title: Patterns of student discourse in solving quantitative science problems
text: While many research studies demonstrate that students often find it difficult to use mathematics in the context of science, even if they have been successful in mathematics courses, there are few which explore how students think and reason as they solve mathematics in science problems. In this study, we use a commognitive approach to explore patterns in student discourse as they solve quantitative science problems in groups. Through paying attention to word use, visual mediators, narratives and routines, we identify four patterns in student discourse while solving these problems: science-dominant discourse; equation-searching; mathematics-dominant discourse and use of a schema. Each of these patterns of discourse can lead to successful outcomes and solutions to the problems. We argue that a commognitive approach can be a useful methodology in exploring students’ thinking as they solve mathematics in science problems. Identifying these patterns in student discourse is an important step in the ongoing research agenda seeking to understand how students bring mathematics and science together in problem solving.
keywords: student discourse, mathematics in science, group problem solving, discourse patterns, visual mediators, student thinking

title: What does validating a variable representation assessment tell us about how introductory chemistry and geology students use multiple external representations?
text: A key challenge for students in science classrooms is learning how to use multiple external representations (MERs) properly; when the information depicted by a representation is misunderstood, or understood correctly but misapplied, students can make improper conclusions and predictions when problem-solving. To better understand students’ rationale when interacting with MERs, 16 chemistry and geology undergraduates from a large public research university in the midwestern United States completed a card sorting activity. The activity asked each student a set of discipline-specific questions. For each question, they were given a set of 15 note cards depicting different representations and asked to select any pertinent representations for the question. As representations were selected, participants explained aloud their rationale for each. A mixed-methods analysis of the activity revealed that participants from each discipline used a standard set of five reasons for using representations: recall, visual, discipline-specific knowledge, pairing-up, and compare-and-contrast. Descriptions of each reason, along with how their usage compared between chemistry and geology students, are shared. The results from these activities suggest improvements that can be made to the assessment of students’ knowledge of MERs.
keywords: multiple external representations, chemistry students, geology students, disciplinary differences, undergraduate science education, problem solving

title: Cognitive characteristics of pre-service teachers in understanding chemical models: an eye-tracking design and evidence
text: Understanding scientific models is emphasized and promoted in international science teaching. This study aimed to assess the level of meta-modelling knowledge of pre-service chemistry teachers. The assessment instrument was a closed-choice task. The instrument covered five aspects: Nature of Models, Multiple Models, Purpose of Models, Testing Models and Changing Models. Each aspect contained three hierarchical levels of understanding. Implicit cognitive activities during pre-service chemistry teachers’ understanding of models were recorded and quantitatively analysed using eye-tracking technology. In this study, the percentage of dwell time and the fixation count were used as indicators of attention allocation, and the differences in pupil size was used as an indicator of cognitive load. The results showed that the understanding level of pre-service chemistry teachers varied in different aspects but was overall at the moderate level. Pre-service chemistry teachers paid more attention to model-related textual content than visual image and showed higher cognitive load. As the task changed, pre-service chemistry teachers’ attention allocation to the textual content varied. Pre-service chemistry teachers with different understanding levels showed similarities in attention allocation and cognitive load to information in the same task. These results suggest that pre-service chemistry teachers’ model understanding levels and cognitive characteristics are both context-dependent.
keywords: pre-service chemistry teachers, scientific models, model understanding, eye tracking, attention allocation, cognitive load, dwell time, fixation count, nature of models, multiple models, testing model

title: Nurturing science learning amidst adversity: a portraiture of science teaching with refugee students in refugee camps
text: In the contemporary world of science, providing high-quality science education is imperative for all students. While a growing body of research in science education is increasing our understanding of science education for many marginalised populations, very little of that research has focused on science education for refugee students, particularly in refugee camps. This study provides an understanding of how refugee teachers in the Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh engage in science teaching with their Rohingya refugee students. Observations, field notes, and interviews were used to construct the portraits to depict the teaching practices in refugee camps. The findings in this study portray the teaching practices of four refugee teachers in the Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh, which reveal how refugee teachers, along with their co-teachers, enact science teaching within these complex contexts. The portraits are used to view practice and future research in co-teaching, specifically concerning science teaching and learning approaches with refugee students in under-resourced and constrained environments in refugee camps.
keywords: science education, refugee students, refugee camps, refugee teachers, Rohingya refugees, co-teaching, teaching practice, resource-limited settings

title: The role of perceiving data as confirming or contradicting to expectations in data-based decisions
text: This article presents an empirical study with 125 university students that investigates the influence of perceiving a confirmation or a contradiction between expectations regarding a hypothetical experiment in physics and empirical evidence from measurement data on data-based decisions. The decisions were analysed for correctness (multiple choice) and for the quality of the justification (free response). The results show that perceiving empirical data as contradicting (anomalous) or as confirming leads 1. to more scientifically consistent responses when data are given (keeping or changing a decision), 2. to more scientifically correct final decisions, and 3. to more sound corresponding justifications when compared with students who do not perceive a contradiction or a confirmation between expectations and data. This finding calls for putting more emphasis on helping students to explicitly focus on and analyse the relation between expectations of a science phenomenon and collected data to recognise a possible conflict or confirmation.
keywords: data-driven decision making, anomalous data, scientific reasoning, physics education, university students, measurement data interpretation

title: A quest for epistemic fluency in STEM: the interplay of views on the nature of science, STEM teaching efficacy and intention among science and mathematics teachers
text: The call for STEM education implementation at various levels has challenged many of the teaching and learning traditions. Yet despite the many drawbacks, the call for STEM education is increasing, considering its impact on economic development and overall national progress and competitiveness. Aimed at contributing to the discourse in STEM education research and the quest for epistemic fluency in STEM, the present study explored the interplay of views on the nature of science, STEM teaching efficacy, and intention among 179 public school upper intermediate and high school science and mathematics teachers in Biliran Province and Leyte, Philippines. Using a five-point Likert scale survey whose items were adapted from the literature, data collected underwent partial least squares-structural equation modelling using SmartPLS 4. The results show that STEM teaching efficacy predicts intention and both could be predicted by views on the nature of science. Moreover, views on the nature of science mediated between STEM teaching efficacy and intention. Informed by the findings vis-à-vis the literature, the researcher elucidated the role of views on the nature of science, STEM teaching efficacy and intention in the quest for epistemic fluency in STEM.
keywords: STEM education, teacher intentions, science teachers, mathematics teachers, teacher beliefs, mediation

title: Does self-regulated learning happen? Learning socio-scientific argumentation through self-Assessment strategies
text: The current study addresses a notable gap in our understanding of what self-assessment design improves students’ socio-scientific argumentation. We investigated the effects of three self-assessment designs: (1) Prediction-only, where students predicted their performance; (2) Standards-informed, where students predicted their performance and compared it against evaluation criteria; and (3) Reflective-adaptation, which additionally engaged students in reflecting on and adjusting their learning strategies. A total of 116 eighth-grade students were assigned to one of these three groups. Over the course of three units focused on energy-related socio-scientific issues, we examined students’ cognitive and metacognitive outcomes – including the quality of their arguments (supporting claims and rebuttals), the accuracy of their self-assessments, and their self-regulation growth from pre – to post-test. Results showed that only the Reflective-adaptation group exhibited a significant improvement in self-regulation. Moreover, this group demonstrated the most substantial gains in argumentation quality over time, particularly in generating well-supported claims. These findings highlight the pivotal role of adaptation tasks in helping students move beyond monitoring toward active regulation. This shift not only enhanced cognitive performance but also strengthened metacognitive skills, underscoring the value of comprehensive self-assessment approaches in science education.
keywords: self-assessment, socioscientific issues, argumentation, student self-regulation, metacognition, performance prediction, eighth grade students, argument quality

title: High school students’ engagement in science learning: scale adaptation and relationship with epistemological beliefs
text: Research worldwide is looking for ways to reform science education and increase student engagement in science education. Determining students’ engagement in science education can provide insight into the effectiveness of teaching and learning activities. For this reason, the Student Engagement in Science Learning scale, which was previously developed in a different sample, was adapted into Turkish. In this context, a two-way study was conducted. First, the validity and reliability study of the scale was conducted. 625 high school students participated in the study (M = 16.01, SD = 1.21). The results showed that the scale had good fit values for its four-dimensional and 20-item structure. Then, with the help of the adapted scale, the relationship between engagement in science learning and demographic variables and epistemological beliefs was tested. In this context, it was found that participation in science learning differed in some dimensions of the scale in favour of male students. In addition, the level of participation in science learning varied according to grade level. A weak relationship was found between students’ engagement in science learning and epistemological beliefs. The study provides pioneering results in students’ engagement in science learning and includes predictions about the variables that must be considered.
keywords: student engagement in science learning, scale adaptation, Turkish adaptation, epistemological beliefs, high school students, gender differences, grade level differences, scale reliability and validity

title: Evaluating Students’ Chemistry Quantitative Reasoning Skills (QRSC) in lower-secondary schools
text: In response to 21st-century demands for students’ Quantitative Reasoning Skills (QRS), the unique quantitative reasoning characteristics of the lower-secondary school chemistry, and the need for QRS assessment in the discipline, this study developed an instrument to assess Students’ Chemistry Quantitative Reasoning Skills (QRSC). The QRSC assessment, designed based on the SOLO taxonomy, curriculum standards, and the Higher Secondary School Entrance Examination (HSSEE) criteria, comprised 26 items and was administered to 237 students. After using Rasch analysis to score students’ performances, the study conducted descriptive statistics, independent samples t-tests, ANOVA, and the general linear model to analyse students’ overall QRSC, gender and academic achievements differences in QRSC, and the interactive effect between gender and academic achievement on QRSC. The results showed that the students’ overall QRSC level was relatively good and widely distributed. Gender had no significant effect on lower-secondary school students’ QRSC; however, there was a significant difference in QRSC among students with different academic achievements. In addition, the study found a significant interaction between gender and academic achievement in QRSC. Specifically, academic achievement can mediate the influence of gender on QRSC. Based on these findings, the study made some pedagogical recommendations for students’ QRSC development.
keywords: chemistry education, junior high school students, scale development, SOLO taxonomy, gender differences, academic performance, chemistry achievement, Rasch analysis

title: Integrating nature of science in science instruction: introducing a hermeneutic and discussion-based approach
text: While significant progress has been made in integrating the nature of science into science education through conventional approaches, considerable scope remains for further research, particularly in the context of classroom-based instruction and teacher pedagogical design. The present article expounds upon the Hermeneutic and Discussion-based Approach (HDA) for integrating science studies issues into science education, with a particular emphasis on classroom-based instruction. The approach is characterised by its interpretive nature and its focus on implicit content analysis, followed by discussion-based techniques. A laboratory activity is employed to illustrate this method, presenting a case from a physics classroom that has been examined from the perspectives of pedagogy and philosophy of science. The study demonstrated that the method exhibited certain characteristics, including the Content and Teacher Dependency Rule (CTDR), the Freedom of Decision and Action Rule (FDAR), and the No Preference or Priority to any Branches of Science Studies Rule (NPSR). This approach is conducive to the provision of science instruction that is situated, minimalistic, and coherent, encompassing the teaching of science studies tenets.
keywords: nature of science, science studies, classroom teaching, discussion method, philosophy of science, physics education, situated learning

title: The elephant in the science staff room: an investigation into the mathematical skills and confidence of pre-service science teachers
text: This paper explores the importance of mathematical skills for teaching science effectively to 14–16-year-olds and evaluates the support pre-service science teachers (PSTs) receive during their postgraduate initial teacher education (ITE) in England. Triggered by increased mathematical demands in the science curriculum, the study gathered data from 18 ITE providers (11% of national providers) during the 2023/2024 academic year. These providers completed a qualitative questionnaire on the mathematical support they offer. Additionally, 236 PSTs (11% of the national cohort) voluntarily completed a marking exercise with eight questions reflecting mathematical skills needed in secondary science teaching. Results highlight wide variability in mathematical preparation across ITE programmes. Only 13.5% of PSTs completed the exercise both correctly and confidently. Performance differences emerged by gender and subject specialism, with male PSTs and physics specialists performing better. Greater prior mathematics education also correlated with higher competence. The study recommends developing a mathematics skills audit and intervention tool for PSTs, integrating stronger mathematical content into ITE programmes, and conducting further research on PSTs’ mathematical development needs. These steps aim to address gaps in mathematical competence and ensure science teachers are well-prepared to deliver the curriculum effectively.
keywords: pre-service science teachers, mathematical skills, mathematical confidence, initial teacher education, secondary science teaching, gender differences, mathematics intervention

title: ‘She asked very much’ – primary school students’ views about scientific inquiry
text: This article presents an in-depth analysis of the Swedish data from the international VASI-E (Views about Scientific Inquiry – Elementary) study. The purpose is to contribute to further knowledge on what younger students know about scientific inquiry (SI). Data were collected by using the VASI-E instrument and were administered to 110 students in the 3rd grade. Furthermore, 24 students were interviewed in order to obtain a deepened qualitative understanding of the students’ views about SI. As already shown in the international VASI-E study, the majority of the students did not have an adequate understanding of SI. Many students seem to embrace a view of SI as following a unique ‘scientific method’, sometimes described as ‘doing experiments’, often in combination with the posing of hypotheses. Furthermore, several students seemed to be unaware of the central role of posing questions as the first step of conducting SI. According to several students, a scientist is a person who should know answers rather than pose questions. A possible reason for this obscured view of SI is the focus on conducting scientific investigations rather than on understanding the different aspects of SI in their teaching. Methodological aspects of the VASI-E instrument are also discussed.
keywords: scientific inquiry, elementary school students, scientific method, questioning, hypothesis generation, role of scientists, science education, 3rd grade

title: Investigation of pre-service science teachers’ scientific text activities as a way of reading comprehension in science education
text: Reading comprehension in science education is seen as a skill that students should acquire today and plays an important role in achieving international goals for science education. It is even more important to investigate the competences and opinions of pre-service science teachers who will introduce reading comprehension into science lessons. In addition, the level of preparation of the students was assessed using the BMDART key developed by the scientists. When the texts with scientific content prepared by most of the pre-service science teachers are evaluated within the framework of the BMDARTs activities, they are at a sufficient level. It was observed that they were more successful in terms of question variety and higher order thinking skills when they prepared questions for the science texts they created according to the DARTs strategy. The pre-service science teachers were found to be inadequate in finding and using resources for reading comprehension texts.
keywords: reading comprehension, pre-service science teachers, scientific texts, higher-order thinking skills, science teacher education

title: Development of a spatial ability test for pre-service science teachers
text: This study aims to develop a spatial ability test specifically designed for pre-service science teachers studying astronomy. Unlike existing spatial ability tests, which primarily use angular geometric objects, this test is constructed entirely with spherical structures to better reflect the nature of celestial bodies in astronomy education. Initially, a review of existing spatial ability tests was conducted, revealing a gap in assessments tailored to astronomy-related spatial reasoning. To address this, a 16-item test based on spherical representations was developed. The initial version was reviewed by experts, and revisions were made based on their feedback. A pilot study was conducted with pre-service science teachers (N = 354) enrolled in astronomy courses at three universities in Türkiye during the 2023–2024 academic year. The test’s validity and reliability were assessed using item analysis, including internal consistency. Results showed an average difficulty index of 0.59, a discrimination index of 0.45, and a reliability coefficient of 0.66, indicating acceptable psychometric properties. Findings suggest that the test effectively measures spatial reasoning skills essential for understanding astronomical phenomena such as eclipses and moon phases. Its implementation in astronomy education may enhance spatial thinking. Future research could expand the test’s scope and examine its applicability in educational settings.
keywords: spatial ability test, spatial reasoning, pre-service science teachers, astronomy education, spherical representations, celestial bodies, test development, psychometric properties, eclipses, lunar phases

title: What can be learned from laypersons’ scientific practices in everyday life: a perspective on causal reasoning
text: Science education aims to cultivate ‘competent outsiders’ – individuals who apply scientific reasoning in real-world contexts. Analysing public engagement with science provides insights into how real-world science is intuitively used and its effect on decision-making. Beyond identifying credible information sources, scientific engagement involves reasoning about causal relationships and underlying mechanisms. This study examines how cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy integrate scientific knowledge through mechanistic reasoning. Data from medical records and surveys captured reasoning on causal phenomena, decision-making self-efficacy, and emergency room (ER) visits. Findings revealed the prominence of scientific reasoning, with patients constructing either parallel or interconnected causal relationships between cause and effect. The identified causal pathways did not indicate greater or lesser accuracy but rather illustrated how laypersons integrate their scientific reasoning into a causal structure that supports decision-making. Some patients incorporated mechanistic components into their causal reasoning structures; these patients demonstrated higher decision-making self-efficacy and had fewer ER visits, underscoring the role of mechanistic reasoning in effective functional decision-making. These findings demonstrate that laypersons engage in scientific reasoning in ways that include both systems and mechanistic perspectives, highlighting the potential effect of such engagement on decision-making. Implications for science education, particularly the integration of mechanistic reasoning with systems thinking, are discussed.
keywords: causal reasoning, mechanistic reasoning, systems thinking, cancer patients, chemotherapy, decision-making self-efficacy, emergency department visits, public engagement with science, causal pathways

title: To change or not to change: a comparison of first-year chemistry demonstrator teaching models
text: This study investigates the impact of two laboratory demonstrator allocation models in first-year chemistry courses at an Australian university. A mixed-methods approach was employed to compare the ‘carousel’ model, where students rotate between demonstrators, with the ‘assigned’ model, where demonstrators work with the same group of students throughout the semester. Results show that both students and demonstrators prefer the ‘assigned’ model, citing enhanced student-teacher relationships as the primary reason. Notably, students’ initial preferences for the ‘carousel’ model shifted significantly after experiencing the ‘assigned’ model. The findings suggest that adopting the ‘assigned’ model can lead to improved learning and teaching outcomes. This study provides valuable insights for educators and administrators seeking to optimise laboratory learning environments.
keywords: laboratory demonstrator, first-year chemistry, student preferences, teacher-student relationship, teaching model comparison

title: The dichotomous key as an active-learning tool in STEM-based biology teaching: effects on students’ self-efficacy, attitudes, and knowledge
text: The dichotomous key has emerged as an active learning tool that can support both students and teachers in learning and teaching biology. The present study is one of the first to examine the dichotomous key within a STEM-integrated active-learning framework; it aimed to investigate the impact of this tool on students’ knowledge, retention, attitudes toward biology, self-efficacy, and also spending time in classrooms. A quasi-experimental research design was employed, involving control (N = 51) and experimental (N = 140) groups selected from five different schools (N = 191) with varying knowledge levels. Pre-, post-, and retention tests were conducted. The findings show that the dichotomous key significantly enhanced knowledge, attitudes toward biology, and self-efficacy, particularly among low-achieving students. The tool also promoted student-centered learning by increasing peer interaction and reducing teacher-led questioning. Moreover, although both the experimental and control groups exhibited overall score increments, the experimental group showed stronger associations with achievement, attitude, and self-efficacy. These findings suggest that the dichotomous key can serve as an effective and sustainable STEM-based active-learning tool, particularly for enhancing engagement and academic development among diverse student populations.
keywords: dichotomous key, active learning, STEM integration, biology education, self-efficacy, attitudes toward biology, student knowledge retention, low-achieving students, student-centered learning, peer interaction, student engagement

title: A multilevel modelling approach to investigating factors associated with middle school students’ systems thinking in biology education
text: Science education has increasingly emphasised the importance of teaching systems thinking (ST), particularly in biology education. However, existing studies have yet to provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing students’ ST in a biological education context. We explore the factors related to students’ biological ST (BST) from individual, class, and school perspectives through multilevel modelling analysis, t-test, and linear regression analysis. A total of 1,408 7th- and 8th-grade students from seven schools in China participated in the study. At the individual level, students’ family socioeconomic status (SES), attitude towards biology, and biological content knowledge (BCK) were significantly associated with BST. Students with higher SES, a positive attitude towards biology, and greater BCK were more likely to achieve higher levels of BST. At the class level, a novel finding is that teachers with more teaching experience and a focus on ST in their practice had students who performed better in BST. Furthermore, urban school students performed better than their rural county counterparts, and school SES was positively related to students’ BST. Our findings may inform educators and researchers about factors that could enhance students’ BST; for instance, efforts should be made to improve students’ attitudes towards biology and BCK.
keywords: systems thinking, biology education, junior high school students, socioeconomic status, teaching experience, urban-rural differences, school socioeconomic status

title: Analysing the relationships between argumentative reasoning and justification beliefs and the effects of prior experience of scientific information
text: This study explored the relationships between argumentative reasoning, justification beliefs, and prior experience with scientific information. Over 300 engineering students from India, aged 20–23, participated. An online science reading and reasoning survey with open-ended questions assessed reasoning behaviours. Prior experience with scientific information was assessed through self-reported measures of reading frequency and the number of sources consulted. The Justification for Knowledge Questionnaire (JFK-Q) measured students’ justification beliefs. Content analysis evaluated reasoning performance while descriptive statistics, correlation, regression, cluster analyses, and ANOVA identified key relationships. The results showed that students struggled to use evidence and consider counterarguments, but could identify certain knowledge to support their claims. Justification by research-based authority was the most agree-upon beliefs. Personal justification and justification by research-based authority both significantly predicted reasoning performance but in contrasting ways. Cluster analysis identified four types of information experience. Students with moderate experience exhibited more adaptive justification beliefs and better argumentative reasoning.
keywords: argumentative reasoning, engineering students, scientific reading, scientific literacy

title: Playing with the experiments and learning new things: science teacher identity through autobiographies
text: Teacher identity is dynamic and continuously evolving, particularly as preservice teachers (PSTs) reconcile past experiences with the expectations of their future roles. For early childhood PSTs, the formation of science teacher identity presents unique challenges, as they must integrate child-centred pedagogies with the demands of teaching science, often in the context of being reading teachers, math teachers, and social studies teachers. While research has explored science teacher identity in middle and high school contexts, less attention has been given to PSTs who aim to teach a STEM (science, technology, engineering, math) subject in elementary school. This study investigates how early childhood PSTs participating in a science methods course navigate the complexities of their developing science teacher identity. The research used autobiographies to examine how PSTs described their prior experiences as science learners and how these experiences shape their identity as future science teachers. Findings provide insights into the intersection of personal history, pedagogical approaches, and identity negotiation in shaping science teacher identity within early childhood education.
keywords: science teacher identity, pre-service teachers, early childhood education, science methods course, child-centred pedagogy, STEM education, elementary science teaching, identity negotiation

title: Exploring students’ understanding of evolutionary biology through large-scale national university entrance examinations
text: Evolutionary biology is essential in science education, yet students often struggle with basic principles due to misconceptions and sociocultural influences. This study investigates Brazilian high school students’ understanding of evolutionary biology using big data from the National High School Examination (ENEM). We aimed to identify changes in comprehension over time, detect prevalent misconceptions, and analyse the association of socioeconomic and cultural variables. We examined over 150 million responses to 66 questions administered across 26 years, employing descriptive and inferential statistical methods. Results revealed very low comprehension (27.9%) and frequent reliance on intuitive reasoning, especially Lamarckian and progressivist thinking. School type was significantly associated with performance, highlighting the role of educational quality and access to resources. Despite this, even private school students showed limited understanding. Religiosity and scientific reading habit were also associated with scores, with less religious students and scientific readers scoring higher. Religious affiliation also appeared important, given substantial differences between some groups. However, multivariate logistic regression showed these variables had only modest discriminative power, indicating other contributing factors. These findings emphasise the urgent need for curricular reforms, improved teacher training, continuing education, and more engaging, conceptually grounded instructional strategies to correct misconceptions and enhance students’ understanding of evolution.
keywords: evolutionary biology, student misconceptions, ENEM, high school students, progressive politics, religiosity, socioeconomic factors, school type, intuitive thinking, evolution education, Brazil

title: ‘Entertainment’ or ‘good for the self’: use and exchange-value cultural capital in White British working-class students’ constructions of science
text: Diversifying science remains an ongoing challenge, and while there is a good understanding of the barriers to participation for women and ethnically minoritised groups, there is far less research about the experiences of those from working-class backgrounds. White working-class students are often generally framed as suffering from a deficit of aspirations, values and understanding. Drawing on interview data with 12 White British working-class students and their parents from a longitudinal project in the United Kingdom, this study utilises a novel theoretical framework of use and exchange-value science-related cultural capital to understand how White working-class students construct the value of science and discusses the implications for their ongoing science participation. Participants’ framing of out-of-school science as either ‘entertainment’ or ‘good for the self’ tended to align with their intentions to continue studying science; with the former group ‘growing out of science’, while the latter group attempted, but often struggled, to maintain a ‘recognisable science identity’ when access to objectified science-related cultural capital diminished and their adolescent selves diverged from classed and gendered discourses of ‘who does science’.
keywords: science participation, science identity, gender and science, parental influence

title: Effectiveness and use of optional scaffolds: an intervention study in biology lessons on phylogenetic trees
text: In heterogeneous classes, students require different levels of support to effectively learn complex content such as interpreting phylogenetic trees. Incremental scaffolds are a promising approach that considers students’ knowledge and skills and offers individual ways of working on tasks. These scaffolds consist of an initial prompt followed by a worked-out example. Current research on the effectiveness of incremental scaffolds for cognitive (knowledge) and motivational (self-efficacy expectations, intrinsic motivation) outcomes is inconsistent. This study explored the effects of incremental scaffolds (treatment 1) and their key components, prompts (treatment 2) and worked-out examples (treatment 3), when offered as voluntary, optional support. The comparison of the three treatments (N = 108 upper secondary school students; grade 11 and 12) showed no significant differences regarding students’ cognitive and motivational outcomes. Subsequent analyses revealed that optional support was mainly used by students with lower pre-knowledge, lower self-efficacy expectations, and lower intrinsic motivation. Simultaneously, students who used support scored lower on post-knowledge assessments and on a specific indicator of intrinsic motivation (interest/enjoyment). Our findings suggest that students who need support are the ones who use it. However, using support alone does not appear sufficient to compensate for differences compared to students who do not require support.
keywords: worked examples, prompting, phylogenetic tree, biology education, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, heterogeneous classrooms, high school students, prior knowledge

title: Fostering scientific practices through structured peer critique: cross-age feedback in ninth-grade science writing
text: This study examines the impact of structured peer feedback from younger students within an argument-based inquiry (ABI) framework on the writing quality and conceptual understanding of ninth-grade students. Guided by the Science Writing Heuristic (SWH) approach, the research investigated how feedback provided by fourth-grade students influenced older students’ revisions. Participants were 95 students across two grade levels in a Midwestern school district in the United States. A quasi-experimental pre – post design was used to assess changes in writing quality across four dimensions: content knowledge, argumentation, rhetoric, and multimodal representation. Results showed statistically significant improvements in argumentation and rhetorical skills, underscoring the value of structured feedback templates in guiding effective revisions. Gains in content knowledge were modest and not statistically significant, and no significant changes were observed in multimodal representation, indicating a need for targeted scaffolding in this area. These findings highlight the potential of structured peer feedback, even in cross-age contexts, to improve specific aspects of scientific writing, while also identifying areas for further instructional support and research.
keywords: peer feedback, argument-based inquiry, Science Writing Heuristic, scientific writing, ninth grade science, writing quality, argumentation, rhetorical competence, writing revision, content knowledge, multimodal representation, scaffolding

title: Motivating science learning when shifting from face-to-face instruction to distance learning: comparing teachers’ and students’ perspective
text: During COVID-19, science instruction in Israel switched from face-to-face (F2F) to distance learning (DL), without teacher preparation or curriculum changes. Instruction in Junior High Schools (JHSs) continued in DL format until the end of the school year and again in the following school year (2021). To support student learning of science, both in F2F instruction and in DL, it is important to motivate them, foster their desire to learn science and encourage them to take part in learning activities. However, science teachers’ motivational practices in F2F instruction may not have worked as well in DL, which offers different opportunities to motivate students. We interviewed JHS science teachers known for motivating their students in F2F instruction and their students, then examined how the teachers’ motivational practices changed during the shift to DL and considered their students’ perceptions of these changes. We identified motivational practices that may help science teachers to enhance the motivation of their students in DL environment.
keywords: student motivation, science learning, distance education, face-to-face teaching, COVID-19 pandemic, junior high school, student perceptions

title: Pre-service teachers’ attitudes towards vaccination before and after targeted teaching interventions
text: Despite recent proof on the usefulness of vaccination during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, global vaccine hesitancy persists, driven by emotional biases and selective information processing. Education can help students acquire the necessary knowledge, critical thinking, as well as improve their decision-making skills. Teachers can play a pivotal role in health promotion and vaccination acceptance, and their training in this domain is essential. Vaccine education through school-based programs for children and adolescents could serve as an effective means to reduce vaccine hesitancy in the broader population. This quantitative study examines Greek pre-service teachers’ vaccination attitudes in general, and in certain aspects of vaccine acceptance (VA; vaccine safety, effectiveness and necessity, vaccination program, affect towards vaccination, mandatoriness) and their potential reconsideration after targeted educational interventions focusing on the importance of vaccines in the past and present and considering cognitive biases. Initial attitudes were positive, and educational interventions significantly improved VA. Pre-service teachers mainly recognised the effectiveness and necessity of vaccines but were less confident about vaccine safety. The lowest acceptance was noticed in the legitimacy of authorities mandating vaccination. The findings underscore the importance of integrating comprehensive, bias-aware vaccination education early in curricula, to enhance public awareness and encounter misinformation effectively.
keywords: vaccine hesitancy, pre-service teachers, vaccine attitudes, vaccine acceptance, vaccine education, cognitive biases, vaccine safety, vaccine effectiveness, mandatory vaccination, health promotion, teacher professional development, misinformation

title: Promoting social emotional learning through socio-scientific issues: a case study of designer baby debates in primary and high schools
text: This study explores the potential of short-term SEL interventions integrated into science curricula to enhance students’ SEL competencies in Chinese primary (Grade 5, N = 52) and high school (Grade 11, N = 55) classrooms. The SEL intervention targeted three dimensions: self-awareness, social awareness and responsible decision-making. Learning outcomes were assessed via role-playing and sharing session activities, with data analysed using non-parametric descriptive statistics. Results revealed that all participants exhibited strong baseline self-awareness (MD = 3, IQR = 2–3 in primary; MD = 3, IQR = 2.5–3 in high school) and moderate social awareness (MD = 2, IQR = 2–2 in primary; MD = 2, IQR = 2–3 in high school). High school students showed statistically significant improvement in responsible decision-making post-intervention (z = −3.368, p < 0.001, r = 0.355), whereas primary students demonstrated no measurable gains (z = −0.378, p = 0.705, r = 0.047). These findings indicate that short-term SEL interventions can produce medium effects in secondary education but may lack efficacy in primary settings. The study highlights the critical need for China’s K-12 education system to adopt comprehensive, age-appropriate SEL interventions across the entire educational continuum to ensure its continuity and progressive development.
keywords: social-emotional learning, socioscientific issues, designer babies, genome editing, science curriculum integration, self-awareness, social awareness, responsible decision-making, role play, elementary school students, high school students, age-appropriate interventions, K-12 education, China

title: Whether, what, and how should we discuss evolution and faith in biology classes? insights from semi-structured interviews and a Delphi study
text: This study explores the challenges of teaching evolution in the context of religious beliefs. The primary objective was to understand the perspectives of biology education experts on discussing evolution and faith in biology classes, and to provide culturally responsive solutions to the challenges encountered by students and educators. Participants included science education experts from diverse ethnic backgrounds in Israel. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and a Delphi study. We identified three key questions regarding the discussion of evolution and faith in biology classes: Should we discuss it? What should we discuss? How should we implement such discussions? There was no consensus on how to conduct these discussions, except for the suggestion to address the evolution-faith conflict through teaching the Nature of Science (NOS). This highlights the importance of culturally responsive teaching in diverse educational settings. Several key issues related to the evolution-faith controversy can be addressed without prioritising one perspective over the other. Support for the discussions was grounded in their educational significance, while opposition stemmed from concerns about their practical implementation. Therefore, it is recommended that these topics be included in teacher professional development (PD) programmes to prepare educators for any related questions that may arise in class.
keywords: evolution and religion, biology education, evolution education, nature of science, culturally responsive teaching, teacher professional development, expert opinion, Israel

title: From reaction to regulation: the emotional trajectory of pre-service primary teachers in science education
text: This study explores the emotional responses and teaching self-efficacy of 455 preservice primary teachers across ten science topics in biology, geology, and physics, using a cross-sectional cohort design. A Likert-scale questionnaire measured ten discrete emotions (e.g. enthusiasm, confidence, boredom, frustration) and allowed comparisons between four academic years. Emotional changes followed two distinct patterns: short-term shifts after instruction (reaction response) and longer-term stabilisation over time (regulation response). In physics topics (second year), positive emotions and self-efficacy increased clearly after instruction, while biology and geology topics (third year) showed more stable emotional profiles. Frustration tended to rise temporarily when students faced complex or ethically sensitive topics. By fourth year, both emotional responses and self-efficacy appeared more balanced, particularly in biology themes. The link between emotion and self-efficacy also changed, moving from isolated patterns in early years to more connected, cross-disciplinary associations in later stages. These findings highlight the importance of engaging students emotionally early on and maintaining that engagement through structured reflection and emotionally supportive learning environments. The study also offers relevant insights for curriculum design and teacher education, particularly in relation to emotional engagement and the development of self-efficacy, both essential dimensions of science teaching competence.
keywords: pre-service primary teachers, teacher self-efficacy, emotion regulation, emotional engagement, frustration, enthusiasm, biology education, geology education, physics education, teacher professional development, curriculum development, emotional reflection

title: Comparing learners’ conceptions of natural and educational scientists: relations to study interest and self-image
text: Learners’ conceptions of scientists are often assumed to influence their academic interests – but empirical evidence for this relationship remains limited and inconsistent. Moreover, little is known about how students perceive scientists beyond STEM domains and how these conceptions relate to their academic interests. These blind spots are uncovered in the present study by investigating secondary school students’ conceptions of educational scientists compared to natural scientists, and how these conceptions relate to their study interest and self-image. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 64 students and used Epistemic Network Analysis to analyse their conceptions. Findings reveal that natural scientists are more strongly associated with scientific activities and cognitive abilities than educational scientists. Notably, students with high study interest and self-image in educational sciences have more inaccurate conceptions, conflating educational scientists with pedagogical roles. Across disciplines, students with low interest and self-image tend to hold pessimistic, stereotypical views of scientists, whereas those with high interest and self-image view them more positively, associating them with communion-oriented activities and prosocial characteristics. This study highlights the need to promote more accurate student views of different scientific disciplines to better align their expectations and career choices, ultimately improving their engagement and reducing dropout rates.
keywords: natural scientists, student learning interest, self-image, high school students, stereotypes of scientists, epistemic network analysis, career expectations, dropout

title: Learning science and the illusion of understanding: exploring the effects of integrating learning tasks after explainer videos
text: Explainer videos are increasingly used to support science learning. While prior research has demonstrated their potential, studies have also identified limitations – particularly their tendency to foster an illusion of understanding, where learners overestimate their grasp of a topic despite gaps in their actual knowledge. Pairing explainer videos with cognitively engaging elements may help mitigate this effect. This paper reports two experimental studies examining the immediate and long-term effects of learning tasks following a physics explainer video on learners’ illusion of understanding. Study 1 (N = 244 physics students) compared high-level learning tasks with watching the video alone. Study 2 (N = 175) compared high-level and low-level tasks. Results show that high-level learning tasks significantly reduce the illusion of understanding immediately after the intervention compared to watching the video alone (t(88) = 6.50, p < .001, d = 0.69). Over the long term, both high- and low-level tasks are similarly effective. Learners with lower prior content knowledge are more susceptible to an illusion of understanding. We conclude that explainer videos should not be used in isolation in science classrooms. To prevent misjudged understanding – particularly among students with limited prior knowledge – they should be combined with cognitively demanding follow-up activities.
keywords: explanatory videos, illusion of understanding, learning tasks, physics education, prior knowledge, misconceptions, video-based instruction, follow-up activities, self-assessment of understanding

title: Exploring the structural relationships among high school students’ epistemological beliefs, critical thinking, and science process skills
text: The purpose of this study was to examine the relationships among epistemological beliefs (EB), critical thinking (CT), and science process skills (SPS) in high school students by comparing two alternative structural models representing different directional pathways of influence. The Critical Thinking Disposition Assessment, the Epistemological Beliefs in Science Scale, and the Science Process Skills Test were employed to acquire data from students at three distinct high schools. The results indicated a robust and positive correlation between EB and CT, indicating that these constructs are mutually reinforcing. In both models, EB demonstrated a more direct impact on SPS than CT, underscoring its critical role in enabling students to develop investigations, evaluate evidence, and support conclusions in a manner that is consistent with scientific reasoning. Additionally, EB mediated the impact of CT on SPS, suggesting that a robust epistemological framework is necessary for the most effective translation of critical thinking into advanced scientific competencies. Comparison of two models showed that Model 2 (EB → CT → SPS) had a more significant overall impact on SPS than Model 1 (CT → EB → SPS). These findings support the integration of critical thinking instruction with epistemic reflection into science curricula by using inquiry methods.
keywords: epistemological beliefs, critical thinking, science process skills, high school students, mediation, structural model, inquiry-based learning, science curriculum, epistemic reflection

title: Third-hand evaluation of science-related information
text: In this position paper, we introduce an Extended Epistemic Vigilance Framework that expands traditional approaches to critical evaluation of science-related information in education. While science education has historically emphasised first-hand evaluation (assessing the quality of claims) and more recently more strongly second-hand evaluation (evaluating source credibility), we argue for the critical importance of an additional dimension, third-hand evaluation, which examines how receivers’ own biases, experiences, and perceptions influence their interpretation of science-related information. The Extended Epistemic Vigilance Framework addresses a significant gap in science education research by focusing on students’ awareness of their own and others’ cognitive biases, sociocultural influences, and decision-making factors that shape information processing. Neglecting awareness towards third-hand evaluation diminishes students’ capacity to become competent evaluators of science-related information, making them more vulnerable to misinformation and disinformation, for example, in digital media environments. Several recent publications in science education support this direction, emphasising the need for students to recognise their own biases and develop self-regulation abilities. We highlight the need for developing professional development programmes for teachers, creating appropriate curricular materials, and designing assessment tools to measure third-hand evaluation competencies in science education.
keywords: epistemic vigilance, cognitive biases, source credibility, misinformation, disinformation, self-regulation, teacher professional development, science curriculum

title: Effectiveness of a school scientific model to address buoyancy in the training of prospective early childhood teachers
text: Buoyancy is a recurring topic in early childhood education and provides an opportunity to introduce scientific modelling. This study is framed within the need to improve the training of prospective early childhood teachers (PECT) in this scientific practice and examines the effectiveness of a teaching intervention that models the buoyancy of objects in water as balanced forces. The research analyses responses from a pre-test and post-test questionnaire administered before and after the intervention. A qualitative content analysis was used to categorise responses. In general, a positive progression was observed in the models used by the PECT to explain buoyancy as balanced forces. Most PECT correctly assimilated that the upthrust exerted by water is equivalent to the weight of the amount of water displaced by the object, and that this upthrust therefore depends on the volume of the portion of the object submerged. The conclusion is that, with interventions such as this, it is possible (1) to initiate the PECT in the practice of scientific modelling as part of their training to teach science at early childhood education, and that (2) they assimilate a school scientific model to be able to explain buoyancy.
keywords: buoyancy, scientific modeling, early childhood teacher education, Archimedes' principle, science teacher education, educational intervention

title: Validity and reliability evidence for the science diagram comprehension test
text: College science students are expected to learn from and with diagrams. Although a substantial body of research exists regarding efforts to improve students’ diagram comprehension, little attention has been paid to this comprehension ability as an individual difference affecting learning and performance in science courses. This lack of attention can be at least partially attributed to a lack of tools available to measure diagram comprehension ability. This paper introduces and evaluates a new measure, the Science Diagram Comprehension Test (SDCT), to address this need. The SDCT is a multiple-choice test, intended for undergraduates, that includes a variety of diagram types from a variety of introductory science courses. This paper presents evidence for the reliability and validity of SDCT scores across four phases. Scale-level descriptive statistics, correlations, IRT, and EFA demonstrate that the SDCT has acceptable psychometric properties, holds expected relationships with other variables (e.g. major and GPA), and has a single factor structure. Expert review confirms that all SDCT diagrams are similar to those used in college science courses. The final version of the SDCT contains 27 items corresponding to 14 different diagrams. Results indicate that the SDCT captures diagram comprehension ability and is appropriate for use in research.
keywords: diagram comprehension, psychometric validation, test reliability, test validity, factor structure, individual differences in learning, introductory science courses, multiple-choice tests

title: Exploring climate-friendly cities: a case study of elementary students’ systems thinking
text: This qualitative case study explores how elementary students’ systems thinking emerges and evolves through engagement in climate change-focused design tasks. Despite growing interest in systems thinking within science education, research at the elementary level, especially concerning complex socioscientific issues like climate change, remains limited. Guided by the Components – Mechanisms – Phenomena (CMP) framework, we analyzed interviews, student artefacts, and field notes collected over 12 weeks involving Grade 6 students in Western Canada. Findings reveal that students effectively identified key system components (e.g. vegetation, oceans, atmosphere, renewable energy sources) and recognised emergent phenomena such as global warming and climate-friendly urban design. However, they often struggled to articulate mechanisms of how these components dynamically interact to produce broader outcomes. It was evident that design tasks and structured scaffolds, such as CMP-informed prompts, provided immediate opportunities for component identification and phenomenon recognition, while perturbation activities prompted dynamic reasoning about system interdependencies and trade-offs between efficiency and equity. Findings also supported that students’ systems thinking skills were multifaceted and context-dependent rather than strictly hierarchical. The study contributes conceptually (reframing development as context-sensitive), methodologically (CMP as scaffold and analytic lens), and practically (a classroom-ready toolkit, including CMP-informed prompts and design-plus-perturbation tasks).
keywords: systems thinking, climate change, elementary school students, design tasks, scaffolding, socioscientific issues, emergence, global warming, urban design

title: Advancing students’ NOS understanding: the power of history of science-based instruction within the reconceptualised family resemblance approach
text: This study examined the effect of history of science (HOS)–based instruction on sixth-grade students' understanding of the nature of science (NOS) through the Reconceptualized Family Resemblance (RFN). RFN conceptualizes NOS across five categories: aims and values, scientific practices, methods and methodological rules, scientific knowledge, and the social–institutional system of science. A mixed-methods Embedded Experimental Model was employed. The sample consisted of 101 students from a public middle school in Türkiye, drawn from four intact classes randomly assigned to experimental and control groups. Quantitative data were collected using the RFN Student Questionnaire administered as pre- and post-tests, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with eight purposively selected students who demonstrated moderate science achievement and balanced gender representation. Pre-test MANOVA results indicated no statistically significant differences between the groups. Post-test MANOVA results showed that students receiving HOS-based instruction achieved significantly higher NOS understanding in the categories of aims and values, scientific knowledge, and the social–institutional system. Although differences in scientific practices and methodological rules were not statistically significant, the experimental group displayed higher mean scores in these dimensions. Qualitative findings supported the quantitative results.
keywords: nature of science, history of science, sixth grade students, junior high school science, scientific practice, scientific knowledge, methodological principles

title: Cultivating STEM aspirations: relationships, experiences, and beliefs of students in resource-limited communities
text: STEM workforce development remains a critical component of K-12 education, yet many students face systemic barriers, including unequal access to opportunities and resources, that typically foster STEM interest and career aspirations. This study investigates STEM relationships and learning experiences among students in a low-socioeconomic status (SES) urban middle school, examining how these factors relate to STEM self-efficacy, outcome expectations, interests, and goals through the lens of Social Cognitive Career Theory. Results demonstrated that relationship to someone outside of the family who is involved in STEM related to increased beliefs across the STEM disciplines. STEM activities with the family were associated with increased science and engineering outcome expectations while teacher discussion of STEM careers was connected to science interest. The study also indicated that students in this low-SES school were unlikely to have family STEM connections or participate in extracurricular activities such as STEM camps or clubs, underscoring the systemic barriers to STEM engagement for underserved populations. Implications for this research include strategies for improving student connections to STEM professionals, professional development tools for teachers to facilitate meaningful STEM career discussions, and targeted efforts to expand external STEM opportunities for students with limited existing resources.
keywords: STEM aspirations, low socioeconomic status students, junior high school students, STEM self-efficacy, outcome expectations, science interest, social cognitive career theory, resource-limited communities, urban schools, STEM workforce development

title: Wellbeing in science education: a qualitative exploration of students’ values
text: Supporting student wellbeing has become a global priority in schools, yet subject-specific foci on wellbeing are limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring science wellbeing (ScWB) through value fulfilment theory, defining it as the fulfilment of students’ values in science, accompanied by positive feelings (e.g. enjoyment) and functioning (e.g. belonging, engagement). Building on an existing ScWB framework, this qualitative study analyses responses from 320 Australian Year 8 (ages 13-14) students to three open-ended questions about what they consider important for positive science learning experiences. Thematic analysis identified 51 instrumental values that mapped to eight ultimate values. Students primarily valued cognitive aspects (e.g. understanding science concepts), engagement (e.g. interest in science), and relationships (e.g. teacher and peer support). Females and males demonstrated similar value hierarchies; however, females more frequently valued relationships in science. The study also identified co-occurring values; for instance, teacher support was often valued alongside enjoyment and understanding. This is the first known study to systematically extract and document students' science-related values, providing empirical support for a values-based ScWB framework. The findings can help teachers identify and fulfil students' values in science classrooms, potentially enhancing enjoyment, engagement, and participation in science education.
keywords: student values, instrumental values, ultimate values, student engagement, teacher support, peer relationships, gender differences, science education, eighth grade students

title: Combining expert K-maps with cued recall to improve students’ conceptions of learning science: a quasi-experimental study
text: Inappropriate restudy can impair students’ conceptions of learning science (COLS), a construct linked to learning approaches and related outcomes. This study examined whether optimising restudy by integrating encoding materials with retrieval tasks can improve COLS in physics. We conducted a three-group pre–post quasi-experiment with 98 Grade 8 students in the Chinese mainland. Group A used linear knowledge summaries (LKSs) with exercises; Group B used LKSs with cued recall; and Group C paired expert-generated knowledge logic structure maps (K-Maps) with cued recall. Outcomes were overall COLS and its reproductive and constructivist dimensions. Relative to LKSs with exercises, K-Maps with cued recall produced significantly more constructivist overall COLS, while LKSs with cued recall showed a smaller, tentative advantage over exercises, whereas no reliable difference emerged between the two recall-based conditions on the overall index. For the subscales, both recall-based conditions tended to increase constructivist COLS, and K-Maps with recall showed a tentative reduction of reproductive COLS compared with LKSs with recall. These findings suggest that restudy designs that prioritise generative retrieval and make relations among ideas explicit can nudge students’ learning conceptions toward more constructivist orientations. Implications for classroom restudy and study-strategy design are discussed.
keywords: restudy, cued recall, generative retrieval, constructivist learning, reproductive learning, physics learning, junior high school students, study habits

title: Cultural context and the development of students’ naïve and scientific knowledge: an example from volcanic processes
text: Despite extensive research on naïve knowledge/conceptions, few studies examine the socio-economic and cultural influence of students, particularly their perceptual experience, on knowledge construction. This study explores how students’ everyday environment shapes their understanding, using embodied cognition, analogy, and knowledge development, including naïve knowledge. It investigates factors influencing students’naïve and scientific knowledge of volcanic processes and risks, focusing on socio-economic and cultural status, and life experiences related to volcanoes and earthquakes (perceptual experience, social environment, school learning). It examines the extent to which these forms of knowledge are shared or differ based on these factors. Conducted among 1,059 Tanzanian students (832 in secondary schools) from two geologically distinct regions exposed to different levels of risk but following the same school curriculum, the study employs a questionnaire-based approach and statistical analysis. Results show that certain perceptual experiences linked to students’ interactions with their daily environment influence the activation of specific naïve knowledge. When perceptual experiences are widely shared, students’ naïve knowledge tends to be similar; conversely, when such experiences are less shared due to differing material and cultural contexts, naïve knowledge are expressed in more varied ways. These differences highlight the potential impact of some pedagogical approaches based on perceptual experience.
keywords: scientific knowledge development, volcanic processes, volcanic risk perception, embodied cognition, analogy, perceptual experience, high school students, earthquakes, geoscience education, knowledge construction

title: Utility value intervention in elementary science classes: analyzing temporal changes in utility value perception and individual interest in science
text: This study aimed to implement a utility value intervention in elementary school science classes and analyse changes over time in elementary students’ utility value perceptions and individual interest in science. We designed a utility value intervention based on (Hulleman, C. S., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2021). The utility-value intervention. In G. M. Walton, & A. J. Crum (Eds.), Handbook of wise interventions: How social psychology can help people change (pp. 100–125). Guilford Press) utility-value-intervention model and applied it to fifth-grade science classes for one semester (16 weeks). The study was conducted with a total of 194 students randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 97) and a comparison group (n = 97), with data collected at five time points. Latent growth modelling analysis revealed that the experimental group showed significant linear increases in both utility value perceptions and individual interest in science, while the comparison group showed minimal changes. Through multivariate latent growth modelling analysis, we confirmed that changes in utility value perceptions significantly predicted changes in individual interest in science. These findings empirically demonstrate that systematic utility value interventions can effectively enhance elementary students’ individual interest in science through improved perceptions of science’s utility value. This study contributes to understanding the developmental dynamics between utility value perceptions and individual interest in science, extending beyond simple pre–post comparisons in existing research.
keywords: utility value intervention, science interest, elementary school science, fifth grade students, science education, wise interventions, student motivation

title: Inquiry-based instruction and its influence on perceived authenticity and maintained situational interest—a cluster-randomised field experiment in a chemistry learning setting
text: Learners’ perceived authenticity is related to the design of a learning setting and learning outcomes such as maintained situational interest (MSI). Further, perceived authenticity can be conceptually linked to inquiry-based instruction (IBI) as a design element of learning settings. This study investigates students’ perceived authenticity and MSI under two conditions: high and low IBI. Under low IBI, learners were asked to reproduce a standard operation procedure, while high IBI included a research question and an investigation with reaction temperature as the independent variable. The sample comprised n = 263 high school students (age M = 16.48 years) for the two conditions: n(high) = 157 and n(low) = 106. Data were collected via a questionnaire with multidimensional perceived authenticity (location, instructors, methods, and innovation) and MSI (emotional, value-related, and epistemic) scales. The results revealed a higher perceived innovation and an unexpectedly lower MSI for learners under the high IBI condition. Still, a higher perceived innovation led to a positive indirect effect on MSI. This complex relationship between IBI, perceived innovation, and MSI can inform the design of science education practices and leads to questions about further mediating factors between IBI design and learners’ MSI.
keywords: inquiry-based teaching, perceived authenticity, perceived innovation, chemistry education, high school students, learning environment design, epistemic interest, emotional interest, standard operating procedures

title: Combining video and virtual experiments to foster online scientific inquiry learning: insights from mediation and lag sequential analyses
text: In recent years, computer-based online inquiry has become a prevalent mode of learning in science education. Growing evidence suggests that using multiple experimental formats can be more effective than single-format approaches in supporting scientific inquiry learning. However, the mechanisms and efficacy of combining video and virtual experiments in online environments remain underexplored. This study investigated the effects and underlying processes of this combination using mediation and lag sequential analyses. A total of 117 middle school students were assigned to one of three conditions: a combined video and virtual experiment condition, a video-only condition, or a virtual-only condition. Results indicated that the combined condition led to significant improvements in students’ inquiry process performance and conceptual understanding. Furthermore, inquiry process performance fully mediated the effect of experimental format on conceptual understanding. Lag sequential analysis showed that students in the combined condition engaged in more effective experimental manipulations and exhibited fewer trial-and-error behavioural patterns than those in the virtual-only condition. These results not only affirm the benefits of combining video and virtual experiments in online scientific inquiry but also elucidate the inquiry process mechanisms, offering valuable insights and implications for both practice and theory in science education.
keywords: virtual experiments, conceptual understanding, junior high school students, experimental manipulation, mediation analysis, lag sequential analysis
