title: Latent profiles of resilience in chemistry: tracking chemistry performance during critical educational transitions
text: This study examined changes in senior high school students’ chemistry performance over a semester and how these changes varied based on their academic resilience in chemistry. Participants were 684 first-year senior high school students from 14 schools. Latent profile analysis revealed three distinct profiles: low (19.152%), moderate (64.766%), and high (16.082%) levels of academic resilience in chemistry. Subsequently, a two-way repeated measures analysis of variance was conducted to compare changes in chemistry achievement across the three profiles over the transition period. Results indicated that students in the low-resilience profile showed a declining trend in chemistry achievement, those in the high-resilience profile demonstrated improvement, and those in the moderate-resilience profile exhibited relatively stable achievement. These findings highlight resilience as a universal asset in chemistry learning, extending its relevance beyond at-risk groups. By identifying student profiles and their associated achievement trajectories during the transition period within China’s highly selective educational system, this study provides a person-centred framework that can inform differentiated early support in cognitively demanding science subjects and offers a valuable reference point for other selection-oriented systems internationally.
keywords: academic resilience, chemistry achievement, achievement trajectories, latent profiles, high school students, educational transitions, student profile, science learning, student support

title: Perspectives on natural science teaching
text: School curricula should give prominence to content that is relevant to both societies and individuals. For this reason, global challenges are increasingly being highlighted in discussions. However, global challenges and how people need to deal with them can only be understood if they are the focus of teaching for an appropriate amount of time. We, therefore, need a new subject that draws on many disciplines but is based on educational theory. The present article presents a perspective on natural science teaching, predicated on the assumption that Central European Theory or Concept of Bildung engenders favourable conditions for the advancement of our societies, and indeed, for the establishment of conditions conducive to both socially adequate and fulfilling individual development. This article argues that it is imperative to prioritise the needs of both society and the individual within an educational framework by examining the most significant constraints on current natural science teaching and learning, such as time on task, socio-metacognition (mainly introspection and evaluation of collective information), in combination with sense making.
keywords: natural science teaching, Bildung, global challenges, curriculum relevance, self-reflection, sensemaking, time on task, personal and social development

title: What knowledge do different experts think should be taught about climate change in compulsory school science? Results from a Delphi study
text: Recent research has focused on the question of what ought to be taught about climate change in compulsory secondary school science from the perspectives of policymakers, teacher educators, and teachers. This study investigates the question from the perspectives of three groups of experts: science teachers, climate scientists, and youth climate activists. Using a three-round Delphi method with 38 experts, 45 knowledge statements were identified and organised into a coherent ‘story model’ for teaching climate change in school science. The model begins with the human drivers of climate change, before explaining the scientific mechanisms and processes that produce immediate impacts and future risks. The model incorporates the scientific consensus and evidence for these three aspects, linking them to future projections which link to knowledge of affective elements, action, adaptation, and mitigation in relation to climate policy and climate justice. The model integrates knowledge of scientific evidence with values, attitudes, and action, offering a means for justice and action to be taught alongside core scientific content. This provides students with an understanding of not only the complexity of the climate system but also the interaction between Earth systems, climate change, and society.
keywords: climate change education, science curriculum content, expert opinion, climate scientists, science teachers, story model, climate justice, climate policy, adaptation and mitigation, scientific consensus, values in science education

title: Formulating a framework on social responsibility of science in primary science education: an approach based on grounded theory
text: The integration of the Social Responsibility of Science (SRS) into primary education requires a coherent framework to address current issues of fragmentation and ambiguity. This study employs grounded theory coding to construct an SRS framework by examining twelve national science curriculum standards from ten innovation-driven countries and regions. Findings reveal that the central aim of SRS is to support the identity transformation of students into two responsible agents: responsible professionals and scientifically literate citizens. To achieve this, we propose a framework structured around three concentric circles of responsibility: the micro level (individual/community), the meso-level (national), and the macro level (global/future generations). Within this structure, the framework should integrate four core themes: environmental sustainability, disaster resilience, healthy living, and representation of Indigenous knowledge. These SRS themes are taken along with five essential competencies: STSE knowledge, prudent judgment, science communication, ethical considerations, and positive innovation. This comprehensive framework offers a roadmap for educators to embed scientific responsibility effectively into future primary science curricula.
keywords: social responsibility of science, elementary school science, science curriculum standards, curriculum framework, scientific literacy, citizenship education, environmental sustainability, disaster resilience, healthy living, indigenous knowledge, science communication

title: Student teachers’ syntheses of knowledge on biodiversity loss from relevant, irrelevant and fake sources
text: Scientific literacy is becoming increasingly important for teachers in the current knowledge landscape, where fake information is gaining ground. However, little is known about how fake content becomes part of ordinary knowledge in science education. This study investigated how Finnish student teachers recognised fake content on the topic of biodiversity loss in an online learning environment and how they used it. Seventy-one first-semester primary student teachers at a Finnish university were given the task of writing a synthesis using online sources and evaluating those sources. The learning environment included relevant, irrelevant and fake texts. The analysis used quantification, content analysis and discourse analysis. The findings showed that nearly half of the participants used fake content in their synthesis, while they also succeeded in synthesising relevant texts. We focused on the use of fake content and identified three discourses referring to it: (1) fake as fact, (2) fake as second opinion and (3) fake as suspicious. The study’s implications regard improving curriculum development and programme design in teacher education.
keywords: fake news, misinformation, biodiversity loss, pre-service teachers, primary teacher education, source evaluation, scientific literacy, information synthesis, virtual learning environments, teacher knowledge

title: Developing and validating the motivation toward virtual reality scale: its associations with science anxiety, academic buoyancy, and grit
text: As immersive technologies gain traction in education, understanding their psychological impacts becomes crucial. This study developed and validated the Motivation toward Virtual Reality Scale and examined its associations with science anxiety, academic buoyancy, and grit. Three studies were conducted with middle school students. Study I (N = 301) involved exploratory factor analysis for scale development. Study II (N = 292) confirmed construct validity and reliability using confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency metrics (α, ω, λ), Item Response Theory (IRT), measurement invariance, and criterion-related validity. Study III (N = 418) tested a structural model examining the mediating roles of academic buoyancy and grit between VR motivation and science anxiety. Results supported a 14-item, three-factor structure with strong psychometric properties. IRT analyses showed high item discrimination, and invariance analyses confirmed stability across gender. VR motivation was positively associated with VR attitude and acceptance. Structural equation modelling revealed that academic buoyancy and grit mediated the link between VR motivation and science anxiety. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and related frameworks, findings highlight the role of VR motivation in reducing science anxiety and enhancing students’ resilience in technology-integrated learning environments.
keywords: virtual reality, scale development, science anxiety, academic buoyancy, grit, junior high school students, self-determination theory, technology acceptance, gender invariance, mediating effect, immersive learning

title: Investigating eye tracking metrics involved in organic chemistry question – solving processes of pre-service science teachers
text: The objective of this study was to investigate pre-service science teachers’ question-solving processes in organic chemistry using eye-tracking technology. The study involved 51 students from a science education programme at a state university. The findings showed that participants’ attention, visit duration, and frequency varied according to cognitive load, problem complexity, and prior knowledge. Despite focused attention to some questions, substandard performance suggested superficial conceptual understanding and inadequate visuospatial processing. After accounting for participants and questions as random effects and correcting for multiple comparisons, no robust differences in eye-tracking metrics were observed for achievement, anxiety, or grade level. A positive correlation was found between fixation duration and success, while a high total visit duration did not guarantee success, suggesting that attention quality may be more important than its duration in determining success. The regression analysis revealed no significant overall relationship (R = .500, R² = .25) between eye-tracking metrics and organic chemistry test scores (F (7, 43) = 2.050; p > .05). Similarly, eye-tracking metrics did not significantly predict (R = .336, R² = .11, p > .05) organic chemistry anxiety levels (F (7, 43) = .783; p > .05), with the model explaining limited variance.
keywords: eye tracking, organic chemistry, pre-service science teachers, fixation duration, visit duration, cognitive load, problem complexity, prior knowledge, visuospatial processing, academic performance, attention quality

title: Shaping excellence: a case study of elite science education programs through a Bourdieusian analysis
text: Recent decades have witnessed increased global focus on science education policy and growing international recognition of how science capital shapes educational participation patterns, particularly regarding access to elite science programs. Israel offers a unique case study to understand the efficacy and impact of excellence programs due to its geopolitical position and reliance on human capital as a strategic resource. This research examines the evolution of two elite Israeli science programs: Alpha and Odyssey. Using Bourdieu's social reproduction theory and Archer's concept of science capital, this study examines the complex interplay between policy entrepreneurs and state institutions, by investigating relationships among stakeholders and demonstrating how these programs can reproduce social inequalities while seeking to promote meritocracy. Through qualitative methodology, incorporating interviews with 20 experts and analysis of 24 policy documents, the research traces these programs’ historical development, shifting objectives, funding transitions, and approaches to equality and diversity. We show that although the Alpha and Odyssey programs successfully create valuable opportunities for gifted students, they fail to deliver equity. This study illuminates the tension between academic excellence and equity, enhancing understanding of how excellence programs reflect broader educational policies.
keywords: science capital, social reproduction theory, educational inequality, gifted students, meritocracy, educational equity, science education policy, policy entrepreneurs, Israel, human capital

title: Evaluating explanations of scientific concepts using image schemata
text: Textual descriptions and simplified examples (non-formal explanations) are commonly used to introduce science topics to students, e.g. in geoscience, but may be ambiguous and understood in different ways, potentially leading to misconceptions. This exploratory study considers how image schemata, mental patterns based on bodily experiences, can be used to investigate how non-formal explanations can be (mis)understood. We illustrate this approach by analysing undergraduate textbooks' non-formal introductions to isostasy, a geoscience concept incorporating the physics concepts of elasticity and buoyancy. Our analysis reveals that the explanations can be understood through different image schemata, some of which are not well aligned to the current scientific understanding of isostasy. Moreover, many of these image schemata can logically lead to misconceptions and do not accurately reflect the corresponding physics. The analysis also highlights how introductions may require that students reconceptualise isostasy to transition to the current scientific understanding. Image schemata may therefore be useful for teachers and education researchers to identify productive, and avoid problematic, understandings when using non-formal explanations.
keywords: image schemas, science misconceptions, isostasy, geoscience education, reconceptualization, elasticity, buoyancy, conceptual understanding

title: Exploring teachers’ learning through teaching experience: formal opportunities, teaching experience, and personal characteristics
text: Our understanding of elementary teachers’ science subject matter knowledge (SMK) development through teaching experience is incomplete. In this study, we explored the relationships with factors that may be associated with SMK. 346 elementary teachers completed one test for evolution and another test for force. They provided information about formal opportunities (college science coursework, professional development programmes), features of teaching experience (years, required curriculum materials, weekly team interactions), and personal characteristics (interest in science, science identity). The strongest predictors of teachers’ science SMK were personal characteristics of interest and identity. Teaching more grade levels and being required to use curriculum materials were negatively associated with SMK for evolution. Interacting with colleagues at least once a week and years of experience were not related to SMK. Similarly, formal opportunities like college science coursework and hours in science professional development did not predict SMK.
keywords: teacher learning, elementary science teachers, teaching experience, professional development, science identity, science interest, evolution education, force and motion, curriculum materials, teacher collaboration

title: Unlocking the potential of innovations: how resource networks support teachers transforming cPCK into pPCK
text: To implement innovations successfully, science teachers must enhance and refine their pedagogical content knowledge (PCK). More specifically, they must transform collective PCK (cPCK) (i.e. what is known about the innovation) into personal PCK (pPCK) (i.e. their own understanding). In this paper, we combine the Refined Consensus Model (RCM) of PCK and the Network of Resources Model to investigate the mechanisms underlying the transformation of cPCK into pPCK. We adopted a qualitative case study approach to analyse how teachers accessed resources in the form of resource networks and how their prior pPCK influenced this process. We took field notes and conducted interviews with seven science teachers who implemented a digitally enhanced unit on the concept of energy. Through the combined model, we identified distinct patterns in teachers’ access to material and social resources and how these patterns shaped opportunities for transforming cPCK into pPCK. The study provides evidence that the combined model provides a lens for understanding and supporting PCK development during innovation uptake. In doing so, it highlights how resource networks can support teachers in meeting the instructional demands associated with integrating digital technologies in contemporary science education.
keywords: pedagogical content knowledge, resource networks, science teachers, innovation adoption, energy concept, teacher professional development

title: Culturo-Techno-Contextual Approach: a new horizon in teaching genetics
text: Despite years of educational reform, systemic barriers in science education across many African contexts continue to limit equitable learning opportunities, underscoring the need for culturally grounded innovations such as the Culturo-Techno-Contextual Approach (CTCA). Grounded in Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory and culturally relevant pedagogy, this study examined the impact of CTCA on students’ academic performance in genetics. A quasi-experimental design was adopted, involving 114 Senior Secondary II students (equivalent to Grade 11) from two purposively selected schools. Intact classes were assigned to experimental (n = 53) and control (n = 61) groups. The Genetics Achievement Test, with a reliability index of 0.86, was used for data collection. The experimental group received instruction through CTCA, integrating culturally relevant strategies and technology, including reading online content and watching YouTube videos. The control group had identical content and activities, minus the innovation. Data was analysed using analysis of covariance. Results showed a significant improvement in the performance of students taught using CTCA, with a partial eta squared effect size of 0.44. This finding underscores the value of contextualised and technology-supported instruction. It is recommended that educators enhance existing teaching practices by incorporating structured frameworks like CTCA to improve learning outcomes in genetics.
keywords: Culturo-Techno-Contextual Approach, genetics education, culturally relevant pedagogy, Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, technology-supported instruction, YouTube videos, online learning resources, high school students, academic performance

title: Building students’ science identity in introductory undergraduate science courses
text: Introductory undergraduate science courses can be profound experiences in which students are engaged actively in scientific practices and develop their identities as scientists. We explored the impact of substantial course revisions to focus on authentic investigations and equitable learning environments on the development of students’ science identity, particularly self-efficacy and interest. We developed a pre-/post-survey, the Beliefs in Investigation and Design Survey (BIDS), through which we collected responses from students at 11 institutions in courses with and without the use of new materials and strategies. Matched pre-/post – responses (n = 770) were subdivided into non-treatment (n = 555) and treatment (n = 215) groups. Treatment participants showed greater self-efficacy gains and more frequently described how they would use science skills in their careers. Our findings highlight that introductory courses can support the development of students’ science identity. Although the role of an introductory course is often perceived as an introduction to the content of a discipline, we envision it as an introduction to an identity and an opportunity to cultivate and nurture that identity through participation in the practices of a discipline. This is a fundamentally different approach with broad impact on who participates in and persists in STEM learning.
keywords: science identity, self-efficacy, student interest in science, equitable learning environments, course revision, STEM persistence, scientific practice

title: Prospective science teachers’ use of generative AI in chemistry lab reports: patterns in questioning and conceptual understanding
text: This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) tools on the questioning skills and conceptual understanding of prospective science teachers (PSTs) in completing chemistry laboratory experiment reports. Before the intervention, a survey assessed PSTs’ AI usage experiences. During the intervention, PSTs used AI tools while preparing experiment reports, incorporating AI-related questions at the end of each report. These questions were analyzed based on difficulty level, topic, and type. Conceptual understanding questions were also posed weekly. A chi-square analysis examined the relationship between PSTs’ conceptual understanding and question difficulty. Results showed a significant relationship between questioning skills and conceptual understanding in the first two experiments. In the last three, PSTs with complete understanding posed moderately difficult questions, whereas those with alternative understanding contributed fewer questions, though no significant correlation was found between question difficulty and conceptual understanding. After the intervention, PSTs reflected on their AI experiences, noting faster access to information, cross-checking AI-derived data, and improved critical thinking and data interpretation. However, they struggled with diversifying their questions to AI. The findings suggest that AI-supported chemistry laboratory reporting provides opportunities for PSTs to refine their questioning and conceptual understanding.
keywords: generative AI, prospective science teachers, questioning strategies, conceptual understanding, question difficulty, critical thinking, teacher professional development

title: Prior attainment in science, maths, and language in relation to science subject choices in sixth forms in Wales, UK
text: While young people express interest in science at school, many do not pursue science beyond compulsory education, threatening the scientific literacy that is demanded of citizens by an increasingly technology and scientifically driven world. This study presents a large-scale analysis of science subject choices in Wales; a bilingual nation undergoing curriculum reform. Using administrative data from 8,010 pupils who completed their core education at the age of 16 in 2016/17, logistic regression models examined the role of academic– pupil– and school-factors in choosing biology, chemistry, and physics for study in Sixth Forms. Findings reveal that prior attainment in science and maths strongly predicted further science choice, while higher language attainment was negatively associated with physics choice and positively associated with biology choice. While increased science teaching in earlier study increased the likelihood of continued science education, its influence was unequal across attainment groups. Sex, school language medium, and school geography revealed subject-specific effects. Results contribute further understanding on the role of language in post-compulsory science study and underscore the importance of disaggregating science subjects in research and policy. The study offers timely insights and broad implications for curriculum design, equity, and bilingual education in science that are of international relevance.
keywords: sixth form, prior attainment, scientific literacy, mathematics achievement, language achievement, bilingual education, gender differences, educational equity, curriculum reform

title: Framing evolution – semantic framing and conceptual blending explains students’ hybrid conceptions of natural selection
text: While research on students’ difficulties in explaining evolution has shifted focus from isolated concepts to the role of intuitive ideas, few studies have yet applied cognitive linguistics. Drawing on frame semantics and conceptual blending, this study examines how upper-secondary students use semantic frames to make sense of natural selection. It employs a qualitative analysis of semantic frames in 31 upper-secondary students’ written explanations of natural selection before and after interacting with an educational visualisation of antibiotic resistance. The results show that students used semantic frames such as adjusting, immunisation, or learning in their explanations. Furthermore, students frequently maintained their initial framing, even after instruction, sometimes leading to mixed and hybrid explanations that combined intuitive and scientific ideas. Conceptual blending was applied to explain how such mixed explanations may emerge when elements from different semantic frames and mental spaces are fused. The findings suggest that semantic frame analysis of student explanations may complement traditional concept-based assessments of natural selection understanding. The results also imply that evolution teaching may require explicit attention to reframing students’ interpretations, thus helping them to transition from everyday conceptions to scientific understandings. The article concludes with implications for visualisation designs for teaching evolution.
keywords: natural selection, evolution education, conceptual blending, frame semantics, cognitive linguistics, student misconceptions, antibiotic resistance, mental spaces, high school students

title: Scientific literacy in higher education: revisiting institutional proximity through engagement and attitudes
text: Scientific literacy is widely regarded as a key competence for informed participation in science-related social and civic contexts. Drawing on civic and functional conceptualizations, this study examined how demographic characteristics, academic role, disciplinary context, attitudes toward science, and engagement with scientific content are associated with adults’ scientific literacy within a higher education setting. The sample comprised 442 university students and academic staff from diverse disciplinary backgrounds in Türkiye. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to differentiate the contributions of distal background characteristics and more proximal meaning-making processes. The findings indicated that neither disciplinary context nor academic role explained unique variance in scientific literacy after demographic factors were taken into account. In contrast, attitudes toward science were strongly associated with scientific literacy, and engagement with scientific content contributed additional explanatory value. Age remained a significant correlate, whereas gender was not. Taken together, the results suggest that variation in scientific literacy within higher education is more closely linked to engagement practices and orientations toward science than to institutional proximity to science.
keywords: scientific literacy, university students, university faculty, attitudes toward science, disciplinary context, academic roles, demographic factors, age, gender, Turkey

title: Students’ STEM career expectations: effects of science and mathematics abilities and attitudes relative to language abilities and attitudes
text: In response to growing concerns about low participation in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) careers, there is a need for more understanding of the underlying cognitive and motivational mechanisms affecting students’ STEM career expectations. This study examined whether relative strengths of abilities and attitudes in science, mathematics, and Chinese language could predict STEM career expectations among junior secondary school students. Data were from the Hong Kong PISA 2022 sample. Data were analysed using person-centred approaches and structural equation modelling (SEM). Results revealed six distinct attitude classes (Passionate, Prefer Chinese, Prefer Science/Math, Prefer Chinese/Math, Persistent, and Uncommitted) and four ability profiles (High-achieving, Above-average, Below-average, and Low-achieving). Students in the Prefer Science/Math class with a clear science/mathematics preference over the Chinese language were the most likely to select STEM careers, whereas the other groups (e.g. Passionate, Prefer Chinese, Persistent, and Uncommitted) were less likely to pursue them. Additionally, the Prefer Science/Math class positively mediated the relationships between student ability profiles and career expectations, whereas the Prefer Chinese/Math class negatively mediated these relationships. Overall, this study underscores the importance of attitudes toward science and mathematics relative to other subjects (e.g. language) in shaping adolescents’ career expectations and future STEM participation.
keywords: STEM participation, science ability, mathematical ability, Chinese language ability, attitudes toward science, attitudes toward mathematics, subject preference, ability profiles, junior high school students, career choice motivation

title: Cutting-edge science education model: implementing a professional learning community between teachers and astronomers
text: This article examines the implementation of an interdisciplinary Professional Learning Community (PLC) comprising teachers, astronomers, and science education researchers, aimed at promoting the integration of cutting-edge scientific topics into school-level physics and mathematics classes. Within the framework of this collaboration, the team developed six instructional sequences based on authentic astronomical data, aligned with the Chilean national curriculum and grounded in principles of active and situated learning. To support this initiative, a pilot Cutting-Edge Science Education Model (CESEM) was designed and implemented, structured around five stages: Content, Design, Implementation, Analysis, and Sharing. The effectiveness of the PLC and the feasibility of introducing frontier science into schools were evaluated using questionnaires administered to participating teachers and astronomers, with the resulting data subjected to content analysis and research triangulation. This article does not report student learning outcomes; instead, it focuses on characterising the PLC’s working model and describing its members’ experiences. Findings highlight the model’s potential to foster authentic, contextualised, and interdisciplinary science teaching, and its capacity for replication and transfer to other areas of cutting-edge science. The article concludes with a discussion of the model’s limitations and future prospects, alongside recommendations for strengthening both initial and continuing teacher education.
keywords: professional learning communities, interdisciplinary science teaching, instructional sequence, active learning, situated learning, physics and mathematics education, teacher professional development, curriculum alignment

title: Relevance and trust in science education: an expectancy-value case study of ninth-grade students
text: Students' declining interest in school science as they transition from primary to secondary education has raised concerns about how science education connects to students' lives and their beliefs about science. This study examines ninth-grade students' attitudes towards school science through two value-related dimensions: perceived relevance and trust in science. Drawing on Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT), we empirically examine students' interest in school science and investigate its relationship with their perceptions of relevance (utility and attainment value) and trust in science as a problem-solving resource. A convergent mixed-methods case-study design was employed with 63 students (age 15) in one Swedish lower secondary school. Quantitative data were collected using selected items from the ROSES survey and analysed through descriptive statistics and separate regression models for relevance and trust. Qualitative data consisted of students' argumentative texts responding to paired statements on relevance and trust, which were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings indicate that perceived relevance has the strongest association with interest, while trust is positively related but insufficient on its own. Qualitative themes illustrate how students experience science as personally meaningful, societally important, or abstract and distant. The study discusses implications for designing science teaching that supports both perceived relevance and informed trust.

title: Paper-based or digital tool?: Investigating equitable student participation in scientific sensemaking on plant structures and functions
text: This study examines the potential of digital platform-based activities, implemented through Canva, to support more equitable student participation during scientific sensemaking. In this paper, ‘equity’ is defined as how participation opportunities are distributed during sensemaking, specifically whether more students can enter the work, contribute ideas that are taken up, and share responsibility for evaluating and revising explanations. A total of 243 sixth-grade students participated in both paper-based and digital platform-based activities across two science units. Survey results showed that most students preferred the digital format (79%), citing access to multimodal resources, ease of revision, and generative AI support. Qualitative analysis then examined students’ participation processes in digital platform-based sensemaking, using interviews, screen recordings, and student artifacts. Three features were associated with more equitable participation: (a) multimodal resources supported students facing barriers in expressing ideas through text or drawings; (b) comment threads enabled revisitable teacher prompts and supported collaborative revision; and (c) real-time artifact creation and revision supported distributed contribution during explanation building. Across these features, students treated platform resources as candidates to be checked and revised against a target causal account, rather than as final answers. These findings highlight how designed platform environments can support more inclusive participation in sensemaking.
keywords: digital learning platforms, Canva, multimodal resources, collaborative revision, comment threads, generative AI, sixth grade students

title: Exploring the roles, tools, and contexts of inservice elementary science teachers: an activity theory perspective
text: This position paper uses an activity theory ( Blunden, 2023) lens to analyze the work of science teachers in elementary settings. We explore the interplay between teacher identity, teacher goals, and instructional tool use in these settings. Through carefully curated scholarship, we illustrate how teachers form their professional identities through interactions in elementary settings and through leadership roles. We discuss findings on how instructional goals, like equitable science instruction and students' sensemaking, can help mediate teacher identity and tool use. We also explore teachers' use of tools in their settings, including project-based learning (PBL) and adaptive technologies. Additionally, we examine how tensions and contractions between policy and practice can bring about changes for elementary teachers.
keywords: teacher identity, learning objectives, activity theory, project-based learning, adaptive learning systems, teacher leadership, policy-practice tensions, elementary school science

title: Development and validation of a scale for evaluating STEM teachers’ identity in the Chinese context
text: A clear and stable STEM teacher identity is a core element driving teachers’ professional development and optimising teaching practices. However, existing research on STEM teacher identity evaluation mostly focuses on single dimensions such as self-efficacy and teaching attitudes, lacking a multidimensional assessment of identity. This study aims to develop and validate a multidimensional measurement scale for STEM teacher identity using large-scale quantitative data. A STEM teacher identity scale was developed and validated with 535 Chinese STEM teachers. The scale was refined using item analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis. Additionally, the study identified how key personal factors relate to STEM teacher identity. The findings of this research are as follows. (1) The final scale comprises 36 items and eight sub-dimensions: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, individual teacher attributes, collective teacher attributes, designer self-efficacy, implementer self-efficacy, outcome-based task perception, and process-based task perception, all demonstrating good reliability and validity. (2) The overall level of STEM teacher identity and its dimensions are positively correlated with teaching experience. (3) Teachers in information technology and science score higher in multiple dimensions compared to those in other subjects.
keywords: scale development, multidimensional measurement, teacher self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, teacher characteristics, task perception, teaching experience, information technology teachers, science teachers

title: Investigating students’ scientific thinking process during online inquiry learning: a process mining approach
text: Scientific thinking is a critical mental process in education, one that relies on investigation, hypothesis development, and critical evaluation. This study explores how scientific thinking evolves during online scientific inquiry, specifically examining students’ use of logic and systematic inquiry strategies to ask questions, gather data, analyse data, and draw conclusions. Using process mining, the research identified effective patterns in scientific thinking by analysing learning process data, offering insights into the cognitive processes underlying students’ learning behaviours. A total of 143 fifth-grade students participated in a science inquiry learning module and completed a science inquiry competency test afterward. Three scientific thinking patterns were identified: proficiency from the start, revision after failure, and stagnation. Students demonstrating proficiency from the start achieved the highest learning performance. Furthermore, high-performing students were more likely to adopt the revision after failure pattern when faced with initial setbacks compared to their low-performing peers. The study underscores the importance of understanding the scientific thinking process in science inquiry learning, with implications for enhancing instructional design to support student learning.
keywords: scientific thinking, process mining, fifth grade students, learning patterns, student learning behavior, instructional design

title: Exploring science teachers’ questioning patterns for learning support through a computational grounded theory approach
text: Teacher questioning is pivotal for students’ conceptual construction and cognitive growth, yet prior studies rely on predefined taxonomies and static analyses. Using a computational grounded theory (CGT) approach that integrates lag sequential analysis (LSA) and pretrained language model–based semantic representations, we systematically examine questioning types and patterns in 32 upper-secondary physics lessons. We identify 19 types organised across three levels – behavioural regulation, cognitive development, and reflective questioning – and two recurring dynamic patterns: cyclical reinforcement and progressive scaffolding. These patterns guide key cognitive processes, including conceptual elaboration, causal reasoning, experimental design, and reflective integration. The study illustrates the value of CGT for semantic analysis of classroom discourse and, when combined with LSA, offers a data-driven yet theoretically grounded pathway to model questioning dynamics. Findings refine theoretical accounts of teacher questioning as a multilayered cognitive scaffold and provide empirical evidence on how exemplary science teachers orchestrate diverse questions to support learning.
keywords: teacher questioning, science teachers, physics education, upper secondary school, classroom discourse, lag sequential analysis, scaffolding, reflective questioning, conceptual elaboration, causal reasoning, experimental design, learning support

title: Understanding climate scientific uncertainty: how undergraduate students’ epistemic views shape climate concern and action
text: This study investigates how students’ perceptions of scientific uncertainty influence their concern and actions regarding climate change. Using the Uncertainty Intensification Hypothesis, which suggests that uncertainty increases emotional responses; Construal Level Theory, which connects psychological distance to abstract thinking; and the Nature of Science (NOS) framework, which highlights uncertainty as inherent to scientific inquiry, we define climate uncertainty as a multidimensional construct that includes measurement uncertainty, perceived ambiguity, and uncertainty about future impacts. We surveyed 633 Taiwanese undergraduates using a validated instrument that measured three dimensions: climate uncertainty, climate concern, and climate action. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was used to examine the relationships among these variables. Perceived ambiguity and future uncertainty were negatively associated with climate concern, whereas measurement uncertainty was positively associated with concern and, indirectly, with action. These findings indicate that recognising uncertainty as an inherent aspect of science can strengthen climate engagement. Integrating NOS principles into climate education builds epistemic trust and resilience, enabling students to make informed judgments and take responsible action. By empirically demonstrating how different dimensions of scientific uncertainty affect students’ climate concern and action, this study supports the need for NOS-informed climate education that prepares learners for reflective, evidence-based reasoning and responsible engagement.
keywords: climate change uncertainty, scientific uncertainty, climate change concern, climate action, construal level theory, psychological distance, nature of science, measurement uncertainty, perceived ambiguity, climate change education, undergraduate students, epistemic trust

title: What professional judgements do teachers make in utilising resources on contemporary science?
text: There is continuing policy interest in engaging students with contemporary science and with scientists’ practices to enhance their learning and interest in science. Calls to action advocate for supporting teachers to establish new approaches to science teaching that widen the scope of science education. This research explores how we can support teachers to engage with specifically created curriculum resources to develop innovative science teaching approaches that forefront scientists’ research and practices. Implementing design-based research methodology, I collaborated with three teachers in a process of adapting these resources to provide students with contextual, contemporary science learning experiences. Data collection involved semi-structured interviews with teachers describing their experiences in implementing these resources, classroom observations involving journal writing and digital video recording of classes during resource use. Findings show that teachers were agentic in exercising professional judgement to link the resource with their own personal practices for productive learning. The study demonstrates that, with appropriate support, resources that represent scientists’ contemporary research and practices can stimulate teachers’ innovative curriculum planning to align these with their professional beliefs and practices. Such resources can support teacher growth into new directions in science education.
keywords: professional judgment, contemporary science, curriculum materials, science education, teacher agency, curriculum adaptation, contextual science learning, teacher professional development

title: Trust in climate science and scientists: secondary science teachers’ climate change views and teaching
text: Climate change is an urgent problem that will require action guided by the work of climate scientists. Education is critical for preparing a knowledgeable citizenry mobilised by expert guidance and able to identify trustworthy sources of information. This mixed methods study characterises secondary teachers’ trust in climate science and scientists and elucidates how trust in climate science and scientists is approached in the classroom. The survey sample consisted of 86 Northeast Ohio secondary middle and high school science teachers, and 26 of these teachers completed interviews. Survey instruments ascertained teachers’ trust in science and scientists, attitudes towards climate change, and climate change teaching practices. Qualitative interview approaches allowed teachers to explain their ideas about trust in science, climate change, and teaching connected to trust in science. Data analysis included statistical analyses to ascertain relationships. Findings include that a majority of teachers discussed climate change in their classes, and more than half included increasing student trust in science as an instructional goal. Teachers’ trust in science and scientists, attitudes towards climate change, and trust-teaching intentions were correlated. Qualitative findings include teachers’ concerns about student mistrust of science and the use of nature of science instruction to increase student trust in science.
keywords: public trust in science, trust in scientists, climate change education, secondary science teachers, scientific literacy

title: Trends in elementary preservice teachers’ lesson planning for socioscientific issues
text: Socioscientific issues (SSI) instruction has been shown to strengthen students’ critical thinking, problem solving, and scientific discourse skills. However, opportunities to engage with SSI remain limited in elementary classrooms across the United States (U.S.). This gap is driven, in part, by U.S. elementary teachers’ reliance on scripted curricula and a lack of access to high-quality, developmentally appropriate SSI resources. Because preservice preparation plays a central role in shaping beginning teachers’ instructional decision-making, teacher education programmes represent a critical site for developing the skills needed to design rigorous, student-centered SSI lessons. This study explores how elementary preservice teachers incorporated elements of SSI (scientific content, moral and ethical considerations, stakeholder perspectives, and assessment) into lesson plans developed within an elementary science methods course. By analyzing trends across these lesson plans, the study provides insight into how elementary preservice teachers conceptualise and design SSI-based instruction and identifies areas where additional pedagogical support may be needed. Findings highlight the promise of preservice preparation for cultivating teachers’ capacity to integrate real-world scientific issues into elementary classrooms and underscore the importance of continued research on how this early preparation has potential to influence teachers’ long-term instructional practices.
keywords: socioscientific issues, pre-service primary teachers, lesson planning, elementary science methods course, teacher professional development, instructional decision-making, stakeholder perspectives, assessment design, scripted curriculum, student-centered instruction

title: Nature through children’s eyes: a phenomenological inquiry using the storyline method
text: This study examines third-grade primary school students’ perceptions of nature within a science education process structured through the Storyline method, grounded in a constructivist learning approach. The research was conducted using a qualitative descriptive phenomenological design with 22 students attending a public primary school in Istanbul, Türkiye. Data were collected through observations, focus group interviews, student artifacts, a Nature Perception Form, mind maps, and a Word Association Test, and were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings indicate that students’ perceptions of nature are organised around three interrelated dimensions: functionality of nature, emotional perception of nature, and protecting nature. Students conceptualised nature not only as a physical environment but also as an interconnected system, a source of emotional meaning, and a shared value requiring protection. Furthermore, students’ explanations regarding environmental concepts such as natural – artificial distinctions, extinction, recycling, and responsibility became more elaborated over the course of the learning process. The study suggests that the Storyline method provides a meaningful pedagogical context for supporting students’ socially mediated meaning-making about nature in early science education.
keywords: children's perceptions of nature, storyline method, early childhood science education, third grade, constructivist learning, environmental protection, extinction, recycling, environmental responsibility, meaning-making

title: Seeing climate change: developing professional vision through interactive data visualisations
text: This article examines how interactive data visualisations can foster professional vision in science teacher education, focusing on socioscientific issues (SSIs) related to climate change. Drawing on video-recorded teaching at a Swedish science centre exhibit, we analyse how an experienced educator engaged two pre-service teachers in exploring dynamic visualisations of sea-level rise and urban vulnerability projected onto a large-scale city model. Using interaction analysis and Charles Goodwin’s concept of professional vision, we identify key episodes that illustrate how professional ways of seeing are enacted in interaction. The analysis shows how the educator established a visual frame, interpreted risks, and projected futures. Professional vision was not only disciplinary and centred on interpreting scientific categories such as sea-level rise, infrastructural systems, temporal and scenario-based reasoning, and data-literacy practices. It was also pedagogical, oriented towards what might be teachable, engaging, or confusing for students. We propose the notion of dual-layered professional vision to capture this intersection of scientific and pedagogical seeing. The study contributes to research on SSI pedagogy and teacher education by demonstrating how interactive visualisations can be orchestrated to cultivate interpretive expertise, enabling pre-service teachers to engage with complexity, uncertainty, and the entanglement of science and society in an out-of-school context.
keywords: professional vision, interactive data visualization, climate change, socioscientific issues, science teacher education, pre-service teachers, sea level rise, urban vulnerability, data literacy, uncertainty, Charles Goodwin

title: Elementary teachers’ use of educative support materials for citizen science projects: affordances, obstacles, and impacts
text: Formidable obstacles constrain elementary teachers’ efforts to provide science instruction that creates opportunities for students to engage with science. These include limited instructional time, inadequate access to high-quality instructional materials and professional learning, and teachers’ self-efficacy. Citizen science, or community science, supports teachers by offering ways to engage students in science and in collecting and interpreting data connected to students’ lives. While citizen science projects emphasise gathering accurate data fundamental for scientific success, they may not align with teacher needs. Using Remillard’s model of teachers’ participatory relationship with curriculum materials, we studied how project-specific educative supports could facilitate teachers’ use of citizen science projects in formal settings. We selected two projects and developed educative support materials. We present data from 52 teachers in a randomised controlled trial investigating (1) how teachers used the materials and (2) how the materials impacted use. Access to project-specific educative supports has a large positive effect on teachers’ and students’ use, and teachers value some supports more than others. We situate our work in research on teachers’ relationship with instructional materials, design of educative curriculum materials, and school-based citizen science. We discuss the implications for project designers, science education researchers, and science teacher educators.
keywords: citizen science, elementary science teachers, teaching materials, teacher self-efficacy, school-based citizen science, student engagement in science, data collection and interpretation

title: Exploring rural and small-town students’ pathways to STEM and factors related to their STEM engagement
text: This study extends Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory to examine how interacting social and institutional contexts shape rural students’ engagement with STEM in Kazakhstan, a country experiencing widening rural-urban disparities. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 23 rural and small-town students enrolled in STEM-related university programmes, the analysis explores how micro-, meso-, exo-, and macro-level systems converge to shape educational trajectories. The findings suggest that rural students’ STEM pathways are not shaped by isolated ecological levels but by interlocking mechanisms linking family expectations, school resources, teacher shortages, gender norms, and broader structural inequalities affecting rural schooling. Constraints such as limited parental familiarity with STEM careers, teacher shortages, and gendered expectations narrow rural students’ perceived horizons of possibility. At the same time, teacher mentorship and supportive school environments emerge as critical relational resources sustaining aspirations and facilitating transitions to higher education. Building on Bronfenbrenner’s framework, the study advances an ecological interpretation of rural STEM engagement that foregrounds cross-level mechanisms shaping aspirations, belonging, and persistence in STEM pathways. By situating these dynamics within Kazakhstan’s post-socialist rural context, the study contributes to international scholarship on rural STEM participation while distinguishing widely observed patterns of rural educational inequality from context-specific dynamics.
keywords: rural students, STEM engagement, STEM pathways, urban-rural differences, ecological systems theory, family expectations, teacher shortage, gender norms, teacher mentoring, school resources, educational inequality, Kazakhstan, post-socialist education, student persistence in STEM

title: Pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) about scientific reasoning in different groups of science teachers and its relation to other variables
text: Scientific reasoning (SR) is a major goal in science education and, hence, science teachers at various levels (i.e. elementary, secondary, and higher education) need pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) of how to promote students’ SR competencies (i.e. PCKSR). However, because these teacher groups usually differ, e.g. regarding the curricula and learning goals the teachers pursue, it can be assumed that their PCKSR also differs from each other. To test this assumption, we used a multiple-choice instrument to assess the PCKSR of science teachers at elementary (n = 113) and secondary schools (n = 201), as well as teacher educators (n = 41). In addition, we conducted a regression analysis to investigate to what extent teachers’ PCKSR can be predicted by their epistemological beliefs about transmission, their openness to innovation, and their teaching experience. It was found that the groups differed significantly regarding their PCKSR. In addition, the considered variables predicted the PCKSR for each group differently. The results not only provide fundamental insights into how the PCKSR of different groups of teachers differs and how it can be predicted by related variables, but also on the development of PCKSR for practicing teachers as well as the assessment of PCK in general.
keywords: pedagogical content knowledge, scientific reasoning, science teachers, teacher educators, primary school teachers, secondary school teachers, epistemological beliefs, openness to innovation, teaching experience, science education

title: Students’ views around scientific research, the nature of science, and their intentions to choose science and science-related careers
text: Students often have positive views about science, although can also feel that doing science or being a scientist is less feasible or appealing. Accordingly, this study explored associations between students’ intentions to choose science and science-related careers and their views around scientific research and the nature of science. 289 school students were surveyed, covering Year 9 to Year 13 (13/14–17/18 years old) from England and Guernsey, and their questionnaire responses were analysed through predictive modelling (ordinary-least-squares regression) that accounted for differences across academic years, gender, home/family circumstances, and a number of other factors. The modelling revealed that students’ views about scientific research (encompassing awareness around working as a scientist, knowing what scientific research involves, and interest and confidence in doing scientific research) independently and positively associated with their intentions to choose science and science-related careers, together with other factors, including their personal views of the gains from studying science and having a career in science, and their personal confidence in doing science in general. Essentially, students’ views around scientific research had relevance over and above their other views, which suggests these as an avenue towards enhancing trajectories towards science and science-related careers.
keywords: nature of science, science career choice, science education, student confidence in science, student interest in science, high school students, gender differences, family situation

title: Agentic actions of women science teachers: how do secondary school educators navigate gendered experiences?
text: This qualitative study focuses on women science teachers’ lived experiences in secondary co-education schools in Bangladesh. Employing gender and agency as the analytical framework and anchored in feminist standpoint theory, the study draws on the narratives of eight women science teachers from urban and semi-urban areas to unveil their agentic actions. A thematic analysis revealed that these teachers navigate the gendered experiences within schools, communities, and families, through different forms of agency. The findings are organised around three patterns of action: micro-resistance that alters immediate conditions, patriarchal accommodation within institutional expectations, and compliance within socio-cultural constraints. Drawing on women science teachers’ accounts of classroom practices, household responsibilities, and career decisions, the study shows that even when actions involve accommodation or compliance, they maintain classroom authority, deliver science lessons, and continue their careers. These everyday practices reveal the interplay of masculinities and femininities in science teaching and highlight how these teachers sustain in science teaching despite gendered constraints.
keywords: gendered agency, micro-resistance, compliance, masculinity and femininity, classroom authority, household responsibilities, career choice, Bangladesh

title: Investigating Arabic diglossia in Bedouin society: a case study of high school biology students’ use of adapted primary literature.
text: The specialised language of biology presents substantial challenges for Arab Bedouin students navigating the gap between spoken Arabic and formal literary Arabic. This diglossic divide can hinder reading comprehension, delay scientific understanding, and weaken student confidence when engaging with scientific texts. This qualitative study investigates the linguistic barriers faced by 12th-grade Bedouin high school students while reading an Adapted Primary Literature article in biology. Using task-based, semi-structured interviews, the research explores how students living in a diglossic context interpret and cope with the linguistic demands of reading scientific texts in Literary Arabic. Participants included thirteen female students from Bedouin villages in the Negev region of Israel. The findings reveal two central linguistic barriers: semantic challenges that disrupted reading comprehension and lexical limitations that affected written expression. Students also reported cognitive overload due to complex vocabulary and sentence structures. A key coping strategy identified was language style-shifting, translating literary Arabic phrases into more familiar spoken Arabic. The study underscores how diglossia impacts scientific literacy and highlights the pedagogical value of adapted scientific articles in supporting comprehension. These findings offer actionable insights for educators aiming to bridge linguistic gaps for Arabic-speaking students in science education, particularly those from marginalised communities.

title: Analysis of academic and non-academic time use patterns in scientific inquiry supported classes through video observations
text: Teachers have raised concerns about insufficient instructional time and challenges in managing time effectively during classroom activities. This study developed a unique observation tool to systematically evaluate teachers’ time management in scientific inquiry-supported classes, analysing both academic (e.g. research process, analysis, conclusions) and non-academic time (e.g. lesson start/end, discipline, materials, off-topic behaviours). The study was designed as descriptive study using systematic observation, and the participants were selected using purposeful sampling. The study group consisted of 10 teachers (five science teachers at secondary level and five primary teachers at primary level) who had completed scientific inquiry-supported e-mentorship in-service training within the scope of a research project. The study data were collected through lesson videos recorded by the participating teachers during the final stage of a four-phase mentorship process. To assess the reliability of the Time Use Observation Scale (TUOS), differences in total durations coded by four observers were analysed using the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test. The findings indicate that mentorship support and effective planning enabled teachers to use limited lesson time efficiently, while class size and physical conditions significantly influenced time management. The research contributes to the literature by offering insights into instructional efficiency in scientific inquiry-supported lessons.
keywords: instructional time management, scientific inquiry, continuing teacher education, teaching efficiency, class size

title: Unveiling the explanatory problem in nature of science research: a critical epistemological assessment
text: Despite decades of research into the Nature of Science (NOS), widespread learner misconceptions persist and questions about why learners hold particular misconceptions, or why some NOS aspects are consistently more difficult to understand than others remain largely unexplored. This paper identifies and analyzes this explanatory limitation from an epistemological standpoint and calls for a shift from merely describing learner misconceptions to explaining their underlying epistemological foundations. Anchored in a framework that spans ontology, scientific practice, epistemology, and science education, we propose a model that clarifies the nature of explanation in NOS studies. Applying this model through the lens of a domain-specific approach to NOS, namely the Nature of the Sciences (NOTSs) approach and drawing on empirical findings from our previous research, we demonstrate how NOTSs can account for entrenched misconceptions documented in NOS literature. We also analyze the consensus-based approach to NOS as a scientific field in its own right, critically evaluating the sources of its limited explanatory power. Finally, we assess the explanatory capacity of the Family Resemblance Approach (FRA) to NOS, considering whether it can effectively respond to the limitations identified in the consensus-based approach or whether it encounters similar challenges. Implications for science education are also discussed.
keywords: nature of science, student misconceptions, epistemology of science education, explanatory power, ontology of science, scientific practice, family resemblance approach

title: Supporting systems thinking in environmental science education with large language model chatbots
text: Understanding the climate system requires systems thinking to consider intersecting components and interrelationships within the atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, and biosphere. Developing systems thinking is challenging, as students often identify simple, linear relationships instead of more complex causal ideas. Modelling practices, including developing, evaluating, and refining models, can enhance systems thinking. While research on modelling has focused on ecological and physical processes, we designed chatbots powered by large language models (LLMs) to highlight perspectives about biodiversity and climate change’s impact. We piloted the chatbots in a two-week high school environmental science curriculum. Students created system models in groups and engaged in open-ended interactions with the chatbots to revise models. Data sources included students’ group models before and after chatbot interactions, written reflections, and chat logs. We qualitatively coded the data for shifts in systems thinking (indicated by components and causal relationships in models) and perspective taking (how students articulated sociocultural and economic factors, scientific facts, and system complexity). Analyses revealed that students incorporated more system components and complex causal ideas following chatbot interactions. We found shifts in perspective taking regarding socioeconomic and scientific climate issues. We discuss how science instruction can scaffold complex causal ideas and effective interactions with LLMs-based tools.
keywords: systems thinking, large language model chatbots, environmental science education, climate change, biodiversity, system modeling, causal relationship, perspective taking, high school students, AI-assisted learning

title: Mediating sexuality as lived biology in science teacher education: the SciSexTed model
text: This article examines how the SciSexTed model mediates preservice science teachers’ engagement with sexuality education when scientific content becomes emotionally charged, ethically uncertain and normatively complex. The model is a campus-based instructional design that provides practice-near and closely supervised skills training in teaching puberty and sexuality. Upper primary pupils visit the university campus and participate in station-based teaching led by preservice teachers, enabling repeated teaching encounters, adjustment, reflection and re-teaching. Methodologically, the study is anchored in Design-Based Research, combined with the Constant Comparative Method. The empirical material consists of focus group interviews, podcast reflections and observation notes from three iterations conducted between 2022 and 2024. Through comparative analysis of controversial, emotional and sensitive incidents, the study examines how preservice teachers respond when sexuality education exceeds reproductive physiology and becomes entangled with pupils’ questions, emotions, identities and values. The analysis shows that reproductive biology initially functioned as a perceived safe ground, but that pupils’ questions unsettled this framing. The article argues that SciSexTed makes ethical tension, uncertainty and friction pedagogically available through repeated teaching, mediating artefacts and collective reflection. It contributes by conceptualising sexuality education in science as lived biology, where bodies, meaning, vulnerability and scientific knowledge are mediated together.
keywords: sex education, science teacher education, pre-service science teachers, puberty education, ethical uncertainty, teacher reflection, reproductive biology

title: Scientific literacy and generative AI: embracing nature of science for social justice
text: This paper explores how generative AI (GenAI) can be leveraged in science education to cultivate a socially responsible form of scientific literacy. It argues for a social justice (SJ)-oriented praxis to help students critically engage with nature of science (NOS) and socioscientific issues (SSIs), thereby fostering scientific literacy essential for democratic participation. While GenAI, NOS, SSIs, and SJ have been explored in the literature, this paper uniquely examines their intersections within K-12 science education. The paper highlights why a science education praxis committed to SJ is of high importance in today’s era of GenAI expansion. It accomplishes this objective by analyzing the impact of GenAI on everyday life and showing how it generates a unique set of SSIs that raise SJ concerns. The paper also highlights how SJ as a framework can be utilised in K-12 science education for guiding learners to critically explore NOS and SSIs within the context of GenAI. The paper ends with a discussion of the contribution of the proposed ideas to a more critical, reflective and participatory form of scientific literacy, which aims to prepare students to critically explore science and its changing nature, deliberate access to science, and act responsibly in society.

title: Spurring and siloing: cultural and linguistic identity (CLI) navigation in scientific writing among Asian student researchers
text: Scientific writing and publication are critical sites where students must navigate between personal identities and presumed scientific objectivity. For non-white student researchers, particularly those stereotyped as ‘model minorities,’ this process involves complex negotiations. This qualitative study examines how Asian and Asian American students navigate their cultural and linguistic identities within scientific writing processes. Using an integrated theoretical framework combining cultural community wealth, narrative identity, and border crossing, we analyzed how participants deployed cultural resources while navigating institutional expectations. Drawing on interviews with 23 student participants who engaged with the Journal of Emerging Investigators (JEI), we identified two primary approaches: ‘spurring,’ wherein ethnic and cultural backgrounds catalyze research questions, and ‘siloing,’ wherein these identities are deliberately compartmentalised during writing. Findings reveal that while participants drew upon familial capital to inform research interests, most practiced disciplinary compartmentalisation and adhered to perceived scientific norms. This tension demonstrates how students negotiate cultural scripts while developing professional identities. Our findings suggest that science educators could help students recognize their cultural backgrounds as valuable epistemic resources rather than sources of bias, explicitly address the myth of value-neutral science, and provide models of how scientists integrate personal and cultural perspectives into rigorous scientific work.
keywords: linguistic and cultural identity, scientific writing, Asian American students, model minority stereotype, narrative identity, border crossing, scientific objectivity, professional identity formation, familial capital, epistemic resources

title: Examining the impact of virtual reality on middle school students’ biology learning outcomes and experiences
text: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly posited to transform biology education by visualising complex, microscopic, and abstract structures. However, prior research has yielded inconsistent findings regarding the comparative efficacy of different visualisation modalities, particularly when integrating cognitive, affective, and technological acceptance variables. This study conducted a six-week quasi-experimental investigation at a middle school, examining 225 eighth-grade students’ academic performance, learning motivation, flow experience, cognitive load, and technology acceptance using knowledge tests and validated questionnaires, employing MANCOVA and ANCOVA. Across twelve biology lessons, students were assigned to three instructional conditions (n = 75 each): (a) immersive VR (IVR) learning via head-mounted devices; (b) desktop VR (DVR) presented on an interactive whiteboard; and (c) two-dimensional (2D) content via PowerPoint (PPT). The results revealed that compared to the PPT group, the IVR group showed significantly higher academic achievement and learning motivation. Compared with the DVR group, the IVR group demonstrated a significantly better flow experience, although no significant differences were found in other measured variables. These findings suggest that to fully harness IVR’s immersive experience, instructional design should focus on stimulating students’ active learning and curiosity, shifting toward problem-based learning. This approach can transform the potential of IVR to support students’ sustained engagement.
keywords: virtual reality, immersive virtual reality, biology education, junior high school students, academic performance, student motivation, flow experience, cognitive load, technology acceptance, head-mounted devices, interactive whiteboards, instructional design, problem-based learning, student engagement

title: Assessing students’ interdisciplinary understanding of socio-scientific issues in STEM education through concept mapping
text: Socio-scientific issues such as climate change represent complex societal challenges that cannot be addressed solely through scientific knowledge but instead require interdisciplinary and societal perspectives. To enable secondary school students to make informed future decisions, fostering interdisciplinary knowledge in STEM education is essential. This study investigates the extent to which students (n = 44) connect terms from different interdisciplinary teaching environments in the context of socio-scientific issues addressing climate change. At the end of the teaching series, students’ interdisciplinary understanding was assessed using semi-open concept maps to visualise their holistic understanding of climate change. A mixed-methods approach was employed. First, the number of connections within and between concepts from the different teaching environments was analysed quantitatively. Second, a multiple-case study using qualitative analysis to identify and categorise different forms of interdisciplinary connections. The analysis shows that students establish connections both within and between teaching environments. Additionally, the findings reveal how students link terms through conceptual, methodological, and model-centred integration when engaging with the complex social-scientific issue of climate change. Overall, this study demonstrates that students can meaningfully connect terms from interdisciplinary STEM learning environments and apply multiple forms of integration to address complex societal challenges such as climate change.

title: Digital or analog? Students’ Instrument choices in science lessons and their associations with authenticity beliefs and science career aspirations
text: This study examined associations between Emirati students’ choices of digital versus analog measuring instruments in science lessons and their perceptions of authenticity, accuracy, scientists’ practices, and science career aspirations. An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design was used with survey data from 429 students (Grades 5–11) in two UAE government schools, supplemented by focus group interviews with 107 students. When given a choice in curriculum-aligned experiments, 68.2% selected digital instruments. Preferences were stable across gender and grade but showed a significant experiment effect. Qualitative findings indicated analog choices were driven by perceived challenge and historical authenticity, while digital choices were motivated by ease, familiarity, novelty, safety, and alignment with modern professional practice. Stronger beliefs in an instrument’s authenticity and accuracy predicted higher likelihood of choosing that type. Ordinal logistic regression showed that perceptions of authenticity, accuracy, and enjoyment significantly predicted science career aspirations, whereas actual instrument choice did not. Interpreted through Social Cognitive Career Theory, results suggest classroom instrument-selection experiences can shape self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and perceptions of science practice. Implications include fostering informed decision-making based on accurate views of contemporary scientific work.
