title: Exploring the associations of curiosity, scientific interest, and scientific identity with 4th and 6th graders’ scientific knowledge understanding, reasoning, and inquiry
text: Scientific literacy serves as a common foundation and core objective of STEM education. While non-cognitive factors such as curiosity, interest, and identity are recognised as crucial for STEM engagement, research on collective relationships to cognitive factors remains insufficient. To investigate these associations, this study employed structural equation modelling (SEM) and multi-group path analysis on data of 5,939 fourth- and sixth-grade students in central China, examining the associative pathways between affective and cognitive factors within scientific literacy. SEM results indicated that: (1) Affective dimensions exhibited significant inter-associations, wherein curiosity showed a positive relation with scientific interest, which in turn was associated with science identity. (2) Among cognitive factors, content knowledge demonstrated a positive correlation with scientific reasoning, which was subsequently linked to scientific inquiry. (3) In specific pathways, affective factors exhibited direct associations with cognitive outcomes, predominantly linking curiosity to scientific inquiry and scientific identity to content knowledge. Furthermore, multi-group path analysis revealed that the overall model structure differed significantly in its associative patterns between the two grade levels. Specifically, the sixth-grade cohort exhibited significantly stronger associative coefficients along the pathways from curiosity to interest, and from knowledge to reasoning and inquiry.

title: Digital incremental scaffolds during experimentation in biology lessons – beneficial for competence experience and intrinsic motivation?
text: Experimenting in heterogeneous learning groups requires the use of instructional learning supports. Given the recent boom in digital technologies, adding digital elements to such supports could help to address challenges during experimentation. For example, digital incremental scaffolds could promote the learners’ competence experience and intrinsic motivation while experimenting. The aim of the present study was thus to investigate the effectiveness of digital incremental scaffolds during experimentation in biology lessons. In a quasi-experimental study, data was collected from 175 students regarding their motivational regulation in biology, competence experience, and intrinsic motivation during experimentation. The experimental group received digital incremental scaffolds while experimenting whereas the control group did not. By assessing competence perceptions phase by phase, the study provides a more detailed understanding of how incremental scaffolds impact learners throughout experimentation. The findings indicate positive effects of using digital incremental scaffolds on the learners’ experience of competence during the various experimental phases. No statistically significant effects were evident for the learners’ intrinsic motivation. However, the students in the experimental group reported lower levels of pressure and tension. The results are discussed in the context of biology experimentation in the classroom, followed by a consideration of limitations and implications for educational research.
keywords: competence experience, intrinsic motivation, motivational regulation, heterogeneous learning groups, science education

title: Everyday certainty and scientific uncertainty: potentials of scientists’ perspectives from microplastics research to address uncertainty in science education
text: Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in human blood represent an emerging research field characterised by uncertainty and public interest. While scientific knowledge is often portrayed as certain in public and educational contexts, scientific literacy approaches emphasise that today’s socio-scientifically relevant problems are complex with changing evidence. In this article an educational perspective on uncertainty for science education is proposed, using the extended Model of Educational Reconstruction (MER) as research framework. Drawing on interviews with MNPs researchers (n = 5), we analyse how they understand and experience uncertainty, differentiating between objectifying (e.g. construction of scientific concepts) and subjectifying (e.g. emotional engagement) approaches. The article focuses on two contrasting cases: one is mainly characterised by objectifying conceptions of understanding and dealing with uncertainty, whereas the other shows a strong intertwining of objectifying and subjectifying conceptions linking limits of detection to experiences of fear. Based on our findings, we discuss refinements of existing classifications of uncertainty integrating interdisciplinary science-in-the-making contexts. We further argue that the heterogeneity of scientists’ understandings and experiences can support reflective engagement with uncertainty in science education by fostering students’ individual meaning-making processes. The findings therefore indicate that the extended MER enables a systematic integration of objectifying and subjectifying perspectives for science education.
keywords: scientific uncertainty, micro- and nanoplastics, scientists' perspectives, Model of Educational Reconstruction, science in the making, scientific literacy, socioscientific issues, detection limit, fear, meaning-making, science education

title: Students’ pre-instructional reasoning about evolution: interactions among conceptual, epistemic, and positioning dimensions
text: Students’ engagement with biological evolution remains challenging due to conceptual demands and sociocultural influences. Research suggests that engagement is shaped not only by scientific knowledge but also by epistemic trust, evaluation of evidence, scientific authority, and learners’ positioning toward scientific explanations. However, little qualitative work has examined how these factors interact prior to instruction. This study investigates how upper secondary students reason about evolutionary explanations before formal instruction. A qualitative descriptive approach was used, based on semi-structured interviews with 25 Grade 12 biology students in western India. Thematic analysis identified dominant reasoning patterns and epistemic positions. Findings reveal fragmented conceptual understanding, scale-dependent acceptance of evolutionary claims, and varied reliance on authority and evidence. Many students expressed conditional acceptance grounded in epistemic trust, while others negotiated tensions between scientific explanations and personal belief frameworks through reconciliation or resistance. Students also articulated preferences for instructional approaches emphasising evidence, dialogue, and conceptual clarity. These findings show how conceptual reasoning, epistemic evaluation, and epistemic positioning interact in shaping students’ reasoning prior to formal instruction, with implications for evolution education. The study provides a process-oriented account of how these dimensions interact prior to instruction, a phase underexplored in evolution education research.
keywords: evolution education, epistemic trust, epistemic positioning, conceptual understanding, high school students, scientific authority, evidence evaluation

title: ‘Going against the grain’: science teachers’ socio-political and social justice-informed praxis in secondary school science
text: Science educators have been advocating a socio-political and social justice-informed turn in science education (SE) in the face of growing socio-justice science issues (SJSIs). This encompasses a shift from downplaying science’s connections with wider socio-political and social justice arenas to it being grounded in critical reflection on its complexities, including political, economic and ethical. Through individual semi-structured interviews with science student teachers, practising schoolteachers and university-based teacher educators in England, this study examined their perspectives and practices regarding such a socio-political and social justice turn. Grounded in an ecological model, our findings reveal that participants primarily linked social justice issues to their immediate teaching environments (micro and mesosystems), and socio-political concerns to broader systemic contexts and issues (exo and macrosystems). However, structural barriers centred in conformity and one-size-fits-all curricula and pedagogies, such as top-down standardised curricula and assessments, anti-activism rhetoric and a lack of a national agenda for anti-racism and anti-misogyny action, limited their capacity to engage with social justice and socio-political dimensions of science. This study highlights both the transformative potential of socially just and socio-politically informed SE driven by science educators themselves, and the challenges posed by entrenched socio-political structures around the teaching profession and schools’ work.

title: Science teachers’ views of Toulmin’s argument pattern: an investigation framed by expansive learning theory
text: The paper presents an empirical study aiming to investigate science education teachers’ views of Toulmin’s Argument Pattern (TAP) when the pattern was introduced to them for the first time and throughout a yearly intervention at primary schools in Cyprus. Four teachers participated in a constructed microcosm, which refers to a methodological setting stemming from Expansive Learning Theory (ELT). Datasets included, amongst others, the recorded discussions at the arranged meetings between teachers, and examples from students’ argumentation. Teachers’ subjectivity and reflective voices were amplified, and the teachers were free to act upon TAP and envision it as an evolving concept. An inductive analysis of the datasets revealed that teachers made adaptations to the pattern, related to its form (e.g. abandoning the rebuttal, allowing alterations to the argument’s starting element or the components’ sequence), and to the way they conceptualised some of its components, like the rebuttal and the warrant. As an implication, we argue that future studies need to take teachers’ reflective subjectivity into serious consideration, concerning the introduction of TAP in practice, as their teaching experience is too valuable to ignore. Finally, we encourage the use of ELT as a methodological framework for investigating teachers’ views on TAP.
keywords: Toulmin model, science teachers' views, teacher subjectivity, argumentation in science education, warrants, rebuttal, teacher professional development, primary science teaching, Cyprus

title: Exploring science teacher adaptive expertise through the framework of pedagogical content knowledge
text: Contemporary societal challenges require teachers to possess not only a strong foundation in science content but also the ability to adapt their instruction to address diverse student needs. This capacity, known as adaptive expertise (AE), requires teachers to apply knowledge flexibly and creatively in response to new situations, while maintaining efficiency in routine tasks. Adaptive expertise aligns closely with Shulman’s framework of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), which integrates knowledge of subject matter, pedagogy, and context to inform effective teaching practices. This study explores how high school science teachers use both their PCK and their AE to address societal challenges such as biotechnology and climate change and simultaneously meet the needs of diverse students. In the study, we explore the dynamic interplay between PCK and AE, particularly in contexts that demand attention to students’ different learning needs. As such, this research provides a better understanding of how teaching about contemporary science requires new skills and capabilities from teachers, and how teachers draw on and transform their PCK in new teaching and learning situations, and how PCK and AE interact in this process.

title: Implicit and explicit conceptual knowledge of gear mechanics in preschoolers: comparing minimal guidance and instructional modelling
text: Preschool science education aims to foster foundational conceptual knowledge, yet young children’s understanding often first appears implicitly in behaviour before it can be articulated explicitly. Acquiring scientifically valid knowledge poses challenges for learners and is thought to benefit from instructional guidance. This study examines how preschool children develop conceptual knowledge about gear mechanics under different forms of guidance. Children (N = 338; Mage = 5.7 years) engaged repeatedly in a gear construction task (GCT) and were assigned to one of four conditions: minimal guidance or brief instructional modelling (gestural, verbal, or combined). Two assessment approaches were used: a paper-pencil-test on turning direction as an indicator of explicit knowledge, and solution quality in the GCT as an indicator of implicit knowledge. Results showed no significant gains in paper-pencil-test scores across conditions. By contrast, solution quality improved in all conditions, with instructional modelling producing immediate gains and minimal guidance supporting gradual improvement. Paper-pencil-test scores as an indicator of explicit knowledge and solution quality as an indicator of implicit knowledge were only weakly related. These findings highlight distinct trajectories of performance on action-based and paper-pencil measures of conceptual knowledge and underscore the importance of considering multiple assessment approaches in early science learning.
keywords: early childhood science education, conceptual knowledge, tacit knowledge, explicit knowledge, turning direction, early science learning, assessment methods

title: Dispositions towards scientific uncertainty navigation (DSUN): relationships with epistemic curiosity and science learning before and after uncertainty-driven instruction
text: Epistemic curiosity (EC) is widely recognised as a driver of science learning, yet less is known about how it is stimulated through students’ encounters with scientific uncertainty. This study examined how students’ dispositions towards scientific uncertainty navigation (DSUN) relate to EC and learning achievement, and how these relationships shift after participation in an uncertainty-driven learning environment. Survey data were collected from 857 middle school students across 32 science classrooms taught by 11 teachers. Five dimensions of DSUN, epistemic orientation towards uncertainty, positive and negative affective reactions, self-efficacy in uncertainty navigation, and uncertainty navigation strategies, were examined in relation to interest-type (I-type) and deprivation-type (D-type) EC using mediational path analyses adjusted for baseline EC and achievement. Results showed that, after instruction, epistemic orientation and positive affective reaction indirectly predicted learning achievement through I-type EC, pathways not observed before instruction. In contrast, D-type EC did not predict achievement. Negative affective reaction predicted less I-type EC but more D-type EC. In addition, self-efficacy predicted achievement before instruction but predicted EC rather than achievement directly after instruction. These findings suggest the importance of supporting productive engagement with scientific uncertainty to foster curiosity and science learning.

title: Unpacking multimodal assessment in primary science: a teacher's view on task design, implicit criteria and representational challenges
text: This exploratory study investigates a primary science teacher?s reasoning when assessing students? multimodal knowledge representations in Biology. Findings reveal tensions between multimodal teaching and assessment practices, highlighting the teacher?s emphasis on written and oral components despite encouraging multimodal expression. Drawing on a multi-layered data set including a reflective conversation with the focal teacher, video observations and student-created posters, this study examines how her assessment of multimodal knowledge representation unfolded in teaching practice. Building on multimodal theory, the analysis identifies four key themes relative to the assessment of multimodal knowledge representations: exploring and searching for central concepts, challenges in assessing single multimodal representations, the influence of task design and the emergence of implicit assessment criteria. The study underscores the need for assessment approaches that recognise and support the use of diverse representational modes and related formative assessment strategies. By foregrounding the teacher?s lived experiences, this research contributes to science education by offering insights into the complexities of assessing multimodal knowledge representations, and by advocating for inclusive practices that better reflect students? varied ways of meaning-making.

title: Characterising the motivations of learners in a massive open online course on astronomy
text: This research project focused on learners in the Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) titled Astronomy: Exploring Time and Space on Coursera. This class was designed as an introductory survey course for a public audience. The goal of this project is to understand the learning identities and motivations of MOOC participants to take a science course designed for learners who are pursuing a personal interest rather than a degree or career advancement. Two survey instruments were used in this study. The first examined learning identities, and the second measured science learning motivations. Using these instruments together allowed us to understand what drives students to learn science by taking this course. The learners we surveyed were found to fall into two main categories: individuals who have a general interest in the subject material (Explorer identity) and knowledgeable individuals who want to dive in more deeply into the specific topic of the course (Hobbyist identity). Participants had high levels of intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and self-determination to learn science, and reported lower grade-related and job-related motivations. These results suggest that this course is reaching the intended audience and that, for these MOOCS, identity can be a useful lens for understanding learner motivations.

title: Student experiences of Ocean Literacy in the Blue School Programme: learning, engagement and action
text: This study examines how students experience and interpret Ocean Literacy (OL) within Portugal’s Blue School Programme and how these experiences relate to broader aims in science and sustainability education. Drawing on a convergent mixed-methods design, data from 3451 students were analysed to explore patterns of OL across cognitive, affective, behavioural, and civic dimensions, as well as students’ accounts of learning, engagement, and action. Quantitative findings indicate generally positive self-reported outcomes across the dimensions retained in the analysis, with younger students reporting higher scores, particularly in Awareness and Knowledge. Qualitative findings show that experiential and emotional engagement helped students connect ocean-related learning with personal meaning, communication, and everyday practices.Rather than presenting OL as a purely knowledge-based outcome, the study highlights its situated and participatory character within formal education. The integrated findings suggest that Ocean Literacy develops through the interaction of knowledge, emotion, social context, and opportunities for participation. They also show that action-oriented engagement is socially mediated and may require specific pedagogical support, particularly among older students. The study contributes a student-centred account of Ocean Literacy in the Blue School context and offers insights into how science education can support meaningful engagement with socio-environmental issues.

title: The interaction effects of emotional feedback and cognitive feedback on elementary students’ learning performance, cognitive load, and inquiry behaviours in an online scientific inquiry learning environment
text: Few studies have explored the combined effect of emotional and cognitive feedback, which are essential components of effective instruction, on students' learning performance in an online scientific inquiry learning environment. This study employed a 2 × 2 factorial design to investigate how emotional feedback (neutral vs. positive) and cognitive feedback (directive vs. reflective) influence students' performance, cognitive load, and inquiry behaviours in an online scientific inquiry environment. A total of 211 sixth-grade students (98 males, 113 females) were recruited from a public elementary school in China and divided into four groups. The results revealed that directive feedback improved performance on original tasks, whereas reflective feedback enhanced performance on transfer tasks. Compared with directive feedback, reflective feedback imposed less of a cognitive load on students in all dimensions. Positive emotional feedback helped reduce the mental effort associated with cognitive load. With respect to behavioural patterns, reflective feedback increased students' engagement in the targeted reverse transition rate, thus indicating deeper cognitive processing. In addition, positive emotional feedback was associated with significantly greater engagement in idea evaluation. In conclusion, reflective feedback may foster higher-order thinking and support knowledge transfer, and emotional support can reduce cognitive load during complex tasks.

title: Exploring the affordances and limitations of PCK: a three-year case study of model-based teaching through a conventional and expansive lens
text: Pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) has long served as a framework for understanding how science teachers can transform disciplinary content into forms that are accessible and meaningful for students. However, as science education increasingly emphasises equitable and knowledge-generative practices, questions remain regarding PCK’s capacity to capture the complexity of these instructional shifts. This longitudinal single instrumental case study examines the affordances and limitations of PCK mapping for understanding a high school biology teacher’s enactment of model-based teaching over three years. Drawing on video-recorded lessons, ancillary materials, and interviews, we analysed instructional sequences using two lenses: conventional modelling and expansive modelling. Findings indicate that PCK maps effectively captured shifts in conventional modelling practices, particularly those involving increased coordination of conceptual, epistemic, and representational dimensions of modelling. However, PCK maps were less sensitive to shifts toward equitable modelling practices characteristic of expansive modelling. In several instances, the strongest PCK maps aligned with multidimensional modelling rather than broader expansive modelling practices. This suggests that while PCK mapping is useful for examining instructional coherence and professional growth, it may obscure equity-oriented dimensions of model-based teaching. We argue for analytic pluralism, combining PCK with complementary frameworks to more fully capture the complexity of contemporary science teaching.

title: Human-in-the-loop: leveraging generative artificial intelligence to transform disciplinary learning in science
text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered science classrooms, teacher preparation, and research, carrying promise and risk. This editorial introduces a special issue of nine studies, spanning biology, chemistry, physics, and science teacher education across four continents, that trace the arc along which GenAI reaches learners. Where data and models are built, the studies show that synthetic student texts, automated scoring, and formative feedback become trustworthy only when experts encode disciplinary theory into prompts and correct the model's reasoning. Where GenAI meets classrooms, they show that when it drafts lesson plans, differentiates instruction for under-resourced schools, and answers students’ questions, quality varies so widely that human mediation is essential. Beyond the classroom, they document how teacher education courses and eight national systems build educators’ capacity for responsible use. Synthesising this evidence, we read the collection through a Human-in-the-Loop framework: GenAI not as an autonomous instructional authority, but as a socially embedded, fallible partner requiring sustained human judgment. Cross-cutting analysis reveals four tensions: affective uptake outpacing cognitive gain; generic AI literacy versus discipline-specific pedagogy; trade-offs among accuracy, equity, and data sovereignty; and teacher agency that scales up, not away, as models improve. Together, their open questions set the agenda for future research.

title: A knowledge-in-pieces approach to students’ self-identified analogies in the inception of nascent (mis)conceptions
text: The use of teacher-generated analogies as a productive conceptual technique to help with concepts, phenomena and situations that are abstract and difficult to understand has been well documented in the science education literature. What has been less researched is how students independently identify and utilise analogies to reason about novel situations (situations not considered before) and the nature of the knowledge they draw on in that process. Data in this study are drawn from questionnaires as well as small focus group discussions in which students (n = 166) aged 9–17 years were asked to make, and explain, their predictions about the outcome of a future event in six novel situations. The article reports on the nature of knowledge and the role of what we refer to as self-identified, and in many cases inapposite, analogies in the inception of nascent (mis)conceptions. The findings suggest that teaching and learning might be made more effective if teachers were more aware of the analogies students are likely to self-identify in particular situations and the knowledge elements activated in these and, as a consequence, better understand how to mitigate against their use so as to prevent the inception of nascent misconceptions.

title: Affective salience and context-sensitive knowledge use in spider-related science tasks
text: Affective responses can shape how learners engage with science tasks, especially when organisms are culturally associated with fear, disgust, or danger. This historical analytical case examines spider-related science tasks administered in Brazil in 2006 to 81 undergraduate biology students and 29 certified science teachers (N = 110). Using a convergent mixed-methods logic, the study integrated taxonomic responses, graphical representations, emotional descriptors, and brief written narratives at the aggregate level. Analyses showed low taxonomic accuracy, uneven identification of classificatory and diagnostic criteria, and a strong concentration of emotional responses in threat- and aversion-related categories. The descriptors fear, disgust, and scared accounted for 63.6% of responses (70/110). The findings do not support participant-level claims about emotional interference or causal mechanisms. They do, however, support a cautious aggregate interpretation: negatively charged spider framings co-occurred with uneven use of disciplinary criteria in science-task products. The study contributes to science education by showing why classificatory difficulty should not be read only as missing conceptual knowledge, and by clarifying how affectively salient task contexts may matter for the context-sensitive use of disciplinary criteria in biology learning and teacher mediation.

title: ‘I drew a flower!’ Improving young children’s observational accuracy through inquiry-based drawing
text: This preliminary randomised controlled trial study examined whether a structured drawing intervention, supported by inquiry-based teacher scaffolding, enhances observational accuracy in kindergarten children. Twenty-five K2 children were randomly assigned to an intervention group receiving the inquiry-based drawing intervention or a control group engaging in routine drawing activities. Observational accuracy was assessed via a validated drawing rubric at pre-test, post-test, and a six-month delayed post-test. A planned contrast comparing baseline to the average of post-intervention scores indicated significantly greater overall improvement for the intervention group relative to the control group. Findings provide preliminary empirical evidence that drawing, when coupled with inquiry-based scaffolding, is a promising approach for fostering the foundational scientific skill of observational accuracy in kindergarten settings. Implications, limitations, and future research are discussed.
keywords: observational accuracy, teacher scaffolding, kindergarten children, early childhood science education, observation skills

title: Seeing nature differently: a phenomenographic study on middle school students’ nature-inspired thinking
text: Biomimicry has been recognised as an approach to fostering creativity, sustainability awareness, and interdisciplinary thinking in science education. While it is applied in higher education, research on how younger students conceptualise biomimicry remains limited. This study explored the qualitatively different ways in which middle school students understand inspiration from nature in the context of science education. A phenomenographic research design was employed to capture the variation in students’ conceptions. Data were collected from 280 students (aged 10–14, grades 5–8) attending two public schools (urban and rural) in Türkiye through an open-ended questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The analysis followed a phenomenographic procedure, including open coding, constant comparison, and collaborative validation among researchers. The findings revealed five categories: (1) product-oriented inspiration – comprising (a) Adaptive Inspiration, (b) Inventive Inspiration (with two sub-dimensions: Innovative and Facilitating), and (c) Imitative Inspiration; and non-product orientations, namely (2) Peace and Well-being, (3) Material Resource, (4) Creative Arts; and (5) Learning Resource. The outcome space maps variation in students’ conceptions of nature-inspired thinking – ranging from imitation and adaptation to invention – while capturing non-product meanings of inspiration from nature. The outcome space can inform biomimicry teaching by helping educators address imitation, adaptation, invention, and non-product conceptions.

title: From dual constraints to developmental pathways: a comprehensive study on assessment literacy of high school chemistry teachers in inquiry-based laboratory teaching
text: This study develops the Assessment Literacy Scale for High School Chemistry Teachers in Inquiry-Based Laboratory Teaching (ALS-HSCT-IBLT). The scale comprises a background survey, a five-point Likert scale on assessment philosophy and ethics, and an open-ended scale on assessment practice capability. It measures high school chemistry teachers’ assessment literacy in inquiry-based laboratory teaching. The study was conducted in two phases. In the first phase, the instruments were developed and refined through a pilot test (n = 75). In the second phase, the scales were administered in a formal test (n = 206), which confirmed their reliability and validity. The survey findings reveal that high school chemistry teachers generally exhibit a phenomenon of ‘high conception, low capability’ in IBLTAL. Attribution analysis indicates that this phenomenon arises from deficiencies in teachers’ assessment identity and pedagogical content knowledge in chemistry, coupled with the constraints imposed by the Gaokao-oriented external assessment culture on their professional autonomy. Based on this and the analysis of the impact of demographic variables (e.g. gender, teacher education background, length of service), a ‘pre-service foundation to in-service deepening’ development pathway was established, providing a clear operational framework for systematically enhancing assessment literacy of high school chemistry teachers in inquiry-based laboratory teaching.

title: Uncovering hidden dimensions of meaningful learning in the laboratory
text: Meaningful laboratory learning is a multidimensional process encompassing cognitive, affective, and social dimensions that standardised self-report instruments may only partially capture. This mixed-methods study investigated the laboratory learning experiences of first-year preservice chemistry teachers in the Czech Republic (N = 60), combining a Czech adaptation of the Meaningful Learning in the Laboratory Instrument (MLLI) with a thematic analysis of 16 semi-structured interviews. The Czech MLLI showed acceptable reliability and reproduced structural patterns reported in prior research. Pre–post comparisons indicated a recalibration of students' expectations: affective outcomes improved, whereas cognitive self-assessments declined, suggesting metacognitive adjustment during authentic laboratory engagement rather than diminished learning. Interview data revealed additional dimensions extending beyond the instrument's construct boundaries, including the temporally distributed development of conceptual understanding, the role of social support and instructional guidance, and organisational conditions shaping epistemic engagement. Based on these findings, we propose a Contextually and Temporally Mediated Model of Meaningful Laboratory Learning, which positions cognitive, affective, and conative processes as embedded within social and organisational conditions and subject to metacognitive recalibration over time. The findings provide a more nuanced conceptualisation of meaningful laboratory learning and illustrate the value of mixed-methods approaches in chemistry teacher education.

title: Investigating science teachers’ experiences of generative AI in science teaching and learning from a GenAI-TPACK perspective
text: This study examines how science teachers report using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools in their classrooms. It employs an interpretivist, qualitative design using semi-structured interviews with twenty secondary science teachers (1–11 years’ experience) on temporary leave while enrolled in Master’s courses at a London university, all of whom had had exposure to GenAI while teaching science to school students. Findings reveal that participants reported using GenAI tools to do such things as generate inquiry prompts, scaffold experiments, and create personalised quizzes for science lessons, all aligned with Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) principles. Confidence in GenAI varied: teachers felt more secure using GenAI privately for lesson planning than when using it directly with their students. They were confident about GenAI’s future potential but less so about currently applying GenAI in their classes. Many reported becoming more confident after professional development. Most of the teachers had considerable awareness of ethical issues around GenAI, but they sought clearer guidance on handling these issues in lessons. This research contributes to understanding how teachers can navigate the complex interplay of technology, pedagogy and subject content to foster critical and ethical scientific learning with GenAI.
keywords: generative AI, science teachers, TPACK, secondary science teaching, teacher confidence, professional development, AI ethics in education, lesson planning, technology integration in pedagogy

title: Gendered pathways to STEM identity: comparing the role of stereotypes across science, technology, engineering, and mathematics
text: STEM identity often declines during the middle school years, coinciding with the increased salience of stereotypes about STEM people and careers. Existing research typically examines stereotype–identity relationships within single STEM domains, leaving a limited understanding of how stereotypes operate across different STEM fields and for boys and girls. Addressing this gap is essential for developing more precise models of identity formation. This study investigates how STEM stereotypes predict identity in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics using a mediational framework in which stereotypes influence identity through self-efficacy, interest, and recognition. The participants included 604 middle school students. The study's data were collected with STEM identity and stereotype measures, enabling field-specific structural equation modelling. Results showed that gender-based stereotypes, but not SES-based stereotypes, significantly predicted identity-related outcomes across multiple fields, operating primarily through self-efficacy and its effects on interest and recognition. Indirect pathways varied by gender and domain, demonstrating that stereotype influence is context-specific rather than uniform. Direct effects of stereotypes on identity were generally non-significant, underscoring the mediating role of self-efficacy and recognition processes. Findings highlight the need for targeted, domain-sensitive practices that counter stereotype-linked barriers and strengthen self-efficacy and recognition to support diverse students’ STEM identity development.
keywords: STEM identity, gender stereotypes, junior high school students, self-efficacy, STEM interest, recognition, social class stereotypes, identity construction, science, technology, engineering and mathematics, gender differences

title: Science practical work as a signature pedagogy under threat: an ecological analysis of teacher agency and pedagogical change
text: Practical work is a longstanding feature of school science, yet concerns persist about its effectiveness. This paper explores practical work as a signature pedagogy of science education, examining how teachers achieve agency for its enactment within changing policy contexts. We use reflexive thematic analysis to analyse interviews with 15 highly experienced science teachers. We synthesise Shulman’s concept of signature pedagogy with Priestley et al.’s ecological model of teacher agency to analyse practical work at the level of its surface, deep and implicit structures. Four themes are identified: responses to assessment changes; loss of inquiry learning; learning the deep and implicit structures of practical work pedagogy; and ecological conditions enabling and constraining practical work. Teachers described learning to use practical work effectively through experience, professional dialogue and participation in subject-specific communities, while school contexts shaped their agency to enact these approaches. We argue that because practical work functions as a signature pedagogy, its effective enactment depends on specialised pedagogical knowledge and judgement. Constraints on teacher agency risk eroding the professional knowledge through which its deep and implicit structures are sustained. Supporting teachers’ ecological agency is therefore essential if practical work is to remain a productive feature of science education.

title: From conceptual foundations to enacted PCK: a mixed-methods study with primary teachers teaching the human body
text: Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) represents a core component of teachers’ professional knowledge and one of the strongest predictors of effective science instruction. This study examines how teachers’ Conceptual Knowledge (CK) relates to both their personal and enacted PCK among 13 in-service primary school teachers teaching the human body. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed, combining a CK test, an analytic PCK rubric, and pre- and post-lesson interviews supported by classroom video recordings. Results revealed a low correlation between CK and PCK, suggesting that they are distinct yet interrelated constructs. However, a functional conceptual threshold was identified, beyond which teachers were able to enact more coherent and scientifically grounded PCK. The qualitative analysis uncovered different patterns of CK–PCK articulation, ranging from routine-based strategies to reflective practices aimed at promoting students’ conceptual understanding. These findings reinforce that PCK develops not only through disciplinary mastery but also through sustained reflection and engagement in authentic teaching contexts. Implications are discussed for both preservice and in-service teacher education, highlighting the importance of integrating content learning with didactic analysis experiences that support the development and enactment of PCK across scientific topics and classroom situations.
keywords: pedagogical content knowledge, conceptual knowledge, primary school teachers, human body, science education, teacher reflection, didactic analysis, conceptual understanding, continuing teacher education, initial teacher education

title: Relationship between understanding of the Nature of Science (NOS) and pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) of NOS in a group of biology teachers before and after a professional development programme
text: This study describes changes in the understanding of the Nature of Science (NOS) and Pedagogical Content Knowledge for NOS (PCKNOS) among 15 in-service biology teachers following a professional development programme (PDP). Data on teachers’ understanding of NOS were collected using a modified version of the VNOS D+ questionnaire, which included two additional questions from the VASI questionnaire related to ‘The Scientific Method’. Teachers’ understanding was classified into three levels – Informed, Mixed and Naïve – according to a validated rubric. To obtain data on PCKNOS, semi-structured Content Representation (CoRe) interviews were used. To describe the changes between pre and post, a comparison was made between each teacher’s personal PCKNOS and a collective PCKNOS. Specifically, three criteria were used for the comparison: (a) total map area; (b) map shape and (c) identity of the codes. The results show that teachers’ understanding of NOS improved after the PDP. The development of teachers’ pPCKNOS was reflected in an increase in map area resulting from the inclusion of new concepts related to knowledge of students’ learning (e.g. preconceptions about ‘The scientific method’) and knowledge associated with instructional strategies (e.g. the use of the history of science). Implications for PDPs and the development of teachers’ PCKNOS are discussed.
keywords: nature of science, pedagogical content knowledge, biology teachers, in-service teacher professional development, scientific method, teaching methods, history of science

title: Biology teachers’ personal and enacted pedagogical content knowledge of evolution (PCK EVO ): is classroom practice enough for PCK development?
text: An exploratory study of teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) of evolution, drawing on the Magnusson et al. (1999) and Vergara et al. (2015) models, is presented. To capture PCK of two Chilean female biology teachers, a Content Representation (CoRe) interview was conducted before and after they taught the evolution unit in Grade 9. All lessons in the unit were video recorded and analysed using the PCK rubric. Based on these recordings, specific situations were selected, and video-based reflection provides opportunities for teachers to make their knowledge explicit. All interviews were analysed through qualitative content analysis, using the components of PCK as pre-existing categories. In terms of personal PCK, both teachers recognise the importance of genetics for understanding evolution and the persistence of preconceptions related to evolution by need in students. Regarding enacted PCK, the teacher with lower initial PCK exhibits more pronounced development, whereas the teacher with higher initial PCK experiences a more constrained progression throughout the unit. Reflecting on practice within a structured accompaniment process facilitated the mobilisation of specific PCK’ components; however, this did not lead to uniform effects on the development of their PCK.
keywords: pedagogical content knowledge, evolution education, biology teachers, teacher professional development, video reflection, misconceptions about evolution, initial teacher education

title: Science capital, science identity and economic utility beliefs in core STEM degree choice
text: This study investigates how science-related sociocultural resources, science identity and perceived economic utility are associated with young adults’ transition into core STEM degree programmes in England. Using ASPIRES 3 survey data from undergraduates aged 20–22, the study compares students enrolled in core STEM degrees with peers in non-STEM programmes. Structural equation modelling examined direct and indirect associations among science capital, science identity, economic utility beliefs and core STEM degree enrolment while controlling for demographic and educational variables. The controlled primary model demonstrated excellent fit (CFI = .996, TLI = .992, RMSEA = .039, SRMR = .023). Science identity showed the strongest direct association with core STEM degree enrolment. Science capital showed no significant direct association with enrolment but strongly predicted science identity and had a significant indirect association with enrolment through identity. Economic utility beliefs were differentiated: beliefs about the occupational breadth of science qualifications and the role of science and technology in creating work opportunities were mainly associated with identity, whereas valuing high earnings was directly associated with core STEM degree enrolment. The findings highlight how resources, recognition, identity formation and perceived future value interact in shaping participation in core STEM degree pathways, with implications for science education.
keywords: science capital, science identity, science education, career choice, gender and science

title: Exploring PCK from the perspective of intellectual virtues: pedagogical content intellectual virtues for twenty-first century science education
text: This article contributes to ongoing debates on the relevance of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) in the twenty-first century, in which science, science education and society are constantly evolving. It also addresses long-standing shortcomings of PCK, including limited attention to affective dimensions and concerns about its epistemological clarity. Drawing on philosophy, we propose that virtue epistemology with its concept of intellectual virtues offers a promising way forward. To address the apparent content- and context-specificity of teachers’ intellectual virtues for educational purposes, we introduce the novel concept of Pedagogical Content Intellectual Virtues (PCIVs). We explored the enactment of PCIVs by four science education students who designed contemporary instructional products. Findings suggest that participants demonstrated a range of PCIVs, including intellectual autonomy, carefulness, empathy, and open-mindedness, which appeared to support their instructional design processes. Taken together, the findings indicate that a PCIV perspective can offer additional insight into key aspects of PCK, particularly by highlighting affective, motivational, and judgement-related aspects of teachers’ thinking that are often less visible in existing PCK conceptualisations.
keywords: pedagogical content knowledge, intellectual virtues, virtue epistemology, science teacher education, instructional design, intellectual autonomy, empathy, open-mindedness

title: An integrated STSE–simulation based learning model for enhancing scientific literacy: validation and educational implications
text: Scientific literacy is widely recognised as a fundamental competency that enables individuals to engage with science-related issues in social, technological, and environmental contexts and to make informed, evidence-based decisions. This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated instructional model based on the science, technology, society, and environment (STSE) approach combined with simulation-based learning (SBL) to support scientific literacy. A mixed-methods exploratory sequential design was employed. In the first phase, qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 13 educational stakeholders. The data were analysed using thematic analysis, through which key themes were identified and synthesised into five essential dimensions: learning context, instructional process, media and tools, roles of teachers and students, and assessment and evaluation. In the second phase, quantitative data were collected from science teachers and analysed using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to validate the model. The findings indicated that the proposed model demonstrated excellent fit, confirming its construction validity and reliability. Among the five dimensions, learning context and instructional process emerged as the most influential. These findings suggest that the STSE–SBL model provides a theoretically grounded and empirically validated framework for designing contextualised science instruction aimed at supporting scientific literacy.
keywords: STSE education, science, technology, society and environment, simulation-based training, learning models, scientific literacy, model validation, educational implications

title: The impact of utility value interventions on students’ interest in science education
text: Enhancing students’ interest in science is a central goal of educational research. Utility value interventions, which prompt students to reflect on the personal or societal usefulness of science content, have been widely implemented as a motivational strategy. However, empirical evidence for their impact on interest is mixed. This systematic review synthesises findings from 14 experimental studies conducted between 2009 and 2022, encompassing over 6,000 students across elementary, secondary, and higher education contexts. Results reveal substantial variability. Only three studies report significant positive effects on interest, most find no direct effects, and one documents decreased situational interest among younger students. Effects may further vary according to students’ competence-related beliefs, although the direction of this moderation is inconsistent across studies. Differences in intervention format, autonomy support, educational context, and measurement practices appear to contribute to the observed heterogeneity. Self-generated formats show somewhat more promising patterns than directly communicated approaches, although this comparison rests on few studies and effects remain modest and context-dependent. Overall, the findings challenge assumptions of universal effectiveness and underscore the importance of theoretically grounded design, attention to student characteristics, and methodologically sound measurement in future research on utility value interventions in science education.

title: The role of confidence on long-term conceptual change in biology among secondary school students
text: This study examines how confidence relates to conceptual change and its sustainability in secondary students’ learning of photosynthesis and cellular respiration. Seventy-three Grade 9 students completed a concept test with confidence ratings before, immediately after, and three months after a four-lesson intervention in a botanical garden. Confidence was analysed both as an absolute rating and as a calibration index combining confidence with answer accuracy. The results showed that pre-test confidence alone did not predict conceptual change. By contrast, calibration differentiated three profiles – underconfident, realistically confident, and overconfident – with distinct trajectories. Overconfident students showed little improvement during the intervention. Underconfident students improved the most from pre-test to posttest but regressed at delayed posttest. Realistically confident students improved during the intervention and continued to improve afterwards, showing the most sustainable conceptual change. The findings suggest that, in complex conceptual learning, confidence matters less as a general trait than as a precisely calibrated assessment directly tied to evolving conceptual understanding.

title: Understanding scientific credibility: graduate students’ reasoning about epistemic practices and social certification of scientific knowledge
text: Understanding how scientific knowledge becomes credible is increasingly important in contemporary societies characterised by misinformation and contested knowledge claims. Although research in science education has extensively examined students’ understandings of the nature of science (NOS), less attention has been given to how learners explain the credibility of scientific knowledge, particularly the relationship between epistemic practices and institutional mechanisms. This study investigates how graduate students in science education reason about scientific credibility in response to a historical case. The study involved fourteen graduate students enrolled in science education programs, most of whom were current or former science teachers. The study employed a qualitative design using a contextualised reflection task based on the historical case of Nobel Prize-winning physicist Maria Goeppert Mayer. Participants’ written responses were analyzed using qualitative content analysis within a framework comprising two predefined analytic dimensions: epistemic practices and institutional mechanisms. The analysis revealed two main patterns. Some participants interpreted scientific credibility as emerging from the interaction between epistemic rigour and collective evaluation within scientific communities. Others treated epistemic validity as largely independent from community recognition. These findings suggest challenges in connecting epistemic practices with the institutional mechanisms through which scientific credibility is established, with implications for science education.
keywords: scientific credibility, epistemic practices, graduate students, epistemic trust, peer review

title: Effects of anxiety and enjoyment on engagement and exhaustion among in-service science teachers
text: The main objective was to study the relationships between key motivations for teaching science, emotions, and dimensions of well-being among in-service science teachers, using the Control-Value Theory/ General Theory of Human Emotions. Data from 452 in-service Chilean science teachers, collected via a questionnaire, was analyzed using structural equation modelling (SEM). The findings highlight the strong positive relationship between anxiety and exhaustion, as well as between enjoyment and engagement among in-service science teachers. An important original contribution of this study concerns the mediation of anxiety and enjoyment of science teachers between the four motivations for teaching science (relevance, difficulty, personal efficacy, and outcome expectancy) and engagement of in-service science teachers. Regarding the practical implications, each variable studied should be improved due to its importance for in-service science teachers, and the set of variables should be optimised due to the direct, mediated indirect and total effects among them. In this respect, it is important to highlight how much remains to be done for pre-service and in-service teacher training, where the motivations for teaching science, and especially the emotions and well-being of science teachers, are barely addressed.

title: Exploring the Impact of Artificial Intelligence in Teaching and Learning of Science: A Systematic Review of Empirical Research
text: Abstract The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education is transforming various dimensions of the education system, such as instructional practices, assessment strategies, and administrative processes. It also plays an active role in the progression of science education. This systematic review attempts to render an inherent understanding of the evidence-based interaction between AI and science education. Specifically, this study offers a consolidated analysis of AI’s impact on students’ learning outcomes, contexts of its adoption, students’ and teachers’ perceptions about its use, and the challenges of its use within science education. The present study followed the PRISMA guidelines to review empirical papers published from 2014 to 2023. In total, 74 records met the eligibility for this systematic study. Previous research provides evidence of AI integration into a variety of fields in physical and natural sciences in many countries across the globe. The results revealed that AI-powered tools are integrated into science education to achieve various pedagogical benefits, including enhancing the learning environment, creating quizzes, assessing students’ work, and predicting their academic performance. The findings from this paper have implications for teachers, educational administrators, and policymakers.

title: Translanguaging as Inclusive Pedagogical Practices in English-Medium Instruction Science and Mathematics Classrooms for Linguistically and Culturally Diverse Students
text: Abstract In English-medium instruction (EMI), English-as-a-second-language students will learn all/some subjects through English. Although there are a considerable number of studies which explore classroom interaction in Hong Kong (HK) secondary EMI schools, few studies have investigated EMI lessons which involve South Asian ethnic minorised students. These students share different linguistic and cultural backgrounds and they may not share a common first language with the teacher and other classmates. This study conducts a multimodal conversation analysis of science and mathematics lessons at a HK EMI secondary school, triangulated with interview data, in order to explore how the EMI teacher mobilises various resources to make discipline-specific knowledge accessible and cater for the different needs of all students in the classroom. This study argues that the process of enacting inclusive practices is a process of translanguaging which requires the EMI teacher to mobilise various available multilingual and semiotic resources and draw on what students know collectively for transcending cultural boundaries from the students’ everyday culture to cultures of school science and mathematics.

title: The Efficacy of Inquiry-Based Instruction in Science: a Comparative Analysis of Six Countries Using PISA 2015
text: Abstract This study is a comparative analysis of 15-year-old students’ scientific literacy, and its association with the instructional strategies that students experience, across six OECD countries that participated in PISA 2015. Across the six countries, the study investigates the efficacy of inquiry-based instruction in science in contrast with two other instructional approaches to teaching secondary science: adaptive and teacher-directed teaching. The analysis shows that students who reported experiencing high frequencies of inquiry strategies in their classrooms consistently evidenced lower levels of scientific literacy across the six countries. Benchmark analysis also showed, common to all six countries, a strongly positive association between the frequency of teacher-directed and adaptive teaching strategies and students’ scientific literacy. Additionally, the study disaggregates PISA’s composite variable representing inquiry-based instruction and shows that different components of inquiry are differentially associated with students’ scientific literacy. We discuss the implications of these analyses for science teacher educators, science teachers, and educational policy makers. In doing so, we add nuance to our understanding of the efficacy of inquiry-based instruction in science, suggesting that some components, as conceptualised and assessed in PISA, seem to suggest greater attention and use, and others more moderated use.

title: Interrelationship Between Inquiry-Based Learning and Instructional Quality in Predicting Science Literacy
text: Abstract Recent international comparison studies such as the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) repeatedly argued that inquiry-based learning (IBL) indicated a negative effect on science literacy (SL). However, those studies included two limitations in revealing the relationship between IBL and SL as they did not consider (1) instructional quality and (2) different types of IBL. Accordingly, this study aimed to explore relationships between two types of IBL (open and guided) and SL, and how four types of instructional quality (classroom management, adaptative teaching, teacher–student relationship, and teacher support) moderated the relationships between IBL and SL. For this purpose, a PISA 2015 Finnish sample was used and analyzed by latent moderated structural equation modeling in order to explore the latent interaction between IBL and the quality of instruction. The results of this study presented that the teacher–student relationship was the most potent predictor of SL and moderated the effects of guided and open inquiry on SL. Classroom management also indicated moderation effects for both guided and open inquiry. Also, this study showed the overruling effect of open inquiry on guided inquiry in predicting SL.
keywords: inquiry-based learning, scientific literacy, teaching quality, open inquiry, guided inquiry, teacher-student relationship, classroom management, adaptive instruction, teacher support, moderating effect, PISA 2015, science education

title: Using Local Rural Knowledge to Enhance STEM Learning for Gifted and Talented Students in Australia
text: Abstract In order to supply a future Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) workforce, Australia needs to engage its most capable and gifted secondary students in quality STEM learning, either within school or through extra-curricular opportunities, so that they will continue into STEM-based tertiary degrees. High-achieving students in rural communities may face additional barriers to STEM learning that can limit their ability to pursue advanced STEM studies and occupations. This small-scale research project sought to explore a group of gifted lower secondary students’ engagement and experiences in a STEM programme designed around a local rural knowledge model as reported by Avery (2013), which uses local knowledge as a vehicle for science learning. This multi-method study was conducted with 26 students years 7 and 8 in a rural school. Information about students’ general science class experiences were collected quantitatively. These experiences contrasted the local rural knowledge programme, where the students worked with an ecologist and experienced science educators to rehabilitate small plots of damaged land close to the school site. Qualitative data were collected throughout the programme to determine its influence on students’ engagement and learning in STEM. The research found that the local rural knowledge model enhanced students’ engagement in STEM learning and they felt that they retained knowledge better as a result of the authentic learning experience. Students also engaged the wider community in the process, leading to broader translation of the STEM learning.
keywords: STEM learning, gifted students, rural schools, junior high school students, student engagement, authentic learning, land rehabilitation, community participation, science education, STEM workforce preparation, knowledge retention

title: Pre-service Teachers’ Knowledge and Perceptions of the Impact of Mitigative Climate Actions and Their Willingness to Act
text: Abstract A 44-item questionnaire was created to examine pre-service teachers’ knowledge and perceptions of the impact of mitigative climate change actions and how willing they are to undertake these actions. Responses ( N = 224) were collected from pre-service teachers at the University of Eastern Finland. The findings show that pre-service teachers have a very low level of knowledge of the impact of different mitigative climate change actions. Furthermore, the students tend to overestimate the carbon footprint of low-impact actions and underestimate the carbon footprint of high-impact actions and they are unable to make a clear distinction between low- and high-impact actions, though the impact of the high-impact actions may be many times greater than those of low-impact actions. In general, pre-service teachers were willing to take low-impact actions, somewhat willing to take mid-impact actions, but reluctant to take the highest-impact actions. Knowledge of the impact of actions did not correlate with willingness to act, possibly due to low levels of knowledge. Some correlation between confidence in knowledge and willingness to act was found. This article discusses the importance of considering confidence in knowledge in future research examining the relationship between knowledge and action. The implications of the findings on teacher education and environmental education are also discussed.
keywords: pre-service teachers, climate change mitigation, carbon footprint, willingness to act, knowledge-action gap, knowledge confidence, environmental education, teacher professional development, climate change education

title: Role of Interest and Self-Concept in Predicting Science Aspirations: Gender Study
text: Abstract According to previous theories and studies, interest and self-concept at an early age have played a pivotal role in occupational choices, especially in the fields of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. However, a causal relationship between interest, self-concept, and aspirations in science is still under debate. In addition, few studies have focused on gender differences in these relationships. Therefore, this study aimed to explore the relationships between interest and self-concept in predicting science aspirations between ages 13 and 16 at lower-secondary school, considering gender differences. For the analyses, we conducted cross-lagged modeling and multi-group structural equation modeling in order to examine interrelationships between interest, self-concept, and science aspirations. According to the results, students’ self-concept was high and stable, while interest was low but increased significantly during the lower-secondary school phases. However, there were no reciprocal relationships between interest and self-concept in predicting students’ science aspirations. Interestingly, while girls’ interest was indicated as a sound predictor of aspirations in science, girls’ self-concept had no predictive influence on aspirations. Possible interpretations and implications of the study for lower-secondary science education are discussed.

title: Multimodal Interaction Analysis: a Powerful Tool for Examining Plurilingual Students’ Engagement in Science Practices
text: Abstract Science teaching and learning are discursive practices, yet analysis of these practices has frequently been grounded in theorizations that place language at the forefront of interaction and meaning-making. Such language-centric analytic approaches risk overlooking key embodied, enacted aspects of students’ engagement in science practices. This manuscript presents a case of a plurilingual student’s participation in science inquiry to demonstrate how multimodal interaction analysis can be used to examine the highly diverse array of communicative resources that she draws upon while participating in science, including gestures, facial expressions, vocal intonations, and languages. Grounded in dialogic theorizations of language, we first detail the multimodal interaction approach, and second, we show how multimodal interaction analysis beginning first with her embodied engagement, then coupled with her subsequent written and spoken engagement, reveals robust views of her engagement in science practices. Key to this methodological approach is multilayered analysis that backgrounds verbal or spoken communication to allow for an identification of embodied interaction resources employed. We emphasize how this analytical method allows us to conceptualize science as a practice that unfolds through and in interaction, as compared to a static body of concepts to be learned.
keywords: multimodal interaction analysis, plurilingual students, scientific practice, embodied interaction, gesture, facial expressions, vocal intonation, dialogic theory of language, scientific inquiry

title: Young Students’ Reasoning About Ecosystems: the Role of Systems Thinking, Knowledge, Conceptions, and Representation
text: Abstract Regarding future ecological challenges, it is highly relevant for students to understand the processes within ecosystems and the effects of external influences on their conservation. Since ecosystems are complex, difficulties in learning are often examined from a systems thinking perspective. However, challenges also arise in other areas, particularly in the application of knowledge, conceptions, and exploration of conventionalized representations of ecosystems. Hence, we aim to determine the factors that influence reasoning about ecosystems and how they interact. We conducted a thinking-aloud study with 20 students aged between nine and 12 years while reviewing a food chain ecosystem. Our results indicated that students’ reasoning was based on mixed reasoning originating from their systems thinking skills, knowledge, conceptions, and individual understanding of the ecosystem’s representation. Further, they revealed that students referred to these factors according to the individual cognitive requirements of the systems thinking skills performed and independently of their age and systems thinking abilities. Additionally, students partially demonstrated complex levels of systems thinking, but their assumptions about systems elements and relationships did not support scientific conventions. Our results indicated that systems thinking was largely guided by systems-specific patterns, as basic assumptions about systems elements and relationships played a major role in reasoning about ecosystems at all levels of systems thinking. We assume that identifying systems characteristics with the identified factors of systems-specific knowledge, conceptions, and representations are an effective blueprint for investigating challenging patterns in students’ understanding of ecosystems and advances knowledge on how systems properties influence students’ reasoning during systems thinking.

title: Science Concept Formation During Infancy, Toddlerhood, and Early Childhood: Developing a Scientific Motive Over Time
text: Abstract A substantial number of empirical studies in the field of Early Childhood Science Education have explored science concept formation in early childhood educational settings. Most of these studies focus on the process of science concept formation during a teaching intervention or a school year period. However, less is known about how children form science concepts over the first years of their lives. This longitudinal study aimed at studying the process of science concept formation during the first five years of children’s life within educational settings. Following a cultural–historical approach, the study explored how children develop a science motive from infancy, toddlerhood, and into early childhood and how teachers create the conditions for the development of a motive orientation towards science over time. A cohort of 50 children in Australia participated in the study. Indicative case examples are presented. The research design drew on the Conceptual PlayWorld model, a collective form of practice for learning and development through imagination and play. Digital visual methods were used for data collection and analysis. The findings illustrated that a science motive is developed when the motive of play and the motive of learning in science are dialectically interrelated over time. It was also shown that teachers create a motive orientation towards science by introducing, maintaining, and transforming an ideal form of science in the children’s environment and by stimulating children to interact with mature forms of science. The study concludes with insights into early childhood science education research methodology, and implications that inform practice are discussed.
keywords: science concept formation, early childhood science education, infancy, toddlerhood, early childhood, play and learning, cultural-historical approach

title: Fostering Secondary School Science Students’ Intrinsic Motivation by Inquiry-based Learning
text: Abstract Background Intrinsic motivation plays a unique mediating role in student academic performance. An inquiry-based learning (IBL) physics practical is studied in terms of effects on secondary school students’ intrinsic motivation towards performing science practicals. Results After performing IBL experiments on ionizing radiation, 38 secondary school physics students were interviewed and expressed their need for support in two main areas: the inquiry process and non-salient tasks, i.e., operating the equipment. The IBL experiments were revised accordingly, providing scaffolding through revised worksheets and videos on the use of the equipment. Subsequently, a quasi-experiment was carried out. One experimental group received both a revised worksheet and a video (N = 88), the other only received the worksheet (N = 67). Students performing the same practical on the basis of a step-by-step instruction sheet were used as a control group (N = 87). Five subscales of the intrinsic motivation inventory were used as a pre- and post-test for all three groups. Results show significant gains in the Interest/Enjoyment as well as Effort/Importance subscales favouring both IBL groups. With an instructional video, all five subscales show a significant increase as compared to the control group. Conclusions The results point to the advantages of using an IBL approach for practicals, provided appropriate scaffolding is used in terms of equipment operation and inquiry process.
keywords: intrinsic motivation, inquiry-based learning, physics practicals, secondary school science, scaffolding, educational videos

title: Investigating Relationships Between Learning Environment Perceptions, Motivation and Self-Regulation for Female Science Students in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
text: Abstract The global lack of student motivation towards learning science and gender imbalance in STEM careers provided the impetus for this study, which had two key aims: (1) to examine the influence of female students’ perceptions of the psychosocial learning environment on their motivation towards and self-regulation in science learning,; and (2) to investigate the influence of their reported motivation on their self-regulation of effort. Data were collected from 338 female students in grades 6 to 9 science classes across 16 government schools in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates. Structural equation modelling was used to explore the hypothesised relationships, which indicated that there were statistically significant relationships between learning environment perceptions, motivation and self-regulation. The results provide exigent information to both teachers, policy-makers and researchers with regard to the influences of the psychosocial learning environment on female students’ motivation towards science, as well as the influence of motivation towards science on their self-regulatory behaviour within science classroom settings.
