title: Infusing Medical Ethics into Organic Chemistry Education for Clinical Medicine: A Blended OBE-BOPPPS Approach to Teaching Amino Acids, Peptides, and Proteins
text: Current reforms in medical education call for future physicians who are both scientifically competent and ethically aware. However, foundational chemistry courses often emphasize mechanistic content over the formation of professional values, creating a gap between chemical knowledge and clinical practice for medical students. To address this, we developed and evaluated a blended instructional model for teaching “amino acids, peptides, and proteins” in an organic chemistry course for first-year clinical medicine students. The model integrates an Outcome-Based Education (OBE) approach with the BOPPPS (Bridge-in, Objective, Preassessment, Participatory Learning, Postassessment, Summary) framework and was delivered via a digital learning platform. It incorporates clinical case analyses, molecular visualization, ethical debates, and project-based learning to simultaneously advance students’ conceptual understanding, practical competency, and ethical reasoning. Implementation data show high engagement: 95.2% of students completed online self-study modules and 91.0% actively participated in ethics-focused discussions. Learning gains were significant, with post-test accuracy on protein structure–function relationships improving from 62.4% to 88.7%. Qualitative analysis revealed that 56% of students achieved “Exemplary Integration”, demonstrating clear connections between molecular concepts and ethical considerations. The OBE-BOPPPS model thus offers a structured, replicable strategy for embedding humanistic and ethical dimensions into foundational chemistry instruction, effectively preparing students to become scientifically adept and ethically conscious practitioners.

title: “Error Checking-and-Correcting” Exam Questions Developed for Powder X-ray Diffraction Program: Assessing Critical Thinking and Real-World Application Competence
text: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is one of the most powerful and frequently used methods for phase and structural studies. However, the traditional type of explanation-calculation exam questions developed for the PXRD program is incapable of fully assessing the students’ spectrum of cognitive competence. Here, a new set of “error checking-and-correcting” exam questions was developed for the program. The exam questions aid teachers in assessing the true level of students’ understanding and grasp of basic knowledge and important concepts/theory of PXRD, as well as critical thinking ability to solve real-world problems. The similar philosophy can be used to pedagogically improve the teaching and learning of other characterization methods.

title: Heterogeneous Peroxymonosulfate Activation for Efficient Degradation of Dye Wastewater: A Comprehensive Experiment for Junior Undergraduate Students
text: Effective treatment of organic wastewater is still a challenge, making it a valuable topic for integrating cutting-edge research into undergraduate chemistry education. This 24 h comprehensive experiment is designed to introduce novel water treatment materials and remediation technology to junior undergraduates and first-year graduates. Centered on the pedagogical goals of knowledge mastery, skill development, problem-solving ability improvement, and experimental literacy cultivation, the experiment engages students in a complete research chain: synthesis of Co-doped AgFeO 2 catalysts (AgFe 1– x Co x O 2 ) with variable Co contents, characterization of microscopic morphology, crystal phase and structure, and evaluation of catalytic performance for peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation by monitoring methyl orange (MO) degradation kinetics and mineralization degree. This experiment is highly feasible to replicate, and its uniqueness lies not only in bridging frontier catalysis research with teaching but also in integrating catalyst synthesis, performance testing, and modern instrumental analysis. Effectiveness is validated by objective data from three cohorts (2023–2025, n = 90 students). This cutting-edge teaching module effectively consolidates core knowledge, advances practical skills, nurtures social responsibility, and inspires the engagement of students in contemporary scientific challenges by linking learning to real-world pollution solutions.

title: Synthesis and Applications of Biomass-Derived Carbon Dots
text: At many universities, foundational chemistry laboratories remain dominated by verification-style experiments with limited connection to contemporary research, which can hinder students’ awareness of disciplinary frontiers. Here we report an upper-division undergraduate laboratory module that integrates the green synthesis, characterization, and applications of biomass-derived carbon dots (CDs) into the curriculum. Common cnidium fruit (CCF), an inexpensive and renewable herbal material, serves as a natural carbon and nitrogen source to prepare highly luminescent CDs (CCF-CDs) via a one-step hydrothermal process (160 °C, 4 h), followed by filtration and dialysis. Students observe bright blue fluorescence under 365 nm UV irradiation and relate the optical behavior to surface functional groups and photoluminescence mechanisms. TEM characterization (performed by a departmental technician, with students observing data acquisition) reveals uniform spherical particles (5–7 nm; 5.29 ± 0.22 nm) with a graphite-like core (0.23 nm lattice spacing). Students then evaluate three applications of CCF-CDs: selective fluorescence quenching for Fe 3+ detection against 18 competing metal ions, antibacterial activity toward Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus using plate-count assays, and an anticounterfeiting demonstration using CD-based fluorescent ink on filter paper. The module requires modest instrumentation, provides clear visual outcomes, and supports extensions, such as tuning hydrothermal conditions or designing additional sensing targets. Implementation with ∼200 students (teams of three) showed high attainment of learning objectives (the post-test average score is 95.8%) and strengthened students’ competencies in experimental design, nanoscale materials characterization, and data interpretation. Overall, this sustainable, low-hazard experiment offers a practical pathway for incorporating contemporary nanomaterials into undergraduate chemistry laboratory teaching and serves as a foundational activity within the Undergraduate Innovation and Entrepreneurship Program at the University.

title: A Lego-Built Spectrophotometer: An Accessible and Engaging Tool for Teaching Molecular Absorption Spectroscopy
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Spectrophotometry is a fundamental analytical technique in science education. Commercial instruments are often viewed as “black boxes”, due to their ready-to-use design, limiting student understanding of operational principles. While recently reported three-dimensionally (3D) printed spectrophotometers with smartphone-based detectors offer low-cost, accessible platforms for exploring internal components, their fabrication remains time-intensive. In this paper, we present a Lego-built spectrophotometer that eliminates the need for 3D printing, while enhancing student engagement in the construction process. We provide a comprehensive overview of the design and discuss some of its inherent limitations. Student-performed quantitative analyses of blue food coloring in a sample beverage demonstrated sufficient accuracy and precision compared to those of commercial instruments for analytical applications. Post-laboratory surveys revealed that students found the Lego spectrophotometer to be an effective and engaging pedagogical tool. This work demonstrates that modular construction approaches can provide accessible, educational alternatives to both commercial and 3D-printed instrumentation in undergraduate teaching laboratories.

title: Organic Chemistry in Practice: Student Learning from Wittig and Epoxidation Experiments in a CURE Framework
text: Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in undergraduate teaching laboratories are a growing tool for establishing science retention, confidence, and tolerance for obstacles. However, very few examples demonstrating these results have been reported in primarily undergraduate institutions (PUIs), subject to related limitations of scale and instructor support. This article describes the design and implementation of a CURE for second-semester organic chemistry students, consisting of a multi-week sequence including a Wittig reaction with cinnamaldehyde and subsequent epoxidation of asymmetric diene Wittig products. Students collaborated to collect reaction condition data and were tasked with a presentation at the conclusion of the project, fostering communication and collaboration skills. Students were also asked to provide both quantitative and qualitative feedback. Assessment data indicate gains in student confidence, frustration tolerance, identification of experimental challenges, and presentation skills. This work provides a model for future work adapting the outcomes and goals of a CURE to primarily undergraduate institutions.

title: An Easy, Effective and Dynamical Pedagogical Tool to Learn Chemistry Concepts─Our Kitchen!
text: The conventional way to teach any subject to the students is to give them a lecture, which is generally prepared by reading the books (or net sources). The book is indeed a bridge between a student and a teacher. This teaching–learning process can be made more interactive by using relatable visuals or modules. Linking the complex concepts to real-life experiences made them easier to grasp and understand. This way, not only can the assimilation power of students be increased effectively but also a passion for science can be reignited in the younger generation. Hence, we have proposed a simple, relatable, and cost-effective pedagogical tool, kitchen in our home, to introduce some concepts and apparatus that are used in chemistry laboratories.

title: Sustainable and Cost-Effective 3D-Printed Calorimeters for Undergraduate Laboratory Experiments
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide The widespread use of disposable polystyrene (PS) coffee cups as calorimeters in undergraduate chemistry laboratories for thermochemistry and thermodynamics experiments raises environmental and economic concerns, especially in institutions serving large numbers of students. This study explores the practicability of replacing polystyrene (PS) calorimeters with 3D-printed alternatives fabricated from polylactic acid (PLA) and polypropylene (PP). These materials were chosen for their differing cost, sustainability, and chemical resistance profiles. Calorimetric experiments measuring the heats of dissolution of KBr and Na 2 SO 4, and the heat of neutralization of HCl with NaOH, were conducted using both the conventional PS calorimeters and the 3D-printed calorimeters (PLA and PP). Results showed that the PLA and PP calorimeters provided comparable accuracy, improved precision, and excellent agreement with reported literature values while requiring reduced reagent volumes. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) calculations confirmed no statistically significant differences between all the calorimeters used. The PLA calorimeters were identified as the most sustainable and cost-effective option, demonstrating chemical resilience and reproducibility across repeated use. This work offers a practical roadmap for integrating sustainable practices into chemistry education without compromising experimental quality.

title: Students’ Perceptions of Staple Elements of the Doctoral Program: Research, Courses, Exams, and Seminars
text: For decades, the core elements of doctoral programs (dissertation research, courses, exams, and seminars) have been used to train independent scientists and prepare them for their careers. Despite this, a lack of systematic job outcome data and a saturated academic market have led to sharp criticism from major organizations regarding the effectiveness of these programs. While previous student surveys have shown general satisfaction, they fail to provide insight into the perceived benefits of each individual program element. This study addresses that gap by characterizing student perceptions of these staple elements, which is crucial for evaluating their efficacy and understanding student engagement. We developed a survey based on a prior qualitative study to measure chemistry doctoral students' perceptions of the benefits of four key program components. Distributed to over 6400 students, the survey yielded a final sample of 837 participants for quantitative analysis and a subset for qualitative coding of open-ended comments. Quantitative results revealed few differences in student perceptions across their year in the program, division, or career interest. Qualitative analysis showed that while students acknowledged the potential to gain knowledge and skills, their perceptions were largely influenced by the element's perceived relevance to their careers, the quality of instruction, and, for exams, the mental stress involved. Ultimately, this study found that students expressed general satisfaction with their programs while simultaneously holding cynical views. Their perceptions are narrowly focused on the relevance of each element to their specific research and career goals, reinforcing the critique that doctoral education often prioritizes hyperspecialization (depth) over a broader, more valuable skill set (breadth).

title: Best Practices for Question Prompt Design of Creative Exercise Assessments in a Two-Semester Organic Chemistry Sequence
text: Creative exercises (CEs) are open response-style questions where students must list as many correct, relevant, and distinct statements as they can about a given prompt. In this study, students in a two-semester organic chemistry sequence were given CEs as part of recurring assessments for the course. Student response types were placed into one of three categories – basic, standard, or advanced – based on the extent to which CE statements revealed meaningful concept linking and included deeper explanations. Results show that a majority of students fell into the standard category with limited distribution in the advanced and basic categories. Minimal movement across category types was observed over time. Additionally, analysis of prompt design indicates that asking students to write statements about simple structures were less effective at eliciting detailed statements that reflect concept linking than prompts that asked students to analyze two related structures or synthetic transformations. We also identify the critical role of defining and rigorously evaluating the relevance criterion of CEs in the context of organic chemistry and offer several best practices to guide CE implementation in organic chemistry courses. Overall, creative exercises can be easily implemented into exams across a course sequence, providing instructors with valuable insight and an opportunity to address student misconceptions and knowledge-building in class.

title: An Exploration of Students’ Perceptions of Organic and General Chemistry Laboratories: A Pilot Study
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Previous studies have found that chemistry laboratories can inspire students’ interest in STEM fields but often fall short by focusing on routine procedures and verification exercises. This lack of connection with real-world issues like pollution and sustainability might leave students uninspired and disengaged. This study explores factors influencing undergraduate students’ perceptions of chemistry laboratories, focusing on differences between general chemistry (GChem) and organic chemistry (OChem) courses, gendered experiences, and the alignment of student and teaching assistant (TA) perspectives on student engagement. A mixed-methods approach combined an online survey with interviews. The conveniently sampled survey data from 128 West Virginia University students were analyzed using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, revealing critical factors such as student interest, course content, lab environment, and external contributors. The Mann–Whitney U test compared gender differences and differences between OChem and GChem. Findings show significant differences in course content perceptions ( p < 0.05), with GChem students more likely to see connections between lab and lecture topics. Qualitative results showed that external contributors had a greater influence on both GChem and OChem students, aligning with their career-driven motivations. There was no significant difference in perceptions between males and females ( p = 0.910). TA interviews highlighted the importance of TA communication, cultural background, and students’ preparation levels in shaping lab experiences. This study will inform educators and researchers about key factors such as improving TA communication, connecting lab content with students’ interests, and fostering a more inclusive learning environment. Improving these areas can enhance student motivation, deepen understanding, and cultivate greater interest in STEM fields through chemistry laboratories.

title: Polymer Warriors: A Gamified Virtual-Real Integration Model for Task-Driven Learning in Polymer Chemistry Laboratories
text: Polymer chemistry is a pivotal discipline with widespread applications, necessitating educational approaches that effectively integrate theoretical knowledge with advanced practical and innovative skills. Traditional experimental teaching methodologies, often characterized by prescriptive “recipe-following”, face significant challenges, including reduced student engagement, safety concerns, and limited development of critical thinking abilities. This study addresses these pedagogical challenges by designing, implementing, and evaluating an innovative situational task-driven teaching model that incorporates virtual simulation technology within a polymer chemistry experiment course. The model is framed within an immersive “Polymer Warriors” narrative, integrating game-based elements such as role-playing, a point/level system, and collaborative challenges to enhance the learning experience. A quasi-experimental study involving 140 sophomore materials chemistry students was conducted to investigate three research questions focused on student engagement, skill acquisition, and teamwork development. The results demonstrate that the situational task-driven approach significantly improved the experiment completion rate compared to traditional methods (96.2% vs 77.4%), enhanced student interest (average self-reported score 8.9/10 vs 5.8/10 in the control group), increased practical skill scores (85.4 vs 73.1), and improved perceived teamwork skills (89.7% agreement vs 53.2% in the control group). The “virtual-physical integration” framework provided a safe, immersive environment for skill development and successfully fostered greater cognitive engagement, collaborative problem-solving abilities, and innovative thinking. Detailed assessment data and an implementation guide are provided to facilitate adoption in diverse educational settings.

title: Materials Chemistry Education at an Inflection Point: Integrating Design, Sustainability, and Artificial Intelligence
text: Abstract Materials science and engineering education is at an inflection point. The knowledge and practices that defined the field a generation ago are no longer sufficient preparation for graduates who will work at the intersection of sustainability, computation, and design. Curricula that emphasize foundational mastery without cultivating design literacy, systems thinking, or data fluency risk producing graduates ill-equipped for the challenges ahead. The integration of design thinking, sustainability, and artificial intelligence (AI) into materials education is not a matter of adding new topics to existing courses, but of fundamentally rethinking how the discipline is taught, assessed, and experienced by students. This Special Issue offers a curated snapshot of how the global materials education community is responding to this challenge. The contributions span classroom instruction, laboratory practice, assessment design, and industry engagement, and collectively provide both conceptual frameworks and practical strategies that educators can adapt across a wide range of institutional contexts.

title: Pseudo-Solid-State Bipolar Zn–I 2 Batteries: A Laboratory Experiment for Teaching Ionic Transport and Bipolar Cell Configuration in Advanced Solid-State Batteries
text: The rapid expansion of the battery industry has created an urgent need for graduates equipped with modern knowledge of solid-state battery systems. However, most teaching laboratories still rely on simple liquid-electrolyte cells. Herein, we introduce a three-session (∼13 h) graduate laboratory module based on an accessible Zn–I 2 platform that models key features of solid-state electrolytes and bipolar battery configurations; both are essential for next-generation solid-state battery design. Students begin by synthesizing a pseudo-solid-state single-ion hydrogel electrolyte and comparing its ionic conductivity and cation transference number to those of a traditional liquid electrolyte. These results are then used to introduce Sand’s time analysis for dendrite initiation and to correlate transference number with metal anode deposition morphology. Using the same hydrogel electrolyte, students assemble monopolar, 2-stacked and 3-stacked bipolar Zn–I 2 coin cells, measure open-circuit voltages, perform LED-lighting demonstrations, and conduct galvanostatic cycling to quantify output voltage and energy-density improvements from bipolar stacking. Pre- and postlab exercises, together with detailed safety guidelines reinforce both conceptual understanding and safe experimental practices. These hands-on experiences are expected to help cultivate the skilled workforce needed for emerging solid-state battery industries.

title: GlycUno: A Card Game to Enhance Engagement and Academic Achievement in Glycolysis
text: Understanding glycolysis remains challenging for secondary students due to the complexity of its sequential reactions, enzyme specificity, and representational demands. This work presents Glyc-Uno, a card-based instructional game designed to support mastery of the glycolytic pathway through structured, rule-based sequencing. Using a design and development approach with a one-group pretest–posttest implementation, the game was introduced to 42 Grade 12 STEM students and evaluated by five biology teachers. Teacher ratings confirmed the game’s curricular relevance, organizational clarity, and instructional quality. Students reported high levels of affective, behavioral, cognitive, and sociocultural engagement, while game-experience data indicated moderate challenge and positive affect. Pretest–posttest comparisons showed substantial learning gains (d = 1.89), suggesting that repeated retrieval, enzyme matching, and pathway sequencing during gameplay support conceptual understanding of glycolysis. A significant gender difference in psychological involvement–empathy was also observed, with female learners reporting higher levels of interpersonal engagement. Overall, Glyc-Uno operationalizes biochemical pathway logic within rule-based gameplay, offering a structure-aligned supplementary tool for teaching metabolic pathways. Implications for instruction, along with limitations and directions for future research, are discussed.

title: “ It was a dark and stormy night... ”: The Use of a Crime Story to Apply (Not Only) Introductory NMR Spectroscopy
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Here, the game-based final session of a short course aiming to introduce high school students to NMR spectroscopy is proposed. The intention was to provide a game fiction in the form of a crime story, encouraging students to work in teams, in order to make STEM disciplines more straightforward and playful. The activity consists of 4–6 h of introductory lessons in NMR spectroscopy to help students understand how to interpret the spectra of simple molecules. After that, the crime investigation takes 2 h, and the story is given to the students little by little in the form of a fictional newspaper text. The chain of events, the clues, and methods used during the scientific investigation will reveal the identity of the culprit. The story can be modified by the instructor to be used to introduce the students to other analytical techniques. title: A WebApp for Digitalized Exploration of Binary Vapor–Liquid Equilibria and Distillation
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide The understanding of vapor–liquid equilibrium (VLE) is of great importance as it provides data and theoretical support for applications in chemical and environmental engineering. Undergraduates in Chemistry and Chemical Engineering are expected to be capable of understanding, drawing and applying VLE phase diagrams. In this paper, we built theoretical models for VLE calculations and distillation column design for binary systems. VLE theory (Raoult’s Law), activity models, and Antoine equations were used, with parameters from literature. Using technology frameworks react.js and d3.js, we developed an interactive and user-friendly WebApp for students to explore VLE and distillation. This WebApp covers typical binary systems and visualizes the results as graphs, tables, and animated cartoons as users play with the system and operating parameters. Our intention with implementing this WebApp is that, through deepened and broadened explorations, students will enhance their understanding in VLE knowledge and will be able to learn in their own way and pace individually; however, the effectiveness should be studied through rigorous education research.

title: Developing a Culture of Laboratory Safety in Undergraduate Chemistry Programs: A Case-Based Educational Intervention in Emerging Departments
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Promoting laboratory safety awareness is a key educational objective in undergraduate chemistry programs, particularly within newly established departments where safety cultures are still emerging. This study presents a structured, educationally driven assessment of laboratory safety knowledge and behavior among students in the Department of Chemistry at Democritus University of Thrace, Greece. The methodology involved the design and administration of a standardized questionnaire incorporating demographic variables, Likert-scale assessments of safety attitudes, and knowledge-based questions aligned with the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labeling of Chemicals (GHS). The results were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to evaluate the impact of gender, academic year, and lifestyle factors on safety awareness. The findings revealed critical gaps in hazard symbol recognition─especially regarding fire-related risks─and highlighted the influence of student demographics on preparedness and adherence to personal protective measures. These outcomes underscore the educational importance of early, structured safety training integrated into the chemistry curriculum. The study advocates for institutional investment in ongoing safety education, modern infrastructure, and the establishment of dedicated safety oversight structures in academic environments.

title: Preparation and Properties of Virus-Like Nano-Photothermal Agents: AI-Enabled Innovative Experiment for Undergraduates
text: In this study, an innovative experiment for undergraduates was designed. Inspired by the efficient cellular entry mechanism of viruses, a virus-like nanophotothermal agent (AuNS@CuS) was constructed. This agent is composed of a gold nanostars (AuNS) core, which mimics viral surface protrusions, and a functional shell of in-situ-grown copper sulfide quantum dots (CuS QDs). Its morphology, physicochemical properties, and photothermal conversion performance were systematically studied. The experiment integrates material synthesis, characterization and performance testing. The operation is safe and controllable, and the results are intuitive and significant. It not only cultivates students’ abilities in material preparation, performance characterization, and data analysis but also effectively fosters their understanding of nanotechnology, interdisciplinary application skills, and innovative practical capabilities. The experimental process deeply integrates artificial intelligence (AI) technology, including the use of AI for literature research and analysis, experimental feed prediction, and mechanism exploration and scheme optimization of growth anomalies. The results show that the AI-assisted preparation of the virus-like nanophotothermal agent AuNS@CuS endows it with excellent near-infrared (NIR) photothermal conversion performance, good photothermal stability, and efficient cell uptake capability due to its virus-like structure, providing a new strategy for tumor photothermal therapy. This experimental design provides an interdisciplinary scientific research practice platform for undergraduates, effectively cultivates students’ interdisciplinary thinking and AI-enabled scientific research ability, and improves students’ cognition and application ability of the combination of nanomaterial preparation and AI technology.

title: From Lunar Soil to Lunar City: An Interdisciplinary Project-Based Learning Module on In-Situ Resource Utilization for High School Chemistry
text: The critical need for lunar in situ resource utilization (ISRU) to enable long-term lunar habitation provides a compelling context in chemistry education. This paper introduces “Simulating the Construction of a Lunar Base”, a Project-Based Learning (PBL) module for high school chemistry. Students, acting as “Lunar Engineers and Geochemists”, apply core chemical principles to the design and construction of a lunar base. A key feature of this module is the rigorous integration of core chemical principles─including redox reactions, chemical equilibrium, and nuclear chemistry─into a comprehensive, open-ended design challenge. The activities encompass model-based lunar resource exploration, chemical feasibility analyses of nonmetal resources such as silicon (for photovoltaics), water (for life support and fuel), and helium-3 (for nuclear fusion), and a hands-on experiment simulating the extraction of titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) from ilmenite (FeTiO 3 ). This approach fosters interdisciplinary thinking by connecting chemistry to engineering, geology, physics, and environmental science. The project cultivates students’ innovative abilities, systems thinking, and sustainable development awareness. Its effectiveness was validated through a qualitative analysis of student design proposals by using a specially developed performance assessment framework.

title: Teaching Quantum Dot Size Estimation Using Smartphone-Based Image Analysis
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Quantum dots (QDs) are semiconductor nanocrystals whose size-dependent optoelectronic properties make them an effective platform for introducing nanoscale concepts in chemistry education. However, direct QD size characterization typically relies on advanced instrumentation that is rarely available in teaching laboratories. This work presents an accessible educational activity for estimating QD size using digital images, including those acquired with a smartphone, are analyzed using a standalone software application executed on Windows or Linux systems to estimate emission wavelength and quantum dot size. The application extracts RGB values from digital images, converts them into approximate emission wavelengths, and estimates QD size using a simplified physical model based on the Brus equation. Although CdTe quantum dots are used as an illustrative example, the software has been expanded to accommodate different quantum dot materials for instructional use. The activity was implemented with 23 undergraduate students from a nontechnical program using a pretest and post-test design. Results indicate learning gains in students’ conceptual understanding of the relationship between QD size, emission wavelength, and band gap energy, along with increased awareness of approximation and model limitations. Overall, this contribution demonstrates how low-cost digital tools can support meaningful engagement with nanoscience concepts in chemistry education.

title: Design of a Safe and Sustainable Laboratory Exercise: Simulation of a Mercury Spill and Effective Disposal Method for Chemical Safety Education Using a Mercury Spill Kit
text: This study presents a novel and safe laboratory exercise designed to actively involve students in simulating and managing a mercury spill without the toxic risks associated with elemental mercury. Addressing the limitations of passive multimedia demonstrations, this hands-on approach uses silver-colored plastic beads as a nonhazardous visual surrogate for illustrating dispersed droplets or particles during a simulated spill scenario. Students engage directly in containment and cleanup procedures using a commercially available Chemizorb Hg Mercury Absorbent Kit, learning standardized protocols for spill response, neutralization, and waste handling. Through multiple pilot sessions and outreach implementations, the 15–20 min protocol demonstrated high procedural fidelity (up to 95%), improved efficiency (25% reduction in completion time), strong knowledge retention (92% correct 1 week after training), and robust transfer-readiness for understanding professional spill-response procedures. By combining tactile simulation with authentic spill-response tools, this exercise promotes active learning, procedural memory, and risk awareness, supporting practical training in chemical safety and laboratory spill-response procedures. This easily replicable model offers educators an accessible way to teach chemical safety and toxicology while fostering critical thinking and environmental responsibility across diverse educational contexts.

title: OrgaChem Deck: An Educational Card Game for Learning Fundamental Organic Reactions
text: To address the challenges of learning organic reactions, which can be tedious and difficult to apply flexibly, this study designed a card-based teaching game called “OrgaChem Deck.” The core of the game lies in simulating the logical reasoning process of organic synthesis through a card system that includes group cards and substance cards. It guides learners to actively combine cards in a competitive setting to understand and apply organic reactions, thereby transforming fragmented knowledge into dynamic connections. Teaching practice has shown that participating students not only deepened their understanding of reaction principles through the game but also experienced a significant increase in learning interest and classroom engagement. According to student feedback, the game has been widely recognized for promoting knowledge integration, cultivating strategic thinking, and enhancing the learning experience, providing an effective complement to traditional teaching methods.

title: Releasing the Full Potential of Videos in Chemistry Teaching: The DAC Method
text: Instructional videos are widely used in chemistry classrooms, yet their impact often remains limited if student engagement is passive. This article introduces the DAC method (Decide–Analyze–Commit), an evidence-informed framework designed to maximize the pedagogical value of video-based learning. The method structures student activity before, during, and after video viewing, incorporating prediction, evaluation of statements, and reflection. A model worksheet and classroom implementation are presented, demonstrating how this approach aligns with Johnstone’s triangle and facilitates the integration of macroscopic, submicroscopic, and symbolic representations. Additionally, survey results from chemistry teachers ( N = 94) who piloted the DAC method reveal teachers’ perceptions of its potential to foster critical thinking, learner autonomy, and engagement. While challenges such as cognitive load and the risk of misconceptions were noted, overall teacher responses indicated strong support for the relevance and usability of the method. The DAC method provides chemistry educators with a practical, adaptable strategy for integrating videos into lessons, thereby promoting active learning and strengthening key study skills (focusing on key points, assessment of truthfulness and argumentation for or against it, and critical thinking).

title: From Plant to Practice: Exploring Justicia spicigera as a Natural pH Indicator in Chemistry Education
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Chemistry education seeks materials for inspiring students for deep analysis to reinforce fundamental concepts. This study explores the potential of Justicia spicigera (commonly known as muicle), a plant traditionally used in Mexican herbal medicine and known for its intense pigmentation, as a low-cost, natural acid–base indicator. A chlorophyll-diminished aqueous extract of J. spicigera (CDE) was prepared and characterized spectrophotometrically within a pH range of 2–10. The extract exhibited a distinct color change from orange to purple in the pH range of 3.5–5.5, consistent with the behavior of anthocyanin-based indicators. The apparent dissociation constant (p K In, app ) was 5.6 ± 0.2. Eighteen undergraduate students successfully used this natural extract as an indicator in an acid–base titration of sodium bicarbonate with hydrochloric acid. The students used JAMOVI software to statistically analyze the experimental data to analyze the performance of the indicator. The natural and synthetic indicators exhibited comparable precision and accuracy within the studied experimental context. Furthermore, the natural indicator provided distinct and consistent color transition at the titration end point, confirming its suitability for analytical applications. The proposed activity promoted green chemistry principles and student engagement and highlighted the cultural and scientific value of traditional plants while developing essential data analysis skills.

title: Science Outreach: Providing an Authentic Independent Research Opportunity in Materials Science to School Students
text: Through the emerging field of bio-nanotechnology, students from UK high schools were provided with an opportunity to explore the use of DNA as a self-assembly building material to create unique DNA origami designs and evaluate these using web-based software. The project helped widen awareness of the cutting-edge research within materials science, enabled the participants to work with a high degree of independence, and reinforced the practical techniques required to synthesize a predesigned origami structure at school. This article describes the results of a study of this long-term, student-led independent research project. We collected data from 51 young people aged 16-19 engaged in the project using group interviews and found authentic research experiences can foster greater personal autonomy, sustain engagement, and be used to improve the perception of subjects such as materials science. The project also gave participants a greater understanding of the broader scene relating to careers within STEM and research as well as improved research skills through thinking and acting like a researcher.

title: Visualization of the Effects of Hydrogen Bonding in Self-Healing Hydrogel
text: The research develops an instrument-free classroom demonstration using a self-healing hydrogel to visualize hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) interactions. Students directly experience the re-formation and breaking of H-bonds through cutting and stretching cycles, thereby gaining an intuitive sense of their tangible strength. Tailored for different educational levels, high school students grasp H-bond formation through autonomous self-healing, while university students connect fundamental chemistry to polymer science via macroscopic evidence. Student feedback from classroom implementation with over 2000 high school students indicated notable differences in self-reported understanding: the proportion of students who reported correctly identifying H-bonds as interaction forces was 91.7% in the demonstration group, compared to 50.3% in traditional lecture settings. This work provides educators with an accessible platform to bridge macroscopic phenomena and molecular interactions, achieving visualization without expensive instruments.

title: A Multifaceted Lesson on TEM, Image Analysis, and Emerging Concerns in Image Manipulation
text: We present a low-cost, hands-on activity to introduce undergraduate students to image interpretation, digital image analysis, and current ethical issues around data bearing images in the literature. Here, a flatbed scanner was utilized to prepare “pseudo-TEM” images that emulated the properties of TEM micrographs. These were used for a series of image analysis activities incorporating ImageJ. Then, students were engaged in a discussion about image manipulation and scientific fraud. Students further engaged with their skills of image interpretation by identifying image manipulations in known cases of image fraud. Due to the use of alternative resources, this activity was low-cost and did not require any specialized equipment or materials. Student responses to the activities were generally positive and students demonstrated mild learning gains.

title: Exploring Intercalation Chemistry of Graphite Negative Electrode in Lithium-Ion Batteries under Various Electrolytes: A Comprehensive Experiment for Undergraduates Based on X-ray Diffraction Characterization
text: To stimulate students’ research interest, cultivate their innovative abilities and enhance their data analysis skills, a comprehensive three-week experiment based on X-ray diffraction (XRD) is designed by integrating instrumental analysis chemistry course content with frontiers of scientific research. In lithium-ion batteries, the structural integrity of the graphite negative electrode determines the reversibility of lithium-ion batteries. Structural damage caused by solvent cointercalation leads to rapid capacity loss of battery. In this advanced independent comprehensive experiment, XRD is used to investigate and assess the impact of electrolytes on solvent cointercalation into graphite electrodes by analyzing the structural changes of graphite electrodes before and after charge–discharge cycles in three representative electrolyte systems. This course not only deepens students’ understanding of XRD instrument and improves their XRD data analysis capabilities but also enables them to acquire fundamental principles underlying secondary battery technologies, thereby promoting knowledge acquisition, skill development, and innovative thinking.

title: From Star Anise Oil to (3+2) 1,3-Dipolar Cycloaddition Reactions: A Comprehensive Approach to the Extraction, Characterization, and Application of trans -Anethole with a Focus on Experimental Chemistry Education
text: This work describes an integrated undergraduate laboratory sequence combining essential oil extraction, spectroscopic characterization, and the synthetic application of trans -anethole in a (3+2) 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition reaction. These experiments involved three key steps: extraction, synthesis, and spectroscopic characterization. They were specifically designed for students studying Chemistry, Pharmacy, and Chemical and Food Engineering. To facilitate learning, the experiments were organized into two separate phases, allowing students to focus on each stage carefully and build a solid understanding of the processes involved. The first phase involved the extraction of star anise oil from star anise ( Illicium verum Hook.f.) fruits, followed by the comprehensive characterization of the oil obtained, which is predominantly composed of trans -anethole. The second phase consisted of organic synthesis experiments using trans-anethole as the starting material for the preparation of 3,5-diarylisoxazolines through a (3+2) 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition reaction. In both phases, routine laboratory techniques were employed, together with full structural characterization by proton and carbon-13 nuclear magnetic resonance ( 1 H and 13 C NMR) spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). In addition, SC-XRD analysis was performed on the final cycloadduct, with single crystals isolated for further structural analysis. The project can also be carried out in separate parts, with one focusing solely on the extraction process and the other exclusively on the synthesis process. In both cases, the laboratory procedures and spectroscopic characterization requirements are fulfilled.

title: Analysis of Vocational Education Content in High School Chemistry Textbooks in Mainland China
text: Implementing vocational education at the secondary school helps awaken students’ career awareness early and lays the groundwork for their future career development. Unlike other countries or regions that deliver vocational education through courses or programs, integrating vocational education content into high school chemistry textbooks and embedding it within subject-based curricula is a distinctive feature of vocational education in mainland China. Based on existing research, an analytical framework was developed to examine the ways and features of this integration, and interviews were conducted with textbook writers. The study found that adding a “Chemistry and Careers” section serves as the primary way of integration. This section highlights vocational education content, aligns with the textbook’s overall structure, and expands career knowledge. The content is presented in an engaging format that combines text and visuals, while the use of third-person narration enhances objectivity. The selection of career reflects a careful integration of career directories and curriculum content, with the introduction of career information taking into account factors such as information volume, depth, and student familiarity. This study provides new perspectives and insights for international chemistry curriculum developers and textbook writers in integrating vocational education content into chemistry courses and textbooks.

title: Addressing Basic Psychological Needs in a Pre-Scientific Initiation Program in Chemistry: A Triangulated Analysis in Light of Self-Determination Theory
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Motivation to learn chemistry depends not only on cognitive factors but also on the satisfaction of basic psychological needs, as proposed by the Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Despite evidence on the motivational role of inquiry practices, there are still gaps to be filled when it comes to understanding how Prescientific Initiation Programs meet these needs in basic education. This study investigated how participation in a Prescientific Initiation Program, linked to a Chemistry department, contributes to the satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness (bonding) among high school students, in light of the SDT. The study was carried out using a convergent mixed-methods design approach; the approach involved the conduct of 13 interviews with students, 5 interviews with supervising teachers, and a questionnaire administered to 15 students, analyzed using the Basic Psychological Needs at Work Scale (BPNWS) database. The interviews were examined by using content analysis, and the quantitative data collected were treated by using descriptive statistics. The results suggest high perceived satisfaction with autonomy (mean = 4.38) and competence (mean = 4.40), reinforced by reports of freedom of choice, responsibility, and the development of scientific skills. Relatedness presented greater variability (M = 3.87), reflecting differences in the consistency of the social support. The findings indicate that participants perceived the program as supporting self-determined motivation, engagement, and strengthening of scientific identity. The study suggests the implementation of practices and actions geared toward improving social integration and encouraging the expansion of similar programs in chemistry education. Future research should employ larger sample sizes and longitudinal analyses in order to obtain more comprehensive results.

title: Solid-Phase Synthesis of an Ultrafine Intermetallic Electrocatalyst for Hydrogen Evolution: A Comprehensive Laboratory Experiment for Undergraduates
text: With the continuous rapid development of materials science, integrating innovative synthesis strategies into undergraduate experimental courses is crucial for bridging fundamental knowledge with cutting-edge research. This study proposes a comprehensive experimental scheme for undergraduates, focusing on the solid-phase synthesis of ultrafine intermetallic compounds within a mesoporous carbon matrix. Students will synthesize nanoscale intermetallic compounds through confined solid-state reactions and use physicochemical characterization techniques to elucidate their atomic structures. This experiment demonstrates the nanoconfinement effects in mesoporous materials and explores their impact on the structural properties of the synthesized compounds. The interdisciplinary experiment covers key concepts such as solid-state synthesis, structural characterization, properties of mesoporous materials, and laboratory safety, integrating core principles from inorganic, physical, and materials chemistry. Through participation, undergraduate students will gain hands-on experience in advanced nanomaterial synthesis, develop a deeper understanding of how confined environments regulate material properties, enhance their experimental and scientific analytical skills, and foster an interest in frontier research in materials science.

title: A Critical Review of Green Chemistry Integration in Vocational Education: Theoretical Frameworks and Pedagogical Strategies
text: Green chemistry education has focused almost exclusively on university scientists, leaving technicians in Vocational Education and Training (VET) largely unsupported. To map this specific sector, we utilized PRISMA guidelines to screen and analyze 80 documents addressing sustainability in trade-level curricula. The results show a fragmented picture. Unlike undergraduate courses, VET instruction still focuses heavily on “end-of-pipe” compliance, such as disposing of hazardous waste, rather than preventing pollution at the source. We define this persistent gap between industrial needs and educational output as the “vocational lag”. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework that integrates Systems Thinking with Work-Integrated Learning (WIL). This approach transforms standard safety protocols into pedagogical tools for developing “Middle-Level Green Competence”. This review offers a roadmap for aligning vocational training with the chemical industry’s sustainable transformation.

title: Effects of a Single-Session Study Skills Workshop on Exam Performance in General Chemistry Courses
text: First-year college students in general chemistry and other introductory STEM courses often lack knowledge of effective study strategies and skills to apply them. In this study, the impact of a one-time, 90 min study skills workshop delivered by the course instructor following the first exam in General Chemistry 1 was evaluated across three cohorts of students (three separate years/six academic semesters, extending into General Chemistry 2). Students choosing to attend the workshop were compared to students who did not attend. The workshop featured instruction on evidence-based learning strategies, mindset, and time management, along with reflection on exam performance by students leading to the formulation of study plans shared with others. Results suggested that, after controlling for lower performance on the first course exam in General Chemistry 1, workshop attendees outperformed nonattendees on all subsequent exams, extending into a General Chemistry 2 course. Further, when comparing a matched group of students based on initial exam performance, workshop attendees outperformed nonattendees on the remainder of exams in General Chemistry 1 and General Chemistry 2. We discuss possible explanations for the lasting effects of the intervention, implications for introductory STEM course instructors, and directions for future work to explore.

title: Copper Analysis by Ion Exchange and Acid Base Weight Titration

title: Nanoparticle Analysis, from Standards to Sunscreens: Teaching Graduate Students Single-Particle ICP-TOFMS through a Hands-On Laboratory Course
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (sp-ICP-MS) enables the characterization of individual nanoparticles (NPs) on a particle-by-particle basis and represents a major advance in analytical chemistry. Time-of-Flight mass analyzers (TOFMS) have emerged as a powerful platform for single-particle analysis thanks to their fast acquisition rates and simultaneous multielement detection capability. Despite its growing relevance and use in environmental and material sciences, sp-ICP-MS is rarely included in graduate teaching laboratories. This advanced lab course introduces students to the principles, operation, and data analysis of sp-ICP-MS and ICP-TOFMS through a combination of theory and hands-on experiments. First, commercially available monodisperse spherical Au and Ag NPs are analyzed so that students become familiar with the fundamental principles of sp-ICP-TOFMS, including transient signal acquisition, calibration, and particle event interpretation. Then the students apply the same workflow to consumer products using sunscreens and cosmetics to detect and quantify titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) NPs. Through these experiments, students strengthen their understanding of plasma-based mass spectrometry, quantitative data evaluation, and NPs characterization in complex matrices. This laboratory class bridges classical ICP-MS education with modern single-particle analysis, providing students with practical experience in advanced mass spectrometry.

title: Opportunities and Limitations of AI Voice Synthesis in Chemistry Teaching

title: Enhancing Student Understanding of Polymer Processing through a Multi-module Laboratory Course: Bridging Simulation and Practice
text: Polymer processing and characterization are core components of materials science and chemical engineering curricula, yet undergraduate students often encounter these topics only through theoretical instruction, computer-based simulations, and isolated polymer-related experiments. This experience limits their ability to fully appreciate the relationships between polymer structure, processing conditions, and material properties. To address this gap, a multimodule laboratory course was developed that introduces students to polymer synthesis, thermal behavior, and mechanical testing through three interconnected experiments: (i) gel time determination of reacting thermosetting resins, (ii) glass transition temperature analysis of common polymers using differential scanning calorimetry, and (iii) specimen fabrication via injection molding followed by mechanical property evaluation using a universal testing machine. Each module was designed to complement students’ prior theoretical knowledge while emphasizing practical laboratory techniques and data interpretation. Student engagement with these modules fostered deeper comprehension of polymer chemistry and processing, while also strengthening critical skills such as experimental design, data analysis, and technical reporting. This work demonstrates an effective framework for bridging the gap between simulation-based learning and experimental practice, thereby enhancing undergraduate education in polymer science and engineering.

title: Student Perceptions of Diverse Assessment Methods in a Second-Year Organic Chemistry Laboratory
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Undergraduate laboratory courses use multiple assessment formats to evidence conceptual understanding, practical skills, safety, and communication, but research rarely examines how students experience several methods used together in one course. This study investigated second-year chemistry students’ perceptions of multiple assessment formats in a compulsory organic laboratory course, including laboratory reports, video presentations, postlaboratory quizzes, laboratory notebooks, risk assessments, and formative peer- and self-assessment. An anonymous online survey ( n = 65 of N = 130 enrolled students) collected Likert-type ratings and free-text comments on eight assessment formats. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively to compare ratings for each format, and qualitative data were analyzed thematically to characterize perceived benefits and challenges. Students attributed different strengths to different formats: laboratory reports were most frequently described as deepening understanding, video presentations as developing concise communication, postlaboratory quizzes as reinforcing key ideas with rapid feedback, and laboratory notebooks and risk assessments as supporting good laboratory practice and safety awareness. Students distinguished between feeling comfortable with a format and viewing it as valuable for learning, with some assessments described as demanding yet worthwhile. Within this course context, the findings suggest that combining complementary assessment types can support a broad range of laboratory learning goals when workload, timing, and feedback are carefully managed.

title: A Virtual Reality Platform for Molecular Visualization in Undergraduate Chemistry
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Many chemistry concepts require students to interpret three-dimensional structures from their two-dimensional representations. To support molecular visualization, a modular, gallery-style virtual reality (VR) platform was developed for undergraduate organic and inorganic chemistry courses. Built-in Unity and deployed on standalone headsets, the application allows students to interact with 3D molecular models through grabbing, rotation, and scaling. The platform is adaptable to multiple chemical topics and scalable for single- or multiple-headset classroom implementation. An exploratory mixed-methods approach was used to understand student perceptions via pre/post surveys, content-specific surveys, and semistructured interviews. title: Beyond the Ideal Gas Behavior: Using a Sampling Valve to Determine the Fugacity of CO 2
text: The aim of this laboratory activity is to provide students with a practical understanding of the concept of fugacity through a hands-on learning approach. Rather than using the traditional method of calculating the gas fugacity by employing a parametrized equation of state in the classroom, we propose an alternative and more realistic strategy. This approach involves measuring the compressibility factor of a gas and using the results to evaluate its fugacity as well as its second virial coefficient. While this method can be used to analyze other gases, the present study focuses on determining the fugacity of CO 2 as a function of pressure and temperature in conditions where the system’s nonideality is significant. The apparatus employed in the measurement is a highly simplified and safer variation of previous implementations. A sampling loop connected to a six-port injector, as those used in the field of HPLC chromatography, eliminates any possibility of sudden discharge of large amounts of gas, and hence a risk of explosion, due to incorrect valve operation.

title: Enhancing High School Students’ Spatial Thinking in Organic Chemistry through Digital Molecular Visualization (KingDrawHD)
text: In today’s evolving educational landscape, digital tools offer new opportunities to support learners in subjects such as organic chemistry that rely heavily on visualization. This study examines the effectiveness of integrating KingDrawHD, a digital molecular visualization application, into the teaching of organic chemistry to improve grade 11 students’ spatial thinking skills. This research is important given the significant role of spatial thinking in interpreting the molecular structures that are central to organic chemistry. A quasi-experimental design was implemented with two groups: an experimental group receiving instruction supported by KingDrawHD and a control group receiving instruction without digital molecular visualization-based support. A validated 20-item Spatial Thinking Scale was administered pre- and postintervention. Pretest results showed no significant differences between groups (t = 0.782, p = 0.437), confirming baseline equivalence, while post-test results indicated a statistically significant improvement for the experimental group (t = 4.374, p < 0.01). The effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.962) reflected a large impact, demonstrating that the use of KingDrawHD was effective in enhancing students’ spatial reasoning within the context of organic chemistry instruction. While the findings highlight the potential of interactive visualization tools to support spatial skill development, an ability theoretically linked to understanding complex molecular structures, they do not provide evidence for gains in chemistry learning itself, which was beyond the scope of this study. The results contribute to ongoing discussions in technology-enhanced STEM education and suggest that targeted digital applications can play a meaningful role in strengthening foundational cognitive skills needed for STEM learning.

title: A Comparative Aldol and Benzoin Reaction Design for the Undergraduate Organic Laboratory
text: The aldol reaction and benzoin reaction are fundamental nucleophilic additions of the carbonyl group in the undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory. We herein describe a parallel experimental design combining the two reactions into one experiment, in which the same reactant under different reaction conditions bifurcates into aldol and benzoin products. The notable improvement to current independent practice saves time and expense at the undergraduate level. The learning objectives also encompass a range of basic synthetic techniques that enable undergraduate students to master the setup and workup procedures of organic reactions. Reagents and equipment required in the experiment are adaptable and feasible at different colleges and universities. The comparative design makes notable updates to current organic laboratory curricula, providing pedagogical value in head-to-head learning of the reaction mechanism and hands-on experience. It also advances learning to a wide range of fundamental topics in organic chemistry studies such as heterocycles and umpolung.

title: Bringing Chemical Kinetics to Life: A Week-Long Mini-Unit of Classroom Activities for High School Students
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Chemical kinetics remains a conceptually and mathematically demanding topic for many high-school and undergraduate chemistry students. This paper presents a weeklong, inquiry-based instructional unit designed to build conceptual understanding of reaction rates without relying heavily on mathematical instruction. Implemented in a diverse Title IX high school setting, the activity sequence included visually rich, hands-on experiences such as a marble-based collision theory simulation, a fruit ripening investigation, and a catalyzed milk curdled experiment. These activities were scaffolded with guided discussions and kinesthetic modeling to support key kinetic concepts. Pre- and postassessments revealed significant learning gains across all targeted concepts, with average scores increasing from 1.7 to 7.7 out of 10, and over 89% of students demonstrating proficiency by the end of the unit. Anecdotal observations also indicated heightened student engagement and conceptual buy-in. The described approach offers a low-cost, adaptable model for teaching the kinetics conceptually and experientially, with potential for extension to diverse student populations and instructional settings.

title: Using Multivariate Image Analysis to Teach Chemometrics through Antioxidant Capacity Determination of Honey Samples: A Grounded Theory Analysis
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide The teaching of chemistry mediated by digital technologies favors the formation of critical and autonomous students, but there are still no laboratory activities that integrate data acquisition through digital images and partial least-squares (PLS) regression analysis. This study evaluated the contributions of using RedGIM as a technological resource for the construction of chemical knowledge in students of the subjects digital technologies for chemistry teaching and general experimental chemistry 1, in undergraduate chemistry courses at Federal University of Espírito Santo (UFES). To this end, the theoretical-methodological strategy of problematized experimental activity (PEA) was adopted. This approach included the determination of the antioxidant capacity of honey samples from stingless and stinging bees using the FRAP (ferric reducing antioxidant power) method associated with UV–vis spectrophotometry. In parallel, digital images of the samples were recorded and processed in RedGIM, and the data were modeled using PLS. Learning was analyzed based on the experimental execution, the processing of data in spreadsheets, and the socialization and interpretation of results on a digital board (Padlet). At the end of the PEA methodological process, the analytical process followed the grounded theory (GT) model. According to the substantive theory developed, the use of RedGIM as a resource for teaching chemistry within the PEA structure effectively contributed to the development of chemical knowledge and to the interpretation of multivariate data. Evidence of this contribution was observed in students’ written responses and in their final products. The data showed that the proposal enabled the integration of chemical and digital concepts at different levels of complexity, promoting meaningful learning and demonstrating pedagogical applicability in higher education in chemistry.

title: Enhancing STEM Learning with Adaptable Virtual XRD Laboratories
text: Cloud-based virtual laboratories and digital twins of physical equipment have gained significant popularity, particularly in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper explores the implementation of virtual X-ray powder diffraction laboratories (v-XRDLabs) and a synchronized collaborative online platform (SCOP) combined with traditional X-ray diffraction (XRD) laboratory at the National University of Singapore (NUS) and other institutions for various educational applications. The online laboratories are comprised of a digital diffractometer, auxiliary simulations, associated software for processing and interpreting powder XRD patterns, open repositories of samples and student assignments, as well as just-in-time learning resources and performance-based assessment tool. The v-XRDLabs are used for (a) authentic online experimentation, (b) homework and controlled assessments in traditional and blended learning environments, (c) preparation for hands-on laboratory work, (d) lecture demonstrations, and (e) performance-based assessment of students’ ability to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world equipment and problem-solving. SCOP enables remote students to perform tasks individually or in groups, with or without instructor supervision. The virtual XRD laboratories have been successfully integrated into the materials science and chemistry curricula at NUS, enhancing both accessibility and experiential learning.

title: The GFP Rainbow: An Educational Tool for Teaching Molecular Modeling and Molecular Dynamics
text: This work presents a computational biochemistry activity designed for advanced undergraduate or graduate students who wish to explore the relationship between structure, dynamics, and energetics in Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) variants through structural biology and computational modeling. The activity integrates practical skills in molecular visualization with conceptual understanding of molecular mechanics, thermodynamics and intermolecular interactions. The students learn to prepare complex systems containing nonstandard residues, such as the GFP fluorophore, generate the corresponding parameter files, and perform GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics simulations under realistic solvated conditions. The resulting trajectories are analyzed to evaluate thermodynamic stability, structural evolution, and energy contributions. Monitoring the evolution of kinetic, potential, and total energies reinforces fundamental principles such as energy conservation and equilibrium. Structural analyses, including Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD), Root-Mean-Square Fluctuation (RMSF) and hydrogen bonding networks, provide insight into protein stability and fluorophore interactions, while energy decomposition quantifies per-residue contributions to fluorophore stabilization. Through this integrated workflow, students connect theoretical principles with computational practice, learning to interpret numerical data in terms of physical meaning. The complete set of input files, scripts, simulation results and analysis for several GFP variants is provided through an open GitHub repository, thus facilitating adoption and adaptation for classroom or research-based learning environments.

title: Demonstration of Tautomerism in Organic Chemistry through Intuitive Colorimetry and UV–Vis Spectroscopy
text: Compared with classical experimental design of tautomerism based on NMR technology, it is believed that convenient, interesting, and colorful experimental design will be popular among students. In this work, the classical keto–enol tautomerization was introduced into common organic dyes (naphthalimides) as key experimental reagents. Three prototropic tautomer experimental reagents based on a naphthalimide chromophore were designed and prepared. During the experiment, students were able to intuitively observe the occurrence of tautomerization by visualizing changes in color and UV–vis spectra. By comparing the color and spectral characteristics of three preset molecules in different polar solvents, students were made aware of the structural and environmental factors that affected the occurrence of tautomerism and the law of isomerization.

title: Quantum Chess as a Pedagogical Tool for Teaching Quantum Information Science in High Schools
text: Recent advances in quantum information science and engineering (QISE)spanning theoretical algorithms and quantum hardware developmenthave intensified the need for broader education in foundational quantum concepts. Yet, the abstract and counterintuitive nature of quantum phenomena presents major barriers to incorporating QISE into high school chemistry curricula. To address this, we developed a game-based instructional workshop designed to introduce secondary students to key quantum mechanical principles, such as quantum superposition and measurement. Grounded in experiential learning theory, the workshop combined guided exploration, structured gameplay, and conceptual explanation to foster engagement and understanding. Pre- and postworkshop assessments indicated high levels of student engagement, as well as demonstrated and perceived learning. These results demonstrate the potential of combining game-based approaches with targeted instruction and collaborative activities to create effective tools for introducing QISE at the secondary level.

title: The Graduate Student Safety Certificate: A Standard, Universal, and Innovative Safety Certificate
text: The Graduate Student Safety Certificate (GSSC) hosted by the Campus Safety, Health, and Environmental Management Association is introduced and described. The GSSC is a unique certificate program aimed at combining online safety training (coursework currently offered by the American Institute of Chemical Engineers), practical experiences, and collaborative efforts through industry partnerships. The GSSC offers graduate students standardized safety training for their careers in science, especially in lab-based careers, by expanding their laboratory safety exposure and training beyond the microcosm of their home institution, department, and research laboratory. This safety certificate strives to help bridge the gap that exists between the industry and academic safety culture. The GSSC is also aimed at professional development and advancement of the graduate students with these certificates by providing them with unified recognition of their commitment to safety culture.

title: Sniffing Out Chirality: Your Nose as a “Sides” Recognizer
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide In this experimental investigation, final-year high school students and first-year university students were presented with a series of pairs of enantiomeric compounds for olfactory assessment. Five pairs of enantiomeric odorants (limonene, carvone, menthol, linalool, and dihydrocarveol) were presented at equal concentrations, and participants reported the perceived odor quality and intensity through an anonymous questionnaire. The collected data show that, for several compounds, students were able to discern distinct olfactory characteristics between enantiomeric counterparts, elucidating differential scent perception in agreement with literature descriptions. In other cases, the two enantiomers were perceived as being more similar and were more difficult to describe. Although the participants were not trained sensory analysts, the results indicate that olfactory tests can be used as an effective hands-on teaching activity to illustrate stereochemical concepts and connect chirality with sensory perception. This approach provides a simple and engaging way to integrate experiential learning into introductory courses in organic chemistry and stereochemistry.

title: Synthesis, Characterization and Cage-Confined Photocatalysis of MOC-16-Ru 8 Pd 6
text: This paper presents a comprehensive teaching experiment module designed for senior undergraduates of Chemistry at Sun Yat-Sen University. The module begins with the synthesis of organic ligand L from organic substrates, followed by the preparation of complex RuL 3, and ultimately constructs a metal–organic cage MOC-16-Ru 8 Pd 6 via supramolecular self-assembly. The photocatalytic confinement performance of MOC-16-Ru 8 Pd 6 is evaluated through either the homocoupling of acenaphthylene and 1-bromoacenaphthylene or the cross-coupling between chalcone and cinnamate. Leveraging both the activation by metal sites within the cavity and the stereoselectivity imparted by the confined environment of the cage, the two reactions predominantly yield the thermodynamically disfavored and sterically hindered diastereo- and enantioselective cyclobutane products. These outcomes clearly demonstrate the critical role of MOC-16-Ru 8 Pd 6 in controlling stereoselectivity in photochemical transformations. The experiment embodies a complete research chain, incorporates novel scientific content, and is highly suitable for hands-on instruction of chemical senior undergraduates, effectively enhancing their comprehensive experimental skills. Through this module, students integrate theory with practice, improve synthetic techniques, learn instrumental operation methods, and develop a deeper understanding of scientific research─particularly in supramolecular self-assembly, stereoselectivity in organic reactions, and enzyme-mimetic cage-confined photocatalysis. This teaching experiment has been successfully implemented over multiple academic years and has demonstrated significant educational effectiveness.

title: A Precollege Summer Enrichment Chemistry Workshop and Its Impact on Student Progression and Success
text: We describe the Summer Enrichment Chemistry Workshop (SECW), a unique program in its dual role as both a bridge and a revised placement program. The SECW is a tuition-free, six-week summer program designed for first-time college students who have received a preparatory placement in chemistry. This course offers an opportunity for performance-based revised placement. Students who successfully complete the workshop may take General Chemistry 1 or Comprehensive General and Organic Chemistry. The workshop is held at an urban R1 research university in the Midwest, which has strong affiliations with a hospital and a health sciences system. The workshop focuses on foundational skills necessary for success in a first-semester general chemistry course. Emphasis is placed on mastering chemical vocabulary and concepts and applying them with basic math skills to solve diverse problems. In this paper, we examine the workshop’s structure and goals, highlighting its distinctive features and impact on student success, including graduation rates, STEM retention, and lower DFW (D-grade, fail, or withdrawal) rates in General Chemistry I. Notably, student interviews revealed unanticipated benefits such as enhanced academic preparedness, confidence, mindset, sense of belonging, and placement outcomes, even in the absence of formal grading.

title: Playing with Chemistry: Developing Observation and Classification through Daily Mix-Up
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Game-based learning provides a creative pathway to engage students in scientific inquiry by transforming abstract concepts into tangible experiences. This study presents Daily Mix-Up, a board game developed to enhance vocational students’ understanding of observation and classification─two fundamental scientific process skills in chemistry. The game situates chemical substances within familiar daily contexts, prompting learners to compare, group, and reason through visual and property-based clues. Integrated into the “Explore” and “Elaborate” phases of the 5E instructional model, Daily Mix-Up combines play, discussion, and evidence-based reasoning to connect theory with practice. Classroom implementation with vocational chemistry students demonstrated that the game effectively promoted active participation, collaborative learning, and deeper conceptual engagement. The findings highlight the potential of structured, context-rich games like Daily Mix-Up to bridge the gap between chemical theory and real-world application, supporting both cognitive and motivational dimensions of chemistry learning.
