title: Introducing Molecular Simulation into Undergraduate Numerical Computation Education
text: Traditional numerical computation courses often emphasize abstract mathematical derivations and algorithmic details, which may limit student engagement. To address this challenge, we present a teaching approach that integrates molecular simulations into an undergraduate numerical computation course for computer science students. In this approach, numerical algorithms are introduced within the context of molecular simulation, providing a concrete application scenario for abstract computational methods. Student feedback suggests generally positive perceptions of the course, particularly in conceptual understanding, computational skills, and interdisciplinary interests. In addition, we compared student performance with that of previous cohorts taught using a traditional approach. Students in the redesigned course achieved higher laboratory scores and slightly improved final examination performance. These results suggest that integrating molecular simulation into numerical computation may enhance student engagement and support the development of computational skills. This approach also provides opportunities for computer science students to explore interdisciplinary applications in molecular sciences.

title: Versatile Scientific Single-Molecule Fluorescence Microscopy Experiments for Advanced Chemistry Students
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Although chemistry conceptionally is a molecular science, experiments are rarely performed on individual molecules but rather are typically carried out with an ensemble. Advanced chemistry students often already have considerable expertise in bulk spectroscopic methods. In order to introduce them to methods of single-molecule detection and chemistry, here we present a versatile, potentially low-cost, and easy-to-set-up course in single-molecule fluorescence microscopy. Using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) to image the fluorescence of single terrylene molecules in a solid p -terphenyl matrix, students learn not only to visualize single emitters but also to extract important quantitative photophysical data such as the emitted count rate, the photobleaching quantum yield, and the optical resolution or even to analyze chemical kinetics on the single-molecule level. Besides acquiring advanced experimental skills such as working with lasers and handling optical setups, the primary focus of this experiment lies on the evaluation and interpretation of the data collected, which includes the assessment of the setup and the critical interpretation of the results with reference to existing scientific models.

title: Bridging the STEM Divide: An AI-Assisted Approach to Developing Phyphox-Based Experiments with Low-Cost Sensors
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Digital experiments play an important role in STEM education but remain underused in resource-constrained rural schools due to limited equipment and insufficient technical training. Phyphox provides a low-cost platform for digital experimentation; however, the integration of external sensors typically requires programming skills that many teachers lack. This study employed a five-stage framework, including investigation, specification, design, construction, and testing, to develop a “Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) + Phyphox” model for experiment design. A CO 2 monitoring station was developed as a case study, with GenAI supporting sensor control, code generation, and data visualization. In classroom implementation, the station produced measurement trends consistent with a Pasco CO 2 sensor, and four teachers without prior technical experience successfully replicated the station. These findings indicate that this approach enables teachers to develop low-cost digital experiments suitable for qualitative and semiquantitative secondary chemistry investigations, thereby lowering technical barriers and expanding access to STEM instruction in under-resourced schools.

title: A Python-Based Module for Exploring Machine Learning-Inspired Optimization Algorithms Using Quantum Chemistry
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide This Technology Report describes a Python-based teaching module for introducing function optimization in a chemically meaningful setting. The module combines the open-source PyNOF software with Jupyter notebooks so that students can implement, run, and compare classical and adaptive optimization algorithms while examining convergence behavior and the role of the learning rate. Hartree–Fock calculations provide an accessible entry point, Natural Orbital Functional theory extends the activities to a more demanding optimization landscape, and the dissociation of H 2 serves as an integrative example linking numerical choices to chemical interpretation. The report focuses on the technology, its intended classroom use, and its initial implementation with graduate students. All notebooks, source files, and supporting materials are openly available, making the module easy to adapt to a variety of computational and quantum chemistry courses.

title: Integrating Machine Learning into a CURE: Student-Led Optimization of Terephthalaldehyde Electrosynthesis
text: Terephthalaldehyde is a valuable intermediate for polymers and pharmaceuticals, and its electrochemical synthesis offers advantages of green chemistry and mild reaction conditions. To address the lack of systematic training in multivariable optimization and data science in undergraduate laboratory education, a course-based undergraduate research experience (CURE) module that integrates data-driven inquiry has been developed. Student teams selected key reaction variables (water content in the solvent and supporting electrolyte concentration), designed a multifactor experimental matrix, and employed both OriginPro for response surface regression analysis and Baidu AI Studio for machine learning-based yield prediction. The inquiry cycle was completed through experimental validation of model-predicted conditions. Assessment showed that over 85% of students successfully built valid predictive models and correlated data-derived insights (e.g., feature importance rankings) with an understanding of solvent effects and ionic conductivity. Student reflections indicated significant gains in research confidence and problem-solving skills. A replicable model for integrating experimental design and data science into the advanced chemistry laboratory curriculum has been developed.

title: Visualization of pH Oscillating Reactions with Aggregation-Induced Emission: A Comprehensive Chemistry Experiment for Undergraduates
text: Visualizing nonequilibrium systems remains a major pedagogical challenge for undergraduate chemistry students. To address this gap, this paper presents a comprehensive, vertically integrated laboratory module that bridges organic synthesis, polymer chemistry, instrumental analysis, and physical chemistry. In this module, students synthesize and characterize a novel pH-responsive polymer probe, PEG-TPE-3N, with aggregation-induced emission behavior. This probe is further coupled with a pH-oscillating reaction within a continuous stirred tank reactor. Driven by the protonation-controlled aggregation of the probe, the resulting system transforms abstract nonequilibrium cycles into an intuitive, rhythmic fluorescence oscillation. By making concepts like feedback loops, autocatalysis, and nonequilibrium steady states macroscopically observable, this experiment enhances students’ comprehension of complex chemical dynamics and cultivates essential practical skills in interdisciplinary research.

title: StereoLearn: An Online Platform for Learning and Automatic Grading of Organic Structure Representations
text: Abstract This report introduces StereoLearn, a web-based platform for developing representational competency. While the ability to fluently translate between various styles of 2D diagrams and 3D models for molecular structure is a cornerstone of organic chemistry, assessing student-drawn structures at scale poses a significant challenge due to the manual overhead of grading. StereoLearn (https://en.stereolearn.chemcognitive.online/) integrates interactive e-learning modules with a robust, automated grading system for dash-wedge drawings, Fischer projections, and Haworth projections. By utilizing a hybrid grading approach that combines RDKit-based canonical SMILES with custom rule-based algorithms to parse Molfiles, the platform ensures rotationally invariant and convention-accurate grading. Implemented in an undergraduate Organic Chemistry course, the platform demonstrated efficacy. Statistical analysis indicated an improvement in students’ structure-drawing proficiency, highlighting StereoLearn as a scalable, evidence-based solution for enhancing representational competency while alleviating the administrative burden of manual grading in high-enrollment courses.

title: Using Chalk Sticks to Illustrate How Surface Area Affects Reaction Rate
text: This paper reports on reactions of chalk sticks with acids to illustrate the effect of surface area on reaction rate. Both qualitative and quantitative illustrations are described, with a focus on initial rates of reaction. A lesson was developed based on the illustrations, and statistical analysis showed that the lesson helped with second semester general chemistry students’ understanding of surface area. Students also largely agreed that the lesson helped with their understanding of surface area and reaction rate.

title: A Simplified Haber-Bosch Experiment for the Chemistry Laboratory: A Low-Cost Approach to Teaching Ammonia Synthesis and Green Hydrogen Concepts
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is one of the major global challenges and involves rethinking established industrial processes. Ammonia synthesis using the Haber-Bosch process is fundamental to modern agriculture, but it is also one of the largest sources of CO 2 emissions. This is mainly due to one of the steps in the process in which hydrogen is obtained from fossil fuels. A promising alternative is to replace this step with the use of green hydrogen, obtained by water splitting with renewable energy sources. However, accessible experimental practices addressing this topic are still limited. Here, we describe a low-cost experiment in which students produce hydrogen by water splitting and use it, in combination with nitrogen, to simulate ammonia synthesis by a simplified Haber-Bosch process. This approach enables students to explore the concept of green hydrogen as a more sustainable alternative for industrial hydrogen production. The reaction is conducted in a simple heated reactor, and the product is identified using a pH indicator. The experiment was developed for general chemistry courses and promotes an integrated discussion of fundamental concepts of thermodynamics, chemical equilibrium, kinetics, and catalysis, alongside contemporary issues related to sustainability, including the role of green hydrogen in reducing the carbon footprint of ammonia production.

title: “Stream-to-Learn Method” for Designing Digital Learning Environments
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide In this work, the first theoretically based development of the “stream-to-learn method” as a didactically sound method is described and discussed. To this end, the newly designed series “Basic Negative” was developed and evaluated for use in school chemistry lessons (for students aged 12–15). By using this method, students should acquire interlinked knowledge and their skills for self-organized learning should be supported and therefore promoted. Students can work at their own pace, repeat content as necessary, and decide how to document their work. The method’s suitability was rated by 16 students of a master course which has a clear focus on new didactic methods. The students rated the method as suitable for designing digital learning environments. To their opinion, working with the digital learning environment should be suitable for autonomous learning in chemistry lessons at school. Focusing on electron movement early on in chemistry lessons and introducing electron transitions was also rated as appropriate. Overall, the design of the series was also rated very well.

title: E-CONFIG Cards: Educational Game to Learn Electron Configuration in Atomic Orbitals
text: Abstract Electron configurations of atomic orbitals are basic and essential topics in the chemistry curriculum for understanding atoms through quantum mechanics. Because the mathematical treatment of wave functions is generally omitted from introductory chemistry courses, students learn the process of arranging electrons in atomic orbital energy levels according to the aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund’s rules. Although various game-based educational methods have been developed to enhance motivation for learning electron configurations of atomic orbitals, they do not encompass all content related to electron configurations in ions and excited states, which are covered in the chemistry curriculum. In this work, an interactive board game was designed to include electron configurations not only in the ground state but also in excited and ionized states. Thirty-six 11th-grade students engaged in this game and reported positive perceptions of usage intention and learning effectiveness. The learning activity led to meaningful improvement in students’ understanding of excited-state electron configurations. The game’s competitive and engaging features encouraged repeated play, supporting students’ learning of fundamental chemical concepts related to electron configurations.

title: A Green Chemistry Laboratory Kit Utilizing Natural Indicators to Enhance Students’ Science Process Skills in Cr(VI) Detection
text: Despite its critical role in promoting safe, environmentally conscious, and sustainable laboratory practices, the integration of green chemistry principles in secondary school chemistry education remains limited. This study developed and evaluated a green chemistry-based laboratory kit for detecting hexavalent chromium [Cr(VI)] using a natural indicator extracted from mulberry fruit ( Morus nigra L.) to enhance students’ science process skills (SPS). A quasi-experimental design involved two grade 10 classes (n = 40 students) at an Islamic senior high school in Indonesia. The control group used conventional synthetic reagent (1,5-diphenylcarbazide), while the experimental group used the developed kit. Data were collected through pretests, posttests, and structured observations. The experimental group achieved average SPS scores of 85 ± 6% (Good category) with N-Gain of 0.76 ± 0.13, while the control group scored 64 ± 3% (Fair category) with N-Gain of 0.34 ± 0.12 ( p < 0.001). Integrating green chemistry principles into laboratory learning significantly improved students’ SPS and strengthened their awareness of sustainability and safety. This laboratory experiment demonstrates high potential as an innovative educational tool for secondary chemistry education.
keywords: green chemistry, laboratory kit, hexavalent chromium detection, hexavalent chromium, natural indicators, Morus nigra, mulberry fruit extract, science process skills, high school chemistry teaching, 1,5-diphenylcarbazide, sustainability awareness, laboratory safety

title: From Research to an Undergraduate Lab Bench: An Undergraduate-Level Guided-Inquiry Experiment to Explore a Cp*Ir(III)-Catalyzed ortho- C–H Activation
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Laboratory work is an essential component of science instruction as it offers students the opportunity to complete hands-on work to acquire practical skills. However, students often lose interest in wet laboratory work due to a lack of understanding and because they fail to connect laboratory work and coursework. The classical structure of chemistry curricula often fragments learning, resulting in disconnected concepts rather than an integrated understanding of the discipline. To address this, the purpose of this research was to develop an integrated experiment that simultaneously illustrates concepts and techniques from two or more subdisciplines of chemistry. The iridium(III)-catalyzed ortho -directed C–H activation reaction was developed in a research laboratory and optimized as an interdisciplinary, guided-inquiry experiment for an upper-division inorganic chemistry laboratory. The experiment intentionally integrates concepts and techniques from both inorganic and organic chemistry courses, encouraging connections across subdisciplines. Designed to be completed in three 3-h sessions, the experiment offers a model for unifying laboratory and lecture content, supporting the development of both practical skills and interdisciplinary thinking.

title: Unveiling Conceptual Structures in Chemistry Textbooks through Latent Dirichlet Allocation
text: In chemistry education, textbooks are critical resources for student learning and teacher instruction. However, systematically analyzing their vast content poses significant challenges. This study leverages Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), an innovative computational text analysis technique, to overcome the labor-intensive nature of traditional text analysis and enhance understanding of textbook content. We analyzed six high school chemistry textbooks from Taiwan to identify key topics and their content. The analysis identified 21 topics, which were then grouped into seven major chemical concepts: chemical reactions, kinetics, equilibrium, structure and function, atoms, bonding, and intermolecular forces. The analysis further revealed distinct teaching sequences, including a knowledge-structure approach (Path 1) and a student cognitive-development approach (Path 2), highlighting how different textbook approaches organize conceptual coherence. These findings provide a practical pathway for researchers and educators to develop expertise in selecting suitable materials and aligning them with curriculum standards for effective educational instruction in schools.
keywords: chemistry textbook, high school chemistry, latent Dirichlet allocation, topic modeling, chemical concepts, didactic sequence, conceptual coherence, chemical reactions, reaction kinetics, chemical equilibrium, intermolecular interactions, chemical bonding

title: Chemistry Laboratory Safety: A Peer-Led Observational Learning Program for High School Students
text: While laboratory safety education is fundamental to scientific inquiry, its implementation in high schools often lacks the rigor found in higher education. This study introduces the Chemistry Laboratory Safety ( CLS ) program, a peer-led initiative designed to establish a safety-conscious framework among high school students. Grounded in Bandura’s Social Cognitive Theory, the program realizes observational learning through a structured framework of theoretical lectures, live demonstrations, and hands-on practical training facilitated by experienced peers. The program’s impact was assessed through a prepost observational study. Quantitative analysis revealed a robust improvement in the cognitive domain, with a large effect size, particularly in mastering first aid and technical equipment utilization. While behavioral improvements were observed, the effect size was smaller, indicating a behavioral lag in which cognitive gains outpaced the internalization of spontaneous safety habits. Following the implementation, the laboratory has recorded no major accidents or injuries, providing a practical contrast to the preventable incidents recorded in previous years. These findings suggest that near-peer led structure effectively bridges the gap between theoretical awareness and technical competency, offering a scalable framework for fostering laboratory responsibility in secondary education settings.
keywords: laboratory safety education, chemical laboratory safety, near-peer teaching, observational learning, social cognitive theory, high school students, first aid training, laboratory accident prevention, safety behavior, secondary education

title: A Physical Chemistry Lab for the Evaluation of Size-Dependent Polymer Properties
text: In this manuscript we present a Physical Chemistry Laboratory experiment designed to increase undergraduate chemistry majors’ exposure to polymers and the technique of thermal analysis. The lab involves characterizing the phase transitions and associated thermal properties for poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVOH). Students work in pairs to conduct the experiment using a differential scanning calorimeter and analyze the resulting thermogram to determine the melting point, enthalpy of fusion, and glass transition temperature for PVOH samples of varying molecular weight. Aggregate class data from several PVOH samples are used to determine the size dependence of each of these properties. Furthermore, the Flory–Fox equation is evaluated as a model for the size dependence of the glass transition temperature for PVOH. Given appropriate support, most students are successfully able to identify the melting point, enthalpy of fusion, and glass transition temperature of PVOH from the thermograms obtained. Additionally, almost all students are also able to correctly evaluate the size dependence of the thermal properties.

title: Integrating Fluorescence and Calorimetry to Teach Protein Unfolding Thermodynamics: A Collaborative Laboratory Experiment
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide This laboratory experiment integrates fluorescence spectroscopy and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to teach the thermodynamics of protein thermal unfolding through a collaborative, guided inquiry approach. Using lysozyme as a model system, students determine the melting temperature ( T m ), enthalpy (Δ H ), entropy (Δ S ), and heat-capacity change (Δ C p ) associated with thermal unfolding. The activity combines complementary techniques and analytical methods: groups analyze fluorescence data using three alternative van’t Hoff approaches (linear analysis, derivative method, and nonlinear global fitting), while others perform DSC measurements under different heating rates, protein concentrations, and reversibility conditions. All data sets are processed and fitted using an affordable, cross-platform data analysis program, providing an accessible alternative to proprietary software supplied with commercial DSC instruments. Students appropriately explore the relationships among equilibrium, reversibility, and kinetic effects by comparing fluorescence- and calorimetry-derived thermodynamic parameters within the same two-state model. The collaborative, guided inquiry design promotes a deeper conceptual understanding of protein stability and equilibrium thermodynamics while fostering transferable skills in data modeling, teamwork, and scientific communication. This experiment is suitable for upper-level undergraduate and graduate laboratory courses in physical chemistry, thermal analysis, and biochemistry.

title: Comparable Outcomes, Divergent Learning Pathways: Comparing Metacognitive Reflection and Practice Problems in Organic Chemistry
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Organic Chemistry I presents significant challenges for students, requiring both conceptual understanding and effective study strategies. Two commonly used approaches to support learning are structured practice problems and metacognitive reflection activities; however, these strategies are rarely compared directly within the same course context. In this study, students enrolled in a postbaccalaureate Organic Chemistry I course (n = 31) were randomly assigned to one of two low-stakes interventions: weekly practice problem sets or structured reflection surveys focused on study strategies. Student performance was evaluated using three midterm examinations, a cumulative final exam, and overall course grades, along with measures of participation. Students in both groups achieved similar final course outcomes, with only small, nonsystematic differences across individual assessments (Cohen’s d < 0.3). The reflection group showed slightly higher mean performance on early exams, whereas the practice group performed slightly higher on later assessments, including the final exam, resulting in convergent overall performance. Participation was moderately associated with course performance across all students (r = 0.315). Although students in the reflection group demonstrated higher levels of class participation, this increased engagement did not translate into differences in final outcomes between groups. These findings suggest that metacognitive reflection and practice-based activities may represent different pathways that produced similar academic outcomes in this context. While reflection may promote early engagement and adjustment to course demands, practice-based activities may more directly reinforce the procedural skills assessed in examinations. Instructors may therefore select or combine these strategies based on instructional goals. Findings should be interpreted in light of the small sample size and course-specific context.
keywords: metacognitive reflection, practice questions, organic chemistry education, study habits, student engagement, student participation, course performance, procedural skills

title: Pool-scAN: Experimental Setup for Student-Oriented Wet-Chemical Analysis to Detect Pool Chemicals in Pool Water within a Game-Based Inquiry Learning Approach
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Inquiry-based learning (IBL) has already proven to be an effective approach to promote scientific inquiry skills. However, its implementation in school practice faces several persistent challenges such as limited time, necessary support measures for students, difficulties in assessment or rigid curricula. To address these barriers, a novel experimental setting─Pool-scAN─in a game-based inquiry learning (GBIL) approach was developed for upper secondary chemistry education. In this setting, students investigate a fictional murder case with integrated supportive game elements (e.g. story, feedback, competition, guidance) as forensic scientists through qualitative and quantitative wet-chemical analyses of highly authentic pool water samples. The setting was evaluated with n = 51 high school students in Germany using a pre-post design based on an adapted R-Comp questionnaire assessing research competence according to the RMRC-K model. Results revealed a highly significant improvement in students’ perceived overall research competence ( d = 1.163***) across all subscales, with the largest effect observed for domain knowledge. Considering the limitations of self-assessments, findings indicate that game-based learning combined with inquiry-based learning is beneficial for research competence development. Furthermore, the results suggest that the adapted R-Comp questionnaire could enable a simple and quick assessment of research competence in schools. On the other hand, an effective experimental learning environment on the topic of wet chemical analysis was developed using the novel context of pool chemistry in the game-based inquiry learning approach. For this reason, the specific influence of game-based learning on research competence and other variables such as motivation or cognitive load of students within the learning environment will be examined in more detail in further studies.
keywords: inquiry-based learning, research skills, wet chemical analysis, student motivation, cognitive load

title: Oral Reports in an Organic Chemistry Laboratory Curriculum
text: The importance of teaching chemistry undergraduate students communication skills is widely recognized, but laboratory assessment is dominated by written reports with delayed feedback from instructors. The literature has demonstrated encouraging learning outcomes like positive student attitudes and deeper understanding associated with oral assessments, alongside the significant benefits of immediate feedback, but logistical challenges remain regarding implementation and consistent assessment across different instructors. This report describes an oral lab report in Organic Chemistry II that utilizes a technical, conversational approach and addresses some of the challenges associated with oral assessments, while retaining their previously documented benefits, including the development of oral communication skills. Using a rubric that is focused on principles of the Science Writing Heuristic, a comparison of students' overall score on written and oral lab reports showed that students scored higher on the oral lab report than with an analogous rubric on the written lab reports for a given experiment. Additionally, students score significantly higher on their oral report when compared to their written reports for other experiments that have a similar complexity. Oral reports can be conducted in-person or virtually without a significant difference in scoring. The challenge of instructor bias in scoring is discussed and instructor reflections are included.
keywords: oral reports, oral assessment, organic chemistry laboratory, laboratory evaluation, speaking skills, Science Writing Heuristic, rubrics, undergraduate chemistry education

title: Development and Implementation of Cloud-Based Tutorials on Biomolecules of Colombia’s Biodiversity
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Success in computational biomolecular education requires students to connect chemical structure, molecular recognition, biological function, and data interpretation using authentic scientific resources. However, implementing molecular visualization and bioinformatics activities in undergraduate and graduate courses can be limited by software installation requirements, heterogeneous computational backgrounds, and restricted access to specialized infrastructure. In this Technology Report, we describe an adaptable and reproducible strategy for developing cloud-based tutorials on biomolecules associated with Colombia’s biodiversity. The collection was implemented in Google Colaboratory and includes one introductory notebook and eight biomolecule-centered tutorials focused on chemical structure, receptor exploration, and biomolecule-receptor interactions. Each tutorial follows a standardized sequence composed of contextual introduction, chemical structure visualization, receptor analysis, and an applied activity in which students reproduce the workflow with a related molecule. The tutorials were used as guided in-class activities in undergraduate and graduate courses at Universidad de los Andes, requiring only a web browser and Internet access. A major benefit of this approach is its template-based design: instructors can generate new tutorials by replacing highlighted molecule and receptor-specific inputs without rewriting the underlying code. This design supports reproducibility, facilitates adaptation to new molecular systems, and provides a practical framework for incorporating cloud-based biomolecular activities into different course levels and institutional settings.
keywords: biomolecules, Google Colaboratory, molecular visualization, bioinformatics education, web-based learning

title: Fostering Systems Thinking in Polymer Chemistry Education: A Retrospective Spiral-Integration Model for Teaching Life-Cycle and Green Chemistry Principles
text: The environmental challenges posed by polymeric materials demand chemistry curricula that equip students with systems thinking and green chemistry competencies. This study introduces the sustainability-driven Retrospective Spiral-Integration (RSI) model, a novel framework that embeds sustainability into polymer chemistry education through a final-year capstone course. Unlike conventional approaches that treat sustainability as an add-on, the RSI model uses the capstone as an integrative platform for students to re-examine prior knowledge through life-cycle thinking, green chemistry, and circular economy principles. Over three academic years (2022–2024), the model was implemented and evaluated using a mixed-methods design combining quantitative analysis of Course Learning Outcome attainment ( N = 482) with qualitative analysis of student projects and surveys. Results indicate that over 85% of students achieved mastery of core competencies, with qualitative evidence revealing sophisticated integration of prior knowledge, application of green chemistry principles, and nuanced navigation of design trade-offs. Student perceptions were highly positive, with 90% affirming the career relevance of the knowledge gained. The RSI model offers a replicable framework for integrating sustainability into upper-level chemistry curricula without extensive restructuring, addressing a critical gap in discipline-specific sustainability education.
keywords: systems thinking, polymer chemistry education, green chemistry, life cycle thinking, circular economy, sustainability education, capstone course, course learning outcomes, student perceptions

title: Integrating Project-Based Learning, Design Thinking, and University–Industry Collaboration in STEM Education: A Qualitative Case Study of Student Experiences and Implementation Challenges
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide This qualitative case study investigates the integration of Project-Based Learning (PBL), Design Thinking (DT), and University-Industry Collaboration (UIC) within a semester-long interdisciplinary master module in which small teams work on deep project briefs materials science and engineering. Through thematic analysis of student reflections, project reports, and stakeholder interviews, the perceived benefits, challenges, and overall impact of this integrated pedagogical framework were examined. Findings suggest that the model successfully enhanced students’ transferable skills─including communication, problem-solving, and project management─and increased greater creative confidence, professional identity, and career readiness. The authentic, industry-anchored projects served as a significant motivator, while the DT process provided a valuable structure for navigating ambiguity and developing user-centered solutions. However, challenges persisted regarding team communication dynamics, role clarity, and the full implementation of later DT phases like prototyping and testing. Stakeholder perspectives highlighted the value of the collaboration but emphasized a need for better-aligned expectations and structured scaffolding. This study demonstrates that the synergistic combination of PBL, DT, and UIC offers a valuable, albeit complex, approach for preparing students to tackle real-world challenges, and provides practical insights for designing future curricula at the intersection of academic and industry relevance.
keywords: project-based learning, design thinking, university-industry collaboration, STEM education, materials science and engineering education, transferable skills, creative confidence, professional identity, career readiness, team communication, prototype development, curriculum development, student experience

title: Preparation of a Colorimetric TLC Stain for Amines from Furfural
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide A laboratory experiment was developed for the preparation of a thin-layer chromatography stain from the condensation of furfural and N -methylbarbituric acid. The experiment allows for the introduction of the concepts of selective TLC staining and colorimetric detection of amines. The stain is based on the formation of donor–acceptor-Stenhouse-adducts (DASAs), and its preparation and application allow the introduction of organic chemistry concepts such as the Knoevenagel condensation, ring opening, and Nazarov electrocyclization, as well as photochromic systems. The cheap reagents required for this work and easy setup allow for a straightforward introduction of the work in various settings, including academic laboratories. The use of biomass-derived furfural reinforces the importance of green chemistry and sustainable practices in organic chemistry.

title: Spectacular Science with Everyday Materials: A Do-It-Yourself Luminescence Workshop for Broad Audiences
text: Abstract Chemistry is often perceived as distant and challenging, which can limit public interest and engagement. Hands-on demonstrations offer a way to make chemistry accessible, engaging, and visually appealing, while also enhancing participants’ perception of learning. This article presents a do-it-yourself (DIY) luminescence workshop using only common household materials, designed for high school students and the general public. Built around visually striking experiments illustrating luminescence phenomena, the workshop aimed to achieve five outcomes: engagement and enjoyment, perceived conceptual understanding, increased interest in chemistry and science, DIY transferability, and a strong wow effect. Its impact was evaluated using a questionnaire addressing enjoyment, interest, perceived understanding of luminescence and fluorescence, and willingness to replicate experiments or engage with science beyond the workshop. Results indicate high levels of enjoyment and interest, a perceived improvement in understanding key luminescence concepts, strong motivation to replicate experiments at home, and a compelling wow effect─confirming that simple, safe, and accessible experiments can effectively foster interest in chemistry and support informal science learning without any specialized equipment.

title: Eye-Tracking Informed Design of Instructional Videos: Aligning Student and Expert Attention to Improve Laboratory Tutorials
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide The integration of multimedia tools has reshaped science education, yet the design of laboratory tutorial videos often relies on intuition rather than evidence of how students process visual information. Although experts can articulate critical procedural steps in laboratory tasks, an expert-generated tutorial video does not guarantee that students will notice the same elements. To address this gap, we used eye tracking (ET) to analyze how students visually engage with chemical instructional videos and how their gaze patterns differ from those of the instructor. On the basis of the results obtained, new second-generation videos were created, based on established multimedia learning principles, which were demonstrably better at instructing students on the correct execution of selected basic laboratory techniques than both the original videos and traditional text-based manuals. A diagnostic prestudy showed that only 28% of students could interpret the critical steps without visual support. The study then examined how to present critical steps. ET analysis showed that neither the initial video nor the text ensured that students noticed all of the critical steps. These insights into the application of established multimedia design principles to the redesign of the tutorial include reductions in visual complexity, targeted cueing, and a consistent visual structure that supported expert-like viewing patterns. The second generation ET validated videos were then tested, with new students achieving 87% correct execution. These results show that a video is effective not because it is a video but because it is designed and validated to ensure that no critical steps are missed. This study evaluates how multimedia learning principles can guide the design of laboratory tutorial videos using eye tracking to align student and expert attention and improve the procedural accuracy.
keywords: instructional video design, eye tracking, multimedia learning principles, visual structure, procedural accuracy

title: Synthesis and Antibacterial Evaluation of Azo Dyes: An Interdisciplinary Laboratory Experiment Bridging Biochemistry and Organic Chemistry
text: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Azo compounds, which are widely used as synthetic organic dyes in the textile, food, and cosmetics industries, have also exhibited antibacterial and fungicidal properties, highlighting their potential as antimicrobial drugs. An innovative educational approach was developed to explore the bioactivity of azo dyes for undergraduate chemistry laboratories, offering students an interdisciplinary experiment that integrates organic chemistry with biological applications. The laboratory experiment involved skills and concepts from general biology, microbiology, biochemistry, and organic chemistry. The experiment was implemented in the Biochemistry laboratory and the nonmajor Organic Chemistry II laboratory. In the first laboratory period, students synthesized azo dyes. In the second period, students characterized the compounds based on their physical properties and UV–vis, 1 H NMR, and IR spectroscopy. In the third period, they determined the azo dyes’ minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against two microorganisms. The student’s learning experience was assessed through a pre- and post-test, a student perceptions questionnaire, and a postlaboratory assignment. The pre- and post-test showed an increase in the scores obtained by the students, indicating a positive impact on their knowledge following the completion of the experiment, as evidenced by the t test results. Interestingly, 69% of students had not experimented with synthesis of azo dyes prior to this experiment. Developing this type of practical experience at the undergraduate level is essential, as it allows students to apply and integrate the theoretical and practical techniques learned in courses such as biology and chemistry, thereby expanding their knowledge in organic chemistry and biochemistry laboratories. Furthermore, by studying biological activities, the students gained valuable experience that will allow them to design the synthesis of a biologically active drug.
keywords: azo dyes, azo dye synthesis, antibacterial activity, minimum inhibitory concentration, undergraduate chemistry education, organic chemistry laboratory, biochemistry laboratory, learning outcomes, student perceptions

title: A Modular Teaching Experiment on the Life Cycle of Resin Matrix Composites
text: Dynamic covalent chemistry is an emerging research frontier in polymer science. It is recognized as a pivotal approach to challenging the conventional notion of thermosetting resins as nonrecyclable materials. The integration of these advanced chemical concepts with sustainability principles represents a critical advancement in both materials engineering education and industrial practice. Here, we present a modular course designed primarily for undergraduate students, with adaptable content that can be tailored to learners from lower-year undergraduates to graduate-level students. The course was implemented with 39 participating students and delivered over a total of 14 class hours. The curriculum encompasses: (1) the synthesis of dynamic covalent bond-containing curing agents via condensation reactions between ketone and hydrazide groups; (2) the fabrication of epoxy resin/carbon fiber composites; (3) performance evaluation of epoxy resin composites; and (4) the degradation study of epoxy resin and composites, thereby completing a closed-loop cycle. By incorporating a “synthesis-materials engineering-end of life management” framework, this course integrates multidisciplinary knowledge spanning organic chemistry, analytical chemistry, and polymer science. It translates cutting-edge scientific discoveries into hands-on learning experiences while exposing students to industrially relevant synthetic and processing methodologies. This pedagogical approach not only bridges fundamental research with practical applications but also cultivates sustainability-driven thinking in materials design.
keywords: dynamic covalent chemistry, epoxy composites, carbon fiber composites, resin matrix composites, end-of-life management, curing agents, composite degradation, modular course design

title: Kakemongen Mapu Mew (The Other Forms of Life): Translation of the Periodic Table of Elements into Mapudungun
text: This paper presents a systematic translation of the periodic table of chemical elements into Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche people of Chile. The periodic table is a foundational tool in chemical education, yet for Indigenous students, the exclusively Western framing of its content can create epistemological barriers. This work develops Mapudungun names for the elements of the periodic table, including individual translations for elements 1–89 and the lanthanide series, and a family level translation for the actinide series, using a set of translation criteria that combine etymology, observable qualities, practical uses, historical context, and connection to Mapuche culture. The translation was culturally validated by Mapuche researchers and educators, cross-referencing proposed terms with oral traditions and established Mapudungun dictionaries. Through examples such as hydrogen (Choyükey Ko, “where water is permanently born”) and bismuth (Relmu Pañilwe, “metal of the rainbow”), we illustrate how the translated names ground chemical concepts in Mapuche epistemology. This work represents a linguistic and theoretical proposal that could serve as a foundation for future intercultural chemistry curricula. Potential pedagogical benefits, including improved comprehension, strengthened cultural identity, and more equitable dialogue between knowledge systems, remain hypotheses for future classroom research.
keywords: Mapudungun language, Mapuche language, chemical element names, Indigenous language revitalization, chemistry education, lanthanides, actinides, epistemological obstacles, intercultural curriculum, cultural validation, etymology

title: The Declining Likelihood of Completing the Ph.D. in Chemical Sciences: The Role of Graduate School Experiences
text: Abstract Maintaining a strong and diverse group of Ph.D.s is vital to the growth and productivity of the chemical sciences. Yet there are concerns this group has become relatively smaller over time as fewer Ph.D. students definitely plan to complete their degree. Using survey data gathered by the American Chemical Society (ACS), we analyze factors that may have contributed to this decline. Specifically, we address the following questions: (1) To what extent is the likelihood of chemical science Ph.D. students’ completing their degree related to socio-demographic characteristics, preferences regarding their future careers, and graduate school experiences? (2) To what extent can these variables account for declines in expressed likelihood of degree completion? Using data gathered in 2013 and 2019, we find students’ experiences in graduate school had a substantially greater influence on the likelihood of degree completion than individual characteristics or career preferences. While students who had adequate funding and more support from faculty and other staff were more likely to expect they would complete the degree, these associations declined markedly when encountering problems and interactions with advisors were controlled. Students reported encountering significantly more problems in their graduate program in 2019 than in 2013, and this difference could account for part of the decreased likelihood of degree completion in 2019. Data gathered in 2022 indicate that the decreased likelihood of degree completion became increasingly more serious over time, especially among students who were more advanced in their program.
keywords: graduate school experience, student financial aid, faculty-student relationships, career interest, sociodemographic factors

title: Bridging Observation and Explanation: Scientific Writing as Epistemic Practice in Biochemistry Laboratory Education
text: Abstract Laboratory reports serve as critical tools for assessing students’ ability to engage in scientific discourse. This study examines how allied health students construct written descriptions of biochemical phenomena in laboratory settings, with a particular focus on their ability to observe, describe, and conceptually explain experimental outcomes. We analyzed 320 lab reports using a rubric evaluating clarity, accuracy, and depth. We found that while students performed moderately well in presenting observable features, their ability to connect observations to theoretical concepts remained underdeveloped. Drawing on insights from science education, language theory, and cognitive psychology, we argue that challenges in descriptive writing reflect deeper issues in conceptual understanding and disciplinary discourse. Instructional interventions are proposed to bridge these gaps, including scaffolding, conceptual framing, and formative feedback. Findings inform the design of laboratory courses that prepare future health professionals for the precision and reasoning demanded in clinical communication. This study contributes to understanding the language demands of scientific communication and emphasizes the need to align writing instruction with epistemological goals of science learning.
keywords: scientific writing, laboratory reports, allied health students, epistemic practices, scientific discourse, conceptual understanding, scaffolding, formative feedback, disciplinary language, clinical communication

title: Learning Synthesis and Property Measurements of Nanoporous Metal–Organic Framework ZIF-8
text: Abstract This laboratory module is designed for upper-division undergraduate students enrolled in an applied physical chemistry course and integrates the synthesis, multitechnique structural characterization, and adsorption-based evaluation of zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) within a three-week module. Students prepare ZIF-8 using a water-based synthesis protocol at ambient temperature and pressure, replacing dimethylformamide, and other hazardous organic solvents commonly employed in metal–organic framework (MOF) synthesis. They then characterize the synthesized ZIF-8 using scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and Raman spectroscopy and analyze thermogravimetric analysis, N2 sorption, and CO2 sorption datasets to evaluate thermal stability, microporosity, and adsorption-based structure–property relationships. Student learning outcomes are assessed through performance-based assignments, supervised laboratory activities, interviews, and a self-diagnostic questionnaire. Through this connected workflow, students gain hands-on experience in MOF synthesis and characterization, develop quantitative data analysis skills, and strengthen their understanding of reticular chemistry, porous materials, and CO2 adsorption behavior.

title: The COVID-19 Pandemic and Ph.D. Students in the Chemical Sciences: Influences on Degree Completion and Commitment to the Field
text: Abstract Using survey data collected by the American Chemical Society (ACS), this paper examines the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on doctoral students’ plans to complete their degree, stay in the field, and pursue postdoctoral study. Two research designs are used: a cross-sectional design, using data from 2022 and a trend analysis examining changes from 2013 to 2022. Almost all students were negatively impacted by the pandemic, especially regarding mental health; and issues persisted two years after the pandemic started. Students who experienced more severe personal impacts of the pandemic were significantly less likely to believe that they would finish the Ph.D. or stay in the chemical sciences. Starting in 2013 the likelihood that students would finish their degree declined significantly, but the decline was significantly greater during the pandemic. There were also significant declines in the percentage of students planning to pursue postdoctoral studies.

title: Preparing the Next-generation Chemistry Students for Systems Thinking: Bridging Secondary and Higher Education
text: Abstract Systems thinking emphasizes the analysis of the interconnectedness of system components and processes, making it particularly useful for addressing 21st-century challenges. However, the question is When should we prepare the next-generation students for systems thinking skills? This work started with the anticipation that engaging students with societal challenges in secondary education will make their learning experience meaningful and may enhance their motivation toward contributing to solving them. We developed a set of learning materials and investigated if conceptual modeling can be used as a tool to support students in developing systems thinking skills. The research was carried out with 156 students (eighth and ninth grade at the Dutch VWO-4 and VWO-5 levels) of four secondary schools. We used questionnaires and semistructured interviews to demonstrate that the learning materials could indeed support students’ individual development of conceptual models. In addition, both students and teachers praised that the learning materials stimulated a collaborative learning environment for structuring ideas. Our results suggest that systems thinking skills can already be applied in practice, even without specific prior training, as the development of conceptual models implicitly requires systems thinking. Overall, the learning materials developed in this work could be broadly applicable to many educational settings and we envision that they enable the increase in teachers’ involvement in innovating education and students’ engagement in science, preparing the next-generation researchers for systems thinking.
keywords: systems thinking, conceptual modeling, secondary education, chemistry education, transition to higher education, societal challenges, cooperative learning, learning materials, student motivation, teacher participation, systems thinking skills

title: “Bend to Send”: A Wearable Alginate-Based Hydrogel Sensor for Morse Code Communication
text: Abstract This laboratory experiment introduces undergraduate students to the preparation and utilization of flexible and wearable hydrogel sensors consisted of sodium alginate, poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrenesulfonate, and an ionic liquid. The hydrogel is synthesized through ionic cross-linking and its resistance variation with stretching strain is evaluated, from which the gauge factors are calculated. The bending-sensing performance is then studied via current–time measurements on an electrochemical workstation, allowing students to directly correlate mechanical strain with electrical response. As a practical application, Morse code messages such as “GO”, “SOS”, and “HELP” are transmitted through controlled finger bending, demonstrating the translation of mechanical signals into communication codes. Beyond these guided tasks, students are encouraged to extend the experiment by designing their own messages or modifying sensing conditions. This activity provides hands-on experience in polymer cross-linking, flexible sensor fabrication, electromechanical signal conversion, and basic data acquisition, while fostering creativity in applying chemical principles to real-world communication systems.

title: One-Day Workshops Introducing High School Students to NMR and Mass Spectrometry
text: Abstract There is growing interest in the development of cooperation between universities and high schools. With respect to the chemical education, such a cooperation can be carried out in various ways, e.g., through the use of experiments designed for undergraduates, in the form of high school laboratory courses, or several-day specialized workshops. The workshops reported in this paper consisted of three different experiments, namely, 1H nuclear magnetic resonance, electron ionization-mass spectrometry, and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. The main goal of the workshops was to increase interest in chemical science among high school students by familiarizing them with instrumental methods. At the end of each class, the instructor asked a few questions that the students volunteered to answer. It may be concluded that the main goal of the workshops seems to have been achieved. Therefore, the performed instrumental workshops were found to be suitable for increasing interest in chemical science in high school students in a relatively simple way and a short time.
