title: Interrupted Case Studies: Engaging Students by Connecting Food Chemistry to Real World Issues
text: Abstract The preparation of many foods often involves high temperatures and extended cooking times, which, particularly in the presence of reducing sugars and amino acids, can promote the formation of acrylamide, a potentially carcinogenic compound produced during the Maillard reaction. In educational settings, this reaction is commonly addressed in laboratory courses through food preparation activities that are used to introduce its underlying chemical principles. This study investigated how students engaged with key concepts related to the Maillard reaction and strategies for reducing acrylamide in food through the interrupted case study method. A Descending Hierarchical Classification analysis of 53 students’ texts using IRAMUTEQ revealed students’ engagement with terminology and discussions concerning acrylamide formation and mitigation in foods such as French fries, toasted bread, and roasted coffee. These findings support the use of case-based learning as a pedagogical approach to connect food chemistry with socioscientific issues and support informed decision-making about dietary practices.
keywords: Maillard reaction, acrylamide formation, acrylamide mitigation, food chemistry education, case-based learning, student engagement, socioscientific issues, informed decision-making, IRAMUTEQ, French fries, roasted coffee

title: Evaluation of the Influence of Protein Coatings on Bacterial Adhesion to Biomaterials
text: Abstract Biomaterials used in medical implants are prone to bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation, which can lead to persistent infections. Staphylococcus epidermidis, which is a major cause of prosthesis-associated infections, adheres to biomaterial surfaces and forms biofilms, increasing resistance to antibiotics and immune responses, compromising the osseointegration. Protein adsorption on biomaterial surfaces plays a crucial role in bacterial adhesion. Serum albumin has the capacity to inhibit bacterial adhesion by creating a less favorable surface, whereas fibronectin (FN) promotes bacterial attachment by binding to bacterial fibronectin-binding proteins. This work studies the influence of human serum albumin (HSA) and FN coatings on adhesion of S. epidermidis to polycaprolactone (PCL) scaffolds, commonly used in tissue regeneration. Additionally, changes in surface hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity were analyzed. The findings provide the students with insight into how protein coatings modulate bacterial adhesion, potentially guiding the development of infection-resistant biomaterials, allowing them to gain a deeper understanding of biomaterials, strengthen their capacity for scientific creativity, and develop greater enthusiasm for research.
keywords: protein coating, bacterial adhesion, Staphylococcus epidermidis, biofilm formation, human serum albumin, fibronectin, polycaprolactone scaffolds, surface hydrophilicity, tissue regeneration

title: What Counts in General Chemistry? An Exploratory Look at What Was Emphasized and Rewarded on General Chemistry Exams Across the United States
text: Abstract General chemistry courses are prerequisites for many Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) majors. This reflects a, perhaps tacit, assumption that performance in introductory chemistry relates to one’s suitability for a STEM career. Unfortunately, our field has little idea what is required to succeed in general chemistry courses across the United States. Therefore, we cannot evaluate if general chemistry grades are an appropriate proxy for one’s potential in STEM. Here, we describe the intellectual work emphasized and rewarded on 235 exams administered in general chemistry courses at 57 colleges/universities across the USA. We parsed assessments into items, which might consist of multiple subparts, each with at least one embedded task. We focus on exams as they are ubiquitous in general chemistry courses and typically consequential for students’ grades. First, we used the 3-Dimensional Learning Assessment Protocol to describe exam points allotted to items that prompt students to use core disciplinary ideas to make sense of phenomena (i.e., 3D Learning). Findings showed that prompting for 3D Learning on assessments was rare regardless of institution type, comprising less than 7% of exam points in our data set. Next, we developed and applied a protocol to describe tasks that did not have the potential to engage students in using core ideas in science practices (i.e., 0D tasks). This revealed that rote calculations were overemphasized comprising over 27% of all 0D tasks. Findings indicate that general chemistry courses gate access to STEM by student facility with rote calculations and drawing/labeling specialist pictures. We unpack why this is problematic and provide recommendations for building chemistry assessments that have the potential to be more meaningful and equitable.
keywords: general chemistry, chemistry assessment, exam question analysis, STEM access, assessment equity, chemistry education

title: Boxed Thermodynamics: Agent-Based Visualization of Chemical Equilibrium, Kinetics, and Free Energy Landscapes
text: Abstract This paper introduces an agent-based simulation framework in NetLogo for exploring core principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics. The approach centers on the behavior of noninteracting particles in compartmentalized boxes whose geometry and energy barriers are explicitly linked to reactions’ enthalpy, entropy, and activation energy. By simulating particles within boxes of tunable floor levels and widths, abstract thermodynamic concepts become immediately visible and measurable. The visual logic of the simulations allows users to examine how temperature, chemical potentials, and free energy relate to chemical equilibrium and kinetics, using both multiparticle averages and single-particle traces. The framework supports Master Equation-based predictions, offering a bridge between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic observables. The model provides a conceptually transparent and computationally grounded tool for illustrating the behavior of chemical systems, which can be readily used by students both during class demonstrations and as part of homework exercises.
keywords: chemical thermodynamics, reaction kinetics, free energy landscape, chemical equilibrium, agent-based modeling, NetLogo, activation energy, enthalpy and entropy, chemical potential, master equation

title: Controllable Synthesis of Hydrogen-Substituted Graphdiyne: A Safe Undergraduate Experiment on Advanced Carbon Materials
text: Abstract The incorporation of advanced carbon material synthesis into undergraduate curricula is often constrained by hazardous reagents, harsh reaction conditions, and prolonged reaction durations. To address these challenges, we have developed an integrated laboratory experiment centered on the controlled synthesis of hydrogen-substituted graphdiyne (Hs-GDY). Utilizing mild solution-phase conditions and readily available reagents, the experiment enables students to control the growth of Hs-GDY films on a copper foil surface within an appropriate experimental time frame. By integrating characterization techniques including scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), Raman spectroscopy, UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra, and photoelectrochemical analysis, the experiments guide students through a complete “synthesis-structure-property” research cycle of the advanced carbon materials. Implementation with senior undergraduates has demonstrated that the experiment not only strengthens hands-on laboratory skills and data analysis proficiency but also fosters interdisciplinary research thinking and innovative awareness, providing a scalable and instructive experiment for enhancing materials science education at the undergraduate level.
keywords: undergraduate laboratory experiment, wet chemical synthesis, synthesis-structure-property relationships, photoelectrochemical properties, materials science education

title: An Industry-Engaged Project-Based Learning Module for Undergraduates: Polyimide Films as a Case Study in Scientific and Engineering Thinking
text: Abstract Undergraduate laboratory and project-based learning (PBL) activities can be effective for skill development, yet they often lack sustained industry engagement and explicit structures that connect scientific reasoning with engineering-oriented decision making. This paper reports an Open Innovative Experiment model that integrates Science–Industry–Education collaboration into a course-level PBL framework for undergraduate training. Using polyimide films with tunable branching as a representative case study, students completed a structured workflow that combined laboratory preparation/characterization with simulation-assisted interpretation to examine how structure and testing configurations influence dielectric breakdown behavior. Implementation of the model through an industry-engaged, dual-mentor structure enabled authentic problem contexts and constraints while maintaining nonproprietary boundaries. Student and industry-partner feedback, together with course-level outcomes, indicated strengthened experimental competency, improved awareness of reliability/quality considerations, and enhanced ability to translate classroom knowledge into practice. The model provides a transferable approach for incorporating industry engagement into undergraduate experimental curricula in applied chemistry and related disciplines.
keywords: project-based learning, industry engagement, polyimide films, dielectric breakdown, open innovation, undergraduate laboratory curriculum, applied chemistry education

title: Laboratory Synthesis of Octyl Methoxycinnamate Using Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation Followed by Transesterification
text: Abstract This three-week undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory module details the synthesis of the sunscreen agent 2-ethylhexyl trans-4-methoxycinnamate, commonly known as octyl methoxycinnamate (OMC). In the first week, students perform a modified Knoevenagel–Doebner condensation between 4-methoxybenzaldehyde and monoethyl malonate utilizing a pyridine/morpholine cocatalyst system to yield ethyl trans-4-methoxycinnamate. The second week involves an acid-catalyzed transesterification with 2-ethylhexanol to produce OMC. To address the inherent limitations of this equilibrium-controlled transesterification reaction, students employ preparative thin-layer chromatography in the final week to isolate the pure product. This module integrates multistep synthesis with advanced instrumental analysis, including 1H, 13C, and DEPT-135 NMR spectroscopy. The experiment reinforces critical pedagogical concepts, such as the mechanism of carbonyl condensation and thermal decarboxylation, the application of Le Chatelier’s principle, and the relationship between molecular structure and chromatographic mobility.
keywords: octyl methoxycinnamate, UV filters, transesterification, 4-methoxybenzaldehyde, 2-ethylhexanol, acid-catalyzed esterification, thin-layer chromatography, NMR spectroscopy, thermal decarboxylation, Le Chatelier's principle, undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory

title: Visualizing Solvent Polarity through the Solvatochromism of Brooker’s Merocyanine: A Hands-On Activity for Secondary Students
text: Abstract This laboratory activity introduces solvent polarity through the visually engaging phenomenon of negative solvatochromism using Brooker’s merocyanine (MOED). Students explore the interaction between a dye and eight different solvents, ranging from water to dichloromethane, observing distinct color changes from yellow to blue. The dye is prepared in-house at low cost, enabling routine classroom use. The activity is designed for a 90 min session and integrates hands-on experimentation, molecular model construction, and guided inquiry. Students compare solvents beyond dielectric constant and explore limitations of single-parameter polarity descriptions. The activity was implemented with secondary school students (ages 16–19) who demonstrated high engagement and improved conceptual understanding of solvent effects.
keywords: solvent polarity, negative solvatochromism, dye-solvent interactions, color change, dielectric constant, high school chemistry, hands-on laboratory activities, inquiry-based learning

title: Taking Bragg’s Law to a Higher Cognitive Level: Using Sketches to Assess Misconceptions of X-ray Diffraction Orders
text: Abstract Undergraduate textbooks covering X-ray diffraction and Bragg’s Law typically show diagrams with only one diffraction order. As a result, students often incorrectly visualize X-ray diffraction orders as beams scattered from different crystalline planes rather than beams scattered at distinct angles. I argue that this misconception arises because the labels for crystalline planes, beams, and diffraction orders all share the same integers (1, 2, ...) and because students typically do not analyze the diagrams carefully. Solving Bragg’s Law problems is straightforward and typically does not produce learning at higher cognitive levels. In contrast, sketching different diffraction orders in real space demands a higher level of cognitive skill and is the main theme of my article. This task serves to assess students’ understanding and identify those students who can translate the Bragg’s Law formula into the physical process in real space. Here, I highlight common student misconceptions and propose hint-based questioning to help students apply critical theoretical concepts. When students see and think about an X-ray diffraction pattern with multiple orders, they experience an “aha!” moment and begin to correctly visualize these beams. I find that showing students a real XRD pattern with diffraction orders is more effective in helping them visualize the physical process than drilling Bragg’s Law problems.
keywords: Bragg's law, X-ray diffraction, diffraction orders, student misconceptions, sketching, cognitive load, X-ray diffraction patterns, visualization, undergraduate chemistry education

title: Back to Basics: Supporting Growth in Mathematics Fluency in Developmental General Chemistry and the Regulation of Calculator Use
text: Abstract Traditional paper and pencil activities are valuable for assessing, predicting, and improving student performance in general chemistry, particularly when related to mathematical automaticity─what students can do without a calculator─because graders can gain insight into student understanding. This study tracks the changes in the mathematical fluency of 725 students taking a developmental general chemistry course in the fall of 2025. Two instructors taught the course using similar teaching strategies including paper and pencil exams. One instructor implemented a calculator-free exam on stoichiometry, while the other allowed calculators on all exams and activities. Students in the calculator-free condition also participated in calculator-free recitation sections and calculator-free homework and received practice exams that did not require calculators. The validated Math Up Skills Test (MUST) was administered to both groups on the first day of the course and again during the 11th week after the stoichiometry exam. Students in both conditions started and ended the course with concerning levels of mathematical automaticity. However, both treatment and comparison conditions improved substantially, showing average MUST score gains of 13–14 percentage points (+2.7 item improvement). The calculator-free group outperformed the comparison group on several MUST items at a statistically significant level, particularly for items related to course topics. Results show that the use of mathematical concepts within the developmental general chemistry course enhances mathematical fluency regardless of the calculator use condition, although calculator-free activities may provide small benefits. It is recommended that the reader have a copy of the MUST available to appreciate the context of this study.
keywords: mathematical fluency, calculator use, stoichiometry, student development, chemistry education

title: An Olefin Cross-Metathesis Experiment for an Undergraduate Laboratory Course Exhibiting Various Selectivities
text: Abstract Olefin metathesis is a fundamental discovery in chemistry and has been introduced as an experiment for undergraduate students in laboratory courses. As a major progress, olefin cross-metathesis exhibits multiple selectivities, but these selectivities have not been discussed in undergraduate laboratory courses. In this report, we present an inexpensive olefin metathesis experiment that was designed for undergraduate training. The experiment systematically demonstrates several selectivity issues, including (i) substrate-dependent selectivity, (ii) catalyst-dependent selectivity, and (iii) product stereoselectivity.
keywords: olefin cross-metathesis, reaction selectivity, olefin metathesis, undergraduate laboratory experiment

title: A Classic Experiment, Reimagined: Using Group Theory to Assign Coordination Complex Geometry via IR Spectroscopy
text: Abstract Group theory is a foundational yet abstract component of undergraduate inorganic chemistry, and students often struggle to translate symmetry operations into experimentally observable spectroscopic outcomes. This work addresses the challenge of facilitating students’ movement beyond symbolic manipulation to apply group theory in authentic chemical contexts. We present a modernized laboratory experiment in which students synthesize a molybdenum carbonyl complex and use character tables to predict infrared-active vibrational modes for possible geometric isomers before collecting and interpreting the IR data. Through a guided-inquiry framework, students compare predicted and experimental spectra to make evidence-based stereochemical assignments. Pre- and post-assessment results demonstrate substantial improvements in calculating IR-active modes, refinement in point group assignment, improved vibrational analysis, and marked increases in student confidence, supporting the effectiveness of embedding symmetry analysis within hands-on synthetic and spectroscopic practice.
keywords: group theory, molybdenum carbonyl complexes, infrared spectroscopy, vibrational modes, cis-trans isomers, character tables, stereochemical assignment

title: A Classroom Demonstration of Red Nylon Dyeing with Japanese Madder ( Rubia Akane ) for Teaching Intermolecular Forces and Acid–Base Equilibria
text: Abstract This paper reports a rapid classroom demonstration and instructional activity based on nylon dyeing with Japanese madder (Rubia Akane), designed to support integrated learning of intermolecular forces and acid–base equilibria at the introductory undergraduate level. Using roots of home-cultivated madder, nylon fabric can be dyed a vivid red within approximately 10 minutes, providing an immediate and visually engaging starting point for discussion. The instructional focus then shifts to the molecular structure of the major dye component, purpurin (1,2,4-trihydroxyanthraquinone), enabling students to connect macroscopic color changes with otherwise invisible microscopic interactions. Compared with previously reported demonstrations of blue nylon dyeing using alizarin (1,2-dihydroxyanthraquinone), the present approach improves classroom safety by eliminating the need for strong bases. When implemented in a 50 minute session in a first-year engineering course, the activity led to improved student understanding of the mechanisms of intermolecular attraction and the concept of acid dissociation constants. From the perspective of sustainability and green chemistry, the use of naturally derived and locally grown materials represents a small-scale yet feasible approach to addressing the utilization of Earth’s limited material resources in individual classroom settings. This work aims to broaden access to chemical education by providing a classroom activity that can be implemented without specialized facilities, thereby offering learning opportunities to a wide range of students worldwide.
keywords: nylon dyeing, purpurin, intermolecular interactions, acid-base balance, acid dissociation constants, anthraquinone dyes, alizarin, green chemistry, classroom demonstration, molecular structure

title: A Research-Inspired Chemical Biology Laboratory Module: Synthesis and Evaluation of an H 2 S-Responsive Diselenide Theranostic
text: Abstract Chemical biology integrates organic synthesis, mechanistic insight, and functional evaluation of small molecules in biological contexts, yet undergraduate laboratory instruction rarely reflects this interdisciplinary workflow. Here, we describe a six-week, research-inspired laboratory module, compatible with a standard 4 h undergraduate laboratory course, in which students synthesize and evaluate a hydrogen sulfide (H2S)-responsive diselenide theranostic derived from the clinically relevant anticancer agent SN-38. Through a concise two-step synthetic sequence, students gain hands-on experience with redox chemistry, multistep synthesis, and modern purification and characterization techniques. The module further incorporates fluorescence spectroscopy to investigate stimulus-responsive activation, enabling students to quantify concentration-dependent release behavior and assess selectivity toward H2S over competing biologically relevant species. By integrating disease-relevant biological concepts, molecular design, organic synthesis, and functional evaluation, this experiment exposes students to a complete chemical biology workflow that extends well beyond traditional undergraduate organic laboratory exercises. To our knowledge, undergraduate laboratory modules that guide students through the biological rationale, design, synthesis, and functional evaluation of a stimulus-responsive small molecule remain rare. This accessible and reproducible experiment provides a practical framework for incorporating contemporary chemical biology concepts and research-inspired learning experiences into an upper-division undergraduate curriculum.
keywords: SN-38, redox chemistry, fluorescence spectroscopy, drug release, anticancer agents

title: Introducing Tetrazine Synthesis and Reactivity in Undergraduate Laboratory Internship
text: Abstract Recent advances in click chemistry have opened promising opportunities for instructional laboratory design, yet heterocyclic compounds such as s-tetrazines─despite their visual distinctiveness and synthetic relevance─remain underutilized in undergraduate education. To meet the instructional need, a short-term undergraduate laboratory internship was designed to introduce first- through third-year students to the synthesis and reactivity of a tetrazine in a collaborative environment. Students learn to synthesize and purify the tetrazine through a straightforward one-pot procedure, followed by performing cycloaddition under ambient conditions. The visually striking transformation, characterized by the disappearance of the red to dark red color, is confirmed by UV–visible absorbance analysis. The experimental protocol is compatible with standard undergraduate laboratory facilities, employing catalyst-free conditions and readily available, inexpensive reagents. The experiment provides students with a structured sequence of reaction setup, purification, and spectroscopic analysis, each reinforcing practical competencies in reaction planning, separation techniques, and instrumental interpretation.
keywords: s-tetrazine, click chemistry, cycloaddition, undergraduate laboratory experiment, heterocyclic compounds, catalyst-free synthesis, one-pot synthesis, spectroscopic analysis, cooperative learning

title: Introducing Enzyme Immobilization and Flow Biocatalysis to the Undergraduate Curriculum
text: Abstract An undergraduate flow biocatalysis laboratory practical experiment was developed to introduce to the students the basics of enzyme characterization, enzyme immobilization, and continuous flow processes, from a practical approach. The practical was structured in two parts─enzyme immobilization and flow biocatalysis─and intended to be executed over 4 afternoons. Within this practical, the students were able to expand and solidify their knowledge on concepts such as homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis, flow setups vs batch reactions in a practical manner with dynamic exchanges with teaching assistants. Student performance was evaluated through a written report aligned with the main components of the practical course and mapped to specific learning objectives.
keywords: enzyme immobilization, flow biocatalysis, continuous flow processing, enzyme characterization, heterogeneous catalysis, homogeneous catalysis, learning objectives, student assessment

title: Interdisciplinary Project-Based Teaching in Food Chemistry Experiments Integrating Traditional Culture and Professional Concepts: Optimization of Traditional Chinese Rice Wine Brewing Conditions
text: Abstract To enhance students’ scientific experimentation skills and facilitate their understanding of careers and culture related to food chemistry, this study designed and implemented a food chemistry experimental project. Rooted in traditional culture and professional principles, this experimental project adopts an interdisciplinary project-based teaching approach. It focused on integrating theoretical knowledge from various disciplines into practice to help students master research methods in food chemistry experiments and food production processes, thereby fostering their comprehensive literacy. The teaching case selected was “Optimization of Brewing Conditions for Traditional Chinese Rice Wine”. Throughout the teaching process, students’ thinking and abilities were prioritized for assessment. We effectively combined experimental grades, self-assessment and mutual assessment, and questionnaire survey results to evaluate students’ overall learning outcomes. Compared to traditional laboratory classes, this interdisciplinary project-based teaching model in food chemistry helps stimulate students’ enthusiasm for learning and improves teaching quality.
keywords: project-based teaching, interdisciplinary teaching, traditional culture in education, student assessment, self-assessment and peer assessment, student motivation

title: Electrochemistry in Everyday Life : Evaluation of a Learning Sequence Supported by Digital Tools in Diverse Educational Contexts
text: Abstract This research investigates the efficacy of a structured didactic sequence for teaching electrochemistry in diverse Brazilian educational settings (public, private, and rural). Based on the three pedagogical moments (3 PMs: initial problematization, knowledge organization, and knowledge application), the intervention integrates an offline application and a Web site as mediators to shift from algorithmic memorization to phenomenal comprehension. Adopting a qualitative approach with 118 students and four educators, the study assesses the impact on engagement and meaningful learning. Data collection included participant observation, conceptual assessments, and platform analytics. Results indicate that linking low-cost experiments─such as homemade batteries─with contextualized digital challenges significantly increased engagement, especially in public/rural contexts, where 86% of students completed the tasks. Regarding conceptual understanding, the transition from problematization to knowledge organization led to measurable gains, with 50% of public school students mastering the final assessment. These findings suggest that integrating active methodologies with accessible digital tools (hybrid models’) allows students to bridge the gap between macroscopic phenomena and submicroscopic representations. The approach demonstrates a robust potential to mitigate educational disparities in limited-infrastructure environments, providing a scalable strategy for contextualized chemistry education that prioritizes scientific literacy over mechanical calculation.
keywords: electrochemistry education, learning sequences, Three Pedagogical Moments, low-cost experiments, student engagement, meaningful learning, conceptual understanding, rural schools, public schools, hybrid teaching model, educational inequality, scientific literacy

title: Learning Chemistry in the Kitchen: Designing Flavored Photonic Hydroxypropyl Cellulose Gels as Food Colorant
text: Abstract Structural colors are widely observed in nature. In this laboratory experiment, we designed a hands-on experiment for first-year undergraduate students that involves the fabrication and characterization of edible food gels with vibrant structural colors. In this experiment, food-grade hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) powder and commercial beverages, such as coffee, coke, and red wine, are mixed to obtain photonic gels via the self-assembly of HPC molecules into a cholesteric liquid crystalline phase. During the experiment, students can observe the shifting of structural colors, from red to green to vivid blue, when increasing the HPC concentration. Additionally, the obtained flavored photonic gels can be encapsulated within chocolate as photonic fillings to increase students’ interest in their application. This hands-on experiment is safe, convenient, and adaptable to most undergraduate laboratory courses. Through this practical class, students can evaluate the optical behavior of the photonic gels using UV–vis/NIR spectroscopy and optical microscopy, enhancing their skills in structural characterization and providing a hands-on experience in materials science. By presenting this concept, we aim to inspire students to explore structural color through the bottom-up self-assembly process, which can further stimulate students’ interest and devotion to scientific research in the future. Detailed instructions for assessing student learning, step-by-step protocols, and a student survey are provided, supporting educational value and easy integration into undergraduate teaching.
keywords: structural color, hydroxypropyl cellulose, cholesteric liquid crystals, self-assembly, food colorants, hands-on laboratory experiments, undergraduate chemistry education, materials science education

title: An Undergraduate Laboratory Module Using a Ternary Nitride Electrocatalyst to Teach Structure–Property Relationships in Electrocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
text: Abstract The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in alkaline media is central to sustainable hydrogen production but is limited by sluggish kinetics and catalyst instability. To connect fundamental chemistry, electrochemistry, and materials science with hands-on learning, we designed a laboratory experiment for undergraduate students to synthesize and evaluate a Mo3N2/Ni3Mo3N/Co3Mo3N triple-phase nitride electrocatalyst, composed of three integrated nitride phases. The ternary structure provides abundant active sites and efficient charge-transfer interfaces, which achieve a low overpotential of 33 mV at 10 mA cm–2, surpassing binary analogues and approaching the HER performance of the benchmark platinum-on-carbon (Pt/C) electrocatalyst. Students prepare working electrodes, characterize catalyst structure using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, and perform electrochemical HER measurements. Analysis of polarization curves, Tafel plots, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy data, and electrochemically active surface area, combined with guided comparisons between ternary and binary systems, enables students to relate structural features to the HER activity. This integrated approach demonstrates how multiphase design enhances HER activity, offering students insights into rational electrocatalyst design and sustainable energy research.
keywords: hydrogen evolution reaction, structure-property relationships, alkaline water electrolysis, undergraduate laboratory experiment, electrocatalyst synthesis, overpotential, charge transfer interfaces, sustainable hydrogen production

title: Organic Chemistry Metacognitive Instruction (OChem-MI) Framework: Integrating Think-Aloud and the Science Writing Heuristic in Green and Sustainable Chemistry Context for Teaching Reactions and Mechanisms
text: Abstract Organic chemistry at the preuniversity level is often taught in ways that emphasize outlining mechanisms rather than explaining them, which can encourage rote memorization and limit students’ mechanistic reasoning, metacognitive regulation, and sense of chemistry’s real-world relevance. To address this, the Organic Chemistry Metacognitive Instruction (OChem-MI) Framework was developed and implemented with 62 Malaysian preuniversity students across 16 lessons over 8 weeks. The framework began with a metacognition class and then paired eight think-aloud (TA) lessons with eight science-writing heuristic lessons in a green and sustainable chemistry context (SWH-GSC) to make electron-flow reasoning explicit and connect organic reactions to hazards, greener alternatives, and authentic societal relevance. The framework was evaluated through a preliminary teacher expert review, focus group interviews with nine students, and a longitudinal analysis of the same students’ weekly SWH-GSC written artifacts. Teacher feedback supported the framework’s feasibility and pedagogical acceptability, while focus group interviews suggested that students perceived stronger confidence in mechanistic explanation, strategic monitoring, adaptability, and problem-solving. Analysis of SWH-GSC artifacts showed progression from general hazard awareness toward more differentiated green and sustainable chemistry reasoning, especially in hazard identification and the proposal of greener alternatives. These exploratory findings suggest that the OChem-MI Framework may offer a feasible and pedagogically meaningful approach for supporting perceived chemistry self-efficacy, mechanistic engagement, and emerging green and sustainable chemistry thinking in preuniversity organic chemistry.
keywords: organic chemistry education, metacognition, think-aloud, Science Writing Heuristic, green chemistry, reaction mechanism, hazard identification, chemistry self-efficacy, instructional framework

title: Skill-Based Question-Embedded Videos (sQEVs) as Part of an Integrated Skill-Instruction Model in the General Chemistry Laboratory
text: Abstract In recent efforts to redesign undergraduate chemistry laboratory instruction, strategies that emphasize skill mastery while supporting student learning and confidence have gained increasing attention. Skill Check-Ins (SCIs) were developed as a scalable, formative assessment framework to support the development of core laboratory skills in large-enrollment general chemistry courses. However, SCIs are primarily an assessment tool for in-lab skill execution while providing limited support for skill preparation before attending the lab. To address this limitation, skill-based Question-Embedded Videos (sQEVs) were developed and integrated into an existing course structure utilizing SCIs to support prelaboratory skill preparation. Based on the prior success of Question-Embedded Videos (QEVs), sQEVs were designed to introduce laboratory techniques through short, close-up demonstrations with embedded questions that prompt active engagement and self-monitoring. Student outcomes in a cohort using the integrated SCI and sQEV instructional model (SCI+sQEV) were compared to those from a prior cohort using SCIs alone. Students in the SCI+sQEV cohort showed higher levels of meaningful learning and lower cognitive load, alongside increases in self-reported knowledge and confidence in laboratory skills. Analysis of open-ended survey responses further indicated that students perceived the sQEVs to be helpful for preparing for laboratory work and reducing uncertainty during hands-on activities. Together, these findings suggest that this integrated SCI+sQEV model can enhance students’ perceived laboratory learning experiences and provides a scalable tool for skill instruction in large-enrollment laboratory courses.
keywords: general chemistry laboratory, formative assessment, cognitive load, student self-confidence, meaningful learning, large-enrollment courses, active learning, embedded questions

title: Tipping the Scales: A Mechanical Analogy for Band Filling in Metals
text: Abstract Band theory offers a useful framework for understanding the physical properties of metals, yet students in introductory chemistry courses consistently find the concepts of band filling and bonding versus antibonding states challenging. In particular, the connection between electron occupancy of a broad s–d band and trends in metallic bond strength across Groups 1–12 is frequently misunderstood. To address this difficulty, we describe an inexpensive, interactive classroom demonstration that uses a mechanical seesaw analogy to model band filling and its consequences for metallic bonding. Golf balls placed at fixed positions along the seesaw represent electrons occupying bonding and antibonding regions of a single composite band, while the force measured at one end of the seesaw corresponds to net bond strength. As the seesaw is progressively loaded, the measured force follows an inverted U-shaped trend that mirrors experimental melting point trends for transition metals. Student feedback collected immediately after the demonstration indicates improved conceptual understanding of bonding versus antibonding and a clearer connection between band filling and metallic bond strength. This demonstration provides a tangible, low-cost approach for reinforcing band theory concepts at the introductory level.
keywords: band filling, band theory, metallic bonding, antibonding states, mechanical analogy, transition metals, conceptual understanding

title: Polymeric Hydrogel and Aerogel-Based Physical Chemistry Teaching Experiments about Phase Diagram and Specific Surface Area
text: Abstract Phase diagrams and specific surface area principles are core components of the physical chemistry curriculum. To strengthen the connection of fundamental physical chemistry theories and their practical relevance, a comprehensive undergraduate laboratory experiment based on the fabrication of polymeric hydrogels and aerogels was designed and implemented. Guided by the phase diagram, renewable agarose biomass is utilized to investigate the phase transition of water through the conversion of hydrogels into aerogels using different drying methods, including oven drying, vacuum drying, and freeze-drying. The experiment demonstrates that the phase-transition process governs the microstructures of dried materials. Compared with oven drying and vacuum drying routes, the freeze-drying pathway, which proceeds via the solid-to-gas sublimation, thermodynamically eliminates the capillary forces induced by gas–liquid interfaces, thereby preserving a high-fidelity porous aerogel network. To reinforce the concept that material properties are dependent on structures, a methylene blue adsorption experiment is employed to determine the specific surface area of the aerogels based on the Langmuir monolayer adsorption theory. Furthermore, because of the high specific surface area, the freeze-dried aerogels exhibit effective formaldehyde adsorption, showing their potential utility in pollutant abatement. The experiment extends the applications of physical chemistry principles to the food industry by comparing the morphological characteristics of various dehydrated fruit products. By integrating green chemistry concepts with synthesis, characterization, and practical application, this innovative teaching experiment facilitated by polymer hydrogels and aerogels not only deepens students’ understanding of phase theory and surface chemistry but also enhances their interest in the practical significance of physical chemistry knowledge.
keywords: polymer hydrogels, aerogels, phase diagram, specific surface area, agarose, freeze-drying, drying methods, porous media, methylene blue adsorption, Langmuir adsorption, formaldehyde adsorption, fruit drying, green chemistry, structure-property relationships

title: Promoting Chemistry Education Worldwide: An Introduction to the Festschrift Honoring Professor Mei-Hung Chiu
text: I met Mei-Hung for the first time in March 2007 at the International Committee of the National Association of Research in Science Teaching (NARST).Mei-Hung chaired the committee, and I was one of the members.It is a great pleasure to work with such a wonderful and diligent scholar.Our friendship strengthened during the ICCE meeting that took place in Taipei in July 2010.Mei-Hung nominated me for the Committee of Chemistry Education (CCE), and since then we started to collaborate in different areas: (1) together with colleagues, I wrote two chapters that were publishes in books edited by Mei-Hung, 1,2 (2) Mei-Hung and I together with colleagues wrote a few papers based on our mutual fields of interest, e.g., systems thinking and women scientists in chemistry, 3,4 and (3) Mei-Hung encouraged me to join her in three IUPAC committees (Standards in Chemistry Education, Gender gap in chemistry, and Systems Thinking in Chemistry).Beyond the professional relationship, Mei-Hung became one of my best friends.This Festschrift honors Mei-Hung and brings a lot of happiness to many colleagues who admire her intellectual contributions

title: Photonic Chocolate: A Sweet Holistic Playground To Explain Crystallization, Phase Transitions, Rheology, and Optics
text: Abstract Traditional methods for teaching scientific principles such as crystallization, phase transitions, rheology, and optics frequently struggle to engage younger audiences or individuals lacking a strong and broad scientific background. Many educational tools do not incorporate the tactile, visually engaging, and relatable elements necessary to stimulate curiosity in complex scientific phenomena. To address this gap, we propose the use of photonic chocolate, an educational tool that integrates diffraction grating technology, material structures, and their processing with the familiar appeal of chocolate. By imprinting commercial diffraction gratings onto the surface of tempered chocolate, striking photonic effects emerge through the light diffraction. These vibrant, iridescent colors are not only captivating but also serve as an instructive function, providing an accessible gateway to advanced scientific concepts. The fabrication of photonic chocolate introduces learners to cocoa butter crystal chemistry and polymorphism, the principles of non-Newtonian rheology, nanoimprinting techniques, and the optics underlying diffraction and interference. The scope of this work is 2-fold: first, providing a comprehensive theoretical background on the topic to support teachers in preparing the learning experience; and second, presenting a practical approach for designing engaging seminars and hands-on activities, emphasizing the connection between scientific fundamentals and everyday experiences.
keywords: diffraction gratings, crystallization, non-Newtonian rheology, nanoimprint lithography, optics education, hands-on learning

title: Secondary School Students’ Thinking Schemes in Solving Chemical Stoichiometry Problems
text: Abstract This study aims to examine students’ mastery level, explore thinking patterns, and develop a scheme for problem-solving thinking in chemical stoichiometry, including conceptual, procedural, and conditional knowledge. The instrument used to assess students’ mastery level in solving chemical stoichiometry problems is the Chemical Stoichiometry Mastery Level Test (CSMLT). Students’ thinking patterns and schemes are determined through oral interviews, retrospective interviews, and the CSMLT. All instruments have been validated by five experts in the field. A total of 172 Form Four students from four prominent schools in Sabah answered the CSMLT, and only 15 students were selected for interviews using purposive sampling. Verbal interviews, retrospective interviews, and CSMLT documents were then analyzed using content analysis and triangulation techniques for validity. The research findings indicate that students fail to solve chemical stoichiometry problems that involve conceptual knowledge. A majority of students grasp only the macroscopic level and possess various alternative frameworks at all three levels of chemical knowledge. Also, students struggled to master procedural knowledge due to their inability to connect conceptual knowledge and procedural knowledge in specific knowledge domains. Furthermore, the study found that students fail to master conditional knowledge due to their weakness in connecting specific knowledge domains and general knowledge domains, thus creating an alternative framework, namely the “Chemical Stoichiometry Problem-Solving Framework”. This framework implies curriculum improvements focusing on empowering problem-solving skills in chemistry education. Among the priorities are teaching and learning processes in chemical stoichiometry topics that emphasize the formation of scientifically literate communities with problem-solving abilities.
keywords: stoichiometry, high school students, conceptual knowledge, procedural knowledge, conditional knowledge, alternative frameworks, chemistry education, scientific literacy

title: From Pressure to Perspective: A Pragmatic, Practice-Based Classroom Study of a Brief Metacognitive Workshop in General Chemistry
text: Abstract Student mental health in large, high-pressure STEM courses is a persistent concern. This pragmatic, practice-based classroom study mapped the mental-health landscape in first-year students taking a General Chemistry course and piloted a brief, in-class metacognitive workshop that names common pressures (perfectionism, comparison), reduces stigma, and offers simple regulation and reflection tools. Pre–Post surveys (anonymous; treated as independent samples) assessed anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-8), and perfectionism (SAPS). Confirmatory factor analyses supported the internal structure of the measures, and composite and subscale scores were used to summarize response patterns. Analyses emphasized nonparametric approaches and educator-legible descriptors, prioritizing descriptive characterization over causal inference. Baseline burdens were substantial: 56.6% of respondents fell within moderate–severe anxiety categories, 50.0% were within moderate-to-severe depression categories, 99.3% endorsed high personal standards, and 74.1% reported frequent negative self-perceptions and social comparison. Across survey administrations, distributions varied between respondent pools, while overall patterns remained stable, indicating cross-sectional variation rather than intervention effects. Under authentic teaching conditions, the workshop was feasible, low-burden, and compatible with routine instruction. Ready-to-use materials and practice-based evidence are provided to support adoption and inform future confirmatory work
keywords: student mental health, general chemistry, perfectionism, social comparison, anxiety, depression, stigma reduction, self-regulation, reflection, first-year students, STEM education, mental health interventions

title: Firework Research: A Twist on a General Chemistry Laboratory Practical
text: Abstract Due to their striking colors and rapid progression, precipitation reactions and flame tests are two quintessential phenomena commonly showcased in general chemistry. This work presents a multipart experiment centered on these classic phenomena that is designed as a low-stakes midterm laboratory practical exam during a 150 minute laboratory period in the first semester of general chemistry. In an effort to reduce anxiety associated with high-stakes assessments and increase student enjoyment, this original laboratory practical exam has been reframed as a mini research project where students identify unknown metal salts that are used as firework colorants through flame tests, chemical color trends, and precipitation reactions. The experiment consists of six short parts that assess students’ understanding of various skills developed as part of a scaffolded curriculum in the first half of the laboratory course. The topics assessed include scientific vocabulary, glassware identification, Bunsen burner operation, stoichiometric calculations, standard solution preparation, qualitative observations, precipitation reactions, solubility, and gravity filtration. Instructional materials and information on implementation are presented. The efficacy of the experiment was shown by positive changes in student confidence and correctness when completing comparable questions over the course of the semester.
keywords: flame test, precipitation reaction, low-stakes assessment, qualitative analysis, student anxiety reduction, student self-confidence, solubility, gravity filtration, stoichiometric calculations, standard solution preparation

title: Student-Centered Teaching of the Electron-Transfer Chain in Biochemistry: Integrating Anime Analogies and Microbial Fuel Cell Concepts
text: Abstract Teaching the electron transfer chain (ETC) in biochemistry is challenging due to both its challenging nature and high cognitive load for students. In this study, we developed a student-centered instructional model that uses an anime storyline analogy and a microbial fuel cell (MFC) demonstration to enhance students’ interest, engagement, and understanding of the ETC. The model was implemented with junior undergraduate biology majors. In the experimental class, key steps of the ETC were illustrated through an adventure narrative featuring the anime character Pikachu, and a real-world bioelectricity generation example by MFC was incorporated. Interactive activities such as a jigsaw-puzzle game were used to reinforce knowledge integration. A control class was taught the same content using traditional lecture-based methods. Pre- and post-test scores, a student feedback questionnaire, and classroom observations were used to evaluate learning outcomes. The experimental class showed a significant improvement in post-test scores compared to the control class. The increase indicates a deep understanding of the ETC. Questionnaire responses also revealed that the anime analogy and gamified activities both increased student motivation and lowered their perceived cognitive load. Introducing the MFC case made the challenging concept of electron transfer tangible by linking it to observable electrical current generation. This integrated approach, blending cutting-edge science, core biochemical concepts, and students’ pop-culture interests, proved to be an effective and replicable way to teach an abstract biochemistry topic. It not only improved learning outcomes in the ETC chapter, but also helped foster students’ interdisciplinary thinking. Further adaptation of this model to different classroom settings and other abstract topics is recommended to explore its broad applicability.
keywords: electron transport chain, biochemistry education, student-centered learning, Pikachu, microbial fuel cells, gamification, cognitive load, student motivation, bioelectricity generation, conceptual understanding

title: Thin-Layer Electrochemistry: Visualizing the Diffusion Layer During Chronoamperometry and Cyclic Voltammetry
text: Abstract The phenomena that occur in the diffusion layer play a central role in electrochemical processes but are often challenging for students to understand. Here, we present a demonstration and activity to directly observe and analyze the changes in diffusion layer during chronoamperometry and cyclic voltammetry. Methyl viologen (MV2+), a redox indicator with distinct color changes upon one-electron reduction, was used to generate an observable color change. The reaction was carried out in a homemade thin-layer cell, and the color changes were monitored and recorded using an optical microscope equipped with a digital camera. In chronoamperometry, students examined the time dependence of current decay and diffusion-layer growth, then calculated the diffusion coefficient of the methyl viologen radical cation (MV+ •). In cyclic voltammetry, students visually tracked the appearance and disappearance of the colored diffusion layer during forward and reverse potential scans. Linking these visual observations to the electrochemical responses enhanced students’ ability to comprehend the underlying processes. This activity offers a versatile and visually engaging tool for teaching electrochemistry in both introductory and advanced courses.
keywords: diffusion layer, thin-layer cell, chronoamperometry, cyclic voltammetry, paraquat, diffusion coefficient, redox indicators

title: Linking Chemistry Learning to Careers: Impact of Career-Based Differentiated Instruction (CBDI) on STEM Students’ Self-Efficacy and Outcome Expectations
text: Abstract Despite efforts to achieve Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 4.4, which seeks to increase the number of youth and adults with vocational skills for employment, STEM education in the Philippines continues to face gaps in career relevance that link classroom learning with workforce needs. This study aimed to develop and validate a career-based differentiated instruction (CBDI) resource package in General Chemistry 1 for teachers and evaluate its impact on STEM students’ self-efficacy and outcome expectations. The development phase entailed applying chemistry concepts to fields in engineering, technology, and health. Experts affirmed the relevance of CBDI in these career fields. The implementation phase used a quasi-experimental design with 161 grade 12 STEM students using pre- and post-tests through Career Decision Self-Efficacy (CDSE) and Vocational Outcome Expectations (VOE) scales. Paired samples t-test showed no significant changes in the control group, while the experimental group achieved significant improvements in self-efficacy [t(84) = −9.30, p < 0.001] and outcome expectations [t(84) = −5.95, p < 0.001] after eight (8) weeks of intervention. Independent samples t-test confirmed significantly greater gains for the experimental group in self-efficacy [t(155) = −5.26, p < 0.001] and outcome expectations [t(158) = −4.08, p < 0.001]. Reflexive thematic analysis from classroom observations and student reflections further supported these results, highlighting career-based laboratory experiments, collaborative activities, problem-solving, and case studies as mechanisms of improvement. The study concludes that the developed CBDI resource package is valid and that its implementation significantly improved students’ self-efficacy and outcome expectations. It recommends classroom adoption, school integration, and policy-driven pilot implementation.
keywords: chemistry education, self-efficacy, outcome expectations, STEM students, career relevance, vocational skills, career decision-making self-efficacy, Philippines

title: Molecular Orbital Theory for Octahedral Complexes: Playing with Cards
text: Abstract Teaching Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT) is often challenging due to its abstract concepts and mathematical formalism, which can make it difficult for students to grasp. To make this content more accessible and engaging, we developed a card game based on MOT principles. In this game, each card represents either a metal orbital, a group of ligand orbitals, or the resulting molecular orbitals generated through Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO). The objective is to form trios of cards that represent and require the evaluation of orbital combinations involved in the bonding interactions of octahedral coordination complexes. The activity was implemented in an Inorganic Chemistry II course at the Federal University of Espírito Santo (UFES). A five-question multiple-choice test was administered before and after the game to explore its potential impact on student understanding. Results suggested trends consistent with improvement in student performance, with an increase in the number of correct answers and a reduction in “I don’t know” responses. In addition, a postactivity questionnaire revealed highly positive student perceptions: students highlighted that the game made learning more enjoyable, interactive, and collaborative, while also supporting the understanding of complex concepts. These findings are consistent with the integration of strategies, such as this low-cost and easily reproducible card game, supporting student engagement and contributing to the learning of abstract concepts in coordination chemistry and beyond.
keywords: molecular orbital theory, octahedral complexes, coordination chemistry, card games, game-based learning, linear combination of atomic orbitals, student engagement, inorganic chemistry education, student perceptions

title: Regression and Residual Analysis in the Spectroscopic Study of Conjugated Dyes
text: Abstract The study of conjugated dyes within the framework of the one-dimensional particle-in-a-box (1D PIB) model is a fundamental experiment in undergraduate physical chemistry curricula. This work extends the analysis of this commonplace experiment with the inclusion of regression and residual analysis, which allows students to explore data fitting, parameterization, and model testing in a controlled fashion. The work herein describes an instructor-led activity to optimize an empirical factor used in a 1D PIB model for a series of cyanine dyes and their respective visible absorption spectra. Students gain experiential use of regression and residual analysis within a process that facilitates a consistent experience for all, independent of the quality of data collected. This makes for an effective educational tool for teaching regression and residual analysis and model parameterization.
keywords: cyanine dyes, particle-in-a-box model, regression analysis, residual analysis, model parameterization, visible absorption spectra, data fitting

title: Development and Application of a Customized Board Game, Block Building Biosensors , To Improve the Assimilation of (Bio)Sensor Concepts: An Active Methodology Approach To Tackle the Device Design Challenge
text: Abstract The field of biosensors is currently recognized as one of the most significant areas of research in analytical chemistry. However, designing these devices presents challenges due to the numerous options available and the impact of various components (biological recognition elements, transducers, and modifiers) on the resulting analytical features. Students also often struggle with assimilating the concepts related to this topic. To address this issue, we present a novel board game specifically designed to facilitate this learning process. This work provides a comprehensive description of the game design and fabrication process. Additionally, it includes relevant considerations for guiding future research. The results obtained were highly positive, both in terms of student feedback regarding the game design and their subsequent evaluation of the basic and advanced concepts learned, demonstrating the game effectiveness in development and application.
keywords: board games, biosensors, game-based learning, active learning, game design, student engagement, analytical chemistry education, biorecognition elements, transducers

title: Reconstructing the Teaching of Activity and Activity Coefficients Centered on Intermolecular Forces: Progressive Modular Teaching Reconstruction and Practice Based on Physical Mechanism Classification
text: Abstract Activity and activity coefficients in chemical engineering thermodynamics feature both in-depth microscopic molecular mechanisms and intensive macroscopic engineering calculations, representing a core teaching pain point where students struggle to internalize concepts and tend to solve problems mechanically. Traditional teaching generally introduces activity coefficient models─ideal solution, Margules, Van Laar, Flory–Huggins, Wilson, NRTL, etc.─in chronological order of their development, leading to severely fragmented knowledge points, disconnected physical mechanisms, and a situation where students only apply formulas without understanding engineering model selection. This article breaks away from the outdated teaching paradigm of “listing models by era” and innovatively adopts a new perspective of classification by physical mechanisms. All activity coefficient models are uniformly categorized into four physical types: enthalpy-effect-dominated, entropy-effect-dominated, local composition microscopic enrichment, and energy–volume coupling. An integrated cognitive chain is constructed: “root of molecular forces → two core mechanisms of nonideality → progressive physical classification of models → precise selection for engineering scenarios”. Taking the typical polar–nonpolar ethanol–cyclohexane mixture system as a case throughout the course, the reform is supported by problem-oriented modular teaching, molecular dynamics microscopic visualization demonstrations, and an integrated “prediction–validation–modeling” reform of vapor–liquid equilibrium experiments. This achieves a cognitive leap for students from “memorizing formulas for numerical calculation” to “understanding mechanisms for model selection”. Teaching practice shows that the proportion of students who grasped the physical essence of activity coefficients rose from 12.2% to 88.0% after the reform and that the score rate of students’ ability to select and apply engineering models increased by 38.9%, as verified by standardized pretests and post-tests covering three dimensions, including conceptual understanding, phenomenon interpretation, and engineering application, as well as an independent sample t test. This provides a directly replicable paradigm reference for the advanced teaching reconstruction of core concepts in chemical engineering thermodynamics in universities and is mainly applicable to senior undergraduate students and graduate students majoring in chemical engineering.
keywords: activity coefficients, activity coefficient models, intermolecular interactions, model selection, non-idealities, vapor-liquid equilibrium, molecular dynamics visualization, modular teaching, NRTL model

title: Pick Your Own Adventure: Orthogonal Methods for Analyzing Polyphenols
text: Abstract The analytical chemistry classroom is naturally poised to demonstrate the use of orthogonal techniques to quantify different molecules such as polyphenols. Using food science as a lens and a molecule-centric, inquiry-based approach, this article describes a semester-long laboratory experience for students to adapt and use potentiometric titration, spectrophotometric, and chromatographic methods to analyze polyphenols (i.e., catechin and gallic acid) in instructor-provided samples. Students then are given the agency to select a sample of interest which (theoretically) contains the target analytes (or not) and justify the appropriate method for that sample. The implementation of this experience provides students with many opportunities to authentically engage in scientific practices, such as designing experiments, evaluating their results, and making evidence-based decisions about how to modify procedures and what samples to study. After completing this laboratory experience, students reported significant gains in learning laboratory techniques and moderate gains in designing experiments and analyzing data, while engaging in authentic analyses (including variability) in a supportive environment. Peer evaluations also indicated that students had positive experiences working in groups. Furthermore, the experience is incredibly flexible. Each standard method module (titration, spectrophotometry, chromatography) can be completed independently, or more orthogonal techniques (e.g., gas chromatography) could be added to expand the molecule-centric semester experience.
keywords: polyphenols, catechins, gallic acid, potentiometric titration, spectrophotometry, chromatography, food analysis, inquiry-based learning, laboratory design, food science, analytical chemistry education, student agency

title: The French-Speaking Chemists’ Tournament: A Laboratory-Based Team Debate Competition to Foster Research Skills through Challenge-Based Learning
text: Abstract In the context of teaching laboratory skills, research- and challenge-based approaches are increasingly valued for fostering inquiry, collaboration, and authentic (real-world context) problem-solving. The Tournoi Francophone des Chimistes (French-speaking Chemists’ Tournament, TFChim) implements these approaches through a laboratory-based team debate competition in which senior undergraduate and early graduate students from 13 French-speaking institutions develop and defend original experimental solutions to open-ended chemistry problems. These problems use a challenge-based learning approach, providing authentic opportunities for research, design, and interdisciplinary exploration in real-world or imaginary contexts. Over several months, teams design these solutions before presenting them and critiquing others in structured debates during a two-day tournament. A survey has been administered to the participants at the conclusion of the tournament. Its responses indicate strong perceived gains, particularly in research competencies such as inquiry skills, with most gains occurring during the extended preparation phase. Analyses also show no significant differences between teams, highlighting the consistency of the learning experience across numerous institutions. TFChim offers a novel research-based learning format for laboratory work, and provides a solid framework for developing international online versions or institution-level competitions that engage multiple disciplines in addressing complex problems implemented in authentic situations.
keywords: challenge-based learning, research skills, inquiry skills, undergraduate chemistry education, authentic problem solving, international student competition

title: Implementing a High-Relevance Redox Course in Everyday-Life Contexts: Effects on Motivation, Attitudes, and Perceived Relevance among Middle School Science Teachers and Pre-Service Teachers
text: Abstract Oxidation–reduction chemistry is central to chemistry education, yet it remains difficult because learners must coordinate visible change, particulate explanation, symbolic notation, and electron transfer. This mixed-methods study examined a high-relevance redox course delivered to two intact Arab-majority teacher cohorts in northern Israel: 50 preservice science teachers and 60 in-service middle school science teachers. The course joined everyday and societal contexts with explicit representational work, misconception analysis, demonstrations, guided discussions, and instructional design tasks. Quantitative measures assessed attitudes toward chemistry, science learning motivation, and perceived relevance before and after the course. Final projects and ten semistructured interviews were used to interpret the quantitative patterns. Paired comparisons showed significant motivation gains in both cohorts and a significant perceived-relevance gain only among preservice teachers. Attitude changes were positive, but not statistically significant. Project scores indicated that participants produced contextually grounded redox tasks under course conditions, although the study did not establish their classroom effectiveness. Qualitative evidence suggests that preservice teachers tended to describe relevance as an expansion of chemistry’s civic and explanatory purpose, whereas in-service teachers more often evaluated relevance through feasibility, curricular pressure, and differentiated student needs. The findings are interpreted cautiously because the design lacked a comparison group, and the qualitative sample was limited.
keywords: redox chemistry, redox reactions, pre-service science teachers, perceived relevance, science motivation, attitudes toward chemistry, everyday situations, misconceptions, instructional design, chemistry teacher education

title: Proper Use of Parentheses and Square Brackets in Describing Cycloaddition Reactions: A Discussion on Normative Practices
text: Abstract Cycloaddition reactions constitute a crucial chapter in organic chemistry education and remain a perennial frontier of chemical research. This article addresses the nonstandardized use of bracket symbols commonly observed in current teaching materials and research literature concerning cycloaddition reactions. It systematically clarifies the appropriate contexts and chemical significance represented by parentheses “()” and square brackets “[ ]” in the notation of cycloaddition reactions based on IUPAC recommendations and authoritative teaching practices. Through an analysis of textbook examples and contemporary research articles, we document the prevalence of inconsistent usage. To assess the practical impact of this inconsistency, we conducted a controlled study of organic chemistry students. The results revealed significant initial confusion regarding symbol interpretation, which was effectively remediated by explicit instruction on the IUPAC convention, confirming the pedagogical importance of the standardized notation. Our aim is to provide clear guidelines for the use of these symbols in chemical pedagogy and academic writing, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the instructional expression and the standardization of scholarly communication.
keywords: cycloaddition, parentheses, chemical notation, IUPAC recommendations, notation standardization, organic chemistry education, student confusion

title: Constructing Crystal Structure Models with Poly(vinyl alcohol) Beads
text: Abstract This article presents the construction of metallic, ionic and network covalent crystal structure models using poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) beads. With the assistance of the baseplates, the crystal structure models can be easily constructed layer by layer, and they can be decomposed into multiple parallel crystal planes from a specific perspective to uncover the stacking nature of atoms/ions in crystals. Model construction based on the PVA beads can improve students’ spatial visualization of crystal structures, helping them conceptualize the structural characteristics of various types of crystals. It can not only stimulate students’ enthusiasm for learning but also cultivate their teamwork ability simultaneously. In the teaching practice, students expressed overwhelmingly positive feedback on this model kit, and they exhibited a high level of interest in collaborating with their classmates to construct crystal structure models. In addition, this model kit is cost-effective and portable, and thus it exhibits extremely high practicality for hands-on activities and classroom demonstrations in the teaching of crystal structures.
keywords: crystal structure model, model kits, metal crystals, ionic crystals, spatial visualization, hands-on learning, chemistry education, crystal planes, teamwork

title: Effects of Temperature and Salinity on the Germination of Triticum aestivum
text: In this laboratory exercise, students explore the potential impacts of temperature and salinity on agricultural systems. Specifically, wheat seed germination was evaluated across a temperature range of 15-35 °C and in the presence or absence of sodium chloride (NaCl), thereby simulating scenarios of rising temperatures and increasing soil salinity. The primary objective of this activity was to raise students' awareness of the challenges that climate change may pose to crop production and, consequently, to promote critical thinking about agronomic strategies that could mitigate these adverse effects. The results indicate that both root and shoot growth of wheat seedlings increase as temperature rises within the tested range. However, at elevated temperatures (35 °C), particularly under saline conditions, both root and shoot development were markedly reduced. These findings allow students to examine the interactive effects of temperature and salinity stress while connecting experimental observations to broader environmental and agricultural issues.
keywords: wheat seed germination, wheat, temperature effects, salt stress, sodium chloride, root growth, shoot growth, climate change impacts on agriculture, crop production

title: A Teaching Experiment on Moisturizing Hydrogels for Ivory Protection: From a Single-Layer Acrylic Hydrogel to a Silicone-Modified Bilayer Hydrogel
text: Abstract Chemistry plays an essential role in the conservation of water-sensitive organic artifacts. Unearthed ivory objects from the Sanxingdui site are particularly vulnerable to irreversible damage, such as cracking and powdering, due to moisture loss. This challenge provides a real-world context that naturally stimulates postgraduate students’ interest and engagement. To address it, we designed a laboratory project that integrates professional education with research practice. Students prepared both a single-layer poly(acrylamide-co-acrylic acid) (P(AM-AA)) hydrogel and a bilayer hydrogel combined with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) (P(AM-AA)/PDMS). The materials were characterized (e.g., for chemical structure, optical properties, mechanical behavior, and thermal stability), and their performance was tested under 25 °C and 50% relative humidity (RH). The bilayer hydrogel outperformed the single-layer hydrogel and an untreated control group in preserving the weight and morphology of ivory and plant sample. Based on a post-experiment questionnaire, students reported significantly strengthened awareness of cultural-heritage conservation and enhanced ability to justify material selection and design. The questionnaire also revealed that students deepened their understanding of four core chemical concepts, which are hydrophilicity, hydrophobicity, hydrogen bonding, and interfacial adhesion, and directly applied them to the bilayer hydrogel design. Overall, students expressed high levels of engagement and satisfaction, noting that the authentic research context effectively improved their integrated experimental competencies in polymer materials chemistry and their research capability to solve real-world protection problems. The proposed hydrogel-based approach also provides a potential material strategy for the conservation of other moisture-sensitive cultural heritage materials.
keywords: polydimethylsiloxane, bilayer hydrogel, moisture loss, chemistry education, cultural heritage preservation, student engagement, hydrogen bonding, interfacial adhesion, hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity

title: Interdisciplinary CURE Studying Protein Aggregation with Super-Resolution Fluorescence Microscopy Promotes Student Scientific Self-Efficacy and Sense of Belonging
text: Abstract Research experiences are a powerful means of engaging students and a critical component of education in STEM fields. However, at large universities, the number of STEM undergraduate students greatly outnumbers the positions available in faculty research laboratories. Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) provide research experiences for larger numbers of students and have been shown to support recruitment and retention of diverse student populations in STEM majors. Here, we describe a new CURE developed for first-year and transfer students to study protein aggregation with single-molecule, super-resolution fluorescence microscopy. Super-resolution fluorescence microscopy (the technique recognized by the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry) is a powerful tool for characterizing the growth and structures of protein aggregates associated with human disease. The CURE is highly interdisciplinary, combining biological and chemical wet-lab work with the chemistry and physics of single-molecule, super-resolution fluorescence microscopy and image-processing and analysis on the computer. Assessments of the CURE indicate that it (1) provides students with authentic research experiences of collaboration, discovery and relevance, and iteration, (2) improves factors such as scientific self-efficacy and sense of belonging that have been linked to improved student outcomes and persistence in STEM majors, and (3) contributes to personal student gains in the context of science. The CURE can be adapted to the study of any aggregation-prone proteins, enabling future adoptions and collaborations.
keywords: course-based undergraduate research experiences, protein aggregation, super-resolution fluorescence microscopy, single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, sense of belonging, STEM retention, interdisciplinary research, protein aggregation diseases

title: Interactive Radiative Forcing Learning Tool To Connect Climate Science to Chemistry Curriculum
text: Abstract Radiative forcing, the change in Earth’s energy balance since the beginning of the First Industrial Revolution in 1750, is the ultimate driver of climate change and one of the core Earth system processes that determines whether we are living within our planetary boundaries. Substances that are positive radiative forcers increase Earth’s energy imbalance and contribute to warming, while negative radiative forcers decrease Earth’s energy imbalance and cause cooling. Though radiative forcing is central to understanding the mechanisms that drive climate change, it is an unfamiliar concept to many chemistry students and the public. To bridge this knowledge gap, the King’s Centre for Visualization in Science (KCVS) has developed an online interactive learning tool to help students explore these concepts further and connect climate change to their learning of core chemistry content. The learning tool visualizes changes in radiative forcing over time and quantifies how each of the key substances’ interactions in the atmosphere have contributed to positive and negative radiative forcing. By engaging with this resource, students, educators, and the public can learn about the sources, impacts, and solutions to mitigate anthropogenic emissions of each radiative forcer. Initial assessment of the learning tool with undergraduate introductory chemistry students demonstrated that the learning tool was successful in increasing their foundational understanding of radiative forcing and its most important contributors.
keywords: radiative forcing, climate change, interactive learning tools, Earth's energy balance, anthropogenic emissions, chemistry education, planetary boundaries, climate change mitigation

title: Spiral Integration of Organic Synthesis and Instrumental Characterization Using Ferrocenyl Chalcones
text: Undergraduate chemistry curricula often present organic synthesis and instrumental analysis as disconnected experiences, limiting students' ability to integrate structural, spectroscopic, and materials-focused concepts when interpreting authentic data. To address this problem, we implemented a spiral laboratory experience in a third-year Instrumental Analysis course at a Hispanic-serving research university (n ≈ 48) in which students revisited ferrocenyl chalcones synthesized in a prior organic chemistry course and analyzed them as "unknowns" using complementary chromatographic, spectroscopic, and thermal analysis techniques. This reintegration required students to draw on prior synthetic knowledge while developing new analytical reasoning skills by interpreting data collected across multiple analytical methods.
