A structured artificial intelligence (AI) prelaboratory component asked students to use targeted prompts to predict characteristic signatures, supporting conceptual preparation, and promoting critical evaluation of AI-generated chemical information. Assessment of laboratory reports and postactivity surveys revealed increased student confidence with analytical instrumentation, improved ability to integrate concepts across subdisciplines, and increased engagement with materials-oriented applications of organometallic compounds. This activity provides a replicable model for addressing curricular fragmentation by combining spiral integration, integrative analytical reasoning, and responsible AI use within the undergraduate chemistry laboratory.
keywords: ferrocenyl chalcones, organic synthesis, instrumental analysis, undergraduate laboratory curriculum, responsible AI use, organometallic compounds, materials chemistry, interdisciplinary integration, Hispanic-serving institutions

title: Climate Justice Course Modules and Chemical Forms Scaffolding Tool for Systems Thinking in General Chemistry at Two-Year Colleges: An Exploratory Assessment
text: Abstract Educators and researchers have called for systems thinking in chemistry education to prepare future STEM professionals and citizens to address 21st century sustainability challenges. A variety of frameworks, teaching practices, and classroom resources that support this goal are being developed as chemistry educators work to understand their effectiveness. We used course module interventions centered on climate justice issues to develop systems thinking competencies in students. We embedded these modules into a two-year college general chemistry course and designed a prepost case study assessment to understand their effect on students’ systems thinking competencies. Preliminary results and classroom observations made while developing our assessment led us to develop a scaffolding tool that uses periodic trends to support students’ competencies for identifying the chemical forms in which elements and compounds exist in real-world systems. In this paper, we present our chemical forms scaffolding tool and assessment of students’ systems thinking. Our assessment results suggest that the module interventions and scaffolding tool supported students’ competency development. Based on these findings, we offer our modules, scaffolding tool, and assessment to other chemistry educators and researchers for classroom use and future studies that will further our understanding of effective approaches, teaching practices, and classroom resources that support systems thinking in chemistry education.
keywords: systems thinking, climate justice, general chemistry education, community colleges, chemical form, periodic trends, course modules, case study assessment, sustainability education, chemistry education

title: Enhancing Science Communication through Deliberative Discussions on Water Contamination in a General Chemistry Lab at an HBCU
text: In Spring 2023 (pilot study, n = 24) and Spring 2024 (main study, n = 48; survey respondents n = 36), second-semester General Chemistry II laboratory students at Xavier University of Louisiana, a Historically Black College and University (HBCU), participated in a classroom activity designed to enhance science communication skills through deliberative discussions on water contamination issues. Following qualitative analysis experiments on heavy metal ions, students engaged in structured small-group deliberations evaluating real-world water contamination challenges and policy solutions. The activity was explicitly aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) #6: Clean Water and Sanitation, providing a global sustainability framework for student discussions. Survey results indicate increased student engagement, improved understanding of water contamination, and enhanced confidence in communicating scientific concepts to nonspecialist audiences. While most students reported increased interest in science communication and STEM careers, some indicated the need for additional support to build confidence. These findings demonstrate that integrating deliberative, sustainability-focused discussions into laboratory courses effectively connects experimental chemistry to societal challenges while fostering scientific literacy and communication skills.
keywords: science communication, deliberative discussion, water pollution, general chemistry laboratory, historically Black colleges and universities, heavy metal ions, small group discussion, sustainability education, SDG 6, clean water and sanitation, scientific literacy, student self-confidence, STEM career interest, chemistry education

title: Three-Dimensional Printing of Metal–Organic Framework Crystal Structure Models for Chemical Education: Methods and Applications
text: Abstract Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) pose a substantial challenge for creating high-fidelity physical models for educational use because of their intricate structures. Here, we report two 3D printing strategies designed to overcome limitations in structural accuracy, dynamic visualization, and cost-effectiveness. Using stereolithography, we fabricated millimeter-scale monolithic models of representative MOFs including UiO-66 and MOF-303. To improve color differentiation, scalability, and structural flexibility, we developed a modular “disassemble-then-assemble” approach based on multicolor fused deposition modeling. This method enabled the construction of flexible MOF models (MOF-808, MOF-5, BUC-88, and BUC-95) using PVC tubing as connectors. These interactive models allow students to simulate framework dynamics and explore structure–property relationships. In a small science outreach activity, retrospective pre/post-self-assessment showed a notable improvement in students’ self-perceived understanding: 16 of 17 participants reported higher comprehension levels following the intervention.
keywords: metal-organic frameworks, 3D printing, crystal structure model, stereolithography, fused deposition modeling, UiO-66, MOF-303, MOF-808, MOF-5, structure-property relationships, science outreach, student self-assessment, chemistry education

title: Investigating Relationships Between Environmental Justice and Science Identity in an Analytical Chemistry Course
text: Abstract This work is centered on exploring students’ science identities as they pertain to environmental justice (EJ). Our research is positioned in an analytical chemistry course that incorporates in-depth discussion on EJ, broader discussions of sustainability, and career-focused applications. The curriculum is intended to build communities within and outside of the classroom, empower marginalized students, and recognize student achievement in diverse scientific contexts. The Just Transition Framework centers the worker as key to societal transition from an extractive economy to a regenerative economy and has been incorporated into an environmental justice dialogue. The purpose of the dialogue was to support building community, developing a holistic science identity, and generating ideas related to environmental justice. Students were further asked to prepare a presentation relating systems thinking and United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs) to a recent research publication. In this work we analyze student written reflections on the dialogue and their presentations. We examined how students plan to use EJ in their career. We further examined how students discuss their science identity with respect to EJ and the scientific practices students relate to EJ. We further identified elements of systems thinking that students plan to use in their careers. This work contributes an understanding of student aspirational beliefs and practices associated with EJ.
keywords: environmental justice, science identity, analytical chemistry education, systems thinking, Sustainable Development Goals, student career aspirations, marginalized students, community building, scientific practice, student reflection

title: The Effect of a Flipped-Classroom-Enhanced Guided-Inquiry Curriculum on Attitudes and Course Satisfaction of First-Generation Underrepresented Minority Students in Chemistry Courses
text: Abstract A quasi-experimental intervention presurvey/postsurvey design study was conducted with undergraduate college students in general chemistry and organic chemistry courses to reduce large educational equity gaps in STEM fields that are experienced by Hispanic and other underrepresented minority (URM) students who live in California’s Central Valley. This study encompasses undergraduate student populations from two Hispanic Serving Institutions (HSIs) in the San Joaquin Valley, specifically, a California State University campus and a local community college. A novel combination of two pedagogies was implemented into the course: flipped classroom and guided-inquiry group work (including POGIL and new activities inspired by POGIL). The study compared attitudinal change and change in satisfaction with the chemistry courses via a within group analysis. Findings showed that at the conclusion of the course following implementation of the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry curriculum, attitude toward chemistry (for Hispanic and Latino students, M = 29.81, SD = 4.37; for non-Hispanic or Latino students, M = 29.42, SD = 4.71) and satisfaction with chemistry course (for Hispanic and Latino students, M = 12.17, SD = 5.97; for non-Hispanic or Latino students, M = 10.76, SD = 5.46) were higher for Hispanic and Latino students but not statistically significant. For satisfaction with chemistry course, an independent samples t test showed that there was no significant difference (t(179) = −0.038, p ≥ 0.05) for satisfaction with chemistry course for first-generation (M = 11.56, SD = 5.63) and non-first-generation students (M = 11.59, SD = 5.98) at the conclusion of the course following implementation of the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry curriculum. However, an independent samples t test indicated a statistically significant difference (t(179) = 2.25, p ≤ 0.05) following implementation of the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry curriculum in attitude toward chemistry for first-generation students (M = 30.22, SD = 4.81) and non-first-generation students (M = 28.71, SD = 3.74). These findings suggest that the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry model in undergraduate college chemistry courses may potentially lead to a decrease in equity gaps and consequently lead to an increase in first-generation underrepresented minority students who enter STEM workforce careers.
keywords: flipped classroom, POGIL, first-generation college students, underrepresented minority students, Hispanic students, chemistry education, student attitudes toward chemistry, course satisfaction, educational equity, Hispanic-serving institutions, general chemistry, organic chemistry, Central Valley, community colleges, STEM retention

title: Exploring ChatGPT’s Career-Based Contextualization of Chemistry Content
text: Abstract Contextualizing chemistry problems to connect disciplinary ideas with real-world or career settings has long been an instructional goal, yet analyses of widely used general chemistry textbooks suggest that such a framing is often limited or absent. This exploratory study examines how generative AI produces career-contextualized versions of general chemistry problems using elaboration prompting and how features of the underlying task may influence those outputs. Three second-semester topics differing in chemical specificity and the presence or absence of an explicit problem purpose were used to analyze chatbot-generated questions across six career domains. The chatbot frequently preserved the original chemical systems, calculations, and answer structures while introducing professional narratives, indicating that the model often treated the original problem as a template for contextual variation. Patterns of contextual integration appeared to vary across both chemistry topics and career domains. Problems involving defined chemical systems and explicit purposes more often supported professional decision-making scenarios, whereas problems focused on reporting numerical results tended to retain procedural structures even when narratives were introduced. These findings suggest that AI-generated contextualization often preserves the disciplinary structure of the original chemistry task while layering professional narratives around it, highlighting both the potential and the limitations of generative AI for career-based contextualization.
keywords: generative AI, ChatGPT, chemistry education, professional narratives, AI-generated questions, chemical specificity, disciplinary structure

title: Covalent Organic Framework for Uranium Detection Using Colorimetry: A Simple Chemistry Experiment for Undergraduate Students
text: Abstract The objective of this study was successfully achieved by engaging undergraduate students in the preparation and application of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for the colorimetric detection of uranium. The COFs were synthesized via a one-step condensation reaction followed by nucleation, both of which were accessible and manageable for undergraduate training. Characterization of the COFs and the subsequent experimental procedure were conducted with students, and the resulting data were analyzed and plotted using Origin software. The interaction between COFs and uranium ions demonstrated their effectiveness as a sensor, with a UV–visible absorption spectrophotometer used as the primary detection method. This approach achieved an average limit of detection (LOD) of 1.74 μM with a concentration range of 2.1–13.8 μM. This work highlights several key advantages: (i) the use of a straightforward and environmentally friendly condensation method for COFs preparation, (ii) the feasibility of a 72 h nucleation process suitable for undergraduate laboratory practice, and (iii) the adoption of a colorimetry detection method that is sensitive, cost-effective, and easy to operate. Overall, this experiment provided students with valuable experience in material synthesis, data analysis, and application of UV–visible absorption spectroscopy for real-world environmental challenges, thereby strengthening both their experimental and conceptual understanding of chemistry.
keywords: covalent organic frameworks, uranium detection, colorimetric sensing, nucleation, condensation synthesis, undergraduate laboratory experiment, UV-Vis spectroscopy, detection limit, environmental monitoring, chemistry education

title: Integrating Environmental Justice into Selected Organic Chemistry Topics: Development and Validation of an Innovative Learning Packet
text: Abstract This study developed and provided initial evidence on the use of an environmental justice-integrated learning packet in organic chemistry. The instructional material was evaluated using a multidimensional framework assessing accuracy, inclusivity, instructional effectiveness, and usability, as well as its potential to promote skills development and civic responsibility. Results indicated high expert ratings across all evaluation dimensions. Student data showed positive trends in engagement and improvements in pre- to post-test scores, as analyzed using the Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test (Z = −2.94, p = 0.003), with a large effect size (r = 0.849). While these findings suggest the potential pedagogical value of integrating environmental justice into organic chemistry, the results should be interpreted as preliminary and context-specific. This study contributes a validated instructional resource and offers initial insights into how socially relevant contexts may support student engagement and learning in chemistry.
keywords: environmental justice, organic chemistry education, teaching materials, student engagement, civic responsibility

title: Probing High School Students’ Knowledge and Cognitive Structures in Electrochemistry: A Combined Use of Concept Mapping and Epistemic Network Analysis
text: Abstract The interconnected nature of concepts in electrochemistry (EC) poses significant challenges for students. This study distinguished knowledge structure (KS)─alignment with an intended knowledge system─from cognitive structure (CS)─the mental network that organizes and guides domain knowledge. Using concept mapping (CM) and epistemic network analysis (ENA), this study probed high school students’ KS and CS in EC and compared high- versus low-achieving groups. KS was examined through segment mastery, morphological patterns, and cross-links. CS was characterized via clustering patterns, associative strength, and cognitive emphasis. Group comparisons employed KS typology (classifying students’ maps and comparing distributions), alongside ENA subtracted networks and centroid positions for CS. Six knowledge segments were identified from CM, with the “electrode reaction equation” segment as the primary bottleneck due to superficial recognition and few cross-links. Organized into principle, application, and representation clusters, the CS model exhibited “principle” as the cognitive hub, strongly co-occurring with the others. High-achievers demonstrated more coherent KS and broadly distributed associations, with centroids shifting toward the “representation” dimension; low-achievers showed scattered KS and localized associations, with centroids near the “application” dimension. The findings informed high school EC teaching and helped university educators bridge learning transitions by revealing students’ prior knowledge.
keywords: electrochemistry, high school students, prior knowledge, cognitive structure, knowledge structure, concept mapping, epistemic network analysis, achievement differences, chemistry education, prior knowledge assessment

title: Density Calculation Using Cubic Equations of State: A Python-Based Framework for Thermodynamics Education
text: Abstract Density is a critical thermodynamic property in chemical engineering and physical chemistry. However, many undergraduate students encounter equations of state (EoS) only symbolically, without connecting them to practical computations or visualizations. This work introduces an open-source Python framework for calculating and comparing fluid densities via four classical cubic EoS-van der Waals, Redlich–Kwong, Soave–Redlich–Kwong, and Peng–Robinson methods. The modular CubicEoS class enables learners to compute liquid and vapor densities, visualize temperature–density behavior, and evaluate model accuracy through mean relative deviation metrics. Using experimental methane–propane data, the instructional case study illustrates both predictive (kij = 0) and fitted (kij optimized) modeling modes. The framework was implemented with 25 participants in a guided classroom activity using Google Colab, and pre- and postactivity questionnaires were used to evaluate students’ prior experience, perceived learning, interpretation of results, and confidence in using computational tools. This resource advances computational and conceptual learning in thermodynamics, supporting reproducible and code-based chemistry instruction.
keywords: cubic equations of state, van der Waals equation, Redlich-Kwong equation of state, Soave-Redlich-Kwong equation of state, Peng-Robinson equation of state, thermodynamics education, Python framework, methane-propane mixtures, Google Colab, learning outcomes

title: Hydrogel Biomaterials Laboratory Modules for Biotransport Education
text: Abstract Biotransport, the movement of molecules, energy, and momentum within biological systems, is a foundational concept in biomolecular science and chemical engineering. Acquiring a thorough understanding of biotransport phenomena is essential for the next generation of scientists and engineers to advance applications such as tissue engineering, gene and drug delivery, and biomedical device design. Practical exposure to biomaterial transport phenomena can help develop an intuitive understanding of these concepts. There is a need for accessible, hands-on, and cost-effective laboratory modules to teach biotransport principles at multiple educational levels. As water-swollen macromolecular networks, hydrogels serve as an ideal model system due to their tunable properties and physiological relevance. Here, we present a collection of laboratory modules designed to introduce students to the principles of biotransport and factors influencing molecular diffusion using hydrogel biomaterials. In these laboratory activities, students learn to fabricate both natural and synthetic hydrogels and investigate molecular diffusion as a function of temperature, polymer cross-linking density, polymer concentration, and molecular weight of substance. These modules demonstrate the influence of polymer properties on diffusion but also provide a platform for introducing fundamental polymer chemistry concepts such as polymerization, cross-linking, swelling, and degradation. The experiments are designed to be performed using widely available laboratory materials and equipment, making them suitable for a broad range of educational settings. Together, these hydrogel-based laboratory modules offer an accessible approach for teaching biotransport phenomena, enhancing student engagement, and improving learning outcomes for students with limited background in biomaterials science and engineering.
keywords: hydrogels, biotransport, molecular diffusion, laboratory modules, hydrogel swelling, hydrogel degradation, polymerization, polymer chemistry, hands-on teaching, drug delivery, tissue engineering

title: Smartphone Application throughout Comprehensive Chemistry Experiment: A Case Study of Tofu Preparation Video Recording and Quantitative Detection of Protein in Tofu
text: Abstract Traditional challenges in chemistry laboratory instruction, such as equipment scarcity, limited real-time supervision, difficulty in tracing error sources, and underdeveloped student skills in scientific expression and reflection, have long been recognized. To address these gaps, a smartphone-integrated teaching model was developed for a comprehensive chemistry experiment involving tofu preparation and protein quantification. Students were engaged with concepts of protein chemistry, colloid stability, and quantitative analysis through hands-on activities using homemade photoboxes, smartphone video recording, and mobile video editing. A quasi-experimental design was employed, in which 166 undergraduate chemistry education students were divided into an experimental group (n = 130) that followed the smartphone-integrated model and a control group (n = 36) that used traditional methods with a UV–vis spectrophotometer and paper-based reports. The results indicated that the smartphone-integrated model significantly outperformed traditional instruction: the experimental group showed a significantly lower operational error rate (9% vs 28%); improved scientific expression was reported by 85% of students; enhanced reflective ability was shown by 67%; and the model’s transferability was affirmed by 94% of preservice teachers. For instructors, complete procedural documentation, precise error diagnosis, enriched assessment, and visually specific feedback were achieved. Student perceptions were overwhelmingly positive, with the model recommended by 96% of students. Implementation challenges were manageable through targeted instructor interventions. This work illustrates an effective smartphone-integrated experimental design for resource-limited settings, through which students are trained in laboratory skills, digital literacy, scientific communication, and reflective practice─competencies essential for future science educators.
keywords: protein quantification, colloidal stability, protein chemistry, error diagnosis, scientific expression, reflective practice, pre-service chemistry teachers, resource-limited laboratories, digital literacy, chemistry laboratory skills

title: A Hot-Process Soap-Making Experiment Using Potassium Hydroxide to Explore Triglyceride Structure and Soap Properties
text: Abstract Esters are widely present in everyday materials, and their study is important for understanding fundamental concepts in organic chemistry. This work presents a laboratory activity based on the saponification of different triglyceride mixtures through alkaline hydrolysis with potassium hydroxide. The experiment integrates stoichiometric calculations, hot-process soap preparation, and qualitative evaluation of the final products. Through hands-on experimentation, students investigate how variations in fatty acid composition influence the physicochemical properties of the soaps obtained, including foam formation, texture, and appearance. The activity enables direct observation of the reaction process and supports discussion of the relationship between molecular structure and macroscopic behavior. The proposed experiment connects ester chemistry to real-world contexts such as hygiene and personal-care products and is suitable for high school and introductory organic chemistry courses.
keywords: saponification, triglycerides, potassium hydroxide, fatty acid composition, foaming, structure-property relationships, stoichiometry, laboratory exercises, high school chemistry

title: Applying the CRADLE Method: An Undergraduate Case Study on Machine Learning for Chiral Noble Metal Nanoparticles Using Literature-Mined Data
text: Abstract Integrating artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) into undergraduate chemistry curricula is essential for preparing students for modern research, yet a central challenge remains: providing students with meaningful, research-ready data sets without prohibitive resource demands. To address this challenge, we present CRADLE (Creating Research-ready Data set from Literature for Education), a pedagogical framework in which students construct machine learning-ready data sets through systematic mining of the chemical literature. We demonstrate CRADLE through an undergraduate case study on predicting chiroptical responses in chiral noble metal nanoparticles. Students mined 67 publications to build a 201-entry database, developed a chemically informed feature-encoding strategy, and trained machine learning models. The optimized Extra Trees model (R2 = 0.93) guided the synthesis of gold nanoclusters with an anisotropic g-factor of 0.0035, surpassing the highest literature-mined value in their data set by 95%. Rubric-based course-performance data and anonymous pre/post-project self-assessments suggested that students successfully completed the major project tasks and reported increased confidence in research-related skills; all eight students endorsed the project-based approach. The CRADLE framework is practical and adaptable, offering a scalable model for embedding authentic, data-driven research experiences into undergraduate chemistry courses.
keywords: literature mining, gold nanoclusters, chiroptical properties, feature encoding, undergraduate research experience, project-based learning, student self-assessment

title: An Undergraduate Biochemistry Lab Exploring Elastin-Like Polypeptide Behavior and Degradation: From Purification to Proteolysis
text: Abstract The development of smart biomaterials that mimic the native extracellular matrix forms the basis for many innovations within the field of regenerative medicine. Elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs) are widely used in biomaterials due to their unique physicochemical properties. ELPs exhibit lower critical solution temperature behavior, meaning that, above their specific transition temperature, these polypeptides reversibly phase-separate and start to aggregate. Furthermore, their production via recombinant DNA techniques enables the incorporation of bioactive motifs such as enzyme-cleavable domains. Because of their attractive properties and broad applicability, the purification and characterization of ELPs are very relevant. Therefore, the goal of this laboratory experiment is to purify and characterize an ELP and to investigate its enzymatic degradation. Purification is done via inverse transition cycling, a technique that utilizes the thermoresponsive properties of ELPs. Students analyze the purity of the various fractions obtained during the purification process using sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). Additionally, they incubate the purified ELP with a protease and evaluate the success of the degradation. This practical provides students with both a theoretical background and practical experience in the fields of recombinant protein production and physical chemistry, which can be valuable for their future career paths in biochemistry, biomedical sciences, bioengineering, and biology.
keywords: elastin-like polypeptides, protein purification, inverse transition cycling, thermoresponsive polymers, lower critical solution temperature, phase separation, proteolysis, recombinant protein expression, smart biomaterials, extracellular matrix mimics, undergraduate biochemistry laboratory

title: CSI Fictions As Pedagogical Tools: Promoting Chemistry Engagement in High-School Students
text: Abstract Capitalizing on the enthusiasm generated by CSI-style fiction, a series of chemistry demonstrations were implemented within a set of university events aimed at promoting chemistry and chemical engineering among high school students, aiming at pedagogical innovation, chemistry outreach, and assessment of student engagement. Four simple experiments (mercury heart, copper capture, nitrite poisoning, and the heaviness of lead) were presented by undergraduate students, illustrating key chemical principles, including electrochemistry, redox reactions, metal electroplating, colorimetry, and complexometric titrations. The demonstrations also highlighted how chemistry can help protect environmental and food safety issues. Students participated enthusiastically, showing curiosity about the experiments and their real-world applications, with the mercury heart generating the strongest engagement because of its surprising visual effect.
keywords: chemistry demonstrations, chemistry outreach, student engagement, high school students, chemistry education, electrochemistry, redox reactions, colorimetry, complexometric titration, food safety, environmental safety, university outreach events

title: When Sunlight Makes Materials Move: A Laboratory Experiment Demonstrating Solar-Driven Hydrogel Actuator
text: Abstract Hydrogels, owing to their softness, deformability, and responsiveness to external stimuli, are widely employed in soft robotics as materials for actuation, sensing, and self-healing, enabling biomimetic motion and intelligent control. This laboratory experiment introduces upper-division undergraduate students to the concept of a solar-driven hydrogel actuator by fabricating and demonstrating a temperature-responsive hydrogel. Students prepare a temperature-sensitive poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAm) hydrogel incorporated with polypyrrole, a black photothermal additive that enhances sunlight absorption and photothermal conversion ability. Under solar irradiation, the temperature gradient between the upper and lower hydrogel layers induces asymmetric volume changes, resulting in visible bending or deformation. Conducted over a 4 h session with 32 upper-division undergraduate students, this hands-on laboratory experiment allows students to explore the relationships among polymer chemistry, materials science, photothermal conversion, and soft actuator behaviors. This laboratory experiment not only cultivates students’ practical skills in hydrogel preparation and data analysis but also stimulates their interest in polymer chemistry and materials science through the visual observation of solar-driven hydrogel deformation. Furthermore, it encourages students to explore the potential applications of hydrogel actuators in future intelligent materials and soft robotics.
keywords: thermosensitive hydrogel, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide), polypyrrole, photothermal conversion, soft robotics, hydrogel actuation, temperature gradient, undergraduate laboratory experiment, polymer chemistry education, materials science education

title: Mistake-Based Learning (MBL): A Mistake-Tolerant Teaching Approach for Developing Innovation-Related Competence in Undergraduate Chemistry Laboratories
text: Abstract This study presents Mistake-Based Learning (MBL), an instructional approach grounded in Mistake-Tolerant Teaching and aimed at fostering students’ innovation literacy through the development of observable competencies in undergraduate chemistry laboratories. MBL is organized around a core cycle of mistake emergence, trial-and-error, and mistake transformation. It integrates innovation-literacy development, a mistake-tolerant learning environment, and structured laboratory practice through a five-stage pathway supported by three interacting drivers, with a four-part evaluation providing continuous formative feedback, guiding students to transform naturally occurring experimental mistakes into opportunities for inquiry, analysis, revision, and reflection. In a cocurricular “second classroom” setting with pharmacy-related undergraduates, MBL was implemented, with phenol nitration serving as an illustrative experimental case. Data were collected from pre-, mid-, and postimplementation questionnaires, student reports and presentations, students’ reflective materials, and records of key learning episodes. Under clearly defined safety boundaries and phased instructor support, students identified and worked through recurring problems in controlling reaction conditions, implementing procedures, and responding to unexpected outcomes by examining possible causes and refining their experimental decisions. Descriptive questionnaire results indicated a shift toward more process-oriented views of innovation, accompanied by stronger innovation-related self-efficacy and self-reported growth in adaptive inquiry, iterative resilience, and reflective integration. These findings suggest that MBL may provide a way to turn bound experimental uncertainty into a productive resource for inquiry, revision, and reflection, thereby offering a valuable pathway for cultivating innovation literacy in undergraduate chemistry laboratories.
keywords: innovation literacy, undergraduate chemistry laboratory, trial-and-error learning, formative feedback, self-efficacy, phenol nitration, pharmacy students, second classroom, inquiry-based learning

title: Self-Assembly of Metal–Organic Cages in Microdroplets: An Interdisciplinary Teaching Module
text: Abstract This teaching experiment presents an interdisciplinary platform that offers integrated training in organic synthesis, supramolecular assembly, microfluidics, and spectroscopic characterization by combining subcomponent self-assembly of metal–organic cages with droplet-based microfluidic technology. A microdroplet generation system is constructed to systematically investigate droplet formation at immiscible liquid interfaces, where controlled flow rates enable the reproducible production of size-tunable, monodisperse oil-in-solvent droplets. The influence of spatial confinement on supramolecular self-assembly is then examined by comparing the formation efficiency of cage C1, assembled from L1, 2-formylpyridine (L2), and Zn(NTf2)2 (L3), in conventional bulk vials and microdroplet environments. 1H NMR analysis demonstrates that complete assembly of C1 is achieved within 60 min under microdroplet confinement, whereas the corresponding bulk reaction remains incomplete even after 720 min. In addition, the aggregation-induced emission (AIE) behavior of cage C1 and its ligand component L1 is systematically explored using UV–vis absorption and fluorescence spectroscopy, elucidating the dependence of their photophysical properties on solvent composition. Overall, this experiment highlights the pedagogical value of integrating micro/nanoscale confinement with molecular self-assembly and provides an effective framework for cultivating students’ experimental skills in advanced synthesis, microfluidic manipulation, and spectral analysis.
keywords: metal-organic cages, supramolecular self-assembly, microdroplets, microfluidics, droplet formation, spatial confinement, zinc(II) complexes, 2-formylpyridine, aggregation-induced emission, photophysical properties, solvent composition, monodisperse droplets, interdisciplinary teaching

title: Challenges and Responses to the Misuse of Artificial Intelligence in Chemistry Education in China
text: Abstract The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education presents a dual reality: it functions as a powerful pedagogical tool while simultaneously creating unprecedented challenges to academic integrity. This study examines the impact of AI on academic integrity in chemistry education. Focusing on second-year environmental engineering undergraduates at Jinggangshan University, online physical chemistry examinations (N = 104) were compared with a historical control group assessed through paper-based exams (N = 54). The results revealed significant score inflation in the online format, inconsistent with students’ prior performance in mathematics and general chemistry. Data from the smart examination system further indicated that 18.23% of students engaged in AI-assisted misconduct, employing techniques such as background switching and AI-embedded input methods to evade proctoring. Although the head teacher support model contributed to the development of more constructive learning habits, evidence indicates that moral regulation and technological surveillance alone are inadequate to protect academic outcomes from AI intrusion. Therefore, these findings highlight the urgent need to redesign assessments to be AI-resilient, emphasizing process over final answers, and fostering ethical awareness. The study advocates for a balanced framework of responsible AI use that preserves both pedagogical benefits and rigorous evaluation standards.
keywords: generative AI, academic integrity, chemistry education, online examinations, AI-assisted cheating, score inflation, assessment design, responsible AI use

title: Examining the Consistency of Nature of Science in Chemistry Curriculum Standard and Textbook: An Epistemic Network Analysis
text: Abstract Nature of science (NOS) is a core component of scientific literacy and has been integrated into China’s junior secondary chemistry curriculum standards. This study analyzes the representations of NOS in the Curriculum Standard and the PEP Textbook and examines the consistency between them. Using the reconceptualized family resemblance approach (RFN) and epistemic network analysis (ENA), the study compares NOS representations across documents. Results showed broad consistency in frequency distribution, with the cognitive-epistemic system appearing more frequently than the social-institutional system in both documents. However, structural differences were observed between the two documents. The Curriculum Standard presented a densely interconnected network, particularly among Scientific Knowledge, Methods, and Scientific Ethos, while the textbook shifted focus toward Aims and Values, with weaker ties to Methods and Ethos. Implications for textbook writers, teachers, and curriculum developers are discussed.
keywords: nature of science, chemistry curriculum standards, chemistry textbook, lower secondary education, China, epistemic network analysis, scientific literacy

title: Fostering Scientific Thinking in Primary Education through Chemistry: Addressing Misconceptions with Experimental Learning
text: Abstract Early science education plays an important role in shaping children’s engagement with natural phenomena and in making their intuitive explanations visible before they become more resistant to revision. Beyond the educational findings, the study provides a set of classroom-tested chemistry activities that may support primary teachers in addressing common misconceptions through experimental learning. The research was carried out through a collaborative partnership between university researchers and primary school teachers in an Italian second-grade classroom with pupils aged 7–8. Four experimental modules were developed around everyday phenomena: color mixing, gas mass, air pressure, and water properties. These topics were selected for their relevance to early chemistry education and for their potential to reveal children’s alternative conceptions. Pupils’ written responses, collected through pre- and postactivity reflective worksheets, were analyzed through qualitative content and thematic analysis. The findings suggest that the laboratory activities offered opportunities to mobilize pupils’ prior knowledge, foster engagement with chemical phenomena, and support the emergence of preliminary forms of scientific reasoning, such as making predictions, describing observations, and comparing initial ideas with observable events. However, the results also show that conceptual development was uneven across the four laboratories. In particular, the activity on water properties proved difficult for pupils, whose responses often remained generic or linked to prior intuitive explanations. Therefore, the study does not provide evidence of stable conceptual change but rather highlights the educational potential of guided laboratory experiences for eliciting and discussing children’s naïve ideas in early chemistry education. The results also point to the importance of developmentally appropriate design, reflective scaffolding, and interdisciplinary collaboration among chemistry experts, pedagogical researchers, and primary school teachers.
keywords: elementary school science, misconceptions, experimental learning, scientific thinking, scientific reasoning, color mixing, gas mass, atmospheric pressure, water properties, conceptual change, scaffolding, university-school partnership, second grade

title: Commercially Purified Phycobiliproteins Can Be Substituted for Protein Purified from Spirulina to Save Lab Preparation Time for Undergraduate Thermodynamics and Protein Folding Experiments
text: Abstract Phycobiliproteins purified from Spirulina dietary supplements have been used in undergraduate biochemistry and/or general chemistry laboratories to demonstrate protein folding and thermodynamic concepts such as equilibrium constants and Gibbs free energy. Preparing samples via purification of phycobiliproteins from Spirulina dietary supplements takes approximately 4 h. Instead of purifying phycobiliproteins from Spirulina to use in student laboratories, preparing samples from commercially purified phycobiliproteins, blue Spirulina powder, yields similar results while saving preparation time and avoiding the need for a centrifuge. Student data using phycobiliprotein purified from Spirulina or commercially purified phycobiliprotein provides nearly identical calculations of equilibrium constants and ΔG values at various urea concentrations, which give a ΔG of unfolding at 0 M urea near 10 kJ/mol regardless of the protein source. This suggests blue Spirulina powder’s use will save instructors’ lab preparation time and make this type of experiment more available for settings where the equipment for purifying phycobiliproteins from Spirulina is unavailable.
keywords: phycobiliproteins, Spirulina, protein folding, protein unfolding, Gibbs free energy, equilibrium constants, urea denaturation, undergraduate laboratory experiment

title: Development and Implementation of a Cloud-Based HPLC Teaching Platform Enhanced by Artificial Intelligence
text: Abstract High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is a fundamental component of undergraduate chemistry curricula. However, the high cost of instrumentation and limited laboratory hours often restrict students’ hands-on access. This lack of practical experience hinders their ability to deeply understand HPLC principles, master instrument operation, and develop problem-solving skills. To address these challenges, we developed an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cloud HPLC experiment platform, termed C-HPLC. Specifically, a deep learning model was constructed to predict compound retention time (RT); then, a refined 3D model was established to illustrate the HPLC instrument structure, and a web-based architecture was implemented to enable cross-platform interoperability. C-HPLC allows students to freely explore mixture separation under varied experimental parameters through accurate RT prediction. The platform is accessible on multiple devices, including smartphones, tablets, and computers, and provides online visualization of HPLC instrument structures and operating principles. Through online exploratory learning, students can deepen their understanding of HPLC principles and instrument configurations. Subsequent hands-on laboratory experiments reinforced and validated this knowledge, leading to an improvement in the effectiveness of HPLC experimental teaching. Usage data and questionnaire results demonstrated the reliability and usability of the platform. Among 105 trial users, 94 reported an enhanced understanding of HPLC, and 100 expressed overall satisfaction. C-HPLC offers a promising solution to current challenges in HPLC experimental teaching and supports the achievement of instructional objectives.
keywords: HPLC, artificial intelligence in education, web-based educational software, undergraduate chemistry education

title: The Effects of Blended Learning on Undergraduate Students’ Conceptual Understanding of Chemical Bonding and Molecular Geometry
text: Abstract Understanding how blended learning (BL) influences undergraduate students’ conceptual understanding of chemical bonding and molecular geometry (CBMG) remains an important yet underexplored area in higher education, particularly in developing contexts. This study examined the effects of the BL approach on undergraduate students’ conceptual understanding of CBMG. A mixed-methods approach with a nonequivalent control group quasi-experimental design was employed. A total of 86 undergraduate students (59 male and 27 female) from Bahir Dar University in Ethiopia participated in the study. Two intact classes were randomly assigned to an intervention group (IG; n = 42), which received BL instruction, and a comparison group (CG; n = 44), which was taught using conventional teaching methods (CTM). Quantitative data were collected using a Three-Tier Conceptual Understanding Diagnostic Test (TTCUDT), while qualitative data were gathered through semistructured interviews. The results showed a statistically significant difference in posttest conceptual understanding scores between the groups, favoring students in the BL condition. The findings further indicated that BL enhanced students’ scientific knowledge and reduced misconceptions (MCs) regarding CBMG concepts compared with CTM. However, no statistically significant gender differences were observed in students’ conceptual understanding. Overall, the results suggest that BL is an effective instructional strategyfor improving undergraduate students’ conceptual understanding of chemistry, and supports the integration of technology to promote meaningful learning.
keywords: blended learning, chemical bonding, molecular geometry, conceptual understanding, chemistry education, misconceptions, undergraduate students, traditional teaching methods, gender differences, technology integration, Ethiopia

title: ExperimentaQuimica : Evaluating an Experimental Continuing Professional Development Program for Primary Chemistry Teaching
text: Abstract This study examined the impact of the ExperimentaQuímica program on the teaching of chemistry in Portuguese primary education, designed as a continuing professional development initiative centered on experimental methodologies and individualized support. The aim was to understand the extent to which participation in the program fostered changes in teachers’ perceptions, pedagogical practices, and motivation, as well as to identify the design features that supported these transformations. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, involving 16 female teachers at this educational level. Data collection included pre- and post-test questionnaires and semistructured interviews, analyzed through descriptive and inferential statistics and qualitative content analysis using a hybrid deductive–inductive coding strategy. The results revealed significant changes in perceptions of experimental teaching, positive emotions associated with chemistry teaching, the perceived importance of instructional resources and institutional support, and teachers’ self-perceived preparation for chemistry teaching, as well as an increase in enthusiasm for teaching chemistry. Quantitative findings also indicated reduced agreement with traditional gender-related stereotypes associated with chemistry teaching. The interviews confirmed these trends, highlighting improvements in classroom practices, greater teacher motivation, and positive effects on pupils, notably in increased curiosity and engagement. The design of the program proved decisive, with particular emphasis on the value of individualized support and the provision of tailored laboratory kits. Despite limitations related to sample size and intervention duration, the study suggests the potential of continuing professional development initiatives that integrate experimental practices and personalized support. These findings offer relevant contributions to the promotion of early chemistry education and to the international debate on teacher education and scientific literacy.
keywords: continuing professional development, experimental teaching, chemistry teacher education, teacher perceptions, teacher motivation, individualized support, laboratory kit, Portuguese primary education, scientific literacy

title: Closing the Theory-Practice Gap in Analytical Chemistry: A Gas Chromatography Simulator for Enhanced Student Learning
text: Abstract Chromatography is a core technique in undergraduate instrumental analysis courses; however, student understanding of chromatographic optimization is often limited by restricted access to instrumentation, time constraints, and the abstract nature of theoretical parameters, such as temperature programming, column dimensions, and detector selection. We report the development and pedagogical evaluation of a MATLAB-based gas chromatography (GC) simulator designed for analytical chemistry courses in science degrees and master’s programs. The simulator allows users to manipulate column characteristics (stationary phase type, length, internal diameter, and film thickness), temperature conditions (isothermal and programmed gradients), carrier gas parameters, and detector types, generating simulated chromatograms that reflect realistic chromatographic behavior. The tool was implemented in a cohort of approximately 200 students enrolled in Pharmacy and Chemistry programs and accompanied by a structured teacher guide, installation instructions, and a student activity manual. Its educational effectiveness was evaluated through a postactivity satisfaction survey and qualitative feedback. Results indicate high levels of student engagement and perceived improvement in understanding chromatographic resolution, selectivity, and detector response. This open-access tool (Zenodo repository – ref 20325295) provides a flexible and scalable strategy to enhance conceptual learning in instrumental analysis courses where hands-on access to GC instrumentation is limited.
keywords: gas chromatography, chromatographic optimization, theory-practice gap, MATLAB simulation, temperature programming, column dimensions, detector selection, student engagement

title: Adopting a Guided-Inquiry Approach for an Undergraduate Liberal Education Course in the Indian Context
text: Abstract India’s national education policy (NEP2020) emphasizes a shift toward experimental, learner-centered inquiry-driven pedagogy. This study focuses on the implementation of inquiry-driven teaching within a newly introduced four-year undergraduate liberal education program. Against the backdrop of predominantly lecture-based instruction in Indian education, this work explores the introduction of guided-inquiry and presents case studies from a first year undergraduate program at the Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management. Student experiences and perspectives on inquiry-based activities related to everyday chemistry, frugal design, and life processes are examined. The findings highlight both the potential and challenges of implementing inquiry-driven pedagogy in theory courses and demonstrate how the core objective of NEP2020 can be meaningfully integrated into science, engineering, and management education in India.
keywords: inquiry-based learning, liberal arts education, National Education Policy 2020, undergraduate chemistry education, frugal design, chemistry in everyday life, life processes, student perceptions, lecture method

title: Didactic Approach on Chemical and Dynamic Equilibrium with the Laboratory Investigation of Oppenauer Oxidation (OPP) and Meerwein–Ponndorf–Verley Reduction (MPV) Reactions
text: Abstract Connecting the textbook definition and mechanisms of oxidation and reduction with practical applications is a lasting challenge for early undergraduate students. This Laboratory Experiment presents the design and implementation of a cost-effective pedagogical experiment of complementary redox reactions (MPV reduction and OPP oxidation) to strengthen first-year undergraduate students’ understanding of the principle of oxidation and reduction with an emphasis on the identification of oxidizing agents, reducing agents and equilibrium through a hands-on lab experiment. This module deals with Meerwein–Ponndorf–Verley (MPV) reduction of acetophenone to 1-phenylethanol using isopropyl alcohol and Oppenauer (OPP) oxidation reactions of 1-phenylethanol back to acetophenone using acetone. This experiment bridges the understanding of students with the laboratory observations monitored by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) with 1H NMR spectroscopy for characterization of products and the Lucas test for confirmation of secondary alcohol formation. Students’ assessment through lab reports achieved 60–93% yields in both (MPV and OPP) reactions. Moreover, the mean score difference for the prelab test (mean = 3.68) and postlab questions (mean = 7.24) supplemented by suitable open-ended structured probing questions was found to be significant at the 0.05 level (p < 0.05), showing a marked improvement in conceptual understanding. This module, which can be replicated in any educational setup with the use of the provided supporting material, has successfully strengthened the core redox terminologies, equilibrium concepts, and practical skills in students.
keywords: Oppenauer oxidation, Meerwein-Ponndorf-Verley reduction, redox reactions, chemical equilibrium, dynamic equilibrium, acetophenone, 1-phenylethanol, isopropanol, acetone, secondary alcohols, conceptual understanding, undergraduate laboratory experiment, probing questions

title: Seeing Molecular Recognition in Action: A Visual, Amplification-Free Sandwich Assay for DNA Detection Using Noble Metal Nanoparticles
text: Abstract This laboratory experiment introduces upper-division undergraduate and early stage graduate students to the design and implementation of a nanoparticle-based DNA sandwich assay for colorimetric DNA detection. The assay leverages sequence-specific hybridization between DNA-functionalized magnetic microparticles (MMPs) and noble metal nanoparticles (Au and Ag NPs), forming a “sandwich” complex in the presence of a complementary target DNA. Students synthesized Au and Ag NPs (20–80 nm) and functionalized them with thiolated DNA. In parallel, streptavidin-coated MMPs were conjugated with biotinylated DNA probes. Upon hybridization, the MMP–DNA–NP complexes were magnetically separated and subsequently dissociated to release signal Au and Ag NPs into solution. The color and absorbance intensity of the released particles, quantified via UV–vis spectroscopy, correlated with target DNA concentration, enabling both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Varying NP size, material, and mixing conditions (vortex vs rotation) revealed that larger NPs and vigorous agitation enhanced assay sensitivity via higher extinction coefficients and increased hybrid formation. The experiment reinforces concepts including plasmonic signal transduction, hybridization thermodynamics, and colloidal stability, while providing hands-on experience with synthesis, conjugation, and spectroscopy. Students demonstrated strong engagement and the ability to relate NP properties to analytical performance, interpreting assay results in the context of molecular recognition and surface chemistry. Overall, this modular, inquiry-driven experiment effectively bridges nanotechnology and bioanalysis in the undergraduate and graduate curriculum, offering a versatile platform for teaching interdisciplinary chemical principles in a visually intuitive and experimentally accessible format.
keywords: colorimetric DNA detection, noble metal nanoparticles, gold nanoparticles, silver nanoparticles, magnetic microparticles, streptavidin-biotin conjugation, DNA hybridization, nanoparticle size effects, colloidal stability, hybridization thermodynamics, molecular recognition, nanoparticle synthesis, undergraduate laboratory experiment

title: The Role of Kitchen Chemistry Activities in Hands-On Science Teaching Across Learning Contexts
text: Abstract The study aims to present inquiry-based kitchen chemistry activities that can be adapted not only to classroom settings but also to diverse learning environments such as distance education, thereby positioning the kitchen as an authentic and accessible space for scientific exploration. The study employed five “Kitchen Chemistry” activities using accessible household materials. This approach transformed the kitchen into a natural laboratory, serving not merely as a substitute but as an authentic inquiry environment. Through these activities, students explored concepts like density and chemical changes, engaging in scientific process skills from prediction to evidence-based reasoning within their immediate reality. The research was conceptualized as a descriptive study involving 24 middle school students (grades 5–7) from two public schools in Western Anatolia. The implementation spanned 7 weeks (28 instructional hours), during which students participated in synchronous online kitchen chemistry activities conducted with home-based materials. Data collection focused on students’ responses to the Kitchen Chemistry Applications Evaluation Scale and their performance on concept tests administered after each activity. Descriptive analyses were employed to examine patterns in student engagement, perceptions, and conceptual understanding. Findings indicate that students responded positively to the activities and were able to engage with scientific concepts in meaningful ways. Overall, the study suggests that inquiry-based kitchen chemistry activities are a feasible and pedagogically valuable approach for supporting science learning in diverse learning environments such as distance education contexts.
keywords: kitchen chemistry, inquiry-based learning, household materials, distance education, home-based learning, junior high school students, density, chemical changes, science process skills, student engagement, conceptual understanding, authentic learning environments

title: Active Learning of Physical Chemistry Principles through the One-Molecule Approach: Crystal Violet for Spectroscopy, Kinetics, and Protein Binding
text: Abstract This integrated laboratory project bridges the gap between fundamental physical chemistry and biochemical application through a cohesive ″one-molecule″ pedagogical strategy. Students utilize crystal violet (CV) as a central probe to explore three core pillars of physical chemistry: spectroscopy, kinetics, and thermodynamics. Initially, students characterize the photophysical properties of CV alongside rhodamine B and Congo red, determining absorption maxima and molar absorptivity while evaluating solvent-induced moves. The focus then shifts to a colorimetric kinetic study of the alkaline hydrolysis of CV, where students derive reaction orders, rate constants, and activation parameters via temperature-dependent studies. The project culminates in a biological context by investigating the noncovalent binding of CV to casein. Students analyze binding stoichiometry and dissociation constants to elucidate the nature of the protein–ligand interaction across varying pH environments. By maintaining a single molecular focus throughout these distinct modules, the curriculum provides horizontal integration across subdisciplines, fostering active learning and data interpretation skills. This approach reinforces the relevance of physical and chemical principles in understanding complex biological systems, making it an ideal candidate for upper-level biochemistry or physical chemistry laboratory courses.
keywords: crystal violet, active learning, physical chemistry laboratory, photophysical properties, activation parameters, protein-ligand binding, dissociation constant, rhodamine B, Congo red, solvent effects, pH dependence

title: Quantifying Chemical Processes in Beer Brewing: A Laboratory Experience for Undergraduates
text: Abstract Real-world laboratory experiences that are familiar, relatable, and engaging are known to solidify challenging theoretical concepts in undergraduate chemical education. Here, we describe a series of laboratory modules where students quantify chemical processes during beer brewing. Each module involves collecting and modeling experimental data by using chemistry and chemical engineering concepts learned in core undergraduate courses. The experiments engage students in the familiar and enjoyable process of beer brewing and are designed to reinforce difficult chemical science concepts from prior core courses. The experiments were implemented in a senior undergraduate elective chemical engineering course and covered concepts in material balances, transport phenomena, chemical kinetics, and fluid mechanics. In addition to reinforcing these core chemical science concepts, the experiments help solidify critical technical skills such as data analysis, theoretical modeling of data, and experimental design. We describe experiments including measuring water absorption in crushed barley, isomerization kinetics of alpha acids during hop boiling, and flow through porous media during wort filtration. The experiments are supplemented by theoretical lectures the week prior to each lab module, which helps students connect theoretical knowledge with real-world experiences. Experiments were designed using simple and readily available equipment and instruments to maximize accessibility. Assessments of historical student work showed that the laboratory experiments were successful in achieving learning outcomes.
keywords: beer brewing, undergraduate laboratory experiment, mass balance, transport phenomena, reaction kinetics, wort filtration, porous media flow, fluid mechanics, experimental design, data analysis, theoretical modeling

title: The Impact of Conscientiousness on Laboratory Safety Behavior Intention of Undergraduates: The Mediation of Safety Perception and Moderation of Chemistry Learning Motivation
text: Abstract This study examined the influence of chemistry learning motivation, conscientiousness, and laboratory safety perception on the safety behavior intention among undergraduates in chemistry-related majors. The results demonstrated that chemistry learning motivation (except amotivation), conscientiousness, and laboratory safety perception positively correlated with the safety behavior intention. Safety perception served as a partial mediator between conscientiousness and laboratory safety behavior intention, accounting for 72.83% of the total effect. Furthermore, amotivation toward chemistry learning significantly negatively modulated the relationship between safety perception and safety behavior intention.
keywords: conscientiousness, perceived safety, chemistry learning motivation, amotivation, undergraduate students, chemistry majors, mediation, moderation

title: Case Studies on Sample Preparation with Diluted Acid for Elemental Determination
text: Abstract Green chemistry provides a framework for redesigning laboratory practices to reduce environmental and safety impacts. In elemental analysis, replacing highly concentrated acids during sample preparation represents an important step toward more-sustainable practices. This study evaluates three didactic case studies based on the use of diluted nitric acid for sediment preparation in analytical and environmental chemistry courses. The participants included secondary technical students in biotechnology (n = 5) and undergraduate chemistry students (n = 43) from the analytical and environmental chemistry course, who were encouraged to critically evaluate conventional procedures that employ concentrated acids. Before classroom implementation, the alternative protocol based on diluted nitric acid was examined to ensure its analytical feasibility. Data were collected through questionnaires, responses completed by students in a structured monitoring form during the activities. The students proposed new alternatives and different approaches to solving problems related to chemical activities. The results demonstrated that this approach enabled students to integrate new knowledge in a critical, creative, and collaborative manner. Furthermore, the didactic strategy provided favorable conditions and essential experiences for training future chemical professionals who are aware of and reflective of their actions.
keywords: green chemistry, sample preparation, sediment preparation, elemental determination, chemistry education, case studies, analytical chemistry education, learning outcomes, critical thinking, cooperative learning

title: Transforming “Cram and Forget” into “Mastery and Retention”: A Longitudinal Analysis of Cumulative Writing-to-Learn in Organic Chemistry Using Linear Mixed Models
text: Abstract Organic chemistry is frequently perceived as a subject requiring overwhelming rote memorization, often yielding “cram-and-forget” study patterns. This study investigates the impact of a structured voluntary remediation program designed to shift at-risk students from surface-level memorization to deep mechanistic understanding. The intervention integrated cumulative retrieval practice with “writing-to-learn” tasks with individualized, remote feedback provided via Google Classroom. Linear mixed-model longitudinal analysis revealed a significant increase in the quality of logical understanding (Mastery Proportion) over eight sessions (β = 0.07, p < 0.001), regardless of initial learning orientation. Notably, a significant gap was observed between students’ low preference for these effortful tasks and their high recognition of their pedagogical value, suggesting the development of sophisticated metacognitive awareness. Individualized remote feedback served as a crucial scaffold, providing psychological safety for struggling learners. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that embedding “desirable difficulties” within a supportive, individualized framework can transform remedial education from rote repetition into a metacognitive process. This scalable approach offers a blueprint for fostering long-term retention and mechanistic reasoning in challenging scientific disciplines beyond organic chemistry.
keywords: organic chemistry education, writing to learn, remedial programme, at-risk students, metacognition, desirable difficulties, Google Classroom, long-term retention, learning orientation

title: Revisiting a Common Cobalt Chloride Equilibrium Experiment with Generative Artificial Intelligence
text: We have developed and implemented a first-year undergraduate laboratory experiment at St. Bonaventure University that augments a well-established thermodynamics lab on the spectrophotometric determination of the equilibrium of cobalt-(II) chloride hexahydrate with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Students utilized the aggregate of their own knowledge, peer discussion, instructor guidance, and free ChatGPT accounts in their analysis of laboratory data to iteratively refine their answers to chemical questions. Overall, the inclusion of GenAI in student workflow did not appear to negatively impact student performance, but there were instances where it struggled to produce correct answers for tasks. Descriptive analysis of student responses, chat logs, and instructor discussions suggests that most students improved their final answers despite potential shortcomings in GenAI responses. However, the analysis additionally identified multiple areas which could be improved in future iterations of this work. This laboratory experiment is designed such that it can be easily adopted by faculty with an interest in exploring the use of GenAI in chemistry curricula. In future work we intend to adapt the iterative framework and Sankey Flow diagrams employed in this work to design assessments which can disentangle the influence of peers, instructors, and GenAI on students' work.
keywords: generative AI, ChatGPT, cobalt(II) chloride hexahydrate, spectrophotometric determination, thermodynamics laboratory, undergraduate chemistry laboratory, student performance, peer discussion, AI-assisted learning

title: Design and Evaluation of Personalized Learning Pathways Based on OBE Principles: A Case Study of Physical Chemistry
text: Abstract The integration of OBE principles into the Physical Chemistry curriculum signifies a shift from merely covering subject knowledge points to achieving multidimensional learning outcomes. To meet contemporary educational demands, constructing personalized learning pathways is crucial for enabling students to explore core disciplinary concepts while enhancing their higher-order thinking skills and comprehensive competencies. This study developed an OBE-based personalized learning pathway model centered on four key modules: goal decomposition, pathway generation, dynamic adjustment, and effectiveness evaluation. The model is implemented through a cyclical process spanning three phases: preclass, in-class, and postclass. The study involved 242 third-year chemistry majors using a mixed-methods approach, embedding quantitative data collection and personalized learning model validation within course design. These findings suggest that students in the experimental condition achieved higher academic performance and self-efficacy. They further demonstrated that under OBE-guided personalized learning pathways, enhancing self-efficacy and reducing cognitive load are two parallel and equally important objectives.
keywords: outcome-based education, personalized learning paths, physical chemistry education, curriculum development, goal decomposition, self-efficacy, cognitive load, higher-order thinking skills, chemistry majors

title: Enhancing Analytical Skills through Quantized-Text Activities in Chemical and Environmental Education
text: Abstract This study presents a methodology for designing quantified text-based tasks for chemical and environmental disciplines aimed at enhancing analytical skills, improving academic performance, and facilitating the comprehension of educational material. The proposed methodology involved structuring tasks into quantized units, each representing a logically complete stage: familiarizing oneself with theoretical material, performing calculations, analyzing environmental consequences, and devising solutions. The methodology was tested on a sample of 140 students from Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University (KazNPU) and Ualikhanov University, divided into experimental and control groups, as well as 7 lecturers who implemented the developed method. The experimental group was taught using the quantized text-based tasks, while the control group followed traditional instructional methods. The findings revealed that the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher levels of academic achievement, analytical skills, and interest in the subject compared with the control group. Furthermore, the time required to complete tasks in the experimental group was reduced by an average of 20–30%. The difference in the average grade improvement between the groups was 17%, confirmed by statistical analysis (p < 0.05). Feedback from lecturers and students also indicated a positive impact of the methodology on motivation and material perception. The results confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed approach in enhancing the educational process and developing professional competencies in the fields of chemistry and ecology.

title: Teaching and Learning about Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Secondary Education Chemistry Classes
text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming chemical research and practice, yet chemistry education has largely focused on students’ use of generative AI tools rather than on understanding AI as a driver of modern chemistry. This mixed-methods study examined the feasibility of teaching “AI in chemistry” in secondary chemistry education (grades 10–13) and developed a practice-oriented model for future implementation and research. To this end, a 3-h professional development (PD) program for chemistry teachers and two 90-min lessons addressing AI applications in chemistry research, as well as associated benefits and risks, were designed and evaluated. Qualitative teacher surveys explored relevance, feasibility, and implementation. Student questionnaires assessed perceived importance of the topic, expectations that teachers address it, interest, attitudes toward AI in chemistry, and science-related AI competencies. Across both samples, prior knowledge of AI applications in chemistry was low but increased following the interventions. Teachers considered “AI in chemistry” highly relevant to the curriculum and emphasized the importance of classroom-ready examples for successful implementation. Students reported higher perceived importance of the topic, stronger expectations that teachers address it, and increased interest after instruction. Attitudes toward AI use in chemistry showed minor changes. In addition, students demonstrated improved ability to identify specific application areas of AI in chemistry. Overall, the findings indicate that instruction on “AI in chemistry” is feasible and educationally valuable. Effective implementation appears to benefit from focusing on tangible, real-world applications of AI in chemistry and from structured discussion of ethical risks, limitations, and trade-offs associated with its use.
keywords: artificial intelligence in chemistry, secondary chemistry education, AI literacy, teacher professional development, generative AI tools, student attitudes toward AI, AI competencies, curriculum implementation

title: A Solvothermal Approach for Synthesizing Pyrite (FeS2) in Undergraduate Inorganic Laboratories
text: Abstract A new upper-level undergraduate laboratory experiment has been developed to synthesize pyrite using a solvothermal method in a pressure autoclave reactor, providing students with a safe and practical introduction to high-pressure synthesis techniques. Pyrite (FeS2) is an important mineral with applications in materials science and energy research, making it an ideal inorganic compound for students to explore structural relationships. The experiment integrates crystal growth under controlled conditions with structural characterization using powder X-ray diffraction, allowing students to determine the phase purity and identify the lattice type of the synthesized material. Analysis of diffraction patterns reinforces key concepts in crystallography, including unit cell symmetry and lattice classification. By connecting synthesis conditions to structural outcomes, the experiment strengthens the solid-state chemistry and materials characterization knowledge of the students. Depending on instructional goals, this laboratory module can be adapted for inorganic or physical chemistry courses, but it is particularly well-suited for advanced laboratory curricula emphasizing interdisciplinary approaches and modern characterization techniques.
keywords: pyrite, FeS2, solvothermal synthesis, high-pressure synthesis, crystal growth, crystal structure, X-ray powder diffraction, crystallography, unit cell symmetry, classification of lattices, phase purity, undergraduate laboratory experiment, inorganic chemistry education

title: A Novel Experimental Setup for the Visualization of Dosing Strategy in Drinking Water Engineering
text: Abstract Drinking water treatment is one of the most important processing techniques in the world, and access to clean water is recognized as a human right by the UN General Assembly. However, the sources and quality of raw water differ immensely in chemical and biological composition, which leads to different treatment strategies. Coagulation–flocculation is an important treatment step used in most water treatment facilities. In this method, the addition of multivalent cations induces flocculation of the negatively charged colloid particles (e.g., clay or humic substances). A novel experimental setup for the visualization of flocculation is introduced, and demonstrations related to two aspects of the dosing strategy of flocculants are presented. This setup complements the traditional jar test used in water management. These demonstrations aim to highlight the practical difficulties in the dosing strategies for coagulation and flocculation when water quality varies, which will benefit students of water engineering as well as students of physical or colloid chemistry.
keywords: coagulation-flocculation, drinking water treatment, multivalent cations, colloidal particles, jar test, water quality variation, colloid chemistry

title: Synthesis of Vanillin from Clove Essential Oil: A 3-Day Laboratory Course on Organic Chemistry (Not Only) for Pharmacy Students Including Modern Aspects of Transition Metal Catalysis
text: Abstract A laboratory course on organic chemistry is presented in the context of isolating and converting natural products for those interested in developing their laboratory curriculum and activities. The course features a robust 5-step laboratory synthesis of vanillin from cloves. It was designed at the Department of Chemistry Education at RWTH Aachen University and successfully implemented in the Bachelor’s program Pharmaceutical Management and Production at DIPLOMA University of Applied Sciences, where it was evaluated with 12 cohorts and a total of 112 second-year undergraduate students. The educational approach enables students to conduct the entire experimental process, from cloves to vanillin, overcoming limitations of an older laboratory synthesis published in this journal. Steps of the original procedure that proved too dangerous or unsuccessful were substituted, employing modern aspects of transition metal catalysis.
