The synthesis involves a wide range of typical laboratory operations that serve as learning objectives, including Soxhlet extraction, the use of rotary evaporators, vacuum distillation, vacuum filtration, crystallization, and purity testing using refractive index, melting point, and gas and thin-layer chromatography. The course offers opportunities to address basic principles of organic synthesis, such as retrosynthetic considerations, protective groups, or acid/base/transition metal catalysis, in the context of daily life natural products, which should increase student motivation and interest in these topics.
keywords: vanillin synthesis, clove oil, transition metal catalysis, pharmacy students, natural product isolation, retrosynthesis, protecting groups, acid-base catalysis, laboratory curriculum design, student motivation

title: Exploring Polar Organometallic Chemistry with Deep Eutectic Solvents in the Undergraduate Laboratory
text: Abstract Polar organolithium reagents are central to modern synthetic chemistry but are rarely used in undergraduate laboratories because of the need for inert atmospheric techniques and cryogenic conditions. This study introduces a deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of choline chloride and glycerol as an accessible reaction medium that enables the nucleophilic addition of n-butyllithium to an imine under ambient conditions and in air. Students prepare the DES, carry out the organolithium addition, and analyze the reaction outcome using FT-IR spectroscopy to confirm imine to amine conversion. Across seven cohorts, the experiment consistently afforded average student yields of approximately 70% and produced reproducible FT-IR spectra that clearly differentiate starting material and product. These results demonstrate that DES-mediated organolithium chemistry can be safely and effectively incorporated into undergraduate teaching laboratories, broadening student exposure to reactive organometallic reagents while reducing logistical and safety barriers.
keywords: deep eutectic solvents, n-butyllithium, imine reduction, choline chloride, glycerol, nucleophilic addition, undergraduate laboratory experiment, reaction safety, FTIR spectroscopy

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Biopolymer Films: A Laboratory Activity for Teaching Sustainable Materials
text: Abstract In recent years, the environmental impact of petroleum-based plastics used in the packaging industry has sparked innovation in bio-based materials. Given the essential role of higher education in tackling the global sustainability crisis, a laboratory activity was developed to integrate bio-based processes and products into the learning processes. This approach promotes learning grounded in sustainability principles and circular economy concepts. In this activity, bio-based films for food packaging applications were synthesized from commercial biomolecules of natural origin and characterized to analyze their physicochemical and mechanical properties through simple laboratory experiments (determination of color, thickness, opacity, moisture content, total soluble matter, swelling capacity, oil absorption and biodegradability) combined with advanced instrumental analysis (SEM, contact angle, tensile test). This laboratory project offers students the opportunity to engage with sustainable development while fostering competencies in critical thinking and problem-solving-based decision-making and strengthening skills in communication, collaboration, conflict management, and planning.
keywords: biopolymer films, bio-based materials, food packaging, circular economy, petroleum-based plastics, swelling power, oil absorption, biodegradability, mechanical properties, physicochemical characterization, laboratory activity design, higher education

title: Post-Pandemic Learning Deficits: Declining Biochemistry Performance among First-Year University Students
text: Abstract The COVID-19 pandemic led to an emergency transition from face-to-face to remote education, disrupting traditional learning and assessment methods. This study evaluates the impact of this transition by comparing student performance in in-person biochemistry courses for first-year undergraduate students before (2019) and after (2022) the pandemic at the University of São Paulo. A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using 21 identical exam questions from two biochemistry courses: Biochemistry and Biophysics (first semester) and Biochemistry of Exercise (second semester). Student scores were analyzed using descriptive statistics, categorical distributions, and Generalized Linear Models (GLM). In 2022, scores were significantly lower in 11 exam questions, compared with 2019. Histograms of mean scores described a significant decline in student performance, with the proportion of students achieving passing grades decreasing by approximately 50%. When analyzed separately, a significant performance decline was observed only in Biochemistry of Exercise, a second-semester course focused on functional and integrative concepts. The performance of first-year university students in biochemistry declined in 2022, after resuming in-person classes, compared with 2019. These findings highlight potential long-term learning deficits from the pandemic years and underscore the need for targeted educational interventions to address post-pandemic academic challenges.
keywords: COVID-19 pandemic, distance education, biochemistry education, first-year students, academic decline, test scores

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Medicinal Chemistry Education: Student Engagement, Confidence Calibration, and Safety-Related Uncertainty in Case-Based Learning
text: Abstract The current study focuses on the function and use of generative artificial intelligence in teaching medicinal chemistry, with particular emphasis on learning process dynamics, decision-making power, and confidence estimation. A total of 101 undergraduate students in pharmacy schools were assigned to work on four case-type medicinal chemistry issues with optional artificial intelligence help. The variables in this research included task-specific AI use, confidence (pre/post), agreement with AI-generated outputs, and perceived certainty regarding chemical correctness and safety. Findings include that while there was considerable variation in usage patterns depending on the task type, there was considerable usage for explanatory tasks, with reduced reliance for higher-stakes decision-making tasks (structural modification/ADMET). Confidence recalibration was also found to vary: while most participants showed increased confidence after interacting with AI, many showed little or no confidence. Notably, there was considerable agreement with the output of AI, even in situations of doubt about its correctness or safety. The qualitative results showed that students mainly viewed AI as an entity for conceptual scaffolding, and their experiences within the disciplines influenced conditional trust and challenges in the process of verification. In general, the research indicates that generative AI is a high-fluency cognitive aid that alters traditionally assessed metacognitive control and monitoring and not just improves it. AI can help students understand medicinal chemistry concepts but also highlights the weaknesses of their capacity for the process of verifying the correctness and safety of the results.
keywords: generative AI, medicinal chemistry education, pharmacy students, case-based learning, confidence calibration, metacognition, trust in AI, chemical safety, student engagement, AI-assisted learning

title: Bridging Nanoscience and Electrochemistry: An Undergraduate Experiment on Soft-Template Synthesis, Characterization, and Electrocatalytic Testing of Mesoporous Palladium
text: Abstract Direct methanol fuel cells (DMFCs) face two major challenges: slow methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) kinetics and catalyst poisoning by CO. These challenges limit their efficiency and lifetime, creating a need for better anode catalysts. This paper describes an undergraduate laboratory experiment on the soft-template synthesis of mesoporous palladium nanoparticles (mesoPd NPs). Students characterize the material by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and evaluate its electrochemical performance for MOR. The experiment introduces students to the structure-function relationship in catalysis, combining nanoscience, electrochemistry, and materials characterization. It provides opportunities for students to develop skills in synthesis, instrumentation, and data interpretation, while introducing them to current research in energy electrocatalysis. Assessment of the module with 20 third-year chemistry majors (n = 20) revealed an improvement from pretest (52%) to post-test (83%) in conceptual understanding. Achievement rates across all success criteria ranged from 80% to 100% across laboratory reports, data analysis, oral presentations, safety compliance, and peer evaluations.
keywords: soft template synthesis, methanol oxidation, direct methanol fuel cells, electrocatalysis, CO poisoning, anode catalysts, undergraduate laboratory experiment, structure-function relationship, nanoscience education, electrochemistry education, student assessment

title: “They Are Students Just Like Me” - Analyzing General Chemistry Student Perspectives on Senior Undergraduate Student Learning Assistants as Laboratory Instructors
text: Abstract Senior undergraduate student learning assistants (LAs) have been utilized as instructors in the General (Introductory) Chemistry laboratories at a primarily undergraduate institution. We investigated what the students liked and disliked about senior undergraduate student LAs as laboratory instructors. Student (n = 102) responses to open-ended survey questions were thematically coded. The most important conclusion was that the General Chemistry students expressed an overwhelming preference for senior undergraduate LAs as laboratory instructors rather than for a staff member. Student responses were primarily positive toward LAs rather than negative toward staff. The most common themes that drove this preference for LAs as laboratory instructors were (1) a feeling of connection with the LAs, (2) liking that LAs are student peers, (3) feeling less (perceived) stress/intimidation with the LAs, and (4) appreciating that LAs have completed the same lab experiments themselves and thus have similar lab experiences. We also tested for significant differences in the frequency of responses between traditionally marginalized student groups vs their nonmarginalized counterparts. Tests for differences between students grouped according to gender (female vs male), race (nonwhite vs white), and access to learning accommodations revealed only a single difference: white students were more likely to identify imperfections in the LAs than their nonwhite counterparts. This suggests that implementation of LAs as general chemistry laboratory instructors is viewed as an equitable practice by students.
keywords: peer instructors, teacher-student rapport, gender differences, racial differences, learning accommodations

title: From Basic Fuchsin to Mixed Dyes: Teaching Electrocatalytic Advanced Oxidation and Digital Image Colorimetry via a Knowledge-Transfer Framework
text: Abstract This article presents an upper-level undergraduate laboratory activity that integrates electrochemistry and environmental chemistry through the electrocatalytic oxidative degradation of the organic dye basic fuchsin (BF). Students assemble a simple two-electrode electrolysis system, operating it under both constant-voltage modes. At the three-dimensional porous nickel-foam cathode, dissolved O2 is reduced via a two-electron pathway to generate H2O2. This H2O2 is subsequently activated at the nickel surface via a reversible Ni2+/Ni3+ redox cycle to yield highly oxidative hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which rapidly degrade BF. Reaction progress is initially monitored qualitatively through time-lapse decolorization. Students then translate these visual changes into semiquantitative trend information using digital image colorimetry. By extracting RGB values from standardized photographs and applying the complementary color principle, students calculate an RGB-derived equivalent absorbance as an operational optical metric, which is compared with UV–Vis spectroscopy to evaluate the degradation trend. Crucially, to foster knowledge transfer, students complete an independent extension task evaluating alternative emerging pollutants to validate the broader applicability of this analytical method. Emphasizing experimental design and variable control, this mechanism-supported, data-driven platform successfully equips students with practical skills in advanced water treatment technologies and accessible analytical techniques.
keywords: basic fuchsin, digital image colorimetry, hydroxyl radicals, nickel foam cathode, oxygen reduction reaction, dye degradation, emerging contaminants, water treatment, undergraduate laboratory, knowledge transfer, RGB color analysis

title: Food Colorants as a Context-Based Approach for High School Chemistry: From Natural Sources to Marketing Practices
text: Abstract This study presents an inquiry-driven teaching approach that draws on students’ everyday experiences with colored foods and beverages. The activity synergistically integrates areas of organic and analytical chemistry to develop students’ experimental and problem-solving skills while supporting their informed decision-making in everyday life. Student engagement was fostered through guiding questions framing two central dilemmas – colorful versus uncolored foods and natural versus artificial colorants – providing an authentic context to address issues related to food safety, current legislation, and environmental sustainability. Within this framework, students carried out inquiry-based learning starting with a simple and rapid test using raw wool as a direct qualitative sensor for natural and artificial dyes. Subsequent analysis of commercial food labels further supported students in making evidence-based assessments and validating preliminary assumptions. Additional techniques, including distillation and UV–Vis spectrophotometry, were introduced to help students uncover misconceptions about color-composition relationships and resolve experimental uncertainties, consistent with a constructivist learning perspective. Finally, the feasibility of coloring foods with natural pigments was tested, highlighting a common but often overlooked industrial practice. Following the experimental work and in line with active citizenship goals, students shared the outcomes of their educational research through public outreach events involving the local community.
keywords: food colorants, natural colorants, artificial colorants, inquiry-based learning, high school chemistry, food safety, food labeling, UV-Vis spectroscopy, distillation, natural pigments, active citizenship, public outreach, constructivist learning, environmental sustainability

title: Drawing Connections: Using a Science Communication Art Project to Bridge the Arts and the Sciences
text: Abstract Previous studies of STEAM initiatives have often emphasized K–12 contexts; comparatively fewer reports describe their implementation and outcomes in undergraduate STEM education. This study provides quantitative and qualitative data on the pedagogical impact of integrating art into undergraduate STEM education. Over the course of a 13.5-week college semester, first year biology and chemistry students completed a science communication project in which they created artwork to convey scientific concepts to a broader audience. They completed pre- and post-surveys assessing their experiences completing the project and perceptions of the arts and sciences. Data analysis revealed significant improvement in students’ understanding of the course material, confidence in communicating science, and recognition that art and science are connected disciplines. Students also reported increased engagement and developed scientific communication skills, despite finding the project challenging. Our findings offer STEM instructors an effective pedagogical tool to support diverse classrooms, while cultivating STEM undergraduates’ ability to convey complex scientific concepts to broader audiences. This work highlights the value of teaching both the arts and sciences in an integrated format that starts early in undergraduate education.
keywords: STEAM education, art-science integration, science communication, undergraduate STEM education, biology students, chemistry students, student art, student engagement, scientific communication skills, first-year students

title: From Equations to Intuition: Interactive Modeling for Teaching Ion Dynamics in Mass Spectrometry
text: Abstract Teaching mass spectrometry (MS) presents a recurring pedagogical challenge: students routinely acquire procedural familiarity with instrumentation without developing a mechanistic understanding of how electric fields govern ion trajectories, stability, and signal generation. We describe an instructional framework comprising three coordinated, browser-based Google Colab notebooks covering quadrupole mass filters, RF multipole ion guides, and Orbitrap-type analyzers, presented within a unified conceptual progression. The notebooks require no software installation or prior programming experience and are freely available as Supporting Information. Each module connects mathematical formalism directly to observable ion behavior through interactive simulation and multiple coordinated visualizations, supporting a shift from procedural competence to a physics-based understanding of modern MS instrumentation. The framework has been implemented in a graduate-level MS course at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and the notebooks, recommended exercises, and assessment materials are provided to facilitate adoption at other institutions.
keywords: mass spectrometry education, ion dynamics, ion trajectories, electric field, quadrupole mass filter, interactive simulation, conceptual understanding

title: Engagement and Achievement in Grade 9 Chemical Reactions: Classroom Demonstrations and Teacher-Curated AI-Assisted Representational Presentations
text: Abstract Chemical reactions require learners to coordinate visible phenomena, particle-level explanations, and symbolic equations. This quasi-experimental study compared two teacher-led approaches in a grade 9 chemical reactions unit: classroom demonstrations organized through prediction, observation, and explanation, and teacher-curated AI-assisted presentations that kept macroscopic, particulate, and symbolic representations visible during interpretation. The study examined a representationally scaffolded classroom format rather than an autonomous AI intervention. Participants were 120 students from four intact classes in one middle school and were classified pragmatically as typical or struggling learners according to prior science achievement. Both conditions addressed the same curriculum, lesson duration, teacher, and postunit measures. Outcomes included learning motivation, scientific curiosity, and chemistry achievement. The presentation condition produced higher scores, especially among struggling learners. Supplementary moderated mediation indicated that motivation and curiosity partially explained the association between instructional condition and achievement. The findings suggest that carefully reviewed visual sequences can support chemistry learning when they connect visible events, particle changes, and symbolic equations.
keywords: chemical reactions, classroom demonstration, chemistry achievement, student motivation, scientific curiosity, struggling students, junior high school chemistry

title: Development of Interdisciplinary SynZyme CURE: A Bridge between Organic Synthesis, Protein Biochemistry, and Drug Discovery
text: The SynZyme Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience (CURE) was developed to immerse students in an interdisciplinary semester-long project integrating organic synthesis and enzyme biochemistry within the context of early stage drug development. Embedded within a bioinstrumental chemistry course, this CURE also emphasizes the practical use of instrumentation in chemical and biochemical research. Eight undergraduate students synthesized a series of five novel triazole-based compounds and performed detailed molecular characterization to confirm purity and identity. Students then performed ADMET analysis and molecular docking before evaluating the inhibitory activity of the compounds against two target bacterial protein tyrosine phosphatases. Student Assessment of their Learning Gains (SALG), along with the Undergraduate Research Student Self-Assessment (URSSA) instrument, was used to evaluate the gains and experiences of the participants. Data revealed increased confidence in conducting independent research and contributing meaningfully to a research project. It also highlights the potential to promote a deeper understanding, skill development, and research competency among undergraduate students. Overall, the SynZyme CURE demonstrates the effectiveness of course-based research in fostering scientific identity, strengthening interdisciplinary literacy, and preparing undergraduates for real-world research environments.
keywords: course-based undergraduate research experiences, interdisciplinary research, organic synthesis, enzyme biochemistry, drug discovery, triazoles, protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibition, ADMET analysis, molecular docking, science identity

title: Embodied Learning for Abstract Concept Teaching in Chemistry: Insights from a Textbook-Based Analysis
text: Abstract To address persistent challenges in teaching abstract concepts in senior secondary chemistry─particularly the gap between macroscopic manipulation and submicroscopic explanation─this study conducted a textbook-based content analysis of Senior Secondary Chemistry (Compulsory Modules 1–2) published by the People’s Education Press and the accompanying teachers’ guides. A four-dimensional coding framework was developed, encompassing concept type, level of bodily engagement, action–concept alignment, and degree of contextual immersion. Nineteen analytical units were independently coded by two raters, yielding high interrater reliability (Cohen’s κ > 0.80). The results indicate a pronounced structural imbalance in the distribution of embodied learning opportunities. Embodied support is predominantly concentrated at lower levels, mainly in observation-based activities (A1) and macroscopic experimental operations (A3–1). In contrast, higher-level embodied designs─including gesture-based action chains (A2), activities supporting structural mapping at the submicroscopic level (A3–2), and immersive simulations (A4)─are markedly underrepresented. Although topics amenable to direct macroscopic manipulation, such as solution preparation and energy transformation, receive relatively strong embodied support, representations that explicitly account for submicroscopic particle mechanisms and symbolic relationships, such as atomic structure and chemical bonding, are largely absent. This pattern suggests that current textbook designs emphasize macroscopic “doing” without sufficiently scaffolding students’ understanding of how submicroscopic interactions give rise to observable phenomena and symbolic representations. Based on the analyzed textbook and teacher-guide materials, these findings suggest that future textbook design may benefit from moving beyond simply increasing embodied activities and instead providing targeted embodied support for concepts that require students to connect macroscopic experience, submicroscopic models, and symbolic representations.
keywords: embodied learning, chemistry textbook, textbook analysis, submicroscopic representation, symbolic representation, gesture-based learning, immersive simulation, People's Education Press

title: Reforming the Course “Chemistry Laboratory Teaching Methods for Secondary Education” Using an Outcome-Based Education Approach
text: Abstract In preservice chemistry teacher training courses at teacher education institutions worldwide, there exist common challenges such as misalignment between course content and secondary school curriculum standards, inflexible instructional models, and inadequate practical competencies. Guided by the principles of Outcome-Based Education (OBE), we proposed a four-dimensional reform framework encompassing Objectives, Content, Models, and Evaluation (OCME), and implemented this framework in Chemistry Laboratory Teaching Methods for Secondary Education─a core course for the chemistry education major at Northwest Normal University. A mixed-method design integrating questionnaire surveys, longitudinal teaching practice tracking, and paired-samples t-test analysis was adopted to evaluate the effectiveness of the reform. Results demonstrated that the OBE-based teaching reform significantly improved preservice teachers’ teaching practice skills (mean score increased by 0.32, p < 0.001), learning engagement (mean score increased by 0.23, p < 0.001), and innovative thinking (mean score increased by 0.28, p < 0.001). Student’ satisfaction with the reformed course reached 90.9%. Collectively, this OBE-based OCME reform framework effectively enhances preservice chemistry teachers’ laboratory instructional performances, and exhibits strong adaptability, thus providing a generalizable model for teacher education institutions worldwide.
keywords: outcome-based education, course reform, teaching practice skills, student engagement, innovative thinking, teacher education curriculum

title: Optimization of Rate Constants in a Mixed-Order Parallel Reaction Mechanism with MATLAB for Undergraduate Students
text: Abstract The treatment of kinetic data and its interpretation is one of the most important topics in most university courses in chemical kinetics. Data handling usually requires mastery of numerical techniques, computer programming, and statistics. In general, many university courses teach mathematics–statistics and programming without kinetic applications. For students, acquiring skills and techniques of kinetic data processing using knowledge of numerical methods and programming is important for their education. This laboratory exercise proposal aims to offer an activity that requires the use of numerical and statistical methods to solve one of the most relevant problems in chemical kinetics: the estimation of the values of constants of a reaction mechanism from experimental values. For its solution, two different approaches are proposed for its development in MATLAB. As a result of the solution of the different variants, it is possible to compare the efficiency of each of the proposed solutions and the modeling of the system over time.
keywords: rate constant estimation, parallel reaction mechanism, reaction kinetics, kinetic analysis, MATLAB, numerical methods, undergraduate laboratory experiment

title: A Low-Cost Broadband Nanosecond Pump–Probe Transient Absorption Spectrometer for Education and Research
text: Abstract Transient absorption spectroscopy offers an effective method to explore excited state dynamics, providing mechanistic insights into fundamental light-induced processes across diverse fields such as organic and inorganic photosystems, biology and medicine, and technological applications like material design and photocatalysis. Commercial transient absorption spectrometers, designed for research laboratories and user facilities, have excellent temporal and spectral capabilities but come at high costs. Alternatively, the affordable teaching kits that introduce advanced molecular photophysics into undergraduate and graduate education probe dynamics at single wavelengths and thus do not capture the full picture of the excited state dynamics. To monitor the overall excited state energy landscape, broad spectral coverage is crucial, revealing spectral shifts and the interplay between different states. We present a low-cost (∼20 000 EUR at the time of publication) transient absorption spectrometer that can be built from individual components or as an extension to an educational single wavelength kit. We validate the spectrometer using a well-characterized zinc tetraphenylporphyrin sample, providing high quality time-resolved spectra that track excited state dynamics in the ns to ms time range with a broad spectral coverage of 450–1000 nm. From an educational point of view, the spectrometer offers a platform for introducing lasers, optics, and time-resolved spectroscopy into the curriculum at both the undergraduate and graduate level. The spectrometer can be built as an introduction to basic optics and alignment, providing hands-on experience in instrument design and implementation, or it can be provided as a complete transient absorption instrument for capturing excited state dynamics of a variety of different samples.
keywords: transient absorption spectroscopy, low-cost instrumentation, excited-state dynamics, nanosecond time-resolved spectroscopy, zinc tetraphenylporphyrin, instrument design

title: Chemistry Instructors’ Interpretations of Assessment Instrument Data for Instructional Action
text: Abstract Assessment instruments enable instructors to collect valid and reliable data about students’ content knowledge and support data-informed pedagogical decisions. Despite the widespread development of assessment instruments in chemistry education research, instructors’ use of these data is often constrained by limited time, interpretive support, and integration into instructional practice. This study investigates how instructors engage with assessment instrument data to interpret student thinking, draw conclusions, and propose instructional actions. Semistructured interviews were conducted during which chemistry instructors interacted with visualizations of their students’ responses, including representations of both correct and alternate conceptions. Instructors’ conclusions and proposed actions were analyzed through the lens of Data-Driven Inquiry to characterize patterns in how assessment data are interpreted and used. This work identifies common trends and challenges in instructors’ sensemaking of assessment instrument data and highlights opportunities for targeted supports. Of note, deficit framing of conclusions from assessment was found to be closely linked to proposal of ambiguous instructional actions, indicating that interpretive stance matters more than the specific conceptual issue identified within assessment data. Future work will focus on designing and evaluating supports that bridge the researcher-practitioner gap by facilitating instructors’ integration of research-based assessments and data-informed instructional practices.
keywords: chemistry teachers, data interpretation, data-informed instruction, student conceptions, deficit framing, data visualization

title: Bringing Lead Awareness into the Classroom: A Multigrade Curriculum Connecting Environmental Chemistry and Public Health
text: Abstract Lead poisoning, a legacy of industrial pollution, remains a serious public health risk in major industrial cities. Aging infrastructure, contaminated soil, and persistent environmental inequities contribute to ongoing exposure, disproportionately affecting low-income communities and children. Recognizing the urgent need for prevention strategies, a student-led research team at Marian University developed “The Lead Poisoning Prevention Program,” an educational outreach initiative that addresses lead exposure risks through school-based learning. “The Lead Poisoning Prevention Program” is a four-session curriculum for students in Pre-K through eighth grade, incorporating hands-on activities, nutrition education, and environmental science. Instruction focuses on building knowledge and practical prevention strategies, including the TCTT method (Test soil, Cover the soil, Take off shoes, Test child). Other topics include sources of lead, the role of diet in reducing lead absorption, and sustainable remediation using phytoremediation techniques. To extend impact beyond the classroom, the program incorporates interactive activities, bilingual brochures, and take-home soil sampling kits that promote family engagement and community action. Across schools in Indianapolis, the program has consistently demonstrated student engagement, gained educator support, and fostered meaningful family participation. Soil analyses collected during implementation indicate that nearly 23% (n = 101) of student-submitted samples exceed the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) threshold screening level. This article describes the program’s scientific background, curriculum design, pedagogy, implementation, and outcomes, highlighting the value of chemistry-based outreach for community health and STEM engagement.
keywords: lead poisoning, lead exposure prevention, environmental chemistry education, public health education, school-based curriculum, soil contamination, phytoremediation, environmental justice, low-income communities, family involvement, STEM engagement, student-led research, community outreach

title: Semipinacol Rearrangement Enabled by Radical-Polar Crossover: An Undergraduate Laboratory Experiment
text: Abstract Organic transformations are traditionally classified as either ionic or radical processes. Ionic reactions, which involve charged intermediates such as carbocations, often provide predictable selectivity but typically require specific conditions and show limited functional group tolerance. In contrast, radical reactions proceed under milder, neutral conditions with broader functional group compatibility, though controlling their selectivity can be challenging. The radical-polar crossover (RPC) reaction merges these two mechanistic paradigms through a single-electron transfer event, combining the mild nature of radical chemistry with versatile and highly selective capabilities of ionic chemistry. This hybrid strategy offers an effective pathway for the semipinacol rearrangement of allylic alcohols, avoiding the competing SN2′ displacement and other side reactions commonly encountered under traditional acidic promotion. Despite its synthetic advantages, the RPC-enabled semipinacol rearrangement has not yet been incorporated into undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory instruction. Here, we present a hands-on experiment that demonstrates a cobalt-catalyzed semipinacol rearrangement via metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) and RPC. Students perform the reaction under an inert atmosphere, monitor its progress by TLC, purify the product by flash column chromatography, and characterize it using 1H NMR, 13C NMR and FT-IR spectroscopy. This experiment not only reinforces fundamental laboratory skills but also bridges textbook knowledge of ionic and radical mechanisms with a contemporary, selective synthetic methodology.
keywords: semipinacol rearrangement, radical-polar crossover, cobalt catalysis, allylic alcohols, SN2 displacement, reaction selectivity, undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory, reaction mechanism

title: From Biobased Materials to Flexible Functional Devices: An Interdisciplinary Innovative Experiment Design for Materials Science and Engineering Students
text: Abstract To bridge the gap between materials synthesis and intelligent systems engineering, this article presents an interdisciplinary innovative experiment based on fully biobased flexible functional devices for undergraduate materials science and engineering students. Students prepare a flexible substrate through latex compounding and acid coprecipitation, using interfacial hydrogen bonding between plant-derived lignin and natural rubber latex to suppress lignin self-aggregation. Direct laser writing is then introduced, in which the photothermal effect of a CO2 laser beam converts the insulating lignin in situ into conductive, porous laser-induced graphene (LIG). On this platform, students construct and evaluate five types of functional devices: resistive strain and pressure sensors evaluated using a universal testing machine and digital multimeters; a serpentine temperature sensor that exploits polymer thermal expansion; a capacitive humidity sensor based on a graphene oxide/NaOH dielectric film, characterized across saturated salt solutions using an LCR meter; and an electrothermal Joule heating actuator evaluated using a DC power supply and an infrared thermal camera. Finally, students collect real-time resistance signals from their self-fabricated knee-joint strain sensors and use a deep-learning model for human motion recognition with over 97% accuracy. Implemented across two consecutive semesters with 58 students, this experiment helps students develop a systematic “Materials–Devices–Data–Applications” engineering perspective in green electronics.
keywords: bio-based materials, lignin, natural rubber latex, direct laser writing, laser-induced graphene, CO2 laser, strain sensors, pressure sensors, temperature sensors, humidity sensor, human motion recognition, deep learning, green electronics

title: Drag-and-Drop PowerPoint Slides for Digital Quizzing and Active Learning in Organic Chemistry
text: Abstract Organic chemistry instruction relies on graphically complex problem types, especially mechanism, synthesis, and bonding questions. These problems cannot easily be reduced to conventional digital input formats without conceptual loss. Because digitization remains essential for scaffolding, active learning, and remote instruction in large service classes, a variety of solutions exist that each introduce their own technical burden and cost. This technology report provides 50 drag-and-drop organic chemistry questions as PowerPoint slides, along with solutions. We performed quizzing and active learning activities using these slides over two common learning management systems (Canvas and Blackboard), in seven semesters. In these activities, students rearranged the movable elements and annotated as directed to generate a response. Students found the format easy to use and appreciated its learning value, according to a detailed survey that was conducted.
keywords: PowerPoint presentations, organic chemistry education, active learning, virtual learning environments, Canva, Blackboard, synthesis problem, remote instruction, student survey

title: Creating Podcasts with Generative AI Using Google’s NotebookLM to Supplement Prelab Activities in Undergraduate General Chemistry Laboratories
text: Abstract Preparation for laboratory in STEM courses is essential to ensure that student learning outcomes are achieved and that the students can participate in the lab in a safe and meaningful way. Often lab preparation comes in the form of prelab assignments, which can range from reading introductory material to completion of an assessment related to tasks the student will be performing in lab. Podcasts are a popular tool for enhancing student learning experiences due to their accessibility for both educators and students. However, the creation of a podcast is often time-consuming, requiring significant effort by the instructor to write, record, and edit the audio file. The work herein discusses how the free version of Google’s NotebookLM can be used to create podcasts using generative AI for a general chemistry laboratory. The podcasts were provided to students to supplement their prelaboratory background reading and preparation. Student survey questions focused on feedback about the AI podcasts, including their design and how helpful students felt they were for the course. Student survey responses are used to highlight the usefulness of traditional course material alongside the podcasts, potentially carving a path for their joint use rather than replacement of traditional resources. The feedback suggests that the use of AI-generated podcasts may be a helpful tool to improve lab preparation and enhance the student learning experience.
keywords: generative AI, podcasts, NotebookLM, general chemistry laboratory, laboratory preparation, student feedback, undergraduate chemistry education

title: Analysis of Safety Competency: A New Assessment of Student Learning Behavior
text: Abstract Chemical laboratory safety is paramount for conducting effective experiments and safeguarding the health of researchers. Traditional teaching methods have often provided a limited perspective on students’ laboratory safety competency assessment. In this work, we presented the data of our course, entitled “Laboratory Safety in Chemistry” from the MOOC platform, which contained six years of discussion forum. By analyzing these data, we explored a new approach to better understand students’ safety competencies. Because discussion forums alone are hard to quantify, we integrated a data-driven approach to analyze learning behaviors. By effectively examining these learning behaviors, we were able to outline their cognitive safety competencies. Based on these findings, course modifications were implemented and received favorable feedback. These results indicated that targeted changes in course content may facilitate a progression from superficial awareness to a deeper comprehension of laboratory safety principles. It reflected the rationality of using the data-driven approach to help understanding students’ learning behaviors, thereby optimizing the course and enhancing students’ safety competencies. It further highlighted the potential of interactive and discussion-based approaches in addressing the evolving challenges of safety education. Representative examples of consistently engaging discussion questions are provided in the Supporting Information.
keywords: laboratory safety, safety competencies, chemistry education, MOOCs, forum, learning behavior, data-driven analysis, course design

title: Growing Crystals, Growing Minds: A STEAM Approach to Introducing Crystallography in Early Education
text: Abstract Crystallography is rarely introduced in early education despite its strong potential to foster inquiry-based chemistry learning through observation, experimentation, and model building. This work presents an STEAM-based educational intervention designed to introduce crystallographic concepts through the integration of experimental activities, narrative, and artistic expression. The proposal was implemented with approximately 420 students across preschool and primary levels, combining crystal growth experiments using sucrose and copper(II) sulfate with a literary framework based on O Veleiro de Crystal. Students engaged in hands-on crystallization activities with sucrose and teacher-guided observation of copper(II) sulfate crystal growth, together with systematic observation and creative production, including drawings and three-dimensional models. The results reveal high levels of student engagement and motivation, as well as the development of early scientific thinking, particularly in relation to crystal growth, material properties, and time-dependent processes. In addition, students demonstrated the ability to connect scientific observations with imaginative interpretation, while collaborative activities supported the development of socio-emotional skills such as teamwork, persistence, and empathy. These findings highlight the potential of crystallography as an effective interdisciplinary context within STEAM education capable of bridging science, art, and humanistic perspectives. The use of low-cost materials, detailed experimental procedures, and accessible methodologies further support the adaptability and reproducibility of this approach, providing a practical framework for introducing crystallography in early chemistry education across diverse educational contexts.
keywords: crystallography, early childhood science education, STEAM education, crystal growth experiments, sucrose crystallization, copper sulfate, inquiry-based learning, art and science integration, 3D model, student engagement, socioemotional skills

title: When Flory Meets the Nano-World: An Experiment Validating the Flory–Huggins Parameter via Block Copolymer Self-Assembly
text: Abstract Ask any student of polymer physics to define the Flory–Huggins parameter (χ), and they will likely recite a cornerstone concept in polymer physics courses for understanding the thermodynamics and phase behavior of polymer solutions and that a high χ value means immiscibility. Yet, few can connect this abstract number to the tangible nanoscale structures it governs. Herein, we describe a laboratory module that makes this connection unmistakable. Using a “phenomenon-driven” approach, students verify the theoretical implications of χ by observing changes in the length of cylindrical micelles (CMs) assembled from a block copolymer in mixed solvents. This teaching practice transforms the abstract χ parameter into observable and measurable experimental results, challenges students to think like scientists by moving “from phenomenon to essence”, and trains them to use classical theory to guide and interpret experiments in complex systems. Consequently, student learning moves beyond rote memorization toward genuine research literacy.
keywords: Flory-Huggins interaction parameter, block copolymer self-assembly, cylindrical micelles, polymer solution thermodynamics, polymer immiscibility, mixed solvents, research literacy, nanostructures

title: Efficient Fabrication of WLEDs for Undergraduate Laboratory: From Phosphors Synthesis to Device Assembly
text: Abstract White light-emitting diodes (WLEDs), as the fourth-generation lighting source, possess remarkable advantages in terms of energy efficiency, environmental friendliness, and prolonged lifespan. Currently, commercial WLEDs mainly achieve warm white light with a low color temperature and high color rendering index by using blue LED chips coated with green and red phosphors. Incorporating the preparation of phosphors and the fabrication of WLEDs into undergraduate experiments is highly meaningful, as it allows students to comprehend the application and development trends of LEDs in modern lighting while experiencing the practical utilization of professional knowledge in both manufacturing and daily life. The experiment comprises three modules: synthesis of copper complexes, characterization and analysis of products, and assembly of light-emitting devices. The solution for synthesizing copper complexes can enable students to become more proficient in basic experimental operations, such as dissolving substances, decantation, centrifugation, and the principle of like-dissolves-like. By observing molecular structures and analyzing the fluorescence of the complexes, students can gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between the structural characteristics and the luminescent properties of copper complexes. In addition, the assembly process of WLEDs not only connects theory with practice but also enhances students’ interest in learning by providing an engaging hands-on experience. The experiment encompasses innovative content, streamlined synthesis, observable phenomena, and a captivating assembly. Besides cultivating students’ practical experimental skills, this experiment also fosters their professional identities. Therefore, this is a very attractive experimental teaching design that is particularly suitable for first-year students.
keywords: white LEDs, phosphor synthesis, copper complexes, fluorescence, undergraduate laboratory experiment, hands-on learning, structure-luminescence relationship, warm white light, energy-efficient lighting

title: Reframing Secondary Chemistry Laboratory Instruction: A Critical Review of Pedagogical Aims, Affordances, and Trade-Offs in JCE and CERP Studies, 2016–2025
text: Abstract Laboratory instruction remains a central feature of secondary chemistry education because it links abstract chemical ideas to observable phenomena, supports practical skill development, and provides opportunities for scientific inquiry. In recent years, research on school chemistry laboratories has expanded across inquiry-oriented practical work, technology-supported and virtual laboratories, and green or microscale approaches. However, this literature is often organized by innovation type rather than by a shared pedagogical logic, making it difficult to compare what different laboratory designs are intended to accomplish, what they enable, and what constraints accompany their use. This paper presents a journal-bounded critical review of secondary chemistry laboratory instruction studies published in Journal of Chemical Education and Chemistry Education Research and Practice between 2016 and 2025. The review was guided by the analytical lenses of pedagogical aims, affordances, and trade-offs and informed by a transparent process of studies identification, selection, and coding. A total of 79 studies were included in the review. Rather than cataloging laboratory innovations by type alone, the review examines how different laboratory designs align with different educational purposes and how their pedagogical promise is shaped by classroom realities. Across the 79 studies, conceptual understanding remained a dominant aim, but many studies also emphasized inquiry, evidence use, scientific reasoning, student engagement, and, in some cases, equity and sustainability. Inquiry-oriented designs, digital and sensor-based approaches, and green or microscale formats each offered distinctive pedagogical affordances. At the same time, these benefits were frequently accompanied by trade-offs involving time, curriculum pressure, teacher facilitation demands, resource availability, technology access, and uneven implementation conditions. This review shifts attention from laboratory formats alone to the pedagogical decisions that shape laboratory teaching within a bounded but influential subset of chemistry education research. It argues that the value of a laboratory design lies less in novelty than in its alignment with intended learning goals under real instructional conditions. The findings have implications for classroom practice, curriculum design, teacher education, and future research on secondary chemistry laboratory instruction.
keywords: secondary chemistry education, chemistry laboratory instruction, inquiry-based learning, virtual laboratory, green chemistry, microscale chemistry, pedagogical affordances, conceptual understanding, scientific reasoning, student engagement, equity in science education, teacher as facilitator, curriculum pressure

title: Processing (Our) Differences: Characterizing Neurodivergent Students’ Experiences Learning Chemistry and Reasoning with Representations
text: Abstract Neurodiversity refers to natural differences in how individuals process and respond to information. It includes established cognitive differences like attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, and specific learning disorders. These differences can become barriers in courses that are not set up to support neurodivergent (ND) students. To design more-inclusive learning environments, it is important to understand how ND students approach chemistry learning and problem-solving. This exploratory study investigated how ND and non-ND students reason through molecular representation tasks in organic chemistry. Eighty-six students completed 40 computer-based tasks requiring translation between wedge-dash diagrams and chair conformations. Each participant then completed a follow-up interview explaining their reasoning for 8 of the 40 tasks. Of the participants, 26 (∼30%) self-identified as ND, allowing for comparisons between groups for accuracy, confidence, time-on-task, and reasoning strategies. Our findings showed that while time-on-task and confidence did not differ substantially, ND students demonstrated lower accuracy and less productive reasoning strategies, including frequent answer switching and reliance on oversimplified rules. We also explored ND students’ reflections on their chemistry learning experiences. Three major themes emerged: (1) ND students perceive meaningful differences in how they learn compared to peers; (2) multiple factors, such as attention span, visuo-spatial ability, and cognitive load, shape their learning; and (3) ND students develop personalized self-accommodation strategies to manage learning challenges. We discuss implications of these findings for instructors and administrators.
keywords: neurodiversity, neurodivergent students, chemistry learning, molecular representation, chair conformation, organic chemistry, inclusive learning environment, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, specific learning disorders, cognitive load, visuospatial ability, student self-confidence

title: Innovative Green Chemistry: Easy and Fast Synthesis of a Universal pH Indicator from Natural Plant Extracts
text: Abstract Plant-derived pigments represent a safe and sustainable alternative to synthetic pH indicators, but single-plant extracts typically suffer from limited pH ranges and poor color differentiation. This study presents the development and educational application of a mixed plant-based universal pH indicator derived from red cabbage (Brassica oleracea) and butterfly pea (Clitoria ternatea). The combination of cyanidin- and delphinidin-based anthocyanins, obtained under mild extraction conditions, yields a smooth and continuous color gradient across the full pH range from 1 to 14. UV–vis spectroscopy confirms that this broad responsiveness results from complementary protonation equilibria and overlapping absorption profiles of the two extracts. A classroom-ready laboratory activity is described in which students investigate the indicator, document color changes, and optionally analyze digital color values as semiquantitative pH proxies. The activity addresses key learning objectives in acid–base equilibria, structure–property relationships, green chemistry, and data literacy. Compared with commercial universal indicators, the plant-based system shows comparable color resolution while offering advantages in safety, cost, sustainability, and pedagogical transparency. This mixed natural indicator therefore provides an effective and conceptually rich tool for teaching acid–base chemistry.
keywords: plant pigments, anthocyanins, red cabbage, Clitoria ternatea, cyanidin, delphinidin, acid-base balance, green chemistry, structure-property relationships, acid-base titration, data literacy

title: Investigating Reaction Mechanism Explanation Sophistication Across a Yearlong Organic Chemistry Course Sequence
text: Abstract Mechanistic reasoning is a central component of organic chemistry learning; however, relatively little is known about how learners’ mechanistic explanations develop and change over time. The work reported herein examined longitudinal changes in learners’ explanation sophistication for reaction mechanisms across a two-semester organic chemistry sequence. A total of 5,942 explanations were collected from 913 learners across 30 reaction mechanisms; learner explanations were evaluated using previously developed level of explanation sophistication rubrics for nucleophiles and electrophiles, comprising four levels: Absent, Descriptive, Foundational, and Complex. Bayesian cumulative logit mixed-effects models were used to investigate changes in explanation sophistication across instructional time points and to examine relationships between explanation sophistication and reaction type and course performance. Results indicate modest increases in nucleophile explanation sophistication across the instructional sequence, whereas electrophile explanation sophistication remained relatively consistent. Although explanation sophistication was found to vary across reaction types, overall longitudinal trends for nucleophiles and electrophiles were mostly consistent. Relationships between explanation sophistication and course performance were present but weak. These findings suggest that development of sophisticated explanations may occur gradually and differently across mechanistic components and reaction contexts. More broadly, this work contributes to understanding how learners develop the language and explanatory practices of organic chemistry, highlighting the need for instructional approaches and future research that supports the long-term development of mechanistic reasoning.
keywords: reaction mechanism, mechanistic reasoning, organic chemistry learning, nucleophiles, electrophiles, course performance, chemistry education

title: A “DBER CURE” for the Replication Crisis: Revisiting Biochemistry Students’ Graphical Reasoning Using a Replication Study
text: Abstract In the past decade, researchers have been concerned about the “replication crisis” in which a high number of studies have not been able to be replicated. Conducting replication studies serves an important role in contextualizing the research in our field, but they are often overlooked given that resources and incentive structures typically favor “novel” and “original” work. In this article, we revisit a previous research project with the intention of conducting a replication study. Specifically, we revisited our own previous work that analyzed biochemistry students’ responses to open-ended exam questions involving graphical reasoning related to enzyme kinetics. Using this framing, we build a case for “replication” within the assumptions of qualitative research, contextualizing our work in relation to tenets of dependability, credibility, transferability, and confirmability. We also discuss the context of the replication study, which was conducted within the scaffolded structured of a “DBER CURE” (discipline-based education research, course-based undergraduate research experience). Based on the flexibility of scope, minimal resources needed, and bounded nature of the project, a DBER CURE can provide a feasible and adaptable approach to authentically engage undergraduate researchers in education research while serving as an ideal setting for conducting replication studies.
keywords: replication crisis, replication study, diagrammatic reasoning, enzyme kinetics, biochemistry education, course-based undergraduate research experiences, credibility, transferability, confirmability

title: LMC’S SPARTAN: An Adapted Peer-Led Team Learning Program in a Malaysian Preuniversity Chemistry Course
text: Abstract Introductory chemistry courses in Malaysia’s one-year preuniversity program leave limited class time for guided problem solving, and many students struggle with foundational topics. This Activity describes LMC’S SPARTAN, a large-scale adapted peer-led team learning (PLTL)-based academic support program implemented in a Malaysian preuniversity chemistry course. The program has been implemented every semester since Semester 1 of the 2024/2025 academic session; this Activity reports the Semester 1 2024/2025 rollout as an illustrative case. Using a Chemistry Diagnostic Test, 1,018 science students were grouped into 288 same-cohort peer leaders (“Titans”) and 730 mentees (“Olympians”) across 144 Spartan teams. A six-phase rollout combined diagnostic placement, data-driven team formation, online leadership profiling, targeted peer-leader training, three multiweek peer-led workshop cycles on core general chemistry topics, and culminating program-level assessment and recognition activities coordinated through Google Workspace and Telegram. In a one-group pre–post program evaluation, adapted Attitudes Toward Group Work and Attitudes Toward Chemistry instruments were administered before the peer-led workshop cycles and at program completion. Students reported significant increases in attitudes toward group work, from 3.990 to 4.365, t(1017) = 15.086, p < 0.001, dz = 0.473, and attitudes toward chemistry, from 3.801 to 4.175, t(1017) = 14.967, p < 0.001, dz = 0.469. Improvements in the two outcomes were positively associated (r = 0.564, p < 0.001). Role-disaggregated analyses indicated positive affective gains for both Titans and Olympians, while supportive dimension-level findings suggested that students perceived chemistry as more manageable. The findings demonstrate that an adapted PLTL-based structure can be implemented at scale in this setting and was associated with more positive affective responses toward collaborative learning and chemistry.
keywords: peer-led team learning, general chemistry, academic support programs, attitudes toward chemistry, peer leaders, cooperative learning, program evaluation

title: What Systems Thinking Do We Seek to Develop in Chemistry Education?
text: Abstract Although systems thinking has become a prominent goal of curricular reform in chemistry education, considerable variation exists in how it is conceptualized and implemented. In this Perspective, I argue that many of these differences arise from underlying tensions that are rarely discussed explicitly. These include tensions between descriptive and inferential engagement, system structure and system dynamics analyses, mechanistic and systemic reasoning, disciplinary depth and interdisciplinary breadth, epistemic and normative aims, and literacy and agency as educational end points. Rather than viewing these tensions as problems to be resolved, I suggest that they reflect different visions of the purposes of systems thinking in chemistry education and provide a framework for examining the educational assumptions that underlie its diverse conceptualizations and implementations. Clarifying these distinctions may help the field articulate more coherent visions of systems thinking and design curricula, instructional experiences, and assessments that support its progressive development across educational contexts.
keywords: systems thinking, chemistry education, curriculum reform, system dynamics, educational purposes, curriculum development

title: From Group Work to Teamwork: Preparing Chemistry Undergraduates for Collaborative Laboratory Practice
text: Abstract Effective teamworking has become a cornerstone of success in higher education, shaping both teaching practices and research outcomes. As universities respond to increasing demands for innovation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and student engagement, the ability to foster cohesive and high-performing teams is more critical than ever. Beyond enhancing academic productivity, teamworking plays a pivotal role in preparing graduates for the modern workforce, where collaboration, adaptability, and communication are among the most highly valued employability skills. Embedding these competencies within undergraduate programs not only benefits students but also aligns teaching practice with professional standards and accreditation requirements, which increasingly emphasize collaborative learning and authentic assessment. This paper describes an evidence-informed, practice-focused workshop designed to move students beyond task-based group work toward effective teamwork. Situated within undergraduate chemistry laboratory education, the workshop uses active and reflective pedagogies to prepare students for collaborative, research-style laboratory practice and offers a transferable model for explicitly teaching teamwork in chemistry curricula.
keywords: teamwork, group work, undergraduate chemistry students, employability skills, active learning, reflective pedagogy, transferable skills

title: Integrating Progressive Contextualization into Inquiry-Based Learning with Fading Scaffolds to Enhance High School Students’ Chemical Experimental Inquiry Skills: A Case Study of “The Mysteries of Polyphenols”
text: Abstract In the context of the county high school revitalization initiative, this study explores the design and classroom implementation of an inquiry-based chemistry laboratory unit integrating situational contexts and scaffolding instruction to promote laboratory inquiry skills among students in Chinese county-level high schools. Using the theme “The Mysteries of Polyphenols”, everyday materials familiar to students (e.g., tea and purple cabbage) were employed to construct a sequence of progressively developed real-life situations centered on the structure and properties of phenolic compounds. An inquiry continuum was designed in which instructional scaffolds were systematically faded as students moved through three levels of inquiry: confirmation, structured, and guided inquiry. Students were guided to progressively complete the full experimental inquiry cycle, including problem interpretation, theoretical analysis, experimental design, implementation, and results discussion. The study was implemented with a group of grade 11 students at a county high school in northeastern China. Students’ development in experimental inquiry skills was evaluated through classroom observations, analysis of student worksheets, and cognitive interviews. The teaching effects suggest that students demonstrated improved ability to connect chemical concepts with real-life contexts, design experimental procedures, and engage in evidence-based reasoning. This teaching design offers an instructive framework for enhancing experimental inquiry skills and promoting learning interests in high school chemistry classrooms.
keywords: inquiry-based learning, polyphenols, high school chemistry laboratory, evidence-based reasoning

title: Self-Regulated Learning and Chemistry Mindset as Predictors of General Chemistry Performance: Evidence from Natural Sciences and Engineering Majors in Turkey
text: Abstract Introductory chemistry courses present significant challenges for undergraduate students, and understanding the factors that support or hinder performance remains an active area of inquiry. This study examined the construct validity of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) and investigated the extent to which self-regulation strategies and chemistry mindsets predict exam performance among natural sciences and engineering majors enrolled in general chemistry courses at a large research-intensive university in Turkey. A total of 871 students completed a 45-item version of the MSLQ and the Chemistry Mindset Instrument (CheMI) during the Spring 2024 semester. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a four second-order factor structure: individual learning strategies, metacognitive self-regulation, social learning strategies, and effort and environment regulation strategies. Regression analyses revealed that prior exam performance was the strongest predictor of subsequent achievement in both of the course contexts. Among the MSLQ factors, social learning strategies were uniquely predictive for students enrolled in the course for natural science majors, while effort and environment regulation strategies were uniquely predictive for students enrolled in the course for engineering majors. The chemistry mindset did not contribute unique predictive variance beyond prior performance in either group. These findings underscore the context-dependent nature of self-regulated learning in chemistry and suggest that targeted instructional supports such as peer learning programs for students in the course for natural science majors and time management interventions for students in the course for engineering majors may better align with students’ distinct regulatory needs.
keywords: student self-regulation, Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, metacognitive self-regulation, social learning strategies, natural science majors, engineering students, peer learning, construct validity

title: Preprocessing Matters: Visualizing the Effect of Spectral Preprocessing on Principal Component Analysis
text: Abstract Principal component analysis (PCA) is widely used in chemistry for the exploratory analysis of multivariate data sets; however, many learners have difficulty understanding how spectral preprocessing influences PCA interpretation. This activity was developed to illustrate the effects of preprocessing on spectral profiles and PCA score plots using guided computational activities implemented in R. During four 50 min class periods, participants compared PCA models generated from raw spectra, Savitzky–Golay (SG) smoothing, first- and second-derivative preprocessing, Standard Normal Variate (SNV) normalization, and combinations of these preprocessing methods (Anal. Chem.1964, 36, 1627.). Guided questions emphasized how preprocessing modifies spectral appearance, sample clustering, intergroup distances, and the proportion of variance explained by the principal components. An assessment using an independent Raman spectroscopy data set evaluated the transfer of these concepts to previously unseen data. Comparison of the different preprocessing strategies demonstrated that smoothing and derivative preprocessing improved spectral discrimination by reducing baseline variation and emphasizing chemically relevant features, whereas SNV normalization minimized intensity differences among spectra. The activities also demonstrated that preprocessing substantially alters the variance structure of spectral data sets, leading to changes in cluster separation and PCA interpretation. By directly relating spectral transformations to multivariate results, this activity provides an accessible instructional activity for teaching spectral preprocessing and principal component analysis in analytical chemistry, spectroscopy, and chemometrics courses.
keywords: spectral preprocessing, principal component analysis, Savitzky-Golay filter, Raman spectroscopy, sample clustering, baseline variation

title: Mechanism-Centered Organic Chemistry Learning on a Chinese Video-Sharing Platform: A Ten-Year Case Study
text: Abstract Mechanistic reasoning is central to organic chemistry because learners must coordinate structure, electron movement, reaction conditions, selectivity, and synthetic logic. Outside formal classrooms, students often seek supplementary explanations through open video platforms, yet the educational functions of these informal resources remain underexamined. This ten-year case study analyzes an organic chemistry video collection on a Chinese video-sharing platform using platform metrics, video metadata, 4,195 comments, and 8,746 time-stamped viewer-generated overlay messages (danmaku). The collection functioned as a durable mechanism-learning infrastructure rather than a set of isolated videos. Foundational lectures supported structured review, named-reaction videos served as just-in-time references, and mechanism-problem videos generated conceptually dense interaction. Across 12,941 text interactions, 2,959 records (22.9%) were classified as mechanism/professional questions, and 3,492 records (27.0%) were classified as expressing high or midhigh cognitive depth. Comments primarily captured reflective learning purposes and affective support, whereas danmaku provided time-resolved evidence of in-video confusion, recognition, correction, and mechanistic discussion. Long-tail interaction patterns further showed that older videos continued to support new learners years after publication. These findings suggest that informal video platforms can extend organic chemistry learning beyond institutional courses by making mechanism-centered explanations searchable, revisitable, and socially annotated.
keywords: organic chemistry education, reaction mechanism, online video platforms, danmaku, viewer comments, named reactions, cognitive depth, Chinese learners, social annotation

title: Bridging the Gap Between Study Skills and the First-Year Chemistry Curriculum
text: Abstract General Chemistry I remains a gateway course for students in STEM fields, with many students dropping out of the course or switching to non-STEM fields after an unsuccessful first semester. The purpose of this article is to provide a framework for improving student performance in general chemistry using direct instruction in study strategies, specifically generative learning strategies. Twelve video-based modules teaching generative learning strategies applied directly to first-year chemistry concepts were implemented with 149 students at an undergraduate-focused university during the fall 2023 and fall 2024 semesters. These modules, which were integrated into a course management system, provided instruction and engagement in six separate literature supported strategies and their direct applications to course chemistry content. Strategies included comparing and contrasting diagrams, drawing, learning by teaching, making inferences, summarizing, and predicting via estimation. Use of these strategies provides insight into skills required for mastery of first year chemistry and also establishes a mechanism for implementing these strategies as a student support tool. The structure of these modules requires a small instructor time commitment after initial implementation and is a nonintrusive way to teach students how to apply study strategies to learning chemistry. Example course material used in the video modules along with preliminary assessment outcomes, suggestions for implementation, and future study are provided.
keywords: study skills, generative learning strategy, first-year chemistry, general chemistry, video-based instruction, student retention, learning by teaching, summarization, virtual learning environments, student support

title: From GROMACS Molecular Dynamics Simulations to Electronic Absorption Spectra: A Tutorial for Small Molecules in Organic Solvents
text: Abstract Classical molecular dynamics is a theoretical method useful for investigating noncovalent intermolecular interactions and conformational flexibility, enabling the simulation of processes such as aggregation/dissolution and adsorption. Molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry are increasingly introduced in chemistry curricula, yet students may encounter difficulties when translating theoretical concepts into robust simulation protocols, particularly outside biomolecular systems. Here, we present a tutorial designed to guide students through the preparation, execution, and analysis of the simulations of small organic molecules in nonaqueous solvents, followed by the calculation of ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) absorption spectra using time-dependent density functional theory. This tutorial focuses on several practical issues: obtaining force-field parameters, building simulation cells, selecting ensembles, and interpreting critical simulation parameters. Custom solvent models are validated against reference density and radial distribution functions, demonstrating how selected observables can be used to assess simulation reliability. We illustrate the usefulness of molecular dynamics by showing that molecular flexibility and solvent interactions broaden the UV–vis absorption band of indigo in chloroform. This contribution is intended as a hands-on educational resource for upper-level undergraduate and graduate students enrolled in physical chemistry and computational chemistry courses, as well as for Ph.D. students working in chemistry, physics, or material science, who are approaching molecular simulations. To support dissemination, we have released a ready-to-use package on GitHub that includes solvent boxes and all the necessary files and data for incorporating new molecules into GROMACS simulations: https://github.com/cippee/SolventSafari-for-GROMACS.
keywords: UV-visible absorption spectra, time-dependent density functional theory, small organic molecules, non-aqueous solvents, chloroform, indigo, force field parameters, ensembles, radial distribution function, molecular flexibility, solvent interactions, simulation-based training

title: Mapping High School Students’ Thinking Patterns in Substance Description and Identification Problems: A Perspective-Based Analysis
text: Abstract Understanding how students reason when solving substance description and identification (D&I) problems is foundational to fostering their chemical thinking. This study employs the theoretical lens of “perspectives” to characterize the diversity and organization of students’ thinking in D&I tasks. Using qualitative content analysis, we examined 634 analytical units from semistructured interviews with 18 tenth-grade students through deductive-inductive analysis and cross-category comparison. Responses were initially organized into four analytical categories: Chemical Perspectives, Interdisciplinary Perspectives, Personal Perspectives, and Unidentified Perspectives. Findings indicate that students most frequently employed chemical perspectives (55.9%), followed by unidentified perspectives (23.2%) and personal perspectives (15.8%); interdisciplinary perspectives were the least common (5.1%). Subcategories were further delineated within each category: chemical perspectives included implicit, explicit, and structured forms; interdisciplinary perspectives primarily manifested as biological perspective; personal perspectives were divided into dailylife and school-life experiences; and unidentified perspectives encompassed heuristic, test-taking schema, and knowledge retrieval approaches. Cross-category comparison showed that these patterns highlighted different aspects of students’ reasoning and revealed four underlying dimensions: the assumptions or attributes orienting attention, the sources of knowledge and experience, the types of reasoning employed, and the explicitness and organization of students’ ideas. Collectively, the initial categories and underlying dimensions provide an integrated account of students’ D&I thinking by characterizing the overall direction of their problem framing and the features through which their responses are constructed and expressed. These findings suggest that instruction should support students in developing productive perspectives and recognizing, evaluating, and coordinating diverse perspectives, knowledge resources, and reasoning processes.
keywords: chemical thinking, high school students, student reasoning, interdisciplinary perspectives, personal perspective, problem framing, chemistry misconceptions, test-taking strategies, knowledge retrieval, tenth grade students

title: Manual Grinding Promoted Synthesis of Functionalized 2,3-Dihydroperimidines: A Useful Introductory Laboratory Experiment in Organic Synthesis
text: Abstract This laboratory experiment presents an enhanced, environmentally benign protocol for the manual grinding synthesis of 2,3-dihydroperimidine derivatives. These conditions make the reaction environmentally sustainable, providing a nontoxic and safer alternative to conventional volatile organic solvents. The main goal of this experiment is to incorporate eco-friendly practices into synthetic organic chemistry while offering a practical educational framework for postgraduate students and highlighting the significance of sustainability in modern chemical synthesis. By engaging in this hands-on demonstration, students will develop essential skills, such as conducting a literature review, designing an experimental procedure, refining synthetic techniques, and evaluating results within a practical context. The activity also offers valuable exposure to green chemistry practices and synthesis strategies.
