Overall, this study demonstrates the practicality of incorporating green and easy-to-use methodologies in academia and supports the continued development of sustainable approaches in organic synthesis that follow green chemistry principles.
keywords: green chemistry, solvent-free synthesis, environmentally benign synthesis

title: A Students-as-Partners Approach to Developing an Advanced Chemistry Laboratory Experiment: Synthesis and Purification of 2-Phenylcyclohexanol
text: Abstract The efficacy of a Students-as-Partners (SaP) approach to the design of an advanced chemistry practical for year 3 undergraduate students is exemplified. Student consultation identified key priorities for laboratory teaching, which subsequently informed a codesign process involving four student partners. The resulting practical integrates air-sensitive synthesis, purification by gradient flash column chromatography, TLC visualization using staining methods, and spectroscopic determination of the reaction outcome within a single laboratory experience. The laboratory experience and subsequent feedback revealed a positive impact on the cohort’s confidence in performing the specific laboratory techniques, while simultaneously being an enjoyable experience. The study illustrates the potential for SaP approaches to develop practical experiments that achieve the desired practical skill acquisition and align with students’ educational priorities and expectations.
keywords: students as partners, student consultation, co-design, undergraduate chemistry education, student feedback

title: Transforming Student Revision: The Pedagogical Potential of Generative AI
text: Abstract The ability and pedagogical potential of ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude AI to create study notes and practice questions were evaluated using undergraduate pharmaceutical science lecture content. A mixed methods approach examined quantitative metrics such as comprehensiveness scores as well as qualitative aspects including accuracy and clarity. Both basic and complex input prompts were used, and a measure of how these models processed different data formats in the form of visual lectures, statistical content, and descriptive teaching formats was also included. All demonstrated potential, yet their performance differed depending on the specific task and type of content. Claude AI produced study notes that were highly reliable, showed high comprehensiveness scores between 0.75 and 1.0. ChatGPT demonstrated exceptional ability to create practice questions at multiple cognitive levels whereas Google Gemini performed better with detailed prompts but faced difficulties with mathematical questions. The study demonstrated that detailed prompting led to higher output quality across all systems especially in generating practice questions at higher cognitive levels. Generative AIs prove to be beneficial educational resource creation tools when their specific attributes and constraints are considered. Their effectiveness depends on the task and subject matter, demonstrating that they work best when used as supplementary tools instead of standalone solutions. This research study advances knowledge about successful Generative AI integration in higher education and identifies areas needing additional development.
keywords: generative AI, ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude AI, student revision, study notes, practice questions, prompting strategies, output quality, higher education, AI in teaching

title: An Undergraduate Laboratory Experiment on Lead-Free Tin-Based Perovskites for Phosphor-Converted Light-Emitting Diodes
text: Abstract Phosphor-converted light-emitting diodes (pc-LEDs) provide an effective platform for introducing undergraduate students to luminescent materials and device fabrication. However, the preparation of conventional phosphors often involves harsh conditions or toxic materials, limiting their use in teaching laboratories. In this work, we present an undergraduate laboratory experiment based on lead-free, tin-based zero-dimensional (0D) perovskites as alternative phosphors. Using a simple antisolvent-assisted method, students synthesize three 0D tin-based perovskites in powder or single-crystal form and investigate their optical properties. The as-prepared materials are subsequently integrated with commercial 365 nm UV LED chips to fabricate orange-yellow, orange-red, and red-emitting pc-LEDs, providing a direct and visually engaging demonstration of wavelength conversion. Through this experiment, students gain hands-on experience in material synthesis, optical characterization, and basic device fabrication. The activity highlights the relationship between material properties and device performance while introducing concepts in photophysics, solid-state materials, and sustainable chemistry. This experiment offers an accessible and interdisciplinary approach to connecting fundamental chemistry with modern optoelectronic applications.
keywords: zero-dimensional perovskites, single crystal synthesis, wavelength conversion, ultraviolet light-emitting diodes, orange-red emission, green chemistry, undergraduate laboratory experiment, photophysical properties, optoelectronic devices

title: Rethinking Organic Chemistry: Enhancing Pedagogies to Explain the Relative Reactivity of Aldehydes and Ketones
text: Abstract In this work, we explore the structure and charge distribution within carbonyl compounds. It is routine in textbook explanations to attribute the relative reactivity of aldehydes and ketones to electron-donating effects of alkyl groups. The results of our computational study indicate that the changes in charge distribution contradict the common textbook explanations. Neither the inductive effect nor the hyperconjugation effect of a methyl group lower the partial positive charge on a carbonyl carbon atom, and the incorporation of halogens adjacent to the carbonyl does not increase the partial positive charge. We must attribute the stabilization exclusively to differing hyperconjugation effects, and we use NBO analysis of hyperconjugation interactions to quantify the relative stabilization of carbonyl compounds by representative groups. As a result, there is an opportunity to develop a more coherent framework for teaching carbonyl chemistry, which intersects with alkene reactivity and carbocation stabilization.
keywords: aldehydes, ketones, carbonyl reactivity, hyperconjugation, inductive effects, electron-donating substituents, halogen substituents, natural bond orbital analysis, carbocation stabilization, alkene reactivity

title: Development and Validation of an Instrument for Assessing Literacy-Oriented Chemistry Achievement for Grades 9 to 11 Students
text: Abstract Assessing students’ chemical literacy is necessary for improving instruction. Schools and regional education authorities require an effective, reliable, and easy-to-use measurement instrument for educational quality monitoring. This study defined a literacy-oriented chemistry achievement assessment framework and developed an assessment instrument for students in grades 9–11. The Rasch model was used to establish empirical evidence for the reliability and validity of the measures. Findings indicate that the instrument meets the requirements of standardized tests for reliability and validity. The Bookmark Method was used to define literacy-oriented chemistry achievement levels into excellent, advanced, proficient, and basic. The instrument can be used to assess students’ progress in literacy-oriented chemistry achievement from middle school to high school, informing regional education policies, accountability, and curriculum and instructional improvement.
keywords: chemical literacy, scale development, Rasch model, Bookmark method, achievement levels, high school chemistry, middle school to high school transition, education quality monitoring, test validity and reliability

title: Microplastic Analysis through High School Classrooms: Leveraging an Authentic Science Experience for Students to Build Global Knowledge
text: Abstract Microplastics are ubiquitous particulate contaminants of concern that are found in all environmental media. While the global reach of this pollutant is well-documented, most monitoring involves densely populated urban areas or remote, pristine locations. Few studies track microplastic abundance and accumulation in everyday, suburban, or residential landscapes where most people live. The identification and quantification of microplastic pollution in a nearby retention pond, neighborhood creek, or popular recreational lake can be an effective means of illustrating the pervasiveness of this contaminant. This activity, designed for high school students, expands awareness around microplastic pollution and also offers participants an authentic hands-on science experience. Pilot tests demonstrate accessibility for this rigorously validated standard operating procedure. In addition to demonstrating fidelity, the activity gives students the opportunity to improve specific laboratory techniques, troubleshoot unexpected problems, consider bias and limits of detection, and develop future scientific questions. Survey questions administered to students piloting this activity demonstrate that it encouraged participants to consider how scientific findings about microplastic pollution could shape behaviors, attitudes, and policies in their local communities.
keywords: microplastics, microplastic pollution, high school science education, hands-on laboratory activities, retention ponds, suburban environment, student attitudes toward science, detection limit

title: Attendance, Pre- and In-Class Engagement, and Pandemic-Era Exacerbated Educational Debts Influence Success in a Flipped General Chemistry I Course
text: Abstract The extent to which pre-, in-, and post-class engagement in flipped undergraduate gateway chemistry courses influence course passing─and for whom─remains underexplored. This study examined factors related to passing a flipped General Chemistry I course for 158 students prior to and 110 students following the COVID-19 pandemic. Attendance and pre-class engagement had some association with passing, but in-class engagement had a stronger association with passing after accounting for other predictors. After accounting for academic predictors, female students had significantly lower odds of passing compared to their male peers. For the post-pandemic cohorts, in-class engagement improved but racial and ethnic disparities increased. Implications for flipped gateway chemistry course design are discussed.
keywords: flipped classroom, student attendance, COVID-19 pandemic, educational debt, gender disparities, racial and ethnic disparities, student success predictors

title: The Allergen Detective: An Undergraduate GC-FID/MS Laboratory Activity for Investigation of Volatile Ingredients in Essential Oil
text: Abstract This laboratory experiment introduces a natural volatile product analysis experiment for undergraduate students majoring in chemistry and pharmacy, helping students to gain a deeper understanding of chromatographic methods in natural-product analysis. It involves the use of gas chromatography–flame ionization detector (GC-FID) and GC-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) in the quantitative and qualitative analysis of allergenic components in a commercial formulated essential oil product (Feng You Jing). The experiment was divided into two parts, each lasting 4 class hours. In the first part, the GC-FID method was employed to qualitatively analyze five known inherent allergenic components in Feng You Jing (eucalyptol, camphor, menthol, methyl salicylate, and eugenol), based on the retention time. The component menthol was selected for quantitative analysis using the internal standard method; in the second part, the GC-MS method was used to qualitatively analyze the five inherent allergenic components through MS signals. Meanwhile, a potential prohibited allergenic component (6-methylcoumarin) was qualitatively identified. By comparing the performance characteristics of GC-FID and GC-MS in qualitative and quantitative analyses, students gained a deeper understanding of the complementarity between the two techniques, providing practical experience for subsequent professional learning and research practice.
keywords: essential oils, allergenic components, GC-FID, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, 6-methylcoumarin, 1,8-cineole, camphor, eugenol, methyl salicylate, natural product analysis, retention time, internal standard method, undergraduate laboratory experiment

title: Design of a Comprehensive Teaching Experiment for Synthesis, Photopatterning, and Device Application of Photo-Cross-Linkable Perovskite Nanocrystals
text: Abstract Perovskite nanocrystals (NCs) have garnered widespread attention for their outstanding optoelectronic characteristics and versatile application prospects. However, the inherently soft structure and dynamically unstable surface ligands of perovskite NCs greatly limit their processability. This work designs a facile and safe undergraduate experiment for the controllable synthesis and photolithography of photo-cross-linkable perovskite NCs. Adopting a mild ambient solution synthesis strategy, the experiment avoids rigorous reaction conditions and reduces teaching risks. In the experiment, students characterize the structural and optical properties of prepared perovskite NCs, analyze the photo-cross-linking mechanism, and explore their potential in photopatterning and light-emitting devices. This experiment integrates nanomaterial preparation, basic characterization, mechanism analysis, and photopatterning, enabling students to master the structure–property–application relationship of functional materials. It effectively cultivates students’ interdisciplinary experimental and analytical abilities, providing a reliable platform for integrating frontier perovskite research into undergraduate practical teaching. It helps students understand the research bottlenecks of photo-cross-linkable nanomaterials and accumulate hands-on experience for their future exploration of advanced optoelectronic materials.
keywords: perovskite nanocrystals, photolithography, photopatterning, undergraduate laboratory experiment, nanocrystal synthesis, light-emitting devices, optoelectronic materials

title: Integrating Values Education into Undergraduate Chemistry Curricula: A Review
text: Abstract This study systematically explores integration pathways and assessment methods for values education in undergraduate chemistry curricula to facilitate effective implementation. Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework, we screened and analyzed 63 peer-reviewed publications from 2016 to 2025 indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, and two targeted chemistry education journals, focusing exclusively on values education in undergraduate chemistry courses. The results reveal that scientific thinking (encompassing scientific inquiry, technical literacy, engineering design, and mathematical thinking) emerges as the most extensively researched domain, followed by ethical and ideal belief education. As a complementary perspective, chemical comprehensive literacy covers eight dimensions, including thinking ability, learning ability, innovative practical ability, and social ethical responsibility, with thinking ability as the focus. However, academic integrity and cultural literacy remain under-studied. In terms of values education integration carriers, experiments serve as the primary carrier, followed by chemistry outline, open-ended questions, calculation, and case-based learning, while innovative tools such as AI-assisted methods remain underutilized. Regarding assessment practices, final investigation assessments dominate, followed by evaluation tools and pre- and postinvestigations. Additionally, most included studies lack a stratified analysis of intervention effects on marginalized student groups. These findings highlight critical gaps in current value education implementation, emphasizing the need for expanded research on neglected domains and validated assessment systems to advance value education in chemistry curricula.
keywords: values education, undergraduate chemistry curriculum, integration pathways, assessment methods, scientific thinking, academic integrity, cultural literacy, chemistry experiments, case-based learning, AI in teaching

title: Bridging the Gap: Enhancing Intermolecular Forces Understanding with IMFs Cards
text: Abstract Intermolecular forces (IMFs) are a fundamental yet challenging topic in chemistry, as students often struggle to connect abstract concepts with observable phenomena. This study reports the development and evaluation of IMF cards, a card-based learning medium designed to integrate multiple levels of chemical representation, including definitions, diagrams, relative strengths, and molecular examples. The activity engages students in structured collaborative gameplay that promotes peer discussion and conceptual reasoning at a foundational level. The effectiveness of the cards was evaluated using a one-group pre-test–post-test design involving 53 students. The results show a statistically significant improvement in students’ understanding of intermolecular forces (p < 0.001), particularly in identifying and describing interaction types. Students also reported positive perceptions of the activity. These findings suggest that the IMF card activity may support students’ recognition and description of intermolecular forces in selected molecular systems, particularly in relation to identifying the dominant interactions between molecules.
keywords: intermolecular interactions, card-based learning, chemistry education, conceptual understanding, collaborative gameplay, chemical representation, peer discussion, molecular interactions, student perceptions

title: Decoding Macromolecular Compactness by Light Scattering: From Measurement to Chemical Insight in the Teaching Laboratory
text: Abstract A critical pedagogical challenge in polymer science is bridging the gap between theoretical concepts and their experimental validation. Herein, we present an integrated laboratory course designed to address this challenge by immersing students in a complete model construction-validation cycle. This course centers on experimentally determining the ρ-value (ρ = Rh/Rg), one of the key quantitative descriptors of macromolecular compactness, using light scattering techniques. Using a series of architecturally defined samples, including linear chain and single-chain nanoparticles (SCNPs) with varying cross-linking densities, students performed static and dynamic light scattering (SLS/DLS) to measure their radius of gyration (Rg) and hydrodynamic radius (Rh). Through guided data analysis, including constructing Zimm plots, fitting correlation functions, and evaluating the appropriateness of analytical models, students actively engaged in the iterative process of scientific inquiry─operating instruments, processing raw data, and comparing results to theoretical predictions. This approach transforms the laboratory from a routine characterization exercise into a coherent investigative experience that connects measurement, model-based analysis, and chemical insights of the structure–property relationship.
keywords: radius of gyration, hydrodynamic radius, light scattering, polymer science education, single-chain nanoparticles, crosslink density, Zimm plot, structure-property relationships, chain conformation, teaching laboratory

title: Bridging the Laboratory-to-Industry Gap: An International Project-Based Learning Model for Hydrogen Plant Conceptual Design
text: Abstract The global energy transition requires a workforce in the chemical sciences and engineering capable of bridging the laboratory-to-industry training gap. This paper presents an international joint Project-Based Learning (PBL) model involving undergraduate students from universities in Brazil and Ecuador, who collaborated on the conceptual engineering design of large-scale green hydrogen production plants for the urban transport sector. Following a PBL framework, three international teams integrated core chemical engineering principles with emerging technologies by utilizing basis of design and engineering criteria, simulation tools, and economic indicators to assess project feasibility. The pedagogical value of this model was evaluated through a student perception survey focusing on student-reported learning, in which 86% of participants recognized high perceived learning and 85.7% recommended the interuniversity format, despite logistical and linguistic hurdles. Subsequently, the technical outputs were subjected to an external evaluation by an industrial expert who validated the realism of the design bases and the rigor of the techno-economic assessments. The results suggested that while international PBL initiatives challenge traditional curriculum structures, they can provide a pathway to bridge the gap between academic theory and industrial reality. In doing so, the framework can foster the technical and transversal skills needed for future professionals to help lead the global energy transition. Ultimately, this study offers a proof-of-concept for an adaptable, international PBL framework that can be implemented across diverse institutional contexts and scaled to other fields of knowledge.
keywords: project-based learning, green hydrogen production, international student collaboration, undergraduate chemical engineering education, techno-economic analysis, student perceptions

title: A Team-Based Learning Activity with AI-Supported Reasoning for Teaching Molecular Dynamics
text: Abstract Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are increasingly included in chemistry and life science curricula, yet students often struggle to interpret outputs and to integrate multiple descriptors into coherent explanations. This paper presents a Team-Based Learning (TBL) activity for a graduate-level physical chemistry course for biotechnology students designed to support this process. The activity emphasizes comparison and integration of protein and ligand root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) time series, regional RMSF values, key hydrogen-bond persistence and pocket occupancy. It also requires collective justification under interpretative ambiguity and uses a deliberately constrained AI-based tutor as a reflective scaffold to prompt explanation without providing authoritative answers. Team discussions during the activity typically involved comparing these indicators and developing collective explanations for alternative molecular scenarios. Student feedback was generally favorable toward the collaborative TBL structure, whereas perceptions of the AI tutor were mixed, indicating that its perceived usefulness varied among students.
keywords: team-based learning, molecular dynamics simulation, AI tutors, reasoning support, protein conformational dynamics, RMSD, RMSF, biotechnology students, student perceptions of AI

title: Guiding Students to Use Spectroscopy to Determine Ligand Coordination Mode in a Cobalt(III) Acetylacetonate Complex
text: Abstract Four inquiry-style activities involving the synthesis and analysis of cobalt acetylacetonate were developed, implemented, and evaluated in an upper-level, undergraduate inorganic chemistry laboratory course. Throughout the two-week laboratory experiment, students are directed via scaffolded worksheets to answer the guiding question: how can spectroscopy be used to determine the coordination mode of a ligand to a metal center? Cooperative learning, student self-efficacy, and concept development and retention were assessed over a two-semester period in four sections of the course. The students worked effectively as teams during these activities by staying focused, communicating, and working collaboratively, and student self-efficacy with respect to confidence, engagement, and/or scientific ability was positively influenced. When working in teams, students were able to use 1H NMR and IR spectroscopic evidence to predict the coordination mode of 2,4-pentanedione to the cobalt(III) center but struggled with concept retention on the cumulative laboratory course final exam. Adoption of this lab experiment can serve to promote student engagement, interpersonal process skills, and student self-efficacy.
keywords: cobalt(III) acetylacetonate, ligand coordination modes, coordination chemistry, acetylacetone, 1H NMR, infrared spectroscopy, cooperative learning, student self-efficacy, concept retention

title: Teaching Practice of Medicinal Chemistry Guided by the Modified CREATE Pedagogy: A Case of Quaternary Ammonium Salt Antimicrobial Agents
text: Abstract We report a modified CREATE pedagogy (Consider, Read, Elucidate hypotheses, Analyze data, and Try Experiments) and implement it in an undergraduate medicinal chemistry course to address limitations of traditional teacher-centered STEM education, particularly the insufficient cultivation of scientific thinking. Compared with the classical CREATE framework, the fifth step was redefined from “Think of the next Experiment” to “Try Experiments”, thereby emphasizing hands-on practice and experiential learning. This approach shifts the instructional focus from passive knowledge acquisition to the development of students’ competencies in reading primary literature, analyzing scientific data, and designing drug discovery strategies. The course was structured around original research articles rather than textbook-based instruction, with modular content organized around the theme of the design and development of quaternary ammonium antibacterial agents, culminating in experimental validation of student-designed strategies. The results show that students enhanced their ability to analyze and synthesize complex literature and interpret scientific data. Their understanding of the scientific process deepened from theoretical awareness to hands-on engagement, creating an integrated, cyclic skill set spanning literature analysis, experimental design, and experimental verification. In addition, students demonstrated enhanced scientific self-efficacy, increased interest in medicinal chemistry and the research process, and made positive gains in classroom engagement and teamwork, highlighting a scalable and effective pedagogical framework for cultivating talent in medicinal chemistry.
keywords: medicinal chemistry education, quaternary ammonium compounds, antibacterial agents, scientific thinking, scientific data analysis, experiential learning, student self-efficacy, undergraduate STEM education, hands-on experiments

title: Graphical Analysis of Ordinary Differential Equations in Biochemical Kinetics: A Pedagogical Framework for Stability and Bifurcations
text: Abstract Graphical analysis provides an intuitive yet rigorous framework for understanding dynamical behavior in biochemical systems. This article develops a pedagogical framework for the analysis of one-dimensional autonomous ordinary differential equation (ODE) models arising in biochemistry and biophysics. Using the production–loss dynamics of a protein P as a foundational template, we systematically introduce increasing regulatory complexity through (i) Michaelis–Menten activation, (ii) cooperative Hill kinetics, and (iii) mutual inhibition. The resulting linear and nonlinear models are analyzed using rate–balance and rate–difference representations, together with phase-line diagrams that encode the underlying one-dimensional vector field. These graphical constructions enable the systematic identification of steady states and determination of their qualitative stability. Slope-based graphical arguments are further employed to detect the onset of bifurcations through the loss of hyperbolicity at equilibrium. Although slope information alone does not fully determine the specific bifurcation type, the vanishing of the local derivative provides a reliable graphical indicator of qualitative change, thereby strengthening the connection between visual intuition and formal dynamical systems analysis. In addition, the instructional implementation of this framework is evaluated through structured classroom deployment and assessment-based analysis. The results indicate improved conceptual understanding, enhanced ability to interpret dynamical behavior graphically, and increased student confidence in linking mathematical formalism with biological intuition. These findings highlight the importance of integrating evaluation-driven pedagogical strategies to validate and refine teaching approaches in mathematical chemistry education.
keywords: graphical method, ordinary differential equations, biochemical kinetics, stability analysis, bifurcation, Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Hill kinetics, reciprocal inhibition, steady state, student conceptual understanding

title: A Guided Size Exclusion Chromatography Demonstration for Teaching Polymer Separation and Characterization
text: Abstract Practical experience with modern analytical instruments is an essential component of undergraduate chemistry education, yet access to advanced instruments varies widely among institutions because of differences in available resources. Although size exclusion chromatography (SEC) is extensively used in polymer characterization in both academia and industry, undergraduate students at Montclair State University previously had limited opportunities to gain hands-on experience to this technique. To address this need, a demonstration using a multidetector-equipped Malvern Panalytical OMNISEC system was developed and incorporated into a second-year organic chemistry laboratory course during the 2025–2026 academic year. This activity engaged more than 300 undergraduate students representing chemistry, biochemistry, biology, psychology, marine science, and exercise science majors and was further extended to 8 undergraduate researchers and 6 K–12 participants through the Summer Polymer Research Program. Educational effectiveness was evaluated using worksheets, pre- and postdemonstration assessments, and anonymous students surveys. More than 95% of participants (n = 169) correctly answered the Fall 2025 postdemonstration worksheet questions, indicating a strong understanding of SEC concepts and instrument operation. In Summer 2026, students (n = 18) completed conceptually equivalent pre- and postdemonstration multiple-choice assessments. Mean scores increased from 7.72 ± 1.23 to 9.00 ± 1.03 (p < 0.001), demonstrating improved understanding following the demonstration. These findings show that a guided SEC demonstration provides an effective and adaptable approach for introducing advanced chromatographic instrumentation and polymer characterization to students from diverse scientific backgrounds.

title: Understanding the Topology of Simple Coordination Structures in Nonmolecular Solids – A Course on Symmetry and Catenation of Polyhedra
text: Abstract We present a course explaining structural features found in inorganic ion crystals aiming to give an outline to lecturers for a stepwise introduction to specific structural phenomena. It deals with the symmetry of polyhedra and its modification starting from isolated ones to their catenation toward the three-dimensional entity. We furthermore treat the sometimes-puzzling interaction of the coordination number, polyhedral catenation, and stoichiometric ratio of the compounds and present working sheets to help with “reading” structures by an analysis of their pictorial presentations. We discuss a variety of effects leading to distortions of polyhedral symmetry induced by typical bonding effects. We also present rules to help understand polymorphic transitions induced by changes in temperature or pressure, and we discuss structural features which are indictive for high temperature or high-pressure regimes.

title: Facile Synthesis and Surface Functionalization of CuInS2/ZnS (Core/Shell) Quantum Dots to Sensitize Green-to-Blue Photon Upconversion
text: Abstract Quantum dots (QDs), semiconductor nanocrystals typically a few nanometers (nm) in size, can exhibit intriguing photophysical properties that are visibly striking and engaging for undergraduate students. Here we present a laboratory experiment where undergraduate students synthesize CuInS2 QDs that they then shell with ZnS, yielding brightly emissive, Cd/Pb-free, and air-stable CuInS2/ZnS core/shell QDs. Students employ an adapted synthetic methodology that is straightforward, reliable, and neither requires air-free techniques nor temperatures >115 °C. Then, students use their QDs and two commercially available molecular fluorophores to assemble a three-component system (i.e., QD sensitizer, 9-carboxylanthracene (9-ACA) “triplet-transmitter” ligands, and emissive diphenylanthracene (DPA) molecules that can perform triplet fusion) that is capable of the fascinating phenomenon of photon upconversion (UC). Specifically, students’ solutions transform the incident green light (λ = 532 nm) from a laser into shorter-wavelength (higher-energy) blue emission (λmax ∼ 430 nm). The blue light from UC can be observed qualitatively with the naked eye (through a short-pass optical filter) and/or quantitatively using photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. Pedagogical analyses of student work and anonymous feedback are consistent with strong attainment of the intended learning outcomes, and suggest that the activity, which introduces contemporary nanochemistry, is interesting and engaging for students.
keywords: CuInS2/ZnS core/shell quantum dots, photon upconversion, diphenylanthracene, triplet fusion, surface functionalization, undergraduate laboratory experiment, photoluminescence

title: When is a Mitochondrial Compartment “Hot” or “Acidic”? Teaching the Limits of Temperature and pH in Small Confined Spaces
text: Abstract Temperature and pH are among the most familiar intensive variables in chemistry and biology and are typically introduced as smooth continuum quantities that can be assigned locally without ambiguity. Yet modern chemistry increasingly probes systems whose dimensions approach those of organelles, vesicles, enzyme active sites, and nanoscopic aqueous compartments, where molecular discreteness and statistical fluctuations become unavoidable. This article examines how continuum thermodynamic concepts emerge from underlying molecular statistics and under what conditions they begin to lose their classical interpretation using intracellular thermometry and proton statistics as pedagogical examples. A central case study is the “hot mitochondrion paradox,” in which fluorescent thermometry experiments suggest mitochondrial temperatures substantially higher (by several degrees) than the surrounding cytoplasm, whereas steady-state heat-diffusion models predict temperature differences of only ∼10–5 K. The pH example is even more striking. At physiological pH, a cell-sized compartment may contain tens of thousands of protons, whereas an organelle-sized volume may contain only tens, rendering pH a fluctuating proton-counting variable rather than a smooth concentration field. Classroom discussions of local equilibrium, thermalization, thermal baths, finite-size fluctuations, transient local heating, operational definitions of temperature and pH, and electronic temperature in quantum systems are suggested. Numerical examples, scaling estimates, and student exercises are also included. The goal is to help students recognize that temperature and pH do not abruptly “fail” at nanoscopic scales; rather, they become statistical, time scale-dependent, probe-dependent, and operationally defined quantities. The accompanying examples, discussion questions, and numerical exercises are intended for upper-level undergraduate physical chemistry and related courses.
keywords: mitochondrial pH, finite-size fluctuations, local equilibrium, thermalization, thermal baths, electronic temperature, quantum systems, thermal diffusion, organelles, vesicles, enzyme active site, statistical mechanics

title: Chemistry Education Research in the DBER Landscape: Insights from Comparative Publication and Citation Patterns
text: Abstract This Commentary examines publication and citation patterns among established researchers in chemistry, biology, and physics education research using data collected from Google Scholar profiles. Comparisons across career stages reveal similar patterns in the accumulation of scholarly visibility and recognition alongside some notable differences across fields. Chemistry education research exhibits relatively consistent relationships between seniority and publication and citation metrics, while biology and physics education research shows greater variability and higher levels of visibility among some researchers. These patterns are discussed in relation to differences in historical development, scholarly contexts, research agendas, and publication venues across fields. The analysis offers a perspective on the distinctive character of chemistry education research and highlights opportunities for reflection on its future development within a broader DBER landscape.
keywords: chemistry education research, biology education research, physics education research, publication trends, citation patterns, research visibility, disciplinary differences, Google Scholar profiles

title: Reflecting Back, Marching Forward: How Do We Ask Quo Vadis? Together in 2026
text: I n August 1976, chemistry educators gathered at the University of Wisconsin-Madison for the Fourth Biennial Conference on Chemical Education (BCCE).The meeting concluded with Gilbert Haight's address, Quo Vadis Chemical Education?�"Whereare you going, chemical education?"A retrospective in the conference report summarized Haight's address with one memorable sentence: "chemical education will not stay unchanged even if we do."1,2 That sentence remains a compelling reason to ask the question.It frames change not as a possibility but as something chemistry educators must expect.Changes in chemistry, technology, institutions, and the students we teach will continue to reshape what we teach, how we teach it, and who benefits.Declining to consider where chemistry education is going would not preserve the status quo; it would merely leave chemistry educators with less influence over the direction of change.The 1976 conference treated that direction as a collective concern.Its participants asked explicitly, "What Is Our Purpose?What Are Our Aims?"They considered what introductory chemistry should accomplish, whom it should serve, and how courses should respond to disciplinary and social change.A single-session program and short talks followed by substantial discussion helped participants examine those questions together.1,2 Quo vadis? was not simply a request for the next instructional innovation.It asked chemistry educators to consider where their field was going, what purposes should guide it, and how a diverse community might decide those questions together.
keywords: general chemistry, educational change

title: Prelab Webinar and Simulator Exercises to Improve Hands-on Learning of GC Temperature Programming in Second-Year Analytical Courses
text: Abstract Capillary-column gas chromatography (GC) is a common topic introduced in second-year analytical lecture courses. However, crafting an effective GC laboratory exercise for students at this curricular level presents many barriers. Most important among them is a novice understanding of chromatography concepts (e.g., analyte migration), a natural unfamiliarity with GC method parameters that must be fixed or controlled in the laboratory (e.g., column type and length, carrier flow rate, and column temperature), and physical limitations imposed by the larger class sizes often encountered in second-year courses, such as the small number of high-quality GC systems typically available for teaching and the limited amount of course time to use them. We describe here a week-by-week sequence of online prelab exercises (webinar followed by simulation) that provides better incremental preparation for these students to tackle the challenging hands-on learning objective of GC temperature programming. Students submit independent reports following each exercise to demonstrate their level of engagement. Our evaluation of these reports showed the webinar not only helps students improve their conceptual understanding of GC temperature programming, but it also helps them learn about key method parameters (e.g., temperature ramp rate and ramp hold) and prepares them to tackle the simulation and hands-on exercises that follow. In the simulation exercise, students familiarize themselves with GC parameters that closely match the method conditions of the hands-on GC system they will use in lab the following week. They can quickly model chromatograms that yield retention times very similar to experimental chromatograms, usually within 10–20%. Students noted that the close correspondence between simulated and experimental chromatograms is a useful tool for optimizing the final experimental temperature program. Also important to our approach, and ultimately to students learning this method in the lab, is the careful choice of the capillary column (nonpolar and relatively short length) and the test mixture composition (10 components including solvent). Both choices help decrease physical barriers to learning noted above by decreasing the time per injection and yet providing a challenging temperature program to optimize.

title: Using RAMP to Incorporate Risk-Based Safety Competencies into the Development of Undergraduate Forensic Chemistry and Toxicology Courses
text: Abstract In forensic chemistry and toxicology laboratories, handling biohazardous specimens and controlled substances is routine and comes with added regulatory and safety restrictions. Therefore, working in these laboratories requires that undergraduate students develop additional safety competencies (SC) and knowledge, skills, and attitudes (KSAs) above those of general chemistry and specific to forensic science. In this context, course developers and educators need to design courses that include student learning outcomes in safety. The hazards encountered in typical forensic experiments are presented with corresponding strategies to minimize their risks. To meet the general and discipline-specific safety considerations in a forensic teaching laboratory, this paper proposes a set of recommendations based on the RAMP risk management framework (recognize hazards, assess risk, minimize risk, and prepare for emergencies). The importance of incorporating regulatory and safety issues and risk assessment into lectures and laboratory procedures is proposed.

title: Kids’ Experiment All Grown Up: Elevating the Classic Red Cabbage Demo for Biochemistry and Food Chemistry University Students
text: Abstract Using red cabbage as a pH indicator is a common experiment in primary and secondary school science classes and even at-home experiments. The fun experiment, often used to spark young people’s interest in STEM, involves changing the color of pH-sensitive anthocyanin pigments in red cabbage juice using common household ingredients. We present an advanced version of the classic experiment for use at the university level. The lab is applicable for both biochemistry and food science students and can be conducted as an in-person lab or a remote experiment students can complete fully at home. The colorful visuals, whole foods, and simple, familiar ingredients effectively facilitate students’ understanding of the complex concepts of pigment chemistry and acid–base equilibrium. Students who participated in the lab demonstrated increased confidence in the subject matter, and improved scores on quiz questions related to pH, acid equilibrium, and anthocyanins. Students conducting the lab remotely reported the experiment was easy to perform, fun, and helped them to better conceptualize challenging course material.
keywords: red cabbage, anthocyanins, acid-base indicators, acid-base balance, food chemistry, biochemistry education, remote laboratory experiments, student self-confidence

title: How Do Inorganic Students and Instructors Describe Conductivity in Solids?
text: Abstract This study investigates how inorganic chemistry students and faculty discuss electrical conductivity differences between a metal and a semiconductor using an open-ended question with temperature-dependent conductivity data. The question was deployed across seven foundation-level inorganic chemistry courses in different institutional contexts. Four overarching categories of ideas emerged from the responses: conductivity, doping, band structure, and the effects of temperature. Responses were analyzed on the basis of these categories. The majority of students discussed conductivity and doping, with fewer discussing the band structure and temperature. Students enrolled in courses with a physical chemical prerequisite referenced more ideas, including more submicroscopic ideas, in their responses compared to students in a course that did not have this prerequisite. Instructor responses included ideas from all four categories as well as more ideas derived from submicroscopic models. This pattern is consistent with experts referring to more resources than novices. Generally, these results provide further evidence of the impact that increased exposure and practice have on learning and development of knowledge. These findings reveal that, although students use ideas from the four overarching categories, they do not fully use those concepts to explain the electronic behavior of solids, which suggests the need for instruction that helps students make connections between macroscopic data and submicroscopic explanations. The resources used by inorganic students and suggestions for how these ideas can be surfaced and integrated during instruction are presented herein.
keywords: electrical conductivity, inorganic chemistry education, student misconceptions, doping, electronic band structure, temperature dependence of conductivity, macroscopic-microscopic connection, instructor knowledge

title: Lessons for Students and Educators in Developing Quantum Mechanical Wave Functions Using Slater Determinant and Sum-of-Permutations Methodologies
text: Abstract Students who are engaged in understanding physical and chemical phenomena and/or designing devices that involve various atomic and molecular systems benefit from an understanding of general concepts that underlie quantum chemistry and quantum mechanics. Wave functions are one of the most basic and important concepts for understanding quantum chemistry, but many students in quantum mechanics courses struggle to write and interpret these functions correctly. This Tutorial presents novel instructional content related to the creation of multiparticle wave functions for multielectron systems using both the Slater determinant and the older sum-of-permutations equations. Late 20th century and early 21st century textbooks typically utilize the Slater determinant for describing multiparticle wave functions. Sum-of-permutations equations that are used in some early and mid-20th century texts and papers can be ambiguous and confusing when compared to the Slater determinant. Herein, we clarify the ambiguity present in the sum-of-permutations equations and provide guidance through examples and lessons to demonstrate that these older equations are equivalent to the newer Slater determinant form. By bridging the gap between past and current approaches for creating multiparticle wave functions, this Tutorial elucidates multidisciplinary teaching and learning opportunities in the area of quantum chemistry and quantum mechanics.
keywords: Slater determinants, many-electron systems, quantum chemistry education, history of quantum chemistry

title: The Science of Design: Introducing Design of Experiments (DoE) through a Hydrogel-Based High School Chemistry Investigation
text: Abstract Creating lessons that connect classroom content to real-world application can enhance high school students’ interest in STEM curricula. The scientific method is one such component of the curriculum that can be meaningfully connected to techniques and practices used across a range of STEM fields. Specifically, Design of Experiments (DoE) is a statistical process widely used in STEM industries and research and development contexts to efficiently collect and analyze scientific data, yet it is rarely taught at the high school level. Importantly, DoE also introduces foundational concepts in structured data generation, multivariable analysis, and pattern recognition that underpin emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches. To bridge this gap between methodological understanding and real-world application, this study implemented a hands-on DoE-based lesson focused on polymer hydrogels, which was assessed in a high school science classroom with students across grades 9–12. Pre- and postlesson assessments, consisting of multiple-choice, short-answer, and conceptual understanding questions, were used to evaluate shifts in students’ content knowledge and understanding of the DoE approach. The median correct response rate for the conceptual understanding section increased from 33.33% to 66.67% between the pre- and postassessments. Additionally, while response rates for conceptual questions increased following the intervention, a statistically significant improvement in response accuracy was not observed. This pilot study serves as a valuable starting point for designing STEM lessons that introduce students to DoE as a framework for experimental design, while also providing insight into student understanding of this approach─an essential skill set for preparing students for future STEM workforce demands.
keywords: experimental design, hydrogels, polymer science, high school chemistry teaching, multivariable analysis, pattern recognition, STEM education, student conceptual understanding

title: Navigating English Medium Instruction in Chemistry: Language as a Barrier or Bridge to Learning
text: Abstract English is the primary language of communication and knowledge exchange in the global scientific community. Therefore, English Medium Instruction (EMI) in undergraduate chemistry education is expected to provide students with broader access to academic resources and enhance their competitiveness for graduate studies and international careers. However, for non-native English speakers, language barriers can pose challenges, potentially hindering comprehension and decreasing learning motivation. In this study, we compared the academic performance of chemistry major students enrolled in EMI and Chinese Medium Instruction (CMI) programs who followed the same curriculum over three different enrollment years from 2022 to 2025. We examined students’ learning outcomes from introductory level courses, General Chemistry and General Chemistry Laboratory, two advanced chemistry courses, Organic Chemistry and Physical Chemistry, and a specific topic course, The Application of Group Theory in Chemistry. Notably, almost none of the EMI students had prior experience with English-based instruction in Chemistry before entering university. Despite this, our findings revealed no clear correlation between English proficiency and academic performance, and the overall achievement levels of EMI and CMI students were comparable across most courses. Interestingly, academic performance in entry-level General Chemistry emerged as a strongly associated factor with subsequent achievement in advanced chemistry courses. However, EMI students’ grades exhibited two distinct groups in some courses and a slightly higher program dropout rate. Our results also found modern technologies such as YouTube videos and ChatGPT play important roles in lowering language barriers. Drawing on Sociocultural Theory, Translanguaging Theory, and Self-Determination Theory, we interpret these findings as suggesting that learning in EMI chemistry contexts is supported by the interaction of mediational resources, translanguaging practices, and learner development. Finally, we discuss pedagogical implications and propose instructional strategies to more effectively support EMI students in undergraduate chemistry education.
keywords: English-medium instruction, chemistry education, language barriers, non-native English speakers, academic performance, Chinese-medium instruction, English proficiency, general chemistry, organic chemistry, physical chemistry, program dropout, YouTube videos, ChatGPT, translanguaging, sociocultural theory, self-determination theory, undergraduate chemistry students

title: Time Capsules of Plastic: An Inquiry-Based Outreach Activity
text: Abstract Declining interest in science among young learners presents a persistent challenge for science education and chemical literacy. This study reports on a 14-month, inquiry-based outreach program implemented with children aged 7–9 in a UK school, centered on the environmental chemistry of plastic degradation. Through hands-on investigation and guided inquiry, pupils explored the breakdown of materials in environmental contexts, linking chemical concepts to real-world sustainability issues. Evaluation of the program indicates that participation increased pupils’ interest in science and enhanced their understanding of environmental processes. Additionally, the activity broadened pupils’ perceptions of scientists and the nature of scientific work. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of early, context-driven inquiry-based approaches in fostering engagement with chemistry and promoting more informed and positive attitudes toward science.
