title: An AI-Assisted Interactive Video-Based System (AI-LabEyes) for Enhancing Visualization, Formative Feedback, and Collaborative Learning in Chemistry Laboratory Instruction
text: Abstract This study describes AI-LabEyes, an AI-assisted, multiangle video system designed to support observation, formative feedback, and teacher-mediated evaluation in secondary-school chemistry laboratories. The system combines synchronized user-facing, side, and overhead video views; computer-vision-based identification of selected titration actions; secure storage for deidentified instructional clips; and tools for teacher or expert review. In a field implementation during a high-school acid–base titration competition, AI-LabEyes scores from 46 valid student videos were compared with teacher-adjudicated scores for six operational actions. Overall agreement was 88%, with stronger performance for visually clear actions such as leak inspection and buret conditioning (96% accuracy for each) and weaker performance for actions requiring finer temporal or judgment-based interpretation. The system effectively promotes the visualization of experimental teaching, formative feedback of students, and collaborative improvement, providing a reference for AI-assisted experimental teaching.

title: Colorimetric-SERS Dual-Mode Detection of Organophosphorus Pesticides Using Au-R-Fe3O4 Nanozyme Cascade Platform: A Practical Approach for Chemistry Education
text: Abstract Organophosphorus pesticides (OPs) pose significant environmental and health risks due to their persistence and neurotoxicity, yet current detection methods rely on sophisticated instrumentation inaccessible to educational settings. To address this pedagogical gap, we developed a recyclable Au-R-Fe3O4 nanozyme cascade reactor integrating robust peroxidase-like activity and surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) capabilities. This platform enables dual-mode detection of OPs through an innovative enzyme cascade (AChE/ChOx/Au-R-Fe3O4), where OP-induced inhibition of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) modulates colorimetric and SERS signals of oxidized 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine. The magnetic Fe3O4 nanorings facilitated efficient catalyst recovery, maintaining 92% activity after five cycles, demonstrating exceptional operational stability ideal for classroom reuse. The dual-mode Au-R-Fe3O4 sensor achieved detection limits for chlorpyrifos and methyl parathion, reaching 8.56 and 5.24 ng/mL via colorimetry and 0.59 and 0.76 ng/mL via SERS, respectively. Particularly significant for chemical education, this system visually demonstrates enzyme kinetics, nanomaterial properties, and environmental analysis principles in a single integrated experiment. We detail its implementation in undergraduate laboratories, enabling students to explore interfacial catalysis, spectroscopic quantification, and environmental monitoring applications through hands-on experience with cutting-edge nanotechnology.

title: Implementing a Course-Specific Chatbot in Undergraduate Biochemistry
text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly available to students, but their educational value depends on how they are configured, constrained, and integrated into course practices. This technology report describes a no-code workflow for implementing a course-specific chatbot in upper-division undergraduate biochemistry using a custom GPT configured with instructor-generated lecture slides, class transcripts, handouts, syllabus information, and custom instructions. The workflow emphasized course alignment, frequent updating, instructor validation, assessment scoping, and student prompt guidance. The chatbot was used in biochemistry I lecture across two consecutive fall offerings and extended to biochemistry II lecture for follow-up use. Student survey responses indicated substantial adoption and generally positive perceptions; peer-led supplemental instruction attendance and course-grade data are presented only as contextual information. The report highlights a practical, transferable approach for using no-code custom GPT tools to extend course-aligned study support while preserving instructor oversight and existing academic support structures.

title: MoS2@DAS Hydrogel Experiment for Interdisciplinary Teaching: Enhancing Undergraduates’ Research Literacy
text: Abstract The comprehensive teaching experiment presented herein exhibits strong interdisciplinary integration, practical relevance, and application potential, making it a suitable experimental teaching program for undergraduates majoring in materials chemistry, polymer science, and other related fields. This experiment successfully integrates organic synthesis techniques, nanomaterial preparation methods, and polymer hydrogel performance characterization skills acquired by undergraduate students, which is critical for enhancing their comprehensive experimental operation capabilities. Through hands-on practice, students not only enhance their ability to solve complex experimental problems but also develop innovative thinking and scientific research literacy. Taking the application requirements of multifunctional hydrogels in the biomedical field as the starting point, the experiment guides students to deeply explore the intrinsic relationship between the chemical structure and properties of materials, thereby establishing a systematic cognitive framework. Throughout the experiment, students complete the synthesis of dopamine methacrylamide (DMA), the preparation of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) nanosheets, and the construction of MoS2 composite hydrogels (MoS2@DAS), followed by evaluating the mechanical, adhesive, catalytic, and photothermal properties of the hydrogels via various characterization methods. The teacher–student interactive teaching mode runs through the entire process of experimental preparation, implementation, and summary, positively expanding students’ theoretical knowledge, improving practical skills, and fostering innovation ability.

title: Line Graph Competence in Chemistry: Introducing the Receptive Graph Competence Model (RGC-Chem)
text: Abstract In chemistry, a visual science, the ability to read, interpret, and reason with graphs is essential for conceptual understanding. However, existing models of graph competence have largely been developed outside chemistry and primarily focus on the formal-representational dimension of graph comprehension. As such, they do not adequately capture the domain-specific cognitive demands that arise when learners engage with chemistry-specific graphs. This paper introduces the Receptive Graph Competence Model for Chemistry (RGC-Chem), a hierarchically structured, domain-specific framework for the analysis, instruction, and assessment of receptive line graph competence in chemistry. The model comprises five hierarchically ordered levels, ranging from the identification of individual function values (Level 1) to the integrated interpretation of more than one graph (Level 5), and integrates two complementary dimensions: a formal-representational dimension addressing the structural conventions of graphs and a domain-specific content dimension encompassing the chemistry-related conceptual knowledge required for comprehensive graph understanding. The RGC-Chem was developed using a deductive–inductive approach, grounded in established theoretical frameworks and empirically refined through a systematic textbook analysis of 371 line-graph-related tasks from German secondary chemistry textbooks. The findings indicate that the model’s competence levels accommodate the full range of graph-related task demands identified in these textbooks and support the model’s practical utility as a research and instructional tool. The paper also discusses the model’s potential for task design, assessment, and instructional planning, as well as its current limitations, particularly the need for empirical validation with learners. Overall, the RGC-Chem provides a theoretically grounded framework for research and practice related to graph competence in chemistry education and highlights the importance of connecting graphical patterns to their underlying chemical meaning.
keywords: line graphs, chemistry education, graph interpretation, chemistry textbook, task design, assessment, instructional planning, graphical representation

title: A Protocol to Identify Large Language Model Use in Undergraduate Chemistry Essays
text: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have been widely adopted by chemistry undergraduate university students as a learning tool, but few methods exist to measure the scope of their influence on essay writing. This report introduces a protocol based on monitoring the frequency of specific words used excessively by LLMs among a sample of 1073 chemistry student essays between 2018 and 2025. Analysis revealed that 54 keywords known to be favored by LLMs simultaneously increased in frequency among essays submitted during the last two years. When the lists of keywords were applied to specific essays, the findings indicated 43% of essays submitted during 2025 had at least some evidence of LLM-generated text. This protocol offers a simple method to generate an approximate scope of LLM uptake among a cohort, which can be combined with student survey data to produce a detailed overall impression of students’ use of generative artificial intelligence. This work’s findings are intended to stimulate discussion on the best practices to update literature review assessment criteria, to ensure it is maintained as a valid assessment option within a curriculum equipped for the widespread adoption of LLMs.

title: The Relationship between Academic Performance and Perceived Competence in General Chemistry
text: Abstract Students’ perceived competence (PC) in a General Chemistry 1 course was explored using the Perceived Competence Scale, a short, well-established instrument grounded in self-determination theory. The PC Scale allows for investigation of whether students perceive that they can achieve their goals in a course, broadly speaking. Students’ PC was explored at the beginning and end of the semester in aggregate and disaggregated by gender, race, and academic performance. Only small statistically significant differences were observed in students’ PC over the course of the semester. Students’ gender was found to have a small effect on PC whereas students’ race did not affect PC. Statistically strong correlations were found between PC and both midterm grades and final course grades measured at both the beginning and end of the semester. These exploratory results signify the importance of students’ PC on academic performance and, conversely, academic performance on PC. Furthermore, the four-question PC instrument can be used as a quick diagnostic tool to assess students’ confidence in a general chemistry course which can alert instructors to the need for interventions to improve students’ learning outcomes.

title: Breaking the Code: Creating Engaging Lock-Based Activities to Transform Student Learning Experiences
text: Abstract General Chemistry serves as a foundational course for STEM students, where early engagement and confidence are critical to academic success. To reinforce core concepts from college-level introductory chemistry courses, we developed an interactive puzzle box game focused on limiting reagents, hybridization, de Broglie wavelength, and dipole moments. Students were asked to help save their chemistry professor and create a fleet of superhumans to stop the evil Dr. Doomfizzle from taking over the chemistry department. They were given four question sets to open three vaults and complete a final task. The game was implemented as a final exam review in the penultimate week of the quarter, and participating students completed pre- and postactivity surveys. Confidence was measured using a self-reported five-point Likert scale. Results indicated significant increases in student confidence across three of the four topics (p < 0.001). Students who participated scored higher on the final exam than those who did not.

title: Engaging Students in Chemistry through Chemical Ecology: A Contextual and Playful Learning Approach
text: Abstract The persistent decline in students’ interest in science, particularly in chemistry, calls for innovative educational strategies that promote engagement and contextual understanding. This study explores chemical ecology as a meaningful and interdisciplinary theme capable of connecting chemistry concepts, such as molecular interactions and structural representation, to students’ daily lives. We designed and implemented a playful pedagogical intervention based on the chemical ecology of Paederus irritans (commonly known as potó), an insect native to northern Brazil whose defensive compound, pederin, is of significant biochemical interest. The intervention involved a brief theoretical introduction followed by a team-based educational scavenger hunt (gincana) with 150 students from two public schools in Brejinho de Nazaré, Tocantins, Brazil. Pre- and post-intervention diagnostic assessment instruments were applied to assess the impact on students’ understanding and attitudes toward chemistry. The results revealed a notable increase in students’ recognition of chemistry in natural phenomena and a greater self-reported interest in chemistry-related topics. The findings suggest that contextualized, playful approaches anchored in chemical ecology may enhance student engagement and conceptual learning in chemistry education.
keywords: chemical ecology, chemistry education, student engagement, playful learning, scavenger hunt, pederin, contextual learning, attitudes toward chemistry, molecular interactions, structural representation, public schools

title: Effects of an Augmented Reality Chemistry Application on High School Students’ Knowledge Gains, Learning Engagement, and Technology Acceptance
text: Abstract Understanding microscopic concepts is a core challenge in chemistry education. Augmented Reality (AR) learning environments address this challenge by providing innovative instructional tools and enabling direct student interaction with molecular representations. To investigate AR’s potential for teaching abstract concepts such as electron density distribution and molecular polarity, we developed a chemistry AR application featuring dynamic visualizations of electron pair displacement and lone pair distribution through Bézier curve scripting. Using a mixed-methods approach, we examined the effects of this AR-supported review activity on 48 high school students in Xinjiang, China, measuring cognitive gains, learning engagement, and technology acceptance. The findings indicate that participation in the AR-supported activity was associated with significant improvements in learning outcomes, with low-achieving students showing greater progress than high achievers, alongside enhanced engagement across cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions, and manageable self-reported cognitive load. Notably, despite minor usability challenges, students reported high levels of technology acceptance. Overall, these findings suggest that AR-supported review activities built around dynamic visualizations of molecular polarity can be positively associated with student outcomes in high school chemistry contexts.
keywords: augmented reality, chemistry education, molecular polarity, electron density distribution, molecular visualization, student engagement, technology acceptance, cognitive load, low-achieving students, high school students, review activities

title: Student Epistemological Thinking and Problem-Solving Approaches: The Case of First-Year International Students in a General Chemistry Course
text: Abstract A common goal of first-year General Chemistry instructors is to encourage students to adopt conceptual approaches to problem-solving rather than algorithmic approaches. This study investigates the role of personal epistemology, with a specific focus on views of the structure of chemistry knowledge in understanding first-year General Chemistry students’ problem-solving approaches. As part of a larger study on student epistemologies, 13 first-year international students enrolled in General Chemistry participated in two task-based and semi-structured interviews. During the task-based interviews, participants solved General Chemistry problems aloud. They also participated in semi-structured interviews that explored their epistemological views. Analysis of the data corpus indicates that students who successfully solved both problems primarily used conceptual approaches and more consistently activated epistemological resources that framed chemistry knowledge as conceptually connected and consisting of interrelated ideas. Of the five students who successfully solved both problems, three consistently framed chemistry knowledge as complex and interconnected. The remaining two recognized chemistry as conceptually connected but distinguished between their views of chemistry as a discipline and their perceptions of what was required for success in introductory chemistry courses. This sentiment was echoed by additional students who solved at least one problem successfully using a mix of both conceptual and algorithmic approaches. Four students were unable to solve either task and primarily relied on algorithmic approaches; these students more frequently framed chemistry as simple, consisting of unconnected facts and formulas, and provided less evidence of attending to conceptual connections across topics. Students attributed inquiry-based learning experiences and instructors’ explicit discussion of conceptual connections among chemistry topics as influences on how they viewed chemistry knowledge. One student who reported a shift toward viewing chemistry as interconnected and conceptually structured attributed the change to concept-focused assessments and opportunities to reflect on her epistemological views. These findings suggest that encouraging students to activate resources consistent with a conceptual and interconnected view of the structure of chemistry knowledge may promote greater use of conceptual approaches to General Chemistry problem solving.
keywords: personal epistemology, chemistry problem solving, international students, first-year chemistry, epistemological beliefs, inquiry-based learning

title: Gold-Nanoparticle-Based Detection of the Iodine Content in Kelp: A Teaching Practice on Colorimetric Sensing for the University Basic Chemistry Laboratory
text: Abstract Gold nanoparticles (Au NPs) are widely used in colorimetric analysis due to their surface plasmon resonance effect. Kelp, being rich in iodine, serves as an important dietary source that is necessary for the synthesis of thyroid hormones in the human body. However, in current undergraduate chemistry laboratory teaching, there is virtually no use of Au NP etching-based regeneration detection systems for analyzing the iodine content in kelp. To address this gap and to align with the principles of green chemistry education, this study designed a teaching activity for university chemistry laboratories. In this design, the iodine in kelp was converted into iodide ions (I–) prior to detection. Kiwifruit juice was employed as both a natural reducing agent and a stabilizer to synthesize Au NPs, which were then used to develop a colorimetric method for I– detection. Finally, students captured color data with smartphones, performed grayscale analysis using ImageJ, constructed calibration curves, and successfully calculated the iodine content in kelp. This activity is designed for second-year undergraduate chemistry majors and can be integrated into an analytical chemistry laboratory course. Feedback from questionnaires and reports indicated a high level of engagement and comprehension of nanoscience concepts. The experiment is safe and feasible, with moderate cost, suitable for widespread adoption in basic university chemistry laboratories.
keywords: gold nanoparticles, colorimetric sensing, iodine detection, kelp, surface plasmon resonance, nanoparticle etching, iodide, smartphone image analysis, green chemistry education, undergraduate chemistry laboratory, iodine content

title: Sensing the Seawater Distillation Process
text: Abstract Accessibility in chemical education requires that laboratory experiments accommodate sensory and functional requirements, and these requirements can be addressed through thoughtful design and technological adaptation. This study presents a modified seawater distillation apparatus tailored for students with blindness or low vision (BLV), incorporating sensors as a key adaptation. The sensors provide auditory feedback, enabling BLV students to participate in the experiment and monitor key parameters of the distillation process, including temperature, volume, salinity, pH, and dissolved oxygen. This approach fosters an inclusive, immersive laboratory experience linking chemistry concepts to real-world applications. Our findings highlight the potential of sensor-based technologies for both online and offline monitoring to enhance the accessibility of STEM education for BLV students.
keywords: seawater distillation, blindness and low vision, sensory adaptation, auditory feedback, inclusive STEM education, salinity measurement, dissolved oxygen, online monitoring

title: Synthesis, Physicochemical Properties Determination, and Absorption Simulation of Phenytoin: An Undergraduate Medicinal Chemistry Experiment for Laboratory Education
text: Abstract Laboratory experimentation plays a pivotal role in the discipline of pharmaceutical chemistry, reinforcing theoretical knowledge and supporting the development of practical skills. Drug synthesis and determination of the physicochemical properties of synthesized compounds are essential topics commonly explored in laboratory-based instruction. In this context, the presently described experimental work comprises two laboratory sessions of 3 h each. On the first day, students carry out synthesis and characterization of phenytoin, while in the second session its solubility is determined, using a solvent series with an increasing polarity index and at different pH values and concluding with a simulated assessment of its absorption when administered orally. The main objectives of this laboratory assignment are for the students to develop confidence in executing standard experimental procedures and deepen their understanding of the chemical concepts related to heterocyclic compounds in order to enhance their research skills, analytical reasoning, and critical thinking. The assessment includes prelaboratory and postlaboratory assignments and in-lab operation and experimental observation. The results obtained from the evaluation of this laboratory exercise are excellent, and the students have demonstrated, through their comments collected in a final survey, a high level of appreciation for this lab project.
keywords: phenytoin, drug synthesis, physicochemical properties, solubility determination, pH-dependent solubility, heterocyclic compounds, undergraduate laboratory experiment, medicinal chemistry education

title: Using NMR Spectroscopy to Analyze and Compare Reaction Progress of Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitutions in Undergraduate Organic Laboratories
text: Abstract The chemistry of aromatic compounds is an important component of second-year organic chemistry. However, lecture courses and laboratory experiments tend to focus on electrophilic aromatic substitution, whereas nucleophilic aromatic substitution is taught as an afterthought. This article focuses on a simple, efficient, and cost-effective nucleophilic aromatic substitution between 2-chloropyridine and benzyl alcohol. In addition to showcasing the utility of this type of reaction, it also introduces students to heterocyclic compounds and demonstrates an instance of their unique reactivity compared with simple benzene derivatives. The experiment also allows students to investigate factors affecting the reaction rate by analysis of the 1H NMR spectra of the crude reaction mixtures of a variety of variable reaction conditions.
keywords: nucleophilic aromatic substitution, 2-chloropyridine, benzyl alcohol, heterocyclic compounds, reaction kinetics, 1H NMR, undergraduate organic laboratory, aromatic chemistry, reaction rate factors

title: First-Year Chemistry Connections: Social Bonds and Disciplinary Belonging
text: Abstract First-year chemistry courses play a pivotal role in shaping student success within science programs, yet they are often characterized by high stakes, large enrollments, and considerable academic challenges. This study explores first-year science students’ sense of belonging across two dimensions: social belonging within the classroom and disciplinary belonging within the field of chemistry. Using a grounded theory approach, we collected data through semistructured interviews and analyzed transcripts using open and axial coding followed by iterative thematic development. Through constant comparison, we constructed a conceptual framework illustrating how belonging emerges from the dynamic interplay between the individual (the student as a system) and their surroundings (including instructors, peers, and context). Our findings suggest that belonging is experienced as a blend of inclusion and the development of professional identity. This preliminary, empirically grounded model offers insights into how first-year chemistry students in this institutional context experience belonging and identity and is intended to inform future studies and practice rather than to generalize across all settings.
keywords: first-year chemistry, sense of belonging, social belonging, professional identity, inclusion, first-year science students, teacher-student relationship, peer relationships, conceptual framework

title: Transforming a Physical Card Game into a Browser-Based Learning Tool: AI-Assisted Digitization of Compound Chain
text: Abstract This study reports the AI-assisted transformation of Compound Chain, a validated physical inorganic chemistry card game, into a browser-based learning application. The development used a “vibe coding” approach, in which educators describe functionality in natural language while an LLM generates and refines the code. We propose a five-step Pedagogical System Architect framework, intended for chemistry educators without programming experience, that covers architectural planning, data design, incremental implementation, AI-assisted debugging, and version control. The digital version extends the original game through automated rule enforcement, a zoom interface, and single-player mode, in a manner consistent with reduced extraneous cognitive load, and supporting self-regulated practice beyond class. In an exploratory classroom deployment, voluntary out-of-class usage (a self-reported approximation of 4.5 sessions per student) suggests that the digital format can transform a classroom activity into an intrinsically motivated practice resource. This exploratory evaluation documents engagement, usability, and voluntary practice; establishing conceptual learning gains from the digital version remains a question for future controlled study.
keywords: card games, inorganic chemistry education, AI-assisted programming, LLM-based code generation, vibe coding, extraneous cognitive load, student engagement, usability

title: Beyond Static Stoichiometry: A Stochastic Lattice Model for Visualizing Kinetic Constraints in H2–O2 Combustion
text: Abstract The ″Fire Triangle″ ─ fuel, oxygen, and an ignition source ─ has long functioned as a foundational pedagogical framework in chemistry education; however, its sufficient-condition interpretation leads students to overlook the physical constraints unique to premixed gas-phase combustion, constituting a source of systematic overgeneralization. This paper introduces a stochastic lattice model, grounded in percolation theory, designed to visualize the ″kinetic connectivity″ required for chain reaction propagation in premixed H2(g)–O2(g) combustion. Propagation is represented as connectivity among lattice sites holding both gases, governed by the active-site density (the fraction of sites occupied by both gases, PH·PO), so students can investigate the physical origins of flammability limits and connect the symbolic representation (the balanced equation) with the sub-microscopic picture of individual particles reacting. Monte Carlo sampling (6000 trials per active-site-density point) shows a sigmoidal connectivity transition; when reduced to standard rules it recovers the known 2-D square-lattice site-percolation threshold (pc ≈ 0.593). An exploratory implementation with 18 preservice chemistry teachers using an earlier prototype showed gains across all three assessment items (Q1: 16.7% → 94.4%; Q2: 27.8% → 88.9%; Q3: 11.1% → 83.3%); these data are reported as preliminary context rather than as an efficacy test of the revised simulation. The tool offers a way to teach stoichiometric and spatial-connectivity reasoning as complementary pedagogical perspectives ─ chemical composition and physical connectivity ─ understanding premixed gas-phase combustion as emergent, probabilistic processes.
keywords: hydrogen-oxygen combustion, stochastic lattice model, percolation theory, site percolation, kinetic constraints, flammability limits, stoichiometry, active site density, pre-service chemistry teachers, chemistry education, Monte Carlo simulation, fire triangle

title: Small Changes, Big Impact: Evaluating the Effects of Green Chemistry Integration in an Organic Chemistry Laboratory Course on Students’ Awareness, Perceptions, and Self-Efficacy Regarding Sustainable Practices
text: Abstract Green chemistry provides an important framework for promoting sustainability and reducing environmental impact in chemical education; however, its integration into undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory curricula remains limited. While previous work described integrating green chemistry principles into an undergraduate lab course through optimized experimental method, the present study evaluated the educational impact of that implementation on student awareness, perceptions, and self-efficacy. A pre-test–post-test survey consisting of Likert-scale and open-ended questions was administered to students enrolled in an undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory course to assess changes in awareness, perceptions, and self-efficacy toward green chemistry concepts and sustainable laboratory practices. Quantitative analysis revealed measurable increases in students’ self-reported understanding of green chemistry principles, confidence in assessing the environmental impact of organic reactions, and recognition of sustainability considerations in laboratory work. Qualitative responses further demonstrated a shift from viewing green chemistry as an abstract concept to recognizing its practical relevance in laboratory practice and future professional applications. These findings suggested that incorporation of a single, well-designed green chemistry laboratory intervention could reinforce core organic chemistry concepts while promoting sustainability awareness, perceptions, and student self-efficacy. This study provided an assessment framework and supporting evidence for broader integration of green chemistry principles into undergraduate laboratory instruction.
keywords: green chemistry, organic chemistry laboratory, undergraduate laboratory teaching, student self-efficacy, sustainability awareness, student perceptions, sustainable laboratory practices, environmental impact assessment, green chemistry education

title: Organic Synthesis Laboratory Challenge: From d -Mannitol to Chiral Building Blocks through Selective Protection and Deprotection
text: Abstract We report a challenge-based laboratory activity designed to introduce undergraduate students to the synthesis of chiral building blocks from d-mannitol. This three-day module combines practical tasks─including reaction setup, synthesis, and purification─with theoretical exercises to build proficiency in organic synthesis with a specific focus on stereochemistry and symmetry. By establishing a synergy between competition and teamwork, the format encouraged students to deeply assimilate the underlying chemical principles. The team-based approach to solving practical and theoretical problems was highly effective, stimulating collaborative learning and rigorous discussion, leading to a hands-on proficient learning approach.
keywords: mannitol, chiral building blocks, selective protection, selective deprotection, stereochemistry, molecular symmetry, organic synthesis, undergraduate laboratory teaching, team-based learning, cooperative learning, challenge-based learning

title: Social Support and Chemistry Learning Engagement: Chain Mediation and Latent Profile Analysis of Chemistry Self-Efficacy and Chemistry Anxiety
text: Abstract Chemistry learning engagement plays an important role in students’ academic development and sustained motivation to learn chemistry. Although previous studies have examined the relationships of perceived social support, self-efficacy, and anxiety with students’ learning outcomes, few have integrated variable-centered and person-centered approaches to investigate the direct and indirect relationships of perceived teacher support, perceived parent support, and perceived peer support with chemistry learning engagement through chemistry self-efficacy and chemistry anxiety. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the direct and indirect relationships among perceived social support, chemistry self-efficacy, chemistry anxiety, and chemistry learning engagement and to further identify students’ self-efficacy–anxiety profiles and their associations with perceived social support and engagement. Data were collected from 1647 Chinese senior high school students. Structural equation modeling was used to examine direct and indirect pathways, whereas latent profile analysis, R3STEP, and BCH procedures were used to identify self-efficacy–anxiety profiles, examine the associations between perceived social support and profile membership, and compare chemistry learning engagement across profiles. The results indicated that (1) perceived teacher support, perceived parent support, and perceived peer support were all positively associated with chemistry learning engagement; (2) chemistry self-efficacy and chemistry anxiety mediated the relationships between perceived social support and chemistry learning engagement; (3) chemistry self-efficacy and chemistry anxiety functioned as sequential mediators in the relationship between perceived social support and chemistry learning engagement; (4) five self-efficacy–anxiety profiles were identified, including two profiles with comparable levels of self-efficacy but contrasting levels of anxiety─the moderate self-efficacy–low anxiety and moderate self-efficacy–high anxiety profiles; and (5) perceived teacher support and perceived peer support, but not perceived parent support, were significantly associated with relative membership in these two profiles. Students in the moderate self-efficacy–low anxiety profile reported significantly higher chemistry learning engagement than those in the moderate self-efficacy–high anxiety profile. Finally, the educational implications and limitations of the study are discussed, and directions for future research are proposed.
keywords: perceived social support, chemistry self-efficacy, teacher support, parental support, peer support, serial mediation, high school students, Chinese students

title: Solvent- and Catalyst-Free Transesterification of Phosphites with 1-Dodecanol: An Undergraduate Experiment Based on 31P NMR Kinetic Monitoring
text: Abstract This laboratory session describes the transesterification reaction involving diphenyl phosphite (DiPhPH) and 1-dodecanol. Based on previous optimization work carried out in our laboratory, the synthesis methodology involves heating the reaction mixture (DiPhPH and 1-dodecanol) in the complete absence of a catalyst or solvent, using a Kugelrohr-type distillation apparatus. Furthermore, the reaction product can be isolated without a time-consuming purification step (chromatography) or recrystallization, which is compatible with the duration of a standard laboratory session (4 h). This experiment has two educational benefits. The first is the study of the reactivity of two other phosphites; diethyl phosphite (DiEtPH) and dimethyl phosphite (DiMePH) compared with DiPhPH, achieved by monitoring the reaction kinetics using 31P nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. The second is demonstrating the importance of implementing experimental procedures that involve more environmentally friendly reaction conditions, such as solvent-free, catalyst-free, and purification-free reactions. The experiment was also seen as an opportunity to introduce students to 31P NMR spectroscopy as an alternative to thin-layer chromatography (TLC) for monitoring reaction progress. To achieve the objectives of this series of experiments, four laboratory sessions of 4 h each were scheduled. Students were evaluated at the end of these sessions based on a literature review they were required to complete prior to the laboratory sessions, as well as a written report they were required to submit in the form of an article published in a scientific journal.
keywords: transesterification, phosphites, diphenyl phosphite, 1-dodecanol, 31P NMR, reaction kinetics, solvent-free synthesis, catalyst-free synthesis, green chemistry, diethyl phosphite, dimethyl phosphite, undergraduate laboratory experiment, reaction monitoring

title: A Classroom-Ready Fluorogenic Nanokit for Hands-On Nanoscience Learning in Resource-Limited Settings
text: Abstract Integrating nanoscience into secondary curricula is frequently hindered by prohibitive equipment costs, stringent safety requirements, and the difficulty of making nanoscale phenomena tangible for students. This work introduces a classroom-ready fluorogenic Nanokit (CRN) designed to bridge these gaps through an accessible, hands-on inquiry module specifically for resource-constrained environments. At the core of the CRN is the microwave-assisted synthesis of bovine serum albumin (BSA)-templated gold nanoclusters (AuNCs). This process uses readily available laboratory materials to produce nanoclusters that exhibit intense fluorescence under ultraviolet illumination. To ground these concepts in real-world utility, students perform a sensing experiment in which fluorescence quenching is used to qualitatively detect copper(II) ions, highlighting how nanomaterials can be applied to environmental sensing contexts. The implementation employs a dual-layered instructional approach, balancing instructor-led safety protocols with student-guided experimentation, to ensure safe operation while maintaining an authentic hands-on learning experience. Data gathered from outreach implementations, including guided worksheets and postactivity questionnaires, indicate notable gains in conceptual understanding and high levels of student engagement. Overall, the CRN demonstrates that fluorescent nanocluster chemistry can be effectively translated into a reproducible and impactful educational tool for diverse classroom and outreach learning settings.
keywords: gold nanoclusters, microwave-assisted synthesis, fluorescence quenching, copper(II) determination, environmental sensing, nanoscience education, resource-limited settings, student engagement, science outreach, secondary school curriculum

title: Unveiling the Chemistry Connection: How General Chemistry Courses Shape Students’ Perceptions of Science and Chemistry
text: Abstract Many students begin their college journey with the intention of pursuing STEM majors, but along the way, they decide to switch paths. One course that often plays a key role in this decision is General Chemistry. It is a required course for many STEM majors and is usually described as a “gatekeeper” course. Due to its significance, this exploratory study examines closely how students perceive both science in general and chemistry in particular and also their attitude towards science through their experience in the General Chemistry course (CHEM 1). Understanding how students feel about this field and what influences those feelings can help us create more effective learning environments that keep students engaged in STEM. We used the mATSI survey to measure students’ attitudes toward science at the beginning and end of the semester. Responses from 841 students in the pre-survey and 643 students in the post-survey were analyzed by gender and the course instructor using ANOVA, a parametric statistical method. Attitudes were measured across four constructs: desire to do science, anxiety toward science, self-efficacy, and the value of science to society. Results showed that male students reported lower levels of science anxiety and higher levels of self-efficacy than female students. While no significant differences were observed among instructors at the beginning of the semester, significant instructor-related differences emerged in the post-survey. Additional questions were included in the post-survey to examine how students’ perceptions of science and chemistry changed after completing CHEM I. Findings revealed that students generally held more positive perceptions of science than chemistry. Course instructors were identified as the primary influence on positive perceptions, whereas exams and course assessments were the main factors contributing to negative perceptions. These insights showed the need to re-evaluate the structure of chemistry courses. If instructors can focus on the most essential concepts, reduce unnecessary content overload, and design fairer assessments, students may begin to see chemistry in a more positive light. In turn, this could encourage more of them to remain in STEM and help strengthen the pipeline for future scientists.
keywords: general chemistry, student attitudes toward science, science anxiety, self-efficacy, gender differences, teacher influence, course evaluation, STEM retention

title: Bridging Cultural Contexts and Scientific Universality: A Philosophical Materialist Analysis of Pedagogical Tensions in Chemistry Education
text: Abstract This paper is a critical reflection on the integration of cultural elements in chemistry education, using philosophical materialism (Gustavo Bueno) as the analytical framework. While it acknowledges the value of culturally relevant teaching for fostering inclusive learning environments, the discussion emphasizes the importance of maintaining gnoseological and epistemological rigor, as well as the universal principles that define chemistry as a scientific discipline. The paper analyzes the potential risks of overemphasizing cultural and emotional dimensions, as this may inadvertently shift attention away from fundamental chemical concepts and the analytical skills essential for understanding and comprehending scientific knowledge. In addition, this contribution also draws attention to broader systemic factors such as socioeconomic inequalities and disparities in resources that play maybe a more decisive role in educational outcomes but are often overshadowed in debates focused solely on cultural inclusion. The paper advocates for more balanced pedagogical approaches that promote cultural sensitivity without compromising the objective and operational nature of chemistry. Such an approach ensures that educational practices not only respect cultural diversity but also preserve the empirical foundations necessary for meaningful engagement with scientific knowledge. This perspective seeks to contribute to current academic discussions on how to design chemistry education that is both equitable and epistemologically robust.
keywords: chemistry education, culturally relevant pedagogy, materialism, Gustavo Bueno, socioeconomic inequality in education, educational equity, scientific knowledge, cultural sensitivity

title: Teaching Relativistic Effects in Undergraduate Chemistry Education: A Fireworks-Based Electronic Structure Perspective
text: Abstract Relativistic effects are essential for explaining heavy-element chemistry, yet many undergraduate chemistry students perceive them as physically abstract and detached from chemical reasoning. We hypothesize that this persistent barrier arises not from the intrinsic difficulty of relativity but from a structural issue in instruction─namely, how relativistic effects are introduced and linked to the breakdown of the nonrelativistic electronic structure description for heavy elements. To address this issue, we designed an instructional module that presents relativistic effects as a conceptually continuous extension of nonrelativistic electronic structure theory. Using fireworks and flame-test colors as motivating chemical phenomena, students compared nonrelativistic and scalar-relativistic descriptions and examined how relativistic effects alter orbital energies and optical transitions. The module was implemented in a single undergraduate quantum chemistry course, and students’ responses were analyzed using Likert-type self-assessment items, multiple-choice questions, and responses to open-ended questions. The results indicate increased self-reported confidence and suggest that some students began to connect observable color differences with underlying changes in electronic structure. Because the study was conducted in a single class without a control group, the findings should be interpreted as preliminary evidence of educational usefulness rather than definitive evidence of learning gains. This work provides an exploratory instructional pathway for repositioning relativistic effects from separate physics to an explanatory concept for heavy-element chemistry in undergraduate chemical education.
keywords: relativistic effects, heavy element chemistry, fireworks, orbital energies, optical transitions, student self-confidence, teaching modules, quantum chemistry education

title: A Undergraduate Laboratory Innovating Project for Chiral Amino Acid Separation and Detection Using a Self-Made Low-Pressure Liquid Chromatography
text: Abstract The separation and detection of chiral compounds are fundamental yet often costly topics in organic chemistry education. To address these challenges, a self-made low-pressure liquid chromatography (SLLC) system was designed and implemented in an innovative laboratory project. The device, assembled from low-cost household items and a smartphone, was used to separate and detect l-phenylalanine obtained from a racemic mixture via diastereomeric salt crystallization. A synergistic strategy combining β-cyclodextrin as a chiral mobile-phase additive and pre-column derivatization with o-phthaldialdehyde/2-mercaptoethanol enabled real-time fluorescence detection using the smartphone’s light sensor. Students assembled the SLLC, performed the chiral resolution, and analyzed enantiomeric excess (ee) using the Phyphox app. The entire project was completed within six class hours at a cost of approximately 100 RMB (≈13 USD) per device. Feedback indicated increased engagement, deepened understanding of chromatography and chiral recognition principles, and enhanced confidence in hands-on experimentation. This approach provides a cost-effective, visually intuitive, and pedagogically robust method for teaching chiral separation in undergraduate curricula.
keywords: enantiomer separation, chiral amino acids, low-pressure liquid chromatography, L-phenylalanine, β-cyclodextrin, chiral recognition, o-phthalaldehyde derivatization, fluorescence detection, enantiomeric excess, low-cost laboratory equipment, undergraduate laboratory project, organic chemistry education

title: Bloom-Blueprinted Multiple-Choice Assessment in First-Year Chemistry: Item Performance, Attainment, and Student Perceptions
text: Abstract Chemistry departments increasingly require summative assessments that are scalable, reliable, and capable of evaluating more than factual recall. This study examines an assessment transition from traditional Short-Answer Questions (SAQs) to Bloom-blueprinted Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs) across a large-cohort first-year undergraduate chemistry sequence tracked over multiple academic cycles. MCQs were designed using a deliberate 4:3:3 blueprint mapped to Bloom’s taxonomy, with 40% lower-order cognitive skills (LOCS), 30% intermediate application and analysis, and 30% higher-order cognitive skills (HOCS)-targeted items. Across successive cohorts, item-level analyses showed a consistent decrease in attainment as intended cognitive demand increased, providing evidence consistent with the intended tiered design rather than direct evidence of students’ reasoning pathways. Overall module-level performance remained broadly within historical ranges, although selected-response formats were associated with narrower score distributions and an initial increase in mean performance in the transition year. Student survey data added an important qualification: students viewed SAQs as better for demonstrating conceptual understanding and deeper reasoning, even when they did not reject MCQs overall. The findings support the conditional claim that carefully designed MCQs can produce reliable, discriminating, cognitively tiered assessment tasks at scale, but their validity depends on careful blueprinting, distractor design, linguistic accessibility, and post-examination review.
keywords: multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, Bloom's taxonomy, first-year chemistry, assessment design, cognitive demand, item analysis, student perceptions, distractor design, summative assessment, conceptual understanding

title: DES Virtual Lab: An Interactive Web Application for Teaching Deep Eutectic Solvents in Undergraduate Chemistry
text: Abstract Deep eutectic solvents (DES) represent one of the most dynamic areas in modern chemistry, yet their incorporation into undergraduate curricula remains limited. This paper presents DES Virtual Lab, a free, installation-free, interactive web application designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts, physicochemical properties, sustainability assessment, and real-world applications of DES. Built as a single-page React application accessible through any modern web browser, the virtual laboratory comprises seven interconnected modules: DES classification by type (I–V), hydrophobicity, and natural origin; interactive solid–liquid equilibrium (SLE) phase diagrams with quantification of eutectic deepness; temperature-dependent physicochemical properties including density and viscosity; ecotoxicity assessment across multiple trophic levels and biodegradability evaluation; application exploration across pharmaceutical, water treatment, gas capture, and food science domains; a DES Designer tool for custom formulations with sustainability scoring; and an integrated assessment module with immediate feedback. The tool addresses a critical gap in chemical education by providing accessible, data-driven exploration of an emerging class of solvents that bridges green chemistry, thermodynamics, and materials science.
keywords: deep eutectic solvents, virtual laboratory, online learning tools, React applications, physicochemical properties, ecotoxicity assessment, biodegradability, green chemistry, sustainability assessment, undergraduate chemistry education, interactive learning

title: A Comprehensive Experiment on the Fabrication and Miniaturized Application of Hole Transport Layer-Free Carbon-Based Perovskite Solar Cells
text: Abstract Laboratory instruction in photovoltaics still lags behind technological advances and lacks systematic training that integrates materials preparation, characterization, and application design. To address this gap, we designed a comprehensive laboratory experiment centered on hole transport layer-free carbon-based perovskite solar cells (HTL-free C-PSCs). Grounded in Kolb’s Experiential Learning Theory (ELT), this experimental program follows the experiential teaching cycle, encompassing the entire research chain of material synthesis, device assembly, performance testing, and system integration. The experiment course design features a basic module on hands-on operation and principle verification, and an advanced module on solvent-additive modulation and multidimensional structure–property characterization. Innovatively, the experiment integrates multiple cell units into a photovoltaic (PV) panel that successfully powers a PV house model with LED lighting, thereby achieving closed-loop teaching from material fabrication to application design. This pedagogical framework effectively bridges fundamental theory and research frontiers, enhances students’ scientific literacy and engineering practice skills, and provides a reproducible, comprehensive practical paradigm for new energy materials education.
keywords: carbon-based perovskite solar cells, experiential learning theory, Kolb's learning cycle, solar cell fabrication, hands-on teaching

title: Development of Sustainability Fact Sheets for Evaluating Undergraduate Organic Chemistry Laboratory Experiments Using AI4Green
text: Abstract Undergraduate chemistry laboratories are essential for practical skills development but can generate substantial environmental and financial costs that are rarely evaluated systematically during curriculum design. Herein, we report a data-driven approach for assessing the sustainability of undergraduate organic chemistry laboratory experiments using AI4Green, a green chemistry-focused electronic laboratory notebook, in combination with experimentally derived student data. Green chemistry metrics, including atom economy, mass efficiency, E-factor, and process mass intensity, were derived using AI4Green workflows and complementary calculations, and integrated with student yield distributions, waste generation, reagent costs, energy usage, and skills profiling. These data are compiled into Sustainability Fact Sheets, which provide a clear, visual comparison of experiments to support evidence-based curriculum decision–making by instructors. A Python-based metric calculator was developed, which automates metric generation and visualization from AI4Green-derived data. Application to a first-year organic chemistry curriculum identified opportunities to reduce waste, hazardous material use, and costs without compromising core laboratory skills. This work demonstrates how AI4Green can be extended beyond reaction-level assessment to support evidence-based evaluation and review of undergraduate chemistry laboratory experiments.
keywords: green chemistry, organic chemistry experiments, electronic lab notebook, sustainability assessment, atom economy, E-factor, process mass intensity, mass efficiency, laboratory waste reduction, reagent cost, energy consumption, curriculum development

title: Measuring Undergraduate Chemistry Students’ Self-Efficacy on Laboratory Scientific Practices (SELSP): Survey Development
text: Abstract Laboratory scientific practices are central to undergraduate chemistry education, yet few instruments are available to assess students’ self-efficacy for engaging in these practices. This study describes the development of the Self-Efficacy for Laboratory Scientific Practices (SELSP) survey and presents evidence supporting the interpretation and use of SELSP scores among undergraduate chemistry students. An initial 39-item Likert scale instrument was administered to students enrolled in General Chemistry II (N = 420). Using a randomly split sample, exploratory factor analysis (N = 212) identified an interpretable factor structure, and confirmatory factor analysis (N = 208) supported a four-factor, 20-item model comprising hypothesis generation and experimental design (HGED), data interpretation and communication (DIC), data collection and measurement (DCM), and data analysis and representation (DAR). Internal consistency estimates indicated a strong reliability across all factors. Evidence supporting score interpretation was further examined by using an independent sample of General Chemistry I students (N = 427), which replicated the four-factor structure and reliability estimates. Measurement invariance analyses conducted using pooled data from General Chemistry I and II students (N = 847) supported configural, metric, scalar, and residual invariances across course context, race, gender, and first-generation college status, indicating that SELSP scores functioned similarly across these groups. Multivariate analyses of covariance controlling for prior laboratory experience revealed significant differences by course numbers and context, with General Chemistry I students reporting higher self-efficacy than General Chemistry II students, whereas no significant differences were observed across other demographic groups. Observed factor means indicated moderately high levels of self-efficacy across all four laboratory scientific practice domains. Collectively, the findings provide evidence supporting the internal structure, reliability, measurement invariance, and intended interpretation of SELSP scores in introductory undergraduate chemistry laboratory contexts.
keywords: self-efficacy, undergraduate chemistry education, chemistry laboratory, questionnaire development, measurement invariance, general chemistry, first-generation college students, gender differences, racial differences

title: Local Scientific Development and Promotion of Scientific Vocations in Africa: The Case of Oilseeds
text: Abstract This article presents an educational outreach initiative to promote interest in chemistry in Africa by connecting science to economic development. The project uses the transformation of oil from local oilseeds into soap as a concrete example of converting a local natural resource into a higher-value product, illustrating how science can become a lever for innovation and entrepreneurship. In outreach workshops throughout the Republic of Congo, high school students engaged in this project, which introduced high-level chemistry concepts through a real-world application in a local context. An assessment study found that the workshops led to the students’ comprehension of key chemical concepts while also increasing their self-confidence and motivation to pursue STEM fields. To create a more significant impact, we call for African scientists to play a more active role in science outreach and popularization efforts in order to strengthen the link between science, education, and sustainable development.
keywords: science outreach, chemistry education, oilseed crops, soap making, STEM motivation, high school students, entrepreneurship, innovation, sustainable development, Republic of the Congo, African researchers, popularization of science

title: Contemporary Use of Click Chemistry and Energetic Functional Groups: Practical Considerations and Competency Assessment in a Senior Undergraduate Lab
text: Abstract Students need to learn about the value of energetic functional groups in order to gain competency in an advanced laboratory setting. By introducing a two-part senior undergraduate laboratory experiment focused around energetic functional groups, students garnered respect for and an understanding of important functional groups used in chemical synthesis. A non-cost-prohibitive experiment utilizing the Sandmeyer reaction and the Huisgen cycloaddition was developed to introduce energetic functional groups, catalytic cycles, and reliable novel crystallization, to senior undergraduate students. With the development of these experiments, an assessment of competency was used, allowing for a more concrete determination of practical skills in a synthetic laboratory setting. Student feedback and instructor commentary were positive toward this novel model for assessing competency of practical skills. Characterization of novel products and crystallization data are included alongside additional details to support experimentation beyond the described procedures. This article describes the synthetic experiment for senior undergraduate students and instructor and student reflections on the learning attained. Intended learning outcomes and a competency rubric are included in the Supporting Information. This experimental design serves as an example of how laboratory instructors can safely include synthetic experiments involving energetic functional groups into their curriculum and use the experiments as a way to assess senior undergraduate laboratory skill proficiency.
keywords: click chemistry, Sandmeyer reaction, 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition, azide-alkyne cycloaddition, competency assessment, competency rubric, crystallization, catalytic cycle, chemical synthesis

title: How to Design a Digital Learning Environment to Address Students’ Needs
text: Abstract Digital learning environments can support students in developing foundational knowledge of chemistry through self-regulated learning, with suitable scaffolding to provide support. This article presents the theory-informed design and development of a learning environment for students at the beginning of their chemistry studies at university. It addresses challenges in learning fundamental concepts by combining structured tasks, self-assessment opportunities, introductory explanations, educational games, and scaffolding. Developed with Genially, the environment covers the periodic table, chemical bonding, chemical formulas, and chemical reactions. Selected components were evaluated by students to examine usability and perceived support. Results show that tasks and games were rated as being particularly valuable for reviewing and applying chemical concepts. The article discusses implications for designing digital learning environments in chemistry education based on the development process and evaluation findings.
keywords: chemistry education, student self-regulation, scaffolding, game-based learning, self-assessment, periodic table, chemical bonding, molecular formula, chemical reactions, Genially, usability evaluation, perceived support

title: Stepping into the Machine Chemist: An AI Vision-Driven Titration Robot for Learning by Creating
text: Abstract In the era of deep integration between artificial intelligence and scientific research, the machine chemist has emerged as a new paradigm for chemical experimental research. Grounded in the philosophy of learning by creating, we have designed an AI vision-driven titration robot (hereinafter referred to as AI-TitroBot) that students can build autonomously. Serving as an entry-level machine chemist, AI-TitroBot is capable of fully automated titration operations. It precisely identifies the titration end point through AI vision, automatically controls the peristaltic pump to cease titrant addition, and calculates both the consumed titrant volume and the concentration of the analyte solution based on calibrated flow rate and titration duration. Experimental results demonstrate that the device exhibits good repeatability. While the accuracy of the redox titration is relatively high, the acid–base titration still shows a systematic negative deviation of approximately 5%. The AI-TitroBot effectively strengthens students’ understanding of chemical principles while integrating interdisciplinary knowledge and skills from artificial intelligence, electronics, programming, and engineering design, thus exploring a feasible pathway for innovation in intelligent chemistry education.
keywords: computer vision, automatic titration, chemistry education, redox titration, acid-base titration, endpoint detection, interdisciplinary STEM education

title: A Case Study in Embodied Cognition: Learning Organic Chemistry as a Blind Student
text: Abstract Organic chemistry presents unique representational challenges that often rely on assumed visual capacity and spatial reasoning, raising important questions about how blind or low-vision (BLV) students access and engage with this content. We employed a case study via participatory action research (PAR) with coauthor Kiandra J. Strickhouser, who is a blind undergraduate student as she navigated the organic chemistry sequence at The Ohio State University, which is a large, public research-intensive institution. Across three semesters, we collaboratively collected and analyzed data including semistructured interviews, course artifacts, lecture and homework observations, as well as reflective sessions. Using embodied cognition as a theoretical lens, we examined how multisensory strategies supported access to different organic chemistry topics. Findings reveal that mechanism-focused topics (e.g., acid–base chemistry, predicting products, retrosynthesis) were accessible through tactile drawing and kinesthetic engagement, while representational topics (e.g., stereochemistry, Newman projections, chair conformations) were more difficult to embody due to the course’s limited modality. These results demonstrate how BLV students can meaningfully engage with organic chemistry when the pedagogy leverages tactile modalities. We conclude by offering implications for instructors and researchers seeking to design multisensory organic chemistry learning environments.
keywords: embodied cognition, organic chemistry education, blind students, low vision, multisensory learning, tactile drawing, stereochemistry, Newman projections, chair conformation, acid-base chemistry, retrosynthesis, tactile modality

title: Why Chemistry? Undergraduate Chemistry Student Perceptions of the Chemistry Discipline in Relation to Science Identity Development
text: Abstract The demand for skilled chemists continues to rise, yet undergraduate participation and degree completion in chemistry remain low. Notably, only half of 2021 chemistry graduates secured science-related employment, with over a quarter unemployed─highlighting a possible disconnect between student expectations and the realities of the scientific job market. While existing literature often centers on faculty perspectives and academia, few studies explore how undergraduate chemistry students perceive and prepare for careers, particularly in scientific industry occupations. This study employs narrative inquiry to examine how chemistry and biochemistry majors at a Midwestern R2 institution develop feelings of career optimism via chemistry identity development through academic experiences. A synthesized theoretical framework, drawing from Gee’s identity theory, Brickhouse et al.’s work on science identity, and Hosbein and Barbera’s chemistry identity model, guides the analysis of how students’ experiences shape their perceptions of viable science careers. Data were collected through semistructured interviews and surveys on career perceptions and experiences in chemistry. From these, detailed narratives were constructed, revealing how unique personal experiences influence career aspirations via identity development. Findings suggest that, while students express strong optimism about securing science-related jobs, this is often based on the belief that scientific disciplines are broadly interconnected and transferable, which may obscure the specialized nature of many science careers. Increased exposure to real-world applications and career pathways during undergraduate education may help align student expectations with postgraduate realities. Future work surrounding facilitated science career exposure with more diverse groups of undergraduate chemistry majors is recommended.
keywords: science identity, undergraduate chemistry students, career perceptions, career optimism, chemistry workforce, identity theory, career exposure

title: The Myriad of Ways That Building and Construction Connect to Chemistry
text: Abstract National Chemistry Week arises every October, and this year the theme is “Chemistry Under Construction” with a look at the chemistry materials commonly used in construction. This area presents a number of opportunities for learning the chemistry of materials as distinctive as concrete and wood. This editorial also connects to a collection of articles from the Journal related to construction to provide ideas to interested teachers looking for National Chemistry Week activities.
keywords: National Chemistry Week, concrete, wood, chemistry education, teaching activities, chemistry outreach

title: A Biochemistry Teaching Activity to Modify the Theoretical Methane Yield Formula in Anaerobic Digestion
text: Abstract Biochemistry not only plays an important role in daily life and industrial practice but also is a core foundational course in universities worldwide. Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a representative catabolic reaction in biochemistry that can promote carbon circulation and maintain ecological balance, but has long been neglected in biochemistry courses. We incorporated AD theories and practices in the course of biochemistry, and Boyle’s formula was used to estimate the theoretical methane yield (TMY) of organic substrates in AD, to evaluate their biodegradability (Bd). However, students were unaware that lignin could not be degraded by AD and used Boyle’s formula to calculate the overestimated TMY of lignocellulosic wastes. To solve these problems, we designed a teaching activity to explain the properties of lignin and guide students to modify the original Boyle’s formula through two methods, to eliminate the interference of lignin. This teaching activity not only helped students learn the non-biodegradability of lignin in anaerobic environment and how to eliminate the influence of lignin on Boyle’s formula, but also provided a more reliable tool for estimating the TMY and Bd in future applications. This teaching activity can provide a reference for teachers who taught biochemistry course in related majors, reflecting its multidisciplinary value.
keywords: anaerobic digestion, lignin, lignocellulosic waste, biodegradability, biochemistry education, teaching activity design, organic substrates

title: When Copper Wire Meets Al-Fed Liquid Metal: A Visual Demonstration of Self-Sustained Oscillation
text: Abstract Oscillation is a fundamental dynamic phenomenon in nature and technology. We present a visually striking and easy-to-implement demonstration experiment suitable for senior undergraduates in physics, chemistry, or materials science. When a copper wire is inserted into a droplet of aluminum-fed gallium–indium liquid metal (LM) immersed in aqueous NaOH solution, the wire begins to oscillate spontaneously and periodically. The motion is driven by a feedback loop between the aluminum–hydroxide reaction, localized hydrogen evolution, and asymmetric capillary forces at the three-phase contact line. The experiment uses only common materials (Ga–In alloy, aluminum foil, copper wire, NaOH), requires no complex instrumentation, and can be completed in less than 30 min. Its vivid, self-sustained oscillation engages students and illustrates core concepts of surface tension, reactive wetting, and chemically induced motion. Detailed safety precautions and waste-disposal protocols are provided, along with open-source video and motion-analysis files to facilitate adoption in the classroom. The demonstration also opens discussions on dynamic systems and the design of soft actuators.
keywords: self-excited vibration, aluminum foil, copper wire, hydrogen evolution reaction, capillary forces, contact line, reactive wetting, surface tension, NaOH solution, soft actuators, dynamical systems, classroom demonstration

title: Faculty Beliefs about the Goals of Doctoral Education in Chemistry: Results from a National Survey
text: Abstract Doctoral education in chemistry (DEC) underpins the United States’ research capacity, innovation ecosystem, and preparation of a highly skilled scientific workforce. The goals that guide doctoral education carry significant national implications as they determine which careers in academia, industry, government, and science-adjacent sectors future scientists are well-prepared for and pursue. In this study, we report results from a national survey of research-active chemistry faculty in the United States examining beliefs about the goals of DEC and their relationship to personal and contextual factors. Faculty demonstrated strong consensus around student-centered goals, including developing independent scientists and preparing students for varying career pathways. Comparatively, endorsement of the institution-focused goal of enhancing rank or reputation was more variable and less strongly prioritized but still a present goal of doctoral programs. No evidence for differences based on academic rank and graduate-education related service role was found. Together, these findings provide national-level evidence of faculty alignment around goals of DEC and offer insight into how consensus and variability in faculty beliefs inform opportunities for doctoral education reform. This pattern highlights opportunities to focus reform efforts on aligning doctoral program structures with faculty-endorsed, student-centered goals.
keywords: faculty beliefs, career paths, institutional reputation, academic rank, graduate education reform, chemistry faculty

title: Teacher and Student Experiences during First-Trial Chemistry Lessons in Immersive Virtual Reality
text: Abstract Virtual reality (VR) is becoming increasingly popular and is being implemented across many areas and levels of chemistry education. When planning to incorporate this technology into teaching, several factors must be considered, such as the cost of these devices, the time required to prepare a VR lesson, and the exhaustion they can cause. Is it worth it? A 90 min lesson in Nanome was prepared and tested with 32 students from lower secondary schools (K8) and 59 students from upper secondary schools (K11). Feedback was collected through a short questionnaire completed by students and semistructured interviews conducted with teachers. This paper presents experiences, opinions, and evaluations from 91 students and two teachers regarding their first attempt to implement VR-based teaching and learning at the secondary school level. VR offers exciting potential for school chemistry education by overcoming physical laboratory limitations and enabling interactive, immersive molecular modeling that boosts student motivation. However, successful integration requires dedicated technical and spatial support to help teachers navigate hardware challenges, lesson preparation, and varying student reactions based on students’ ages and prior VR experience. Successful VR integration requires clear learning goals and an initial time investment, but once teachers master the technology, reusable lesson plans make the effort well worth it.

title: A Foldable Ultraviolet Light Box for Smartphone-Based Fluorescence Spectroscopy Experiments
text: Abstract This work describes the design, assembly, and applications of the TechGlow, a foldable ultraviolet light box for smartphone-based fluorescence imaging. The device is fabricated from heavyweight black cardstock using consumer-grade desktop paper-cutting machines, avoiding the need for 3D printing, laser cutting, specialized machining, custom electronics, or optical alignment. The TechGlow uses an inexpensive LED strip for top-down excitation and holds up to five cuvettes in fixed positions for simultaneous visual comparison and image-based fluorescence measurements. Two quinine-based activities illustrate different levels of quantitative complexity. An introductory activity explores the relationship between dilution and fluorescence intensity, while a more advanced assay uses smartphone images and blue-channel intensity values to construct calibration curves and determine quinine concentrations. The rapidly assembled, portable design provides a reproducible platform for introducing fluorescence, solution preparation, calibration, and graphical analysis in teaching laboratories and outreach settings with limited access to conventional fluorescence instrumentation.
