title: Permittivity and permeability: what they mean and why both should be taught at school level
text: Abstract Permittivity (ϵ) and permeability (μ) are essential concepts in physics, as witnessed by their close relationship with fundamental constants such as the speed of light and the fine-structure constant. In much school teaching, permittivity is encountered at a very basic level, but permeability is rarely included. In this paper, some important differences between the two concepts—especially considering their traditional names and some apparent similarities that could lead to misunderstandings—are explained. A case is made that both concepts ought to be included, at least briefly, at higher school level.
keywords: dielectric constant, permeability, speed of light, fine-structure constant, electromagnetic constants, school physics curriculum, misconceptions

title: Van Gogh’s summer sunsets: an astronomical approach to art analysis
text: Abstract This study applies astronomical analysis to two Vincent van Gogh paintings from the summer of 1888, demonstrating how scientific principles can deepen our understanding of artistic works. While previous research has shown that van Gogh occasionally placed celestial bodies in positions significantly different from their astronomical reality, the analysis of Wheat Field with the Setting Sun and Canal with Women Washing reveals a close alignment with expected astronomical positions. This contrast suggests that van Gogh made conscious decisions about celestial positioning, sometimes prioritising astronomical accuracy and other times favouring creative expression. Furthermore, this study highlights the value of interdisciplinary approaches in modern education, showing how the integration of science and art can enrich both fields.
keywords: Vincent van Gogh, sunset, science and art integration, interdisciplinary teaching

title: Effectiveness of peer instruction in the South African college-level physics classroom
text: Abstract This study investigated the potential of evidence-based physics education research (PER) strategies to improve student outcomes in South African introductory physics courses. Using students from a university in the Eastern Cape as a case study, it assessed the effectiveness of peer instruction (PI) within a traditional calculus-based introductory physics course. Think-pair-share discussion questions were integrated into lectures, and PI’s impact was evaluated through Force Concept Inventory (FCI) gains. To better understand factors influencing these gains, the study also examined the role of class attendance and scientific reasoning skills, measured using the Lawson classroom test of scientific reasoning (LCTSR). The results showed lower-than-expected normalised FCI gains for PI, with attendance and reasoning skills playing a significant moderating role. These findings suggest that for PI and other interactive engagement (IE) methods to be effective in the South African context, course design must prioritise student engagement and attendance. Moreover, the study indicates that implementing PI in isolation may not yield optimal results, and that effective integration of PI and IE strategies should be paired with efforts to develop students’ scientific reasoning abilities. Beyond evaluating the effectiveness of PI in the local context, this study also contributes to the PER literature in South Africa, by providing FCI and LCTSR scores for South African students. While the FCI and LCTSR are widely used internationally in selecting and applying PER tools in the local context, there is limited data available on South African students.
keywords: peer instruction, Think Pair Share, introductory physics education, Force Concept Inventory, scientific reasoning skills, class attendance, interactive engagement, calculus-based physics, South African students, Eastern Cape, course design

title: Skipping ropes and solar storms
text: Abstract There are various locations in the vicinity of the Earth’s orbit around the Sun where centripetal and centrifugal forces are balanced and spacecraft are able to orbit the Sun at the same period as the Earth. These locations are known as Lagrange points, numbered 1–5. The first of these, L1, lies about 1.5 million km from the Earth towards the Sun. Various spacecraft, for example the solar and heliospheric observatory (SOHO) and deep space climate observatory (DSCOVR) sit in halo obits around L1. SOHO provides high resolution images of the Sun, and DSCOVR provides an early warning of coronal mass ejections, and detailed images of the Earth. In a halo orbit, the orthogonal components of the spacecraft-Sun and spacecraft-Earth force vectors provide the centripetal force enabling a spacecraft to orbit a point in space. This is essentially the same physics as in a skipping rope, which can be demonstrated in the classroom using a skipping rope.
keywords: Lagrange points, L1 Lagrange point, halo orbits, solar storms, coronal mass ejections, centripetal force, centrifugal force, SOHO, DSCOVR, physics demonstration

title: Networked observatory for virtual astronomy (NOVA): teaching astronomy with AI
text: Abstract The term ‘artificial intelligence’ (AI) first appeared in the mid-20th century. It was not until well into the 21st century that AI began to flourish. Today, AI has found very diverse applications. One area that is just beginning to be explored is physics education. The aim of this work is to contribute to this burgeoning educational field through a ChatGPT application named networked observatory for virtual astronomy (NOVA). This application provides students with simulated astronomical data in a ChatGPT-based environment, where they can put their scientific skills to work by formulating hypotheses, analyzing data, and drawing verifiable conclusions through interaction with ChatGPT.
keywords: artificial intelligence in education, ChatGPT, astronomy education, Virtual Observatory, hypothesis generation, data analysis, AI-assisted learning

title: Exploring small-angle in-plane oscillations of a rigid pendulum suspended from two points: theory and experiment
text: Abstract This study provides an introductory investigation into the oscillatory dynamics of a rigid bar suspended at both ends by two identical, inextensible strings attached to an adjustable horizontal support. Unlike the typical bifilar pendulum—which undergoes torsional motion—this system oscillates within its own plane, combining translational and rotational motion depending on the geometry of the suspension points. A simple theoretical Newtonian model is developed using the small-angle approximation, allowing predictions of the oscillation period and trajectories of the bar’s endpoints. Experimental validation is performed using slow-motion video analysis and tracking software. The results show good agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental observations, highlighting the educational relevance of this system for undergraduate physics students and high school teachers. The setup effectively illustrates constrained rigid body motion and the associated oscillatory and roto-translational behaviours.
keywords: bifilar pendulum, small-angle approximation, oscillation period, Newtonian model

title: Observing forced oscillations using a charge generator and a homemade capacitor
text: Abstract In this work, we present a didactic experiment involving the observation of forced oscillations in the vertical plane induced by an electric force acting on a dielectric cylinder that forms part of a mass-spring system. The cylinder is placed on a homemade Leyden jar-type capacitor, which is charged over time by a Van de Graaff-type electrostatic generator. Simultaneously, the motion of the cylinder is recorded using a smartphone camera, and the video is later analysed with the Tracker software. During the recording, the generator is switched on for a period, then turned off, and finally, the capacitor is discharged. We developed a simplified theoretical model to describe the cylinder’s motion during the three regimes, allowing us to understand the forced oscillations and the displacement of the system’s stable equilibrium position immediately after the generator is switched on. In the regime of small oscillations, we demonstrate that the system behaves as a forced oscillator with variable frequency when the charge generator is active, due to the coupling between the system’s time-dependent charges and the cylinder’s displacement. Finally, we use the modelling, combined with video analysis, to show the possibility of obtaining an estimate of the product of the charges that remain in the system immediately after the generator is turned off, even when detecting displacements on the order of the experimental uncertainty limit of 1 mm .
keywords: forced oscillations, mass-spring system, dielectric cylinder, electrostatic forces, Van de Graaff generator, equilibrium displacement, smartphone video analysis, Tracker software, charge estimation

title: Pressure in the siphon
text: Abstract The paper reports on direct measurements of pressure inside the siphon. Two apparatuses were designed. The first one allows for detailed measurements of pressure dependence along the siphon tube, the second is the simplified version of the first, which allows for measurements and for visual demonstration of pressure at a few points along the siphon tube. Discussion of measurements uses two approaches, the standard combination of Bernoulli equation, and the resistance due to the combination of viscous and quadratic drag and using the forces acting on object-like small parts of water.
keywords: siphon, pressure measurement, Bernoulli equation, viscous drag, quadratic drag, drag force, fluid dynamics

title: Watching a goldfish swimming in a fishbowl
text: Abstract The problem of determining the position and magnification of a fish swimming in a fishbowl can be solved by means of the small-angles approximation. However, an exact solution, free from such simplifications, yields a more realistic and quantitatively accurate description of what is observed. In this analysis, the curve of the transverse magnification m is determined as a function of the goldfish’s position within the bowl. It is found that the magnification increases as the goldfish moves away from an external observer. This qualitative behaviour can be readily confirmed through simple experiments. Quantitative differences between the exact analysis and the small-angle approximation become significant when the size of the goldfish is not negligible compared to the radius of the bowl.
keywords: goldfish, refraction, apparent position, small-angle approximation, exact solutions, image formation

title: From training to practice: the lasting effects of IBSE on physics teachers’ professional development and classroom practices
text: Abstract This study explores the long-term impact of inquiry-based science education (IBSE) training on teacher professional development and classroom practices, focusing on two experienced educators who participated in the Teaching Enquiry with Mysteries Incorporated (TEMI) training program a decade ago. A qualitative case study approach was adopted, combining semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and teacher self-assessments. Data were analysed to compare the adoption of IBSE, challenges faced, and professional growth achieved by both teachers. Initially skeptical, teacher A gradually integrated IBSE, transforming her teaching into a student-centred approach. Despite challenges in adapting her methods and managing time constraints, she observed increased student engagement and conceptual understanding. Teacher B, enthusiastic from the outset, implemented IBSE rapidly, emphasizing laboratory-based and interdisciplinary learning. She faced logistical challenges but achieved significant improvements in student curiosity and problem-solving skills. Though their journeys differed, both teachers experienced professional growth and enhanced student engagement through IBSE. Teacher A’s gradual adoption reflects the value of persistence, while teacher B’s enthusiasm highlights the benefits of early integration. This study demonstrates the transformative potential of long-term professional development in fostering innovative, inquiry-based teaching practices.
keywords: inquiry-based science teaching, teacher professional development, physics teachers, teaching practice, student-centered learning, student engagement, conceptual understanding, problem-solving skills, student curiosity, interdisciplinary learning, laboratory-based learning

title: Einstein’s cat: a thought experiment on the universality of time dilation
text: Abstract The universality of time dilation is sometimes misunderstood, with claims that it applies exclusively to light clocks and not to mechanical clocks or other material objects, including biological entities. This leads to incorrect interpretations of experiments like the Hafele–Keating experiment, which actually confirm relativistic effects through the use of atomic clocks. To address this issue, we propose a thought experiment, inspired by Schrödinger’s cat, involving a ‘Sync-or-Die clock’, a device that combines a light clock and a mechanical stopwatch, with the life of Einstein’s cat, Tiger, depending on their synchronization. A straightforward analysis shows that both clocks experience time dilation equally, reinforcing the fact that time dilation is not limited to clocks based on light propagation but is a universal feature of Special Relativity.
keywords: time dilation, special relativity, thought experiments, Schrödinger's cat, Hafele-Keating experiment, atomic clocks, light clock, mechanical clocks, clock synchronization, relativity education

title: How internal forces indirectly affect the acceleration of a system: example and insights
text: Abstract The influence of internal forces in classical mechanics is often overlooked in textbooks, despite their crucial role in shaping a system’s response to external forces. In this study, we examine a simple two-body system—a mass on a table connected by a string to a hanging mass—to highlight how internal tension affects acceleration. By varying the angle of the string, we explore how the transmission of force changes in both frictionless and frictional scenarios. Our analysis reveals that in the absence of friction, internal tension merely distributes the driving force, whereas in the presence of friction, it actively alters the normal force, thereby modifying resistive forces. These findings provide new insights into multi-body dynamics and suggest that a deeper emphasis on internal forces in introductory physics courses could enhance the presentation of Newtonian mechanics.
keywords: internal forces, tension, two-body systems, acceleration, friction, normal force, force transmission, introductory physics, classical mechanics, multibody dynamics

title: Uniform circular movement Arduino-based apparatus
text: Abstract We propose the construction of an Arduino-based apparatus to study uniform circular motion (UCM) cartesian axis projection. Using a common step motor Arduino controlled, the apparatus produced a controlled UCM with a specific frequency. The illumination configuration using cellphone flashlights produced UCM projection on x and y-axis and consequentially, this didactic apparatus proposed the possibility of collecting data time position function and studying x and y position, velocity and acceleration component sinusoidal time function and identifying parameters essentials such as amplitude, period, frequency, angular frequency, and phase. The projection can be associated with a single harmonic motion that sometimes was not understood in the physics classroom.
keywords: uniform circular motion, Arduino, stepper motor, harmonic motion, sinusoidal functions, physics teaching apparatus, angular frequency, phase

title: Innovative STEM pedagogies for teaching trigonometric and mensuration concepts at secondary level
text: Abstract The understanding of trigonometry at secondary level overburdens the students and demotivates them towards studying mathematics and in turn physics/science. The present innovative STEM pedagogies based on sensors and Arduino facilitate the understanding of the difficult concepts in trigonometry and mensuration. Various concepts related to angle, Pythagorean triangle, trigonometry in terms of sine, cosine, tangent, height and distance measurements and mensuration involving volume, lateral surface area, total surface area of 3D objects can be easily understood through the STEM pedagogies developed using tilt sensor, ultrasonic sensors and Arduino microcontroller. The results have high accuracy and the hands-on measurements facilitate the visualization of these challenging concepts. The novel and inventive approach may greatly bolster educational attainment by fostering interactive learning and implementing tailored teaching methods that seamlessly blend theory and practical application in mathematical concepts and thus Physics/Science using technology.
keywords: STEM teaching, trigonometry, measurement, high school mathematics, Arduino, inclinometer, ultrasonic sensors, Pythagorean triangles, volume, interactive learning

title: Measuring g using buoyancy: a simple and accurate method for high-school physics lab
text: Abstract This article presents a simple and accurate method for determining the gravitational acceleration g by applying Archimedes’ principle. A cylindrical aluminium rod was suspended and gradually immersed in water, and a digital scale recorded the buoyant force at each depth. The volume of the immersed rod was calculated geometrically with a correction applied to the finite vessel size. By plotting the buoyant force against volume and using the known density of water, the value of g was extracted from the slope of the best-fit line. The result, g = 9.788 ± 0.023 m s−2, agreed well with the accepted value and demonstrated the educational potential of fluid-based alternatives to traditional kinematic methods. This experiment offers a low-cost and conceptually rich opportunity to explore hydrostatics, Newtonian mechanics, and metrology in an integrated manner. As such, it represents a valuable and accessible method for high school physics laboratories.
keywords: gravitational acceleration, buoyancy, Archimedes' principle, hydrostatics, aluminum rod, water immersion, low-cost experiments, metrology

title: The study of shadows—Kepler’s ‘light figures’ and pinhole imaging
text: Abstract Kepler’s theory on pinhole camera imaging is still valid today, its development is well documented and provides an exciting context for optics lessons. Kepler presented a generalised concept of ‘light figures,’ describing the formation of soft shadow images through the interaction between extended apertures and extended light sources. The work marks the culmination of Kepler’s extensive engagement with the ‘Moon Puzzle.’ In this paper, we examine Kepler’s theory and depiction of ‘light figures’ from both historical and experimental perspectives. We provide an overview of Kepler’s theory and its historical context, and present experiments that illustrate Kepler’s theoretical insights, specifically designed for educational use. In this way, a generalised concept of soft shadow imaging can be integrated into optics education, drawing on an authentic historical context.
keywords: Johannes Kepler, pinhole imaging, pinhole camera, soft shadows, extended light sources, history of optics, optics education

title: Correcting the rolling shutter effect in a video analysis experiment
text: Abstract The rolling shutter effect, a well-known source of distortion in pictures captured with sensors that acquire the image line by line rather than at a single instant, significantly impacts video analysis, a common technique in introductory physics labs for studying motion. When a decelerating rotational motion is recorded with such sensors, the measured angular velocity exhibits pronounced oscillations, rather than a uniform decrease. However, these artifacts can be eliminated by advancing or retarding the timestamp of each video frame. This correction, which involves calculating the derivative of data with non-uniformly spaced timestamps (a task achievable through straightforward methods), provides students with a valuable opportunity to understand the necessity of identifying and correcting sensor-induced artifacts. While the rolling shutter effect also introduces errors in projectile motion experiments, including a 4% overestimation of the free-fall acceleration g, its impact is less pronounced than in rotational motion scenarios.
keywords: rolling shutter effect, video analysis, angular velocity measurement, rotational motion, sensor artifacts, derivative estimation, free-fall acceleration, projectile motion, introductory physics laboratory

title: Instability in sugar–salt double-diffusive systems
text: Abstract The International Young Physicists’ Tournament (IYPT) is a worldwide, annual competition for high school students. This paper is adapted from the author’s investigation into problem 8, Sugar and Salt, of the 28th IYPT. When a container with a layer of sugar water placed above a layer of salt water is illuminated, a distinctive fingering pattern may be seen in the projected shadow. This phenomenon is known as double-diffusive convection. Although the theoretical foundations for double-diffusive systems have been established, explicit experimental verifications of the instability condition are limited. This paper aims to qualitatively investigate the dependence of the growth of the fingers on different sugar and salt concentrations, verify the downward flux of sugar, and quantitatively verify the instability condition for the sugar–salt double-diffusive system. This experiment gives students the experience of tackling complicated problems in physical chemistry and fluid dynamics in a laboratory setting, in the spirit of the IYPT.
keywords: double-diffusive convection, fingering instability, Rayleigh-Bénard convection, sugar content, salt concentration, instability conditions, sugar water, salt water

title: The use of computer mathematics systems for performing home laboratory works in physics during distance learning
text: Abstract The possibility of using computer mathematics systems and smartphone for distance learning of physics for students and pupils, in particular, for performing laboratory works at home, was analysed. An algorithm for performing home laboratory work on studying the movement of bodies in a viscous liquid and determining the viscosity coefficient using the modified Stokes method has been developed. The essence of the method consists in video recording of a real experiment, subsequent conversion of the video into a set of JPG-format frames, and processing of the obtained figures by means of computer mathematics systems.
keywords: distance education, smartphones, viscosity coefficient, video frame analysis

title: A token system for incentivising equal contributions in group work
text: Abstract Teamwork is an essential skill for STEM students, but ensuring equitable workload distribution remains a challenge. We propose a token-based method to incentivise equal work sharing. Each team of size N receives 2 N+1 tokens, which students openly discuss how to divide amongst their teammates. Two tokens result in a full grade, while three tokens earn a bonus. This system is implemented in small, frequent team assignments, promoting immediate peer feedback for underperforming teammates. The ability to bank bonus tokens ahead of time also allows flexibility for students who have illnesses or emergencies. The token system was piloted with university undergraduates in an introductory engineering and an upper-level physics course, with surveys conducted at the 16-week semester’s start and end. Results showed that students’ perceptions of group work improved, teams using the token system had more equitable contributions compared to a control group, and students had mostly positive comments about the token system. A few students pointed out some deficiencies, especially social pressure to not penalise underperforming students. Based on survey data and the authors’ experience, we offer the following recommendations for instructors: provide in-class time for token discussions even if the assignments are submitted outside of class, be prepared to mediate conflicts, monitor groups for the social pressure to avoid penalties, set a semester cap of 100% for token points to avoid work hoarding, and be careful when using the system with continually reshuffled teams. Overall though, the token system successfully promotes equitable contributions to team assignments.
keywords: token economy, group work, teamwork, peer feedback, student incentives, STEM education, engineering education, social pressure, grading

title: A simple method of demonstration of characteristics of rainbows using a glass of water and a few laser sources
text: Abstract A rainbow is a captivating natural phenomenon resulting from the refraction, dispersion, and reflection of sunlight within water droplets. Traditional classroom demonstrations often focus on qualitative explanations of the formation of rainbows using prisms or water bowls. This study presents a simple experimental approach to analysing the process of rainbow formation through quantitative analysis using a cylindrical glass filled with water, graph paper, and three semiconductor laser sources emitting red, green, and blue light. By measuring the angles of minimum deviation for different wavelengths, we have found that the experimental values closely match the theoretical predictions. This method offers a hands-on, cost-effective approach to enhance students’ understanding of the physics behind rainbows.
keywords: rainbow formation, optical dispersion, minimum deviation, water droplets, refraction, wavelength dependence, semiconductor lasers, classroom demonstration

title: Measuring and understanding radiation exposure on a commercial flight as a teaching tool
text: Abstract Getting experience with radioactivity as an undergraduate in physics can be difficult for many reasons. Many physics labs simply do not want to deal with the safety and regulatory requirements that come with managing a radioactive source. And for those that do manage their own source, contamination concerns and participant dosimetry can often make lab demonstrations more work than they are worth. As the cost and variety of simple radiation detectors decrease and increase, respectively, a fun and safe way to collect example radiation data might be as simple as getting on a commercial flight for your next vacation. Here we describe a simple method of measuring a portion of the ‘radiation column,’ or the increase in radioactivity that occurs with altitude in the atmosphere. In addition to employing low-cost equipment, it has the added benefit of providing a relate-able context for students to understand radiation safety.
keywords: cosmic rays, radiation exposure, commercial air travel, altitude, radiation protection, radiation detectors, low-cost detector, undergraduate physics education, physics experiment teaching, dosimetry

title: Mobile phone-integrated demonstration of Kepler’s second law of planetary motion and the conservation law of angular momentum
text: Abstract Kepler’s second law states that a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals as it orbits the Sun. The principle is intrinsically linked to the conservation of angular momentum. However, its exploration may be challenging for students mainly due to the complex nature of determining the area of a sector of the chosen planet’s elliptical orbit. This article introduces a simpler and faster way of demonstrating the mentioned fundamental laws by integrating smartphone-based measurements through the mobile application Petiole Pro (or alternatively LeafByte for iOS). With readily available orbital data of planets and comets that can be extracted online, this study provides an accessible and easier method for students and educators to visualize and understand celestial mechanics using a smartphone application.
keywords: Kepler's second law, angular momentum conservation, eccentric orbits, smartphone-based measurement, celestial mechanics, planetary orbits, comets, physics demonstration

title: Helping introductory physics students connect physics with humanities, art, social sciences, and everyday life
text: Abstract In this article, we reflect upon our positive experiences incorporating or working on extra credit projects in algebra-based introductory physics that asked students to connect physics with humanities, social sciences, and everyday life. We give an example of a student project that reflects their creativity and ingenuity and encourages other instructors to offer similar projects.
keywords: introductory physics, interdisciplinary connections, humanities, social sciences, everyday life, student creativity, algebra-based physics, student projects

title: Enhancing secondary school students’ self-concept through Vee-diagram and guided-inquiry strategies
text: Abstract In a world where educational success is paramount, students’ self-concept significantly influences their motivation and performance, especially in challenging subjects like physics. Traditional teaching methods often fail to engage students, resulting in reduced self-confidence and interest in STEM fields. This study investigated the effects of Vee-diagram and guided-inquiry strategies on the self-concept of secondary school physics students. Using a quasi-experimental design, the research involved 413 students selected from a population of 83 981 Senior Secondary Two (SS2) students through multistage sampling, with 225 females and 188 males. The Physics Self-Concept Inventory, validated by experts and showing a reliability coefficient of 0.81, was used for data collection before and after a six-week intervention. Data analysis employed Mean Rank, Kruskal–Wallis, and Mann–Whitney U tests. Results indicated significantly higher mean rank gain in self-concept in both the Vee-diagram (75.03) and guided-inquiry groups (65.36) compared to conventional lecture methods (10.66). No notable gender differences were found in the self-concept ratings within the Vee-diagram (p = 0.618) and guided-inquiry groups (p = 0.442). Structured professional development programs that introduce teachers to these strategies. workshops, peer-teaching sessions, among others, are recommended for effective implementation.
keywords: self-concept, Vee diagram, guided inquiry, high school students, student motivation, STEM interest, teacher professional development, gender differences

title: Demonstrating the shift of acoustic beat frequency with tuning forks and smartphones and its application for measuring the speed
text: Abstract While investigating the phenomenon of acoustic beats using two tuning forks, we observed that the Doppler effect alters the beat frequency of the tones produced. This effect is easily perceived by observers, offering physics students a very direct experience of even very small shifts in frequency, and can be readily explained using the physical principles behind beat formation. For precise speed measurements, we replicated the phenomenon using a small cart, mobile phones, and a computer-based measuring device. The analysis of the recorded data revealed that this setup enables the cart’s velocity to be determined to within 1 cm s−1. The results of the acoustic measurements were verified through video analysis of the motion. The developed experimental setup is suitable for implementation in classroom settings or student laboratories, offering an effective means of increasing student engagement and deepening their understanding of physics.
keywords: beat frequency, Doppler shift, tuning fork, smartphone audio, velocity measurement, physics laboratory experiments, classroom demonstration

title: Lenz’s law and a magnet on the end of a fishing line in a conducting tube
text: Abstract A simple experiment is described that links Lenz’s law to Newton’s laws of motion. A length of fishing line is glued to a rare earth magnet. When the magnet is dropped through the centre of a conducting tube placed on a tared balance, while the magnet is descending at constant velocity, the balance reading becomes equal to the mass of the magnet. When the descent of the magnet is arrested by grabbing the fishing line, the balance reading falls to zero. When the magnet is lifted, the reading becomes negative.
keywords: Lenz's law, electromagnetic induction, eddy currents, Newton's laws of motion, rare-earth permanent magnets, fishing line, physics demonstration

title: Torque calculations
text: Abstract A calculation of angular acceleration involves a torque acting about a given axis, usually passing through the centre of mass. However, the same answer can sometimes be obtained using a different axis.
keywords: torque, angular acceleration, center of mass, rotation axis, moment of inertia, rotational dynamics

title: Temperature mapping in urban biomes using an infrared thermometer: an investigative approach to physics education
text: Abstract In recent years, the frequency of extreme weather events on Earth has significantly increased. This phenomenon is driven by the intensification of the greenhouse effect caused by anthropogenic activities, which leads to temperature variations in urban environments that affect thermal comfort and quality of life. Given this context, the present study investigates temperature mapping in urban biomes using an infrared thermometer, conducted as part of a hands-on workshop offered during the 21st National Science and Technology Week. The initiative involved students from the public school system, and was grounded in physics education, aiming to foster scientific enculturation. Participants engaged in a problem-based learning experience, actively contributing to all stages of the knowledge-construction process. The objective of this study was to examine the relationship between the presence of vegetation and its impact on temperature in urban environments. A qualitative and quantitative methodological approach was adopted, enabling the identification of scientific literacy indicators, such as information sequencing, data organisation, logical reasoning, hypothesis formulation, justification, and explanation of observed phenomena. The analysis of the students’ statements and activity guidelines provided insights into their critical thinking development. The findings indicated that students developed essential skills for understanding physical and environmental phenomena, effectively linking collected data to scientific concepts, and proposing well-supported interpretations. Moreover, experience reinforced the perception of science as a dynamic and investigative process, fostering curiosity and enhancing students’ argumentative abilities. Thus, the workshop proved to be an effective strategy for promoting scientific literacy and engaging participants in the study of environmental impact in urban contexts.
keywords: urban heat island, temperature mapping, infrared thermometer, urban vegetation, scientific literacy, critical thinking, problem-based learning, hands-on workshop, science and technology week, public school students, greenhouse effect, extreme weather events, argumentation skills

title: Kinetic energy change under Galilean transformation
text: Abstract This paper aims to establish a consistent and accurate definition of an inertial frame of reference. The proposed definition adheres to Newton’s Laws and ensures results that remain invariant under Galilean transformation. Additionally, it upholds the principles of energy and linear momentum conservation.
keywords: Galilean transformation, kinetic energy, Newton's laws of motion, energy conservation (physics), conservation of linear momentum, invariance, classical mechanics

title: Using slime to enhance students’ understanding of tidal force and its effect on ocean: two water bulges
text: Abstract Tidal force refers to the difference in gravitational pulls exerted by one celestial body on different parts of another body such as the Moon and the Earth. Tidal force is complicated for students to understand because it is an abstract scientific idea, difficult to demonstrate, touch, or perceive by people’s senses. However, the concept of tidal force is useful for explaining phenomena such as the formation of two water bulges. This is important because some students mistakenly believe there is only one bulge on the side facing the Moon, as typical explanations focus solely on the Moon’s attraction. This paper uses a combination of slime as a physical model and a diagram to help students understand the tidal force and its effect on ocean: two water bulges.
keywords: tidal forces, gravitational pull, physical model, slime, tides, misconceptions, diagrammatic representation, physics education

title: On Joule’s paddle wheel experiment in textbooks II
text: Abstract Joule’s paddle wheel experiment has become famous in the history of physics. Illustrations of the experiment have appeared in textbooks since the 19th century. However, the textbook diagrams of Joule’s experiment differ from each other, and most differ from the original diagram. The differences appear to be significant. The question of whether the results of the experiments are the same in each of the experimental configurations is addressed in this paper. In order to answer this question, a replica of the original calorimeter was built. The results obtained were compared with those obtained using machines that corresponded to the schematics of the experiment in physics textbooks. This comparison gives us a new insight into the potential energy transformed into heat.
keywords: history of physics, physics textbook, mechanical equivalent of heat

title: Epicycle motion of spinning objects
text: Abstract The motion of spinning objects on a horizontal surface can be explained in terms of an epicycle, originally proposed by Ptolemy around 170 AD to explain the motion of the planets. Examples are given of a spinning coin, a spinning egg and a spinning cylinder.
keywords: spinning objects, rolling without slipping, Ptolemy, rotating cylinder, horizontal surface, rotational motion

title: DIY of pencil drawn Seebeck effect
text: Abstract This article explores the fabrication of a thermocouple using different grades of pencils on a wooden substrate to demonstrate the Seebeck effect to the students. By utilising the Seebeck effect, the thermocouple generates a voltage when subjected to a temperature gradient. Experimental results reveal that the output voltage varies with the pencil grade, reflecting differences in their respective Seebeck coefficients. V-shaped single-junction thermocouple composed of HB and 8B graphite produced an output voltage of 0.7 mV at 118 °C, whereas a configuration using HB and 4B graphite generated 0.5 mV at 125 °C. This simple yet effective approach provides an accessible method for teaching thermoelectric principles in educational settings.
keywords: Seebeck effect, thermocouples, pencil graphite, Seebeck coefficient, thermoelectric materials, temperature gradient, output voltage

title: Developing high school students’ experimental competence in radioactivity through problem-based learning
text: Abstract This article describes a problem-based learning (PBL) approach to developing experimental competence in radioactivity among 12th-grade high school students. The study, conducted in the context of the Vietnamese physics curriculum, involved eight students in a series of hands-on tasks. Using equipment such as a Geiger–Müller detector and a self-constructed Wilson cloud chamber, students were challenged to design and conduct their own experiments on the properties and applications of radiation. Our findings indicate that the PBL framework led to significant gains in students’ experimental skills, particularly in planning and execution. We present this case as a successful model for teaching complex physics topics through active, student-cantered inquiry.
keywords: problem-based learning, experimental competence, radioactivity, high school physics, Geiger-Muller counter, cloud chamber, student-designed experiments, inquiry-based learning

title: Real-time data acquisition with ESP32: a didactic approach to Faraday’s law
text: Abstract This paper presents a study of Faraday’s law of induction, using an experimental apparatus based on the ESP32 microcontroller, adopting a practical and pedagogical approach. The setup enables real-time acquisition and both qualitative and quantitative analysis of the behaviours of current, magnetic field, and induced voltage. This enables clear visualization of how the induced voltage is related to the temporal variation of the magnetic field, as described by Faraday’s law. The methodology facilitates the understanding of concepts that are often regarded as abstract and difficult for students to grasp, making them more accessible and intuitive. The integration of the experiment with Excel, employing PLX-DAQ software, provides a customized tool for this application, enabling streamlined data acquisition and analysis. The promising results obtained in this study highlight the potential of using microcontrollers as a valuable pedagogical resource in physics education, capable of fostering more active learning by linking theoretical principles with practical applications.
keywords: Faraday's law, ESP32 microcontroller, real-time data acquisition, induced voltage, magnetic field variations, active learning, Excel data analysis
