title: Bridging the DART mission with scientific and school knowledge: integrating simulations for enhanced learning
text: Abstract NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission tested planetary defence by altering an asteroid’s path, could offer a real-world context for integrating science into education. The objective is to design simulations based on the DART mission to merge scientific and school knowledge, enhance STEM education through experiential learning, and raise awareness of planetary defence. The requirements to reach the objective were set to reflect DART’s key phases—rendezvous and impact—considering 3D modelling, orbital timing, brightness, and adjustable start dates for varied mission scenarios. These classroom tools should allow students to manipulate time and observe orbital dynamics and photometric changes. The results include one simulation that models the spacecraft’s Keplerian motion to rendezvous with the Didymos asteroid, while the second shows the impact and its effect on the orbit. Students can explore planetary movement, analyse data, and evaluate different mission timelines. Bringing DART into the classroom bridges theory and application, strengthens STEM understanding and problem-solving, fosters engagement, and promotes awareness of planetary defence challenges.
keywords: DART mission, planetary defense, asteroid deflection, STEM education, educational simulation, Keplerian motion, orbital dynamics, photometry, mission timeline, experiential learning, 3D modeling

title: Some new ways of looking at the solar system
text: Abstract Four new ways of drawing the solar system are presented and discussed. In the first diagram, Sun-planet barycentres are plotted on the radius of the Sun. Only the centre of the Sun–Jupiter barycentre lies outside of the Sun. A second diagram shows the relative sizes of the planets plotted concentrically revealing a pairing of the planets: Mercury–Mars, Earth–Venus, Uranus–Neptune, Jupiter–Saturn. A third diagram shows the relative positions of the planets on the gravitational potential (GP) well of the Sun. A fourth diagram shows a plot of the relative depth of the GP wells of the planets. All the diagrams are available as supplementary material.
keywords: solar system, gravitational potential well, gravitational potential, planetary orbits

title: Lecture demonstration of heart function as a piston pump for liquid circulation
text: Abstract For the educational use it is suggested to use a simple hemodynamic model of the left heart atrium and ventricle. The model is meant to be assembled by students with subsequent demonstration in a classroom. The model is constructed of large transparent plastic syringes and soft transparent silicone tubes; it is also suggested to use glass balls, an inflatable balloon and other available materials to imitate the valves of the heart. The setup allows a visual demonstration of the heart’s function as a pump: systole and diastole of the atrium and ventricle; the operation of the valves that provides the pumping of liquid by the heart. The model allows demonstration of coordinated functioning of all parts of the heart.
keywords: cardiac function, heart as pump, hemodynamic modeling, left atrium, left ventricle, heart valves, systole and diastole, liquid circulation, classroom demonstration

title: Mathematical modelling of photoperiod: equation to calculate the photoperiod at any location on the planetary surface
text: Abstract Our lives, since ancient times, have been shaped by the position of the Sun in the sky. Not only agriculture, but also the functioning of modern urban societies, depends on the presence—or absence—of light provided by our central star. In this context, the ability to determine the duration of natural daylight (photoperiod) has long held significant interest across various domains of human activity. In this work, we present a new equation that enables the calculation of the photoperiod for any location on Earth’s surface. Although approximate, the equation yields results that closely match observational data. The mathematical tools involved fall well within the scope of an undergraduate course in the exact sciences: chiefly, vector analysis and trigonometry. From astronomy, only elementary principles are employed. This makes the work accessible both for applied investigations and as a pedagogical tool to deepen the understanding of fundamental concepts encountered in undergraduate education. Although it has not yet been implemented in the classroom or developed in collaboration with students, such applications are clearly possible.
keywords: photoperiod, day length, mathematical modeling, trigonometry, vector calculus, solar position, solar declination, solar altitude, undergraduate physics education, astronomy education

title: Laboratory-scale model for air vortex generation using passive and natural heating methods
text: Abstract This work discusses the design of an inexpensive and easy-to-operate experimental apparatus for the creation and visualization of air vortices using natural convection. The experimental setup consists of an upright clear tube with four tangentially mounted air inlets. Three experimental cases were explored: forced convection from the use of a hair dryer, natural convection from the use of a candle, and passive flow using smoke without the application of an external heat source. The experimental results indicated that the candle setup produced successfully an observable and sustained air vortex by creating a thermal gradient forcing the buoyant upward flow. The vortex creation was complemented by tangential air flow from the inlets, leading to spiralling motion as predicted from theory and computer simulations. This system provides an inexpensive teaching tool for vortex dynamics, convention, and atmospheric fluid flow in the educational setting.
keywords: natural convection, forced convection, thermal buoyancy, vortex dynamics, physics teaching apparatus, smoke visualization

title: Which rope breaks? A study of tension distribution in multi-rope systems
text: Abstract We investigate the tension distribution in systems of mass-less ropes under different loading conditions. For a two-rope system, we demonstrate how the breaking scenario depends on the applied force dynamics: rapid pulling causes the lower rope to break, while gradual pulling leads to upper rope failure. Extending to a three-rope Y-shaped configuration, we identify a critical angle θ C = 60 ∘ that determines which rope breaks first. When the angle between the upper ropes exceeds this critical value, the upper ropes fail before the lower one. We further analyse how an attached mass at the junction point modifies this critical angle and establish maximum mass limits for valid solutions. Our results provide practical insights for introductory physics students understanding static forces and system stabilities.
keywords: critical angle, static force, system stability, introductory physics

title: Unveiling gender dynamics in introductory physics labs
text: Abstract The persistent underrepresentation of women and gender minorities within the physical sciences remains a significant issue. This study investigates gender dynamics in introductory algebra-based physics laboratories, focusing on participation, task preferences, and comfort levels. Statistical analysis revealed no significant gender difference in overall participation rates during lab activities. However, significant gender-based disparities emerged in both task preference [ χ 2 ( df = 3 ) = 9.548 , p = 0.023 , α = 0.05 ] and comfort levels [ χ 2 ( df = 3 ) = 7.906 , p = 0.048 , α = 0.05 ]. Male students significantly preferred and felt more comfortable with hands-on equipment handling and data collection, whereas female students more frequently preferred and reported higher comfort with analytical and documentation tasks like note-taking, calculations, and report writing. Qualitative responses highlighted additional challenges reported by some women, including exclusion from group discussions and reluctance to contribute ideas in male-dominated groups. These findings suggest that while overall participation may appear gender-neutral, gendered patterns in task allocation and comfort persist. The results underscore the need for instructional strategies that promote equitable engagement and foster inclusive laboratory environments in physics education.
keywords: gender dynamics, introductory physics laboratory, gender equity, women in physics, gender minorities, student participation, task preference, comfort level

title: The rolling dynamics of a plastic cup on the floor
text: Abstract This study aims to evaluate the generalizability of the rolling motion model proposed by Wibowo et al (2025) by extending its application to a different class of rolling objects, namely plastic cups. The investigation focuses on comparing theoretical and experimental turning radii of circular trajectories formed by cups with distinct sizes and geometries. Four plastic cups—green, blue-patterned, yellow, and dark green—differing in size, shape, and mass were tested. Theoretical radii were calculated based on geometric parameters, while experimental radii were obtained by tracing the cups’ rolling paths. The theoretical values ( R t ) were 35.90 cm (green), 38.88 cm (blue-patterned), 23.69 cm (yellow), and 68.01 cm (dark green), compared with experimental results ( R e ) of 39.09 cm, 40.14 cm, 25.64 cm, and 63.04 cm, respectively. The relative errors ranged from 3.23% to 8.89%, indicating strong consistency and confirming the robustness of the geometric model. Nevertheless, the results also revealed systematic deviations, with larger cups producing tighter curves than predicted, largely due to asymmetric mass distribution and rotational inertia that are not accounted for in the geometric formulation. These findings highlight the limitations of a purely geometric approach while demonstrating that the model remains a reliable approximation for a broader class of rolling objects. In addition to its theoretical contribution, the study underscores the pedagogical value of the rolling cup experiment, offering students a low-cost and engaging activity to explore rotational dynamics, geometric modelling, and error analysis while reflecting on the interplay between idealized models and real-world observations.
keywords: roll motion, plastic cups, turning radius, circular trajectory, rotary inertia, asymmetric mass distribution, rotational dynamics, model generalization, error analysis

title: EM-In: a simple electromagnetic induction experiment kit
text: Abstract In this study, we designed and fabricated an experiment kit, known as EM-In, to investigate factors affecting the magnitude of the induced electromagnetic force (emf) in the coil. It consists of four components: (1) a PVC stand, (2) a cylindrical magnet as a pendulum, (3) copper coils with different diameters and number of turns and (4) a connection box. The EM-In experiment kit offers a simpler method to demonstrate the production of the induced emf by swinging the cylindrical magnet to-and-fro the coil. It was employed with a personal computer installed with Audacity software to differentiate the magnitude of the induced emf in the coils. The EM-In experiment kit can be utilised to determine the effects of coil diameters, number of turns and magnetic field strength on the magnitude of the induced emf in the coil.
keywords: electromagnetic induction, induced voltage, copper coil, coil diameter, number of coil turns, magnetic field strength, Audacity, physics teaching aids

title: The gravity of imagination
text: Abstract This paper discusses some experiences carried out in an Italian high school with third year students (around 14 years old). Each phase of the proposed lesson is used to introduce an oral discussion within the class; the images, words and games used are all aimed at stimulating debate among the students. The practical part of the lesson is used to look for the relationship between physical quantities and their values; in this part, measuring instruments play a central role in guiding the students to find the proportionality between geometric parameters (such as area, distance, orientation, etc). The goal will never be to find ‘the right relationship between the physical quantities involved in the experiment’, but rather to find a correct and repeatedly applicable methodology for working and finding results.
keywords: high school physics, oral discussion, classroom debate, measurement instruments, proportionality, geometric parameters, physical quantities, experimental method, student-centered learning

title: Measurement of lens function of yeast cells using optical microscope and laser pointer
text: Abstract Measurements using an optical microscope, red, green, and blue laser pointers, a diagonal prism mount and a sapphire ball, as well as calculations using the equation for a thick lens, were conducted to investigate the wavelength dependence of the refractive index of micrometre-sized yeast cells. In addition, projection experiments using a lattice pattern and an optical microscope demonstrated that yeast cells can function as lenses. This research method, which uses familiar materials and instruments, such as yeast cells and optical microscopes, is suitable as a teaching method for optical experiments for not only physics students but also biology students to learn the principles of optical microscopes and lenses.
keywords: yeast cells, refractive index, wavelength dependence, optical microscopy, laser pointer, physics education, biology education, optical experiments

title: Explore the physics of soap films with the SoapFilmScope
text: Abstract This paper presents the SoapFilmScope, a versatile and inexpensive device designed for physics teaching at secondary school and undergraduate levels. Built from low-cost and easily accessible materials, the SoapFilmScope enables students to explore key physics concepts–wave dynamics, light interference, and fluid motion–through real-time observation of soap film behaviour under acoustic excitation. Using only a 3D printer, a smartphone, a loudspeaker, and basic components, learners can visualise capillary standing waves, interference patterns, and internal flow structures. The device is particularly suited for classroom demonstrations and student-led inquiry, offering both qualitative insights and entry points for simple quantitative analysis. Aligned with core physics curricula, the SoapFilmScope provides a hands-on platform for reinforcing fundamental topics in waves, optics, and fluid dynamics.
keywords: soap films, optical interference, fluid dynamics, acoustic excitation, classroom demonstration, student-led inquiry, wave dynamics

title: Hawking in a thousand words
text: Abstract British physicist Stephen Hawking’s most important discovery was that ‘black holes are not so black’, as they possess a temperature and emit thermal radiation. In his popular science texts, Hawking offered a detailed explanation of this phenomenon. The aim of this work is to translate that explanation into mathematical language accessible to an advanced high school student, all within a thousand words.
keywords: Hawking radiation, black holes, Hawking temperature, thermal radiation, black hole thermodynamics

title: Assessing Chinese students’ performance in introductory calculus-based physics: a case study
text: Abstract Students’ recurring difficulties in learning reflect to some degree the weakness in an instructor’s pedagogy. This study assesses students’ performance in introductory calculus-based physics, focusing on mechanics, among freshmen at a top-tier university in China. Through statistical analysis of the final exam, students’ common weakness in knowledge acquisition and retrieval is observed and only a small fraction demonstrate transition from novice-like to expert-like problem solving. Thus, the traditional pedagogy of lecturing followed by student-directed learning currently assumed turns out to be insufficient in developing students’ general problem-solving capabilities. Moreover, the practical usage of the Minnesota Assessment of Problem Solving rubric in the assessment indicates that explicit problem-solving instruction is feasible in large-enrolment lectures, which is promising in improving students’ knowledge integration in future teaching practice.
keywords: student performance, mechanics, problem solving, novice to expert transition, knowledge acquisition, knowledge retrieval, physics education, Chinese university students

title: Instructional design and teaching that fosters meaningful engagement in disciplinary practice in a Maker project on projectile-motion
text: Abstract This study contributes to the growing body of work on integrating Making into science education by examining how an open-ended projectile-motion design challenge can foster meaningful disciplinary engagement in physics. We report on an intervention that integrated an extended Making project into the learning of physics at the advanced high school level in the 10th grade. The intervention (18 academic hours, spread over 4 weeks) was videotaped, and post-activity interviews with selected students (5 out of 18) were conducted. We use these data to discuss how instructional design and the interaction with the facilitating teachers fostered the emergence of students’ engagement with core physics practices that organically emerged from their engagement in Making. We highlight key design considerations, how the tradeoff between openness and structure was negotiated and resolved, the teachers’ facilitation strategies and their discursive moves. We also offer practical guidance for educators seeking to support authentic disciplinary learning in Makerspaces without sacrificing students’ creativity, freedom, and ownership.
keywords: maker education, projectile motion, design challenges, disciplinary practices, student engagement, instructional design, open-ended learning, teacher as facilitator, makerspaces, high school physics

title: Schematic representation method for quantum circuits: an intuitive approach to quantum gate effects
text: Abstract In quantum circuits, qubits and the quantum gates acting on them have traditionally been analysed using matrix algebra and Dirac notation. While powerful, these can be unintuitive for conceptual understanding and rapid problem solving. In this work, a new schematic representation method is developed that visualizes the effects of quantum gates on qubits without relying on complex mathematical operations. In the new notation, quantum bits (qubits) are represented using black (|0〉) and white (|1〉) circles. When a quantum gate is applied to a qubit, the circle representing the qubit is visually modified. For example, a Hadamard gate transforms a solid black or white circle into a half-black and half-white circle representing superposition. The work shows how this method simplifies the visualization of quantum algorithms, entanglement, and multi- qubit operations. The work proposes how this method can act as a visual aid to support the understanding of quantum algorithms, entanglement, and multi-qubit operations. Thus, the initial conceptual analysis of basic quantum circuits can be facilitated by simple schematic representations, reducing the immediate cognitive load of complex mathematical operations for beginners.
keywords: quantum circuits, quantum gates, schematic representation, Hadamard gate, superposition, entanglement, quantum algorithms, conceptual understanding, visual aids

title: The ballast metronome
text: Abstract We present an educational activity concerning the realization of a homemade ballast metronome and the experimental investigation of its oscillations that can be varied by changing the position of a movable weight along a vertical rod. The instrument is equipped with a mechanical escapement powered by an elastic rubber band. We analyze the mechanical system in terms of a compound pendulum. However, due to the presence of the escapement and friction, not taken into account in the model, the experimental data are only qualitatively accounted. The proposed experimental activity can be easily carried out in the classroom, at secondary and high school physics laboratory. The ballast metronome can be used for marking musical tempos, as a classical mechanical metronome. Furthermore, it gives the opportunity to teach/learn concepts at an elementary level concerning the elastic potential energy, the mechanism of the escapement, and the pendulum isochronism exploited for measuring time, contributing to increase student’s engagements in physics.
keywords: compound pendulum, escapement mechanism, elastic energy, oscillations, music tempo

title: Teaching non-uniform circular motion through real-world aircraft kinematics
text: Abstract This work proposes a new teaching method for teaching non-uniform circular motion by analysing real-world aircraft trajectories. The method uses video clips captured from Flightradar24, Tracker software for coordinate extraction, and Python scripting for analysing motion. Physical quantities such as total velocity, centripetal acceleration, tangential acceleration, bank angle, and load factor were calculated for different types of commercial aircraft. These calculations were verified against known standard values to confirm their accuracy. The velocity vectors and acceleration vectors both in normal and tangential directions were visualized on the aircraft trajectories. I believe that this method provides students with a connection between physical concepts and real-world examples. It also prepares the students with critical thinking, data acquisition, and analysis skills.
keywords: aircraft kinematics, Tracker software, coordinate extraction, centripetal acceleration, tangential acceleration, bank angle, load factor, commercial aircraft

title: Systematic study on the size effect of the copper tube used in the demonstration of Lenz’s law
text: Abstract Electromagnetic induction and Lenz’s law are very important topics in both university and high school education, as well as in everyday practice. The qualitative demonstration of Lenz’s law with the movement of a magnetic body falling in a copper tube is well known. In this work, in order to expand on the quantitative analyses published in the literature so far, we conducted systematic experiments on the effect of the size of the copper tube used in the demonstration of Lenz’s law. We established important quantitative relationships regarding the effect of both the wall thickness and the inner diameter of the tube, which were also supported by theoretical considerations. The obtained relationships can not only help university students to understand the topic more deeply but can also provide engineers with important knowledge in practical applications and designs. Our low-cost experimental equipment can be easily assembled in a student laboratory, and we plan to implement this experiment as an advanced university laboratory activity.
keywords: Lenz's law, electromagnetic induction, copper tubes, tube wall thickness, inner diameter, eddy currents, physics laboratory experiments, low-cost laboratory equipment

title: Conservation of angular momentum demonstration
text: Abstract A simple experiment is described using a spinning ball to illustrate conservation of angular momentum in the absence of an external torque.
keywords: angular momentum conservation, spinning ball, external torque, physics demonstration, rotational motion

title: Metrology of the simple pendulum, through a study of error analysis and data interpretation
text: Abstract The simple pendulum experiment is a fundamental tool in physics education, illustrating key concepts in mechanics and data analysis. This study presents a comprehensive examination of the experiment, emphasizing the crucial role of metrology – the science of measurement – in obtaining reliable results. We highlight how careful statistical analysis, including assessing the convergence of statistical measures, and uncertainty estimation are essential. A key finding is that even when the calculated acceleration due to gravity ( g ) is close to the expected value, a detailed analysis of the L vs. T 2 relationship can reveal significant systematic errors, such as those arising from inaccuracies in length or time measurements. By systematically analysing these errors, this paper provides valuable insights for educators and students seeking a deeper understanding of experimental physics and the importance of metrological rigor.
keywords: simple pendulum, metrology, error analysis, uncertainty estimation, gravitational acceleration, length measurement error, systematic errors

title: Energy loss in head-on collisions
text: Abstract When two objects collide head-on there is usually a loss of energy that can be quantified in terms of the coefficient of restitution (COR). However, the energy loss also depends on the mass and the velocity of each object, so the role of the COR is not completely obvious. The energy loss is a maximum, and depends only on the COR, if the centre of mass of the two objects remains at rest.
keywords: head-on collisions, energy loss, coefficient of restitution, center of mass, collision dynamics

title: On the derivation of the cosmological Gurzadyan’s theorem
text: Abstract We present a pedagogical, perturbation-based derivation of the cosmological Gurzadyan’s theorem, accessible to advanced high-school and undergraduate students.
keywords: cosmological perturbations, cosmic microwave background, primordial power spectrum, cosmic microwave background anisotropies

title: Work done on an object that translates, rotates and compresses
text: Abstract Two different work-energy theorems can be used to describe the work done on an extended object if it rotates and/or compresses when an external force is applied to the object. An example is presented where a force is applied to a flexible rod that simultaneously translates, rotates and compresses.
keywords: work-energy theorem, rotational motion, compression, flexible rods, external forces, rigid body dynamics

title: An AI for an AI: AI-generated interactive animated questions as a defense against AI-based cheating
text: Abstract The proliferation of advanced large language models (LLMs) in education has created new challenges for academic integrity, as students can now access AI tutors capable of solving traditional text-based problems with high accuracy. To address both conventional peer cheating and emerging AI-assisted cheating, we propose a novel method that leverages Claude AI to generate interactive animated questions integrated with Moodle’s formula question type. This approach creates multiple question versions while incorporating interactive elements that current AI systems cannot effectively process. We evaluated our method using physics problems across one-dimensional motion with friction and two-dimensional projectile motion. Our findings demonstrate that while LLMs like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini can readily solve traditional text-based versions of these problems, they struggle significantly with interactive versions that require user manipulation and real-time observation. The proposed method offers a scalable solution for educators to create AI-resistant assessments without requiring programming expertise, though broader validation across disciplines and AI models is needed.
keywords: AI-generated questions, academic integrity, large language models, Claude, Moodle, physics problem solving, projectile motion

title: Book Review: Discordance by Jim Baggott
text: Book Review: Discordance by Jim Baggott. Keywords: physics education, discordance
keywords: physics education, discordance

title: Cosmic catapults: bringing coronal mass ejections into the classroom
text: Abstract Analogies are used extensively in physics education. In this paper an elastic band analogy is used to teach students about the physical principles behind the generation of coronal mass ejections (CMEs), which are massive balls of plasma ejected from the Sun. If the Earth lies in the path of a CME the plasma interacts with the magnetosphere of the Earth. CMEs are of increasing concern due to their potential to disrupt global telecommunications. In this paper, the basic equations of motion are applied to a CME. Some CMEs are able to accelerate from zero metres per second to 1% of the speed of light in the space of the radius of the Sun in a period of about 7 min. A twisted elastic band on a toy plane is an example of how twisted material can store potential energy which can then be converted into kinetic energy. A stretched and flicked elastic band is another analogy to CMEs. Elastic bands are also a good model of the closed nature of magnetic field lines.
keywords: coronal mass ejections, solar plasma, magnetosphere, space weather, equations of motion, kinetic and potential energy, CME acceleration

title: Exploring students’ critical thinking skills through STEM-PjBL on Newton’s Laws
text: Abstract Critical thinking skills are essential components of 21st-century learning, supporting teaching and learning processes in the classroom. Based on previous results, students’ critical thinking skills are relatively low. Therefore, this research aimed to explore students’ critical thinking skills through the application of a STEM-integrated project-based learning (PjBL) model on the topic of Newton’s laws. The descriptive qualitative research comprised 35 grade XI students in Banyuwangi with a case design. Data obtained through documentation, interviews, and observations were analysed qualitatively using the Miles & Huberman method and tested for data validity through data triangulation. The results showed that the interpretation indicator was relatively low. Meanwhile, indicators of analysis, evaluation, inference, and explanation were in the good category. This research reported the implications of optimising STEM-integrated PjBL models on the topic of Newton’s laws to enhance the contextualisation and applicability of learning. The importance of critical thinking skills was also emphasised in improving the quality of education in the modern era.
keywords: critical thinking skills, STEM education, project-based learning, Newton's laws of motion, high school students, contextual learning, 21st century skills

title: Determining the speed of sound in a home experiment
text: Abstract This paper presents a home experiment for determining the speed of sound in air using simple resonators, such as a ballpoint pen tube, household foil tube, homemade paper tubes, and cylindrical teacup. The study demonstrates that for tubular resonators, the speed of sound can be calculated from the plot of the resonance frequency versus the harmonic number. When a teacup is employed as a resonator, the speed of sound can be determined from the frequencies corresponding to the maxima and minima of the amplitude–frequency response. A specially developed pulse-modulated sound sweep generator was used to accurately identify these frequencies. The results demonstrated that simple, low-cost resonators can provide reliable data on the speed of sound, offering an effective approach for home-based or classroom experiments in physics education.
keywords: speed of sound in air, resonant frequency, harmonic numbers, amplitude-frequency response, low-cost physics experiments, home experiments

title: Real-world physics learning through rowing: a STEM + sport case study with Phyphox and Python
text: Abstract This study examines the impact of integrating sports and physics education on fostering meaningful Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics (STEM) learning among 11th-grade students. Within the framework of a STEM + Sports interdisciplinary approach, a biomechanical analysis of rowing was conducted using the Phyphox mobile app and Python programming in Google Colab. Students collected real-time acceleration data during rowing activities using carbon fibre, aluminium, and composite oars. They then used ChatGPT to generate Python code, interpret the data, and calculate rowing performance, engaging with physics concepts such as force, acceleration, and energy transfer in a real-world context. The findings demonstrate that sports-based experiments not only increase student engagement but also enhance their conceptual understanding of physics. Incorporating such activities into the physics curriculum can help build STEM identity, particularly among students who have shown limited interest in science. Recommendations for classroom implementation and student reflection activities are also provided.
keywords: rowing, STEM education, Phyphox, Python programming, biomechanics, accelerometer data, rowing performance, STEM identity, student engagement, high school physics

title: Modular 3D-printed Circuit Nodes for low-cost and hands-on Electricity Education
text: Abstract We present a modular, low-cost system for teaching electric circuits using 3D-printed components called Circuit Nodes . Each node aligns physically with standard schematic representations and connects magnetically, supporting intuitive circuit construction and reducing abstraction barriers for students. We describe the educational design rationale, technical realization, and cost structure of the system, as well as its current component library. A survey of eight secondary school physics teachers was conducted to evaluate the usability and classroom applicability of the materials. The results indicate high acceptance and perceived benefits in terms of schematic clarity, hands-on engagement, and customization. Concerns regarding production effort and access to 3D printing were attributed primarily to contextual factors, e.g. school infrastructure and teacher experience. The study suggests that 3D-printed, open-source teaching tools such as Circuit Nodes offer substantial potential for scalable and practice-oriented physics education.
keywords: electrical circuits, electricity education, hands-on learning, schematic diagrams, low-cost teaching materials, high school physics

title: Most slippery point of a simply supported bridge
text: Abstract When a pedestrian walks across a simply supported bridge, the bridge deflects under their weight. As the bridge surface becomes sloped at certain points, the pedestrian must be careful not to slip. In this study, we determine the position where the slope of the bridge is greatest—the ‘most slippery point’. This work is expected to aid in the understanding of physics at the university level, particularly with regard to its applications in the mechanics of materials.
keywords: simply supported bridges, bridge deflection, strength of materials, statics, college physics

title: Revisiting the simple model of the late Professor Frank S Crawford for water wave dispersion relations, and thus obtaining a physical explanation of the depth-dependence of shallow water wave speeds
text: Abstract This paper aims to provide an alternative physical explanation for why water waves propagate more slowly in relatively shallow areas compared to relatively deeper regions within shallow water. Our analysis is based on Prof. Frank S Crawford’s model (Crawford 1987 Am. J. Phys . 55 171–2), which demonstrates that the centre of mass of a standing water wave behaves like a simple pendulum. Essentially, the effective length of the pendulum is inversely proportional to the water depth, which forms the foundation of our explanation. Additionally, we elaborate a simple geometric approach to addressing this question.
keywords: shallow water waves, wave velocity, depth dependence, center of mass, effective length, geometric approach

title: An Arduino-enabled barometric validation of the hydrostatic equation using BMP280 sensor in an undergraduate lab
text: Abstract The study aims to validate the hydrostatic equation using a low-cost, Arduino-based pressure measurement system. An Arduino microcontroller was integrated with a BMP280 sensor and LCD display to collect atmospheric pressure and altitude data across different floor levels of a multi-story building. The system included a push-button interface for automated pressure logging at regular intervals. Theoretical pressure values were calculated using the barometric formula, assuming an isothermal atmosphere, and were compared with the measured data. The results showed strong agreement with theoretical results. Minor deviations were observed due to sensor limitations, temperature gradients, and environmental influences. Overall, the experiment demonstrates that such a microcontroller-based system is effective for verifying the hydrostatic principle and holds significant potential for educational use and small-scale environmental monitoring.
keywords: hydrostatic equation, barometric formula, atmospheric pressure, altitude, Arduino, low-cost instrumentation, undergraduate laboratory experiment, isothermal atmosphere, environmental monitoring

title: Experimental verification of the absence of the transverse Doppler effect in sound using a simple rotating system
text: Abstract The absence of a transverse Doppler effect for sound in classical mechanics is well established, yet it is often misunderstood by students who may incorrectly expect a frequency shift whenever relative motion is involved. In this work, we demonstrate experimentally that no such shift occurs when the source moves transversely with respect to the observer. Using a simple rotating system, we provide a direct and reproducible verification of this principle. The setup can be easily implemented in a college laboratory, helping students confront and correct a common misconception while reinforcing the distinction between longitudinal and transverse motion in wave phenomena.
keywords: transverse Doppler effect, acoustic waves, Doppler shift, rotating systems, misconceptions, wave frequency shift, classical mechanics

title: From geocentrism to heliocentrism: an inquiry-based lesson on the nature of science for middle school students
text: Abstract Understanding the nature of science (NOS) is a core component of scientific literacy. This study details the design and implementation of a history-of-science lesson for sixth-grade students that transforms the abstract topic of the shift from geocentrism to heliocentrism into a hands-on inquiry activity. The lesson integrates an explicit-reflective questioning approach with a simple yet effective simulation of the phases of Venus, structured within the PEHDSR pedagogical framework. Analysis of qualitative data, including classroom video recordings and student responses, indicated that the lesson design effectively stimulated students’ interest and enabled them to construct and articulate their understanding of core NOS concepts, such as the tentative, evidence-based, and socio-cultural nature of scientific knowledge. Students also effectively engaged in science and engineering practices, particularly using models and analysing data. This study provides a concrete, replicable blueprint for physics educators worldwide to design inquiry lessons based on the history of science, allowing students to experience scientific discovery firsthand.
keywords: nature of science, geocentrism, heliocentrism, history of science, inquiry-based learning, scientific literacy, junior high school science, science and engineering practices, evidence-based reasoning

title: Reframing spacetime: the emphasis on proper time
text: Abstract The concept of spacetime often conflates mathematical form with physical meaning, obscuring the central role of proper time. This article argues that such ambiguity contributes to persistent difficulties in teaching relativity. Without grounding in proper time, students frequently misinterpret time itself and struggle with the relativity of simultaneity. To address this, the article reframes spacetime by placing proper time at the center—as the primary expression of physical change. Guided by the principle of light, the article reformulates the Minkowski metric equation in temporal units, which exposes its meaning as reflecting the intuitive observation that one experiences distant objects not as they are now, but as they were when their light departed. The article also interprets the metric equation by a metric triangle, a geometric construct that interprets coordinate time as the orthogonal sum of proper time (internal rhythm) and time latency (from spatial separation). This framework clarifies key conceptual distinctions—between proper and coordinate time, simultaneity, and the metric itself—offering a more coherent and physically grounded understanding of spacetime.
keywords: spacetime, proper time, relativity of simultaneity, Minkowski metric, coordinate time, special relativity, conceptual understanding

title: Cost effective experiment to determine the relation between refractive index and wavelength
text: Abstract Students are introduced to the term ‘refractive index’ at the School level. It is an integral and very significant property of any particular material. In this paper, we present a simple and innovative method to determine the relation between refractive index and wavelength. We verify that for any liquid, the refractive index is inversely related to the wavelength of light. The novel approach here is to introduce different colours of LEDs and observe the degree of refraction of light as the wavelength is varied. This method can be incorporated as a school laboratory activity, as yet another way to help the students clearly understand the concept of refractive index. This experimental setup was developed at the Science Laboratory, Nehru Planetarium (Mumbai). This experiment can be used to explain the phenomenon of dispersion of light as a substitute for a prism, using different colour LEDs, and the different degrees of bending of respective light rays can be demonstrated.
keywords: refractive index, wavelength dependence, optical dispersion, refraction, school laboratory experiments, liquid refractive index

title: Golden ratio and stability of 2D laminas: DIY for centre of mass
text: Abstract This study presents do-it-yourself experiment to demonstrate a correlation between the centre of mass (COM) and the golden Ratio ( ϕ ≈ 1.618 ) in various standard 2D laminas. A systematic process of subtracting part of the lamina is shown to shift the COM to a critical point on the lamina’s edge. It is found that this point divides the object’s principal dimensions in a ratio that consistently approximates ϕ . This phenomenon was observed in rectangles, squares, circles, and pentagons, suggesting a correlation that may be independent of the initial shape’s specific geometry. This investigation enables students to improve their understanding of classical mechanics, stability and grows a deep underlying geometric relation prompting mechanical equilibrium.
keywords: golden ratio, center of mass, stability, mechanical equilibrium, critical points, geometric ratios, rectangles, squares, circle, Pentagon

title: Visualizing thermal equilibrium through a simple kinetic simulation
text: Abstract We present a simple simulation code that models, within a purely mechanical framework, the thermalization process between two ideal gases represented as kinetic billiards. The gases occupy adjacent compartments separated by a mechanically impermeable but ‘diathermic’ wall which mediates virtual exchanges of kinetic energy between particles approaching from opposite sides. The simulation shows the approach to a stationary equilibrium in which both gases attain the same average kinetic energy, thereby providing a microscopic visualization of the concept of thermal equilibrium and of the physical meaning of temperature. The model is fully mechanical, free from thermodynamic assumptions, and runs directly in the GlowScript VPython environment, making it suitable for classroom demonstrations and interactive learning activities at various educational levels.
keywords: thermal equilibrium, ideal gas, kinetic energy exchange, mechanical simulation, microscopic visualization, classroom demonstration, VPython

title: Measuring atmospheric pressure using a burette
text: Abstract We present a simple and cost-effective technique for measuring atmospheric pressure. This method is suitable not only for undergraduate level but also for school. The experimental result is nearly 3% less than the standard value of the atmospheric pressure which indicates the reliability and effectiveness of our technique compared to conventional methods that require expensive instruments.
keywords: atmospheric pressure measurement, burette, low-cost experiments, undergraduate physics experiment, school physics experiments

title: The inaccuracies of SUVAT
text: Abstract This report intends to investigate the inaccuracies of the SUVAT equations for motion/kinematics by exploring the unconsidered factors or assumptions used in the SUVAT derivation. This will include an exploration on air resistance and gravitation attraction. This exploration will determine the appropriate conditions for SUVAT to be used, as well as the tipping points for alternatively proposed equations to be used instead for the most accurate model of motion.
keywords: kinematics, aerodynamic drag, gravitational attraction, motion model, projectile motion

title: Friction on a block sliding down an incline—is it constant with speed?
text: Abstract Many articles have been published in this journal quoting measurements of the coefficient of sliding friction for a block sliding down an incline. Results are usually presented for the average coefficient, but that hides the fact that the coefficient might depend on the sliding speed.
keywords: sliding friction, friction coefficient, velocity-dependent friction, inclined plane, friction measurement

title: A literature review on the definition of the phenomenon of refraction of light
text: Abstract Refraction of light is one of the important topics in physics education. Depending on how the refraction is defined, textbooks offer different opinions on whether light waves travel perpendicular to the interface between two media and undergo refraction when passing from one medium to another. We examined twenty-eight fundamental physics textbooks to reveal the differences of opinion in the literature regarding the definition of refraction of light in a single source. It was observed that the majority of textbooks (57.1%) defined refraction of light waves as “the change in direction at the interface.” Additionally, the refraction was randomly defined as “the change in average speed”, “the bending”, or “the transmission” of light when passing from one medium to another. Therefore, some textbooks thought that light waves were not refracted when their direction of travel was perpendicular to the surface, despite changes in the medium. However, 42.9% of textbooks defined the refraction of light waves as “the change in the average speed and wavelength when passing from one medium to another”, and they thought that light was refracted even when it was perpendicular to the surface, regardless of the angle of incidence.
keywords: light refraction, physics textbook, textbook analysis, angle of incidence, light waves
