title: From prompt to physics: evaluating Doppler effect simulation generated by ChatGPT
text: Abstract This study aims to develop and evaluate a Doppler effect simulation generated by ChatGPT. The development process was carried out through iterative prompt engineering, focusing on user interface, user experience, sound wave visualisation, and the accuracy of physics concept representation. The simulation was assessed through self-evaluation and expert evaluation, using a Likert scale and qualitative analysis. The results showed that the simulation accurately represents the underlying physics concepts, achieving maximum scores in both conceptual and visualisation aspects. Nevertheless, some limitations were identified regarding interface flexibility. This study highlights ChatGPT’s considerable potential as a tool for developing physics simulations, although ongoing evaluation is necessary for educational appropriateness.
keywords: Doppler shift, ChatGPT, large language models, physics simulation, prompt engineering, user experience, expert evaluation

title: A learning module on the Sun and the space weather
text: Abstract The term ‘space weather’ indicates the physical conditions at the Sun and in the space environment between the Sun and Earth, that can influence the operation of spaceborne and ground systems and affect human activities and health. Scientific research on the space weather is therefore important to forecast the potential impact of perturbations driven by the Sun activity on biological and technological systems. This work discusses a learning module aiming at introducing high school pupils to the characteristics of the Sun, the relationships with the Earth and the impact that phenomena of solar origin have on our planet. The module consists of experimental observations and of class lectures, both aiming at coupling the curricular teaching at school with actual research topics.
keywords: space weather, sun, solar activity, solar-terrestrial relations, high school physics teaching, learning modules, experimental observation, science education

title: From public databases to the classroom: investigating neutron stars with spreadsheets
text: Abstract Neutron stars, most prominently observed as radio pulsars, are among the most intriguing astrophysical objects because of their periodic emission of electromagnetic radiation. Traditionally, studying pulsar profiles requires access to large radio telescopes and specialized data-processing tools, making such research inaccessible in most educational settings. This work demonstrates that publicly available pulsar data from the EPN Database of Pulsar Profiles can be effectively imported, processed, and visualized using spreadsheet software, a widely accessible tool for data analysis. By applying straightforward data-handling techniques, students can reproduce pulsar profiles such as those of the Vela and Crab pulsars, and explore fundamental concepts including polarization, multiple pulse components, and the geometry of pulsar emission. This approach highlights a cost-effective and pedagogically valuable method for integrating pulsar research into the classroom while simultaneously building computational literacy and data-analysis skills.
keywords: neutron stars, radio pulsars, pulsar profiles, spreadsheet software, Vela pulsar, Crab pulsar, polarization, pulsar emission geometry, computational literacy, data analysis skills, astronomy education

title: Revitalising legacy superheterodyne radios as a teaching resource for amplitude modulation and digital signal analysis
text: Abstract This paper introduces a low-cost teaching resource that integrates legacy analogue hardware with modern digital tools to support the learning of amplitude modulation (AM) and Fourier analysis in undergraduate physics education. A simple AM transmitter is paired with a legacy superheterodyne receiver and Arduino-based data acquisition, allowing students to probe both RF and audio stages of the receiver. By recording signals, applying fast Fourier transform analysis, and exploring aliasing effects, students connect theoretical principles with observable waveforms. The activity is framed around explicit learning objectives and supported by scaffolding strategies, making it a practical and adaptable resource for instructors seeking to bridge classical radio communication with contemporary digital signal analysis.
keywords: superheterodyne receiver, amplitude modulation, Arduino data acquisition, fast Fourier transform, aliasing, radio communication, digital signal analysis, undergraduate physics education, scaffolding

title: Virtual experiments in educational practice to study light interference with small particles
text: Abstract This paper presents the educational application of a Python-based model simulating the interference of light on spherical micron-sized particles deposited on a plane-parallel glass plate. The model integrates the geometric conditions of interference with the angular intensity distribution derived from Mie theory. This approach enables the investigation of the effects of wavelength, source spectral width, refractive indices, particle size, polydispersity, and glass plate thickness on the interference pattern. Virtual experiments have been developed in which students modify model parameters, analyse the results, and solve the inverse problem of determining the modal particle radius. The proposed methodology fosters the development of computational thinking, analytical skills, and a deeper understanding of optical interference phenomena. The model is distributed as open-source software under the MIT licence and is available in a public repository, thereby facilitating its integration into the teaching process by educators and its adaptation to the appropriate level of education.
keywords: optical interference, Mie scattering, spherical particles, virtual experiments, Python simulation, angular intensity distribution, polydispersity, inverse problems, particle size measurement, computational thinking, refractive index, wavelength dependence, open-source educational software

title: Unicorn in the classroom—a student-led experiment on the speed of sound using Arduino
text: Abstract We aimed to familiarise students with the fundamentals of digital measurements early in their physics studies, as this can help maintain their interest and develop their digital competencies. Therefore, in the seventh grade, we used uniform motion—a well-known and easily understandable concept—to introduce this new measurement technique, combining digital tools with classical methods. We employed a simple, Arduino-controlled HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (easily assembled even at home) to determine the speed of sound in air and, if needed, in other media (e.g. carbon dioxide). A key advantage of this experiment is that the results can be directly compared to official reference values, providing students with immediate positive feedback on their work. The novelty of our developed tool lies in its cross-grade applicability and reusability, enabling the discussion of core physics concepts like systematic and statistical errors. As part of the project, we piloted the equipment and task sequence, collecting student feedback via questionnaires. Attitude survey results indicate that students found the experiment highly engaging, suggesting its potential to enhance classroom motivation and foster a positive attitude toward the subject.
keywords: sound velocity, Arduino, HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, digital measurement, uniform motion, carbon dioxide, student motivation, digital skills

title: Integrating space weather into secondary physics: insights from the Mother’s Day solar storm of 2024
text: Abstract The geomagnetic storm of 10–11 May 2024, popularly known as the Mother’s Day storm, was one of the most intense space-weather events of the current solar cycle, reaching G5 (Extreme) levels on the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration scale with a Dst (disturbance storm-time) index minimum of −412 nT. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the storm’s global and regional responses in vertical total electron content, highlighting hemispheric asymmetries and variations in recovery time. Using freely available data sources and public-domain platforms, we demonstrate how this event provides an authentic, real-world context for exploring electromagnetic concepts such as plasma, field–particle interactions, and space-weather effects on communication systems. The pedagogical framework emphasises inquiry-based and data-driven learning approaches that allow students to connect textbook physics with natural phenomena.
keywords: geomagnetic storms, space weather, high school physics teaching, vertical total electron content, hemispheric asymmetry (solar and geophysical), plasma, inquiry-based learning, data-driven learning, Dst index

title: Determining the minimum force to insert or remove a cork from a sealed cylinder
text: Abstract In the case of a difference in internal and external pressure, the cork closing the air filled cylinder remains at rest due to the force of friction. An interesting question is how much can be compressed air in a cylinder using a long tight-fitting cork and what force is needed to remove the cork.
keywords: cork, atmospheric pressure, friction, air compression, pressure difference

title: A portable kit for refractive-index studies: refraction and critical angle in solids and liquids
text: Abstract This paper presents a portable and simple refractive index kit that lets students study refraction, refractive index, and the critical angle in both solids and liquids. In schools, refraction is typically taught using a ray box that produce bright and dim rays, making refraction hard to observe. In addition, the activity also requires drawing lines on paper to trace the rays, which is time consuming and slows the process of teaching and learning. To overcome this problem, the portable refractive index kit uses a monochromatic 532 nm laser beam with a rotating mount and a fixed protractor as the sample stage, making the rays easy to observe without paper tracing and speeding up the lesson. In addition, the kit also offers added value by including a liquid container that enables refractive-index studies of liquids using the same geometry as solids without changing the setup. These additions save time, improve repeatability, and enable clear measurements for both solids and liquids within a single lesson. Refractive index is estimated using Snell’s law from a straight-line Snell plot, and the critical angle for total internal reflection is used as a built-in check. Results for typical classroom samples are n = 1.56 for glass, n = 1.33 for water, and n = 1.45 for cooking oil, with critical angles of 40.17°, 48.75°, and 43.60° respectively. The uncertainties of n , obtained from standard error analysis, range between ± 0.01 and ± 0.02 depending on the measurement method. This project contributed to physics education by providing a low cost, accurate and easy to obtain experimental kit for schools. This innovation adds value to teaching and learning by improving visibility, reducing setup time, and enabling fair comparison between solids and liquids within a single lesson.
keywords: refractive index, refraction, critical angle, total internal reflection, Snell's law, low-cost educational tools, ray tracing, 532 nm laser, glass, water, cooking oil, measurement uncertainty

title: Identifying and comparing misconceptions about atoms and molecules among students and student teachers
text: Abstract Mastering fundamental concepts of atoms and molecules is pivotal for deep learning in physics and chemistry, forming the foundation for topics such as states of matter, chemical reactions, interatomic bonds, gas properties, and quantum mechanics principles in secondary and higher education. Misconceptions about the properties of atoms and molecules can hinder conceptual understanding. This study aimed to investigate misconceptions among students and student teachers regarding the characteristics of atoms and molecules. This explanatory mixed-methods study involved a purposive sample of 27 ninth-grade male students from Shahid Abrar School in Qayn, Iran, and 15 master’s-level student teachers from Farhangian University in Iran during the 2024–2025 academic year. Data were collected using a researcher-developed 57-item questionnaire, validated by experts and with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.85. Results revealed misconceptions in both groups, but their type and intensity differed. A total of 47 misconceptions were identified across 10 conceptual categories. Students exhibited higher misconception rates (85.6%) than student teachers (14.4%), particularly in molecular energy and structure. Chi-square tests showed significant differences in two categories ( p < 0.05). The main misconception categories included molecular structure, composition, size, shape, weight, bonding, energy, atomic structure/shape, size, and animism. This study highlights educational barriers to understanding atomic and molecular concepts, emphasizing the need for curriculum reform and enhanced teacher training. Addressing misconceptions can enhance conceptual science learning.
keywords: misconceptions, atoms, molecules, pre-service teachers, ninth grade students, molecular structure, molecular energy, atomic structure, animism, conceptual understanding, chemistry education, teacher professional development

title: Fish physics
text: Abstract In this paper a series of hands-on demonstrations is described to teach students about hydrostatic pressure and buoyancy using fish. Fish are neutrally buoyant and therefore do not need to expend energy to swim up or down, apart from overcoming friction between their scales and fins, and water. In a first demonstration, the increase in hydrostatic pressure with depth is felt when a hollow plastic cylinder less dense than water is pushed into a tall container of water. In a second demonstration, robot fish of different density are placed at the top of a 1 m tall transparent plastic tube and observed to swim down. A neutrally buoyant robot fish swims steadily to the bottom and is suspended in the water column when not swimming. A negatively buoyant fish sinks continuously to the bottom, and a positively buoyant fish fails to reach the bottom. Archimedes principle can be used to accurately measure and adjust the density of a robot fish as necessary. In a third experiment, a sinker is lowered into an aquarium demonstrating that the weight of an object is independent of depth. Buoyancy brings together physics and marine biology and therefore is a good STEM topic.
keywords: hydrostatic pressure, buoyancy, neutral buoyancy, Archimedes' principle, robotic fish, density, hands-on demonstration, marine biology, STEM education

title: From textbook images to functional models: a model-based teaching intervention on electric current to foster scientific literacy and 21st-century learning skills
text: Abstract This paper presents a model-based teaching intervention designed to introduce the concept of electric current while engaging participants in modelling activities that foster scientific literacy and 21st-century learning skills. Although textbooks often include images representing microscopic phenomena, these are rarely utilised as tools for active exploration, explanation, and prediction. The intervention utilises such textbook images, transforming them into functional models that support both exploratory and expressive modelling. Collaborative work and reflective tasks are integrated to promote communication, critical thinking, and creativity. The intervention is structured around the 5E instructional model, integrating three key dimensions: teaching the cognitive content (electric current), familiarisation with scientific practices (understanding the nature and function of models), and development of 21st-century learning skills. Activities include analysing electron movement within conductors, constructing and comparing models to explain observable phenomena, and predicting the effects of manipulating circuit components. Through the transformation of static images into functional models, students gain metamodelling knowledge, recognising that representations must incorporate theoretical ideas to explain or predict phenomena. A preliminary validation phase, conducted through semi-structured interviews with ten in-service physics teachers, provided feedback on the clarity, feasibility and pedagogical coherence of the intervention and identified specific phases that support students’ use, construction and revision of models. Their feedback also highlighted practical considerations for classroom implementation, informing directions for future refinement. The next step involves classroom implementation to investigate the intervention’s impact on learning outcomes and on students’ perceptions of modelling as a scientific practice.
keywords: electric current, model-based learning, textbook illustrations, functional model, scientific literacy, 21st century skills, 5E instructional model, metamodeling, nature of models

title: Teaching physics and sustainable development: an action research project on the transformation of photovoltaic energy into electricity at a secondary school in Namibe (Angola)
text: Abstract Alternative energies and sustainable development are articulated, for example, in the 2030 Agenda. This articulation should also be made in the educational field, particularly in Physics classes. However, this articulation is still absent, specifically in the official programs for this subject in Angola. This article presents and discusses a study conducted at School Complex No. 101 M—“Álvaro Manuel Boa Vida Neto“ in Namibe (Angola) with 44 students from the 10th Grade (II cycle of Secondary Education in the Physical-Biological Sciences Course). Methodologically, an action, descriptive and interpretative investigation approach was used, as the school teacher, who also took on the role of researcher, is the primary author of this article. Mixed data (qualitative and quantitative) was collected through documentary analysis, researcher field notes and a questionnaire provided to the students at the beginning and end of implementing an innovative, designed-based teaching sequence. The data was treated by content analysis and descriptive statistics. The action research, which, due to time constraints, only includes one cycle, consisted of the planning, implementation and validation of a teaching sequence focused on the inclusion of photovoltaic energy, already being used in the school region where the study was developed. Notice that photovoltaic energy can be used as an alternative method for producing electrical energy as a guarantee in the sustainability of communities. The implementation of the proposed teaching sequence enabled interactions between the purpose of knowledge, the skills and the reality of the students, thereby contributing to individual and collective thinking in search of new ways to approach everyday problems, in addition to improving the quality of teaching. It is suggested that further research should be done on this topic, namely through studies that analyze actions that promote the professional development of Physics teachers from a sustainable development perspective. This study should focus on emphasizing the proposal developed, introducing new action research cycles that enable a focus on the understanding of the educational reality and the construction of knowledge.
keywords: photovoltaic energy, sustainable development, physics education, alternative energy, didactic sequence, high school physics, 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, teacher research

title: Measuring the Faraday effect: an instructive experiment
text: Abstract As discovered by Michael Faraday in 1845, the Faraday effect is a magneto-optical phenomenon in which the plane of polarization of a linearly polarized beam of light is rotated whenever the beam of light passes through a transparent material placed in a magnetic field. In this paper, we present a science project that uses a laser, solenoid, polarizing film, acrylic water cell, and photoresistor to measure the rotation angle of light in water under a magnetic field. Details of the optical layout, solenoid construction, calibration, and measurement procedure are given along with a comparison with published data. This project presents an accessible introduction to magneto-optics and the methods used in optical studies by demonstrating a feasible, low-cost, and instructive experiment for students, science hobbyists and educators interested in magneto-optics.
keywords: Faraday rotation, magneto-optics, optical rotation, plane of polarization, solenoid, magnetic field, polarizing film, light dependent resistor, low-cost experiments, science education

title: PER me si va ne la fisica recente —an educational particle escape room (PER) towards the discovery of the Standard Model of particles
text: Abstract We designed and implemented an educational escape room on particle physics, titled ‘ PER me si va ne la fisica recente ’, to introduce secondary school students to concepts rarely addressed in formal curricula. The activity combines content-driven puzzles, narrative engagement, and structured debriefing, and is now a permanent installation at the University of Pavia. The study involved around 300 participants, with matched pre-/post-test data available for 232 students. The assessment focused on both curricular and extra-curricular items, as well as on the persistence of common misconceptions. Results show significant conceptual gains, particularly on extra-curricular questions related to the standard model, while misconceptions such as the confusion between antimatter and dark matter proved more resistant. The normalized gain analysis confirms that even short interventions can produce measurable improvements in understanding. This work demonstrates that a low-cost, replicable escape room can effectively engage students with frontier physics and complement classroom teaching. It also highlights the importance of targeted debriefing for addressing persistent misconceptions, contributing to the growing body of evidence on the role of game-based and non-formal strategies in STEM education.
keywords: escape rooms, particle physics education, high school students, misconceptions, debriefing, game-based learning, non-formal education, STEM outreach, conceptual change

title: Viability of a low-cost solution for linear air track: a comparative study
text: Abstract Linear air tracks are essential experimental tools used in undergraduate laboratory courses. They facilitate the exploration of kinematic and dynamic topics in a frictionless environment. While commercial air track systems require significant investment, affordable alternatives are valuable for making such apparatuses accessible to high schools and universities. We test and compare a low-cost air track made from medium density fibreboard (MDF) wood as a possible alternative. In this manuscript, we performed new experiments on the uniformly accelerated motion of a glider in an inclined plane to compare the friction of the MDF air track with that of a commercial one. We tested the built and commercial gliders and air tracks for angles of 1, 2, and 5 degrees. Our findings revealed that the friction was about 10 − 4 for all setups analysed. We also observed the influence of air drag on the glider’s movement and attempted to quantify it using the quadratic velocity air drag model. Overall, the results indicate only a slight difference between the MDF air track and the commercial version, suggesting that the MDF air track is a viable and cost-effective alternative to commercial systems.
keywords: low-cost laboratory equipment, medium-density fiberboard, gliders, inclined plane, uniformly accelerated motion, friction, aerodynamic drag, kinematics, dynamics, physics laboratory equipment

title: A simple experimental setup for measuring microparticle diameters with a smartphone and an LED
text: Abstract We present a simple and low-cost experimental setup for quantitatively measuring the size of microparticles in powders. The method requires only inexpensive, readily available materials and can be easily reproduced at home, making it particularly suitable for distance learning applications. The theoretical framework relies on Babinet’s principle, which states that, to very good approximation, a particle generates a diffraction pattern equivalent to that of a circular aperture. In practice, the powder sample is placed on a glass slide and positioned directly over the camera of a smartphone. A small piece of a diffraction grating is attached over the slide, and the resulting diffraction images are captured with the smartphone camera. The images are then quantitatively analysed using the open-source software Tracker. As light sources, light emitting diodes of different colours are employed. This accessible setup provides a robust and reproducible approach to introducing students to diffraction phenomena and particle size measurement.
keywords: powder particle size, Babinet's principle, diffraction gratings, smartphone camera, LED light source, Tracker software, diffraction patterns, low-cost laboratory equipment, distance education

title: Measurements of the moments of inertia of a pickleball paddle
text: Abstract A method is described to measure the three moments of inertia of a pickleball paddle when swinging the paddle as a physical pendulum. The results are relevant to the performance of the paddle as a striking implement.
keywords: moment of inertia, physical pendulum

title: Demonstration of strain-based heating and cooling effects in balloon using smartphone-based thermal imaging camera
text: Abstract This manuscript presents a hands-on experiment designed to help students understand the relationship between mechanical deformation and thermal changes in materials. Using a simple balloon, students observe the effect of stretching and relaxing when it leads to variations in surface temperature, which can be explained through fundamental concepts such as energy transfer and entropy changes. The balloon is incrementally stretched up to 45 cm, during which its surface temperature increases from room temperature (25 °C) to a maximum of 38 °C. Upon relaxing, the temperature drops to as low as 15 °C. These results demonstrate that mechanical strain can induce significant thermal effects, highlighting the practical application of thermodynamics, this effect is also known as Elastocaloric effect. By analyzing the experimental data, students can develop a deeper understanding that mechanical forces can influence thermal behavior. The experiment provides an accessible introduction to energy transformations and the physics of materials, fostering engagement through direct observation and real-world connections.
keywords: elastocaloric effect, mechanical strain, surface temperature change, entropy, energy transfer, thermodynamics, smartphone thermal imaging, hands-on experiments, materials physics

title: Engaging students in electrodynamics: an integrated approach to teaching divergence of electrostatic field
text: Abstract This article explores the teaching of electrodynamics, a challenging yet foundational subject in theoretical physics. It highlights the early hurdle students face in learning vector analysis, a key mathematical tool used to describe electromagnetic fields and their interactions with matter. The manuscript commences with the introduction of two teaching approaches: the classical method, which emphasizes conceptual understanding through examples like the relationship between electric field flux and charge distribution, and the mathematical method, which applies Coulomb’s law and vector calculus directly to compute the divergence of the electrostatic field. While the classical approach fosters physical intuition, the mathematical approach enhances efficiency. The integration of both methods creates a robust and comprehensive educational experience, effectively balancing conceptual depth and analytical precision to accommodate diverse learning levels. Ultimately, this integrated methodology aims to inspire students to master electrodynamics by reinforcing the connection between mathematical tools and physical phenomena.
keywords: vector calculus, charge distribution, Coulomb's law, conceptual understanding, integrated teaching, student engagement

title: Cartoon-based instruction improves concept mastery and problem-solving in secondary physics
text: Abstract This study investigated the efficacy of cartoon-integrated instruction for enhancing concept mastery and problem-solving in secondary physics. A quasi-experimental design employed pre-test equivalence to assign 41 students to experimental ( n = 20) and control ( n = 21) groups. The experimental group learned about sound waves using curated cartoons and animations, while the control group received conventional instruction. Post-test results revealed the experimental group achieved a significantly higher mean score (18.06 vs 13.33) and lower dispersion (SD = 3.88 vs 6.86). A Welch independent-samples t -test confirmed a statistically significant difference, t ( 25.5 ) = 2.388 , p = 0.0247 , with a large practical effect (Cohen’s d = 0.85). These findings provide empirical support for cartoon-integrated instruction as a method to foster effective and more uniform concept understanding among diverse learners.
keywords: animated cartoons, acoustic waves, concept mastery, problem solving, high school students, multimedia teaching, conceptual understanding

title: Collision of a ball with a beam clamped at each end
text: Abstract A collision of one ball with another is a standard problem in elementary mechanics. A collision of a ball with a bat or a racquet is more complicated but can be modelled as a collision between a ball and a uniform beam. Experimental results are presented for an impact of a baseball with aluminium beams of varying length and thickness, showing that the rebound speed of the ball can be increased or decreased as a result of beam vibrations. An increase in the outgoing ball speed is known as the trampoline effect.
keywords: trampoline effect, beam vibration, baseball, aluminum beam, impact

title: It all began with h —a century of quantum mechanics: from Planck to today’s quantum technologies
text: Abstract Quantum mechanics has revolutionised our understanding of reality. At the heart of this theory lies Planck’s constant h , which plays a fundamental role in describing the behaviour of matter on the smallest scales. In this paper we present a teaching approach that combines a concise historical overview of the origin of h with a simple experiment in which students determine its value from measurements on a photovoltaic panel. The article integrates methodologies from Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics and problem-based learning to demonstrate how contemporary educational techniques can not only aid in understanding quantum concepts, but also enable the experimental determination of one of the most fundamental constants of nature. Using low-cost components available in school and introductory university laboratories, students measure the threshold voltage of a photovoltaic cell for different wavelengths of light and, by analysing the linear dependence of the electron energy e U on c / λ to obtain an experimental estimate of h . In contrast to other works where light-emitting diodes have been used to determine Planck’s constant (Chakarvarti and Sharma 1988 Phys. Educ. 23 416; Ward 2013 Phys. Educ. 48 20–1; Morton and Abraham 1986 Phys. Educ. 21 414; Korpal et al 2023 Phys. Educ. 58 045003), this article presents a method of experimentally determining h , by measuring the threshold voltage of a photovoltaic panel as a function of the frequency of incident light. The proposed experiment can be easily conducted in a school setting, for example as a group project under the guidance of a teacher. It illustrates that core quantum concepts can be explored experimentally even at the introductory level. Furthermore, this experiment can complement university-level lectures or laboratory courses.
keywords: Planck constant, history of quantum mechanics, solar cells, threshold voltage, photoelectric effect, quantum mechanics education, problem-based learning, STEAM education, introductory physics laboratory

title: Teaching measurement uncertainty in physics: aligning classroom practice with the modern GUM framework
text: Abstract Uncertainty is a central feature of experimental physics: without it, measurements cannot be compared, validated, or meaningfully interpreted. Nevertheless, in many teaching environments it is introduced only briefly, often through significant figures or approximate ‘error bars.’ This narrow treatment encourages the misconception that uncertainty measures mistakes rather than confidence in a result. This article presents a teaching framework inspired by the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM), providing a clearer and more coherent way to discuss uncertainty in school and university laboratories. The approach highlights the complementary roles of statistical methods (Type A) and non-statistical information (Type B), promotes explicit reporting of uncertainty, and uses accessible mathematics consistent with GUM notation. Several classroom-ready examples illustrate uncertainty propagation, coverage factors, and how uncertainty shapes the interpretation of a measurement. A learning progression and suggestions for assessment are also proposed. Framing uncertainty as a quantitative expression of knowledge—rather than a correction for error—supports better scientific reasoning and encourages students to approach data with greater rigor and confidence.
keywords: measurement uncertainty, Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement, error propagation, coverage factor, uncertainty reporting, laboratory teaching, significant figures, error bars, learning progression, assessment

title: Motion of a simple cardboard boomerang
text: Abstract The flight of a boomerang is conventionally regarded as a complex problem in aerodynamics. However, the problem can be greatly simplified for high school students by treating it as an example of circular motion.
keywords: boomerang, circular motion, flight dynamics, aerodynamics, high school physics teaching

title: Work done on a pendulum bob
text: Abstract If a pendulum is pulled to one side and released from rest, it arrives at the bottom in a horizontal direction. The gravitational force acts only in the vertical direction. The tension force in the string therefore does work to increase the horizontal speed, despite the fact that the string tension acts in a direction perpendicular to the motion of the pendulum bob.
keywords: pendulum, string tension, gravitational force, horizontal speed, energy conservation (physics)

title: Corner cube reflectors
text: Abstract Corner cube reflectors (CCRs) display the interesting behaviour that a reflected beam of light is always parallel to the incident beam. A beam of light incident at any point, at any angle, on a CCR will exit along a path parallel to the incident beam. Three methods of demonstrating the operation of a CCR are described. In one demonstration, a bicycle CCR is fixed to a classroom wall. When students shine their phone lights at the reflector they can see the reflection wherever they are sitting. In a second demonstration, a mirror and a bicycle CCR are immersed in tonic water and a violet laser (wavelength 405 nm) shone alternately onto the mirror and CCR. The laser induces fluorescence in the tonic water. When the laser is directed onto the mirror, the incident and reflected beams are seen. However, when the laser is directed onto the bicycle CCR, only a single beam is seen due to retroreflection. In a third demonstration, a large-scale CCR constructed from plastic mirror squares is immersed in tonic water. In this case, the path of the multiply-reflected beam is visible in the tonic water.
keywords: corner cube retroreflector, retroreflection, light reflection, parallel beam, multiple reflections

title: The electric dipole: pedagogical and research implications of diverging definitions in physics and chemistry
text: Abstract This note examines the conceptual and notational divergence in the definition of the electric dipole moment between physics and chemistry. While the magnitude is consistent across disciplines, a crucial difference in sign convention can lead to confusion for students and miscommunication in interdisciplinary research. Through a pedagogical lens, we explore the historical, theoretical, and educational underpinnings of this divergence, with proposed strategies for instruction and interdisciplinary clarity.
keywords: electric dipole moment, sign conventions, interdisciplinary terminology

title: A partial solar eclipse observed from Rzeszów, Poland, on 29 march 2025
text: Abstract A team of students from the University of Rzeszów observed the partial solar eclipse of 29 March 2025 under clear skies in southeastern Poland. Using three independent optical systems-a projection setup, a digital camera equipped with a Baader solar filter, and a Coudé 150/2250 refractor with a glass filter-we documented the progression of the eclipse and analyzed the observational results. The project was designed to evaluate how structured, hands-on observing activities can support the development of practical astronomical skills and enhance student engagement with scientific inquiry. In the phase of maximum eclipse, the magnitude was k = 0.097, which means that 9.7% of the Sun’s diameter was obscured. From this, a model was used to estimate the perceived change in solar brightness, yielding a subjective decrease of 0.11 magnitudes. Although this phenomenon was a shallow eclipse, it provides a useful quantitative exercise in relating eclipse geometry to radiant flux and visual magnitude. Overall, the event allowed students to practice safe solar-observing techniques, analyze real astronomical data, and develop skills applicable to future eclipse observations and other time-dependent astronomical phenomena.
keywords: partial solar eclipse, solar observation, eclipse magnitude, eclipse geometry, radiant flux, visual magnitude, solar filters, student engagement

title: Simple skating model
text: Abstract We consider the arguably simplest possible model of skating (whether it be ice or roller skating), predicting that the skater’s initial strides should be weaker than her latter ones and briefly consider the influence of stride length and strength on optimal technique. The model is simple enough that it could be understood by upper-level secondary school students.
keywords: skating, ice skating, roller skating, stride length, skating technique, biomechanics, physics models, high school physics

title: Development of a gamified web-based interactive program on constructing free-body diagrams for secondary school students
text: Abstract Constructing free-body diagrams is crucial for solving force and motion problems, yet many secondary school students struggle due to misconceptions and a lack of understanding of fundamental concepts. Existing educational technologies offer interactive and engaging ways to learn free-body diagrams but have limitations, such as insufficient detail in force action points and incomplete representation of forces. To address such, this paper proposes an innovation in the form of a web-based interactive program, created using the ADDIE model as the framework for development and Scratch as the visual programming language, that aims to provide an effective learning experience for constructing free-body diagrams. It is also integrated with game elements and pop-up feedback to guide students. Currently, the study is in the development stage. Preliminary testing and assessment with a group of experts has shown 22 positive results, with suggestions for further improvements. The next stage will be to assess the efficacy of the improved system with actual students.
keywords: free-body diagrams, gamification, force and motion, physics misconceptions, high school students, Scratch, ADDIE model, game elements, expert evaluation

title: Using oscilloscope triggering to teach the Faraday–Lenz law: an inclined-tube experiment
text: Abstract The study of electromagnetic induction and the Faraday–Lenz Law is a cornerstone of basic electromagnetism courses. Traditional demonstrations using galvanometers or digital interfaces often fail to capture the transient nature of the induced emf, limiting students’ understanding of its temporal structure. In this work, we present an experimental approach based on the trigger function of a digital oscilloscope, which enables the clear visualization of the induced voltage as a magnet passes through a coil. This method allows students to observe the polarity reversal predicted by Lenz’s Law, to compare the entry and exit pulses, and to appreciate qualitatively the influence of magnet velocity on the signal amplitude. Although the technique is well known in laboratories, its explicit pedagogical application in introductory physics courses is rarely reported. Here, we show how this approach bridges the gap between simple qualitative demonstrations and more advanced quantitative measurements, offering students an accessible yet powerful way to explore electromagnetic induction.
keywords: electromagnetic induction, induced voltage, polarity reversal, introductory physics education

title: A simple Doppler effect experiment using smartphone sensor and RC car
text: Abstract This study presented a solution to laboratory facility constraints by developing a low-cost, flexible, and accurate Doppler effect experiment using smartphone sensors (microphones) and the remote-controlled (RC) car. A simplified experimental design was employed, utilizing RC car as the moving sound source to ensure stable and measurable speeds under approaching and receding motion conditions. The results confirmed the method’s accuracy, showing observed frequencies close to theoretical values with a relative error ranging from 0.02%–0.26%. The observed relationship between speeds both observer and source and the resulting frequency shift was linearly consistent with theory. In conclusion, the combination of RC cars and the smartphone sensor provided a simple, stable, and accurate platform for the Doppler effect, making it suitable for replication and easy to implement in schools with limited laboratory resources.
keywords: Doppler shift, smartphone microphone, RC car, low-cost physics experiments, frequency shift, moving sound sources

title: Teaching light absorption and the Beer–Lambert law using everyday materials: a tomato juice experiment for introductory physics
text: Abstract I describe a visually engaging experiment to demonstrate the Beer–Lambert law in introductory physics or general science courses. By using diluted tomato juice as a naturally colored absorber and a halogen lamp as a broadband light source, students can explore how light attenuation depends on concentration and wavelength. The activity connects the optical concept of exponential absorption with everyday materials, making it accessible for classrooms with limited resources. Transmission spectra obtained with a compact spectrometer reveal a strong absorption band around 500 nm, corresponding to the green-blue region absorbed by lycopene. Plotting absorbance against concentration allows students to confirm linear behavior at low concentrations and to discuss deviations at higher ones. The experiment emphasizes conceptual understanding of light–matter interaction, quantitative data analysis, and the limitations of ideal laws, providing a memorable learning experience in optics and spectroscopy.
keywords: Beer-Lambert law, optical absorption, tomato juice, lycopene, transmission spectra, halogen lamps, spectrometer, concentration dependence, wavelength dependence, light-matter interaction, introductory physics, low-cost laboratory experiments

title: Challenges faced by autistic students in mainstream physics education: a literature review
text: Abstract Autistic individuals make up an estimated 1%–2% of the population, making it likely that physics teachers will eventually meet autistic students in their classrooms. Though autistic students often express interest in physics, also as prospects of further education and career, they can run into many difficulties in classrooms where their support needs are not known or met. In order to pave the way for dismantling barriers, this paper presents a literature review concerning what difficulties autistic students can face in mainstream school physics classrooms, and presents the current state of research on the matter. With only four papers found in a systematic literature review, this paper highlights many research gaps for future investigation. Possible difficulties are identified based on sensory, cognitive and communication differences of autistic students, and how these traits may interact with the physics classroom.
keywords: autism spectrum disorder, students with autism, inclusive education, sensory differences, cognitive differences, communication differences, barriers to learning, physics classroom, teacher support needs

title: Bringing light to learning: a low-cost spectroscopy kit and experiments for every classroom
text: Abstract This paper presents a low-cost, portable spectroscopy kit and a set of experiments designed to make optics education more accessible through hands-on, active learning in classrooms. Built using a commercial multispectral sensor (AS7263 or AS7262), an Arduino Uno microcontroller, and 3D-printed housing, the kit is a fraction of the cost of commercial spectrophotometers. While maintaining educational accuracy. The designed experiments teach fundamental concepts such as Beer’s law, chemometrics, additive colour mixing in RGB displays, and gamma correction in LCDs. Experimental results for these concepts are also presented, demonstrating the high accuracy that can be achieved.
keywords: optics education, multispectral sensors, Arduino, 3D-printed housing, Beer-Lambert law, chemometrics, gamma correction, LCD, hands-on experiments, active learning

title: Damped harmonic oscillator revisited: a new approach to energy decay in the case of Coulomb, Stokes, and Newton damping
text: Abstract Approximate formulas are derived to describe energy loss in a harmonic oscillator (HO) that experiences three distinct damping mechanisms: constant-magnitude (Coulomb), velocity-proportional (Stokes), and velocity-squared (Newton), using fundamental mathematical methods and physical insight. Our methodology leverages an understanding of the free HO and the inherent link between energy dissipation rates and the power exerted by damping forces. We establish a direct analytical framework for assessing the energy of a damped HO, obviating the need for amplitude-based equations. The simplicity of our findings is accompanied by their remarkable accuracy when validated against exact or computational simulations. In addition to an excellent approximate description of the energy decay, we also show how to derive an exact solution in the case of Stokes damping without relying on the standard procedure for solving second-order differential equations. The theoretical underpinnings and mathematical strategies employed are well-suited to undergraduate-level or advanced high school physics instruction. In the appendix, we propose a MATLAB-based computer experiment for the Newton damping case, illustrating the comparison between the approximate energy-based solution and a numerical reference solution.
keywords: damped harmonic oscillator, energy decay, Coulomb damping, quadratic damping, energy dissipation, approximate analytical solutions, damping force

title: Exploring physics and Welsh identity: using Facebook and Google Maps to make links
text: Abstract Resources are presented that highlight the role of Wales and Welsh people in the history of the development of physics and engineering. These resources are intended to support the Science Capital Teaching Approach by providing contextual links that are local and personal. Well received by teachers, there are a number of barriers presented by the technology as it uses Facebook and Google Maps.
keywords: Welsh identity, history of physics, history of engineering, science capital, contextual learning, local history, Facebook, Google Maps

title: Interactive visualization of the Kronig–Penney model and extended zone scheme using Python programming
text: Abstract In the interest of improving pedagogical clarity, we provide an interactive way to apply Python programming to visualize the extended zone scheme and the Kronig–Penney model in the same window. To investigate how straightforward physical parameters such as lattice spacing, barrier width, and potential height affect band structure characteristics in periodic potentials, the simulation was developed by students as part of an instructional end-of-semester project employing project based learning principles. This article is intended for physics educators seeking interactive tools and for students as a guide to integrating computational methods with theoretical physics. The simulation has several features including sliding graphs in real time. The simulation aims to promote conceptual understanding in solid state physics by connecting theory into the abstract and presenting visual representations. With Python libraries such as matplotlib, numpy , and ttkbootstrap , we create an intuitive user interface appropriate for both undergraduate and graduate level instruction. We discussed how these simulations may broaden pedagogical space in a pedagogical frame in developing interactive capabilities for learning and provided a brief outline of the underlying theoretical principles, programmatic design and pedagogical features of the simulations.
keywords: Kronig-Penney model, electronic band structure, periodic potential, solid state physics education, interactive visualization, Python simulation, project-based learning, lattice spacing, barrier width, user interface design

title: Development and evaluation of a dance-based learning method in physics education for modelling electron motion in materials
text: Abstract Teaching abstract concepts such as electron motion in different materials presents a persistent challenge in physics education and is often accompanied by primary and secondary school students’ misconceptions. We report on the development and classroom evaluation of a novel dance-based embodied learning method designed to support conceptual understanding of electron behaviour in metals, insulators, semiconductors, and superconductors. The method was inspired by observed kinesthetic practices in early childhood education and systematically adapted for secondary level physics instruction. Purpose-designed instructional dance videos were produced in collaboration with a professional dance troupe and used as the core representational component of the method. A quasi-experimental design was implemented with 152 high-school students (aged 16–18) from four schools in Croatia. Students were divided into a control group receiving traditional physics instruction and an experimental group exposed to the dance-based materials combined with guided physical enactment. Identical pre- and post-tests were administered to assess conceptual understanding. The results indicate that students in the experimental group demonstrated clearer conceptual explanations and fewer documented misconceptions regarding electron motion than those taught using traditional methods alone. These findings underscore the global potential of embodied and interdisciplinary approaches to improve science understanding, motivation, and engagement. The study contributes to the growing movement toward STEAM integration and offers a scalable model adaptable across diverse educational contexts.
keywords: dance-based learning, embodied learning, electron motion, physics misconceptions, STEAM integration, high school physics, conceptual understanding

title: Equilibrium and stability of bevel gauges: the role of arm angle and length
text: Abstract We investigate the equilibrium and stability of bevel gauges resting on an idealised punctual support, assuming identical thickness and mass density for both arms and perfect contact. Extending our previous analysis of L-squares, we generalise the model to variable inter-arm angles and examine how equilibrium orientation and stability depend on arm lengths, arm thickness and inter-arm angle. Using the principle of virtual work, we derive a theoretical expression for the equilibrium angle, including its sign, and complement it with a stability analysis that identifies the conditions for stable or unstable equilibria. This leads to the definition of a critical thickness that separates two distinct regimes in the evolution of equilibrium configurations as the longer arm length increases, and below which all equilibrium positions remain stable. Experiments conducted with laser-cut bevel gauges confirm the theoretical predictions. Beyond its mechanical interest, this simple system offers an accessible framework for illustrating how geometry controls equilibrium and stability, and can be rapidly adapted for classroom demonstrations.
keywords: equilibrium, stability, arm angle, arm length, critical thickness, principle of virtual work

title: Correlation between exam score and quiz submission day in an introductory physics course
text: Abstract Students’ learning performance and its correlation with exam scores are examined using a unique factor: the day the online quiz was submitted. By collecting information on quizzes through an online learning management system for each subject in an introductory physics course for first-grade medical students, student learning performance is thoroughly analysed and compared with the final exam score. The results show a statistically significant negative correlation between the exam score and quiz submission day. Furthermore, by combining several parameters that are potentially related to the exam score, we are able to evaluate the student’s learning attitude in more detail. Based on the results, we discuss the negative effects of procrastinating behaviour and successful learning practices.
keywords: test scores, procrastination, learning attitude, introductory physics, online quizzes, virtual learning environments, medical students, student learning performance

title: An AI-supported classroom investigation of energy loss and the coefficient of restitution
text: Abstract A classroom-based investigation is presented in which students study energy dissipation and the coefficient of restitution of a bouncing ball using smartphone-based acoustic measurements and AI-assisted analysis. Impact sounds from successive collisions are recorded with the smartphone microphone using the Phyphox application, and the resulting time-series data are analysed to extract rebound intervals, heights, and associated energy losses. AI is used as an analytical assistant to support routine data processing, while physical interpretation and verification remain the responsibility of the students. The work focuses on the experimental method, timing-based analysis of inelastic collisions, and the practical integration of AI-assisted workflows into a classroom setting.
keywords: coefficient of restitution, energy loss, inelastic collisions, bouncing ball, smartphone sensors, Phyphox, AI-assisted data analysis, energy dissipation

title: Modelling free-fall motion and vortex flows through the use of Tracker software: an inquiry-based teaching learning sequence
text: Abstract This article presents a teaching–learning sequence based on the inquiry-based learning approach, designed to help high-school students gain a deeper understanding of the physical principles of the free fall of bodies and the role of viscous resistive forces. The activity, centred on the use of the open-source video analysis software Tracker, enables students to explore the motion of small-radius spheres of different masses and materials, and to experimentally infer the effect of air viscosity on the motion of a lightweight polystyrene ball by means of the Tracker’s built-in modelling tool. An extension of the activity is also proposed, focusing on the vortex-induced motion to provide a clearer explanation of the observed phenomena. The comparison of the motion laws of balls of different mass allows students to overcome common misconceptions related to dynamics and engage with fundamental aspects of fluid dynamics, which are often addressed only superficially in traditional instruction. The experiment is conceived not simply as a laboratory task, but as an educational experience aimed at developing scientific curiosity and critical autonomy through direct experimentation.
keywords: free-fall motion, viscous drag, aerodynamic drag, vortex-induced motion, inquiry-based learning, high school physics teaching, fluid dynamics

title: Determination of the mutual inductiveness coefficient of coils on a ferromagnetic core
text: Abstract In ferromagnetic cores, the magnetic field inside a toroid is spatially non-uniform, and the relative magnetic permeability μ(H) depends nonlinearly on the magnetic field strength H . In electromagnetism courses, when determining mutual inductance, it is usually assumed that the relative magnetic permeability of the core material is constant, which significantly affects the calculated values of mutual inductance. In the proposed method for determining mutual inductance, a graphical analysis of the function μ(H)/H is used to account for the non-uniform distribution of the magnetic field and magnetization in a toroidal core. When determining the magnetic flux through the cross-section of the core, integration with respect to the magnetic field strength is employed. Since an analytical expression for the relative magnetic permeability μ ( H ) is not available and is given graphically, the required integrals are evaluated graphically. The method is illustrated by calculation examples for a toroidal core made of American Rolling Mill Company iron. The results show that the mutual inductance depends on the current in the primary coil, the number of turns, and the ratio of the outer to inner radii of the core. A comparison with the method based on a constant relative magnetic permeability demonstrates that such an approach can lead to significant errors, especially in regimes where the magnetic field varies considerably across the core cross-section. The proposed method accounts for the nonlinearity of the magnetic properties of the ferromagnetic core and the non-uniformity of the magnetic field. It helps students relate theoretical concepts to the experimental properties of materials. The use of digital tools for determining the areas under the curves of plotted functions helps simplify certain calculations and improve the accuracy of the obtained results.
keywords: mutual inductance, ferromagnetic core, toroidal coil, nonlinear magnetic permeability, magnetic field inhomogeneity, graphical integration, magnetic flux, magnetic saturation

title: An aid or not? Examining ChatGPT-generated visualizations in physics problem solving
text: Abstract The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education is expanding rapidly, yet its effectiveness for supporting conceptual understanding in physics remains uncertain. This study investigates the quality and pedagogical adequacy of ChatGPT-generated diagrams across five mechanics problems of varying complexity. Three university physics lecturers analysed the diagrams in relation to the problem statements. The analysis revealed recurring discrepancies, including missing or misdirected vectors, no coordinate systems, misrepresented forces, and the inclusion of extraneous or misleading elements. Errors were more frequent and severe in complex problems, indicating that the model’s capacity to produce accurate visual representations diminishes with task complexity. These findings highlight the limitations of relying on ChatGPT for physics visualization and underscore the importance of instructor mediation to ensure conceptual accuracy. Involving students in critiquing AI-generated visuals could also promote engagement and deeper conceptual understanding.
keywords: ChatGPT, physics visualization, physics problem solving, mechanics problems, conceptual understanding, task complexity, college physics

title: Using summary sentences to assess scientific reasoning in introductory physics lab
text: Abstract The purpose of this article is to introduce and advocate for experimental sentence summaries as a form of lab assessment in introductory physics labs. We discuss the reasoning which underlies different kinds of scientific experiments and show how summary sentences can capture and make that reasoning explicit to students. We then use examples of summary sentences our students have submitted to illustrate how they allow us to assess student understanding.
keywords: scientific reasoning, introductory physics laboratory, laboratory evaluation, student understanding, explicit reasoning

title: Experimental study on visualisation of the Zeeman effect based on flame shadows
text: Abstract When sodium chloride granules are introduced into a flame illuminated by a sodium lamp, a shadow forms behind the flame. Under the influence of an externally applied steady magnetic field, the Zeeman effect can be directly observed through changes in the shadow’s brightness. This experimental design demonstrates that the Zeeman effect causes the shadow’s colour to lighten as the degree of energy level splitting increases, thereby achieving a visualisation of the Zeeman effect. This experimental approach enables visual observation of the Zeeman effect using low-cost apparatus, thereby resolving the issue of expensive traditional experimental equipment.
keywords: Zeeman effect, sodium vapor lamps, magnetic field, energy level splitting, low-cost laboratory equipment

title: Contact loss on curvilinear surfaces: a video analysis study of the normal force
text: Abstract In this work, we developed a laboratory guide that can be applied in both basic and advanced courses of classical mechanics. It consists of an experimental study of the normal force acting on a small metallic sphere as it rolls along certain curvilinear profiles. Specifically, we considered circular and elliptic profiles, fabricated with a 3D printer. In the method, the sphere’s motion is filmed using a smartphone camera. We also model the system using Newton’s second law, which governs its dynamics. Then, using video analysis, we estimate the magnitude of the normal force along the sphere’s trajectory. These results were used to estimate the height at which the sphere loses contact with the profile’s surfaces, at the point where the normal force is zero. We demonstrate the importance of possible dissipative effects and of the rotational motion, showing how the theoretical aspects addressed during the classes are related with practical and real aspects of the experiment, evidencing their influences on the position where the sphere loses contact with the surface by means of a direct comparison between experimental and theoretical results. The theoretical results describe a sphere that only slides without friction, for which the mechanical energy associated with the translational motion is conserved.
keywords: contact loss, normal force, rolling sphere, curved surfaces, video analysis, smartphone camera, Newton's second law, rotational motion, dissipative effects, mechanical energy conservation

title: A ripple tank made of Lego bricks for student experiments
text: Abstract In this article, we present a wave tank made of Lego bricks, that can be replicated using our freely available instructions. We describe three experiments: single slit (diffraction), double slit (interference) and the behaviour of a wave on a reflective surface. We compare the experimental results from this ripple tank made of bricks with a setup of the commercial demonstration experiment and a simulation. Creating the experimental setup with bricks can motivate learners and enable them to implement their own ideas when varying the experiments.
keywords: ripple tank, LEGO bricks, wave tank, single-slit diffraction, double-slit interference, wave reflection, hands-on physics experiments, low-cost laboratory equipment, student motivation

title: A DIY model to support understanding of the phases of the Moon
text: Abstract Students often experience difficulties in understanding the phases of the Moon, particularly in relating Earth-based observations to the spatial configuration and motion of the Sun–Earth–Moon system. Persistent misconceptions are well documented. This paper presents a simple, low-cost, do-it-yourself model designed to support conceptual understanding by linking two frames of reference: a heliocentric coordinate system, used to explain the physical origin of lunar phases, and a geographic coordinate system, from which the phases are observed. The model combines a planar representation of orbital motion with a three-dimensional viewing element that enables an Earth-based perspective. By explicitly connecting these viewpoints, the model supports the transition from observation to explanation. The model can be easily constructed from readily available materials and is suitable for use in primary and secondary school classrooms.
keywords: lunar phases, Sun-Earth-Moon system, geographic coordinate system, orbital motion, misconceptions, conceptual understanding, low-cost teaching models, 3D model, astronomy education

title: Magnetic force determination using a buoyant probe magnet
text: Abstract A simple and low-cost apparatus is presented to experimentally determine the magnetic force between two cylindrical magnets. The first magnet is a buoyant probe magnet immersed in water and is free to be repelled by a second underneath magnet, with an ability to change the second magnet with another of different height. By analysing the forces under static equilibrium conditions, the mutual magnetic force between the two repelled magnets is experimentally determined each time. The measured values are then compared with those predicted by Cheedket’s formula, showing good agreement within the experimental uncertainty. Owing to its conceptual clarity, minimal instrumentation and direct connection between theory and measurement, the proposed experiment is particularly well suited for undergraduate physics laboratories. It helps students develop practical skills in force analysis, error estimation and experimental verification of analytical models, while deepening their understanding of magnetostatics and equilibrium principles.
keywords: magnetic force, magnetostatics, static equilibrium, low-cost laboratory equipment, undergraduate physics laboratory, error estimation, force analysis

title: Contemporary confirmation of Galileo’s inclined plane experiment using smartphone proximity sensor
text: Abstract Galileo’s theory of accelerated motion, presented in the book discourses concerning two new sciences, was met with skepticism because the experimental procedure lacked an accurate timing method. Many attempts have been made to confirm the experiment using more reliable time-measuring instruments. In this study, a smartphone was used to record the motion of an object on an inclined plane to confirm Galileo’s experimental result. The time interval for the object moving on the inclined plane was measured for several variations in distance. The ratios of distances and the ratio of time squared were calculated and compared with Galileo’s theory. In addition, regression analysis was conducted to examine the relationship between distance and the square of time. This study confirmed Galileo’s theory of accelerated motion.
keywords: Galileo Galilei, accelerated motion, time measurement, history of physics, regression analysis

title: A contextualized and iterative inquiry framework for competency emergence in high school physics
text: Abstract This study explores how a pedagogical model that integrates contextualized learning with iterative inquiry promotes the development of core competencies in high school physics. By combining authentic contextual tasks with iterative inquiry cycles, a competency-oriented instructional framework was constructed and implemented in a 12-lesson kinematics unit for first-year high school students. Student performance was assessed using a six-dimensional competency rubric covering conceptual understanding, experimental skills, reasoning & modelling, explanation & argumentation, reflection & metacognition, and collaboration & communication. The results indicate that contextualized tasks support foundational competencies, while iterative inquiry fosters higher-order competencies. Several competencies became more evident only after sustained engagement and repeated inquiry cycles, highlighting the gradual and relational nature of competency development.
keywords: competence development, contextual learning, inquiry-based learning, high school physics, kinematics, competency rubric, metacognition, communication and collaboration, experimental skills, conceptual understanding, modeling skills

title: Simple teaching tools for hybrid energy systems: a learning media to support renewable energy literacy
text: Abstract The global energy transition toward sustainability demands the integration of renewable energy education into the school curriculum. However, traditional physics education is still missing appropriate experimental aids especially for understanding hybrid energy systems such as solar or wind hybrid system. The objective of this research is to create and assess cost-effective and field weighty school-based hybrid renewable energy education systems tutors for enhancing student’ energy literacy. This study adopted the ADDIE (analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation) development model to develop a hybrid solar panels and mini wind turbine demonstration instrument equipped with digital voltmeter switching system. The developed product was validated by the experts in the subject, media and physics teachers with a very high level of feasibility (above 85%). Energy literacy increased significantly among high school students that used both teaching aids (normalized gain = 0.63), moderately improving conceptual understanding and student engagement, when the teaching tools were introduced. Teacher and student feedback also suggested that it was useful, interactive, and facilitated contextual learning. This study is novel in that it offers an inexpensive, easy‐to‐replicate, and successful instructional intervention to promote renewable energy literacy in physics education.
keywords: hybrid energy systems, physics teaching aids, solar panels, small wind turbines, high school physics teaching, energy transition, contextual learning, student engagement

title: The physics of sound during water bottle filling: a theoretical study of fluid resonance in a closed organ pipe
text: Abstract The rising pitch heard during water-bottle filling is a simple yet instructive example of resonance in a time-varying fluid–air system. This study presents a theoretical analysis of the relationship between water height, discharge rate, and sound frequency by modelling the bottle as a closed-end organ pipe. As the bottle fills, the water–air interface rises and continuously shortens the air column, which acts as a variable-length resonator whose fundamental frequency increases accordingly. Using an idealised, monotonically decreasing volumetric inflow (taken here as linear in time) and neglecting turbulence and Doppler effects, we derive an analytical frequency–time expression. The resulting function predicts a nonlinear frequency increase consistent with standing-wave physics in a compressible medium. For representative parameters H = 0.23 m, A = 3.3 × 10 −3 m 2 , and c = 340 m s −1 , the predicted pitch evolution aligns with everyday observations of bottle filling. Although the governing equation reduces to a Chini-type form that does not generally admit a closed-form solution, a series approximation provides useful insight into its behaviour. The model clarifies how fluid filling kinematics sets a time-dependent acoustic boundary condition, offering an accessible theoretical context for teaching resonance in physics.
keywords: fluid resonance, standing waves, compressible media, discharge rate, water level, series approximation, physics education

title: Cosmic Muon Explorer: a portable detector for cosmic muon flux measurements and outreach
text: Abstract In this paper, we present development of a portable cosmic muon tracker tailored for both on-site measurements of cosmic muon flux as well as for outreach activities. The tracker comprises of two 70 mm × 70 mm plastic scintillators, wavelength shifting (WLS) fibres, and Hamamatsu made silicon photomultipliers (SiPM) S13360-2050VE. The detector uses plastic scintillator panels optically coupled to WLS fibres, which transmit scintillation light to the SiPMs. SiPM signals are routed to an electronics board equipped with op-amp amplifiers and a peak-hold circuit connected to an ESP32 microcontroller module. When muons traverse through both scintillators the light emitted is collected by the SiPMs, and thus generating signals proportional to the incident light intensity. These signals are then amplified and the pulse peak is held for 500 µ s. A high speed discriminator is used to generate trigger logic signals. The peak analogue voltage is digitized using the onboard ADC of the ESP32 when a coincident trigger occurs. The SiPMs are powered by a high voltage bias supply module while an onboard BMP180 module measures temperature and pressure. For real-time event tagging, a GPS module is interfaced with the ESP-32. Housed within an acrylic box measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 100 mm the detector can be powered using a 5 V 1 A USB power bank. An open source mobile application was used for real-time monitoring. This versatile and cost-effective portable detector facilitates cosmic muon research in various experimental settings. Its portability and low power requirements enable on-site measurements in environments such as tunnels, caves as well as high altitudes.
keywords: cosmic ray muons, muon flux measurement, plastic scintillators, wavelength-shifting fibers, silicon photomultipliers, ESP32 microcontroller, low-cost detector

title: A flipped classroom practice that combines gamification and analogy to improve learning outcomes for online students
text: Abstract This study aims to improve the results of online learning of a simple electrical circuit. It provides a solution to the barriers of synchronous distance learning, particularly in terms of interactivity and reducing the role of the teacher. The proposed solution is to adopt a flipped classroom practice that combines gamification and analogy (FCPCGA). The mixed-methods methodology includes quantitative and qualitative measures using multiple-choice questionnaires to assess academic performance and collect feedback on the FCPCGA. It uses a control group and an experimental group and measures learning outcomes before and after the intervention. The results showed an improvement in learning outcomes for students in the experimental group who expressed satisfaction with the FCPCGA.
keywords: flipped classroom, gamification, analogy-based learning, online learning, distance education, electrical circuits, learning outcomes, student satisfaction

title: Work done by sliding friction on a bouncing ball
text: Abstract At glancing angles of incidence, a bouncing ball can slide on a horizontal surface during the whole impact duration. It is shown that the work done to change its horizontal translational kinetic energy is given by the friction force multiplied by the horizontal displacement of its centre of mass and the total mechanical work done to change its horizontal kinetic energy plus the work done to change its rotational kinetic energy is equal to the friction force multiplied by the displacement of the point of application of the friction force.
keywords: sliding friction, bouncing ball, work done by friction, grazing incidence, impact duration, rotational kinetic energy, center of mass displacement

title: Measuring your weight while moving up and down
text: Abstract Suppose that a person standing on a weighing scale bends or squats down then rises back up again. What changes will be noticed in the scale reading? It is the change in the vertical acceleration rather than the vertical speed that determines the change in the scale reading.
keywords: weighing scales, apparent weight, vertical acceleration, Newton's second law

title: A digital storage oscilloscope-based approach to teaching the concept of coherent sources
text: Abstract This study presents a laboratory method for introducing the concept of coherence to undergraduate students using a oscilloscope with a function generator. The approach employs dual-trace measurements and Lissajous figures in XY mode to differentiate signals originating from a common source from those generated independently. A split signal produces stationary Lissajous patterns, confirming a fixed phase relationship and coherent behaviour, while independent generators yield continuously changing figures indicative of incoherence. The results provide a clear, visual framework for conceptualising coherence and establish a pedagogical bridge between electrical signal analysis and optical interference principles.
keywords: coherent sources, optical interference, Lissajous figures, function generator, digital storage oscilloscope, phase equilibria, incoherence, physics experiment teaching, undergraduate physics education

title: The use of microcontrollers and digital fabrication to investigate Ampere’s Law
text: Abstract In this manuscript, we introduce a novel device that computes the magnetic field along the path as a function of the path. This device, comprising 3D-printed parts: a magnetometer and a wheel with an optical encoder connected to a microcontroller that sends data to a computer wirelessly, offers a unique approach to verifying Ampere’s Law. By moving the device in a closed loop, with and without a wire carrying current, the magnetic field can be graphed as a function of position, providing a fresh perspective on this fundamental law.
keywords: Ampère's law, magnetic field measurement, microcontroller, 3D printing, magnetometer, optical encoder, current-carrying wire

title: Origami DIY on auxetic material: negative Poisson’s ratio
text: Abstract Poisson’s ratio is considered an intrinsic material property that characterizes the elastic behaviour of a material under mechanical loading. It is traditionally positive between 0 and 0.5 and theoretically ranges from − 1 to + 0.5 . Negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR) is theoretically permissible, rarely exists in nature and primarily observed in engineered structures.
