This article demonstrates the concept of a NPR through an origami-based activity effectively visualizes behaviour both within and beyond the traditional range.
keywords: negative Poisson's ratio, auxetic materials, origami, hands-on activities, elastic properties, material properties, engineering education

title: The study of the motion of bodies in a non-inertial reference frame
text: Abstract The paper presents an experimental study of the motion of a solid cylinder and a uniform ball on a platform moving with acceleration in the context of studying non-inertial reference frames and the relativity of motion. The kinematic parameters of the bodies were determined using video analysis with the tracker software, and further data processing was performed in the cloud-based environment Google Sheets. The ratio of the platform acceleration to the acceleration of the body on it was determined without considering rolling friction. The coefficients of rolling friction on aluminium and rubber surfaces were also estimated. The proposed methodology combines theoretical analysis, experiment and modern digital data processing tools and can be used as a research educational project in the master’s level training of future physics teachers.
keywords: non-inertial frames, rolling friction, rolling without slipping, solid cylinder, relativity of motion, kinematics, video analysis, physics teacher education

title: Turning social media into a physics laboratory: teaching exponential saturation through inquiry-based learning
text: Abstract Exponential behaviour is a fundamental concept in physics, yet it is often introduced through abstract or idealised systems that may seem disconnected from students’ everyday experiences. This paper presents a concise classroom activity that uses social media viewer accumulation as a familiar and engaging context to teach first-order exponential saturation. Students analyse time-dependent viewer data, identify saturation behaviour, and relate their observations to canonical physical systems such as capacitor charging. The activity emphasises observation, modelling, and interpretation within an inquiry-based framework, allowing students to construct understanding before formal equations are introduced. By linking a familiar digital phenomenon to a well-established physical model, this approach provides an accessible and practical pathway for introducing exponential behaviour in introductory physics courses.
keywords: inquiry-based learning, capacitor charging, introductory physics education

title: The compelling case of the magnetic damped pendulum for undergraduate laboratories
text: Abstract A damped harmonic oscillator is an important theoretical construct that is part of a typical undergraduate curriculum. While the theory is straightforward, an experiment in undergraduate settings, where the theory can be quantitatively verified, is not. I describe a practical realisation of a damped harmonic oscillator in the form of simple pendulum having a magnetic bob and an eddy current brake effected by a metal plate in its vicinity. This set-up has a simple way of controlling damping and yields observations that are amenable to a rigorous analysis. The simplicity of the set-up makes it easy to scale it up in numbers at a low cost and with minimal effort.
keywords: damped harmonic oscillator, eddy current brake, simple pendulum, damping control, undergraduate physics laboratory, low-cost laboratory equipment

title: Time-domain verification of Ohm’s law using a fixed resistor in an RC circuit
text: Abstract Ohm’s law is traditionally verified in physics laboratories under steady-state conditions by varying resistance and measuring corresponding current–voltage pairs. While operationally effective, this approach often obscures the instantaneous and local nature of Ohm’s law and encourages the misconception that the law is valid only for constant currents. In this article, a time-domain verification of Ohm’s law is presented using a fixed resistor in a series resistor ( R )-capacitor ( C ) circuit. The charging and discharging of a capacitor driven by a low-voltage DC source are studied by simultaneously measuring voltage and current as functions of time. Experimental voltage–time and current–time data exhibit the expected exponential behaviour, while the voltage–current plots (voltage versus corresponding current at any instant) obtained from measurements taken at different times during charging and discharging yield straight lines with nearly identical slopes. The results demonstrate that, despite the circuit being globally non-Ohmic, the variation of voltage and current through the resistor obeys Ohm’s law instantaneously at all times. The experiment provides a complementary, conceptually rich alternative to the conventional rheostat-based verification of Ohm’s law, while the present method offers a conceptually richer yet experimentally easier means of understanding the instantaneous and local nature of Ohm’s law in time-dependent circuits.
keywords: Ohm's law, RC circuits, fixed resistors, physics laboratory experiments

title: Measurement of human reaction time using a smartphone camera stopwatch and video analysis
text: Abstract A simple method for measuring human reaction time is presented by comparing a manually operated smartphone stopwatch with a camera-based stopwatch implemented in the Phyphox application. In the experiment, a toy car rolls down a short inclined track and the travel time is recorded simultaneously using both timing methods. While the manual stopwatch is stopped visually by the observer, the Phyphox camera stopwatch automatically detects the finish event via brightness changes in a selected sensing region. The difference between the two measured times provides an estimate of the observer’s reaction delay. To evaluate the coordination delay associated with manually starting the timing devices, the experiment was also recorded and analysed frame-by-frame using QuickTime Player. The measured start delay was small and used to correct the reaction-time values. The corrected mean reaction time obtained from repeated trials is approximately 0.13 s , consistent with reported visual reaction times. The experiment requires minimal equipment and offers a simple classroom activity to investigate human reaction time and the role of measurement methods in experimental physics.
keywords: human reaction time, Phyphox, video analysis, toy cars, inclined tracks, measurement methods

title: Popping of inflatable rubber balloons filled with different gases
text: Abstract The popping of inflatable rubber balloons filled with different gases provides a simple, low-cost and pedagogically valuable experiment to investigate the acoustic signatures of gases with contrasting thermodynamic properties. In this study, balloons of identical geometry were inflated with helium, argon, nitrogen, and air, then burst while the resulting acoustic signals were recorded using a smartphone microphone. Power spectral density analysis was performed. The results reveal clear and systematic differences between gases: helium produces high-frequency-rich, broadband spectra with large spectral centroids and bandwidths, whereas argon exhibits low-frequency-dominated spectra with steep high-frequency attenuation. Nitrogen and air show intermediate behaviour, reflecting their similar molar masses and sound speeds. The study demonstrates that acoustic spectral analysis of balloon explosions enables reliable qualitative discrimination between light and heavy gases using simple instrumentation. This approach is robust, non-invasive, and well suited for educational demonstrations and introductory experimental physics activities.
keywords: power spectral density, helium, argon, nitrogen, air, molar mass, sound velocity, smartphone microphone

title: A low-cost teaching apparatus for charged particle deflection in electric and magnetic fields
text: Abstract This study presents a low-cost teaching apparatus designed to demonstrate the deflection of charged radiation in electric and magnetic fields under ambient laboratory conditions. The system employs a commercially available thorium-based lantern mantle as a radiation source. Thorium decay series isotopes are known to emit predominantly alpha radiation, as documented in international radiation assessment reports (United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) 2000 Sources and effects of ionizing radiation (United Nations) www.unscear.org/). A Geiger–Müller detector equipped with a mica window is used for particle detection. Experiments were conducted using electric-field-only, magnetic-field-only, and combined-field configurations. The detector position was scanned laterally to obtain spatial count distributions and observe deflection patterns. The measurements reveal clear shifts in detected radiation corresponding to applied fields, demonstrating the qualitative behaviour of charged particle motion. The observed deflection directions under both electric and magnetic fields are consistent with positively charged particles, suggesting that the dominant deflection behaviour is associated with a positively charged radiation component. Preliminary attenuation tests using paper and thin plastic absorbers suggest that multiple radiation components may be present; however, only the positively charged component produces the systematic peak displacement observed under applied fields. The results highlight the value of the system as an accessible instructional platform for illustrating Lorentz force effects, radiation attenuation, and the differences between idealized textbook models and real experimental conditions.
keywords: charged particle deflection, Lorentz force, electric and magnetic fields, alpha radiation, Geiger-Muller counter, radiation attenuation, ionizing radiation

title: Ball spin generation with a racquet
text: Abstract The collision of a ball with a racquet is more complicated than the collision of a ball with another ball but can be filmed in slow motion to determine the outgoing speed and spin of the ball. Results are presented where the ball is incident either horizontally or vertically on a racquet incident on the ball, and explained in terms of the forces acting on the ball. The problem is specific to a spinning ball but is a relatively simple example of the generation of rotation by an applied torque.
keywords: torque, rotational motion, collision dynamics

title: Jumping into the second Newton law: conceptualization of the landing process
text: Abstract The second Newton law is one of the basic laws in classical mechanics and therefore, demands deep conceptual understanding by physics learners. This, however, frequently is not the situation. Precisely, students experience difficulties applying Newton Laws in the analysis of real life situations. An interesting real-world context ruled by the principles of classical mechanics is the world of acrobatics and parkour. Here almost every jump creates the ‘Wow’ affect and hence is probable to draw the attention of learners; thus, inspiring a true curiosity regarding its underlying physics principles. Each acrobatic jump requires the skill of safe landing which is the process of zeroing a jumpers’ velocity within a certain time period. The second Newton law describes this situation. In the present study, we analyse a real jump and employ it as a real life case for 5 clinical interviews and 3 focus-group interviews (conducted as whole class dialogic discussions)—69 participants in total. The interviews’ analysis yielded three kinds of misconceptions. We further discuss these misconceptions and suggest practical ways for their review. We believe that physics teaching and classical mechanics precisely, should be based on such practical examples, which are likely to arouse curiosity on the one hand, and can be easily experienced by most of the learners. In our case, the tool is always accessible; it is the body of every one of us.
keywords: acrobatics, parkour, misconceptions, conceptual understanding, classical mechanics, speed reduction, dialogic discussion, physics education

title: Design, implementation, and application of a low-cost ESP32-based anemometer: context-based learning of physics concepts with a focus on weather
text: Abstract The ESP32 microcontroller, with its built-in, low-cost Hall sensor, offers many opportunities for interdisciplinary, practice-oriented physics teaching. In this article we present a fully functional anemometer that was designed using CAD software, manufactured via 3D printing, and calibrated using the ESP32’s integrated Hall sensor’s magnetic detection capabilities. A neodymium magnet embedded in the rotating roof passes near the Hall sensor, enabling the microcontroller to detect each rotation. A custom Python script then converted this rotation rate into the wind speed, enabling real-time measurement. This low-cost and student-friendly device is ideal for outdoor use on school rooftops or in gardens, and can be easily integrated into broader weather monitoring systems. This project situates physics learning in an authentic weather context and demonstrates how digital tools can enhance engagement and relevance in the classroom.
keywords: ESP32 microcontroller, anemometer, Hall effect sensors, wind speed measurement, 3D-printed device, Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets, weather monitoring, contextual learning, low-cost instrumentation, real-time measurement

title: Measuring focal length via real images of virtual objects
text: Abstract Are physics lessons uninteresting? Many students would answer ‘yes’ to this question. Consequently, many high school students do not choose to take physics as an elective. Interest in physics is also waning at the undergraduate and graduate levels. However, physics teachers can prevent this unsatisfactory situation by using instructional approaches that encourage students to think differently. To determine the focal point of various optical devices, this study presents three experiments demonstrating how to obtain a real image of a virtual object using a concave mirror, a convex mirror, and a concave lens, respectively. These examples use virtual objects to encourage critical thinking by prompting students to think in new ways.
keywords: focal length measurement, virtual objects, real images, concave mirror, convex mirror, concave lens, optical instruments, physics education, critical thinking, high school physics

title: Integrating GeoGebra and PhET simulations in mathematics and physics: opportunities and challenges in Rwandan lower secondary schools
text: Abstract This study investigates how GeoGebra and PhET simulations are integrated into mathematics and physics curricula in rural and urban Rwandan lower secondary schools, focusing on both the opportunities they present and the challenges teachers encounter. The study is guided by the following research questions: (i) To what extent are GeoGebra and PhET simulations being used in the teaching and learning of mathematics and physics in rural and urban lower secondary schools in Rwanda? (ii) What are the challenges hindering the effective use of GeoGebra and PhET simulations in the teaching and learning of mathematics and physics in Rwandan lower secondary schools? A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining surveys and interviews with mathematics and physics teachers across selected schools. Quantitative results indicate that while a majority of teachers are aware of GeoGebra and PhET simulations, approximately 56% do not use them regularly, mainly due to limited information and communication technology (ICT) skills, time constraints, and insufficient computer and internet facilities. Qualitative findings further highlight teachers’ perceived benefits of simulations in enhancing conceptual understanding and learner engagement. The study concludes that systematic professional development in digital pedagogy and improved ICT infrastructure are essential for promoting the effective integration of interactive simulations in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics classrooms. These findings have implications for educational policy and teacher training initiatives aimed at advancing technology-enhanced learning in Rwanda.
keywords: GeoGebra, PhET simulation, interactive simulation, mathematics education, physics education, junior high school, rural and urban schools, teacher ICT skills, ICT infrastructure, digital pedagogy, teacher professional development, technology-enhanced learning, Rwanda

title: Laser wavelength with a ruler: easy made apparatus
text: Abstract We describe an easy-to-build low-cost apparatus by which the wavelength of a laser module can be determined by measuring just some lengths. The basic idea is to use a metallic workshop ruler in grazing incidence, similarly to what is done in x-ray spectrographs, where normal optical gratings are used in this configuration. We additionally propose a novel approach to the theory of the phenomenon, enabling exact calculations for a large number of diffraction maxima positions. This new scheme results in a substantial improvement in the accuracy of the calculated wavelength values compared to previous works. The apparatus has been designed for its maximum easy of construction, simplicity, availability of materials and flexibility of use. Detailed instructions on construction and alignment are given.
keywords: laser wavelength measurement, diffraction gratings, grazing incidence, low-cost equipment, diffraction theory

title: Effects of friction on ball spin generation
text: Abstract An experiment is described where a horizontal surface was projected across the bottom of a ball to increase its spin. The roles of sliding and rolling friction were clearly demonstrated.
keywords: friction, sliding friction, rolling friction, ball rotation

title: An examination of the third interstellar object (3I/ATLAS) through the lens of physics education
text: Abstract The interstellar object 3I/ATLAS, which entered the Solar System from the interstellar medium, will soon complete its journey and leave the Solar System. This study seeks to address several questions about this amazing object and presents corresponding answers by reviewing related literature. These questions can be incorporated into physics courses to both enhance students’ motivation to learn physics and to foster a deeper understanding of the interstellar objects.
keywords: 3I/ATLAS, interstellar objects, interstellar medium, student motivation, interstellar travel

title: From optimal engines to minimal refrigerators: the Carnot case
text: Abstract The Carnot limit defines the maximum efficiency for reversible heat engines. However, when applied to reversible refrigerators operating within a fixed temperature range, the Carnot cycle corresponds—counterintuitively—to the minimum possible performance. While this fact is established in formal thermodynamics, it is frequently overlooked or misunderstood by students. This paper presents a physical explanation for this asymmetry without explicitly relying on entropy formalism. A direct, simple mathematical demonstration of this result is provided, along with a concrete illustrative example.
keywords: Carnot cycle, maximum efficiency, thermodynamic efficiency limits, entropy

title: Analysing conceptual understanding in physics education using the APOS framework
text: Abstract This paper explores the application of the Action–Process–Object–Schema (APOS) framework to analyse and enhance conceptual understanding in science education, specifically in thermodynamics, kinematics, and magnetism. Results show that while most students excel at the Action level, performance significantly declines at higher cognitive stages: Process (40%–54%), Object (43%–54%), and Schema (23%–31%). The APOS framework offers valuable insights into students’ cognitive development, with its strengths lying in clear diagnostic modelling and instructional guidance through the ACE cycle (Activities, Classroom discussion, Exercises). However, its focus on individual cognition limits its consideration of affective, social, and contextual factors in learning. This paper argues that integrating APOS with complementary pedagogical approaches can promote deeper, more integrated learning experiences, facilitating students’ progression to higher levels of conceptual understanding.
keywords: conceptual understanding, thermodynamics, kinematics, magnetism, cognitive development stages, student misconceptions

title: A genuine demonstration of the radiative greenhouse effect
text: Abstract Despite its central importance to understanding the Earth’s climate, experimental demonstrations of the radiative greenhouse effect are surprisingly lacking, with many purported tabletop demonstrations inadvertently illustrating other, non-radiative mechanisms. A set of controlled experiments has been devised to close this critical gap. By covering a sky-exposed black surface with panes of differing optical materials, it is shown that panes that are more opaque to infrared radiation causally result in a warmer surface temperature than those more transmissive of it. Systematic control experiments confirmed the radiative nature of the observed temperature differences, ruling out confounding factors. A variant of the experiment is provided which is performable in under an hour. A simple computer model is also made available which closely matches experimental results and may prove useful for illustrating the heat flows involved.
keywords: infrared radiation, greenhouse gases, surface temperature, optical transmittance, infrared opacity, heat flow, climate science education, computer model

title: Measuring mutual inductance with op-amp integrator: a hands-on undergraduate experiment
text: Abstract This paper presents a redesigned undergraduate experiment that emphasizes the practical and pedagogical significance of mutual inductance. The setup enables direct measurement of the mutual inductance between two magnetically coupled coils at various angular orientations (0°–180°). It realizes the role of integrating the induced current to determine the total charge flowing through the secondary coil. The integration is performed by an operational amplifier integrator circuit. The experimentally obtained mutual inductance values are cross-checked and validated by comparing with those derived from the total inductances of the two coils connected in series under aiding and opposing configurations. The experiment enhances students’ conceptual understanding of electromagnetic induction and fosters hands-on engagement with analogue computation in experimental physics.
keywords: mutual inductance, electromagnetic induction, magnetically coupled coils, analog computing, hands-on physics experiments, undergraduate physics education

title: An integrated sequence of laboratory activities to promote modelling and graphical analysis in introductory physics
text: Abstract This paper presents an integrated sequence of introductory physics laboratory activities designed to promote modelling, graphical analysis, and uncertainty reasoning. The approach combines pairs of complementary experiments for the determination of liquid density, the elastic constant of a spring, and gravitational acceleration, while emphasizing the common methodological framework used to analyze experimental data. In each case, theoretical relationships are reformulated into linear forms that allow experimental results to be interpreted through graphical models, with physical parameters obtained from the slopes of fitted lines. The activities also highlight the process of transforming nonlinear relationships into linear representations and comparing results obtained through independent methods. Rather than focusing solely on the numerical determination of physical constants, the proposed sequence emphasizes modelling, data interpretation, and the role of experimental uncertainty in evaluating physical models. Because the experiments rely on standard laboratory equipment and widely accessible measurement techniques, the framework can be readily implemented in undergraduate teaching laboratories to support the development of fundamental experimental skills.
keywords: introductory physics laboratory, modeling, graphical method, uncertainty reasoning, experimental uncertainty, liquid density, gravitational acceleration, data interpretation, experimental skills, undergraduate physics education

title: Enhanced damping of shallow-water sloshing induced by hydrophobic walls: a counterintuitive laboratory experiment for undergraduate physics
text: Abstract It is often expected that hydrophobic walls reduce viscous dissipation. However, our experimental results show that they instead increase the damping of shallow-water sloshing while leaving the natural oscillation frequency essentially unchanged. Two geometrically identical acrylic containers, differing only in wall wettability, are impulsively excited and the subsequent free-surface decay is recorded using a smartphone camera. Contrary to intuitive expectations, the hydrophobic container exhibits a decay time nearly three times shorter than the hydrophilic container. A shallow-water model reduces the dynamics to a damped harmonic oscillator, allowing students to extract frequency and decay rate independently through nonlinear regression and spectral analysis. The experiment provides a clear and accessible laboratory activity for upper-level undergraduate courses, illustrating the separation between restoring forces and dissipative mechanisms, the role of boundary conditions, and the exponential decay of mechanical energy in oscillatory systems.
keywords: hydrophobic walls, wall wettability, damping, viscous dissipation, damped harmonic oscillator, restoring force, boundary conditions, undergraduate physics laboratory, smartphone video analysis

title: Entropy and heat beyond special cases
text: Abstract Starting from the fundamental energy equation and the first law of thermodynamics, we derive a general relation between entropy and heat that helps to avoid common misconceptions encountered in teaching thermodynamics. The approach avoids relying on overly restrictive equations that can lead to conceptual confusion and limited pedagogical insight. Applications to representative thermodynamic processes illustrate the instructional value of the derived relation.
keywords: entropy, heat, first law of thermodynamics, thermodynamic processes

title: Verification of Snell’s law using digital photography and laser light
text: Abstract We present a low-cost, high-precision laboratory method for verifying Snell’s law using laser illumination and smartphone-based digital photography. Unlike the conventional pin-tracing method that relies on manual alignment and angular measurement with a protractor, the present approach determines the refraction angle through geometric analysis of a digitally recorded image in a plane-parallel glass slab.
keywords: Snell's law, refraction, smartphone photography, laser illumination, optics education

title: The physics of gudeg: learning the mechanics and thermal properties using collaborative project based activities for the high school physics
text: Abstract In this paper, we describe a presentation on the physics of gudeg, a traditional food from Indonesia specifically originated in the special district of Yogyakarta. This learning context is designed for the high school physics curricula. The physics presentation focuses on the making processes of gudeg. Qualitative interviews with gudeg makers were carried out by the researchers to thematise the process of making gudeg and highlight its educational connections for the physics learning. Five extracted learning themes are how the density concept behind peeling the jackfruit skin (main gudeg ingredient), how the relation between the young’s modulus concept and the jackfruit sections, how the texture-torque experiment of the sweet and tasty gudeg, how the effect of boiling mechanism on the texture of the jackfruit, and how the conduction and convection of the preserved gudeg. Using our learning strategy which is so-called ‘Collaborative Project based Teaching’, we provide simple experimentations and demonstrations of the physical concepts behind these gudeg processes that are promising for conceptual physics learning by managing triple educational roles between teachers, students, and gudeg practitioners. This approach can be generally adopted beyond physics to promote the excitement of traditional knowledge which can enhance pedagogical approach in educational setting.
keywords: gudeg, traditional food, high school physics, collaborative project-based learning, Artocarpus heterophyllus, density, Young's modulus, torque, boiling, heat conduction, thermal convection, traditional knowledge, Yogyakarta

title: Rolling marbles, energy conservation, and the frontiers of science
text: Abstract A simple classroom experiment is described that uses a marble rolling down an inclined plane to teach students the relationship between gravitational potential energy, and linear and rotational kinetic energy. A marble is rolled down a 1 m-long aluminium channel set at five inclinations, and a mobile phone video camera used to measure the time for the marble to roll from the top to the bottom of the track. Uniform acceleration of the marble is assumed. The acceleration time is used to calculate the final linear velocity and kinetic energy knowing the mass of the marble. The linear velocity is used to calculate the angular velocity of the marble, assuming no slippage. The sum of the linear and rotation energies is plotted against initial potential energy. The experiment is useful for teaching students about conservation of energy, and the role this has played in major discoveries in physics, for example the discovery of the neutrino, dark matter, and dark energy.
keywords: inclined plane, conservation of energy, gravitational potential energy, rotational kinetic energy, angular velocity, uniformly accelerated motion, neutrino discovery, dark matter, dark energy, history of physics

title: Comment on ‘Work done by sliding friction on an incline’
text: Abstract When an object slides across a surface, macroscopic mechanics cannot predict how the total thermal energy that is generated gets partitioned between the object and the surface. However, thermodynamics defines work as a quantity of energy gained (or lost) by one system with an equal amount lost (or gained) by another system (called the surroundings of the first system) as a result of a force acting between them. Using this definition, the work that the object (taken to be the system) performs on the surface (taken to be the surroundings) due to sliding friction cannot be determined solely from knowledge of the initial and final bulk mechanical energies involved.
keywords: sliding friction, work done by friction, heat generation, energy allocation, mechanical energy, incline, heat dissipation

title: Reply to Comment on ‘Work done by sliding friction on an incline’
text: Reply to Comment on ‘Work done by sliding friction on an incline’. Keywords: sliding friction, work done by friction, inclined plane, work-energy theorem, friction force
keywords: sliding friction, work done by friction, inclined plane, work-energy theorem, friction force

title: Development of a low-cost teslameter for study a magnetic dipole moment of permanent neodymium magnets
text: Abstract In this paper, we present the construction of low-cost educational teslameters and the use for the magnetic field measurements of permanent neodymium magnets to demonstrate the behavior of magnetic dipoles. Our framework is based on the Arduino program in an educational context. We observed a good agreement between the experimental results and those obtained using a commercial Tesla meter (Phywe Teslameter). The main purpose of this work is to design and construct a magnetic field measuring device and to help students understand the meaning of the dipole magnetic field, and to determine the magnetic dipole behavior of a magnetic field produced by of permanent neodymium magnets by doing the experiment. They have proved that the magnetic field is inversely proportional to the cube of the distance, B( x ) ∼ 1/ x −3 , which is in agreement with the theoretical analysis. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ubon Ratchathani University.
keywords: Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets, permanent magnets, magnetic dipole moment, magnetic field measurement, Arduino, inverse cube law

title: Enacting simulations in physics micro-teaching: insights into pre-service teachers’ TPACK
text: Abstract Digital simulations are widely used in physics education; however, their instructional value depends not on their mere presence, but on how and when they are pedagogically and epistemically enacted during physics teaching. This study examines how pre-service physics teachers integrate digital simulations within microteaching contexts, with particular attention to the phase-dependent roles assigned to simulations across the 5E instructional model. Adopting a qualitative multiple case study design, the study draws on classroom observations, analytic observation rubrics, lesson plans, instructional artefacts, and semi-structured interviews from three pre-service physics teachers purposefully selected to represent contrasting levels of instructional enactment. Data were analysed through a two-stage process combining within-case analysis and cross-case comparison, aligned with the phases of the 5E model and physics-specific dimensions of technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK). To support analytic transparency, a participant-specific pedagogical enactment heatmap was constructed to visualise the depth and distribution of simulation use across instructional phases. The findings reveal clear differences in both the pedagogical depth and phase-specific distribution of simulation use. Inquiry-oriented enactment of simulations was strongly associated with higher instructional quality, whereas demonstrative or fragmented uses aligned with lower-quality teaching practices. Importantly, effective simulation use was not confined to the explore phase but extended meaningfully into the explain and elaborate phases when simulations were orchestrated as epistemic tools supporting causal-mechanistic reasoning, coordination of multiple representations, and conceptual sense-making. These findings position simulation use as a dynamic, phase-dependent component of technology-enhanced physics instruction and highlight the importance of supporting pre-service teachers in regulating simulations as epistemic resources rather than as visual aids. The study contributes a practice-oriented perspective on TPACK as enacted knowledge and offers implications for the design of simulation-focused learning experiences in physics teacher education. While these findings offer valuable insights into TPACK enactment, the simulated nature of microteaching highlights the need for further research in authentic classroom settings.
keywords: digital simulation, microteaching, pre-service physics teachers, TPACK, 5E instructional model, multiple representations, physics teacher education

title: Using consumer cameras to observe scintillation light from radiation
text: Abstract For a long time, the cloud chamber was the only educational tool available for measuring ionising radiation, such as alpha, beta, and gamma rays. In recent years, simple radiation detectors combining scintillators with silicon photomultipliers have become increasingly common for these purposes. However, students are not able to see the scintillation light, the core process of radiation measurements with scintillators. Therefore, we explored the possibility of detecting scintillation light using two widely available consumer cameras: an ordinary digital camera and an inexpensive cooled astronomical camera. In addition, we examined how differences in the spatial distribution relate to radiation types and energies. Scintillation light could be measured with these consumer cameras, and its spatial distribution reflects the radiation energy. This method could be utilised as an accessible imaging setup to compare radiation properties in a classroom, without the need for specialised, high-cost photodetectors.
keywords: scintillation light, scintillation detectors, consumer cameras, digital camera imaging, ionizing radiation, radiation education, radiation energy, low-cost radiation detector

title: Optimizing smartphone magnetometer measurements: an experimental design for magnetic moment determination incorporating Helmholtz coil calibration
text: Abstract While smartphone sensors offer unprecedented accessibility for physics education, the raw data they produce often suffer from hardware variability, limiting their use in rigorous scientific inquiry. This study proposes a systematic experimental framework designed to transform smartphones into high-precision instruments for electromagnetic measurements. The core of this methodology is a robust two-step calibration process: the precise localization of the internal magnetometer sensor, followed by device-specific standardization using a Helmholtz coil. Experimental results demonstrate that by applying a derived calibration factor ( k = 1.0317 ), the measured vacuum permeability μ 0 achieved a percentage error as low as 0.7083%. Furthermore, in the determination of the magnetic dipole moment M , the relative standard deviation remained below 2%, exhibiting exceptional stability. This framework has been successfully integrated into the introductory physics laboratory at Feng Chia University, involving over 1000 students. The large-scale implementation confirms that the proposed calibration modules effectively bridge the gap between digital sensor outputs and rigorous scientific standards, ensuring reproducibility across diverse hardware and student skill levels.
keywords: smartphone magnetometer, magnetometer calibration, Helmholtz coil, magnetic dipole moment, vacuum permeability, node localization, experimental design, physics laboratory, low-cost instrumentation, reproducibility

title: Effect of e-readiness skills, self-efficacy, and physics literacy on pre-service teachers’ misconceptions
text: Abstract This study investigates the influence of e-readiness skills (ERS), physics literacy (PL), and self-efficacy (SE) on pre-service teachers’ misconceptions in physics. This study utilised a quantitative design using a survey method. Data were collected from 122 participants using validated instruments measuring ERS, SE, PL, and misconceptions. Descriptive results indicate high ERS and SE levels, moderate PL proficiency, and persistent misconceptions across several physics topics. Multiple linear regression analysis reveals that PL significantly predicts misconceptions, whereas ERS and SE show no significant effects. The model accounts for 16.5% of the variance in misconceptions, suggesting that content mastery exerts greater influence than digital readiness or teaching confidence. These findings underscore the importance of strengthening pre-service teachers’ conceptual understanding and scientific reasoning through curriculum and teacher education programmes that integrate digital skills and scientific-based learning.
keywords: self-efficacy, physics literacy, physics misconceptions, pre-service teachers, digital readiness, teacher professional development, conceptual understanding, scientific reasoning

title: Calculating a journey to Mars with introductory physics
text: Abstract The problem of a crewed mission to Mars provides a compelling and realistic context for teaching introductory physics. In this work, we present a coherent set of calculations describing a round-trip journey between Earth and Mars, using only mathematical tools accessible at the high-school level. The treatment integrates key topics that are typically taught separately—such as Newtonian gravitation, energy, circular motion, and basic astrodynamics—into a single coherent framework. The analysis includes Hohmann transfer orbits, travel times, launch conditions, and mission constraints, illustrating how a complex real-world problem can be transformed into an effective classroom resource. This work aims to support teachers and students in exploring interplanetary travel as an accessible and motivating application of fundamental physics.
keywords: Mars missions, Newtonian gravity, circular motion, orbital dynamics, interplanetary travel, travel time, launch conditions, mission constraints, high school physics

title: Active learning strategies on addressing misconceptions in electromagnetic induction concepts
text: Abstract Misconceptions in electromagnetic induction pose significant barriers to effective learning among high school students. This study investigates the effectiveness of active learning strategies in addressing these misconceptions among 11th-grade students in Mahvelat, Iran. A sample of 40 students was randomly assigned to experimental (active learning) and control (traditional teaching) groups. Data were collected using standardized pre- and post-tests with a confirmed validity by physics experts and a Cronbach’s alpha reliability of 0.798. The intervention consisted of 10 sessions of 75 min each. Data analysis using ANCOVA and Bonferroni post-hoc tests revealed that active learning strategies, including group work, hands-on projects, and field trips, significantly reduced misconceptions (from 33% to 9% in the experimental group) and improved conceptual understanding compared to traditional methods. These findings suggest that active learning strategies are effective in enhancing physics education.
keywords: active learning, misconceptions, electromagnetic induction, high school students, group work, hands-on projects, field trips, conceptual understanding, conventional instruction comparison

title: Exploring learners’ understanding and use of positive and negative signs in electrostatics
text: Abstract Electrostatics is a crucial topic in physics, one that requires learners to understand the meanings of signs used to represent electric charges, forces, and fields. This paper reports findings of a mixed method study that explored 395 physical sciences learners’ understanding and use of positive (+) and negative (−) signs in the topic of electrostatics prescribed in the South African curriculum. A test comprising multiple-choice and calculation-based questions was designed to examine learners’ understanding and use of positive and negative signs across various electrostatic contexts. The study was framed by the categories of the meaning of signs in physics, namely direction, opposition, change, and compound. Quantitative and qualitative data were collected and analysed using descriptive statistics and content analysis. The results revealed that some learners lacked an adequate understanding of signs and were unable to use them to solve various problems of electrostatics. Based on the findings, recommendations for teaching electrostatics were made.
keywords: electrostatics, electric charge, electric force, electric field, meaning of signs, physics misconceptions

title: Generating interactive smartphone physics laboratories using artificial intelligence
text: Abstract We present an AI-generated, browser-based interactive laboratory tool designed to support experimental physics education on smartphones and personal computers. The application, produced entirely via conversational prompts to the Claude AI assistant (Anthropic), implements a dual-channel sine-wave generator (0–2000 Hz) and a real-time microphone waveform visualiser within a single HTML file that requires no installation. The Web Audio API, embedded in all modern browsers, provides low-latency audio synthesis and time-domain analysis at sampling rates up to 48 kHz, making the tool functionally comparable to dedicated hardware signal generators and oscilloscopes. We exemplify its use through the acoustic beat phenomenon: two smartphones are deployed simultaneously, one running the generator and one running the visualiser, allowing a classical two-source interference experiment to be reproduced with no additional equipment. Beat frequencies measured for the pairs (400, 450) Hz and (1000, 1050) Hz agree with theoretical predictions to within 1%, demonstrating a level of accuracy suitable for introductory university physics laboratories. The application exports data as CSV files and screen captures as PNG images, enabling quantitative analysis with standard software. The workflow for generating such a tool through AI prompting is described in detail, providing educators with a replicable template for creating custom, zero-cost browser-based physics laboratories.
keywords: Web Audio API, sine wave generator

title: Socratic dialogue and guided experimentation: an approach to teaching mechanics in physics teacher training
text: Abstract This article analyses a didactic activity developed with pre-service physics teachers aimed at investigating the evolution of students’ reasoning when confronted with a novel problem involving forces and the application of Newton’s laws. The proposal integrated guided experimentation and Socratic dialogue as mediating strategies to foster conceptual reflection and critical thinking. Participants were challenged to explain a non-everyday phenomenon—fixing a pen to a wall without using glue—and to represent their ideas through free-body diagrams. The Socratic dialogue, conducted by the researchers, encouraged hypothesis formulation, identification of contradictions, and collective conceptual reconstruction. The dialogues generated during the activity were transcribed and analysed using Bardin’s content analysis methodology within a qualitative research framework. The results indicate that the approach promoted engagement, curiosity, and a deeper understanding of physical concepts, underscoring the pedagogical potential of dialogic interaction and experimentation in physics education. The study contributes to the initial training of physics teachers by evidencing the value of dialogical and inquiry-based practices. Supplementary material is provided, including a detailed description of the activity, excerpts from students’ dialogues, free-body diagrams produced during the intervention, and the analytical procedures adopted, supporting transparency and facilitating replication or adaptation of the proposed approach.
keywords: Socratic dialogue, pre-service physics teachers, physics teacher education, Newton's laws of motion, force, free-body diagrams, conceptual change, critical thinking, dialogic interaction, inquiry-based learning, student reasoning

title: Democratising scientific software in physics education: AI-assisted custom instrumentation for teachers
text: Abstract Published Arduino-based mechanics experiments reveal a continued accessibility paradox: while sensor hardware costs are minimal, the software required for instrumentation control and data analysis can be financially restrictive for school practitioners, limiting access to enhanced analytical techniques. This paper contributes to addressing this gap by showing how AI-assisted Python development enables KS4-5 secondary school physics teachers, without formal programming training, to extend Arduino-based experiments using entirely free software. A worked example is presented in which a complete graphical user interface for spring oscillation measurements is developed with large language models. The development process, challenges encountered, and implications for classroom practice are discussed. The resulting system provides real-time data acquisition, automated analysis, and data visualisation, including curve fitting to anharmonic oscillator models and numerical derivative calculations. Static and dynamic spring constant measurements show good agreement (19.94 ± 0.13 N m −1 and 20.44 ± 0.14 N m −1 respectively), validating the approach. The method generalises to a wide range of Arduino-based experiments and demonstrates that sophisticated data acquisition and analysis are now accessible to individual educators at low cost. A short demonstration video of the apparatus and workflow is available at https://zenodo.org/records/17980784.
keywords: Arduino, large language models, AI-assisted programming, Python, free software, graphical user interface, data acquisition, anharmonic oscillator, curve fitting, numerical differentiation, secondary school teachers

title: Typical approach in technical texts on gyroscopic rigidity and models developed by students
text: Abstract In technical aircraft maintenance courses, concepts such as gyroscopic rigidity are often taught descriptively, without recourse to mathematical or physical formalisation. This study, conducted within a military technical school (Escola de Especialistas de Aeronáutica, Brazil), examined the mental models developed by students after exposure to such an approach, using the attitude indicator—an aircraft navigation instrument—as a contextualising element. The research followed a qualitative, interaction-based methodology grounded in Vygotsky’s sociohistorical framework. Students were first presented with a typical descriptive explanation of gyroscopic rigidity from the technical manuals. They were then asked to graphically represent the behaviour of the rotation of a free gyroscope at different latitudes. Instructor and peer interactions were encouraged, and targeted mediations were applied according to the models initially developed by the students. Two distinct student models have emerged. The first model interpreted rigidity as relative to the earth’s horizontal, meaning that the rotation axis would remain horizontal regardless of latitude. The second model aligned more closely with the physical principle of absolute rigidity in space, wherein the rotation axis maintained its initial orientation independent of latitude. The descriptive approach commonly used in technical texts can lead to divergent and incomplete mental models of gyroscopic rigidity. Effective learning requires structured mediation to address these specific misconceptions, particularly through hands-on interactions with physical instruments and peer dialogue. This study highlights the importance of adapting instruction to students’ cultural and educational backgrounds, especially in heterogeneous classrooms, to foster an accurate conceptual understanding of technical physics education.
keywords: gyroscopic precession, mental models, student misconceptions, attitude indicator, technical manuals, peer interaction, latitude effects, conceptual understanding, heterogeneous classrooms

title: Making thermoelectric current visible: Arduino data acquisition with Blynk mobile visualisation in physics classroom
text: Abstract Thermoelectric generators provide an accessible context for teaching energy conversion because their electrical output varies dynamically with thermal conditions and circuit loading. This paper presents a thermoelectric real-time measurement system (TRMS) as a classroom-ready approach that makes thermoelectric current visible in real time using an Arduino-compatible Wi-Fi microcontroller and Blynk mobile visualisation. In two related configurations, the TRMS supports temperature-gradient monitoring and extended electrical characterisation, allowing temperature, voltage, current, power, and energy to be displayed on a smartphone dashboard as live numerical indicators and time-series plots. Pedagogically, the approach helps students relate temperature difference, load, and electrical response during heating and cooling, rather than treating measurements as isolated values. The TRMS can be used as a ready-to-run instrument for guided inquiry or as a student-built system for measurement-design and project-based learning. Two model investigations are presented to illustrate classroom implementation. The approach offers a low-cost and adaptable alternative for real-time thermoelectric experimentation, while also highlighting practical considerations of Wi-Fi-based mobile logging in school settings.
keywords: thermoelectric generators, thermoelectric current, energy conversion, Arduino, Blynk, real-time data acquisition, temperature gradient, electrical characterization, project-based learning, inquiry-based learning, low-cost instrumentation, physics classroom

title: Diagnosing pre-service teachers’ thermodynamics reasoning: linking definitions to model-based explanations across contexts
text: Abstract Understanding how learners define and mentally model thermodynamic concepts is essential for meaningful conceptual development. This study examined pre-service science teachers’ definitional knowledge of heat, temperature, and internal energy; their model-based explanations across multiple thermal contexts; and the coherence between these two forms of knowledge. Data were collected from written responses to a five-item open-ended assessment administered to forty-eight participants. Qualitative content analysis was conducted using a coding framework informed by conceptual change perspectives, model-based reasoning, and representational approaches. The analysis of definitions revealed three levels of understanding: conceptual confusion, partially correct but relationally inconsistent explanations, and scientifically accurate yet not fully integrated descriptions. Most participants demonstrated transitional patterns, using correct terminology without establishing mechanistic relationships. Explanations generated for contextual thermal problems produced three types of mental models: fragmented single-variable models, context-dependent hybrid models, and integrated macro–micro–symbolic models. Only one participant demonstrated a fully integrated model. Cross-analysis indicated a partial alignment between definitional levels and mental model types. Crucially, correct definitions did not reliably predict coherent causal reasoning across contexts. These findings suggest that learners activate different cognitive resources depending on the thermal situation, even when they can reproduce scientific terminology. For physics teacher education, this implies a shift from definition-focused instruction to model construction, model comparison, and explicit coordination of macro–micro–symbolic representations.
keywords: pre-service science teachers, model-based reasoning, mental models, heat, temperature, internal energy, conceptual change, causal reasoning, physics teacher education

title: Enhancing students’ critical thinking skill and understanding of solar energy through STEM education with Arduino-based sensors
text: Abstract This project aims to integrate STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) education with hands-on applications in high school physics, focusing on fostering critical thinking and problem-solving skills. STEM education encourages students to apply knowledge and skills from various disciplines to solve real-world problems, promoting creativity and innovation. In this project, a 3 ± 0.15 W solar panel (18 V, 0.167 A) serves as the primary energy source, supporting two interconnected circuits: an automatic plant watering system and a traffic light model. The system incorporates a solar charge controller (12 V/24 V, 30 A) and a 12 V, 5 Ah rechargeable battery to efficiently power both circuits while optimizing energy usage. A moisture sensor, connected to an Arduino Uno, monitors soil moisture levels and triggers the watering mechanism for a medium-sized plant and multiple plants. The traffic light prototype, designed with four corners and a pedestrian signal powered by LEDs (1.8 V–3.2 V), is also solar-powered. This project not only demonstrates the principles of energy conversion, storage, and consumption, but also provides students with the application of physics concepts such as voltage, current, energy efficiency, and sustainable energy. Through this project, students develop their critical thinking and problem-solving skills by analyzing the energy supply and calculating the system’s energy balance to ensure the efficient operation of both circuits. By bridging theory with practice, this project encourages students to engage with STEM concepts and apply them to everyday challenges.
keywords: STEM education, critical thinking, solar energy, Arduino sensors, soil moisture sensors, solar charge controller, energy balance, high school physics, hands-on learning, energy efficiency

title: ‘Niñas Atómicas’ (Atomic Girls): an initiative that generates opportunities for young girls in STEM
text: Abstract We report on an initiative that seeks to encourage high school girls to develop critical thinking and transferable skills widely used in scientific work, as well as to generate a concrete space of opportunities for girls to experience how real science is done. Our ‘Niñas Atómicas’ workshop combines the teaching of particle physics, electronics, programming and scientific methodology through building and operating a dedicated experiment: a muon counter. Girls from all over Chile can apply to this workshop, where every year they are guided by female scientists for two weeks. We report on the contents and methodology of our workshop and provide details on how to build the muon detector. We report results on muon flux and proper lifetime, two muon properties which can be extracted from the data collected by the girls with the muon detectors they built themselves. Insights into the girl’s experiences during the 2024 and 2025 editions of the workshop are also detailed, with the aim to contribute to the wider physics education research and outreach communities.
keywords: girls in STEM, high school girls, particle physics outreach, muon flux, electronics workshop, programming, research methodology, critical thinking, transferable skills, science education

title: Exploring a blended laboratory strategy to enhance secondary school students’ achievement in physics practical
text: Abstract Practical activities are essential for effective physics instruction; however, their implementation in secondary schools is often constrained by inadequate or unavailable laboratory apparatus. Advances in educational technology, such as virtual and blended laboratory strategies, provide alternative means for teaching physics practical. This study examined the effects of virtual laboratory and blended laboratory strategies on secondary school students’ achievement in physics practical. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was employed, involving 194 Senior Secondary School II students (72 males and 122 females) selected from a population of 21 576 using a multistage sampling technique. Data were collected using the physics practical achievement test, which was validated by experts and yielded a reliability coefficient of 0.815. The instrument was administered before and after a four-week instructional intervention. Data were analysed using mean, normalised mean gain, and Analysis of Covariance. The findings revealed that students taught using the blended laboratory strategy achieved the highest normalised mean gain (25.8%), followed by those exposed to the physical laboratory method (23.6%), while the virtual laboratory group recorded the lowest gain (13.2%). The results further indicated that gender had no significant effect on students’ achievement in blended laboratory strategy ( p = 0.119). The study recommends increased awareness, teacher training, and professional development workshops to promote effective implementation of blended laboratory strategy in physics practical instruction.
keywords: virtual laboratory, physics practicals, high school students, physics achievement, educational technology, gender differences in achievement, teacher professional development

title: Quantum physics concepts in Greek upper secondary physics and chemistry textbooks: implications for curriculum coherence
text: Abstract Quantum physics plays a central role in contemporary science and technology, while school textbooks mediate curriculum intentions and classroom practice. This study examines how quantum physics concepts are represented in Greek upper secondary physics and chemistry textbooks. A qualitative content analysis was conducted on the officially prescribed student textbooks used in all three grades of the Greek General Lyceum. The analysis investigated the presence, distribution, pedagogical framing, and cross-disciplinary coherence of quantum concepts across subjects and grade levels. The findings indicate that quantum content is largely absent in the first two grades of physics and becomes concentrated in the final grade, where it is predominantly presented descriptively. In chemistry, quantum concepts appear earlier but are mainly embedded within application-oriented discussions of atomic structure. Across both subjects, probabilistic and epistemological dimensions receive limited attention, and cross-disciplinary alignment remains weak. These patterns suggest that quantum theory is presented through parallel disciplinary trajectories rather than as an integrated conceptual framework.
keywords: quantum physics, school textbooks, upper secondary school, curriculum coherence, physics textbook, chemistry textbook, atomic structure, probabilistic interpretation, epistemology of quantum mechanics, textbook content analysis

title: Interactive simulations for teaching geometric optics exploring didactically the paraxial approximation limits
text: Abstract The teaching of geometric optics involving spherical surfaces is generally limited, for pedagogical reasons, to the paraxial approximation in elementary physics textbooks, as well as in virtual simulation platforms. However, quite often, these didactic materials end up excessively stretching the validity of the approximation, applying it in situations in which it could not be simply applied, possibly generating misconceptions about the physical phenomena being conveyed. In this work, we present the development of two interactive simulations from scratch, using GeoGebra, aimed at teaching geometric optics exploring didactically the paraxial approximation limits. The first simulation explores the process of image formation in spherical mirrors, similarly to what is done in textbooks, but not avoiding the distortions in the images (optical aberrations) that occur beyond the validity regime of the paraxial approximation. The second simulation aims to didactically explore how far we can stretch the validity of the approximation while maintaining its reasonableness, and what happens beyond that. It provides an in-depth examination of the conditions for the formation of a focus, specifically considering a hemispherical shaped mirror. We follow a flexible approach in the construction process of the simulations, so that the teacher may implement their own adjustments, according to their specific teaching objectives, without the need for programming skills.
keywords: geometrical optics, paraxial approximation, spherical mirrors, image formation, optical aberrations, focus formation, interactive simulation, GeoGebra, physics education, misconceptions, approximation validity

title: Real-time camera experiments with phyphox
text: Abstract Smartphone-based experimentation tends to split into real-time sensor-based approaches and post hoc analysis of camera recordings. We present a novel approach to use the phone’s camera in real-time experiments using the open source app phyphox. For this, users can select an area of the camera image and choose to determine one or multiple of meaningful aggregated properties as luma, relative luminance and the coordinates of the HSV colour model (hue, saturation and value) for this area. With frame rates of up to 240 Hz, many periodic processes can be captured just by pointing the camera at the experiment. The physical properties derived from the camera data are integrated into the flexible analysis system in phyphox allowing for customizable data analysis for a wide range of new experiments. Examples include but are not limited to measurements at (large) distances, enhancing existing experiments with modern data analysis and various applications for precise timing measurements.
keywords: Phyphox, smartphone camera, real-time measurement, LUMA, relative luminance, image analysis, timing measurement, physics experiments, open-source apps

title: Comment on ‘Work done during a head-on elastic collision’
text: Abstract A general model for a one-dimensional elastic collision between two balls is proposed, and the relevant definitions and calculations of work, kinetic energy, and potential energy are clarified.

title: Discovering cosmic rays: a course for in-service upper secondary school teachers
text: Abstract The refresher course ‘Exploring Cosmic Rays’ took place at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratories in Italy in December 2023 and saw the participation of 17 in-service teachers from all over Italy. The 2.5 d residential course provided an opportunity to delve into the fascinating topic of cosmic rays, the experiments observing them, and to learn more about the messages they can bring from space. During the practical sessions, participants actively contributed to building a muon telescope, conducted a measurement of the muon flux, and analysed the data. Significant focus was placed on developing educational pathways to create concrete and usable outputs. The goal of the course was to provide a diverse overview of the topic, allowing participants to become familiar with the activities, experience them firsthand, and enhance their existing knowledge and skills. In the months following the course the teachers were encouraged to develop teaching pathways based on the course content and to implement the activities in the classroom. In this article we present the goals, structure and content of the course as well as the follow-up work by the teachers. An evaluation of the course is followed by a discussion of the requirements for successful implementation of modern physics in upper secondary school teaching curricula.
keywords: cosmic rays, continuing teacher education, senior high school physics, muon flux measurement, teacher professional development, modern physics education, Gran Sasso National Laboratory

title: Using disc golf to teach the four phases of projectile flight
text: Abstract This article describes how I use disc golf to teach the four phases of projectile flight to advanced ballistics students, including those with naval experience, mapped to internal, transitional, external, and terminal ballistics. Although a disc and a naval round differ in geometry and spin axis, both are governed by the same forces: angular momentum, drag, lift, and gravity. At 20–35 m s −1 , a disc makes these forces observable in real time. Since introducing the exercise, students have reported clearer understanding of the transition and free flight phases, and quiz scores on those topics have improved.
keywords: disc golf, projectile motion, internal ballistics, exterior ballistics, terminal ballistics, drag, lift force, angular momentum, gravity

title: Determining the level of student’s understanding of concepts related to gravitation
text: Abstract This study investigates the level of conceptual understanding and identifies common misconceptions related to gravitation among students of classes IX–XII studying in government schools located in remote hilly regions of Uttarakhand, India. The research was conducted with 102 students from different schools during the academic year 2025–26. A set of 15 descriptive questions was administered to assess student’s understanding of fundamental concepts of gravitation. Student’s responses were evaluated using a rubric-based star rating scale and analysed through descriptive statistical methods. The results indicate that although students exhibit basic familiarity with gravitational concepts, substantial conceptual gaps persist, particularly in mathematical interpretation, conceptual reasoning, and higher-order cognitive understanding.
keywords: gravity, conceptual understanding, misconceptions, high school students, Uttarakhand, conceptual gaps, higher-order thinking skills

title: Systematic heat loss in open calorimetric systems: a modelling-based approach to teaching enthalpy
text: Abstract Laboratory activities aimed at teaching thermodynamic concepts often rely on simplified experimental setups, particularly in educational contexts with limited resources. One common consequence of such conditions is the appearance of systematic discrepancies between theoretical and experimental values, especially when calorimetric measurements are performed using open or imperfect systems. This paper analyses a set of temperature measurements obtained from the dissolution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in water using improvised calorimeters. Rather than seeking to optimise calorimetric accuracy, the study characterises the systematic error inherent to open systems and examines its potential pedagogical significance in the teaching of enthalpy. A simple model incorporating a corrective term, γ , is introduced to represent heat losses to the environment. The analysis suggests that non-ideal experimental conditions can provide a structured context for discussing systematic error, model assumptions and non-ideal behaviour in thermodynamics. In addition, an open-access web application is presented to facilitate exploratory analysis of how variations in temperature measurements influence calculated enthalpy values. The work constitutes a theoretically grounded instructional proposal based on experimental analysis and illustrates how a modelling framework can support reflective discussion of systematic error in resource-limited laboratory settings.
keywords: systematic errors, heat loss, enthalpy, thermochemistry, thermodynamic modeling, temperature measurement, chemistry education

title: The massive dinosaur extinction: revisiting the bases of the asteroid impact hypothesis in primary and secondary school
text: Abstract In this work, the elements constituting the asteroid impact hypothesis for the Cretaceous–Tertiary extinction are revisited. In contrast to standard approaches based on the retrieval of factual information, this approach enables students to follow the logical, interdisciplinary pathway that scientists undertook to reach the current state of knowledge. Specific didactic sequences are designed to address the topic at both upper primary/lower secondary and upper secondary levels.
keywords: dinosaur extinction, Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, asteroid impact hypothesis, science education, elementary school, secondary schools, didactic sequence, interdisciplinary learning, scientific inquiry, history of science

title: Technical development and application of a virtual reality-based physics laboratory exercise
text: Abstract In this study, we present the technical aspect of a physics lab exercise created and executed in a virtual reality setting to help undergraduate students understand the process of gathering measurements and applying statistics. Subsequently, we assessed the effectiveness of the virtual laboratory training approach with two groups of high school students aged 14 years old. The pupils were separated into two groups of 18 participants each. The first group practiced the exercise in the physical laboratory under the supervision of a teacher, and another carried out the virtual reality laboratory independently. To determine the effectiveness of the learning experience, both groups were given four common questions to answer. Their answers show no difference in the scores achieved by the two groups. Additionally, they had to respond to some questions to evaluate their opinion about the virtual reality laboratory exercise, which revealed no difference between the two groups’ answers.
keywords: virtual reality, physics laboratory, high school students, student perceptions

title: Demonstration experiment for observing Haidinger’s interference rings using microparticles deposited on reflective surfaces
text: Abstract A demonstration experiment for observing Haidinger’s interference rings (fringes of equal inclination) is proposed and experimentally implemented. The method uses microparticles deposited on the reflective surfaces of plane-parallel glass plates or flat mirrors. These particles act as localised secondary sources, converting the angular interference structure into a directly observable ring pattern on a screen in the far field. While similar observations have been reported for dusty mirrors, this work extends the technique to glass plates. We demonstrate that microparticles on both surfaces introduce additional coherent scattering paths exhibiting a similar angular phase dependence, leading to a pronounced enhancement of fringe visibility without altering the geometric arrangement of the rings. The experiment employs inexpensive and readily available equipment, such as a low-power semiconductor laser pointer, a glass plate, and a mirror, enabling stable interference patterns with high fringe visibility to be observed under standard classroom lighting. Quantitative analysis of the interference patterns is presented, including measurements of ring radii and determination of the glass plate thickness. The shifts of selected ring radii provide a direct and intuitive demonstration of the wavelength dependence of interference, allowing students to explore optical dispersion without the need for spectrometers. By combining classical interferometry with accessible experimental techniques and digital data processing, this approach makes Haidinger’s fringes readily observable and pedagogically effective for both secondary school and university laboratory exercises.
keywords: secondary sources, flat mirrors, optical dispersion, coherent scattering

title: A classroom activity on global glacier mass balance and glacier climate feedback
text: Abstract This article presents a didactic sequence for upper secondary physics that integrates climate change education through the analysis of glacier mass balance. Using authentic data from the World Glacier Monitoring Service (1980–2023), it is proposed that students engage in a collaborative inquiry and mathematical modelling to explore the accelerated decline of global glacier ice mass. The activity introduces climate feedback mechanisms through a simplified model that students fit to real observational data. By comparing model predictions with measurements, students discover that glacier mass loss acceleration results from positive feedback processes that amplify the effects of atmospheric warming, as quantified through an effective feedback coefficient. Data analysis enables students to project the complete melting of non-Greenland and non-Antarctic glaciers within a century. The pedagogical approach combines authentic scientific data, collaborative modelling, and socially relevant contexts to develop both disciplinary knowledge and transversal competences. The activity is designed for practical implementation using standard computational tools and publicly accessible data, contributing to scientific literacy and informed engagement with contemporary environmental challenges.
keywords: glacier mass balance, climate feedbacks, positive feedback, climate change education, mathematical modeling, scientific literacy, inquiry-based learning

title: Applied teaching of semiconductor physics: design and characterization of a low-cost Schottky diode device at the high school level
text: Abstract Although semiconductor physics is part of the high school curriculum, it often remains abstract and theoretical due to the high cost and complexity of fabrication processes. As a solution to this problem, this study presents a low-cost educational design that adapts the fabrication of an advanced topic, the Schottky barrier diode (Metal-Semiconductor Contact), to high school laboratory conditions. Using the engineering design process methodology, a diode was produced using P-type silicon, aluminium foil (for the ohmic contact), and conductive silver paste (for the Schottky contact). Instead of high-vacuum annealing furnaces, a partially controlled thermal process (15 min) using a 500 W halogen lamp was applied for the diffusion of the aluminium contact into the silicon. The electrical characterization of the produced prototype was performed using a standard component tester and a Keithley 2400 source meter (SMU). The quantitative findings of this study proved that the prototype exhibited a clear rectifying (switching) characteristic, with specific numerical parameters such as an ideality factor of n = 6.3 and a turn-on voltage of U f = 4.41 V. These results demonstrate that the fundamental principles of semiconductor fabrication can be effectively taught at the high school level using a safe, low-cost, and replicable experiment set.
keywords: Schottky diodes, semiconductor physics education, high school laboratories, low-cost fabrication, metal-semiconductor contacts, halogen lamp annealing, ideality factor, turn-on voltage, rectifying characteristics, engineering design process, p-type silicon

title: A burning stick in equilibrium on a thin flat base
text: Abstract The problem of determining the time it takes for a burning stick, resting on a thin flat base, to fall is examined. The kinematics of the burning point is used to determine the motion of the centre of mass of a system composed of three distinct sections with continuous mass distribution. With some caution, experimental proof of the calculation can be given.
keywords: center-of-mass motion, continuous mass distribution, equilibrium

title: How well do AI systems solve AP physics? A comparative evaluation of large language models on algebra-based free response questions
text: Abstract The rapid advancement of large language models has generated growing interest in their potential role in physics education and assessment, yet a focused evaluation of their performance on multi-faceted, free-response physics problems remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically evaluate the performance of four widely accessible AI systems—ChatGPT 4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude 4.0 Sonnet, and DeepSeek R1—on algebra-based advanced placement (AP) Physics 1 and AP Physics 2 free-response questions administered between 2015 and 2025. Model-generated solutions were produced under standardized exam-style prompting and evaluated by three independent physics experts using official College Board scoring guidelines. All models achieved relatively high mean scores (82%–92%), indicating strong capability in structured algebraic problem solving. However, substantial year-to-year variability was observed, particularly for AP Physics 1, where statistical testing revealed no consistent performance hierarchy among models. In contrast, AP Physics 2 results showed statistically significant differences, with Gemini and DeepSeek demonstrating more consistent performance than Claude, and numerically higher performance than ChatGPT, though the latter comparisons did not reach statistical significance.
