A qualitative analysis revealed recurring error patterns across all models, including misinterpretation of diagrams and graphs, incorrect graph construction, incorrect reasoning about vector direction, circuit topology errors, partial and misleading qualitative explanations, and difficulties applying three-dimensional concepts such as the right-hand rule. These findings suggest that while contemporary AI systems can effectively support routine physics problem solving, they remain limited in tasks requiring spatial reasoning, visual interpretation, and conceptual integration. The results highlight both the instructional potential and current pedagogical limitations of AI-assisted learning tools in physics education.
keywords: large language models, free-response questions, physics problem solving, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, model comparison, AI-assisted learning, spatial reasoning, right-hand rule

title: START SMART: reimagining physics education
text: Abstract We have developed a high school outreach and undergraduate recruitment program at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln designed to promote physics while showcasing the versatility of a physics education. Developments in microelectronics, robotics, artificial intelligence, and space exploration have unveiled the shortage of and need for professionals with a robust grounding in physics. Here, I outline our program and share experiences and resources freely accessible for integration with class and club activities or use at other colleges and universities. The workshops are run by physics undergraduates who enthusiastically share their experiences, insight, and ambitions with high school students. Carefully selected topics and activities help demystify the mathematics and physical principles through the creation of art.
keywords: physics outreach, high school outreach, undergraduate recruitment, student-led workshops, undergraduate physics students, arts-based learning, STEM workforce shortage

title: Arduino-based automated I – V curve tracer for physics laboratory
text: Abstract We present an automated current–voltage ( I – V ) curve tracer using the open-source Arduino platform, designed explicitly as structured, multi-stage student project for physics laboratory teaching. Retaining the classical circuit arrangement, the system digitizes voltage and current acquisition to generate accurate I – V curves. The DC variable voltage source is realized using the on-board digital-to-analogue converter, with an operational amplifier buffer to boost the output currents up to 250 mA. A digital temperature sensor extends the setup to explore temperature dependence of device characteristics. The curve tracer is validated against a high-end commercial I – V curve tracer and applied to resistors, silicon and germanium diodes, a light emitting diode, a Zener diode, and an incandescent bulb. Each phase of the project is mapped to explicit learning objectives, covering semiconductor device physics, analogue electronics, digital instrumentation, and experimental data analysis. A five-step guided measurement sequence is described, with commentary on the intended learning outcomes at each step, making the system suitable for both introductory and advanced undergraduate laboratory curricula.
keywords: I-V curve tracer, Arduino, physics experiment teaching, student projects, semiconductor device physics, diodes, Zener diode, light-emitting diodes, incandescent lamps, temperature dependence, digital-to-analog converter, digital instrumentation, analogue electronics, experimental data analysis

title: Identifying and addressing astronomy misconceptions among school students: a diagnostic pre–post assessment study
text: Abstract This study investigates alternative conceptions held by school students (Grades 6–11; approximately ages 11–16) in astronomy in Delhi, India (a context where informal explanations and cultural beliefs may shape astronomy ideas), and examines how classroom instruction influences conceptual change. A diagnostic pre-test was administered to identify prevalent misconceptions related to seasons, phases of the Moon, planets, asteroids, and the work of astronomers. Following a structured instructional intervention, an achievement post-test was conducted. Quantitative analysis of anonymized pre–post data from 150 students shows an overall improvement in performance, with a mean normalized gain of 0.47. Item-level analysis highlights concepts that respond well to instruction as well as misconceptions that remain resistant. The findings underscore the value of diagnostic assessment in astronomy education and provide evidence-based insights for improving instructional strategies in school-level science classrooms in similar contexts.
keywords: astronomy misconceptions, misconceptions, conceptual change, school students, seasons, lunar phases, planets, asteroids, astronomers, cultural beliefs, diagnostic assessment, educational intervention, science education

title: Initiation to science in secondary physics education: a conceptual approach to entropy
text: Abstract This paper examines the role of entropy in supporting an Initiation to Science within secondary physics education. It is argued that conventional approaches, often centred on problem-solving and formal manipulation, tend to weaken the epistemological meaning of key concepts, limiting students’ engagement with the nature of scientific knowledge. In contrast, a conceptual approach to entropy is proposed, in which its introduction is grounded in questions of irreversibility, probabilistic reasoning and the relationship between microscopic and macroscopic descriptions. Rather than presenting entropy as a formal quantity to be applied algorithmically, the approach emphasises its role within a model-based explanatory framework. Illustrative classroom situations are discussed to show how students can be engaged in interpreting physical processes through statistical reasoning, without relying on prescriptive instructional sequences. It is argued that, when approached in this way, entropy provides a productive context for initiating students into central features of scientific thinking, contributing to a broader understanding of physics education as an entry into the epistemological practices of science.
keywords: entropy, irreversibility, probabilistic reasoning, statistical reasoning, model-based explanation, nature of scientific knowledge, epistemology of science, scientific thinking

title: Distinguishing energy conservation from mechanical energy conservation using a bouncing ball: undergraduate laboratory experiment
text: Abstract This paper presents a laboratory experiment designed to help undergraduate engineering students distinguish between the general principle of energy conservation and the conditional conservation of mechanical energy. Using the accessible system of a vertically bouncing ball, the experiment employs temporal measurements of successive rebound intervals. From these measurements, students determine the coefficient of restitution and quantify mechanical-energy loss during impacts without relying on fitting procedures or image analysis. The experiment is configured to minimize the influence of air resistance through the choice of small, relatively dense balls and modest release heights, ensuring that energy dissipation is dominated by non-conservative processes during the collision. The activity was implemented on a large scale with approximately 400 first‐year students across two study programs. Student results exhibit a high degree of reproducibility, with clear distinctions between rigid and soft impact surfaces. The experiment proved robust, conceptually transparent, and well aligned with the learning objective of clarifying the limitations of mechanical‐energy conservation. Its simplicity, scalability, and strong diagnostic value make it a valuable addition to introductory physics laboratory curricula.
keywords: energy conservation (physics), mechanical energy conservation, bouncing ball, coefficient of restitution, energy dissipation, impact, non-conservative forces, introductory physics laboratory, engineering students, conceptual understanding

title: Collisions observed in two different reference frames
text: Abstract A head-on collision between two balls can be examined in different inertial reference frames, such as the laboratory frame or the centre of mass frame, and the impact force is unchanged. However, the spin of a ball bouncing on a horizontal surface differs in the two different inertial reference frames. An experiment is described where the differences are examined.
keywords: head-on collisions, inertial frames, center-of-mass frame, laboratory frame, impact force, ball spin, bouncing ball, horizontal surface

title: Measurements of the damping of oscillations and bending in a suspended multi-pendulum in the form of a flexible bead chain
text: Abstract A simple construction of a multi-pendulum in the form of a flexible chain of beads is described, together with a straightforward experimental methodology for studying a complex phenomenon—the oscillations of this multi-pendulum initially excited by a bending disturbance. The equipment and experimental procedure are accessible to school students and to educational institutions at the introductory level of physics education. The equipment and experiments are safe and can be rapidly implemented in the educational process. Importantly, the study of oscillations of a multi-pendulum allows for unlimited variability in laboratory results, which is essential for developing students’ independent experimental skills. Any student can construct their own multi-pendulum differing in parameters—such as length, number of elements, method of suspension, etc—from that of a neighbouring student. As a result, it is possible, for example, to measure the damping of oscillations and bending in a suspended multi-pendulum.
keywords: vibration damping, flexural vibration, introductory physics laboratory

title: Reply to comment on ‘A unifying network approach for circuits simplification and equivalent resistances, capacitors and inductors evaluation’
text: Reply to comment on ‘A unifying network approach for circuits simplification and equivalent resistances, capacitors and inductors evaluation’. Keywords: electrical circuits, circuit simplification, equivalent resistance, equivalent capacitance, equivalent inductance, network approach
keywords: electrical circuits, circuit simplification, equivalent resistance, equivalent capacitance, equivalent inductance, network approach

title: The forgotten conductor: a discussion about the conductivity of paper in history and in physics textbooks
text: Abstract The classic experiment involving the attraction of small pieces of paper when brought close to a rubbed plastic bar is one of the most popular introductions to electrostatics in physics textbooks at the high school and university level. This experiment is usually explained as a polarisation phenomenon on a non-conductive material: the paper. We will show that the assumption of paper as an insulator—an assumption very common in physics textbooks—prevents us from understanding such an experiment when other materials are included into the experimental setup. These difficulties disappear if a more nuanced view of the conductivity of paper is adopted, a view which takes into account the hygroscopic nature of this material, as it was common in elementary physics textbooks of nineteenth century.
keywords: electrostatic induction, polarization, insulators, hygroscopic materials

title: Comment on ‘A unifying network approach for circuits simplification and equivalent resistances, capacitors and inductors evaluation’
text: Abstract Costa (2022 Phys. Educ. 57 045031) claims that electric circuits with passive elements (resistors, inductors, and capacitors) with respect to its steady-state respose to a sinusoidal voltage source can be simplified by segregating the elements by types and successively eliminating nodes that are not adjacent to an external source. This comment argues that segregation into different types is not applicable and describes a correct method to calculate their equivalent impedances.
keywords: equivalent impedance, equivalent resistance, equivalent capacitance, equivalent inductance, passive components, network theory, node elimination

title: Exploring buoyancy and thermal equilibration with a Galileo thermometer
text: Abstract Galileo thermometers are often used to demonstate buoyancy and density. In this article, a Galileo thermometer is used as the basis of a classroom activity which extends beyond Archimedes’ principle. Observations were made during cooling and localised heating of the thermometer which provide opportunities to discuss measurement range, thermal equilibration, response time, and non-equilibrium behaviour. Photographs and supplementary videos are provided and applications in classroom activities are discussed. The activity may be implemented in introductory thermal physics and fluid dynamics teaching.
keywords: buoyancy, thermalization, density, temperature measurement, thermal expansion

title: Every student’s own optics: low‐cost acrylic sheets for colour, fluorescence, and light guiding
text: Abstract Two transparent acrylic sheets—one orange and one fluorescent yellow—allow students to explore three optical phenomena in a single lesson using coloured LED light: subtractive colour mixing, fluorescence with stokes shift, and light guiding via total internal reflection. Each student holds their own sheets and observes all three effects independently, without lasers, spectrometers or shared apparatus. The activity suits students aged about 14 and above and supports a predict–observe–explain sequence.
keywords: acrylic sheet, fluorescence, Stokes shift, total internal reflection, light guiding, Predict-Observe-Explain, high school physics

title: A research-based online particle physics course for high-school students
text: Abstract We have developed and published CERN’s online particle physics course for high-school students. The course design is grounded in educational reconstruction, cognitive load theory, and research on the nature of science, with particular attention to linguistic accuracy and model-based representations. The course was evaluated during a three-month pilot phase involving 3841 users, out of which 35% completed all chapters, and survey data showed high perceived enjoyment (89%), easiness (89%), and interest (87%). In this article, we outline the main design principles, curriculum decisions, and evaluation results, demonstrating how research-based approaches can support engagement and conceptual understanding in physics education.
keywords: online course design, particle physics education, high school students, educational reconstruction, cognitive load theory, nature of science, linguistic accuracy, student engagement, conceptual understanding, pilot evaluation, CERN

title: Inquiry-based teaching of circuit laws with black-box experiments: evidence from Angola
text: Abstract Understanding electrical circuits remains a persistent challenge in physics education, particularly in technical–vocational contexts where laboratory resources may be limited. This study investigates the impact of an inquiry-based instructional intervention using a black-box experimental methodology on students’ conceptual understanding, confidence, and motivation related to electrical circuit laws. The study was conducted in a technical secondary school in Angola, providing evidence from an educational context that remains underrepresented in physics education research. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control group design was implemented with 70 Grade 11 students (typically aged 16–17 years) enrolled in an Energy and Electrical Installations programme. The experimental group engaged in hands-on black-box investigations designed to promote model-based reasoning using Ohm’s Law and Kirchhoff’s Laws, while the control group received traditional lecture-based instruction. Students’ responses were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analysed using Mann–Whitney U and Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests. Pre-test results showed no statistically significant differences between groups ( p > 0.05), indicating comparable initial levels. After the intervention, statistically significant differences were observed between groups across all measured constructs (Q1–Q3: p < 0.001; Q4: p = 0.012). Effect-size analysis revealed large effects for confidence, application of circuit laws, and conceptual understanding ( r = 0.72–0.75) and a moderate effect for motivation ( r = 0.30). Additional post-test survey items applied only to the experimental group indicated very positive student perceptions of the activity (Q5 mean = 4.89, SD = 0.32; Q6 mean = 4.97, SD = 0.17). These results suggest that black-box experimental activities provide an effective and low-cost strategy for promoting inquiry-based learning and improving conceptual understanding of electrical circuits in resource-constrained technical education environments. The findings highlight the potential of black-box investigations as an accessible experimental strategy for teaching electrical circuits in technical and secondary physics classrooms.
keywords: inquiry-based learning, Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws, technical and vocational education and training, conceptual understanding, student self-confidence, student motivation, model-based reasoning, high school physics, Angola

title: Embodied learning through theatre: students addressing misconceptions in electric circuits
text: Abstract This study presents a theatre-based embodied learning approach for addressing students’ misconceptions in electric circuits within a non-formal educational setting. Eighteen secondary school students (aged 15–16) participated in a science club, where they explored electric circuits through the collaborative development and performance of a theatrical play. The approach aimed to engage students in reflecting on and externalising their alternative conceptions through embodied representations. Students initially explored their ideas through discussion, experiments, and simulations, focusing on key concepts such as the role of the source, electron movement, and the function of the switch. They subsequently developed and performed a theatrical play representing both misconceptions and scientifically accepted models at macroscopic and microscopic levels. Data were collected through semi-structured group interviews and analysed using thematic analysis. Findings suggest that students perceived the embodied and theatrical representations as helping them reflect on and reconsider their initial ideas about electric circuits, while also fostering metacognitive awareness. In addition, students described the process as engaging and supportive of collaboration, creativity, communication, and critical reflection. The study suggests that theatre-based embodied learning can serve as a promising complementary approach for teaching abstract physics concepts, particularly those involving non-observable phenomena.
keywords: embodied learning, theatre-based learning, misconceptions, electrical circuits, non-formal education, science clubs, high school students, metacognitive awareness, cooperative learning, microscopic representation

title: A power-law current–voltage relationship in a 3.6 V Zener diode
text: Abstract We present a simple experiment in which the current–voltage ( I – V ) characteristic of a 3.6 V Zener diode under reverse bias provides a clean realisation of a high-degree polynomial model. The measured I – V data are empirically described by the power-law relationship I = a V n , with a measured exponent of n = 8.08 ± 0.08 . Because the system is inexpensive, robust, and yields an unusually clear example of high-order dependence, it is well suited for high-school and undergraduate laboratories that emphasise data acquisition, nonlinear fitting, and model assessment.
keywords: Zener diode, current-voltage characteristics, power-law relationship, reverse bias, nonlinear fitting, physics laboratory experiments, data acquisition

title: A 3D-printed optical kit for a crime-solving educational escape room: a service-learning outreach initiative
text: Abstract Geometric optics constitutes a cornerstone of the physics curriculum, yet its instruction is frequently hindered by persistent misconceptions regarding light propagation, image formation, and the visual process. This study details a pedagogical intervention that integrates an educational escape room within a Service-Learning framework to mitigate these conceptual barriers. To address the scarcity of experimental resources, we designed 3D-printed structural components (including optical benches, lens holders, and an eye model) to complement commercial optical element. The activity, anchored in a forensic crime-solving narrative, was facilitated by undergraduate optics students acting as mentors for a cohort of fifteen 12th-grade students. Qualitatively, initial student sketches exposed significant gaps in their grasp of ray tracing and physiological optics. Data from a pretest–posttest design indicated a substantial improvement in conceptual understanding, with mean knowledge scores rising from 35.1% to 77.6% ( p < 0.001). Beyond student gains, undergraduate mentors reported enhanced scientific communication skills, while high school teachers emphasised the kit’s high replicability. By disseminating the open-access 3D-printing files and pedagogical guide, this project offers a sustainable and engaging model to foster STEM interest and enhance optics education.
keywords: educational escape rooms, service-learning, ray tracing, physiological optics, image formation, high school outreach, STEM interest

title: When intuition fails: exploring counterintuitive mechanics using python simulations in high school physics
text: Abstract Students often rely on intuitive reasoning when interpreting motion in introductory mechanics. However, many physical situations produce results that contradict these intuitive expectations. Such discrepancies can create valuable learning opportunities when explored through visual and computational tools. This paper presents a set of Python-based simulations designed to investigate several counterintuitive phenomena in high school mechanics. The simulations illustrate cases where common assumptions about motion fail, including projectile motion launched from an elevated position, comparisons of straight and curved descent paths, and situations in which a slower object overtakes a faster one due to different acceleration conditions. Using accessible computational tools implemented in Python, the simulations generate clear visualisations including trajectory plots, position–time graphs, velocity–time graphs and phase-space diagrams. These visual representations allow students to explore relationships between position, velocity and acceleration while comparing intuitive predictions with computational results. The approach demonstrates how accessible computational simulations can support conceptual understanding in introductory physics and encourage students to critically examine their intuition about motion. The simulations are designed to be easily implemented in classroom activities, allowing students to explore counterintuitive mechanics through computational modelling.
keywords: introductory mechanics, projectile motion, Python simulation, computational modelling, high school physics, conceptual understanding, overtaking, acceleration, phase space diagrams

title: Content–method coupling in students’ physics research practices: a two-track analysis
text: Abstract Inquiry-oriented approaches in physics education emphasise students’ engagement in scientific practices. However, school-based inquiry often constrains opportunities for students to organise research content and select methods in relation to their investigative focus. This study examines how research content and research methods are structured and coupled in student-led physics research. We analysed 400 physics Research and Education reports produced in Korea between 2021 and 2025 using a two-track approach that combines topic modelling and dictionary-based method analysis. Topic modelling was used to identify content-topic structures, and method keywords were analysed to examine patterns of method use and content–method coupling. The results show that students’ research topics are organised less around conventional physics subfields and more around the character of phenomena and problems under investigation. Five content-topic categories were identified: motion and dynamics, sound and vibration, force and stability, energy and efficiency, and fields and measurement. Method use was structured more clearly by content–method coupling than by year-to-year trends. Simulation was strongly coupled across all content topics, whereas other methods differentiated topics in systematic ways. For example, FFT and sensor methods were prominent in sound and vibration, CFD and wind tunnel methods in Energy and Efficiency, and laser and sensor methods in Fields and Measurement. These findings suggest that student physics research involves the joint organisation of content and method. The study provides large-scale empirical insight into student research practices and offers implications for supporting physics inquiry learning that connects research questions, content, and methods.
keywords: research methodology, research content, inquiry-based learning, student-led research, physics education research, simulation methods, sound and vibration

title: Teaching Newton’s laws through model rocketry within Kolb’s experiential learning cycle
text: Abstract Understanding Newton’s laws is often challenging for students due to persistent misconceptions and the abstract nature of the concepts involved. This study explores the use of model rocketry within a teaching sequence structured according to Kolb’s experiential learning cycle. A teaching unit on Newtonian mechanics was implemented with three groups of secondary school students: a traditional instruction group, a Kolb cycle–based activity group (KOLB), and a Kolb cycle–based group that additionally participated in a model rocket project (ROCKET). Students’ conceptual understanding was assessed in a quasi-experimental design using a researcher-developed knowledge test administered before and after the instructional unit. The results were analysed using a repeated measures analysis of variance. A significant improvement between pre-test and post-test scores was observed across all groups. However, the interaction between time and instructional group was not statistically significant, indicating that the magnitude of learning gains did not differ significantly between the instructional approaches. Students’ perceptions of the rocket project were also examined through selected items from an end-of-year questionnaire. A large majority of students in the ROCKET group identified the rocket project as their favourite physics learning activity. The findings suggest that instruction structured according to Kolb’s experiential learning cycle can be as effective as traditional instruction in supporting students’ understanding of Newtonian mechanics. While the rocket project did not produce a measurable additional effect on learning gains, student feedback indicates that it can provide an engaging context for learning physics.
keywords: Newton's laws of motion, model rocketry, Kolb's learning cycle, classical mechanics, misconceptions, high school physics, student perceptions, conceptual understanding

title: Low-cost 21 cm hydrogen-line detection for physics education using software-defined radio and a simple antenna
text: Abstract The 21 cm hydrogen line offers a practical way to introduce students to radio astronomy, spectral analysis, and Doppler shifts using authentic data from the Milky Way. However, the technical and financial barriers of conventional hydrogen-line detection systems often limit accessibility, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study presents the design, implementation, and field testing of a low-cost, autonomous radio telescope system based on a Raspberry Pi and software-defined radio for detecting Doppler-shifted hydrogen emission near 1420.405 MHz. The system operates without continuous user input and records raw signal and intensity data for later spectral analysis, enabling extended observations and a post-processing workflow suitable for student use. Field trials conducted in Jasaan, Misamis Oriental, Philippines demonstrate detection of a hydrogen-line peak with both redshifted and blueshifted cases over different observing times. The results support the feasibility of an affordable and replicable set-up for physics education, public outreach, and introductory research activities.
keywords: 21 cm hydrogen line, software-defined radio, Raspberry Pi, Doppler shift, radio astronomy education, spectral analysis, public outreach

title: Theory meets real-life experiment - understanding electric circuits with the ‘PUMA : Spannungslabor’ AR-app
text: Abstract The use of digital support materials is becoming increasingly popular in teaching. One promising use for teaching physics is the joint presentation of a real-life experiment and the theoretical model utilised to explain the experiment’s phenomenon. This holistic approach facilitates the creation of a mental link between model and reality, supporting the students’ understanding and learning. The ‘PUMA : Spannungslabor’ app was developed to enable this approach, allowing it to be used when teaching about simple electric circuits. The application visualises the base quantities voltage (abstracted via a height- or pressure-analogy based model), current (abstracted via moving electrons) and electrical resistance (abstracted via a collision-analogy based model). The visualisations can be shown either via a video-see-through augmented reality (AR) mode (in combination with a real experiment setup) or as a fully digital simulation. To evaluate the impact the app’s use in teaching has on the learning process, a student laboratory study was conducted with N = 441 8th grade students (ages 13–14). The empirical results revealed a significant difference in the development of conceptual knowledge between using the app as AR or as a simulation. Additionally, it was found that using the AR-app to display model representations lowered the students’ cognitive load and its use for data acquisition significantly reduced the amount of time the students needed to finish their tasks. These results provide information for a target group-oriented design and implementation of AR-apps for school lessons. The benefits of using this AR-app are currently examined in an intervention study in classroom practice. A teaching unit was developed which utilises the app at various points to support the students’ learning process. This course, together with the AR-app, simulation and additional supplementary material, is available free of charge for students and teachers on the website https://go.uniwue.de/puma-voltagelab .
keywords: augmented reality, electrical circuits, voltage, electric current, electrical resistance, conceptual understanding, physics simulation, cognitive load, data acquisition, eighth grade students, digital teaching materials

title: Seeing vs measuring revisited: a mirror modification of Greene’s presidents thought experiment
text: Abstract Brian Greene’s presidents-on-a-train thought experiment vividly illustrates the relativity of simultaneity in special relativity: two presidents seated at opposite ends of a moving train sign a peace treaty simultaneously in the train frame, while ground observers conclude that the signings were not simultaneous. This paper introduces a mirror arrangement at the train’s centre that reflects light from both signings outward toward the ground observers. The mirror creates an apparent paradox: the same observers who infer non-simultaneity from Greene’s original analysis now receive mirror-reflected signals together, apparently indicating simultaneity. The resolution is that the mirror cancels two asymmetries. Light from the earlier of the two presidential signings takes longer to reach the train-centre mirror, while light from the later signing takes less time. The example provides a compact classroom illustration of the distinction between what observers see and what they observe, where observing means reasoning from visual signals to physical conclusions.
keywords: relativity of simultaneity, special relativity, thought experiments, Brian Greene, specular reflection, visual signals, light travel time

title: How might we improve recruitment into postgraduate teacher preparation programmes? Insights from undergraduate physics students’ views about becoming a secondary school physics teacher
text: Abstract Recruitment of physics teachers is internationally recognised as challenging. One pool of potential recruits into physics teacher preparation programmes is undergraduate physics students. In this paper, we explore the insights into this challenge that can be provided by understanding undergraduate physics students’ views about becoming a secondary school physics teacher. In response to these insights, we suggest four points for consideration, action, and further discussion that may lead to gains in the recruitment of physics teachers. These suggestions have relevance for those teaching physics at all levels of education, as well as those who employ physics graduates.
keywords: teacher recruitment, physics teacher education, high school physics teaching, undergraduate physics students, student perceptions, teacher education curriculum, physics graduates

title: Exploring blackbody radiation using RGB measurements from an iPhone 12 Pro Max camera
text: Abstract A low-cost experimental method for investigating blackbody radiation is presented using a heated filament and smartphone-based colour detection. The red, green, and blue intensities of emitted light were measured as a function of electrical power. Analysis of the intensity ratios shows that the blue-to-red ( B / R ) and blue-to-green ( B / G ) ratios increase with increasing power, whereas the red-to-green ( R / G ) ratio decreases. These trends indicate a progressive shift of the emitted spectrum towards shorter wavelengths as the filament temperature increases. The observations are in qualitative agreement with Planck’s law and Wien’s displacement law. A comparison with theoretical trends suggests that the iPhone 12 Pro Max camera used in this study can function as a three-channel, low-resolution spectrometer. To assess measurement consistency, the experiment was repeated using two independent iPhone applications (physics toolbox and colorimeter), which produced similar qualitative trends. The method provides an accessible approach for exploring thermal radiation in classroom settings.
keywords: blackbody radiation, thermal radiation, smartphone camera, Wien's displacement law, Planck's law, low-cost spectrometer, wavelength shift

title: Effectiveness of steam-integrated project-based learning to improve problem-solving ability and conceptual understanding of seventh-grade students in the density topic
text: Abstract This study evaluates the effectiveness of the STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics)-integrated project-based learning (PJBL-STEAM) model in enhancing problem-solving abilities and conceptual understanding among seventh-grade students studying the topic of density. A quasi-experimental design with pre-test and post-test assessments was employed, involving an experimental group (PJBL-STEAM) and a control group (traditional instruction). The population consisted of seventh-grade students from Mosleynejad Girls’ High School in Mashhad, Iran, during the 2023–2024 academic years. A sample of 30 students (15 per group) was selected using cluster random sampling. Both groups participated in the pre-test, post-test, and retention test. Data were collected via a researcher-made questionnaire, validated by physics professors, with a Cronbach’s alpha reliability of 0.759. The experimental group underwent four 90 min PJBL-STEAM sessions, while the control group received traditional instruction. Post-test results indicated a significant improvement in problem-solving abilities and conceptual understanding in the experimental group compared to the control group ( p < 0.05). A retention test conducted six months later revealed a significant difference ( t (28) = 3.79, p < 0.01), indicating that the experimental group maintained superior performance over time. The PJBL-STEAM approach fostered active engagement, creativity and conceptual understanding of density. These findings suggest that PJBL-STEAM is an effective method for teaching abstract physics concepts and enhancing problem-solving skills student. Recommendations include broader adoption of PJBL-STEAM in science education to develop 21st-century skills.
keywords: STEAM education, project-based learning, density, physics problem solving, conceptual understanding, seventh grade students, physics education, learning retention, 21st century skills

title: Fostering lower secondary school teachers’ professional development: a teaching experiment in classical mechanics
text: Abstract Teacher professional development in science education often struggles to translate theoretical knowledge into meaningful classroom practice, particularly at the lower secondary level. This study presents an original teaching experiment in classical mechanics, designed to foster both pedagogical content knowledge and conceptual change through a situated, inquiry-based approach. Grounded on situated learning theory, our methodology integrates the PEC model (prediction, experimentation, comparison) within modular teaching episodes enabling authentic engagement with physics concepts through low-cost, hands-on activities. Unlike many top-down professional development programs, this initiative builds from teachers’ intuitive knowledge, actively confronting and reconstructing misconceptions through guided inquiry and collaborative reflection. Relying on qualitative data—collected through classroom observation, discussion transcripts, and informal interviews—we document how teachers revised deeply held misunderstandings about motion, force, mass, and weight. Findings reveal a substantial shift in participants’ conceptual frameworks and teaching practices, including increased use of student-centred experimentation, more accurate use of scientific language, and improved ability to model inquiry-based instruction. This research contributes original evidence that sustained, situated learning environments can effectively promote long-term professional growth and epistemological transformation in science teachers, even in structurally constrained educational systems.
keywords: teacher professional development, classical mechanics, pedagogical content knowledge, conceptual change, situated learning, inquiry-based teaching

title: A hands-on activity for exploring temperature measurement and Newton’s law of cooling with a low-cost thermistor
text: Abstract This article presents a low-cost hands-on activity for exploring temperature measurement and Newton’s law of cooling using an NTC thermistor and a digital multimeter. Students calibrate the thermistor through graphical analysis and use the calibrated sensor to investigate cooling behaviour experimentally. The activity promotes understanding of sensor calibration, data transformation, uncertainty, and thermal physics through active student participation and collaborative investigation. Its simplicity and low cost make it suitable for secondary and introductory undergraduate physics laboratories.
keywords: Newton's law of cooling, temperature measurement, NTC thermistor, sensor calibration, thermistor calibration, uncertainty, data transformation, thermal physics, hands-on laboratory activities

title: Earthquake in the courtyard: an experiential learning activity for epicentre triangulation and wave phase identification
text: Abstract Seismology is often perceived by students as an abstract ‘big science’ confined to global networks and complex digital datasets. To bridge the cognitive gap between theoretical wave physics and real-world observation, we developed an experiential learning activity titled ‘earthquake in the courtyard’. This study utilises a professional seismic recording system for geophysical surveys to replicate a small-scale seismograph station in a university setting. Using an impulsive source (hammer-and-plate), students manually identified longitudinal (P-waves), transverse (S-waves), and dispersive surface waves. By applying site-specific velocity structures, students performed 2D triangulation methods to locate the epicentre. Results from five independent student trials demonstrate that calculating coordinates with the statistically averaged velocity structure significantly improves accuracy, yielding a low mean Euclidean distance error of 0.6 m. Furthermore, the analysis of error triangles provided a tangible framework for students to quantify experimental uncertainty and picking precision. This laboratory exercise demonstrates that high-fidelity geophysical methods can be effectively adapted into an accessible, hands-on curriculum that reinforces the scale-invariance of physical laws and the importance of site-specific empirical data.
keywords: P wave, S-waves, surface waves, experiential learning, seismology education, experimental uncertainty, hands-on laboratory exercises

title: Where is the world’s largest capacitor?
text: Abstract Students often regard RC circuits as abstract ideas that appear only weakly connected to observable phenomena in the real world. This article presents a teaching approach that introduces RC circuits through the global atmospheric electric circuit. By interpreting the Earth–ionosphere system as a planetary-scale capacitor, students can estimate its capacitance and compare it with that of a handheld 1-F supercapacitor. A simple classroom demonstration using a supercapacitor and a light bulb illustrates RC discharge and provides a visual analogue for the relaxation time of the global electric circuit. This approach connects basic circuit concepts with atmospheric electricity and helps students recognise how the same physical principles apply across vastly different scales.
keywords: RC circuits, global atmospheric electric circuit, capacitance estimation, supercapacitors, relaxation time, atmospheric electricity, classroom demonstration

title: Artificial intelligence and computer vision as allies in the teaching of kinematics concepts
text: Abstract This paper presents a technological tool designed to support physics teachers in addressing kinematics and graph construction and interpretation. The software uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to recognize the human body and estimate the positions of specific joints. From these coordinates, the program generates graphs of the user’s hand position. The tool also includes a self-correction feature for activities. Examples of use and suggested activities are provided in the text. A brief discussion of the tool’s potential is presented in the concluding remarks.
keywords: kinematics teaching, artificial intelligence, computer vision, human pose estimation, joint position estimation, self-correction, PhET, educational software

title: STEM project design: blending quantum and computational physics with Tic-Tac-Toe
text: Abstract Quantum physics remains a conceptual hurdle in physics education due to the non-intuitive nature of superposition, entanglement and wavefunction collapse. The Quantum Tic-Tac-Toe is a rule-based game specifically designed to visualise these concepts. While the game is proposed, some numerical and algorithmic subtleties about implementation of this quantum game remain unaddressed and there are no explicit results to validate the code and the strategy. This article serves as a resource for physics educators looking to integrate quantum concepts into the capstone projects with reference material to the numerical results. To support project mentorship, we also provide a 10 week project mentoring schedule and highlight specific technical challenges encountered during implementation. We present numerical benchmarks and reference code for instructors to cross-check students’ results. This project offers a new approach for early physics learners to turn abstract concepts from quantum physics and statistical physics into a hands-on game design. These skills could lay the students’ foundation towards quantum information science.
keywords: quantum superposition, quantum entanglement, wave function collapse, game-based learning, capstone projects, computational physics, statistical physics, quantum information, STEM education

title: Weighing photons and gravitons through astrophysical observations
text: Abstract This paper explores some physical consequences of assigning a non-zero rest mass to photons and gravitons. While classical electromagnetism and General Relativity assume these particles are massless, leading to a constant speed c , a minimal mass would imply frequency-dependent propagation speeds. We demonstrate how this phenomenon, though only detectable over cosmological distances, provides a gateway to discussing the frontiers of modern physics. Using mathematical tools accessible to advanced secondary school and introductory university students, we show how to model the arrival time differences of signals from remote astrophysical events.
keywords: photon mass, light propagation, time difference of arrival, cosmological observations, general relativity, electromagnetism, massless particles

title: Polarization of mechanical waves in a plucked string: a low-cost device for classroom visualization
text: Abstract Polarization is a fundamental property of transverse waves, yet it is seldom explored in the context of mechanical waves on strings. When a string is plucked, the initial conditions typically excite two orthogonal transverse modes, producing linear or elliptical polarization of the resulting wave. This article presents a simple homemade device that amplifies the transverse motion of a plucked string and allows students to visualize the polarization of mechanical waves on strings. The device is inexpensive, easy to build, and suitable for classroom demonstrations.
keywords: polarization, mechanical waves, plucked strings, transverse waves, elliptical polarization, linear polarization, transverse modes, wave visualization, classroom demonstration

title: Beyond uniformity: variations in the implementation of cognitive conflict strategies in physics education
text: Abstract Instructional strategies are central to science education research, yet they are often evaluated as if they were uniform treatments, whether in classroom experiments or meta-analyses. This assumption masks the internal variation that shapes how strategies function in practice, limiting both theoretical development and instructional improvement. This article introduces a framework for studying instructional strategies beyond uniformity, using cognitive conflict—a central strategy in conceptual change research—as a case. We conducted a qualitative content analysis of 229 reported implementations in physics education, identifying variation across four dimensions: the misconceptions targeted, the methods used to generate dissatisfaction, the instructional tools employed, and the content areas addressed. These dimensions not only varied internally but also interacted systematically, revealing patterns such as empirical falsification paired with conceptual relations and implemented through student experimentation. By mapping these dynamics, we move beyond treating cognitive conflict as a monolithic strategy and instead highlight how it operates as a dynamic configuration of interacting components in science classrooms. This methodological shift offers a new lens for understanding instructional strategies in science education, demonstrating why studying their variation is essential for advancing theory, guiding instructional design, and strengthening future research.
keywords: cognitive conflict, teaching methods, conceptual change, misconceptions, student experimentation, instructional design, science classroom

title: Diagrammatic approaches to teaching special and general relativity
text: Abstract This paper presents two purely diagrammatic methods for teaching central ideas of special and general relativity. The relativity of simultaneity and time dilation are derived through axis tilting in spacetime diagrams, emphasizing geometric consistency over algebraic formalism. The same reasoning is then extended to gravity by representing the universality of free fall and the influence of gravity on light through the local variation of light cones. This approach visualizes spacetime curvature in terms of causal structure rather than curved surfaces and provides a coherent conceptual bridge from inertial motion to black holes. The constructions offer an accessible yet physically faithful introduction to relativistic spacetime making them particularly suitable for secondary school students and general-audience outreach.
keywords: special relativity, general relativity, diagrammatic reasoning, spacetime diagrams, relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, weak equivalence principle, light cone, spacetime curvature, causal structure, black holes, high school students, public outreach

title: Smartphone-assisted acquisition of diode characteristics using SeeLab 3 for determining the energy band gap of silicon
text: Abstract This work presents a simple and cost-effective approach to determine the energy band gap of silicon in an undergraduate laboratory. By using a 1N4007 silicon diode along with the SeeLab 3 interface, the experiment overcomes the common limitations of traditional methods, such as time-consuming manual data recording and the likelihood of human error. The use of smartphone-based data acquisition allows students to observe the behaviour of the semiconductor in real time and obtain instant graphical outputs. The measured band gap value of silicon is found to be 1.05 ± 0.06 eV , which is reasonably close to the standard value of 1.12 eV . This method simplifies the experimental process and shifts the focus from tedious data collection to better understanding and interpretation of the underlying physics.
keywords: silicon band gap, silicon diodes, smartphone data acquisition, undergraduate laboratory experiment, semiconductor physics, diode characteristics

title: Development of a physics test instrument to assess students’ analytical thinking skills in particle dynamics using Rasch analysis
text: Abstract This study aimed to develop and validate a constructed-response assessment to measure analytical thinking skills in the context of particle dynamics. Grounded in Sternberg’s theory of analytical intelligence, the instrument comprised seven open-ended items aligned with indicators such as analysing, critiquing, evaluating, explaining, logical reasoning, drawing conclusions, and sorting. A five-point rubric was developed for each item to evaluate the accuracy, depth, and logical coherence of student responses. Content validity was established through expert judgment involving six specialists in learning evaluation and physics, using Aiken’s V index. The instrument was pilot-tested with 106 undergraduate students from the Physics Education Program, and data were analysed using the Rasch model. All items demonstrated good fit (infit/outfit mean square 0.5–1.5) and high item reliability (0.99), while person reliability was moderately acceptable (0.79). The wright map confirmed good targeting, though a ceiling effect suggested limited challenge for high-performing students. Unidimensionality assumptions were satisfied, supporting construct validity. The findings provide empirical support for a theoretically grounded instrument that captures analytical thinking in physics and suggest directions for extending the assessment to broader science domains and instructional contexts.
keywords: analytical thinking, particle dynamics, physics assessment instrument, constructed-response assessment, open-ended questions, rubric development, content validity, Rasch model validation, ceiling effect, unidimensionality, undergraduate physics students

title: Using the SOLO taxonomy to analyse students’ conceptual understanding of friction force
text: Abstract Effective assessment plays a crucial role in improving the quality of learning by identifying learners’ mental schemata and misconceptions. This study examined twelfth-grade students’ conceptual understanding of friction force based on the structure of the observed learning outcome (SOLO) taxonomy and explored their common misconceptions. The research employed a descriptive survey design, and 216 students were selected through multistage cluster sampling. Data were collected using a nine-item open-response test aligned with the levels of the SOLO taxonomy. The content validity of the instrument was confirmed by subject-matter experts, and its reliability was established using Cronbach’s alpha coefficient ( α = 0.749). The findings showed that, on average, students produced responses at the unistructural (83%), multistructural (30%), and relational (3%) levels of the SOLO taxonomy, while no responses reached the extended abstract level. Based on the ceiling-performance measure (the highest level demonstrated by each student), 52% of students produced at least one response at the unistructural level, 40% at the multistructural level, and 8% at the relational level. According to the mastery measure (consistent performance across items), no student demonstrated mastery at the relational or extended abstract levels, whereas 41% of students remained at the prestructural level, 47% demonstrated mastery only at the unistructural level, and 12% attained mastery at the multistructural level. Common misconceptions were identified through qualitative analysis of students’ written responses, including misunderstandings regarding the direction and magnitude of friction force and confusion between static and kinetic friction.
keywords: friction force, conceptual understanding, SOLO taxonomy, misconceptions, static friction, sliding friction, high school students, mental models

title: Integration of metaverse Spatial.io as a pre-laboratory medium to enhance conceptual understanding of Newton’s laws
text: Abstract This study aims to integrate and evaluate the effectiveness of a metaverse Spatial.io-based pre-laboratory environment in enhancing students’ conceptual understanding of Newton’s laws. Conventional pre-laboratory media are often passive and provide limited opportunities for immersive, interactive preparation, which may restrict students’ ability to develop a robust conceptual foundation before examination. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was employed, involving two groups of physics education students (experimental n = 30; control n = 30). Conceptual understanding was assessed using a validated and reliable test instrument. The results indicate that the experimental group engaging with Spatial.io achieved significantly greater improvement in conceptual understanding than the control group using 2D video media, with an independent sample t -test showing a significant difference in normalizedgains ( t (58) = −3.199, p = 0.002). These findings suggest that immersive pre-laboratory experience can better facilitate active cognitive engagement and support the formation of more concrete mental models of fundamental mechanics concepts. Overall, Spatial.io appears feasible and promising as an innovative pre-laboratory medium that bridges theory and practice in physics learning and offers a scalable approach to strengthening conceptual readiness before laboratory activities.
keywords: metaverse, Newton's laws of motion, conceptual understanding, immersive learning, virtual reality in education, mental models, mechanics

title: Kinetic energy of rolling motion from the contact point
text: Abstract We make use of the fact that the instantaneous velocity field of a body in a planar, pure rolling motion is identical to that of a rigid rotation about the contact point. As a consequence, the total kinetic energy can be written with respect to that point. For bodies with circular symmetry, the usual Koenig decomposition into translational and rotational contributions is immediately recovered, and remains valid for any radially symmetric mass distribution.
keywords: roll motion, kinetic energy, contact points, instantaneous velocity field, rigid body rotation, König's theorem, circular symmetry, planar motion

title: Hands-on aerodynamics: kirigami-inspired parachutes as a vehicle for cultivating innovative thinking
text: Abstract Innovation is a key force driving global development and solving complex problems. A recent study published in Nature introduced kirigami-inspired parachutes, which offer a unique and engaging approach to cultivate innovative thinking in students. Based on this cutting-edge research, we designed a hands-on classroom teaching activity that guides middle and high school students through the process of designing, testing, and iterating their own kirigami-inspired parachutes using simple materials. Experimental results demonstrated that the cut parachute exhibited excellent vertical and attitude stability, maintaining a consistent shape throughout the descent, while the uncut parachute experienced multiple curling and deviated from the release point. This activity is ideal for science fairs, physics classroom projects, or youth innovation competitions, promoting both scientific thinking and creative problem-solving skills.
keywords: aerodynamics, parachute design, hands-on classroom activities, innovative thinking, creative problem solving, middle and high school students, science fair projects

title: Exploring detail-oriented education in undergraduate physics experiments
text: Abstract Detail-oriented education, which emphasizes developing the ability to leverage critical details for problems discover, analysis and resolution, is invaluable for cultivating comprehensive innovation capabilities in science and engineering education. This study integrates detail-oriented education into undergraduate physics experiments through a ‘three-dimensional four-stage’ model, which spans knowledge, ability and quality dimensions across four stages, including theory and experimental design, experimental precautions, experimental operations, experimental summary and reflection. Using photoelectric effect experiment as a case study, results demonstrate that the group received detailed-oriented-training outperformed the control group in plan completeness, operational compliance, task efficiency and error analysis capabilities. This framework not only reinforces the foundational role of physics experiments in undergraduate science education, but also provides a replicable approach for systematic detail-oriented instruction across various experimental courses.
keywords: undergraduate physics experiment, experimental skills, experimental design, error analysis, innovation ability

title: Building an analogue simulator of a photonic quantum computer with transparent tape, maple syrup, and cat lasers, and implementing first quantum algorithms in the classroom
text: Abstract This work presents the implementation of single-qubit gates, including Rx and Rz gates realized using transparent adhesive tape, and Ry gates obtained with optically active maple and agave solutions. These gates form the native gate set of a simple photonic system and are subsequently used to construct a Hadamard gate. Two forms of two-qubit gates are introduced using a combination of a calcite crystal and transparent tape. The setups employ both the polarization and the path degree of freedom of a photon as qubits, illustrating how readily accessible materials can be used to manipulate and transform the quantum information they convey. Calculations are performed to determine the birefringence of two different types of tape and to quantify the specific rotations introduced by multiple layers of transparent tape. Finally, simple algorithms and exercises are proposed for students. These experimental setups are designed to facilitate hands-on manipulation of quantum effects while lowering the barrier to accessing quantum systems, with total costs kept below $50 CAD for the singlequbit gates and below $100 CAD for all experiments combined. The configurations presented serve as an analog simulator of a photonic quantum computer: although the laser beams used can be described classically, all theoretical considerations and experimental procedures remain valid for quantized systems employing single-photon emitters and single-photon detectors.
keywords: photonic quantum computing, single-qubit gates, Hadamard gate, two-qubit gates, calcite crystals, birefringence, maple syrup, agave syrup, optical activity, polarization qubits, quantum algorithms

title: A machine learning approach to free-fall experiments: predicting drop height from acoustic signals
text: Abstract Experiments involving falling objects are fundamental in introductory physics to illustrate uniformly accelerated motion. However, traditional approaches often rely on idealized models that overlook real-world experimental variability. In this work, we present an educational framework in which students infer the drop height of a metallic ball from acoustic recordings of its successive impacts using a supervised random forest regression model. By extracting temporal descriptors from the audio signal, students analyse how physically meaningful features emerge from noisy experimental data. The model achieves high predictive accuracy ( R 2 = 0.996 ), but the primary pedagogical value lies in enabling students to identify which aspects of the physical process are most stable and informative. In particular, intermediate rebound intervals are found to be more reliable than the first impact, highlighting the limitations of traditional kinematic approaches. This activity integrates experimental physics, signal processing, and computational modelling within a Google Colab environment, promoting a transition from idealized problem-solving to data-driven scientific reasoning. The proposed framework provides a connection between classical mechanics and modern data science, preparing students to interpret complex experimental data in realistic settings.
keywords: free fall, acoustic signals, impact noise, random forest regression, uniformly accelerated motion, introductory physics education, audio feature extraction, Google Colab

title: Our place in the universe: comparing the solar system to other planetary systems
text: Abstract This article presents an educational proposal that uses exoplanet research as a motivating context to promote active and situated learning of physics both at the school level and in introductory university courses. Working with real data, students are encouraged to investigate how planets form by analysing exoplanet populations and the architecture of extrasolar systems, including commonly observed arrangements such as the pea-in-a-pod configuration. This approach aims to foster the development of higher-order cognitive skills through authentic engagement with contemporary scientific research. The article discusses the scope and limitations of the proposal and offers concrete suggestions for its implementation in the classroom.
keywords: exoplanets, extrasolar planetary systems, planet formation, solar system, situated learning, active learning, higher-order thinking skills, school physics

title: Entropy of simple gas models: an accessible approach to information-theoretic and thermodynamic concepts
text: Abstract A simple derivation of the entropy of the ideal and the dilute hard-sphere gas up to a normalization constant is presented, using only high school-level mathematics. The connection between information theory and thermodynamics, as well as the role of Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle in the transition from the classical to the quantum description of physical systems, is highlighted in a concise manner accessible to non-experts with a general interest in the natural sciences. A brief discussion is also devoted to the ultra-relativistic gas which can be analysed with the same elementary approach used for the non-relativistic case.
keywords: entropy, ideal gas, hard-sphere gas, dilute gases, information theory, thermodynamics, uncertainty principle, quantum-to-classical transition

title: Interactive block-format teaching and forensic science students’ attitudes to physics: a three-year study
text: Abstract This three-year pre-post study investigated changes in undergraduate forensic science students’ attitudes and beliefs about physics during a four-week interactive block-format course in Physics in Forensic Sciences. A total of 216 s-year students completed the Colorado Learning Attitudes about Science Survey (CLASS) at the start and end of instruction, providing both personal responses and estimates of a perceived expert-like view. Personal favourable responses increased from 40.1% to 61.3% (gain = 21.2%, 95% CI [18.46, 23.94], Cohen’s d = 0.50, Hake’s g = 0.35). Perceived expert-like responses increased from 72.6% to 91.4% (gain = 18.8%, 95% CI [16.64, 20.96], Cohen’s d = 0.98, Hake’s g = 0.69). Positive shifts were observed in all CLASS categories, with the largest gains in Problem Solving Sophistication (+24.2%) and Real World Connections (+22.9%). Female students entered with lower personal scores than male students but showed larger gains, narrowing the initial gap. In the absence of a control group or historical course data, the findings are interpreted as evidence that the instructional design may have contributed to more favourable beliefs when physics was consistently connected to forensic practice.
keywords: forensic science education, student attitudes toward physics, interactive teaching methods, Colorado Learning Attitudes about Science Survey, gender differences, problem solving, real-world connections, undergraduate physics education

title: Measuring g via the minimum period of a physical pendulum
text: Abstract This paper presents a simple experiment using the minimum-period condition of a physical pendulum as an alternative to traditional simple pendulum setups used in undergraduate physics laboratories. Rectangular plates were designed and fabricated using 3D printing, with pivot locations positioned at their respective radii of gyration relative to the centre of mass of the plate. Under these conditions, the oscillation period of the plate is mathematically equivalent to that of a simple pendulum with an effective length, ℓ , equal to twice the radius of gyration. The period of oscillation T was experimentally measured using an Arduino micro-controller coupled to a rotary encoder, enabling accurate determination of angular displacement and period. Measurements obtained from plates of different dimensions produced a linear relationship between 4 π 2 ℓ and T 2 , as predicted by theory, with a slope of about 9.80 m s − 2 corresponding to the local acceleration due to gravity. The experiment provides an intuitive framework for exploring rotational dynamics, oscillatory motion, moment of inertia, and the determination of gravitational acceleration in undergraduate laboratory courses.
keywords: physical pendulum, gravitational acceleration measurement, radius of gyration, moment of inertia, simple pendulum, Arduino data acquisition, rotary encoder, rotational dynamics, oscillatory motion, undergraduate physics laboratory

title: Motion of a projectile launched from a ramp
text: Abstract We present a pedagogical activity for undergraduate physics students designed to demonstrate the measurable differences between the material point (Model 1) and rigid body (Model 2) models in projectile motion. We propose a computational experiment that simulates the launch of a sphere from a ramp, an activity that is often performed in introductory practical classes. We provide Python code that generates simulated data for both models and adds random noise to reproduce real conditions. Analysing the simulated data, students can visualise that the rigid body model (which includes rotational energy) provides a much more accurate prediction. The simulated data yield a slope ( A vs h ) that is only 1.40 % different from the rigid body theory, whereas it is 16.7 % different from the simpler material point model. This computational approach serves as a valuable and resource-efficient teaching tool for classrooms without access to laboratory equipment or as a preparatory exercise before a real experiment.
keywords: projectile motion, rigid body model, rotational energy, computer simulation, introductory physics laboratory

title: Biographical digital storytelling in physics education: a pedagogical framework for book trailer production
text: Abstract This study presents the biographical book trailer production (BBTP) framework, a theory-based pedagogical model for humanizing physics education through biographical reading, conceptual reconstruction, and multimodal storytelling. BBTP comprises three interrelated components. First, physicist selection is guided by seven interdependent criteria, including curricular alignment, the epistemic and social dimensions of the family resemblance approach (FRA) to the nature of science (NOS), historical and conceptual relevance, and identity and representation, all of which are grounded in the model of educational reconstruction. Second, students are guided through a four-stage production cycle, from biographical immersion to digital production and peer-reviewed presentation, in which historical material functions not only as motivational context but as a resource for reconstructing the conceptual emergence of physics ideas. Third, a five-dimensional, weighted evaluation rubric assesses physics content, the cognitive-epistemic and social-institutional dimensions of NOS independently, narrative design, and creative execution, operationalizing the distinction between surface and deep engagement with physics and NOS. An example centred on Lise Meitner and nuclear fission illustrates the framework’s application while deliberately resisting heroic or lone-genius narratives common to biographical science teaching. BBTP positions students as active interpreters, producers, and critical communicators of scientific knowledge, supporting four interconnected outcomes: enhanced engagement with the cognitive-epistemic and social-institutional dimensions of FRA; strengthened scientific agency and identity; conceptual reconstruction of physics content through historical narrative; and the development of critical science communication literacy. BBTP offers physics educators a flexible, empirically grounded, and assessable approach to integrating the historical, social, and human dimensions of physics into classroom practice.
keywords: biographical reading, nature of science, family resemblance approach, multimodal storytelling, conceptual reconstruction, educational reconstruction, Lise Meitner, nuclear fission, science identity, assessment rubrics

title: Charged ring and rod: visualizing convergence to point charge to prevent misconceptions
text: Abstract This article details a supplementary investigation on the electric fields due to a uniformly-charged ring and a line of charge. Specifically, this study examines the well-known textbooks’ approximations associated with these classic problems in elementary electromagnetism: rings and rods behaving as point charges. The analytical approach presented in texts is rather cursory, which is based on the supposition of large distances and as a consequence, hiding potentially relevant effects, pertaining to location, regime, or transition. The intended ease in this approximation could lead students to the unintended consequence of its liberal use. This scenario unnecessarily exposes students to further misconceptions. This study is aimed to help students overcome potential pitfalls by providing a more intuitive presentation of the problem. To achieve this, a simple remedial visualization approach, based on synthetic data, is used, demonstrating the transition from the electric fields of the ring and rod to that of a point charge.
keywords: electric field, point charge approximation, student misconceptions, visualization, synthetic data, electromagnetism education

title: The design and construction of a learning material based on collaborative problem solving to develop system thinking in circuit electricity
text: Abstract This study reports the design, development, and initial validation of collaborative problem solving based learning materials for dynamic electricity, targeting first-year physics teacher education students. The materials were developed using the ADDIE instructional design model and focus on building students’ systems thinking skills through structured inquiry and peer collaboration. Four expert validators assessed the materials and rated them as highly valid overall, with content and presentation receiving the maximum score and language rated as adequate. Following expert revision, the materials were implemented with 23 students. Learning gains were measured using normalized gain (N-gain), yielding a class average of 0.43, classified as moderate. While no student reached the high-gain category, 82.61% demonstrated moderate improvement and 17.39% showed low improvement. These findings indicate that learning materials based on collaborative problem solving can meaningfully support the development of systems thinking in introductory physics, though sustained implementation over multiple learning cycles is needed to reach higher levels of competency.
keywords: collaborative problem solving, systems thinking, dynamic electricity, physics teacher education, instructional materials development, ADDIE model, peer collaboration, inquiry-based learning, introductory physics

title: A thematic analysis of A-level physics examiner reports on gravity
text: Abstract Examiner reports from six major United Kingdom exam boards published between 2017 and 2025 are analysed using a mixed-methods thematic analysis. Focusing on questions relating to gravity, the objective is to understand where students commonly drop marks. Findings reveal that the source of difficulty is dependent upon topic and question style. Mathematical errors account for the majority of lost marks in calculation-type questions, while a lack of conceptual understanding commonly results in lost marks on questions relating to fields, energy and gravitational potential. Pedagogical strategies for teaching gravity must emphasise algebraic skills for orbital mechanics topics while prioritising qualitative modelling and precise definitions for field theory.
keywords: gravity, A-level physics, examiner reports, student misconceptions, mathematical errors, conceptual understanding, gravity field, gravitational potential energy, orbital dynamics, field theory, algebraic skills

title: General Physics for Earth Sciences, an undergraduate introductory physics course for students majoring in the Earth Sciences at the University of Johannesburg
text: Abstract Curriculum development for science degrees in higher education is of great relevance to service courses, i.e. courses designed to cater to students majoring in scientific disciplines different from that of the service course. Not only do service courses provide general scientific literacy to future scientists, but (if properly designed) they also address preconceptions around the relevance of a particular science discipline within the broader scientific context. Physics service courses are not exempt from this. A first-year physics course for Earth Sciences majors developed at the University of Johannesburg is described. The course was developed to address the poor performance of the students in the old ‘content-neutral’ general physics service course, and the lack of engagement of students with the content. The content of this fourteen-week course spans topics from vector algebra and two-dimensional mechanics to the properties of solids and fluids. Particular care has been put into enriching each section with relevant examples within the geosciences context, and making links between physics principles and laws to more advanced geoscience subjects. Examples of these include: the relevance of vector addition for the triple-junction stability in plate tectonics; projectile motion to model the effect of volcanic eruptions; Archimedes’ principle and buoyancy at subduction zones; the effects of stress and strain on fossils; and many others. The pedagogical approaches adopted in the teaching of the course are described. These approaches together with the relevance of the course content to students, have tremendously contributed to increasing student performance and the holistic experience of the course. Finally, arguments are proposed to support the claim that the emphasis on relevance of the content is the appropriate answer to address the issues around decolonization of the curriculum within the South African higher education landscape.
keywords: curriculum development, student engagement, student performance, decolonization of curriculum, South African higher education, vector algebra, plate tectonics, volcanic eruptions, subduction zone, buoyancy, teaching methods

title: Introducing the concept of photons to primary school students: an exploratory study on teaching light in a modern context
text: Abstract Despite modern physics providing the most accurate description of the Universe and underpinning current technology, school students are mostly taught classical physics concepts, such as light as waves and gravity as an instantaneous force. In this study, we report on our trials of an eight-lesson progression on the quantum nature of photons. We used appropriate child-friendly language, such as ‘ bulletiness’ for momentum and ‘ waviness’ for the wavelength of photons, to describe its quantum properties, and innovative teaching methods in which concepts emerge from hands-on activities. The study involved 113 students aged 10–11 from two primary schools in Australia. An eight-item conceptual assessment was administered as a pre- and post-test, with responses evaluated using a structured rubric. Statistical analyses, including paired t -tests and ANCOVA, were conducted to examine learning progressions between cohorts. Results showed statistically significant improvements in student learning, with mean scores increasing from 28% to 64% for Cohort 1 ( n = 41) and from 12% to 69% for Cohort 2 ( n = 72), including 29 participants scoring above 80% in the post-test. While participants developed solid foundational knowledge, their ability to analyse and apply it to new situations remained somewhat limited, indicating the need for further scaffolding for higher-order thinking across all students.
