Our findings corroborate prior research that quantum science can be introduced in schools with the caveat of including more tangible activities to support primary-level students.
keywords: photons, quantum nature of light, elementary school science, hands-on activities, conceptual understanding, conceptual assessment, learning progression, higher-order thinking skills, science curriculum reform

title: Where does the mechanical lifting force of a lever come from?
text: Abstract The principle of the lever is one of the oldest in human history. The force applied at one end of a lever (called the effort) results in a force at the other end of the lever in order to lift a load situated there, the weight of which exceeds the size of the effort. Where does the mechanical force which lifts (or otherwise moves) the load come from? An answer to this question is presented.
keywords: levers, mechanical advantage, force transmission, simple machines, physics misconceptions

title: From online videos to physics problems: engaging students through real-world scenarios
text: Abstract Online videos are widely consumed by students, often even during class time. Many of these videos feature situations rich in physical phenomena and can serve as useful starting points for problem-based activities. In this work, we explore how such content can be incorporated into introductory physics teaching by transforming selected video-based scenarios into structured problems. We present three examples that illustrate how such situations can be formulated as quantitative problems suitable for first-year courses, with possible extensions for classroom discussion. By connecting visual experiences from widely viewed online media with formal analysis, this approach offers a way to engage students and relate physics concepts to contexts that already capture their interest.
keywords: online video, problem-based learning, introductory physics, real-life situations, student engagement

title: Work done by the friction force on a toy car
text: Abstract The acceleration of a pull-back toy car was measured and compared with the measured drive torque applied by the axle. The drive torque was only slightly larger than the opposing torque arising from the static friction force on the wheels. The total work done by the static friction force on the wheels of the car was zero since the work done by the friction force to accelerate the car was equal and opposite the work done by the friction torque. That result differs from the conclusion of many authors that no work is done by the static friction force on the drive wheels of an accelerating car.
keywords: static friction, work done by friction, driving torque, wheel torque, acceleration, work-energy theorem

title: Analysis of frequency change due to time dependent tension variation in the kotsuzumi using acoustic measurements and video-based timing analysis
text: Abstract This research introduces a new approach to studying pitch glide in the traditional Japanese drum kotsuzumi through acoustic analysis and controlled tension release. The approach uses a smartphone camera to record the experiment and frame-by-frame video analysis to obtain timing measurements. A simple automated setup was also developed to examine how changes in membrane tension influence vibration frequency during sound production. The study highlights the educational value of music as a context for learning physics by making the relationship between vibration and sound easier to observe experimentally. Unlike a conventional drum, the kotsuzumi allows pitch glide to be observed when the membranetension is released during vibration. This makes the kotsuzumi a useful educational tool for helping students understand the acoustic behaviour of the membrane.
keywords: pitch glides, membrane tension, tension release, vibration frequency, smartphone video analysis, sound production

title: Teaching momentum and impulse in lyceum physics through Fishbone-diagram-supported problem-based learning
text: Abstract This study examined the effectiveness of a Fishbone-diagram-supported problem-based learning (PBL) approach for teaching momentum in lyceum physics. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was conducted with 42 tenth-grade students divided into a Traditional group ( n = 21) and a PBL group ( n = 21). Both groups studied the same core concepts—momentum and impulse—but through different instructional approaches. In the Traditional group, the topic was taught through teacher explanation and worked examples. In the PBL group, learning was organised around the real-life question of why airbags reduce the risk of injury during car collisions and was visually structured using a Fishbone diagram. Pretest and posttest results were analysed using descriptive statistics, t -tests, and ANCOVA. Both groups showed higher posttest scores, but the PBL group demonstrated stronger post-instruction performance. The mean posttest scores increased to 66.00 in the Traditional group and to 73.00 in the PBL group, with gain scores of 8.00 and 14.62, respectively. The findings suggest that Fishbone-diagram-supported PBL can strengthen students’ conceptual understanding of momentum and provide a more meaningful alternative to traditional instruction in lyceum physics.
keywords: momentum, impulse, problem-based learning, fishbone diagram, conceptual understanding, airbags, car collisions, physics education, tenth grade students

title: A low-cost engineering design challenge for exploring geometrical optics: the ‘Safe Room’ activity
text: Abstract This paper presents a low-cost engineering design challenge—the ‘Safe Room’ activity—designed to support the teaching of geometrical optics through an engaging, hands-on, problem-based scenario. Working in teams, participants design and build a laser-based ‘security system’ that must satisfy specific optical constraints (including multiple reflections and at least one refraction) while triggering an alarm when the beam is interrupted. The task combines simple optical components (plane mirrors and a prism) with an Arduino-based sensing system, encouraging planning, prototyping, testing and iterative refinement within an engineering design framework. The activity was implemented with eight pre-service physics teachers during a physics didactics course, allowing them to experience this approach from the learner’s perspective as a model for future classroom practice. Evidence was collected through a post-activity Likert questionnaire, structured observation of group work, and individual SWOT reflections. Results indicate high levels of engagement, mobilisation of key geometrical optics ideas, and positive evaluations of the approach for future teaching use. Observations further indicate that participants enacted core design practices, including systematic planning, iteration and troubleshooting, while also revealing practical implementation challenges such as alignment, mechanical stability and safety routines. The ‘Safe Room’ is therefore proposed as a replicable, low-cost and adaptable engineering design activity that can enrich optics instruction and teacher education. For introductory school contexts, it can be implemented as a progressive sequence comprising reflection-focused and refraction-focused challenges before learners undertake the integrated version.
keywords: geometrical optics, engineering design challenges, problem-based learning, pre-service physics teachers, teacher professional development, refraction, plane mirrors, PRISM, iterative design

title: Why do seated passengers feel tired after a long trip? A context for teaching mechanics and vibration
text: Abstract Why do passengers often feel tired after a long trip even when they have only been sitting? This familiar experience can be explained, at least in part, through physics. A seated passenger is not in true mechanical rest during travel, but is subjected to repeated acceleration, oscillatory disturbance, and vibration transmitted through the vehicle and seat. The body therefore remains mechanically active even without deliberate motion. This paper uses passenger tiredness as a context for teaching reference frames, acceleration, vibration, forced motion, and system response in introductory mechanics. To examine how students initially think about this phenomenon, a short exploratory questionnaire was administered to 21 students enrolled in an introductory mechanics course. The results show that students readily recognise the experience but usually describe it in ordinary language such as prolonged sitting, rough roads, shaking, vehicle movement, and lack of sleep. These responses can be translated into mechanics concepts, making the topic a practical bridge from an everyday question to formal physics.
keywords: vehicle vibration, seat vibration, acceleration, reference frames, forced motion, system response, student misconceptions, contextual learning

title: A compendium of thermodynamic identities with outlines of derivations
text: A compendium of thermodynamic identities with outlines of derivations. Keywords: thermodynamic identity, thermodynamics, first law of thermodynamics, second law of thermodynamics, internal energy, entropy
keywords: thermodynamic identity, thermodynamics, first law of thermodynamics, second law of thermodynamics, internal energy, entropy

title: Investigating experts’ and teachers’ perspectives on teaching special relativity theory at secondary school: didactical approaches, historical controversies, hero narratives, and gender disparities
text: Abstract Special theory of relativity (STR) is a cornerstone of modern physics; however, its introduction in secondary education continues to pose significant conceptual and pedagogical challenges. Although STR is increasingly incorporated into secondary school curricula in Europe, its effective classroom implementation remains uneven and problematic. This study investigates the perspectives of 34 Italian high school teachers and 31 academic physics experts on the educational reconstruction of STR, using a structured questionnaire specifically developed for this research, the ReCon-STR. The first objective of the questionnaire is to explore whether STR should be included in secondary school curricula and to examine the underlying reasons for positions of the participants. The findings reveal a strong consensus on the cultural and epistemological value of STR. The second objective of ReCon-STR is to identify which core topics and experiments should be prioritised in teaching. The results show substantial agreement among teachers, experts, and textbook content, indicating a shared view on the fundamental conceptual elements of STR that should be addressed at the secondary level. The third objective concerns how STR should be taught. Here, significant divergences emerge between what textbooks provide (kinematic-algebraic approach) and what educators and experts prefer (kinematic-geometric approach). Notably, the kinematic-geometric approach—often recommended by physics education researchers and theoretical physicists—is generally not preferred by teachers or other experts. The fourth objective examines the historical accuracy of the narratives commonly presented in teaching and textbooks. The study identifies a persistent acceptance of ‘pseudohistorical’ accounts, such as the role attributed to the Michelson–Morley experiment in the origin and development of STR. In addition, responses from both groups reveal a continued marginalisation of various scientific contributors, including female figures such as Mileva Marić. These findings suggest that STR instruction is often ‘historically flattened,’ underscoring the need for instructional frameworks that present science as a collective, dynamic, and contested human enterprise. Overall, the results of this study provide valuable guidance for the design of targeted teacher training programmes.
keywords: special relativity, high school physics teaching, teacher perceptions, history of relativity, Michelson-Morley experiment, Mileva Marić, gender and science, textbook content, teacher professional development

title: Making a wooden quarter-wave plate for microwaves
text: Abstract The paper presents a simple experimental method for making a wooden quarter-wave plate for microwaves. In addition to the obvious birefringence of wood, absorption must also be considered when making a suitable wooden sample to serve as a quarter-wave plate for microwaves. Two parameters must be determined to obtain circularly polarised microwaves after linearly polarised microwaves pass through a wooden plate: the thickness of the plate and the orientation of the polarisation of the incident linearly polarised microwaves. Due to microwave absorption in wood, experimentally finding appropriate values for both parameters may be non-trivial and time-consuming. The main advantage of the method presented is that it divides the search for the two parameters into two steps. In each step, only one parameter is determined, making the method straightforward and fairly robust, so it can be used as a laboratory exercise in physics courses at pre-university or university level.
keywords: quarter-wave plate, birefringence, wood, microwave absorption, circular polarization, linear polarization, plate thickness, polarization direction, physics laboratory exercises

title: Enhancing retention in physics among secondary school students through Vee-diagram and guided-inquiry strategies
text: Abstract The ongoing underachievement of Nigerian secondary school students in Physics has been attributed to the use of teacher-centred instructional strategies among other factors. Therefore, it is essential to explore innovative student-centred approaches that enhance long-term retention of physics concepts. This study examined whether the use of Vee-diagrams or guided-inquiry instruction can significantly improve students’ retention of physics concepts. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was adopted. The sample comprised 413 students drawn from selected secondary schools. Data were collected using a validated Physics Retention Test (reliability coefficient = 0.89). The data were analysed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and post hoc tests. The results revealed a significant effect of instructional strategy on students’ retention, F(2, 410) = 87.96, p < .001, η 2 p = 0.30, indicating a large effect size. Students exposed to Vee-diagram or guided inquiry strategy performed significantly better than those in the control group. However, no significant difference was found between the two experimental groups. In addition, gender had no significant effect on students’ retention. The study concludes that Vee-diagram and guided inquiry significantly enhance students’ retention in physics. It is recommended that physics teachers adopt these strategies to promote meaningful learning and improve long-term retention among students.
keywords: Vee diagram, guided inquiry, student-centred instruction, high school physics, meaningful learning

title: Modelling the coefficient of restitution for a bouncing ball
text: Abstract A standard experiment in elementary physics is to measure the coefficient of restitution (COR) of a bouncing ball. When dropped vertically on a rigid horizontal surface, the COR is defined as the ratio of the bounce speed to the incident speed. The COR is a measure of the energy loss and depends on the elastic properties of the ball. A simple model is presented to show how the COR of a ball can be calculated in terms of its elastic properties.
keywords: coefficient of restitution, bouncing ball, energy loss, elastic properties, collision

title: Simple method of determining the liquid dielectric constant using a variable capacitor
text: Abstract Various methods are used to measure dielectric constant, particularly in pedagogical settings to illustrate the concept of capacitance. This study presents a sequence of three experiments using two types of variable capacitors to investigate the dependence of capacitance on plate area and the medium. In the first experiment, a single-gang variable capacitor was used to determine the dielectric constant of a liquid by comparing capacitance measurements in air and in the liquid medium. The second experiment determined the dielectric constant by measuring the capacitance of capacitors connected in parallel, with a set of capacitors in air and the other immersed in liquid. The third experiment employed a dual-gang variable capacitor, enabling direct and simultaneous capacitance measurements in air and in liquid. The dielectric constants of transformer oil, coconut oil, and castor oil were measured. The results aligned with published values. The experimental setup requires minimal equipment, a variable capacitor and an LCR meter. The concise procedure makes it suitable for instructional laboratory use. Through these experiments, students gain practical insight into the fundamental properties of capacitors and dielectric materials.
keywords: variable capacitor, capacitance measurement, parallel plate capacitor, transformer oil, coconut oil, castor oil, LCR meter, physics laboratory experiments

title: A low-cost, homemade lysimeter for exploring evaporation and water balance in physics education
text: Abstract Evaporation, infiltration and soil-water exchange are governed by fundamental physical principles, yet they are rarely explored experimentally in school physics due to the cost and complexity of professional instrumentation. This article presents a simple, low-cost homemade lysimeter designed to make these processes measurable and pedagogically accessible in a laboratory setting. The device, built from inexpensive materials, allows students to determine precipitation, infiltration, soil-water storage and actual evapotranspiration directly from mass differences. A practical measurement protocol is outlined, suitable for lab sessions. It is illustrated how the resulting data can be analysed to identify first-stage (linear) and second-stage (square-root) evaporation regimes using basic least-squares techniques on a spreadsheet. The activity provides a real-life context for applying concepts of heat transfer, phase change and water balance, while connecting physics learning with sustainability and environmental processes observable in school gardens. The lysimeter offers a versatile tool to support inquiry-based learning, quantitative reasoning and discussions of real-world water-management challenges.
keywords: lysimeter, evaporation, water balance, infiltration, soil water storage, evapotranspiration, low-cost laboratory equipment, inquiry-based learning, heat transfer, phase transitions, water management, school gardens, sustainability education

title: What really happens to energy and longitudinal momentum when a transverse wave pulse hits a linear mass density discontinuity in a taut string? Comment on ‘A simulation tool for exploring pulse dynamics in connected strings with different densities’
text: Abstract In a recent paper, Ladino and Rondón (2025 Phys. Educ. 60 045026) discuss ‘an interactive simulation tool designed to investigate the dynamics of a Gaussian pulse propagating along two connected strings with different linear densities.’ In its conclusions, the paper states that ‘longitudinal momentum was found to be non-conserved,... this observation suggests [that] an underlying cause... warrants further investigation.’ This paper provides that investigation by showing that Newtonian longitudinal momentum is conserved in the process, but that one needs to take into account the necessary coupling between transverse and longitudinal modes of oscillation to determine that. It is also noted that transverse-longitudinal mode coupling significantly changes the required potential energy density analysis, unless one restricts the analysis to Slinky springs for which purely transverse motion of string points is possible. However, if one restricts the analysis to Slinky springs, purely transverse pulses do not have any Newtonian longitudinal momentum, and this remains the case throughout the whole reflection and transmission across a linear mass density discontinuity process. Consequently, in that case there is no apparent ‘non-conservation of longitudinal momentum’ conundrum to resolve. All results are determined by modelling a taut string as a chain of point masses joined by massless springs obeying Hooke’s law and solving the resulting set of coupled ordinary differential equations numerically. The results are of importance for instructors more generally by revealing the limits of applicability of neglecting longitudinal motion when analysing energy transport around taut strings.
keywords: taut string, energy transport, potential energy density, classical mechanics

title: No left-hander left behind: finding the right way in the physics laboratory
text: Abstract Laboratory work is central to physics education, yet the design of laboratory instruments, demonstrations, and safety procedures almost universally assumes right-handed operation. This study investigates the disadvantages that left-handed students face in high school physics laboratories through two complementary approaches. First, a handedness survey of 4226 Grade 10–12 students across three public high schools in China revealed that while 9.5% of students were naturally left-handed, over three-quarters had been corrected to write with their right hand, leaving only 2.2% who still used their left hand—a finding that highlights the extent to which cultural correction masks the true scale of the affected population. Second, a measurement experiment using vernier calipers ( N = 583 ) showed that both left-handed and corrected left-handed students exhibited higher error rates (53% and 52%, respectively) than right-handed students (31%), with a Kruskal–Wallis test confirming significant group differences ( H = 11.73 , p = 0.003 ). Video behavioural coding ( N = 51 ) further revealed that left-handed students required longer task completion times (median 165 s vs 118 s) and substantially more frequent re-grasping of the instrument (median 9 vs 2), patterns corroborated by thermal imaging of grip distributions. Importantly, overall academic performance showed no meaningful differences among handedness groups, indicating that the observed laboratory disadvantages are environmentally imposed rather than intrinsic. The paper concludes with practical inclusive teaching strategies, including pre-laboratory handedness audits, body-neutral safety language, positional compensation training, and the use of symmetrically designed instruments as transitional scaffolding.
keywords: left-handedness, physics laboratory, task completion time, infrared thermography, inclusive pedagogy, high school physics teaching, instrument design, safety procedures, scaffolding

title: Visualizing convection currents: a sequence of experimental activities
text: Abstract This paper presents two experimental activities for teaching heat convection to upper-primary and lower-secondary students. The sequence is designed to make the interaction and exchange of warm and cool water masses visible and to support students in constructing an explanatory mechanism. The first activity focuses on the vertical motion of warm and cold water, while the second extends this understanding to the full cyclic pattern of convection currents. Structured according to the predict–observe–explain strategy, the activities link visible fluid motion with temperature differences, density differences, and the cyclic motion of water masses, thereby supporting an explanatory understanding of convection.
keywords: convection currents, thermal convection, convective cells, density difference, temperature difference, fluid flow, Predict-Observe-Explain, explanatory understanding, upper elementary students, junior high school students, hands-on experiments

title: From abstraction to measurement: a low-cost experimental study of friction torque using a physical pendulum and a smartphone
text: Abstract This article proposes a low-cost experiment to overcome the didactic obstacles associated with the abstract concept of solid friction torque for students. By simply using a smartphone equipped with a free application (Fizziq) to analyse the oscillations of a physical pendulum, this study allows for the indirect measurement of a constant solid friction torque τ s at a fixed rotation axis, by exploiting the relationship between this torque and the observed linear decay of the oscillation amplitudes. The results show that the solid friction torque τ s remains constant regardless of the pendulum’s geometry, thus confirming the validity of the theoretical model. Finally, the introduction of measurement uncertainty analysis gives this approach a scientific rigour and didactic significance that are essential for students.
keywords: physical pendulum, smartphone sensors, low-cost physics experiments, damped oscillations, amplitude decay, measurement uncertainty evaluation, rotational dynamics, physics education

title: Teaching blackbody radiation through thermal camera, simulation, and land surface temperature mapping
text: Abstract The teaching of blackbody radiation in secondary physics is often challenging due to its abstract nature and limited availability of appropriate instructional resources. This study aims to implement an integrated learning design incorporating a thermal camera-based apparatus powered by the MLX90640, virtual simulations, and project-based learning (PjBL) to support the teaching of blackbody radiation in secondary education. The study employed a research-and-development approach using the 4D model (define, design, develop, and disseminate). The developed materials were validated by experts and implemented in two 12th-grade classes. The results indicate that the learning apparatus and module are highly feasible. Throughout the PjBL, students mapped land surface temperature using Google Earth Engine and presented their findings as posters, thereby connecting abstract physics concepts with real-world environmental data. In addition, students reported positive perceptions regarding environmental awareness, engagement, and collaboration. This study illustrates how science, technology, engineering, and mathematics and education for sustainable development can be integrated into physics instruction through thermal camera demonstrations, simulation, and real-world environmental data analysis. The proposed learning design offers practical references for teachers seeking to implement technology-enhanced and sustainability-oriented instruction in secondary physics education.
keywords: blackbody radiation, thermal camera, virtual simulation, land surface temperature mapping, Google Earth Engine, project-based learning, STEAM education, sustainability education, technology-enhanced instruction, environmental awareness

title: From gloves to photons: a case study of upper secondary students’ understanding of classical and quantum correlations after ordinary classroom instruction on entanglement
text: Abstract Quantum entanglement is increasingly being discussed in upper secondary physics education, yet little is known about how students understand entanglement after ordinary classroom instruction. This small-scale case study investigates how 12 German upper secondary students distinguished between classical and quantum correlations after a lesson in which entanglement was introduced through a classical glove example and a photon-polarisation scenario. Students’ written responses were analysed using a qualitative coding approach to identify their dominant reasoning orientations and associated misconceptions. Three main reasoning orientations were identified: object-oriented, relation-oriented and measurement-oriented reasoning. Many students explained quantum correlation by referring to properties of individual quantum objects, such as uncertainty or superposition, rather than by treating the correlation as property of a composite system. Some students also transferred classical ‘opposite-pair’ intuitions to the quantum case, leading to the assumption that entangled photons must always show perfect anti-correlation. In addition, several responses indicated students’ confusion between superposition and entanglement. These findings suggest the need for greater attention to the relational and measurement-dependent character of quantum correlations in introductory instruction on entanglement at the upper secondary level. Classical examples and simplified quantum scenarios should therefore be accompanied by discussion of their limitations, so that these teaching examples do not unintentionally reinforce students’ misunderstandings.
keywords: quantum entanglement, quantum correlations, classical correlations, student misconceptions, photon polarization, superposition, measurement dependence, relational reasoning, anticorrelation, conceptual change

title: Improving physics students’ communication skills through interdisciplinary teaching
text: Abstract The interdisciplinary nature of science and technology in the 21st century requires scientists to communicate across disciplines and non-specialist audiences. We ran a four-year collaboration pairing an upper-level physics laboratory course with an inorganic chemistry course, focusing on superconductivity and nanotechnology. Physics students analysed the materials synthesized by chemistry students and then presented their results to campus-wide audiences, including non-science majors. The presentations evolved from separate discipline-specific discussions to integrated poster sessions. Using rubrics and self-reflection exercises, we assessed how physics students developed into communicators. The student responses showed that they increasingly recognized audience needs and adapted their explanations accordingly. This study demonstrated that structured interdisciplinary experiences can enhance physics students’ ability to communicate complex scientific ideas.
keywords: science communication, interdisciplinary teaching, superconductivity, nanotechnology, poster sessions, audience adaptation, self-reflection, rubrics, non-specialist audiences

title: Investigating projectile motion in a liquid: an educational experiment with a ball launched at an angle
text: Abstract This paper presents an educational investigation of projectile motion in a viscous medium using a simple laboratory setup and smartphone-based measurements. A magnetic launcher installed inside a water-filled container was used to launch a spherical projectile at different angles. The launch angle was measured using the mobile application phyphox, while the trajectory was recorded in slow-motion mode with a smartphone camera. The motion of the projectile was analysed theoretically and experimentally in water using drag-force models. Particular attention was given to the radial distance between the projectile and the launch point. It was shown that the critical launch angle associated with non-monotonic motion changes in a viscous medium. For the experimental conditions considered here, the theoretical critical angle was 62.5 ∘ , while the experimentally measured value was ( 53 ± 0.5 ) ∘ . For launch angles above the critical value, the projectile first moves away from the launch point, then approaches it again, and finally moves away once more. This counterintuitive behaviour provides an engaging demonstration of resistive forces and projectile motion for students studying mechanics.
keywords: projectile motion, viscous media, drag force, launch angle, critical angle, resistance force, smartphone-based measurement, Phyphox

title: Effectiveness of a low-cost 3D magnetic field visualization device in enhancing students’ conceptual understanding of fundamental magnetism concepts
text: Abstract This study investigated the effectiveness of a low-cost fluid-based three-dimensional (3D) magnetic field visualization device in enhancing students’ conceptual understanding of fundamental magnetism concepts. The study employed a quantitative pre-experimental research design, specifically the one-group pretest-posttest design, involving 40 student participants. The developed device utilized suspended iron filings enclosed within a transparent liquid medium, integrated with LED lighting and magnets of varying sizes to facilitate 3D visualization of magnetic field behaviour. The intervention focused on competencies related to magnetic field patterns, magnetic strength, visualization of invisible magnetic forces, and scientific inquiry through observation and comparison. Results revealed substantial improvements in students’ Mean Percentage Scores across all learning competencies, with post-test results indicating moderately high to high understanding levels. Paired t -test results further showed statistically significant differences between pre-test and post-test scores across allcompetencies at the 0.05 level of significance, suggesting that the device effectively improved students’ conceptual understanding of magnetism. Thematic analysis additionally revealed that students perceived the device as engaging, interactive, practical, and helpful in visualizing abstract magnetic concepts. Overall, the findings suggest that the developed 3D magnetic field visualization device is an effective and low-cost instructional material that supports visualization-based and inquiry-oriented learning in Physics Education.
keywords: conceptual understanding, iron filings, magnetic field patterns, magnetic field strength, inquiry-based learning, student perceptions

title: Reversing the sign of Hooke’s law
text: Abstract Hooke’s law for ideal springs describes the linear relationship between the restoring force exerted by a spring and the distance by which the spring is displaced from its equilibrium length. In its basic form, the law states that if a spring is compressed or extended by some displacement away from equilibrium, the spring will exert a force proportional to this displacement in the opposite direction. The resulting motion of a particle feeling such a restoring force is the commonly studied harmonic motion of a one-dimensional oscillator. In this work, we describe a hypothetical situation in which the sign of the Hooke’s law expression for the restoring force is reversed. This means that now the particle is being acted upon by a repelling force proportional to the displacement in the same direction. Apart from trivial cases, one might naively think that the expected outcome of the motion will see the particle being pushed to infinity by the repelling force. However, we show here that this is not always the case. We illustrate the idea and introduce various scenarios in which some curious results are obtained. This pedagogical work shows to an audience of undergraduate students that differential equations can exhibit extreme sensitivity to initial conditions, where even tiny changes can lead to dramatically different outcomes.
keywords: Hooke's law, repulsive force, restoring force, one-dimensional oscillator, harmonic motion, differential equations, sensitivity to initial conditions, chaotic dynamics, nonlinear dynamics

title: Design, calibration, and classroom implementation of a low-cost gear apparatus for secondary physics education
text: Abstract Hands-on apparatus can make rotational mechanics more observable and measurable for secondary students, yet many gear instructional kits are costly, small-scale, or impractical for classroom deployment. This study reports the design and calibration of a low-cost, scalable hands-on gear apparatus for upper secondary physics, enabling students to investigate gear ratio relationships through direct measurement of rotational motion and torque transmission, quantitative comparison between theoretical and experimental values. The apparatus was designed using two-dimensional modelling (Rhinoceros) and fabricated from 3 mm plywood via laser cutting to ensure reproducibility and rapid replacement of parts. The learning set was evaluated with upper secondary students ( n = 90) during classroom-based investigations in which experimentally measured outcomes were compared with theoretical predictions derived from gear tooth ratios. Calibration results showed mean percentage errors of 1.57% for revolutions per minute measurements and 2.19% for torque measurements, demonstrating satisfactory accuracy for classroom use. The apparatus cost approximately USD 8, indicating strong potential as an affordable and accessible physics learning tool. The apparatus may support inquiry-based learning and help students connect theoretical rotational mechanics concepts with observable mechanical behaviour.
keywords: gear ratio, torque transmission, hands-on learning, instrument calibration, laser cutting, inquiry-based learning

title: Development and evaluation of a lesson sequence in heat and temperature using transformative learning in a blended-online setting
text: Abstract This research focused on a transformative learning (TL) lesson sequence to determine how effectively they helped Bachelor of Secondary Education major in Science (BSEd Science) students develop a better understanding of the concepts of heat and temperature in a blended online learning framework. Using a Concurrent Embedded Mixed Methods Design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected using heat and temperature conceptual evaluation (HTCE), semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and students’ reflective journal logs. The intervention was implemented within a two-week period, consisting of 20 blended, synchronous and asynchronous, online, instructional hours. Conceptual understanding was assessed using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, as post-test conceptual gains violated the assumption of normality. Participants’ post-test scores showed a statistically significant positive change in conceptual understanding ( Z = –2.580, p = .010), with a medium effect size ( r = .48). Although participants’ HTCE post-test scores fell within the poor achievement range, HTCE (Cronbach’s α = .724) was deemed a suitable test for measuring students’ conceptual understanding. Despite some persistence of abstract misconceptions and some misconceptions within the domain of heat, topics like heat and temperature, perception of hotness, calorimetry, thermal conductivity, rate of cooling, and specific heat capacity, evidenced a significant decrease in misconceptions among participants. Qualitative data complemented the quantitative findings and described participants’ challenges and positive experiences with critical reflective and collaborative learning. Overall, findings suggest that TL is a viable approach to developing physics concepts; however, more extensive instructional implementation may be warranted to affect greater conceptual change regarding heat and temperature concepts.
keywords: transformative learning, temperature and heat, conceptual understanding, misconceptions, pre-service science teachers, conceptual change, reflective learning, calorimetry, specific heat, thermal conductivity

title: Distinguishing medium displacement from acoustic pressure in two-dimensional sound interference
text: Abstract Sound interference is often taught using the rule that sound becomes louder when two waves meet in phase and quieter when they meet in opposite phase. The rule applies directly to acoustic pressure, but it can be misleading if students interpret it as the simple addition of medium-particle displacements. This ambiguity becomes especially clear when two sound waves travel in perpendicular directions. Vector addition of two orthogonal medium displacements can produce resultants with the same magnitude in the in-phase and opposite-phase cases, differing only in direction. Medium-displacement magnitude alone therefore cannot distinguish constructive from destructive interference. The difference becomes clear from the inflow and outflow of neighbouring medium. At a constructive-interference point, the surrounding medium alternately converges and spreads out, producing a large acoustic-pressure oscillation. At a destructive-interference point, inflow from one side is balanced by outflow through another, so acoustic pressure changes very little although the medium continues to move. This paper presents time-sequence diagrams and a browser-based dynamic display that visualise this two-dimensional motion and help students interpret the path-difference condition in terms of acoustic-pressure superposition.
keywords: acoustic interference, acoustic pressure, constructive interference, destructive interference, perpendicular wave propagation, path difference, wave superposition, dynamic visualization

title: Can artificial intelligence solve school-level physics exam questions? A decade-based evaluation using Turkish university entrance exams
text: Abstract Background. Large language models LLMs are increasingly used by students as informal learning tools; however, their reliability in solving school-level physics questions remains uncertain. Aim. This study evaluated the performance of three LLMs—ChatGPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and DeepSeek V3.1—in solving physics questions from Turkish university entrance examinations administered between 2016 and 2025, comprising the Yükseköğretime Geçiş Sınavı (YGS; Transition to Higher Education Examination) in 2016–2017 and the Temel Yeterlilik Testi (TYT; Basic Proficiency Test) in 2018–2025. Methods. A total of 84 publicly available physics questions—28 from the 2016–2017 YGS examinations and 56 from the 2018–2025 TYT examinations—were presented to each model under identical testing conditions using the same neutral student-style prompt, without revealing the examination source. Responses were scored for final-answer correctness using official answer keys. Correct-answer accuracyand net scores were calculated, and model performance was compared using Cochran’s Q test. Results. DeepSeek V3.1 achieved the highest numerical correct-answer accuracy at 78.6% (95%CI 68.7%–86.0%), followed by Gemini 2.5 Flash at 69.0% (95% CI 58.5%–77.9%) and ChatGPT-5 at 65.5% (95% CI 54.8%–74.8%). However, the difference in correct-answer performance among the three models was not statistically significant (Cochran’s Q = 4.732, df = 2, p = 0.094). Conclusion. LLMs may support physics learning and exam preparation, but their responses should be used critically and under teacher guidance rather than as substitutes for structured physics instruction.
keywords: large language models, ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, physics problem solving, LLM performance comparison, student learning tools, exam preparation

title: Investigating ultrasonic reflection at perpendicular and oblique incidence: a context-based classroom model for understanding urban bat collisions
text: Abstract Ultrasonic distance sensors are widely used in school experiments and technical applications based on time-of-flight measurements. However, the influence of surface orientation on echo detection is rarely addressed experimentally, despite playing a crucial role in real-world acoustic systems. This article introduces a classroom experimental model set in an authentic and socially relevant real-world context: bat echolocation in urban environments. Smooth, vertical glass façades can suppress ultrasonic echoes during oblique approaches, potentially leading to fatal collisions. This scenario enables context-based physics learning by connecting geometric reflection principles to phenomena directly linked to students’ everyday environments. The presented setup, based on an Arduino and an HC-SR04 sensor, deliberately reduces the complex real-world phenomenon to its essential geometric mechanism. This reduction allows for a phenomenon-based and model-oriented investigation of ultrasonic reflection. The experiment is specifically designed for the lower secondary level, providing age-appropriate cognitive stimulation through a controllable and reproducible setup. Due to its low-cost and easily accessible components, the model offers a low-threshold opportunity for classroom implementation. It thus combines authentic framing, conceptual clarity, and practical feasibility, contributing to context-based physics education in secondary school settings.
keywords: ultrasonic reflection, oblique incidence, perpendicular incidence, bat echolocation, glass facades, time-of-flight, high school physics, Arduino, HC-SR04 sensor, low-cost laboratory equipment, reflection geometry

title: Developing, validating, and preliminarily testing a Basic Science examination item bank contextualized for technical officer training: a case study at a military technical officer school
text: Abstract This article reports the development, expert validation, and preliminary testing of a Basic Science examination item bank contextualized for technical officer training at a military technical higher-education institution. The study responds to the need to renew assessment in alignment with outcome-based education and competence-oriented learning. In particular, it addresses the tendency for examination questions in Advanced Mathematics, General Physics, and Applied Chemistry to focus mainly on knowledge recall and decontextualized calculation, while insufficiently showing the relationship between foundational knowledge and technical-professional contexts. The study adopted a mixed-methods case-study design with a design-and-development orientation. Data were collected from 60 cadets, 10 Basic Science lecturers, and 10 specialized-subject lecturers. The resulting item bank contained 180 items distributed across Advanced Mathematics, General Physics, and Applied Chemistry and organized by cognitive level, professional context, and accompanying data type. The item bank was reviewed by 20 experts and preliminarily tested with 36 cadets. The survey results show that participants clearly recognized the role of Basic Science courses, strongly supported the development of context-integrated examination items, and positively evaluated the pedagogical value of this approach. Expert appraisal indicated high levels of appropriateness in terms of disciplinary accuracy, professional contextualization, clarity, and usability for assessment, with S-CVI/Ave = 0.91 and Kendall’s W = 0.64. Preliminary item analysis produced a mean difficulty of 0.62 and a mean discrimination index of 0.38; 28 of the 36 pilot items met both difficulty and discrimination criteria, 6 required revision, and 2 were recommended for removal or redesign. The main contribution of the study is a structured process for developing an examination item bank based on the alignment among learning outcomes, a content–competence–context matrix, expert validation, preliminary testing, and item-quality analysis. The study extends discussions on authentic assessment, contextualization, and assessment literacy in military technical education.
keywords: item development, item validation, contextualized assessment, authentic assessment, outcome-based education, competency-based education, item difficulty and discrimination, assessment literacy, basic science education, higher mathematics, general physics, applied chemistry, military higher education

title: Tracking uniformly accelerated motion using a smartphone magnetometer: a low-cost investigation based on time-derivative analysis of magnetic field data
text: Abstract Smartphone magnetometers are widely used for measuring static magnetic fields but have received comparatively little attention as sensors for investigating motion. I present a simple, low-cost experiment in which the magnetic field produced by a cylindrical neodymium magnet attached to a toy car is recorded by a smartphone running the Phyphox application as the car moves down an inclined plane. Rather than converting the magnetic-field data into displacement through calibration, the magnetic field is analysed directly as a function of time. The first and second temporal derivatives of the magnetic field are calculated numerically to investigate how the magnetic signal changes during uniformly accelerated motion. The maximum values of both derivatives increase systematically with the inclination angle and show a strong linear correlation with sin θ . The experiment combines mechanics, magnetism, numerical differentiation and data analysis within a single accessible activity. It demonstrates that a smartphone magnetometer can serve as a dynamic motion sensor while providing students with practical experience in experimental data acquisition and numerical analysis using inexpensive equipment.
keywords: smartphone magnetometer, uniformly accelerated motion, Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets, toy cars, inclined plane, Phyphox, numerical differentiation, motion sensing, low-cost physics experiments, kinematics

title: Effectiveness of active teaching in addressing students’ misconceptions in static electricity using SOLO Taxonomy
text: Abstract This study investigates the effect of active teaching methods on students’ SOLO taxonomy levels in learning static electricity concepts (electric charge, force, and field) among 11th-grade female students, aged 16–17 years, during the 2024–2025 academic year. Using a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-tests, 30 students were divided into experimental (active teaching) and control (traditional instruction) groups. Researcher-developed assessments with acceptable reliability (Cronbach’s alpha: 0.708–0.743) were used. The 14-session intervention included hands-on experiments, PhET simulations, and collaborative learning activities. MANOVA results showed significant improvements in the experimental group at higher SOLO levels: relational (electric charge), extended abstract (electric force), and multistructural (electric field), with moderate to large effect sizes ( η 2 = 0.15–0.41). Qualitative findings indicated a reduction in common misconceptions, such as misunderstandings about charge transfer and electric fields. Overall, active teaching enhanced higher-order thinking, improved conceptual understanding, and effectively reduced misconceptions in physics learning.
keywords: active teaching methods, student misconceptions, static electricity, SOLO taxonomy, conceptual understanding, electric charge, electric force, electric field, PhET simulation, hands-on experiments, cooperative learning, higher-order thinking skills

title: Investigating wireless power transfer using a homemade pickup coil and a Qi wireless charger
text: Abstract Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction is commonly demonstrated using moving magnets or laboratory signal generators, which may not adequately connect the underlying physics with modern technologies. We describe a simple, inexpensive classroom experiment that uses a commercial Qi wireless charger to demonstrate electromagnetic induction and wireless power transfer. A homemade 200-turn receiving coil, a Schottky diode, a smoothing capacitor, and an ordinary digital multimeter are used to convert the induced high-frequency AC voltage into a measurable direct current voltage, eliminating the need for an oscilloscope or function generator. By varying the separation between the transmitting and receiving coils, students directly observe the decrease in induced voltage as the distance increases, illustrating the reduction in magnetic coupling predicted qualitatively by Faraday’s law. The experimental data are well represented by a physics-informed phenomenological fit, providing an opportunity to discuss curve fitting and the distinction between idealized physical models and commercially optimized devices. The apparatus is inexpensive, easy to construct, and well suited for secondary-school and undergraduate teaching laboratories, providing an effective bridge between textbook electromagnetism and the everyday technology of wireless charging.
keywords: wireless power transfer, Faraday's law, pickup coil, electromagnetic induction, magnetic coupling, phenomenological fit, curve fitting, physics-informed modeling, classroom demonstration

title: Determine the internal resistance and electromotive force (EMF) of alkaline battery by using Raspberry Pi Pico
text: Abstract This paper presents the findings from utilizing the Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller in an educational context to measure the internal resistance and electromotive force (EMF) of both old and new alkaline batteries. The experiment aimed to bridge theoretical concepts with practical applications and was conducted with graduating physics teacher students. Current and voltage were measured with high precision, and the data were processed using Microsoft Excel. Additionally, measurement uncertainty and errors were calculated. Through the analysis of the experimental results, students used the measured current–voltage relationship to determine the internal resistance and EMF by linear regression while developing practical skills in data analysis, uncertainty evaluation, and interpretation of experimental results.
keywords: alkaline batteries, internal resistance, electromotive force, Raspberry Pi Pico, microcontroller-based measurement, current-voltage characteristics, measurement uncertainty, physics teacher education, hands-on physics experiments, linear regression

title: Time as a teaching object: beyond the variable t
text: Abstract Time is central to physics, yet in physics teaching it is often treated mainly as an operational variable in equations. This article argues that time can also be addressed as a teaching object. It offers physics teachers a practical framework for making different meanings of time explicit in upper secondary and introductory undergraduate contexts. To this end, we analyse time from physical, historical, cultural and philosophical perspectives and present a content-analysis framework organised around conceptual structure, systems of representation and phenomenology. This framework helps teachers identify key meanings of time and is operationalised through short classroom activities that connect physical models, representations and students’ everyday experiences. Rather than adding a new topic to the curriculum, the article proposes brief conceptual windows for discussing models, measurement, irreversibility, lived time and the situated nature of scientific knowledge.
keywords: time in physics, meaning of time, physics education, upper secondary school, irreversibility, lived time, timekeeping, phenomenology, representation systems, situated knowledge, classroom activities

title: Corrigendum: Comment on ‘A unifying network approach for circuits simplification and equivalent resistances, capacitors and inductors evaluation’ (2026 Phys. Educ. 61 048001)
text: Corrigendum: Comment on ‘A unifying network approach for circuits simplification and equivalent resistances, capacitors and inductors evaluation’ (2026 Phys. Educ. 61 048001). Keywords: electrical circuits, circuit simplification, equivalent resistance, equivalent capacitance, equivalent inductance, network approach
keywords: electrical circuits, circuit simplification, equivalent resistance, equivalent capacitance, equivalent inductance, network approach

title: The swing weight of a baseball bat
text: Abstract The moment of inertia (MOI) of simple objects is easy to calculate, but is not so easy for objects with a complicated shape. In the present paper, the MOI of a baseball bat is calculated using a simplified model of a bat, and is shown to be closely related to the distance between the end of the handle and the centre of mass. The results are compared with measured results, indicating that the MOI may be easier to calculate than to measure.
keywords: baseball bats, moment of inertia, center of mass, rotational dynamics

title: Comparative effects of collaborative strategies in a Quizlet gamified learning environment on secondary school physics students’ achievement
text: Abstract Gamification is increasingly recognised as a vital strategy for enhancing students’ learning outcomes. In science education, particularly in physics students often experience learning as abstract, difficult, and disengaging, which negatively affect their achievement. This study evaluated how four collaborative learning strategies could enhance secondary school physics students’ achievement through Quizlet gamification. The study was guided by two research objectives. A pretest, posttest, non-equivalent quasi-experimental research design was employed. The sample size was 317 physics students. The instruments for data collection were Quizlet gamification software in four collaborative learning strategies and physics achievement test (PAT). The instruments were validated by physics education experts. The PAT was pilot tested on 49 physics students and analysed using spearman ranking correlation which yielded 0.89 confirming its validity. The instrument was used to generate data which were analysed using mean, standard deviation, analysis of covariance and Sidak post hoc. Sensitivity and fidelity analysis were carried out to confirm the findings and implementation of problem based learning. The data analysed showed that the use of collaborative learning strategy in gamified environment enhances physics students’ academic achievement in think–pair–share (TPS), Jigsaw, reciprocal peer tutoring (RPT) and problem-based learning (PBL). Male students outperformed their female peers in RPT and Jigsaw however, in TPS and PBL, gender differences in achievement were negligible. The study concluded that the use of four collaborative learning strategies in Quizlet gamified environment enhances physics students’ achievement in TPS, Jigsaw, RPT and PBL. Therefore, teachers should integrate Quizlet gamification into collaborative learning setting to improve physics students’ achievement. Also, gender-responsive strategies should be incorporated into RPT and JIGSAW to bridge performance gaps, while maintaining inclusive practices in TPS and PBL.
keywords: gamification, Quizlet, collaborative learning strategies, physics achievement, high school physics, Think Pair Share, Jigsaw cooperative learning, reciprocal peer tutoring, problem-based learning, gender differences in achievement, student engagement

title: Using generative AI to support students’ interpretation of kinematics graphs: a classroom-based approach
text: Abstract This paper reports a classroom intervention in which secondary vocational students used generative artificial intelligence (AI) to discuss and check their reasoning with kinematics graphs. The intervention was conducted within the AI4Physics project and consisted of five 90 min workshops. The activities focused on common difficulties such as confusing graph shape with motion, graph height with slope, and the area under a graph with a visual feature rather than a physical quantity. Students worked with position–time, velocity–time, and acceleration–time graphs and were guided to use AI for explanation, comparison and checking rather than for obtaining final answers. Students completed complementary test of understanding graphs in kinematics-based pre- and post-test item sets. Descriptively, their mean score was 2.91/13 on the pre-test item set and 5.50/13 on the post-test item set. Because the two item sets were not independently validated as equivalent and the study involved only one class, the results are interpreted with caution. The distinctive pedagogical contribution of the paper is a teacher-guided checking routine in which AI-generated explanations, including incorrect ones, become objects for physics reasoning: students are required to test AI claims against axes, units, slopes, areas and graph intervals before accepting or rejecting them.
keywords: generative AI, kinematic diagrams, physics reasoning, secondary vocational students, position-time graphs, velocity-time graph, acceleration-time graphs, AI-generated explanations, classroom intervention

title: From star patterns to sky map: a simple activity to clear misconceptions about constellations
text: Abstract The concept of constellations is one of the cornerstones in observational Astronomy. However, there are many misconceptions about constellations among middle school students. In this article, we introduce a simple activity that can be readily performed in a typical middle school classroom, which can rectify misconceptions.
keywords: constellations, misconceptions, star patterns, sky maps, observational astronomy, junior high school students, astronomy education, hands-on classroom activities

title: A heuristic derivation of gravitational redshift in a high school
text: Abstract Modern physics topics increasingly appear in upper secondary school curricula, creating a need for approaches that remain conceptually rigorous while staying within students’ mathematical background. This paper presents a lesson introducing gravitational redshift to 17–18-year-old students through Einstein’s equivalence principle and elementary special relativity. Inspired by Einstein’s original 1907 reasoning, the proposed derivation avoids the formalism of general relativity while preserving the physical logic underlying the phenomenon. The lesson is designed to help students connect concepts from Newtonian mechanics, Newtonian gravitation and special relativity within a coherent explanatory framework rather than treating the redshift formula as an isolated result.
keywords: gravitational redshift, equivalence principle, special relativity, high school physics teaching, heuristic derivation, Newtonian gravity, classical mechanics, conceptual understanding

title: Teacher-guided AI-assisted development of virtual physics laboratories: classroom case studies in secondary physics
text: Abstract This classroom case study examines the teacher-guided artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted development of virtual physics laboratory activities for secondary education. A generative AI system was used as a rapid prototyping partner to create and iteratively refine interactive simulations, digital measurement tools, and supporting laboratory worksheets for Grade 10 and Grade 12 physics. The first case study focused on a single-slit diffraction laboratory emphasizing conceptual visualization, measurement calibration, and error analysis. The second case study focused on Grade 12 electricity and electromagnetism activities, including transformer and series LCR circuit simulations, and illustrated how previously established design patterns enabled faster development using simpler prompts. Classroom implementation and exploratory student feedback are discussed in relation to engagement, usability, visualization, and perceived support for experimental understanding. The study highlights how generative AI may support rapid development of curriculum-linked virtual laboratories when the teacher remains central in directing pedagogy, verifying physics content, and adapting tools for learners.
keywords: generative AI, virtual physics laboratory, single-slit diffraction, measurement calibration, error analysis, transformer simulation, rapid prototyping, interactive simulation, student engagement, usability

title: A unified model for voltage-dependent capacitance in supercapacitors for physics teaching
text: Abstract This work presents a conceptually accessible analytical framework for teaching voltage-dependent capacitance in supercapacitors by extending the classical concept of capacitance. While conventional capacitors are characterised by a constant capacitance and a linear charge–voltage relationship, supercapacitors exhibit nonlinear behaviour due to the coexistence of electrostatic double-layer capacitance and voltage-dependent pseudocapacitive processes associated with fast faradaic reactions. The proposed framework develops a unified analytical model in which the total stored charge is expressed as the sum of a linear electrostatic contribution and a nonlinear, voltage-activated component. The resulting formulation captures the transition from ideal capacitive behaviour at low voltages to enhanced charge storage at higher potentials and predicts a voltage-dependent effective capacitance with a characteristic enhancement near the activation region. The model parameters are directly linked to physically meaningful and experimentally accessible quantities, including double-layer capacitance, pseudocapacitive strength, activation potential, and transition sharpness. A qualitative comparison with representative cyclic voltammetry behaviour in carbon–metal oxide composite electrodes demonstrates that the model reproduces key features of non-ideal capacitive response. Beyond its analytical simplicity, the framework provides a unified conceptual bridge between electrostatics and electrochemistry, supporting students in connecting mathematical expressions, graphical representations, and the underlying physical mechanisms of voltage-dependent charge storage. Its graphical and computational accessibility, together with the accompanying python implementation, make the framework well suited for upper-level undergraduate physics instruction and for exploring how model parameters influence observable system behaviour.
keywords: supercapacitors, voltage-dependent capacitance, pseudocapacitance, faradaic reactions, charge storage, analytical capacitance model, cyclic voltammetry

title: Constrained vs. unconstrained free-fall and projectile-motion AI problem-to-simulation generation: a pilot study
text: Abstract Many students fail in introductory mechanics because physics problem-solving involves algebraic as well as conceptual understanding Ceberio et al (2016 J. Sci. Educ. Technol. 25 590–609). This pilot study compares a constrained-AI-problem-to-simulation approach, NewtonSimAI, with unconstrained-AI-generated simulations of five Force Concept Inventory free-fall and projectile-motion questions. Simulations were graded using a technical and physics accuracy rubric evaluating setup, modifiable variables, vectors, time control, qualitative graphs, and the physical accuracy of the motion. NewtonSimAI fulfilled all applicable rubric criteria in the simulations that were tested, whereas unconstrained generations had much more variability, including a catastrophic generation failure. These findings support the use of constrained simulation systems to prevent AI hallucination prior to classroom studies of learning outcomes.
keywords: physics problem solving, free-fall motion, projectile motion, Force Concept Inventory, AI hallucination, introductory mechanics, classical mechanics

title: Exploring weightlessness in the classroom with a liquid hourglass
text: Abstract This paper describes a simple and inexpensive classroom demonstration based on a commercially available liquid hourglass (approximately US$10–20) that allows students to observe some consequences of weightlessness directly. The hourglass was released into free fall together with a smartphone camera, enabling slow-motion recording from the co-falling frame of reference. Analysis of the recordings reveals two simultaneous effects. Droplets that are elongated under normal gravitational conditions become more spherical during free fall as surface tension becomes the dominant influence on their shape. At the same time, moving droplets continue their motion in accordance with the principle of inertia.
keywords: microgravity, free fall, droplet shape, surface tension, inertia, slow-motion video, smartphone camera, classroom demonstration

title: A soft-drink battery: beyond electromotive force
text: Abstract We present a quantitative classroom experiment comparing Zn–Cu cells prepared with Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Sprite and salt water with a commercial D cell. Open-circuit voltage, terminal voltage under load, delivered energy, effective ohmic internal resistance and power as a function of load resistance were measured over 48 h. Although the Zn–Cu cells maintained open-circuit voltages of the order of 1 V , they delivered far less energy than the commercial cell because their internal resistance was large and strongly time dependent. The experiment provides an accessible way to connect electromotive force, terminal voltage, internal resistance, power and useful energy.
keywords: electromotive force, terminal voltage, internal resistance, open-circuit voltage, delivered energy

title: Space, time, and energy: a pedagogical derivation of the Schrödinger equation
text: Abstract A heuristic derivation of the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation is presented based on an energy interpretation of the wave function. The spatial derivative naturally produces a term proportional to the kinetic energy, while the temporal derivative yields a term proportional to the total energy. By relating both contributions through the classical relation for total mechanical energy, the Schrödinger equation is obtained. The proposed approach provides a simple and intuitive framework to introduce this equation in modern physics or introductory-level quantum mechanics courses.
keywords: Schrödinger equation, kinetic energy, spatial derivatives, temporal derivatives, one-dimensional quantum mechanics, introductory quantum mechanics

title: Narrative ingenuity: storytelling and poetry in an introductory astronomy course for non-science majors
text: Abstract The study of astronomy and physics extends well beyond experimental and mathematical skill: it also requires students to interpret models and communicate ideas clearly. This paper describes a classroom practice in which storytelling, poetry and comic strips are used as an alternative, formative assessment tool in an introductory astronomy course for non-science majors at a university in Colombia. When covering stellar evolution, students combine multimedia instruction with a required creative-writing task in which they represent the life cycle of a star as a story, poem or comic strip; the exercise is completed in class, without electronic devices, so that the work can be trusted to reflect the student’s own understanding rather than machine-generated text. We describe how the activity originated, how oral and iterative feedback is used to bring student’s work into line with the underlying physics, and we share a representative student poem depicting stellar evolution. The paper does not present systematic quantitative results; rather, it offers a practitioner’s account, intended for colleagues considering similar creative-writing assessments, and situates the practice within the wider and rapidly growing literature on narrative pedagogy in physics and astronomy education.
keywords: narrative pedagogy, storytelling, poetry, comic strips, stellar evolution, introductory astronomy, non-science majors, formative assessment, verbal feedback, iterative feedback, multimedia teaching

title: A modern version of Newton’s pendulum ball collision experiment
text: Abstract A modern version of Newton’s pendulum ball collision experiment is described to help explain how the coefficient of restitution (COR) provides a measure of the fractional energy loss when two balls collide. The COR itself is determined by the impulse acting on each ball. The experiment would be suitable in a student laboratory and illustrates why 17th century physicists had trouble interpreting the results.
keywords: coefficient of restitution, ball collision, energy loss, impulse, collision experiments, history of physics

title: Study of acoustic resonance in a cylindrical Helmholtz resonator excited by a tangential jet of air through a lateral slit
text: Abstract We report an experimental investigation of a cylindrical Helmholtz resonator with a lateral slit, excited by an oblique air jet generated by a rotational motion of the resonator. Despite the small size of the cavity, the system produces clearly audible tones. The acoustic response can be analysed using a smartphone-based audio spectrum analyser. The dominant resonance frequency is found to vary systematically with the slit length. The experimental results are described by the classical Helmholtz resonance model, which relates the observed frequencies to the geometrical parameters of the resonator through an effective mass–spring description. The apparatus is inexpensive, easy to construct, and suitable for both classroom activities and undergraduate laboratory experiments. The activity provides a clear and quantitative framework for exploring acoustic resonance, connecting concepts from mechanics, thermodynamics, and acoustics.
keywords: Helmholtz resonator, acoustic resonance, resonant frequency, physics laboratory experiments, classroom demonstration

title: Science CAMP for girls: an immersive experience for Brazilian high-school girls
text: Abstract Women remain underrepresented in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), particularly in physics and related disciplines. Outreach initiatives that provide positive scientific experiences and opportunities to interact with women role models have been proposed as one strategy to address this imbalance. In this paper, we describe two editions of the Science CAMP, an immersive residential programme organised by the outreach initiative Tem Menina no Circuito and aimed at girls from public schools in socially vulnerable regions of the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The programme combined astronomy observations, programming activities, electronics workshops, creative projects, and discussions on gender and scientific careers, all conducted by an entirely female team of researchers, teachers, and university students. The first edition, held in 2024, involved 41 participants from two schools, while the second edition, held in 2025, involved 74 participants from three schools. We describe the programme structure, the educational activities developed, and participants’ responses to the workshops. Participant feedback and preliminary follow-up data suggest that immersive STEM experiences may support engagement, confidence, and interest in higher education. The Science CAMP offers a case study of how scientific learning, mentorship, and community building can be combined in outreach programmes aimed at broadening the participation of girls in STEM.
keywords: science camp, STEM outreach, girls in STEM, gender gap in physics, programming workshop, electronics workshop, female role models, mentoring, community building, public schools, Rio de Janeiro, participant engagement, interest in higher education

title: Teaching heat transfer and thermodynamics through a Peatland-Smart project: an environmental context for physics education
text: Abstract Tropical peatlands are critical carbon sinks, yet their degradation contributes significantly to global greenhouse gas emissions and environmental challenges. This study developed the Peatlands-Smart project as an authentic learning ecosystem within the framework of sustainable physics learning to promote contextual and sustainability-oriented learning about thermodynamics. Following the Plomp educational design research approach, the study involved preliminary research, prototyping, and assessment phases to develop an integrated learning ecosystem consisting of a contextual peatland laboratory, internet of things (IoT)-based environmental monitoring, a digital dashboard, a content framework, and student worksheets. Expert evaluation indicated that the developed learning ecosystem achieved high validity, demonstrating its suitability for implementation in physics education. The findings reveal that authentic environmental data generated through IoT-based monitoring functioned as a primary pedagogical resource that enabled students to investigate real peatland phenomena, interpret empirical evidence, and construct scientific explanations of thermodynamic processes. The developed content framework explicitly connected environmental variables, sensor-generated data, physics concepts, scientific analysis, and learning activities, extending the role of IoT beyond environmental monitoring toward an integral component of authentic physics learning. Furthermore, the Peatlands-Smart project supported the integration of thermodynamics concepts with peatland conservation and climate change mitigation, fostering scientific reasoning and environmental literacy. The proposed framework demonstrates how authentic environmental contexts and digital technologies can bridge abstract physics concepts with real-world phenomena while supporting education for sustainable development.
keywords: thermodynamics education, heat transfer, tropical peatlands, Internet of Things, environmental monitoring, authentic learning, sustainability education, carbon sink, peatland conservation, climate change mitigation, environmental literacy, digital dashboard

title: Feeling tilted, then heavier: smartphone measurements of specific force during aircraft takeoff
text: Abstract Smartphone sensors provide an accessible way to connect familiar experiences of motion with quantitative physics. This study analyses three-axis specific-force data recorded by a smartphone placed in a seat-back pocket during the takeoff of a commercial aircraft. Gyroscope data were used to distinguish the ground roll from a later rotation-associated transition. During the ground roll, the mean specific-force vector changed direction by approximately 15 ∘ , while its magnitude increased by only 3.1% relative to the stationary reference. During the later transition, the directional change remained comparable, but the mean magnitude increased by 21.1%. The measurements therefore separate two effects that are often combined in everyday descriptions of takeoff: an initial change in the direction of the specific-force vector and a subsequent increase in its magnitude. The activity provides an authentic classroom context for teaching vector decomposition, specific force, apparent weight, and non-inertial reference frames. It also enables students to compare a simplified ground-roll model with measured data and to identify the conditions under which that model is no longer adequate.
keywords: aircraft takeoff, specific force, apparent weight, non-inertial frames, vector decomposition, smartphone sensors, gyroscope, accelerometer, ground roll

title: Implementing departmental standardised exams in introductory university physics: institutional experience and pre–post evidence
text: Abstract This study examines the implementation of standardised departmental examinations in an introductory Physics I course at a higher education institution in the Dominican Republic. The implementation involved institutional endorsement, coordination among instructors teaching parallel sections, common assessment procedures, and supporting resources for instructors and students. Quantitative evidence was obtained using a quasi-experimental pre–post design based on historical cohorts, comparing an academic term without standardised assessment (2023-2, N = 37) with a subsequent term in which common examinations were administered across all course sections (2023-3, N = 44). Academic performance was examined at the overall course level, by assessment component, and by instructor, together with intra-term performance change indicators and the coefficient of variation (CV). Mean final grades remained relatively stable (71.4 ± 9.9 in 2023-2 versus 69.4 ± 12.0 in 2023-3), while the CV of the final course grade increased from 0.14 to 0.17.
