title: A workbook and assessment scheme implemented for engineering students with an aim of increasing their motivation for mathematics
text: This article reports on a small-scale study, investigating engineering students' motivation to engage with mathematics through a workbook and assessment scheme (WAS). The study analysed anonymous responses to a questionnaire from all 181 students in a mathematics course, using Situated Expectancy Value Theory (SEVT) and thematic analysis. The research question was ‘How does the task-organization influence the students' engagement with the mathematics content and how is this engagement related to motivational values?'. Findings revealed three thematic aspects: intrinsic values as adoption to self, attainment values as outcomes and cost values as challenges. The course implementation was less successful than anticipated, and we discuss this considering research and our experiences. We recommend that WAS must be supported by adjusting the teaching style and with the students’ maturity taken into account.
keywords: mathematics learning motivation, engineering students, situated expectancy-value theory, intrinsic value, attainment value, cost value, task organization, student engagement, mathematics education

title: The potential for planning competence development and transformative learning in the Life – Cycle Assessment learning process
text: Frameworks on sustainability competencies suggest students should be equipped with abilities allowing them to craft sustainability action plans, and the call for transformative sustainability learning expects these abilities to be acquired in a manner that transforms the way they make sense of the world. Ensuring these in engineering education is both an opportunity and a challenge. Engineers are historically seen as problem solvers, so the responsibility to master tools, such as Life – Cycle Assessment (LCA), for assessing sustainability performance and recognising improvement potential falls naturally on them. We investigated the LCA learning process to find out if the potential for transformative learning and the development of systems–thinking, futures–thinking, values–thinking and strategies–thinking is already present in engineering education. Our results indicate the potential for both sustainability competence development and transformative learning, offering a perspective of how sustainability learning could be brought into the praxis of engineering education.
keywords: life cycle assessment, transformative learning, sustainability competencies, systems thinking, futures thinking, sustainability education, engineering education

title: Students’ changing accounts of chemical engineering: a longitudinal study in three countries
text: In this article we examine how students’ accounts of chemical engineering change during their undergraduate degrees and whether these changes were related to the educational intentions of their degree programs in two English, two South African and two US universities. Based on interviews with forty-five students over the course of their undergraduate chemical engineering degree, we found that initially most students did not know what chemical engineering was or thought it was about undertaking chemistry on a large scale. By the end of their degrees, most students had reached a watershed account of chemical engineering and saw it as about the design of large-scale processes of production. The changes in students’ accounts of chemical engineering appeared to be related to the educational intentions of their degree programs. We explore the implications of these outcomes for curriculum development in chemical engineering.
keywords: chemical engineering education, student conceptions, undergraduate students, educational intentions, degree programs, curriculum development, engineering identity

title: The impact of participation in technical student-run organisations on loneliness among engineering students
text: Students across several countries have reported high levels of loneliness. The consequences of loneliness are severe, often linked to mental health issues such as depression, self-harm, excessive media consumption, and poor sleep quality. Engineering students involved in technical student-run organisations (TSROs) have reported that participation in these organisations positively affects their well-being. This paper adopts a mixed methods approach, combining interviews and a questionnaire to examine the effect of participation in a TSRO on perceived loneliness. The results from this study indicate that engineering students who had three key factors present in their lives experienced reduced feelings of loneliness compared to other engineering students. The influential elements were participating in a student-run organisation or a TSRO, being in a romantic relationship, and not living alone. The study contributes to understanding the factors influencing loneliness among engineering students and has important implications for university practice.
keywords: loneliness, engineering students, student participation, romantic relationships, living arrangements, student well-being, mental health, university students

title: A competency assessment model for free-body diagrams construction in mechanical engineering students: a case study
text: The concept of a free body diagram is central to Mechanical Engineering. Beyond its correct layout, a series of analysis concepts in the development of this skill allows one to visualise, understand, and analyse mechanisms and other complex applications. The correct assessment of the skill goes beyond the simple application of a test because it is expected to be a lifelong skill and, therefore, long-term learning must be evaluated for the ability to recover learning. Concept inventory tests are usually an ideal tool for this evaluation. In this research, after a proposal to build and interpret this tool, we applied a test-of-concept analysis associated with free-body diagrams to mechanical engineering students. The analysis allows for quantitative visualisation of the behaviours of specific groups during the test application, particularly those related to the gender of the students and the campuses. In addition, the results were cross-analysed for possible causal errors in the associated concepts. Finally, the test items and distractors were analysed for improvement.Abbreviations: CIT: Concept Inventory Test; FBD: Free-Body Diagram; ICC: Item Characteristic Curve; IT: Inventory Test
keywords: free-body diagrams, competency assessment, concept inventory, item characteristic curves, mechanical engineering students, gender differences, distractor analysis, engineering mechanics education, long-term learning

title: ‘I couldn’t be more of a female’: the ‘World-Travelling’ of Black South African women into industry engineering and STEM academia ‘worlds’
text: In recent times, there's been an increase in calls for the engineering terrain to be transformed. To show how Black South African female engineering development are implicated, this paper untangles the salient aspects of raced, gendered and aged related exclusions, and resistance strategies at the intersection of critical gendered principles of recognition and decolonial feminist World-Travelling encounters. It incorporates a participatory storytelling approach, whereby data were collected from 9 Black South African women in the engineering industry and Science, Technology, Engineering, Maths (STEM) academic work context who were at various stages of their careers. The paper contributes by empirically highlighting how aspects related to exclusion, stereotyping and resistance strategies feature in the professional development of young Black South African women in engineering industry and STEM academic workspaces. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates how two related, yet distinct framings on transformation can be weaved together in order to facilitate equitable masculine study and employment contexts.
keywords: black South African women, women in engineering, gender and race intersection, decolonial feminism, engineering industry, professional development, resistance strategies, participatory storytelling, gender equity in the workplace

title: Straight from the source: exploring engineering experts’ views of nature of engineering
text: Understanding the Nature of Engineering (NOE) is essential for engineering literacy and a key goal in K-12 education. A clear understanding of NOE may help learners grasp engineering as a creative, iterative, and socially situated endeavour, supporting their ability to engage with engineering-related issues and make informed decisions. It is important to investigate engineering experts’ views on the NOE using an open-ended NOE assessment tool. This study explored how engineering experts including professors, practicing engineers, and educators conceptualise NOE using the open-ended instrument. Rather than generating new NOE constructs, the study examines how expert perspectives correspond with and contextualise an established conceptual framework for NOE. Findings indicate that experts’ responses generally reflect well-informed views that articulate the framework’s core tenets through professional examples and experiences.
keywords: nature of engineering, engineering literacy, K-12 engineering education, professional engineers, engineering teachers, iterative design

title: Factors influencing mental health among engineering students in India
text: Background Mental health challenges are a significant concern among emerging adults, particularly college students. An increasing body of research highlights a mental health crisis in India’s engineering institutions.Purpose The current study examines whether socio-psychological factors such as sociodemographic variables, departmental pride, batchmate mattering, self-esteem, parental control, and academic stress significantly predict the mental health status of students.Data/methods This study utilised a concurrent nested mixed-method design. An online survey, with quantitative measurements and open-ended qualitative questions, was conducted. The participants were 839 engineering undergraduates from different engineering institutes in India.Findings Multiple regression analysis revealed that self-esteem, batchmate mattering, academic stress, departmental pride, gender, and parental control were significant predictors.
keywords: mental health, engineering students, emerging adults, self-esteem, parental control, academic stress, sociodemographic factors, gender differences, India

title: Fostering engineering design teaching in secondary schools: Q-study of science teachers' engineering capital
text: To address the growing demand for engineering competencies and engage students in science, K-12 science teachers are increasingly expected to integrate engineering into their teaching. This study examines the engineering capital of 21 secondary school science teachers participating in a professional development programme focused on problem-oriented engineering projects. Using Q-methodology, the 21 secondary school teachers sorted 35 statements related to engineering capital offering insights into their perceptions and experiences. The Q-sort served both as an analytical tool and a means of reflection, helping teachers articulate their readiness and potential for teaching through engineering. The study identifies key competences and prior experiences that support this transition, it offers teacher profiles based on their engineering capital and suggests differentiated pathways into engineering education. Findings indicate that Q-methodology is effective for uncovering and developing teachers’ engineering capital, with implications for designing targeted professional development initiatives.
keywords: secondary science teachers, teacher professional development, teacher perceptions

title: Teaching excellence programmes – lessons learnt at two universities
text: Teaching excellence initiatives are emerging internationally, as universities seek ways to strengthen the educational competence of faculty and to raise the status of educational merits. This study compares the experiences of initiatives for promoting teaching excellence in one Swedish and one Dutch technical university. In both programmes, participants work on their own project for an extended time, while also being part of a community with meetings and coaching. The main differences are the programme duration, number of participants, and whether the projects address a given theme or are formulated by the participants. In both programmes, participants were generally highly satisfied, despite tension regarding diverse goals and backgrounds. While participants were positive about their own learning, they were cautious about the results at the organisational level. We reflect on findings at the individual and organisational levels, and provide recommendations for programmes for teaching excellence in higher education.
keywords: faculty development, engineering education, technical universities, coaching, peer learning communities, participant satisfaction, organizational change, higher education teaching quality

title: Multidimensional characteristics of design thinking and project-based learning (DT-PBL) in higher education: a grounded theory study
text: This study investigates the underlying mechanisms of Design Thinking and Project-Based Learning (DT-PBL) in engineering education through a grounded theory approach. Based on classroom observations and semi-structured interviews, four interdependent dimensions—self-confidence, reflective interaction, knowledge integration, and iterative refinement—were identified, forming a closed-loop learning ecology. The findings reveal that DT-PBL operates as a recursive, dynamic process: self-confidence drives participation, reflection deepens understanding, and iteration progressively transforms knowledge into actionable insights. Beyond generating project deliverables, DT-PBL cultivates reflective judgment, integrative thinking, and sustainable problem-solving competencies vital for contemporary engineering practice. This study contributes a theoretically grounded and pedagogically actionable framework for advancing DT-PBL implementation in higher education.
keywords: design thinking, project-based learning, engineering education, self-confidence, reflective interaction, knowledge integration, iterative refinement, reflective judgment, integrative thinking, problem-solving competencies, university teaching

title: Student and instructor perceptions of data science integration into science and engineering courses
text: Data science literacy is vital for undergraduate engineering and science students, yet questions remain about effective integration in curricula. This study investigates the impact of integrating discipline-specific data science modules into existing undergraduate STEM courses at three US universities through a research-practice partnership. Using mixed methods to analyze survey responses from 877 students and instructor grades and interviews across six courses, we examined changes in student data science perception across various demographics, academic levels, and disciplines and compared student and instructor perspective. Results show significant increases in student self-reported perception after completing one or more modules irrespective of course and institution differences. Analysis revealed alignment between student self-assessments and instructor evaluations. Students highlighted benefits including real-world applications and career relevance, while identifying challenges with data analysis tools and varying experience levels. These findings provide insights for educators seeking to integrate data science into curricula.
keywords: student perceptions, instructor perceptions, research-practice collaboration, data analysis software, career relevance, student self-assessment, engineering education, science education

title: Staying the course: investigating motivations for first-semester engineering students
text: This mixed methods study examined influences on early motivation among first-semester Bachelor of Engineering students at a Danish university. A 32-item Likert survey (n = 342) was analysed using exploratory factor analysis, yielding a three-factor structure – Institutional Belonging & Environment, Supportive Teaching & Curricular Value, and Motivation & Mindset – explaining 45.6% of variance (α = .83, .79, .70). Inter-factor correlations were moderate (.42–.57). Interviews with 16 Study Leaders and 11 students contextualised these results, showing how students’ readiness to study, perceived psychological safety, sense of belonging, and curriculum relevance shaped the ways they interpreted difficulty, sought support, and maintained engagement. Some students described a clear sense of purpose and curricular value, though experiences of teaching and access to support varied. Overall, the findings offer exploratory insight into how institutional, instructional, and individual conditions influence students' early motivation. Interpretation is limited by the cross-sectional design and single-institution context, yet the results indicate opportunities to strengthen early motivation through psychologically safe teaching, clearer curricular signalling, and accessible support.
keywords: student motivation, first-year students, sense of belonging, psychological safety, curriculum relevance, student support services, student engagement, mindset, engineering education

title: Investigating the impact of augmented reality in machine operation training: A case study on laser-cutting machines
text: Although augmented reality (AR) has shown promising effects in education, its application in manufacturing training remains underexplored, particularly beyond assembly and maintenance tasks. This study examines the impact of AR on learning machine operation using a laser-cutting machine as a case study. The initial hypothesis that AR enhances performance and the learning experience was not fully supported by this experiment. The inexperienced learners who used AR produced fewer errors than instructor-led learners when reproducing the cutting task, but the control group performed faster than the AR group. The experiment also revealed a significant difference in the amount of additional information needed by both groups. These findings highlight the importance of design and challenge the notion that AR consistently enhances learning. However, these results offer valuable insights for future AR-based training system designs, emphasising the need for more nuanced approaches to optimise AR's educational efficacy.
keywords: augmented reality, machine operation training, laser cutting machine, manufacturing training, learning performance, instructor-led training, learning errors

title: Enhanc(e)ing engineering education in Europe – cross-national perspectives on challenges and opportunities for university teaching practices

title: Factors affecting motivation in a community of undergraduate makerspace assistants
text: Engineering programs are often supported by makerspaces with student staff, which we refer to as Undergraduate Makerspace Assistants (UMAs). These UMAs often work independently and take the initiative to learn skills and assist users. This research took a qualitative approach by examining our own makerspace through interviews with our UMAs using reflexive thematic analysis. We sought to understand the factors that contribute to the development of UMA motivation through the lens of Basic Psychological Needs Theory, a subtheory of Self-Determination Theory. We interpreted three themes of shared meaning, those being: we want to make stuff, UMA is a mentoring position, and people can just hang out together. These themes are representative of a community of UMAs who engage in activities that develop and reinforce their motivation to grow as makers and foster it in each new generation. Our findings will be of interest to those managing makerspaces that have student employees.

title: Choosing engineering education: understanding the motives of Indian young women-a narrative inquiry
text: Young women in India are now seen choosing engineering education in the institutes of national importance, marking the beginning of inclusivity. With the aim of sustaining this positive momentum, this study explores the experiences of young women which led them into engineering education. Polkinghorne’s Two kinds of analysis – ‘Analysis of narratives’ and ‘Narrative analysis’ are adopted to understand the narratives. The study revealed a nuanced understanding of their motives and triggers. The stories of nine students are shared under two narrative types – ‘Engineer by choice’ and ‘Engineer by chance’. ‘Engineer by choice’ captures the narratives of those women who employed their agentic self in realizing their dream, while ‘engineer by chance’ captures the stories of those women who used engineering education as a fallback option when their dreams did not materialize. McAdam’s Narrative identity theory and Gotfredson’s theory of circumscription and compromise are used in analysis to understand the nature of contextual support needed in the growing years. Interventions at the school level by career counselling cells are proposed. Exposure to potential careers, awareness of favourable policies in organizations, and conduct of workshops with opportunities to solve real-life challenges, are proposed to create favourable disposition towards engineering among girls.
keywords: women in engineering, female engineering students, career choice, gender in engineering, narrative identity theory, career guidance, school-based intervention, India

title: Building inclusive engineering education conferences: a responsive approach to identifying and mitigating barriers
text: Academic conferences are a key development activity due to their role in capacity building and identity formation. However, meaningful participation is limited by barriers which differentially impact individuals, influencing their career development and progression. This work aims to understand how organisational practices (i.e. established norms) support participants with diverse identities when participating in the European Society of Engineering Education (SEFI) conference, and their perceptions regarding initiatives to reduce barriers to inclusion. Data from two surveys (prior to and during SEFI2024) are discussed in relation to the concept of inequality regimes. Implemented initiatives appear to have reduced some of the identified barriers to submission and attendance; however, the apparent disconnect between value statements and disparate levels of individual awareness underlines the need for inclusion to be integrated transversally into the conference culture and organisational structures. The paper concludes with reflections and recommendations for future conference organisers.
keywords: inclusive engineering education, academic conferences, barriers to inclusion, inequality regimes, diversity and inclusion, conference organization, organisational practices, identity construction, career development, SEFI, conference culture

title: Challenges and opportunities in the introduction of relevant content from the social sciences and humanities in engineering curricula: perceptions from civil engineering academics
text: Addressing today’s complex global challenges requires interdisciplinary thinking. Yet, engineering education has traditionally prioritised technical knowledge, often sidelining the social sciences and humanities (SSH). This study explores how SSH content is integrated into civil engineering programs, drawing on qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with faculty members at Spanish universities. Findings reveal four interrelated and overarching themes that shape integration processes: ability, preparedness, willingness, and conduciveness. These form the basis of a conceptual structure that explains key barriers and enablers to curricular change – from institutional rigidity and resource constraints to disciplinary identity and faculty motivation. The study offers new insights into how engineering educators conceptualise SSH content and highlights that integration depends not only on content availability but also on shifting mindsets and organisational cultures. This research contributes to the growing discourse on interdisciplinary engineering education and provides a foundation for future policies and practices for fostering socially responsible engineers.
keywords: interdisciplinary engineering education, curriculum integration, teacher perceptions, disciplinary identity, engineering education policy, Spanish universities

title: Engineering faculty’s emotional response during emergency remote teaching
text: Emergency remote teaching (ERT) during the COVID-19 pandemic entailed drastic changes in education. Faculty faced challenges in their teaching role while immersed in an unprecedented emotional atmosphere. With the aim of characterising potentially vulnerable groups of engineering faculty (those reporting more self-perceived negative emotions), our study analyses answers of 577 faculty members of a Technical University to a survey in 2020. The focus is on emotions in relation to contextual factors and perceived teaching performance. Results show that vulnerable groups in ERT include females, younger generations and individuals with family load. Emotions also impacted faculty's perception of teaching performance, in aspects such as students' competencies and their own teaching improvement. Engineering faculty members feeling negative emotions more frequently could also be unable to recognise their students' and their own development. As teaching performance can be affected by faculty's emotional response, emotional management should be central in professional development plans.
keywords: emergency remote teaching, COVID-19 pandemic, engineering faculty, emotional responses, negative emotions, teaching performance, vulnerable populations, gender differences, age differences, family responsibilities, emotional management, professional development, student competencies

title: Analysis of social responsibility perceptions: the case of undergraduate science and engineering students
text: Higher education institutions play a central role in societal development, acting as catalysts for change and reflecting the evolving nature of our world. Particularly, in the fields of science and engineering, higher education holds immense societal importance and is crucial for addressing complex global challenges outlined by the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals. Despite this recognition, research about science and engineering students does not usually focus on understanding these students’ perspectives on social awareness and responsibility. Accordingly, this paper aims to examine the perceptions of undergraduate science and engineering students regarding social responsibility. Applying a grounded theory framework for characterizing perceptions of all stakeholders regarding social responsibility in higher education, which is illustrated in this paper for the case of undergraduate science and engineering students.
keywords: social responsibility, student perceptions, undergraduate science students, engineering students, higher education, Sustainable Development Goals, social awareness, stakeholder perspectives

title: ‘I know I won’t be employed here forever’: exploring career self-management in early-career engineers
text: This study investigates how early-career engineers engage in career self-management (CSM) and the role of educational experiences, particularly in a problem-based learning (PBL) environment. Through 10 life history interviews with recent engineering graduates, the authors explore how participants navigate career uncertainty, refine goals, and proactively manage their development. The findings reveal that participants adopt a pragmatic and adaptive approach, combining strategic planning with openness to emerging opportunities. Proactivity was seen in trial-and-error career exploration, continuous learning, and value-driven career preferences, with many prioritising opportunities for hands-on, applied work, as well as societal impact. Participants reported challenges in aligning personal values with visible career opportunities and balancing technical aspirations with leadership ambitions. The results highlight the importance of integrating CSM-supporting practices into PBL curricula, emphasising career reflection, goal setting, and exposure to real-world work environments. Additionally, this study contributes to discussions on fostering career resilience and adaptability in dynamic, technical professions.
keywords: career self-management, young engineers, problem-based learning, career uncertainty, career exploration, career resilience, goal setting, career reflection, engineering graduates, career adaptability, engineering curriculum

title: To be a teacher, to be many other things and always to do the best. The identity and narratives of engineering professors
text: Our investigation focused on the perceptions and views of engineering professors regarding their understanding of the meaning of being a teacher, including their life stories and relationships with others and themselves. By doing so, the idea was to identify the characteristics, elements or factors of their identities. This study considered a narrative inquiry approach to explore the stories and experiences of engineering professors who teach in higher education through unstructured interviews and field records. Our study revealed two key themes that intimately reflect the identities and perceptions of these engineering professors as teachers: (a) To be a teacher and always to do the best, and (b) To be a teacher and to be many other things. From the results, we can observe that the identity of engineering professors is being constructed/modelled as the meanings of what they understand about what it means to be a teacher are negotiated in their work environments and contexts, thus directing their actions.
keywords: engineering faculty, teacher identity, meaning of teaching, engineering education, university teaching, life stories, professional identity, work environment, narrative inquiry

title: Operationalising generic employability frameworks within specific disciplines: a transparent example from engineering
text: Employability has become a central concern in engineering and higher education, with universities increasingly expected to prepare graduates for both initial employment and long-term career development. Within this context, effective frameworks are essential for guiding competency assessment and redesigning engineering programs to better equip students for professional life. Despite the availability of generic employability frameworks, there is limited empirical evidence regarding their efficacy within specific disciplines. Specifically, this study provides a transparent case example of applying a generic employability framework to categorise engineering-specific employability items and examines the challenges encountered in this process. A total of 88 employability items identified across 29 review papers were classified using the selected framework. The analysis revealed significant conceptual overlaps and several items that defied neat classification. These findings highlight the need for overarching institutional frameworks complemented by discipline-specific frameworks that accurately capture how employability manifests in particular disciplines.
keywords: employability, engineering education, competency assessment, graduate employability, career development

title: Operationalising Jonassen’s design theory of problem solving: exploration of a problem typology scaffold in an introductory aerospace engineering course
text: This mixed-methods study explores a PBL facilitation model based on Jonassen's design theory of problem solving. Jonassen's theory was operationalised in two different sections of an introductory aerospace engineering course. One was facilitated through problem-typology (PT-section) while the other used no formal scaffold (NPT-section). The impact of the scaffold on students' problem engagement was explored through students' solution artefacts, a pre/post self-efficacy survey and debrief interviews. Results show that PT-section artefacts evidenced more information related to the resolution of problem ill-structuredness and complexity than NPT-section artefacts. PT-section students were also more confident in their problem solutions and their ability to solve similar problems in the future. Two important implications stem from this study. First, a better understanding of how classroom discourse impacts the salience of structuredness and complexity for students is needed. Additionally, developing the technical communication skills of undergraduates is vital for a holistic assessment of their problem-specific reasoning.
keywords: problem typology, scaffolding, problem-based learning, aerospace engineering education, ill-structured problems, problem complexity, self-efficacy, technical communication skills, introductory engineering course

title: ‘Les Petits Constructeurs': principles of construction explained to children
text: ‘If you cannot explain a concept to a six-year-old child, it means you do not fully understand it.' This study investigates the 'Les Petits Constructeurs' program, where architecture Master’s students are tasked with transmitted complex concepts of structural morphology and construction logic to children aged 6-10. Research aims to determine if this mediation enhances students' technical understanding. A comparative evaluation with a control group reveals that students involved in teaching children showed a significantly higher progression in technical knowledge acquisition. Paradoxically, their self-reported confidence and perception of the discipline exhibited limited variation, highlighting a dissociation between measured learning outcomes and perceived competence. Ultimately, the findings suggest that knowledge mediation—simplifying expertise for a non-specialist audience—is a powerful pedagogical tool. It enhances conceptual clarity more effectively than standard methods, proving that the challenge of explaining “how things hold up” to a six-year-old is a rigorous path to professional expertise.
keywords: architectural education, structural morphology, construction principles, teaching children, knowledge mediation, architecture students, perceived competence, conceptual understanding, engineering pedagogy

title: Steps for designing research to compare how one believes they will behave to how they behave
text: Gaps between how individuals believe they will behave and how they actually behave can be consequential, particularly in engineering education and engineering practice. Research addressing such gaps must first identify where they exist. This paper presents research design steps intended to support scholars in systematically comparing beliefs about intended behaviour with observed behaviour. We articulate three key steps: operationalising a phenomenon as a measurable behaviour and belief about that same behaviour, designing data collection and analysis methods that validly capture each construct, and creating an appropriate means of comparison. For each step, we describe key considerations, relevant prior work, and guiding questions. We illustrate implementation via case study examining engineering students’ ’process safety judgements. Although the examples centre process safety, these steps are intentionally generalisable across engineering education and professional practice. This framework enables actionable insights and provides a foundation for future work aimed at reflection, change, and improved beliefs-behaviours.
keywords: research design, operationalization, measurement validity, engineering students, engineering education

title: Engineering students’ agency for sustainability in a PBL context: Q methodology research
text: Sustainability has become a central concern in engineering education, requiring future engineers to address complex ecological, social, and economic challenges while exercising professional agency. This study examines engineering students’ perceptions of their sustainability agency within a Problem-Based Learning (PBL) environment, using Q methodology to capture diverse viewpoints among students enrolled in the same course. The analysis identified four key factors shaping sustainability agency: (1) educational opportunities combined with institutional support, (2) societal engagement through teamwork and collaboration, (3) emotional and motivational drivers, and (4) knowledge of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) within a supportive learning framework. These factors represent complementary pathways through which students enact agency. The findings demonstrate that diversity of perspectives functions as a generative and enabling condition for learning in PBL, as it fosters dialogue, negotiation, and collective sense-making around complex sustainability problems. The study highlights the importance of intentionally designing large-scale, interdisciplinary PBL projects that connect students with real-world sustainability challenges and provide institutional support for sustained engagement. Such learning environments can strengthen engineering students’ capacity to navigate uncertainty, work across disciplinary boundaries, and act as proactive agents of sustainable change.

title: Mis(alignment) in engineering doctorates: insights from industrial doctorates
text: In recent decades, reduced public funding for higher education and growing pressure for research impact have led to diversification of engineering doctoral programmes. One variant, the industrial doctorate, involves sharing costs, supervision, and project aims between industry, funding bodies, and academia. This creates a distributed supervisory and accountability arrangement that differs from traditional doctoral models. In this study, industrial doctoral programmes are used to examine how variations in engineering doctorates shape students’ decision-making, professional development, and experiences. Data from interviews with thirteen UK-based participants were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. While some experiences reflect broader doctoral challenges, features specific to industrial doctorates introduce additional complexities, particularly around accountability, alignment between students’ aspirations, and expectations, and definitions of success. Findings highlight the importance of evidence-based design, including transparent communication of programme structures and project options before enrolment, and defined supervisory roles, providing insights to support engineering doctoral students operating across academic – industry boundaries.

title: ‘Not just one winner’ – where empathy and community engagement meet
text: Prior research has demonstrated that service-learning is valuable for supporting empathy development in students. However, the specific aspects of undergraduate engineering students’ service-learning experiences that contribute to empathy development remain unclear. This study aimed to (i) explore the role of empathy as described by undergraduate engineering students in service-learning programs, and (ii) investigate elements of service-learning programs that shaped these students’ empathy development. We conducted semi-structured interviews with fourteen participants in service-learning programs from two United States institutions and analysed their responses using thematic analysis. Four themes indicate the role in the students’ experiences – having a sense of responsibility toward others, keeping an open mind, learning from stakeholders, and understanding others’ situations. Structured, loosely structured, and unstructured program elements contributed to the students’ empathy development. These findings provide further support to existing literature that suggests service-learning is a productive learning environment for promoting students’ empathy development. We suggest key areas that engineering educators could focus on in their design of service-learning programs and similar learning contexts to nurture empathy.

title: Bridging higher education and practice: a one-week live-case model supporting interdisciplinarity and lifelong learning
text: Universities face the dual challenge of preparing full-time students for real-world work-life challenges and offering practitioners lifelong learning (LLL) opportunities. The purpose of this article is to develop and assess a small-scale live-case model that focuses on both full-time and LLL students’ learning, reflecting on its implications for students, practitioners, and universities to better understand how to simultaneously promote lifelong learning and work-life integration in higher education. The model addresses two key challenges in previous live-case literature: high resource demands and the tendency to focus on organisational rather than individual learning. By focusing on a shared, small-scale live case involving quality improvement in healthcare, the small-scale live-case model offers a resource-efficient and time-bound format promoting mutual learning and engagement between engineering students and healthcare practitioners.
