title: Adaptive capacity in graduate engineering education: synthesising a multilevel framework for student success in the United States
text: This review synthesises 26 recent studies (2019-2025) on graduate engineering education in the United States using an inductive, conceptually driven approach. Unlike much of the student success literature focused on undergraduate performance-based outcomes, this work examines graduate success across dimensions including persistence, identity negotiation, and career adaptability. Through structured narrative synthesis, we identify five interconnected domains shaping student experiences: persistence and attrition; student development and well-being; systemic and institutional factors; advising and mentorship; and career trajectories. These results inform a multilevel resilience and adaptive capacity framework for understanding how graduate students and institutions respond to evolving demands. Recurring challenges, such as high attrition rates, mental health concerns, inequitable advising, and limited career preparation, are examined alongside emerging responses such as identity-affirming mentorship and integrated career development models. The framework reconceptualizes success as outcomes of dynamic, adaptive processes operating at individual, relational, and systemic levels, with implications for equity-informed, systems-level change.
keywords: graduate engineering education, student success, adaptive capacity, student persistence, attrition, student well-being, identity negotiation, academic advising, career development, career adaptability, resilience, equity in engineering education, multi-level framework

title: Crafting a sustainable development metrics framework in engineering education
text: Existing Sustainability Assessment Tools primarily focus on the institutional level, addressing broader issues that limit their applicability for assessing individual degrees. This research addresses that gap by developing a tool to assess the integration of sustainable development in engineering education.The tool draws on the Education for Sustainable Development principles, existing Sustainability Assessment Tools, and literature to define three main categories: Education Offer (6 subcategories), Education Quality (8 subcategories), and Students (4 subcategories) which are operationalised through 23 measurable indicators. For validation and improvement, the tool was used to assess the bachelor's and master's degrees in Environmental Engineering offered at a public university in the North of Portugal. Overall, the tool offers a transparent, adaptable, evidence-based framework that supports programme analysis, benchmarking and continuous improvement of ESD, while providing a baseline that should be refined through future research.
keywords: sustainability education, engineering education, sustainability assessment tools, evaluation metrics, program evaluation, benchmarking, continuous improvement, higher education sustainability

title: One-year internship program on software engineering: students' perceptions and educators' lessons learned
text: The inclusion of internship courses in Software Engineering (SE) programs is essential for closing knowledge gaps and improving graduates' readiness for the software industry. Our study focuses on year-long internships at RMIT University (Melbourne, Australia), which offers in-depth industry engagement. We analysed how the course evolved over the last 10 years to incorporate students' needs and summarised the lessons learned that can be helpful for other educators supporting internship courses. Our qualitative analysis of internship data based on 91 reports during 2023–2024 identified three challenge themes the students faced, and which courses were found by students to be particularly beneficial during their internships. On this basis, we proposed recommendations for educators and companies to help interns overcome challenges and maximise their learning experience.
keywords: software engineering education, university-industry collaboration, student perceptions, lessons learned, internship challenges, graduate employability, experiential learning

title: A systematic review of empirical research in engineering ethics education (2020–2025): global trends, teaching practices, and challenges
text: Engineering ethics education faces growing pressure to remain relevant amid rapid technological and digital transformation. This systematic review maps how engineering ethics has been taught, studied, and challenged across recent empirical research. Following PRISMA 2020, 42 empirical studies on engineering ethics education published between January 2020 and March 2025 were selected from Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore and appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Multi-method synthesis revealed growing academic interest and stronger visibility in high impact journals, yet the field remains concentrated in Western and undergraduate contexts. Across studies, engineering ethics teaching is frequently fragmented and constrained by weak curricular integration, limited faculty preparedness, and culturally misaligned content. Case-based learning continues to dominate, while experiential, digital game-based, and AI-enabled approaches remain underexplored. The review calls for more context-sensitive, innovative, and pedagogically integrated ethics education.
keywords: engineering ethics education, ethics education, teaching practice, case-based learning, experiential learning, game-based learning, AI-assisted learning, faculty readiness, curriculum integration, digital transformation, research trends

title: Qualitative evaluation of engineering teaching assistants’ current mentorship capabilities
text: Contribution This paper reports on the qualitative results of open-ended items from a questionnaire designed to understand the teaching capabilities of engineering teaching assistants.Background Teaching assistants are vital for many universities, taking on several responsibilities to complement their professors’ instruction and improve student learning. Knowing the importance of this role, investigating variables related to teaching assistant effectiveness has become a prevalent topic among researchers, with self-efficacy, pedagogical practices, and class organization serving as popular frameworks.Methodology A teaching assistant evaluation survey with four open-ended questions was shared with several US-based colleges. After data cleaning, 400 participants remained. Their answers underwent a process of open coding followed by focused coding to develop themes across the data.Findings Ultimately, the results of the questionnaire suggest most teaching assistants are adequately prepared to serve students. However, they might benefit from improved institutional support around training, faculty relationships, and classroom structure.
keywords: teaching assistants, mentoring, engineering education, institutional support, faculty relations, classroom structure, teaching assistant training, student learning

title: Self-perceived imagination and conceptual problem solving in engineering dynamics
text: This study investigates the thinking modes employed by students when they solve conceptual problems in engineering dynamics, with a focus on the role of imagination. It explores whether students self-report using imagination, how thinking modes are associated with problem-solving success, and how students’ scores are related to their learning preferences. Data were collected through self-reported surveys that contain conceptual problems, selection of thinking modes and opinion questions (n = 111). In the findings, 44.1% of total instances using the ‘Imagine’ thinking mode, which was associated with the highest rate of correct answers (73.5%). Students who could moderately engage imagination with other thinking modes tended to be associated with higher scores. High-score participants tended to prefer lectures, whereas more low-score participants preferred online resources. With the relevance of imagination in conceptual understanding, future research should investigate the cognitive processes of imagination and other thinking modes through qualitative research and modified survey instruments.
keywords: imagination, conceptual problem solving, engineering dynamics, thinking mode, learning styles, conceptual understanding, physics education, problem-solving success

title: The relations between ethical reasoning and moral intuitions among engineering students in the US, Netherlands, and China
text: Ethical reasoning has been adopted as a goal of engineering ethics education, and measures of reasoning have been developed by researchers and with participants in mostly the US. However, US participants are outliers on various psychological and social characteristics, and it is unclear whether reasoning results in more ethical judgments or behaviours. To address these issues, this study sought to better understand the natures of and relations between ethical reasoning and moral intuitions among engineering students in the US, Netherlands, and China. It was found that: students in the US scored higher on postconventional reasoning than those in the Netherlands or China; ethics education was associated with lower rates of preconventional reasoning; postconventional reasoning was positively related to intuitions about care and fairness, and negatively relations to intuitions about loyalty, authority, and sanctity; and students in China cared more about loyalty, authority, and sanctity, and less about care and fairness.
keywords: moral reasoning, moral intuitions, engineering ethics education, engineering students, cross-cultural comparison, moral judgment

title: Making competencies visible: evaluating the effects of stimulating lifelong learning in engineering education
text: In an era of rapid change and evolving workforce demands, engineering education must equip students with lifelong learning (LLL) competencies to ensure adaptability. This study explores effectiveness of explicitly integrating LLL competencies into problem-based learning (PBL) within a first-year engineering programme. Using a quasi-experimental design, four PBL groups participated in varying interventions including adapted peer assessments and reflective essays targeting LLL competencies. A mixed-method combined pre- and post-intervention surveys with reflective essays. While the Lifelong Learning Scale showed no significant changes, students reported increased perceptions of importance and presence of LLL competencies and improved confidence in their abilities. Group 4, receiving both interventions, demonstrated notable gains in self-reflection. Reflective essays revealed that engaging in deeper reflection results in articulating both LLL and professional competencies. These findings underscore the value of embedding structured reflective practices and targeted interventions to better prepare students for dynamic demands of the engineering profession.
keywords: lifelong learning, engineering education, problem-based learning, first-year engineering students, peer assessment, reflective essays, self-reflection, professional competence, student self-confidence, competence development

title: Engineering educators’ readiness for change in adopting PBL through participating in an international faculty professional development programme: experiences from India
text: This study explores how engineering educators perceived their readiness for change in adopting Project-/Problem Based Learning (PBL) through participating in an international faculty professional development programme involving 40 educators from Indian universities. Using Q methodology, four distinct collective viewpoints emerged: 1) PBL enhances student learning and employability; 2) PBL offers personal benefits for both students and educators; 3) PBL strengthens teaching competence with institutional support; and 4) PBL improves student learning with leadership support. Participants reported diverse perceptions of change readiness, valuing student benefits, personal growth, or institutional support to varying degrees according to their institutional contexts and personal priorities. These findings highlight the importance of systemic strategies and supportive institutional culture in addressing the various needs of educators and fostering their readiness to implement PBL effectively.
keywords: project-based learning, problem-based learning, engineering education, faculty professional development, readiness to change, institutional support, institutional culture, student employability, teaching competence, Q methodology

title: Great expectations: a systemic perspective on aligning expectations among stakeholders in challenge-based learning projects
text: Challenge-based learning (CBL) is an educational approach that emphasizes co-creation among students, educators, and external stakeholders to address real-world, interdisciplinary challenges. While CBL effectively engages students, it also requires coordination across disparate stakeholders, posing organizational challenges that remain underexplored in existing literature. This article addresses this by examining how expectations are aligned among stakeholders in three CBL courses at a technical university in the Netherlands. Drawing on Niklas Luhmann’s systems theory, organization is conceptualized as a process of decision-making grounded in shared expectations. Narrative case analyses were developed and synthesized using causal loop diagrams to visualise feedback-driven processes of change. The study finds that early alignment – particularly between educators and challenge owners – supports long-term success but must avoid rigid deliverable fixation to preserve CBL’s open-ended nature. Managing expectations is shown not as a constraint but as a necessary condition for meaningful collaboration, contributing to more sustainable and coherent CBL ecosystems.
keywords: challenge-based learning, stakeholder expectations, systems theory, Niklas Luhmann, organizational decision-making, co-creation, causal loop diagrams, open-ended learning

title: Durability of descriptive geometry competence in engineering education: a 12-month longitudinal comparison of CADOP-based and traditional instruction
text: Descriptive geometry is central to engineering graphics education, supporting spatial reasoning, representational fluency, and technical drawing interpretation. Although CAD is now fundamental to engineering practice, limited evidence exists on how CAD-integrated instruction affects the long-term durability of descriptive geometry competence. This study presents a 12-month longitudinal comparison of traditional Monge-based instruction and a CAD-integrated approach aligned with orthographic projection principles (CADOP) in a first-year engineering graphics course. Student performance was assessed immediately after instruction and at six- and twelve-month follow-ups using an analytic rubric capturing conceptual, spatial, and procedural dimensions. Linear mixed-effects models showed that CADOP students achieved higher performance at all time points and experienced slower skill decay, especially in procedural competences. Although all students declined over time, conceptual and spatial competences were more resilient and remained more strongly integrated under CADOP. The findings show that instructional design shapes both the durability and organization of descriptive geometry competence.
keywords: descriptive geometry, engineering graphics education, orthographic projection, skill decay, long-term retention, spatial reasoning, procedural competence, conceptual competence, technical drawing, instructional design, first-year engineering students

title: Planning intercultural group work in engineering education: the importance of a multilevel approach
text: Intercultural group work (IGW), where students from different cultures work together, can play a crucial role in contributing to international and group work learning outcomes, yet presents significant pedagogical challenges. Despite this, the teacher perspective has largely been overlooked in IGW research. This qualitative study takes a multilevel approach to the planning of IGW at two European universities, focusing on the teachers. Data sources include interviews with programme and course managers and documentation from international to course level. The results highlight the extent to which multilevel learning outcomes and teacher purposes for group work influence the planning of IGW, exemplified through choices around group forming, facilitation and assessment. A conceptual framework has been developed, highlighting the dynamic interplay between context and group work planning, and emphasizing the importance of both the structural setting and human interactions. The findings underscore the necessity of considering context in future IGW planning and research.
keywords: engineering education, multilevel approach, teacher perceptions, international students, group formation, group facilitation, group work assessment, conceptual framework, internationalization of higher education

title: AI chatbot as Socratic Butler: effects on metacognitive awareness, cognitive load, and learning performance in introductory programming for engineering education
text: Introductory programming is a foundational course in engineering education, yet many students struggle to connect coding exercises with underlying theory. Standard lab instructions often lead to superficial engagement, with students copying code without deeper conceptual understanding. Socratic questioning can foster critical thinking and self-explanation, but is rarely applied consistently due to constraints in teacher availability and dialogue skill. This study introduces the Socratic Butler, a dual-role AI chatbot that guides students through question-based dialogue while providing instructors with insights into student progress. A quasi-experimental design was implemented involving 95 electrical engineering students divided into three groups: Socratic Butler, conventional chatbot (ChatGPT), and no-chatbot control. Students using the Socratic Butler showed significantly higher learning performance and metacognitive awareness than the other groups. They reported greater cognitive load, due to the reflective effort required. These findings support dual-role AI tools to foster deeper conceptual engagement and provide scalable engineering education support.
keywords: AI chatbots, Socratic questioning, metacognitive awareness, cognitive load, learning performance, introductory programming, engineering education, self-explanation, ChatGPT, student engagement, electrical engineering students

title: Engineering leadership education: a PRISMA-based systematic review and comparative analysis with business leadership models
text: Purpose This paper systematically examines how leadership development is integrated into engineering education and evaluates whether engineering leadership constitutes a distinct socio-technical paradigm rather than an extension of traditional business leadership models.Design/methodology/approach Guided by the PRISMA 2020 protocol, a systematic review of 68 peer-reviewed articles published between 2005 and 2024 was conducted across five major academic databases. Studies addressing leadership frameworks, curricular models, and institutional practices in engineering education were analysed using iterative qualitative coding to generate cross-cutting themes and enable structured comparison with business leadership paradigms.Findings The review demonstrates that engineering leadership is grounded in technical credibility, systems thinking, and ethical accountability, diverging in substantive ways from managerial leadership models. However, leadership integration remains uneven globally, frequently constrained by curricular density, accreditation ambiguity, and institutional silos. Programmatic innovations vary across national contexts, reflecting structural and cultural conditions rather than a unified global template.Originality/value By positioning engineering leadership as a socio-technical leadership paradigm, this study advances conceptual clarity and offers evidence-informed recommendations for curriculum reform, institutional alignment, and policy development.
keywords: engineering leadership, leadership development, engineering education, leadership curriculum, systems thinking, ethical accountability, accreditation, institutional silos, curriculum reform

title: Sources fostering engineering students’ academic well-being in PBL environments: a cross-national comparative analysis
text: This study explores students’ perspectives on academic well-being, employing a theoretical framework to identify sources of support across two distinct educational institutions that adopt Project-/Problem-Based Learning (PBL) as the core learning approach for the curriculum. The research highlights how both internal (e.g. personal drive) and external (e.g. peer and institutional support) factors influence academic well-being in diverse educational settings. While emphasizing the critical role of motivation and self-efficacy in shaping students’ experiences, this study highlights the diverse learning needs of students from different PBL environments to support their academic well-being. The study contributes to a deeper understanding of academic well-being and offers insights for future research. It calls for the exploration of the long-term effects of these factors on academic success and well-being, particularly in addressing disparities across different educational contexts.
keywords: academic well-being, engineering students, project-based learning, problem-based learning, student motivation, self-efficacy, peer support, institutional support, student perceptions, cross-national comparison

title: Team up and learn across cultures: Chinese students’ reflections on teamwork in UK engineering education
text: Teamwork is a central component of engineering education, particularly within UK programmes where project-based collaboration is widely embedded. Despite the large presence of Chinese students in these environments, limited research has examined how they interpret and navigate teamwork in intercultural settings. This study investigates how Chinese engineering postgraduates understand and adjust to collaborative practices in UK universities. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 22 Chinese students, and the data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal four interconnected patterns: students encountered general teamwork challenges such as uneven contribution and unclear expectations; they experienced language-related barriers that constrained participation; they navigated differences between Chinese and UK educational norms that shaped communication and role positioning; and they gradually developed better collaborative competence over time. The study highlights the need for engineering programmes to provide clearer guidance on teamwork expectations, scaffold intercultural communication, and create structured opportunities to promote their engagement. By foregrounding the perspectives of Chinese engineering students and drawing on an insider-informed interpretive approach, this research contributes to ongoing discussions about diversity, inclusion, and non-technical skill development in global engineering education. The findings reveal four interconnected patterns: students encountered general teamwork challenges such as uneven contribution and unclear expectations; they experienced language-related barriers that constrained participation; they navigated differences between Chinese and UK educational norms that shaped communication and role positioning; and they gradually developed better collaborative competence over time.
keywords: teamwork, cross-cultural collaboration, international students, project-based learning, collaborative competence, language barriers, educational standards, role positioning, student reflection, diversity and inclusion, global engineering education, non-technical skills

title: The importance of transferable skills according to Finnish first-year engineering students, university staff, and technology companies
text: We examined the views of first-year students (N = 102), university staff (N = 46), and company representatives (N = 15) concerning the importance of and attitudes towards transferable skills in engineering. Data were gathered from a questionnaire, and statistical methods were utilized in the analysis. The groups shared similar views concerning the order of importance of transferable skills: critical thinking was evaluated as important, whereas awareness of political and social issues was ranked with low figures. Statistically significant differences were absent between students and university staff, but company representatives rated 12 of 38 skills as lower importance. The groups had positive attitudes towards learning and assessing transferable skills, but significant differences emerged in views concerning the importance of these in comparison to technical academic knowledge/skills, developing these in extra-curricular activities, and giving credits for developing these. We suggest that companies’ views be considered when integrating transferable skills into curricula.
keywords: transferable skills, engineering education, first-year engineering students, student attitudes, university staff perspectives, industry perspectives, critical thinking, extracurricular activities, curriculum integration

title: Examining college student mental health in engineering and computer science education: relevant factors, relative importance, and demographic differences
text: Mental health challenges pose significant barriers to academic success and well-being among university students, particularly in engineering and computer science. While prior research has examined factors influencing students' mental well-being, a gap remains in how these factors rank in relative importance and vary across demographic groups. This study identifies and ranks factors predicting mental health changes among engineering and computer science undergraduates in the U.S., and examines how these relationships vary by gender, race/ethnicity, and first-generation status. Using random forest analysis on the nationally representative BPS 12/17 Survey (2011-2014), we found that physical health was consistently the most important predictor of mental health outcomes, followed by academic preparation, institutional characteristics, social support, and psychological factors that varied in importance. Sub-population analyses revealed significant heterogeneity and distinct additional challenges faced by marginalised and first-generation students navigating compounding intersectional pressures.
keywords: student mental health, engineering students, computer science students, physical health, academic preparation, institutional characteristics, social support, gender differences, race and ethnicity, first-generation college students, intersectionality, marginalized students, predictors of mental health

title: Confusion, interest, and achievement in introductory physics: insights from student self-reflections
text: Self-reflection is associated with improved learning outcomes, but relatively little is known about how introductory physics students’ self-reflection on confusion and interest relates to their academic performance. This mixed-methods, observational study on 208 introductory physics students examined three questions: (1) how does number of submitted reflections, specificity of reflections about confusing and interesting aspects of learning, and perceived levels of confusion and interest relate to academic performance; (2) how does reflections from high-, mid-, and low-performing students differ in what they describe as confusing or interesting; and (3) how often do students’ reflections on what they found confusing and interesting overlap? Quantitative analyses showed that number of submitted reflections and perceived level of interest significantly predicted academic performance. Qualitative analyses revealed distinct reflection patterns and overlaps between confusing and interesting aspects of learning. These findings have implications for designing instructional strategies that use self-reflection to better support student learning.
keywords: self-reflection, introductory physics, student confusion, student interest, academic performance, instructional design, physics education

title: Metacognitive awareness in model-making activities: impacts on students’ conceptual understanding of construction details in engineering education
text: Metacognitive awareness can support deeper learning in engineering education. However, its role in activities such as model-making in construction education remains underexplored. This study examined whether integrating a model-making metacognitive awareness intervention (MMAI) into model-making activities improved students’ understanding of construction details. Using a quasi-experimental design, students were assigned to either a control group or an experimental group (with MMAI). Short-term learning gains were assessed using pre- and post-test quizzes that measured conceptual understanding of construction details. Long-term learning gains were evaluated through the accuracy of final technical drawings. Paired-samples t-tests, Welch’s t-tests, and ANCOVA were used to analyse within-group change, between-group differences, and the effect of baseline performance. Both groups improved significantly in quiz performance, and the experimental group showed a larger average gain. Between-group differences in gain scores and drawing errors were not statistically significant. ANCOVA results showed that baseline performance significantly influenced post-test outcomes.
keywords: metacognitive awareness, model making, construction details, conceptual understanding, engineering education, technical drawing, metacognitive intervention, construction education, drawing accuracy

title: Which way to go? Approaches to learning for engineering students
text: This study includes the consideration of learning approaches and self-regulating learning strategies in use by first-year engineering students with the intent to reduce the probability of academic disengagement in future college years due to inadequate academic preparation in the first year. Fifteen engineering students were interviewed to identify their learning approaches and strategies as applied to specific study habits. Certain approaches and strategies were found to be similar for both technical and non-technical courses, while others were dissimilar. The most interesting result was that many participants stated that their overall purpose for studying was to achieve high grades rather than to acquire knowledge, yet their learning strategies often reflected a deeper than expected engagement with learning. This little-explored area of research provides a starting point for guided practice in the use of self-regulated learning strategies for more meaningful learning, mitigating the probability of second-year academic disengagement through more effective academic preparation for higher-level courses.
keywords: learning methods, self-regulated learning strategies, engineering students, first-year students, student disengagement, study habits, academic preparation, meaningful learning

title: Can role-play play a role in authentic learning? Investigating two pre-university engineering education design projects
text: This study investigates the framing, implementation, and experience of role-play and challenge-based learning in design projects, and what aspects of authenticity they reveal in two Swedish upper secondary school engineering courses. In two different schools, students were to assume the role of engineering professionals and organise work with different roles and areas of responsibility, and act in suitable ways when interacting with ‘customers’ and ‘managers’. Observations and interviews with students and teachers revealed themes related to weak and strong role assignment and authenticity concerning learners, activity preparation, cross-cutting, and discipline-specific obstacles. Findings indicate that while role-playing is not necessarily equivalent to authentic engineering scenarios, it fulfils a substantial and situated learning process that may simulate real-world experiences, making it a compelling component of future engineering education. The study contributes novel knowledge on authenticity and challenge-based learning in engineering education, in particular, how teachers and students perform and perceive such projects.
keywords: role play, authentic learning, challenge-based learning, engineering education, design projects, upper secondary school, situated learning, role assignment, student and teacher perceptions

title: Impact of using interactive materials on student beliefs and self-efficacy in a materials science classroom
text: This study investigated the impact of interactive course materials on engineering students’ confidence and self-efficacy in problem-solving within a retention-critical materials science course. The research assessed students’ attitudes, beliefs, and academic performance for 218 sophomore-level engineering students across four academic terms at a rural university, employing a 13-question Likert scale instrument administered at six checkpoints throughout each term. The research hypothesised that engagement with interactive content would positively influence problem-solving self-efficacy, enhance confidence levels, and improve academic achievement. Overall, findings revealed that students’ problem-solving self-efficacy did not conclusively increase or decrease when utilising the interactive web-native textbook. These results provide empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of interactive digital learning resources that does not conclusively increase or decrease student learning experiences, academic performance, and self-efficacy development in engineering education, with important implications for inclusive pedagogical practice.
keywords: self-efficacy, student beliefs, problem-solving self-efficacy, engineering students, materials science education, digital learning resources, student engagement, academic performance, student self-confidence

title: Practitioner perspectives on developing professional competencies in engineering education in South Africa
text: The development of professional competencies is central to preparing engineering students to develop solutions for global challenges. It has been argued that this requires a holistic, integrated curriculum supported by transformative pedagogies. This study explores how professional competencies are developed and assessed in South African engineering curricula, and the possibilities for an integrated curriculum, through focus groups and individual interviews. The findings indicate that while professional competencies are acknowledged, they are rarely explicitly taught or systematically assessed. They are frequently marginalised by limited early exposure in the curriculum, fragmented placements, and significant confusion about the meaning of integration. Accreditation requirements are often misunderstood, reinforcing a compliance-driven rather than developmental approach. Despite these challenges, some success stories emerge, particularly from institutions with strong industry connections and work-integrated learning models. The study provides several recommendations for integrating professional competencies more effectively into engineering curricula.
keywords: professional competence, engineering education, curriculum integration, competency assessment, accreditation requirements, work-integrated learning, industry partnerships, practitioner perspectives, South Africa

title: Distributed learning in interdisciplinary teamwork: the role of the social organisation of work
text: Engineering education increasingly relies on interdisciplinary project-based learning (PjBL) to prepare students for complex real-world problems. Yet bringing students from different disciplines together does not automatically produce interdisciplinary collaboration. This paper addresses a central question: under what conditions do interdisciplinary intentions translate into interdisciplinary practices and outcomes? The paper advances a theoretically grounded approach using the theory of practice architectures to analyse how collaboration is socially organised in practice. Rather than aiming at empirical generalisation, it presents a conceptual exploration illustrated through a single case from a master’s course in interdisciplinary teamwork. The analysis shows how the degree of task interdependence in the organisation of work shaped whether the students’ collaboration became interdisciplinary or remained multidisciplinary. By adopting a sociomaterial view of learning, the paper conceptualises learning as changes in shared practices rather than solely in individual competencies. The study contributes a process-oriented framework for understanding how interdisciplinary collaboration is enabled or constrained in engineering education contexts.
keywords: interdisciplinary teamwork, distributed learning, practice architectures, task interdependence, interdisciplinary collaboration, multidisciplinary collaboration, project-based learning, shared practice, engineering education

title: Understanding academic interest in engineering students: the interplay of identification, effort, support, and reward
text: Academic interest is a key motivational construct influencing students’ learning and engagement, yet its development within structured educational contexts remains underexplored. This qualitative study investigates how engineering students experience and make sense of academic interest. Semi-structured interviews with 55 undergraduate students were analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings indicate that students recognise their interest through experiential cues such as competence, curiosity, voluntary engagement, and flow, while its development is shaped through effort, academic support, and perceived rewards. These dimensions interact in non-linear, context-dependent ways rather than following a predetermined sequence. To support interpretive grounding, peer discussion sessions were conducted with 63 students, which affirmed the relevance of the findings while highlighting variability in experiences. The study offers a configurational understanding of academic interest as emerging through multiple interacting pathways and contributes by foregrounding the role of interest identification. Implications are discussed for fostering meaningful engagement in engineering education.
keywords: student learning interest, engineering students, effort, academic support, perceived rewards, competence, curiosity, flow, student engagement, motivation, undergraduate engineering education

title: Understanding and evaluating engineering creativity: development and factor solution of the engineering creativity assessment tool (ECAT)
text: This study reports the initial development and validation of the Engineering Creativity Assessment Tool (ECAT), a performance-based rubric evaluating creativity in engineering design products using observable product features rather than self-report. Grounded in creativity theory and the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking product-scoring tradition, ECAT was implemented among undergraduate engineering students (N = 199) at a northeastern U.S. public university, who completed an open-ended design task; trained raters scored final artifacts on four dimensions—Fluency, Originality, Elaboration, and Cognitive Flexibility—using structured descriptors that support consistent interpretation while preserving expert judgment. Exploratory Factor Analysis (via Jamovi) yielded a coherent, multidimensional structure aligning with ECAT’s intended subscales, though this solution is provisional and requires cross-validation. Findings provide initial evidence that ECAT can be scored reliably and yields interpretable, theoretically consistent scores. ECAT offers engineering education a transparent, practical rubric for assessing creative products, supporting formative feedback and research. Future work should replicate the factor structure across contexts and conduct confirmatory analyses with larger samples.
keywords: engineering creativity, creativity assessment, Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, fluency, originality, elaboration, cognitive flexibility, factor structure, undergraduate engineering students, formative feedback

title: Design for transfer of design thinking development in undergraduate bioengineering students
text: Whereas design thinking (DT) constitutes a foundational competency in undergraduate engineering, many students fail to apply it. This study used a theoretical framework of students’ role identity and motivation to investigate students’ transfer of DT across tasks. Students engaged in weekly reflections on work product created during a Biodesign course, and purposely selected students were interviewed at the end of the course and again following the capstone course. Evaluation of the capstone data indicated minimal DT transfer. The analysis indicated that students struggled with learning and applying DT in their Biodesign projects. Students’ Biodesign role identities involved an orientation to the ‘right’ solution, focus on grades, and lack of agency over their prototypes. The findings point to the need for early hands-on experiences with DT that encourage student agency and ownership over projects to promote development and internalization of this important competency into their emerging engineering role identity.
keywords: design thinking, transfer of learning, bioengineering education, undergraduate engineering students, role identity, student motivation, student agency, capstone design, competence development, reflective practice

title: Technology-supported interventions to facilitate self-regulated learning in vocational education: a systematic literature review
text: Despite the increasing emphasis on self-regulated learning (SRL) as a critical competence in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), there remains a lack of clarity on how technology can effectively support its development within vocational contexts. This study aims to systematically review existing literature to identify the characteristics, benefits, challenges, and needs of technology-supported interventions for facilitating SRL in TVET settings. Using the PRISMA method, this systematic review analyzed 15 peer-reviewed studies published between 2008 and 2024 that focused on technology-facilitated SRL in vocational education. The findings reveal a concentration of research in Western and East Asian contexts, with a predominance of quantitative designs. They also highlight the potential of technologies such as learning management systems, multimedia tools, and web-based platforms to enhance SRL. Future research should investigate emerging technologies, such as 3D modeling and 3D printing, to better support authentic SRL in engineering and vocational education.
keywords: student self-regulation, technology-based interventions, vocational education and training, virtual learning environments, multimedia resources, online learning platforms, 3D modeling, 3D printing, engineering education, authentic learning

title: An integrative model of project-based learning for sustainability in engineering capstones: insights from students across industry-based and service-learning contexts
text: This study investigates how engineering capstone projects influence students’ academic motivation and understanding of sustainable development. Drawing on qualitative interviews with twenty final-year engineering students, it examines how course design, basic psychological need satisfaction, and project contexts shape students’ capstone learning experiences. The findings indicate that perceived competence gaps, structured autonomy, and interdisciplinary collaboration serve as powerful motivators. In contrast, time constraints, competing academic priorities, limited budgets and resources, and insufficient stakeholder engagement constrain opportunities for deeper learning, experimentation, and critical reflection. Although most participants initially viewed sustainability primarily through an environmental perspective, those involved in service-learning projects developed a broader understanding that encompassed engineers’ social responsibilities and the Sustainable Development Goals. Based on these findings, the study proposes a transferable integrative model of project-based learning that demonstrates how contextual factors, basic psychological need satisfaction, and motivational regulation interact to foster academic motivation and sustainability-oriented learning in engineering capstone education.

title: Agency for sustainability across the university-to-workplace transition: senior student and early career engineer perspectives from Qatar
text: Engineers play a central role in achieving sustainability goals, yet a value-action gap appears when graduates move from university into work. This qualitative study compares how senior engineering students (n = 10) and early career engineers (n = 10) in Qatar perceive their agency for sustainability across the university-to-workplace transition, using Bandura’s theory of human agency as an interpretive lens. Thirteen sub-themes emerged from the thematic and cross-group analysis, grouped under these themes: (1) multiple pathways for conceptualising sustainability, which captured four recurring conceptualisations, (2) intrapersonal sources as foundational to agency, and (3) structural and contextual supports and constraints of agency. Together, these findings show that enacting agency for sustainability requires a dynamic interplay between the thinking and being dimensions, which are further mediated by contextual structures that enable or constrain sustained action. This study offers implications for engineering education and early career development for sustainability action across the transition into the workplace.

title: Career choice process in Peruvian and Spanish engineering students: a cross-cultural study
text: The Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT) was tested in a cross-cultural study, Spain and Peru. This model explains career-related decision encompassed in following variables: self-efficacy, interest, outcome expectations, goals, perceived social supports and barriers. 1,005 undergraduate engineering students, 580 from Spain and 425 from Peru completed the Spanish adaptation of the Engineering Fields Questionnaire. Multiple-group structural equation modelling (SEM) was carried out to examine the model’s fit for Spain and Peru. Two models are established to clarify the role of the two dimensions of self-efficacy (academic and coping) in the SCCT career choice process model. There were founded differences by country in the role of coping self-efficacy in the SCCT model. Peruvian students exhibited better protective factors than Spanish students did. Although both countries share the same language there are clear social and cultural differences which concerning the Engineering degrees.

title: Attitudes toward engineering: investigating pre-service teachers’ perceptions of engineering in STEM education
text: There is limited understanding of engineering within Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education, particularly among pre-service teachers, despite its critical role in innovation and future workforce capabilities. The research is guided by the research question: ‘What are pre-service teachers’ perceptions of, and attitudes toward, engineering within STEM education?’ with the goal of enhancing understanding of engineering within STEM education. Engineering is often the least understood STEM component in primary schools, despite its significance. Following the method of Nadelson et al. (2013) data were collected from pre-service teachers to evaluate their confidence and perceptions of engineering using adapted versions of the Teaching Confidence Scale (Woolfolk Hoy 2000), the Science Teaching Efficacy Belief Instrument (STEBI, Riggs and Enochs 1990), and the Pittsburgh Freshman Engineering Attitudes Survey (PFEAS, Besterfield-Sacre, Atman, and Shuman1998). Participants were Australian and international primary/elementary pre-service teachers enrolled in initial teacher education programs (N = 65). Results indicated generally positive attitudes, though detailed knowledge was lacking, particularly about engineering. The study found that addressing problem-solving and creativity in teacher education could improve understanding. Furthermore, significant correlations between perceptions of engineering and self-efficacy in teaching STEM suggest that increasing engineering visibility could benefit STEM education overall. The findings underscore the need for targeted teacher development programs to integrate engineering effectively into curricula, ensuring educators are equipped to teach all STEM elements and prepare students for future technological challenges.
keywords: attitudes toward engineering, pre-service teachers, STEM education, teacher self-efficacy, teacher professional development, engineering curriculum integration

title: Engineering leadership: definition, skills, taxonomy, and identity from the perspectives of engineering leaders in ABET and industry professional engineers
text: There is a lack of consensus on the definition of leadership in engineering and the specific skills that should be emphasized in engineering leadership training and discussions. This knowledge gap affects the quality of leadership education in engineering programs. Most existing definitions of leadership in engineering were borrowed from management and psychology literature. To foster a holistic definition that effectively embodies the principles of leadership in the engineering profession, this qualitative study explores leadership through the lens of engineering leaders in the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET) and industry. The Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) methodology guided data collection through semi-structured interviews and subsequent analysis. The study resulted in a proposed definition of engineering leadership, an identification of 18 important engineering leadership skills, a proposed taxonomy of engineering leadership skills, and a re-envisioning of the leadership identity of engineering professionals, reiterating engineering as a leadership profession.
keywords: engineering leadership, leadership skills, leadership identity, engineering profession, engineering education, ABET accreditation, leadership training, professional engineers

title: Engineering Role identity scale for women in professional contexts
text: Engineering identity research has largely focused on students, leaving professional practice underexplored. Existing engineering identity instruments were developed primarily for academic settings, where social roles, recognition, and expectations for professional practice differ from those experienced by practicing engineers. Because these features underpin the operationalization of engineering identity, student-focus instruments may not adequately capture identity in professional settings. These limitations are compounded in Spanish-speaking contexts, where no validated instrument for practicing engineers currently exists. This study addresses these limitations by developing and gathering validity evidence for the Engineering Role Identity Scale for Professionals (ERISP) among Colombian women engineers. The instrument captures three dimensions of engineering identity: interest, performance/competence, and recognition. Factor analyses supported a three-factor structure with strong reliability. Structural equation modelling provided evidence of predictive validity. This work provides a psychometrically sound scale for practicing engineers that enables workforce analysis, evaluation of organizational interventions, and research on professional persistence.
keywords: engineering identity, women engineers, professional engineers, scale development, psychometric validation, recognition, competence, interest

title: Sustainability in engineering education: an editorial and interpretive synthesis
text: This editorial provides an introduction to and interpretive synthesis of the seventeen contributions to the European Journal of Engineering Education special issue on Sustainability in Engineering Education, and the current state, emerging trends, and future directions of the field. The special issue contributions indicate that sustainability in engineering education is moving beyond early add-on approaches towards broader curricular integration, yet transformative ambitions remain only partially realised and unevenly enacted across institutional, disciplinary, and national contexts. These insights are complemented by two additional perspectives: a reflective insider account of current trends at one European university and a critical challenge to dominant European viewpoints through South African scholarship on transformation and decolonisation. Beyond further curricular integration, the next phase of sustainability in engineering education is argued to depend on enhanced institutional reflexivity, epistemic plurality, and critical engagement with the purposes, assumptions, and societal responsibilities of engineering education and engineers.

title: Understanding variation in students’ perceptions of faculty encouragement: the roles of faculty connection breadth and interaction quality
text: Faculty encouragement may help students persist through academic challenges and recognise future possibilities, yet less is known about variation in students’ perceptions of faculty encouragement. This study examined whether two dimensions of faculty–student interaction, namely breadth of faculty connection and perceived interaction quality, were associated with challenge-focused and potential-focused faculty encouragement across Engineering, Science, and non-STEM fields. Survey data from 351 undergraduate students at a midsized public university in the United States were analyzed using structural equation modelling. Both interaction quality and breadth of faculty connection were positively associated with both forms of encouragement. Engineering students reported fewer faculty connections than non-STEM students, and women in Engineering reported lower interaction quality; both patterns were indirectly associated with lower encouragement. Findings suggest that strengthening faculty encouragement in engineering education requires attention to both students’ access to faculty and the relational quality of faculty–student interactions.

title: When the room is left to hold the tension: orientations towards learning to fail and ‘fail better’ when ‘doing emotions’ in engineering education
text: This collective autoethnography emerged from our experiences at the Emotions in Engineering Education Symposium 2025. Multiple moments of tension, discomfort, and rupture generated a sense of failing the community, prompting reflections on emotions as sites of meaning and struggle in international scholarly communities. Rooted in and building on African communitarian philosophy, particularly Ubuntu, as well as decolonial, queer and Western feminist theory, we conceptualize emotions as made in community and entangled with power, (in)justices, and (un)even distributions of (dis)comforts and labours. In a meta-affective reflexive thematic analysis of our collective ethnographic practice, we constellate four themes as starting and continuation points for collective reflections on our abilities to build emotionally responsive communities. We wonder: How can we design and inhabit scholarly spaces that centre emotions while collectively developing the response-abilities needed to hold discomfort, interrupt harm, transgress systemic oppression, share emotional labour, and learn to fail, and fail better, together.

title: Students’ metacognitive regulation strategies use during self-assessment and reflection across an engineering course
text: Technological advancements have influenced how tasks are performed in the workplace, increasing the need for engineers who have life-long learning skills to adapt quickly to rapid change. That is, engineers need to be self-regulated learners who can employ metacognitive regulation strategies (i.e. planning, monitoring, and evaluating) to improve their learning and effectiveness. Reflection activities in engineering courses can assist students in developing their metacognitive abilities. The purpose of the study was to investigate engineering students’ use of the metacognitive regulation strategies in a course in which they had multiple opportunities to self-assess their work and reflect on their learning. Students’ written self-assessments and reflections were analysed to identify the level at which they used these strategies. Clustering techniques were used to identify distinct patterns of use. The results showed students predominantly used these strategies at low-to-medium levels. Additionally, three distinct patterns of use were identified. Implications for practice are provided.
keywords: self-assessment, reflection, student self-regulation, engineering students, lifelong learning

title: Social and cognitive dimensions of engineering students’ learning: bridging theory and practice in living labs
text: This study explores how Living Labs (LLs), as innovative higher education (HE) environments, support engineering students in addressing real-world challenges alongside academic and external stakeholders. LLs facilitate the integration of theoretical knowledge and practical application supported by digital and virtual tools. Grounded in situated learning theory and the 4Es framework of cognition (embedded, embodied, enacted, extended), this research investigates how students bridge theory and practice, collaborate, and intertwine social and cognitive learning processes. Data consist of in-depth interviews with eight engineering undergraduates and are analysed using theory-driven methods for cognitive aspects and inductive thematic analysis for social collaboration. The results have been validated through the experiences of teachers and lab leaders and demonstrate the importance of all four Es in LLs. Social aspect analysis revealed four key themes: informal discussions, helping, finding close collaborators, and expansion of professional networks, which underscore the interaction between social and cognitive aspects.

title: Beyond self-regulated learning: a multi-dimensional framework of students’ regulation of learning during collaborative open-ended problem solving
text: Engineering students increasingly engage in collaborative open-ended problem solving, which involves navigating uncertainty and ambiguity, and which sometimes triggers emotional responses. Existing models of self-regulated learning offer limited explanatory power for such contexts because they under-theorise regulation through collaborative scaffolding, prioritise cognitive regulation over emotional and behavioural regulation, and conflate objects and mechanisms of regulation. This paper introduces a multi-dimensional framework of students’ regulation of learning that integrates four types of regulation – self-regulated learning, co-regulated learning, socially shared regulation of learning, and a newly proposed form, shared co-regulated learning – with three dimensions of regulation (cognitive, emotional, behavioral) at two levels. We illustrate the framework using empirical data (interviews and video-recorded group work) from two studies of engineering students in Sweden and the United States. We conclude that the framework can support research and educational design aimed at developing students’ capacity to collaboratively navigate complexity and uncertainty in engineering education.

title: From problems to challenges: a genealogical literature review of challenge-based learning and future directions
text: This article presents a genealogical literature review of Challenge-Based Learning (CBL) in engineering education, examining how ‘challenge’ became established as a pedagogical category. Drawing on Foucault and critical discourse analysis, it analyses seven literature reviews and 106 primary studies. Historical reconstruction identifies three phases: foundation (2001–2014), consolidation (2015–2018), and expansion (2019–2022). External partnerships increased from 9% of studies in the foundation phase to more than 77% in the expansion phase, making stakeholder participation a prominent marker of authenticity. Across seven analytical dimensions, the review shows how CBL discourse combines innovation, urgency, external relevance, and student agency while obscuring the histories, conflicts, and power relations through which challenges are constituted.CBL discourse promises innovation without genealogy, engagement without conflict, and relevance without resistance. The article proposes six principles for CBL’s maturation: explicit politicization, collective agency and solidarity, reflexive self-authorship, historical and temporal reflexivity, epistemic pluralism, and decolonial reciprocity.

title: Why students skip class: exploring absenteeism in first-year engineering education
text: Student attendance has been found to be a crucial factor impacting their learning in higher education. In recent years, however, student absenteeism has been a growing problem, suggesting that attendance is not viewed as essential for students. This study aimed to explore why students in their first years in engineering education decide not to attend learning activities. A qualitative study including focus group interviews was conducted, showing that high workloads and time constraints, together with the availability of alternative learning resources, are the main reasons for students’ prioritisations, leading to absenteeism. Furthermore, two types—temporal and strategic absenteeism are identified, often triggered by perceived poor teaching and lack of time to develop constructive study strategies. The study calls for a reevaluation of how absenteeism is viewed by university teachers.

title: Student profiles on sustainability in interdisciplinary engineering education: European insights into motivation, abilities, and learning contexts
text: Student profiles on sustainability remain underdeveloped, particularly in interdisciplinary engineering fields such as Industrial Engineering and Management (IEM). This study examines how IEM Bachelor’s students perceive sustainability through their motivations, abilities, and external learning contexts, and how these perceptions configure student profiles. Drawing on qualitative workshops and interviews with 44 students in three IEM programs in Portugal, Germany, and Turkey, we identify three profiles: motivation-driven Sustainability Anticipators, ability-grounded Sustainability Pragmatists, and context-sensitive Sustainability Sceptics. Cross-profile insights reveal that (i) profiles are context-dependent configurations dominated by one of the profile components, (ii) transferable and interdisciplinary competences ground perceived sustainability ability, and (iii) students’ reasoning and articulation of sustainability motivation are conditional and dimensionally asymmetrical: intrinsic environmental sustainability concern becomes conditional on whether sustainability engagement is perceived, under prevailing labour-market conditions, as compatible with personal economic and social sustainability concerns. The study contributes to the theory and practice of sustainability in engineering education.

title: Pedagogical equivalence and motivational superiority of game-based learning in engineering graphics: a multi-campus RCT
text: This multi-campus randomised controlled trial (N = 227) tested whether teacher-authored educational videogames could match traditional lectures pedagogically while improving motivation in Engineering Graphics. Two one-sided tests (TOST) and Bayesian analysis showed a mixed pattern on immediate knowledge assessments: dimensioning and surface tolerances fell within a ±0.4 SD equivalence margin, whereas dimensional tolerances did not, with the experimental group scoring lower. The game-based approach yielded superior final course grades (d = 0.71), with 81.7% of game-based students earning good or outstanding marks against 60.2% of controls, and better motivational outcomes. Because the trial spanned two campuses and three instructors, instructor effects were tested directly. Clustering was negligible except for dimensional tolerances (ICC = 0.116), likely reflecting an instructor or section effect. The findings are consistent with a motivational rather than cognitive pathway, though this was not formally tested. Teacher-authored videogames appear a scalable alternative for some content.
keywords: game-based learning, engineering graphics, student motivation, engineering education

title: Examining engineering students’ perceptions of global competence using Q methodology
text: Global competence is increasingly recognised as essential for engineering graduates to effectively address complex, global challenges, yet its definition remains contested and dominated by Western frameworks with limited input from engineering students. This study examines how Hong Kong engineering undergraduates themselves understand global competence. Using Q methodology, 21 students sorted 58 statements reflecting diverse conceptualisations of the construct. Factor analysis identified four distinct viewpoints: (1) the Socially Responsible Global Citizen, (2) the Technically‑Oriented Pragmatic Global Engineering Professional, (3) the Localised Ethical and Caring Engineer, and (4) the Intercultural Open‑Minded Explorer. These perspectives both align with and challenge existing models, illustrating that global competence in engineering is multidimensional and interpreted in varied ways by learners. The findings highlight the need for a pluralistic, students‑as‑partners approach to global competence education, one that values students’ diverse understandings and better prepares them for the complexities of global engineering practice.
keywords: global competence, engineering students, student perceptions, Q methodology, engineering education

title: Gender dynamics in engineering education: instructor gender, students’ course expectations, and diversity value and inclusive behavior
text: This study examines how instructor gender is associated with engineering students’ course expectations, diversity value and behaviour, and perceived inclusive climate. Data were collected from 380 undergraduate students in an introductory engineering course taught by six instructors across 16 sections. Using hierarchical linear modelling, we analysed how instructor and student gender are associated with students’ course outcome expectations, diversity values, and behaviours. Results showed that instructor gender significantly moderated the relationship between pre- and post-course outcome expectations, with students showing stronger positive changes under male instructors. Women students demonstrated higher diversity value scores and greater willingness to challenge discriminatory behaviours compared to men students. No significant gender differences were found in perceptions of inclusive classroom climate. These findings suggest that both instructor and student gender are related to engineering students’ educational experiences and provide insights for creating more inclusive engineering educational environments.
keywords: gender dynamics, engineering education, teacher gender, course expectations, diversity values, inclusive behavior, gender diversity, student perceptions

title: Navigating ethical and equity challenges in the workplace: a qualitative study of early-career engineers’ transition to practice using social cognitive theory
text: The early-career phase is an important period in the formation of engineers, during which the combined influences of education and workplace environments shape their ethical decision-making. This study includes interviews with thirteen engineers from North America. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis a theoretical lens of social cognitive theory. We found four main themes from participant responses: (1) University does not fully prepare early-career engineers (2) Characteristics of individuals’ workplaces strongly shape the early-career experiences of engineers. (3) Engineers make decisions based on their personal attributes and the support provided or limitations imposed by their workplace. (4) Self-confidence and self-worth affect ethical decision-making. While improvements in engineering education can help smooth the transition process, this study shows the limits of engineering education in developing ethical and equitable engineers. Enhancing ethical and equitable engineering practice depends on intentional workplace reforms that bridge the gaps between academic preparation and workplace realities.
keywords: young engineers, transition to practice, workplace ethics, social cognitive theory, engineers, professional development

title: Engineering judgment: undergraduate epistemologies
text: Engineering judgment is a crucial competency present in ABET’s outcomes. However, a consensus-driven definition for it was only recently published in the education literature, with limited formal instruction and assessment to date. Therefore, the present study used this definition to analyze undergraduate epistemologies of engineering judgment using a mixed methods design, including student views on the relevance of concepts of engineering judgment from the literature, personal definitions for it, and beliefs about learning it. Students in two courses rated the concepts decision making, application of knowledge/experience, and recognition of mistakes/errors among the most relevant to engineering judgment. Per a deductive content analysis, students consistently discussed decision making, ethical factors, and use of explicit knowledge in their personal definitions. Although students viewed our lecture on engineering judgment as useful, others believed experiential learning was more impactful for engineering judgment knowhow. This study can inform education on engineering judgment for engineer formation.
keywords: engineering judgment, student beliefs, engineering education, ABET outcomes, decision-making, experiential learning, engineering ethics, explicit knowledge

title: Teachers’ perception of STEM integration and education: a systematic literature review
text: For schools to include quality STEM education, it is important to understand teachers’ beliefs and perceptions related to STEM talent development. Teachers, as important persons within a student’s talent development, hold prior views and experiences that will influence their STEM instruction. This study attempts to understand what is known about teachers’ perceptions of STEM education by examining existing literature. Study inclusion criteria consisted of empirical articles, which aligned with research questions, published in a scholarly journal between 2000 and 2016 in English. Participants included in primary studies were preK-12 teachers. After quality assessment, 25 articles were included in the analysis. Thematic analysis was used to find themes within the data. Findings indicate that while teachers value STEM education, they reported barriers such as pedagogical challenges, curriculum challenges, structural challenges, concerns about students, concerns about assessments, and lack of teacher support. Teachers felt supports that would improve their effort to implement STEM education included collaboration with peers, quality curriculum, district support, prior experiences, and effective professional development. Recommendations for practice include quality in-service instruction over STEM pedagogy best practices and district support of collaboration time with peer teachers. Recommendations for future research are given.
keywords: STEM education, teacher perceptions, teacher beliefs, STEM assessment, teacher support, professional development, peer collaboration, district support, STEM teaching

title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
text: Abstract The successful irruption of AI-based technology in our daily lives has led to a growing educational, social, and political interest in training citizens in AI. Education systems now need to train students at the K-12 level to live in a society where they must interact with AI. Thus, AI literacy is a pedagogical and cognitive challenge at the K-12 level. This study aimed to understand how AI is being integrated into K-12 education worldwide. We conducted a search process following the systematic literature review method using Scopus. 179 documents were reviewed, and two broad groups of AI literacy approaches were identified, namely learning experience and theoretical perspective. The first group covered experiences in learning technical, conceptual and applied skills in a particular domain of interest. The second group revealed that significant efforts are being made to design models that frame AI literacy proposals. There were hardly any experiences that assessed whether students understood AI concepts after the learning experience. Little attention has been paid to the undesirable consequences of an indiscriminate and insufficiently thought-out application of AI. A competency framework is required to guide the didactic proposals designed by educational institutions and define a curriculum reflecting the sequence and academic continuity, which should be modular, personalized and adjusted to the conditions of the schools. Finally, AI literacy can be leveraged to enhance the learning of disciplinary core subjects by integrating AI into the teaching process of those subjects, provided the curriculum is co-designed with teachers.
keywords: AI literacy, K-12 education, artificial intelligence in education, competency framework, curriculum development, AI in teaching, teacher co-design, unintended consequences of AI

title: Research and trends in STEM education: a systematic review of journal publications
text: Abstract With the rapid increase in the number of scholarly publications on STEM education in recent years, reviews of the status and trends in STEM education research internationally support the development of the field. For this review, we conducted a systematic analysis of 798 articles in STEM education published between 2000 and the end of 2018 in 36 journals to get an overview about developments in STEM education scholarship. We examined those selected journal publications both quantitatively and qualitatively, including the number of articles published, journals in which the articles were published, authorship nationality, and research topic and methods over the years. The results show that research in STEM education is increasing in importance internationally and that the identity of STEM education journals is becoming clearer over time.
keywords: STEM education, research trends, scientific publications, journal publishing, research topics, research methodology, international research collaboration

title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
text: Abstract Background The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in STEM education (AI-STEM), as an emerging field, is confronted with a challenge of integrating diverse AI techniques and complex educational elements to meet instructional and learning needs. To gain a comprehensive understanding of AI applications in STEM education, this study conducted a systematic review to examine 63 empirical AI-STEM research from 2011 to 2021, grounded upon a general system theory (GST) framework. Results The results examined the major elements in the AI-STEM system as well as the effects of AI in STEM education. Six categories of AI applications were summarized and the results further showed the distribution relationships of the AI categories with other elements (i.e., information, subject, medium, environment) in AI-STEM. Moreover, the review revealed the educational and technological effects of AI in STEM education. Conclusions The application of AI technology in STEM education is confronted with the challenge of integrating diverse AI techniques in the complex STEM educational system. Grounded upon a GST framework, this research reviewed the empirical AI-STEM studies from 2011 to 2021 and proposed educational, technological, and theoretical implications to apply AI techniques in STEM education. Overall, the potential of AI technology for enhancing STEM education is fertile ground to be further explored together with studies aimed at investigating the integration of technology and educational system.
keywords: artificial intelligence in education, STEM education, general systems theory, education system

title: Developing student 21st Century skills in selected exemplary inclusive STEM high schools
text: Abstract Background There is a need to arm students with noncognitive, or 21 st Century, skills to prepare them for a more STEM-based job market. As STEM schools are created in a response to this call to action, research is needed to better understand how exemplary STEM schools successfully accomplish this goal. This conversion mixed method study analyzed student work samples and teacher lesson plans from seven exemplary inclusive STEM high schools to better understand at what level teachers at these schools are engaging and developing student 21 st Century skills. Results We found of the 67 lesson plans collected at the inclusive STEM high schools, 50 included instruction on 21 st Century skills. Most of these lesson plans designed instruction for 21 st Century skills at an introductory level. Few lesson plans encouraged multiple 21 st Century skills and addressed higher levels of those skills. Although there was not a significant difference between levels of 21 st Century skills by grade level, there was an overall trend of higher levels of 21 st Century skills demonstrated in lesson plans designed for grades 11 and 12. We also found that lesson plans that lasted three or more days had higher levels of 21 st Century skills. Conclusions These findings suggest that inclusive STEM high schools provide environments that support the development of 21 st Century skills. Yet, more can be done in the area of teacher professional development to improve instruction of high levels of 21 st Century skills.
keywords: 21st century skills, non-cognitive skills, lesson planning, teacher professional development, STEM education, high school instruction, student work samples, STEM workforce preparation

title: A systematic review on trends in using Moodle for teaching and learning
text: BACKGROUND: The Moodle Learning Management System (LMS) is widely used in online teaching and learning, especially in STEM education.
