title: STEM immersions + pedagogical PD drives multi-domain growth in multi-disciplinary teachers: qualitative findings from the Kenan Fellows Program for Teacher Leadership
text: Abstract Background Preparing students for evolving STEM careers requires teachers who understand workforce skills and pathways, yet most professional development (PD) and STEM Experiences for Teachers (SETs) are studied in isolation. This study examines [Fellowship Program] (TFP; Pseudonym), a year-long model that integrates a 120-hour summer industry or research immersion with 80 hours of pedagogical and leadership PD. We analyzed 56 interview and 3 focus-group transcripts from seventy-three K–12 teachers who participated in TFP between 2018 and 2024. Using Atlas.ti, we employed inductive coding and then mapped emergent categories to Clarke and Hollingsworth’s Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) to examine professional growth in teachers’ Personal Domain, the Domain of Practice, and the Domain of Consequence. Results Our findings indicate that teachers most frequently reported changes in the Personal Domain (n = 371), with more references to Knowledge (n = 160) than Beliefs (n = 128) or Attitudes (n = 69). Growth in the Domain of Practice (n = 211) centered on Pedagogy (n = 136) and forming new Community Connections (n = 54). Reports in the Domain of Consequence (n = 241) highlighted teacher outcomes (n = 162) and new student opportunities (n = 95). Co-occurrence analyses linked knowledge gains to Professional Development and Industry Connections (72 co-occurrences) and belief change to Program Infrastructure/Values and Brand Recognition (52 co-occurrences). A salient pathway traced Increased Self-Efficacy → Agentic Action → new Community Connections → Opportunities for Students. Conclusions The results of this study highlight how integrating SETs with sustained pedagogical and leadership PD drives multi-domain teacher growth and bridges the “knowing–doing gap” often seen in professional learning. Findings show that TFP’s SET + PD model enhances teachers’ knowledge, self-efficacy, and networks, which in turn catalyze agentic actions that expand classroom opportunities for students. Using Clarke and Hollingsworth’s IMPG, the study demonstrates that external supports—such as industry experiences, high-quality PD, and program infrastructure—produce personal growth that translates into new pedagogical practices, leadership roles, and student engagement. This study positions the TFP model as a replicable framework for workforce-aligned teacher professional development and offers design and policy recommendations for scaling SET + PD initiatives to strengthen K–12 STEM education and career readiness.
keywords: teacher professional development, pedagogical professional development, self-efficacy, knowledge-practice gap, teacher networks, teacher beliefs, STEM workforce preparation, teacher knowledge and beliefs

title: The use of school labs as extracurricular STEM programmes and their effects on STEM career intentions
text: Abstract Background Extracurricular science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) programmes are very popular and are actively used by teachers and students. Studies evaluating these initiatives show positive effects on cognitive, affective, and motivational student traits, which in turn can influence career choices in STEM. Based on attendance at such programmes, specifically school labs, we measured students’ learning gain, the enjoyment experienced during attendance, the change in interest and self-efficacy beliefs in STEM, and how these factors related to STEM career intentions. To this end, 2605 students who had attended a school lab in Switzerland or in the Principality of Liechtenstein were surveyed with a questionnaire. Results Based on a structural equation model, it could be shown that learning gains and enjoyment of the visit correlated strongly. Furthermore, in the model these two variables did not have a direct effect on STEM career intentions, but an indirect one via the change in self-efficacy beliefs. This shift in beliefs related strongly to STEM career intentions as well as the development in interest in STEM, which was also highly associated with STEM career intentions. Conclusions Overall, we could demonstrate the importance of four direct and indirect factors resulting from attending a school lab that are important influences on the fostering of students’ STEM career intentions.
keywords: STEM self-efficacy, STEM interest, learning gains, enjoyment, student motivation

title: Snapshots of team functioning: development and validation of the team member perceptions of instructional change collaborations (TM-PICC) survey
text: Team-based efforts to improve undergraduate STEM instruction have many potential advantages over individually-focused efforts. Team-based instructional change efforts can address broad student learning challenges across degree plans and/or enable changes to develop and solidify over multiple semesters. Instructional change teams can also function as communities of practice that support individual members’ learning about STEM teaching and learning. Yet not all teams are equally successful, and a dysfunctional team can result in perceptions of wasted time, energy, and resources. In our prior work, we used grounded theory to develop a model that describes instructional change team functioning. The model includes key aspects of how teams are set up, how team members collaborate, and the team outcomes. Building on this model, we developed the Team Member Perceptions of Instructional Change Collaborations (TM-PICC) survey and collected pilot data to examine its factor structure and initial validity. The pilot survey was completed by 219 team members across 34 instructional change teams at nine institutions. The survey contained 67 items spanning Team Inputs, Team Processes, Emergent States, and Team Outcomes. In this study, we focus on the Team Processes and Emergent States portions of the instrument and conducted exploratory factor analysis on 39 items representing these constructs. Exploratory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure for Team Processes and a three-factor structure for Emergent States. The Team Processes domain was represented by the factors Communication and Decision-Making Clarity and Team Commitment, while the Emergent States domain was represented by Team Cohesion, Psychological Safety, and Shared Vision. All five factors demonstrated strong internal consistency and aligned closely with the underlying theoretical model. The final Team Processes and Emergent States models explained 54% and 65% of the variance, respectively. We also demonstrate the practical application of the TM-PICC survey through an example team report designed to provide actionable feedback to instructional change teams. The TM-PICC survey provides a research-informed instrument for evaluating and supporting instructional change teams in undergraduate STEM education. In addition to informing team development and improvement efforts, the survey offers a foundation for future research examining the factors that contribute to successful instructional change collaborations.

title: Engaging future scientists: the effect of science museum visits on high school students’ science identity development
text: Abstract Background Expanding participation in STEM fields has been a longstanding national priority, with growing attention to informal learning environments as contexts for fostering students’ science identity. Science museums offer hands-on, inquiry-based experiences that complement formal classroom learning, yet large-scale quantitative evidence on whether museum visits contribute to science identity development remains limited. This study addresses this gap by examining whether visiting science museums or planetariums during high school is associated with stronger science identity at the end of eleventh grade. Grounded in science identity theory and situated expectancy-value theory, the study applies a quasi-experimental design combining inverse probability of treatment weighting with doubly robust estimation to nationally representative longitudinal data from the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009 (HSLS:09), with an analytic sample of 7,290 students across 935 high schools. Results Students who visited science museums or planetariums between ninth and eleventh grade reported significantly higher science identity at the end of eleventh grade than comparable peers who did not visit, even after adjusting for baseline science identity, demographic characteristics, and a comprehensive set of school- and student-level covariates. Propensity score analyses revealed a steep socioeconomic gradient in museum visitation, with students from the highest SES quintile more than twice as likely to visit as those from the lowest. Women and Latino students were more likely to visit science museums, yet they reported significantly lower science identity than male students and the broader student population. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that the estimated treatment effect was robust to plausible levels of unobserved confounding. Conclusions and implications These findings suggest that visiting science museums during high school can meaningfully support students’ science identity development. However, these benefits are embedded in a stratified opportunity structure that distributes access unevenly across socioeconomic, gender, and racial lines. Implications for equitable informal science education and directions for future research are discussed.

title: “I learned a lot, but…”: preservice elementary teachers’ integrated STEM teaching self-efficacy and perceived challenges
text: Abstract Background Recent K-12 education reforms emphasize integrated STEM (iSTEM) instruction to prepare young learners for interdisciplinary careers. However, elementary teachers often find iSTEM teaching challenging, partly due to limited emphasis on iSTEM training in teacher preparation programs. As a relatively new and evolving field, there remains a limited understanding of the challenges that preservice elementary teachers (PSTs) perceive and how these influence their iSTEM teaching self-efficacy. This mixed-methods exploratory concurrent research addresses this gap in the literature by investigating changes in PSTs’ self-efficacy and perceived challenges at the beginning and end of their science or STEM methods coursework. Data were collected from 465 PSTs across five institutions in the United States using the Self-Efficacy for Teaching Integrated STEM instrument (SETIS) and an open-ended questionnaire. Results Multivariate analysis of variance and paired t-tests revealed significant positive gains in iSTEM teaching self-efficacy, while McNemar tests indicated a significant decrease in overall perceived challenges by the end of the semester. Qualitative content analysis identified six major categories of perceived challenges: (1) teacher affect and experience, (2) student-related concerns, (3) content and curricular challenges, (4) pedagogical challenges, (5) support from others, and (6) time and resources. Structural equation modeling results showed a significant negative effect for the challenge related to lack of science or STEM content knowledge, with lower SETIS scores among those reporting this concern on the post-survey. In contrast, the challenge of technology access had a significant positive effect, suggesting that PSTs with higher SETIS scores were more likely to identify this concern. Conclusions The overall gains in PSTs’ iSTEM teaching self-efficacy highlight the potential benefits of methods coursework, whether these experiences are situated within science methods coursework or a designated STEM semester with multiple STEM-themed methods courses. PSTs reported fewer challenges at the end compared to the beginning of the semester, suggesting that participation in science or STEM methods coursework alleviated, though did not entirely eliminate, some concerns. Recognizing perceived challenges can better prepare PSTs for iSTEM instruction and help reduce future surprises. Accordingly, these findings offer valuable implications for PST preparation in iSTEM coursework and future research.

title: Exploring the effectiveness of a digital metaphor game-mediated STEM PBL approach for primary students’ perceived scientific inquiry competence, learning experience, and cognitive load
text: In the age of rapid scientific and technological advancement, cultivating primary students’ scientific inquiry competence has become an educational priority. STEM project-based learning (STEM PBL) offers an authentic context for inquiry, yet its open-ended tasks often require students to coordinate multiple resources across inquiry steps. This can fragment attention, undermine motivation following unsuccessful inquiry attempts, and leave students unsure how to organize the inquiry process. To address these challenges, this study developed a digital metaphor game-mediated STEM PBL (DMG-STEM PBL) approach. Specifically, a front-loaded digital metaphor game was used as a mediating scaffold to introduce a metaphorical inquiry framework, which was then reinforced through metaphor-recall prompts and metaphor-supported reflective narration during STEM project work. A quasi-experimental study was conducted to examine its effects on primary students’ perceived scientific inquiry competence, learning experience (including learning motivation and flow experience), and cognitive load. Two sixth-grade classes were randomly assigned at the class level to the experimental group ( N = 48), which adopted the DMG-STEM PBL approach, or the control group ( N = 42), which used conventional STEM PBL. Results showed that students in the DMG-STEM PBL group reported significantly higher scores on overall perceived scientific inquiry competence and on the dimensions of planning, experimenting and data collection, and analyzing and concluding. They also reported greater learning motivation and flow experience. For cognitive load, students in the DMG-STEM PBL group reported higher overall cognitive load, with higher mental effort but no significant between-group difference in mental load. These findings provide insights and practical implications for future research on STEM PBL instruction and the development of primary students’ scientific inquiry competence.

title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
text: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education and the resulting institutional responses have prompted research to support evidence-based policy decisions. As policies change to adjust to this disruptive technology, it demands agility from educators. The impacts of these policy changes on student behaviours and outcomes are currently poorly understood. This study examines how students used GenAI across three assessments in an undergraduate physics unit after assessment redesign forced by institutional policy that permitted purpose-specific and open use. Using a mixed-methods approach, student declarations of GenAI use were coded into four functional categories and mapped to the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition (SAMR) framework. Learning and Formatting dominated early use and aligned with substitution and augmentation for a presentation assessment type. Later assessments showed a marked growth in Feedback uses, which spanned all SAMR levels and became the most common pattern. ‘Doing Task’ uses appeared in smaller numbers but illustrated modification and redefinition when GenAI generated step-by-step solutions for unfamiliar problems. Across all assessments, GenAI users achieved slightly higher scores, although differences were not statistically significant, so this trend should be interpreted as a tentative observation. Findings suggest that assessment design, which rewards understanding and requires student judgement, aligns with the theoretical markers of evaluative judgement. While this study did not directly measure internal cognitive states, the observed change in functional behaviour, specifically the transition toward iterative feedback loops, suggests that GenAI could serve as a catalyst for learning. This study provides empirical evidence on how assessment redesign based on policy shifts influences GenAI use patterns and proposes design principles for authentic assessment in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) contexts. It highlights authentic assessment and constructive alignment as guiding principles for sustainable policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era, ensuring coherence among learning outcomes, activities, and assessment.
keywords: generative AI, institutional policy, assessment redesign, undergraduate physics, SAMR framework, authentic assessment, constructive alignment, evaluative judgments, feedback loops, assessment design, STEM education

title: AI literacy and STEM education: emerging frontiers and research priorities
text: Abstract This article examines the state of the art in AI literacy and STEM education and identifies emerging frontiers and research priorities to inspire cutting-edge empirical and theoretical research. The reviewed research is grounded in established AI literacy frameworks and shows that there is potential for students’ development of a critical and technologically informed AI literacy. However, the research is unevenly spread across the STEM disciplines and the potential for AI to transform STEM learning remains unclear. Thus, while the field has expanded rapidly, particularly with the emergence of generative AI (GenAI), fundamental challenges remain. The conceptual ambiguity surrounding AI literacy, combined with the rapid evolution of AI technologies, demands continued theoretical refinement and empirical investigation. Critical questions remain regarding how AI literacy intersects with disciplinary STEM literacies, how GenAI tools both support and reshape teaching and learning processes, and what opportunities and trade-offs arise when students engage with AI as learning partner. The ethical dilemmas of AI integration, including bias, data privacy, and environmental sustainability, also warrant urgent attention. As STEM education increasingly engages with AI as both a subject of learning and a learning tool, future research must move beyond one-size-fits-all frameworks toward context-sensitive approaches that empower educators and learners to critically and responsibly engage with AI while preserving core STEM learning goals. This article highlights key research frontiers and priorities for advancing scholarship at the intersection of AI literacy and STEM education.
